exam.title: Why Freedom of Speech? Historical Suppression and the Birth of Article 19(1)(a)

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
One-paragraph summary (read this last, the night before the exam)

Speech is a natural, pre-political human capacity (the newborn's first cry is the first "speech" and society celebrates it). The Constitution still had to guarantee it because, historically, whoever held power (the State, the Church, the King) suppressed ideas that challenged the "established knowledge". Western history is full of such suppression (Socrates, Copernicus/Galileo, the Inquisition, Nazi Propaganda Ministry) so Western constitutions (USA, First Amendment, 1791) put speech first. In India the pressing problem was inequality (caste, untouchability), so the Constitution put Equality (Art 14) before Freedom (Art 19). The British colonial State, however, imported suppression (e.g. Official Secrets Act, 1923), so the framers re-asserted free speech in Art 19(1)(a), but only for citizens.

sections.title: 1.1 The starting point: speech is natural, so why is it a constitutional right?
sections.html:
The professor opened with an illustration: a newborn's first cry is the child's first act of communication ("I am alive"), and the family rejoices. "Speech" therefore means communication by any means, not only words. If this is a natural right, nobody has to grant it, so the real question is why it needed constitutional status at all.

  • Answer in one line: because it was suppressed; a right is guaranteed in writing only when someone has been taking it away.
  • Who suppresses? In Dr. Ambedkar's style of brevity: the State (anyone more powerful than the individual: King, Church, Government).
  • Why does power suppress? (i) to hide its own wrongdoing; (ii) to protect the "established system of knowledge" or religion it rests on; (iii) because those in authority treat their word as final and take a challenge as an insult; (iv) to preserve their superiority and keep their hold on power.
  • The student answer that the other side also has a right "not to be provoked into violence" is the seed of Art 19(2) reasonable restrictions (public order). The professor's point is that the right comes first and restrictions are the exception.

sections.title: 1.2 Historical suppression of ideas (the examples the professor told you to know)
sections.html:
The professor repeatedly asked students to be able to give these examples. Below, each one has the "professor's version" and a verified/precise version so that you do not lose marks for factual slips.

ExampleWhat the professor saidPrecise, safe-to-write version
Socrates (Athens)Asked questions (method of teaching), challenged existing knowledge/religion; made to drink poison.Tried in Athens in 399 BCE on charges of impiety (not honouring the city's gods) and corrupting the youth; sentenced to death by drinking hemlock. The Socratic method = teaching by relentless questioning. (Note: this was a Greek, not a Christian, authority.)
Copernicus / GalileoSaid the Earth goes round the Sun, contrary to the Church's belief that the Sun circles the Earth; the Church acted against them.Copernicus published the heliocentric model (De revolutionibus, 1543) and died a natural death; his book was later placed on the Church's Index (1616). Galileo was tried by the Roman Inquisition in 1633, forced to recant and kept under house arrest until death (1642). Giordano Bruno was burned at the stake in 1600. If asked "who was punished", write Galileo; do not write that Copernicus was executed.
The InquisitionA historical institution that actively searched for and suppressed ideas contradicting the established knowledge/religion, with capital punishment for writing against the dominant belief.A system of Church tribunals (medieval Inquisition from the 1230s; Spanish Inquisition 1478; Roman Inquisition 1542) to detect and punish heresy. It also maintained the Index of Prohibited Books (first issued 1559), i.e. prior censorship of books.
Propaganda MinistryA ministry whose job was to ensure nothing was written against the existing authority; "Hitler had a Propaganda Ministry".The Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda (1933, Joseph Goebbels) controlled press, radio, film, literature and art in Nazi Germany. It is the standard example of State control of information.
BlasphemySome religions treat criticism of the dominant belief or God as blasphemy; such a concept (and word) did not exist in classical India.Blasphemy = speech showing contempt for the sacred. In India the nearest provisions are ss. 295, 295A and 298 IPC (now BNS ss. 298, 299 and 302), and they are limited by Art 19(2) (public order) and Art 25.
Colonial State in IndiaBritain brought suppression to India (Official Secrets Act, 1923).Press Act 1799, Vernacular Press Act 1878, Sedition (s. 124A IPC, 1870), Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act 1931, Official Secrets Act 1923 (replacing the 1889 Act).

Professor's claims you should NOT repeat as facts in an answer

"Copernicus was killed", incorrect, see table above. "Socrates was punished by Christianity", incorrect, Socrates (399 BCE) predates Christianity. Safe sentence: "Socrates, Galileo and Giordano Bruno were punished by the political or religious authorities of their time for questioning received wisdom".

"Anyone with a top-secret document gets death", the Official Secrets Act, 1923 prescribes imprisonment (up to 14 years for the gravest offences under s. 3, up to 3 years for others such as wrongful communication under s. 5), not death.

The professor's remarks about contemporary politicians, parties, elections and about particular religious communities are his personal commentary. They are not exam material and have been left out of these notes.

sections.title: 1.3 The idea behind free speech: "marketplace of ideas"
sections.html:
The professor used this phrase: "speech is the marketplace of ideas: when new ideas come and we discuss, a better solution can emerge". Be ready to name the theories:

TheoryThinker / caseCore idea
Truth discovery / Marketplace of ideasJ.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859); Milton, Areopagitica (1644); Holmes J. dissent in Abrams v. US (1919)Truth emerges from free competition of ideas; suppressing an opinion robs everyone, whether it is true or false.
Democratic self-governmentMeiklejohn; Indian cases: Romesh Thappar, Bennett ColemanCitizens can govern only if they can discuss and criticise government freely.
Individual autonomy / self-fulfilmentKant, Mill; Maneka Gandhi (1978) linking speech with personal libertyExpression is part of human dignity and personality.
Safety valveBrandeis J., Whitney v. California (1927)Allowing dissent releases pressure and prevents violence.

sections.title: 1.4 India v. the West: the "tradition of dialogue" argument
sections.html:
• Professor's thesis: classical India encouraged debate (the Shastrartha tradition: formal philosophical debate; Gargi challenging Yajnavalkya in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad; the tradition of question-and-answer contests, e.g. Yaksha Prashna in the Mahabharata). Hence there was little *need* for a speech right in India.
  • Social reformers (Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule) wrote and spoke against caste despite social hostility (Savitribai was pelted with mud and dung on her way to teach girls; she carried a spare sari). The professor used this to show that the Indian problem was social inequality, not state censorship.
  • Counter-point to keep in mind (for balance in an answer): India has never been free of suppression: caste hierarchy silenced large groups, and colonial laws (Vernacular Press Act, sedition, Official Secrets Act) were severe. Courts have also had to deal with post-1950 restrictions (First Amendment 1951).
  • The professor's conclusion: free speech in India is partly an import from the West through colonial rule, retained because it is one of the most valuable freedoms.

sections.title: 1.5 Official Secrets Act, 1923: the colonial example of suppression
sections.html:
• What it is: an Act (replacing the 1889 Act) to punish spying and unauthorised disclosure of official information.
  • Professor's four levels of classified information: Restricted, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret. (Strictly, these categories come from government security instructions, not from the text of the Act itself, which speaks of "secret official code or pass word, sketch, plan, model, article, note, document or information". In an exam, you can say "official information is classified into four grades".)
  • Key sections: s. 3 (spying: entering a prohibited place, making sketches, obtaining information useful to an enemy; up to 14 years if connected with defence); s. 5 (wrongful communication or receiving of secret official information, even possession of a document found by chance, as the professor said: "if you pick up a document lying on the road and keep it, you can go to jail"); s. 6 (unauthorised use of uniforms, false reports); s. 8 (duty to give information); s. 9 (attempts and abetment).
  • Modern angle: the Right to Information Act, 2005 s. 22 gives it overriding effect over the Official Secrets Act, and s. 8(1)(a) exempts only information that would affect sovereignty, security etc. Journalists have been charged under the Act, which is why it is a free-speech and press-freedom topic.

sections.title: 1.6 Why Article 14 comes before Article 19 in India (reverse of America)
sections.html:
This was the professor's favourite "no-textbook-answer" question (he says he asks it in interviews). Learn the answer as a short argument:

  • USA: the first thing the American founders wrote into the Bill of Rights was the First Amendment (religion, speech, press, assembly, 1791). The long history of censorship in Europe made speech the first demand; equal protection arrived only with the Fourteenth Amendment (1868), after the Civil War.
  • India: the Constitution was framed to solve India's own problems. The deepest problem was inequality (caste, untouchability, religion, gender). So the chapter on Fundamental Rights begins with equality (Arts 14 to 18) and then freedoms (Art 19).
  • Logic: equality needs speech first, but speech needs equality too. "If you cannot speak, you cannot even say that you are unequal; if you are treated as unequal, you cannot speak." India chose to attack the first evil first.
  • The sentence the professor said to remember: "The Indian Constitution was made to solve our problems; the Western constitutions solved theirs: suppression first for them, inequality first for us."

sections.title: 1.7 Why is Article 19 only for "citizens"?
sections.html:
The professor posed this question and left it open. Here is a structured answer:

  • Text: Art 19(1) begins "All citizens shall have the right...", whereas Art 14 says "The State shall not deny to any person", and Art 21 says "No person".
  • Reason 1, political character: the freedoms in Art 19 (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession) are rights of membership of the political community; the Constituent Assembly reserved them to citizens.
  • Reason 2, security and propaganda: foreign nationals (and enemy aliens) could misuse speech, assembly and association to spread propaganda or incite division (the professor's concern with foreign propaganda).
  • Case law (supplementary): Hans Muller of Nuremberg v. Superintendent, Presidency Jail (1955): a foreigner cannot claim Art 19 (but can claim Art 14, 21, 22). State Trading Corporation v. CTO (1963): a company is not a citizen and cannot claim Art 19. Bennett Coleman (1972) allowed shareholders (citizens) to challenge a measure affecting the company's press freedom (lifting the veil).
  • Criticism: Art 19 excludes non-citizens, but expression is a human right; the courts compensate by reading Art 21 broadly (e.g. Maneka Gandhi) and by treating the press as exercising citizens' rights.

sections.title: 1.8 Questions asked by the professor in Lecture 1, with model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. Speech is a natural right (a baby cries on birth), so why did it need constitutional status?

Context: Opening question of the lecture; the student answered "so that people can speak freely" and "because those above us in power try to suppress us".

Model answer

Because rights are written down only when somebody has taken them away. The State and those more powerful than the individual suppressed free expression (Socrates, Galileo, the Inquisition, Propaganda Ministry), so the framers gave the natural freedom a constitutional guarantee that is enforceable against the State under Art 32 and 226.

Question asked in class

Q2. Who suppresses the freedom of speech, and why? (Give a one-word answer in Ambedkar's style)

Model answer

The State. Reasons: (1) to prevent its wrongdoing from coming out; (2) to protect the established system of knowledge or religion on which its authority rests; (3) because rulers consider their statement final and a challenge a personal affront; (4) to maintain power.

Note the counter-reason given by a student: the other side has a right not to be provoked into violence; this is why the Constitution lets the State impose reasonable restrictions under Art 19(2) but only on the eight listed grounds.

Question asked in class

Q3. What happened to Socrates? What was his "fault"?

Model answer

He questioned prevailing knowledge, religion and authority in Athens (the Socratic method). He was convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth and executed by drinking hemlock in 399 BCE. His case shows that questioning was treated as a crime.

Question asked in class

Q4. What happened to the one who said the Earth revolves around the Sun? Who was it, and who punished him?

Model answer

The heliocentric theory is associated with Copernicus (published 1543), and defended by Galileo. The Church (through the Roman Inquisition, 1633) forced Galileo to recant and placed him under house arrest, because the accepted view (Ptolemaic geocentrism, backed by religious authority) was that the Sun moved around the Earth. (Giordano Bruno was burned in 1600.)

Question asked in class

Q5. What was the Inquisition?

Context: A student read out the NotebookLM definition at the professor's request: "an institution that actively sought out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established knowledge".

Model answer

A historical institution of the Roman Catholic Church that actively searched out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established religion and knowledge; punishment for heresy could be imprisonment or death. It also operated the Index of Prohibited Books, an early form of prior censorship.

Question asked in class

Q6. What is the Official Secrets Act, 1923, and how does it classify information?

Model answer

A colonial law (replacing the 1889 Act) punishing spying and unauthorised communication or even retention of official secret information. Government information is graded Restricted, Confidential, Secret and Top Secret. It is a classic example of a law that restricts speech in the name of State security and is read now with Art 19(2) (security of the State) and the RTI Act, 2005.

Question asked in class

Q7. Why is Article 14 placed before Article 19 in India when America put speech (First Amendment) first?

Model answer

See section 1.6. Short form: the West's main problem was suppression of ideas, so speech came first; India's main problem was social inequality, so equality came first. The Constitution is designed to solve the problems of its own society.

Question asked in class

Q8. Why is Article 19 given only to citizens?

Model answer

See section 1.7. Short form: Art 19 freedoms are political rights of members of the nation; non-citizens can seek only the "person" rights (Arts 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22), and foreign propaganda was a concern.
sections.text: Question asked in class Q1. Speech is a natural right (a baby cries on birth), so why did it need constitutional status? Context: Opening question of the lecture; the student answered "so that people can speak freely" and "because those above us in power try to suppress us". Model answer Because rights are written down only when somebody has taken them away. The State and those more powerful than the individual suppressed free expression (Socrates, Galileo, the Inquisition, Propaganda Ministry), so the framers gave the natural freedom a constitutional guarantee that is enforceable against the State under Art 32 and 226. Question asked in class Q2. Who suppresses the freedom of speech, and why? (Give a one-word answer in Ambedkar's style) Model answer The State. Reasons: (1) to prevent its wrongdoing from coming out; (2) to protect the established system of knowledge or religion on which its authority rests; (3) because rulers consider their statement final and a challenge a personal affront; (4) to maintain power. Note the counter-reason given by a student: the other side has a right not to be provoked into violence; this is why the Constitution lets the State impose reasonable restrictions under Art 19(2) but only on the eight listed grounds. Question asked in class Q3. What happened to Socrates? What was his "fault"? Model answer He questioned prevailing knowledge, religion and authority in Athens (the Socratic method). He was convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth and executed by drinking hemlock in 399 BCE. His case shows that questioning was treated as a crime. Question asked in class Q4. What happened to the one who said the Earth revolves around the Sun? Who was it, and who punished him? Model answer The heliocentric theory is associated with Copernicus (published 1543), and defended by Galileo . The Church (through the Roman Inquisition, 1633 ) forced Galileo to recant and placed him under house arrest, because the accepted view (Ptolemaic geocentrism, backed by religious authority) was that the Sun moved around the Earth. (Giordano Bruno was burned in 1600.) Question asked in class Q5. What was the Inquisition? Context: A student read out the NotebookLM definition at the professor's request: "an institution that actively sought out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established knowledge". Model answer A historical institution of the Roman Catholic Church that actively searched out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established religion and knowledge ; punishment for heresy could be imprisonment or death. It also operated the Index of Prohibited Books, an early form of prior censorship. Question asked in class Q6. What is the Official Secrets Act, 1923, and how does it classify information? Model answer A colonial law (replacing the 1889 Act) punishing spying and unauthorised communication or even retention of official secret information. Government information is graded Restricted, Confidential, Secret and Top Secret . It is a classic example of a law that restricts speech in the name of State security and is read now with Art 19(2) (security of the State) and the RTI Act, 2005. Question asked in class Q7. Why is Article 14 placed before Article 19 in India when America put speech (First Amendment) first? Model answer See section 1.6. Short form: the West's main problem was suppression of ideas, so speech came first; India's main problem was social inequality, so equality came first. The Constitution is designed to solve the problems of its own society. Question asked in class Q8. Why is Article 19 given only to citizens? Model answer See section 1.7. Short form: Art 19 freedoms are political rights of members of the nation; non-citizens can seek only the "person" rights (Arts 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22), and foreign propaganda was a concern.

sections.title: 1.9 Homework and instructions given in Lecture 1
sections.html:
Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 1.1: Write a short article on the examples used in class (Socrates, Galileo/Copernicus, the Propaganda Ministry) and circulate it (professor: "make a small article... circulate by email/video")

Model answer

Model article (about 250 words, ready to submit):

Why the Constitution Protects Speech: Lessons from History. Freedom of speech is as old as the human voice, yet it has always been fragile. In 399 BCE Athens tried Socrates for questioning the city's gods and for "corrupting the youth"; he was made to drink hemlock. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition, the Church tribunal charged with enforcing orthodoxy, forced Galileo Galilei to recant his support for Copernicus's heliocentric model and confined him to his house for the rest of his life. The Church also maintained an Index of Prohibited Books to control what people could read. In the twentieth century Nazi Germany set up a Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda (1933) which controlled press, radio and film.

These episodes explain why modern constitutions turn a natural human capacity into an enforceable right. The American First Amendment (1791) placed speech first. In India, colonial laws such as the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and the sedition law showed how the State could suppress dissent; the framers therefore guaranteed freedom of speech and expression in Article 19(1)(a) to citizens, subject only to reasonable restrictions on the eight grounds in Article 19(2). Because India's own central problem was inequality, the Constitution places Article 14 before Article 19. The lesson of history is that a society which punishes questions stops learning; free speech is the marketplace in which better ideas defeat worse ones.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 1.2: Remember this sentence (professor: "ये सेंटेंस याद रखना")

Model answer

"Wherever Western powers went they suppressed freedom of speech (e.g. the Official Secrets Act, 1923), and therefore freedom of expression became essential: Western constitutions listed speech first because suppression was their problem; India listed equality first because inequality was ours."

Use it as the opening line of any answer on the historical background of Art 19(1)(a).

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 1.3: Be ready with the definition of the Inquisition and the Official Secrets Act (professor asked students to look them up and read aloud)

Model answer

See Q5 and Q6 above. Learn them word-for-word. The professor expects the phrases "actively sought out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established knowledge" for the Inquisition and "Restricted, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret" for the Official Secrets Act.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 1.4: Habit task: follow the news and general knowledge (professor repeatedly asked students to read news daily and to check facts themselves rather than rely on his statement)

Model answer

Answer-writing tip: when you cite a historical or current example, make sure you can name the year and the authority (for example "Roman Inquisition, 1633"). Accuracy in examples earns marks; vague examples do not.

exam.title: Article 19(1)(a) Freedom of Speech & Expression: Scope, the Eight Grounds of Restriction and the Early Cases

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Art 19(1) is for citizens only (so are Arts 15, 16, 29, 30; Art 14 and 21 are for "any person"). Art 19(1)(a) = speech and expression, and it includes publication, circulation (Romesh Thappar), the right to reply (LIC v. Manubhai Shah), the right to telecast (Odyssey) and the right to receive information (Cricket Association of Bengal).

Restrictions: only by "law", only on the eight grounds in Art 19(2), and they must be reasonable (State of Madras v. V.G. Row). No right is absolute, not even Art 21.

Eight grounds: (1) sovereignty and integrity of India, (2) security of the State, (3) friendly relations with foreign States, (4) public order, (5) decency or morality, (6) contempt of court, (7) defamation, (8) incitement to an offence. The professor wants all eight memorised before you enter the exam hall.

Prior censorship: bad for print (Brij Bhushan) but allowed for cinema (K.A. Abbas). Obscenity: Hicklin → community standards (Aveek Sarkar); Khushboo = discussion of pre-marital sex is not obscenity.

sections.title: 2.1 Text of Article 19 and who can claim it
sections.html:
Heading of the Article (professor read it out): "Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc." Art 19(1): "All citizens shall have the right (a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions [or co-operative societies, added by the 97th Amendment, 2011]; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; [(f) deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978]; and (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business."

  • The professor drew attention to the first words: "All citizens shall have the right". It is a right, and it belongs only to citizens. Non-citizens cannot claim Art 19 (they get Arts 14, 20, 21, 22 etc.).
  • Equality group: Art 14 is for everybody ("any person"); Arts 15 and 16 are for citizens; so Arts 15, 16 and 19 are citizens' rights. (Also Arts 29 and 30 speak of "any section of citizens".)
  • Art 17 (abolition of untouchability): the professor chose not to teach it in detail (a student once joked that "untouchability abolished means I can touch anybody"). Exam-safe summary: Art 17 abolishes untouchability in any form, makes its enforcement an offence punishable by law (Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989). It is an absolute right with no exception and is enforceable even against private individuals (People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India, 1982). "Untouchability" means the social practice of treating certain castes as polluting, not the literal act of touching.
  • Art 18 (abolition of titles): (1) State shall confer no titles except military and academic distinctions; (2) citizens cannot accept titles from foreign States; (3) a non-citizen holding an office of profit/trust cannot accept foreign titles without President's consent; (4) no gifts/emoluments from foreign States without President's consent. The professor explained: titles such as "Sir", "Rai Bahadur", "Diwan Bahadur" (colonial rulers conferred them to create loyal local elites) were abolished because all citizens are equal. "Doctor" or "Advocate" is a professional/academic qualification, not a State title.
Case

Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1996 SC 770 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India).

Facts
  • Petitions challenged the National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri) as "titles" prohibited by Art 18(1).
Issues
  • Are national awards "titles" within Art 18(1)?
Held (Decision)
  • No. They are awards/distinctions, not titles; they do not create a class of hereditary or social superiority, and Art 18 does not forbid recognising merit. But they must not be used as a prefix or suffix to the name; misuse can lead to forfeiture (Awards Rules).
Ratio decidendi

Art 18 prohibits titles that denote nobility or social hierarchy; honours conferred for merit without privileges are consistent with equality.

Use in the exam

Professor mentioned this case ("there is a case on this, see it") as the authority on awards vs titles.

sections.title: 2.2 Why is free speech valuable? (professor's points)
sections.html:
• Democratic accountability and transparency: the people decide who governs; if the Government errs it can be criticised, questioned and corrected. "Speech is the marketplace of ideas".
  • Participation in public life, criticism of government, supporting democratic debate, political accountability, citizenship. Leaders who persuade by speech can bring reforms.
  • The professor's phrase: free speech is "not merely a personal liberty; it is an institutional guarantee" (the press, publishers and broadcasters are protected, not only the individual who speaks).
  • International parallels: First Amendment of the US Constitution; Art 19 UDHR (1948); Art 19 ICCPR (1966); Art 10 European Convention on Human Rights; French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, 1789 (Art 11).

sections.html:
The professor's list (learn as a checklist; each item is backed by a case in later lectures):

sections.title: 2.4 The four-five cases on dissemination (circulation / telecast / receiving information)
sections.html:
The professor said: "These cases show that we have a fundamental right to give and to receive information. Read them in that light." (He later asked students to fit each case to this theme.)

Case

Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1950 SC 124; 1950 SCR 594 (Supreme Court; decided 26 May 1950, 4 months after the Constitution came into force).

Bench / Author

Patanjali Sastri J. wrote the majority opinion; Fazl Ali J. dissented (the professor noted that Fazl Ali J. wanted "public order" and "security of the State" read liberally because disorder can lead to threats to the State).

Facts
  • Romesh Thappar printed and published Cross Roads, an English weekly, in Bombay (printed in Madras). The Madras Government, under s. 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949, banned the entry and circulation of the journal in Madras State.
  • The professor's framing: "Nehru's Government gave permission to *print* but banned *circulation*. Who prints a paper to keep it in his room?"
Issues
  • Does the freedom of speech and expression include freedom of circulation?
  • Is a law that restricts a publication to prevent disturbance of "public order"/"law and order" valid under the then Art 19(2) (which allowed restrictions only for matters affecting the security of, or tending to overthrow, the State)?
Held (Decision)
  • Freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, and that freedom is ensured by the freedom of circulation. Without circulation the right is empty.
  • Because Art 19(2) (before 1951) did not list "public order"/"law and order" as a ground, s. 9(1-A) could not be saved. The section was void.
  • The Court distinguished "public order" from "law and order" and from "security of the State": the last is the narrowest; not every disturbance of public order endangers the State.
Ratio decidendi

Freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation; a restriction must fall within the grounds listed in Art 19(2); "law and order" is not a ground (the Court said that Art 19(2) as then worded could not support curbs for mere public disorder).

Significance / Later treatment
  • Together with Brij Bhushan it triggered the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951, which added "public order", "friendly relations with foreign States" and "incitement to an offence" and made restrictions "reasonable" and applicable retrospectively.
  • The three concentric circles are later described in Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1966): law and order (widest), public order, security of State (narrowest).
Use in the exam

The professor repeatedly asked: "What did the Supreme Court say?" Two things: (1) law and order is not a ground; (2) circulation is covered by Art 19(1)(a). He asked students to read the original judgment, which explains the three terms well.

Case

Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana (1988)

Citation / Court / Year

(1988) 3 SCC 410 (Supreme Court of India).

Facts
  • Odyssey produced the Doordarshan TV serial "Honi Anhoni". A public-interest organisation, Lokvidayan Sanghatana, objected that the serial promoted superstition and sought to stop its telecast.
  • The professor recalled the case as "Doordarshan denied permission to telecast a serial" and said the Court recognised a right to telecast. (Exam-safe version: the dispute was about stopping a telecast, and the Court upheld the producer's right to exhibit it.)
Issues
  • Does the right to telecast a film/serial on the national broadcaster form part of Art 19(1)(a)? Can it be stopped at a third party's instance?
Held (Decision)
  • A citizen's right to exhibit films on Doordarshan, subject to the terms and conditions of the broadcaster and the restrictions in Art 19(2), is part of freedom of speech and expression. The challenge to the serial failed because no Art 19(2) ground was made out.
Ratio decidendi

The right to disseminate by television is part of Art 19(1)(a), and the right cannot be defeated except on grounds in Art 19(2).

Use in the exam

Professor: "Read the case; the right to telecast was held to be a fundamental right and it cannot be denied (except on Art 19(2) grounds)". A student pointed to Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) (telecast of the serial Tamas, based on Bhisham Sahni's novel on Partition), where the Court refused to ban the serial; effect of a work must be judged from the standpoint of reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous persons, not of those with weak and vacillating minds.

Case

LIC of India v. Manubhai D. Shah (1992)

Citation / Court / Year

(1992) 3 SCC 637 (Supreme Court of India). Also reported as Life Insurance Corporation v. Professor Manubhai D. Shah.

Facts
  • Prof. Manubhai Shah (Consumer Education and Research Centre, Ahmedabad) wrote a study criticising LIC's policies/premiums. LIC's in-house magazine, Yogakshema, published a rebuttal and defence of the policies. When Shah asked to publish his reply in the same magazine, LIC refused.
  • Professor's analogy: "If the university magazine praised the university and a student wrote a criticism and the Registrar refused to print it, the student can say: I want to publish my account too."
Issues
  • Does the freedom of speech include the right of reply and the right to publish a counter-view in the organ of a body that has published criticism?
Held (Decision)
  • Refusal to publish the reply violated Art 19(1)(a). A one-sided presentation by a State instrumentality, which refuses an opposing view, denies fair debate.
  • LIC, as a statutory corporation (State within Art 12), was bound by Art 19 and had to give space to the reply; it could not rely on its "proprietary" rights over the magazine.
Ratio decidendi

Free speech includes the right to reply / the right to a fair and balanced presentation when the State or its instrumentality uses its own platform to put forward a view.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Professor's summary: "publish, because that is also public"; he added the example of a private institution. (Caution: the holding is about LIC as State, not about every private publisher; horizontal application of Art 19 is addressed separately in Kaushal Kishor, see Lecture 19.)
Case

Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)

Citation / Court / Year

(1995) 2 SCC 161 (Supreme Court of India).

Bench / Author

Sawant J. (for himself and Kuldip Singh J.), with Jeevan Reddy J. concurring.

Facts
  • The Cricket Association of Bengal hosted the Hero Cup one-day international matches (1993) at Eden Gardens and gave telecast rights to a foreign production company (Trans World International, TWI). The Government and Doordarshan (state broadcaster with a monopoly on terrestrial telecasting) insisted that only Doordarshan could telecast/uplink the matches within India.
  • The professor's version (BCCI contract of "thousands of crores" to a foreign company; Doordarshan could not afford it): the simplified point is that the State monopoly over broadcasting was challenged.
Issues
  • Are airwaves public property? Can the State claim a monopoly over broadcasting? Is there a fundamental right to telecast and to receive information?
Held (Decision)
  • Airwaves/frequencies are public property, to be used for public good and in line with Art 39(b) and (c) (distribution of material resources of the community).
  • The right to impart and receive information (through any medium: print, electronic, audio-visual) is part of Art 19(1)(a); a State monopoly over broadcasting is not mandated by the Constitution.
  • The right to broadcast is not unlimited: licensing and regulation are permitted if they fall within Art 19(2) (and 19(1)(g)).
  • The Court recommended an independent, autonomous public authority representing all sections of society to control and regulate the airwaves.
Ratio decidendi

Freedom of speech includes the right to receive and impart information through electronic media; airwaves are public property and cannot be monopolised by the Government.

Use in the exam

The professor wanted the full name: Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (not "of India": "आपने इंडिया कह दिया तो ... यही सब गड़बड़ हो जाता है"). Remember the proposition: right to receive information.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.1: Fit each of the following cases to the theme "we have a fundamental right to give and to receive information" (the professor asked "what are these cases focusing on?")

Model answer
CaseGive (impart/disseminate)Receive
Romesh Thappar (1950)Right to circulate the journalReaders' access is the purpose of circulation
Odyssey v. Lokvidayan (1988)Right to telecast the serialViewers' right to see lawful content
LIC v. Manubhai Shah (1992)Right to reply / publish counter-viewReaders get both sides
Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)Right to telecast sport through chosen agencyPublic's right to receive information on air

One line for the exam: "Together these cases establish that Art 19(1)(a) protects not only the speaker but the entire chain: production, publication, circulation, broadcast and reception of ideas."

Facts Romesh Thappar printed and published Cross Roads , an English weekly, in Bombay (printed in Madras). The Madras Government, under s. 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 , banned the entry and circulation of the journal in Madras State. The professor's framing: "Nehru's Government gave permission to *print* but banned *circulation*. Who prints a paper to keep it in his room?" Issues Does the freedom of speech and expression include freedom of circulation ? Is a law that restricts a publication to prevent disturbance of "public order"/"law and order" valid under the then Art 19(2) (which allowed restrictions only for matters affecting the security of, or tending to overthrow, the State )? Held (Decision) Freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, and that freedom is ensured by the freedom of circulation . Without circulation the right is empty. Because Art 19(2) (before 1951) did not list "public order"/"law and order" as a ground, s. 9(1-A) could not be saved. The section was void . The Court distinguished "public order" from "law and order" and from "security of the State" : the last is the narrowest; not every disturbance of public order endangers the State. Ratio decidendi Freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation ; a restriction must fall within the grounds listed in Art 19(2); "law and order" is not a ground (the Court said that Art 19(2) as then worded could not support curbs for mere public disorder). Significance / Later treatment Together with Brij Bhushan it triggered the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951 , which added "public order", "friendly relations with foreign States" and "incitement to an offence" and made restrictions "reasonable" and applicable retrospectively . The three concentric circles are later described in Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1966) : law and order (widest), public order, security of State (narrowest). Use in the exam The professor repeatedly asked: "What did the Supreme Court say?" Two things: (1) law and order is not a ground ; (2) circulation is covered by Art 19(1)(a) . He asked students to read the original judgment, which explains the three terms well. Case Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana (1988) Citation / Court / Year (1988) 3 SCC 410 (Supreme Court of India). Facts Odyssey produced the Doordarshan TV serial "Honi Anhoni" . A public-interest organisation, Lokvidayan Sanghatana, objected that the serial promoted superstition and sought to stop its telecast. The professor recalled the case as "Doordarshan denied permission to telecast a serial" and said the Court recognised a right to telecast. (Exam-safe version: the dispute was about stopping a telecast, and the Court upheld the producer's right to exhibit it.) Issues Does the right to telecast a film/serial on the national broadcaster form part of Art 19(1)(a)? Can it be stopped at a third party's instance? Held (Decision) A citizen's right to exhibit films on Doordarshan, subject to the terms and conditions of the broadcaster and the restrictions in Art 19(2) , is part of freedom of speech and expression. The challenge to the serial failed because no Art 19(2) ground was made out. Ratio decidendi The right to disseminate by television is part of Art 19(1)(a), and the right cannot be defeated except on grounds in Art 19(2). Use in the exam Professor: "Read the case; the right to telecast was held to be a fundamental right and it cannot be denied (except on Art 19(2) grounds)". A student pointed to Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) (telecast of the serial Tamas , based on Bhisham Sahni's novel on Partition), where the Court refused to ban the serial; effect of a work must be judged from the standpoint of reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous persons, not of those with weak and vacillating minds. Case LIC of India v. Manubhai D. Shah (1992) Citation / Court / Year (1992) 3 SCC 637 (Supreme Court of India). Also reported as Life Insurance Corporation v. Professor Manubhai D. Shah . Facts Prof. Manubhai Shah (Consumer Education and Research Centre, Ahmedabad) wrote a study criticising LIC's policies/premiums. LIC's in-house magazine, Yogakshema , published a rebuttal and defence of the policies. When Shah asked to publish his reply in the same magazine, LIC refused . Professor's analogy: "If the university magazine praised the university and a student wrote a criticism and the Registrar refused to print it, the student can say: I want to publish my account too." Issues Does the freedom of speech include the right of reply and the right to publish a counter-view in the organ of a body that has published criticism? Held (Decision) Refusal to publish the reply violated Art 19(1)(a) . A one-sided presentation by a State instrumentality, which refuses an opposing view, denies fair debate. LIC, as a statutory corporation (State within Art 12), was bound by Art 19 and had to give space to the reply ; it could not rely on its "proprietary" rights over the magazine. Ratio decidendi Free speech includes the right to reply / the right to a fair and balanced presentation when the State or its instrumentality uses its own platform to put forward a view. Significance / Later treatment Professor's summary: "publish, because that is also public"; he added the example of a private institution. (Caution: the holding is about LIC as State , not about every private publisher; horizontal application of Art 19 is addressed separately in Kaushal Kishor , see Lecture 19.) Case Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995) Citation / Court / Year (1995) 2 SCC 161 (Supreme Court of India). Bench / Author Sawant J. (for himself and Kuldip Singh J.), with Jeevan Reddy J. concurring. Facts The Cricket Association of Bengal hosted the Hero Cup one-day international matches (1993) at Eden Gardens and gave telecast rights to a foreign production company (Trans World International, TWI) . The Government and Doordarshan (state broadcaster with a monopoly on terrestrial telecasting) insisted that only Doordarshan could telecast/uplink the matches within India. The professor's version (BCCI contract of "thousands of crores" to a foreign company; Doordarshan could not afford it): the simplified point is that the State monopoly over broadcasting was challenged . Issues Are airwaves public property ? Can the State claim a monopoly over broadcasting? Is there a fundamental right to telecast and to receive information? Held (Decision) Airwaves/frequencies are public property , to be used for public good and in line with Art 39(b) and (c) (distribution of material resources of the community). The right to impart and receive information (through any medium: print, electronic, audio-visual) is part of Art 19(1)(a) ; a State monopoly over broadcasting is not mandated by the Constitution. The right to broadcast is not unlimited : licensing and regulation are permitted if they fall within Art 19(2) (and 19(1)(g)). The Court recommended an independent, autonomous public authority representing all sections of society to control and regulate the airwaves. Ratio decidendi Freedom of speech includes the right to receive and impart information through electronic media; airwaves are public property and cannot be monopolised by the Government. Use in the exam The professor wanted the full name: Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (not "of India": "आपने इंडिया कह दिया तो ... यही सब गड़बड़ हो जाता है"). Remember the proposition: right to receive information . Homework / instruction HOMEWORK 2.1: Fit each of the following cases to the theme "we have a fundamental right to give and to receive information" (the professor asked "what are these cases focusing on?") Model answer Case Give (impart/disseminate) Receive Romesh Thappar (1950) Right to circulate the journal Readers' access is the purpose of circulation Odyssey v. Lokvidayan (1988) Right to telecast the serial Viewers' right to see lawful content LIC v. Manubhai Shah (1992) Right to reply / publish counter-view Readers get both sides Cricket Association of Bengal (1995) Right to telecast sport through chosen agency Public's right to receive information on air One line for the exam: "Together these cases establish that Art 19(1)(a) protects not only the speaker but the entire chain: production, publication, circulation, broadcast and reception of ideas."

sections.title: 2.5 Nothing is absolute: Article 21 and the death-penalty illustration
sections.html:
The professor said: "In our country no right is absolute, not even a fundamental right. Even the right to life can be taken away by procedure established by law (death sentence); so freedom of speech obviously cannot be absolute." He illustrated with a recent murder trial (a husband killed and his body hidden in a blue drum; his wife and her lover were accused) and set a homework (below).

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.2: Research why, in the "blue drum" murder case, the wife was (as the professor believed) not given the death penalty while the lover was; the professor said "research and tell me why the wife was not hanged"

Model answer

What the professor said: the lover was sentenced to death, the wife only to about 20 years, and he asked whether the wife (the alleged informer and mastermind) should have been hanged. Students gave different answers (equal participation; the woman has a child; pregnancy).

Legal framework for the answer (valid for any such question):

  • Death is the exception: only in the "rarest of rare" cases (Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, 1980), after weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances for each accused separately (Machhi Singh, 1983). Parity between co-accused is not automatic: courts examine role, age, criminal record, probability of reform, family circumstances.
  • Possible mitigating factors for a woman accused: a young child dependent on her; pregnancy (a death sentence on a pregnant woman is postponed, and customarily commuted: s. 416 CrPC, now the corresponding BNSS provision); no previous criminal record; the possibility of reform.
  • Death sentences by trial courts must be confirmed by the High Court (CrPC s. 366 / BNSS s. 407); the accused can appeal to the Supreme Court and seek mercy under Arts 72 and 161.

Factual update (verify before using in an exam answer): news reports found while preparing these notes state that on 14 October 2026 the Meerut trial court sentenced both the wife and her lover to death. If that is right, the premise in class (wife got 20 years) is outdated or wrong. In an exam, use the case only as an illustration that even Art 21 yields to procedure established by law.

sections.title: 2.6 The eight grounds of Article 19(2): history and meaning
sections.html:
Art 19(2): "Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence."

#GroundCame in byKey points to remember
1Sovereignty and integrity of IndiaSixteenth Amendment, 1963Words "sovereignty and" were added in 1963 (after the Chinese war and secessionist demands). The professor: "you cannot talk of breaking the country", but mere words without imminent danger do not amount to an offence.
2Security of the StateOriginal (1950: "undermines the security of, or tends to overthrow, the State")Narrowest of the three circles; covers serious and aggravated forms of public disorder, e.g. rebellion, waging war, insurrection (Romesh Thappar).
3Friendly relations with foreign StatesFirst Amendment, 1951Added after the Nehru Government wished to stop anti-Pakistan writings (the Organiser case). Not yet widely litigated.
4Public orderFirst Amendment, 1951Disturbance of public peace, safety and tranquillity (see 2.7). Wider than security of State, narrower than law and order.
5Decency or moralityOriginalIncludes obscenity (see 2.9). Tests: Hicklin → community standards (Aveek Sarkar).
6Contempt of courtOriginalContempt of Courts Act, 1971 (civil and criminal contempt).
7DefamationOriginal ("libel, slander, defamation")Civil (tort) and criminal (s. 499/500 IPC, now BNS s. 356). Libel: permanent form; slander: transient (see Q4 below).
8Incitement to an offenceFirst Amendment, 1951Mere advocacy is protected; incitement needs a proximate link to violence (Shreya Singhal; S. Rangarajan "spark in a powder keg").

Trap: do not forget what the First Amendment (1951) did

(1) Added three new grounds: friendly relations with foreign States, public order, incitement to an offence; (2) replaced "undermines the security of, or tends to overthrow, the State" by the simpler "security of the State" (so that public disorder of a serious kind is covered); (3) inserted the word "reasonable" (so that courts can review the restriction); (4) inserted "in the interests of" (wider than "relating to") and made the amendment retrospective (to overrule Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan and similar decisions).

The professor said the framers of the amendment "cancelled the old cases and applied the new text from the date of the Constitution". The Sixteenth Amendment (1963) later added "sovereignty and". Do not attribute any other amendment to Art 19(2).

Memory aid for the eight grounds: Sovereignty-Security-Friendly relations-Public order-Decency/morality-Contempt-Defamation-Incitement = "SS FP DC DI" (or remember the pairs: two of State (sovereignty, security), two of society (public order, decency), two of foreign (friendly relations) and the three of law (contempt, defamation, incitement)). Note that "hate speech", "national interest", "law and order" and "fake news" are NOT grounds.

sections.title: 2.7 Law and order, public order and security of the State (concentric circles)
sections.html:
The professor explained with campus examples and said "this is explained beautifully in Romesh Thappar; read it".

LevelProfessor's exampleLegal meaning
Law and order (widest circle)Two children quarrel; two families or neighbours fight.Any breach of law affecting individuals. Not a ground under Art 19(2) (Romesh Thappar).
Public order (middle circle)Clash between communities (Hindu-Muslim) or between whole batches (third-year v. first-year students).Disturbance of public peace, safety and tranquillity, affecting the community at large (Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar, 1966: "public order" is the even tide of life of the community). Ground added in 1951.
Security of the State (narrowest circle)A threat to the nation; "insurrection, war".Serious and aggravated forms of public disorder: rebellion, waging war against the State, insurrection. Ground from the beginning.
  • Test of "public order" (professor): there must be an approximate (proximate) and reasonable nexus between the restricted activity and public order; a remote, far-fetched or hypothetical connection does not satisfy the test. (Rangarajan: the anticipated danger must be "like a spark in a powder keg", not remote.)
  • Fazl Ali J. (Romesh Thappar dissent): a liberal reading, since "law and order" can lead to public order and public order to the security of the State. The majority rejected the slippery-slope.
  • Imminent danger / clear and present danger: the professor explained that mere words such as "Muslims cannot live in India; it is time to break the country" are not criminal unless the danger is imminent; "if someone gives a speech like a madman that nobody listens to, there is no imminent danger, so no offence". He said the US test of clear and present danger (soldiers urged not to join the army during war, Schenck v. United States, 1919) is relevant, "the same thing is going on today; study it". In India the closer Indian cases are Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962), Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995) and Shreya Singhal (2015).

sections.title: 2.8 Requirements of a valid restriction (State of Madras v. V.G. Row, 1952)
sections.html:
Case

State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1952 SC 196; 1952 SCR 597 (Supreme Court of India).

Bench / Author

Patanjali Sastri C.J.

Facts
  • V.G. Row, an office-bearer of the People's Education Society, Madras, challenged a Madras notification declaring the Society an unlawful association under the Indian Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1908 (s. 15(2)(b)), claiming violation of Art 19(1)(c) (right to form associations).
Issues
  • What is a reasonable restriction under Art 19(2)-(6), and who decides reasonableness?
Held (Decision)
  • The Court held that the Act (as it existed) was unreasonable: it allowed the executive to declare an association unlawful on its own opinion, with no judicial review, no hearing and no objective standard.
  • The Court laid down the factors for reasonableness (applied to all restrictions in Art 19(2)-(6)): the restriction must be in the interest of the general public; the Court looks at both substantive and procedural aspects: nature of the right, underlying purpose of the restriction, extent and urgency of the evil, disproportion of the imposition, prevailing conditions; the standard is objective, not subjective, and not what the legislature thinks.
Ratio decidendi

A restriction is reasonable only if it is not arbitrary or excessive, bears a real and direct connection with the object, and is accompanied by fair procedure (including judicial review).

Use in the exam

The professor listed what a valid restriction needs: (1) imposed by law (Act of Parliament/State Legislature); (2) only for a ground mentioned in Art 19(2): no other ground can be used; (3) a real, approximate connection between the speech and the protected interest (a "rational nexus"); (4) reasonable (nowadays tested as proportionate); (5) fair procedure. He asked students to cite State of Madras v. V.G. Row for the definition of reasonable restriction.

  • "Law": the professor stressed that "law" in Art 19(2) means a law duly enacted by Parliament or a State Legislature; it is not to be read as widely as the definition in Art 13(3)(a) (which includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs). Executive instructions without statutory backing cannot restrict Art 19 (compare Kharak Singh, Bijoe Emmanuel).
  • Restrictions are valid only "in the interests of" the listed grounds; there are no other grounds. Reasonableness is justiciable: the courts, not the legislature, decide whether a restriction is reasonable.
  • Modern formulation: the doctrine of proportionality (Modern Dental College, 2016; Anuradha Bhasin, 2020): legitimate aim → rational nexus → necessity (least restrictive means) → balance. (See later lectures.)

sections.title: 2.9 Obscenity, decency and morality: Hicklin, Aveek Sarkar and Khushboo
sections.html:
The professor warned that "obscenity" (he joked about mis-hearing it as "obesity") is a ground inside "decency or morality" and said students must study Aveek Sarkar and S. Khushboo, and prepare presentations on them.

Case

Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014)

Citation / Court / Year

(2014) 4 SCC 257 (Supreme Court of India, two-Judge bench: K.S. Radhakrishnan and A.K. Sikri JJ.).

Facts
  • The German magazine Stern (1993) carried a photograph of tennis star Boris Becker posing naked with his fiancée Barbara Feltus, a Black Afro-German model, as a statement against racial discrimination (apartheid). The photograph was reprinted in the Kolkata-based magazine Sports World and in Anand Bazar Patrika (publisher/editor Aveek Sarkar). A complaint under s. 292 IPC (obscenity) followed.
  • The professor: "A German tennis player's girlfriend from South Africa, a Black woman; he said skin colour makes no difference to love, and published their nude photograph; an Indian magazine reprinted it."
Issues
  • Is the publication obscene under s. 292 IPC? Which test governs: the old Hicklin test or a community standards test?
Held (Decision)
  • The Court rejected the Hicklin test and adopted the community standards test: the work must be judged as a whole, from the standpoint of an average, reasonable person applying contemporary community standards, not by looking at a single isolated passage and not from the viewpoint of a hypersensitive or the most susceptible reader.
  • The photograph, in context (a message against racial prejudice), did not appeal to prurient interest; hence not obscene; the proceedings were quashed.
Ratio decidendi

Obscenity is judged by contemporary community standards and the whole work and its context; nudity is not obscene per se.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Followed Ranjit D. Udeshi (1964) (which had applied Hicklin) → Samaresh Bose v. Amal Mitra (1985) (moved away) → Bobby Art International (1996) → Aveek Sarkar (2014) (formally buried Hicklin).
Use in the exam

The professor asked a student to present this case. Know the test sentence above by heart.

Case

S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010)

Citation / Court / Year

(2010) 5 SCC 600 (Supreme Court of India; K.G. Balakrishnan C.J., Deepak Verma and B.S. Chauhan JJ.).

Facts
  • In a 2005 magazine interview, the South Indian film actress Khushboo said that pre-marital sex is not wrong in itself but that girls should be careful about sexually transmitted diseases and pregnancy. About 22-23 criminal complaints (obscenity, defamation, Indecent Representation of Women Act, s. 292, 499, 500, 504, 505 IPC etc.) were filed across Tamil Nadu alleging that she corrupted Indian culture.
  • Professor: "She was asked whether physical relations before marriage are right or wrong; she said there is no harm but be careful; a case was filed that she is corrupting our girls."
Issues
  • Do these remarks constitute an offence (obscenity, defamation, incitement)? Where is the line between expression of views and criminal liability?
Held (Decision)
  • The Court quashed the complaints. Expressing a view on pre-marital sex, even if unpopular, is protected speech; a mere discussion or even advocacy of a popular or unpopular cause is the heart of Art 19(1)(a) and is not a crime unless it is an incitement to commit an offence.
  • Living together / pre-marital sex is not an offence in itself; no obscenity (no appeal to prurient interest; no incitement); the complaints amounted to harassment. The Court also stressed that multiple complaints in different places for one statement is an abuse of process.
Ratio decidendi

Unpopular opinions on morality are protected by Art 19(1)(a); obscenity requires material that is lascivious / appeals to prurient interest; mere advocacy is not criminal.

Use in the exam

Khushboo , and prepare presentations on them. Case Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014) Citation / Court / Year (2014) 4 SCC 257 (Supreme Court of India, two-Judge bench: K.S. Radhakrishnan and A.K. Sikri JJ.). Facts The German magazine Stern (1993) carried a photograph of tennis star Boris Becker posing naked with his fiancée Barbara Feltus , a Black Afro-German model, as a statement against racial discrimination (apartheid) . The photograph was reprinted in the Kolkata-based magazine Sports World and in Anand Bazar Patrika (publisher/editor Aveek Sarkar ). A complaint under s. 292 IPC (obscenity) followed. The professor: "A German tennis player's girlfriend from South Africa, a Black woman; he said skin colour makes no difference to love, and published their nude photograph; an Indian magazine reprinted it." Issues Is the publication obscene under s. 292 IPC? Which test governs: the old Hicklin test or a community standards test ? Held (Decision) The Court rejected the Hicklin test and adopted the community standards test : the work must be judged as a whole , from the standpoint of an average, reasonable person applying contemporary community standards , not by looking at a single isolated passage and not from the viewpoint of a hypersensitive or the most susceptible reader. The photograph, in context (a message against racial prejudice), did not appeal to prurient interest ; hence not obscene ; the proceedings were quashed. Ratio decidendi Obscenity is judged by contemporary community standards and the whole work and its context ; nudity is not obscene per se. Significance / Later treatment Followed Ranjit D. Udeshi (1964) (which had applied Hicklin) → Samaresh Bose v. Amal Mitra (1985) (moved away) → Bobby Art International (1996) → Aveek Sarkar (2014) (formally buried Hicklin). Kanniammal (2010) Citation / Court / Year (2010) 5 SCC 600 (Supreme Court of India; K.G. Balakrishnan C.J., Deepak Verma and B.S. Chauhan JJ.). Facts In a 2005 magazine interview, the South Indian film actress Khushboo said that pre-marital sex is not wrong in itself but that girls should be careful about sexually transmitted diseases and pregnancy . Living together / pre-marital sex is not an offence in itself; no obscenity (no appeal to prurient interest; no incitement); the complaints amounted to harassment . The Court also stressed that multiple complaints in different places for one statement is an abuse of process . sections.title: 2.10 Pre-censorship: Brij Bhushan and K.A. Abbas
sections.html:
Case

Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1950 SC 129; 1950 SCR 605 (Supreme Court of India; decided 26 May 1950 on the same day as Romesh Thappar).

Bench / Author

Patanjali Sastri J. for the majority (6-judge bench; Fazl Ali J. dissented).

Facts
  • Brij Bhushan was the printer/publisher of The Organiser, an English weekly (RSS-affiliated) in Delhi. Under s. 7(1)(c) of the East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949 (applicable in Delhi), the Chief Commissioner ordered the weekly to submit for scrutiny, before publication, all communal matter and news and views about Pakistan, including photographs and cartoons.
  • The professor: "After Partition many things could be said abusing Pakistan; Nehru said you cannot abuse Pakistan, and imposed press censorship: check with us first."
Issues
  • Is pre-censorship of a newspaper a valid restriction on Art 19(1)(a), particularly when "public order" was not a ground in Art 19(2) (before 1951)?
Held (Decision)
  • The order was unconstitutional. Pre-censorship of a journal is a restraint on the liberty of the press and is not saved by Art 19(2) as then worded (only matters undermining the security of, or tending to overthrow, the State).
Ratio decidendi

Prior restraint on the press is a direct restriction of freedom of speech and expression and is invalid unless within Art 19(2). "Pre-censorship in print media is not acceptable."

Significance / Later treatment
  • First Amendment (1951) overruled the result by adding "public order" and "friendly relations with foreign States". Pre-censorship remains disfavoured: Kharak Singh, Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1959), Sakal Papers (1962).
Use in the exam

The professor: "name the case on pre-censorship of print media: Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi." He said a student wrongly named a case on incitement to an offence (a different matter) and asked to keep them apart.

Case

K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1971 SC 481; (1970) 2 SCC 780 (Supreme Court of India; Hidayatullah C.J.).

Facts
  • K.A. Abbas (film-maker and journalist) challenged the censorship provisions of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 after the Censor Board gave his documentary "A Tale of Four Cities" an "A" certificate (adults only), objecting to pre-censorship and to the classification into "U" and "A".
  • Professor: "Brij Bhushan said prior restraint is bad for print; films are certified before release; Abbas asked how can you impose prior restraint?"
Issues
  • Is pre-censorship of films consistent with Art 19(1)(a), given Brij Bhushan?
Held (Decision)
  • Pre-censorship of films is valid under Art 19(2): the cinema has a unique impact on the audience (sight and sound together; emotional power; audience sits in the dark, absorbed, with a lasting effect), so it can be treated differently from the press.
  • Classification into U (universal) and A (adults) is a reasonable restriction.
  • The standard of the censor must be that of an ordinary person with common sense and not one who is over-sensitive or prudish; guidelines must be specific and applied with freedom for artistic expression.
Ratio decidendi

Prior restraint on films is permissible because motion pictures are a different medium with greater impact than the printed word; the classification system is valid.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Statutory system today: Cinematograph Act, 1952 as amended in 2023: certificates U, UA 7+, UA 13+, UA 16+, A, S. Certification by the CBFC (Central Board of Film Certification, the "Film Censor Board" whose office the professor said he visited).
  • S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989): the State cannot ban a certified film because of the threat of violence by objectors (heckler's veto); danger must be like a "spark in a powder keg", proximate and direct.
  • Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (Bandit Queen) (1996): scenes of nudity and violence must be judged in the context of the film's message.
Use in the exam

The professor: "Broadcasting things need prior sanction because the impact is larger; people see and hear; reading takes effort. Telecast reaches lakhs at once and influences the mind more." He asked students to read Abbas (theory only) the next day.

MediumCasePrior restraint?Reason
Print media (newspapers, magazines)Brij Bhushan (1950)Not allowedDirect restriction on liberty of the press; not within Art 19(2) as then worded; later disfavoured generally.
Cinema / broadcastingK.A. Abbas (1970)Allowed (with guidelines)Greater impact: audio-visual, simultaneous mass audience, emotional power.

sections.title: 2.11 Defamation: libel and slander; is a tape recording libel or slander?
sections.html:
• Libel = defamation in permanent form (writing, printing, pictures, effigy, statue, morphed photographs). The professor's example: "morphed pictures of a girl to defame her" (a modern form). Slander = defamation in transient form (spoken words, gestures).
  • Professor's question: if someone abuses me and it is tape-recorded, is it libel or slander? A student first said slander (because it is "verbal"), another said libel. Answer: libel, because the record is permanent (it can be replayed and proved later). The professor said "this kind of question should be discussed in the classroom".
  • Why it matters: in tort law libel is actionable per se (no proof of special damage), while slander generally requires proof of special damage (except for imputation of crime, loathsome disease, unchastity of a woman, or professional unfitness). In Indian criminal law (s. 499 IPC / BNS s. 356) there is no libel/slander distinction; "words, spoken or intended to be read, signs or visible representations" are all covered.

sections.title: 2.12 United States comparison (as explained by the professor)
sections.html:
• The First Amendment (1791) says "Congress shall make no law... abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press", and also protects religion. It has no list of grounds for restriction. The professor stressed: "that does not mean there are no restrictions in the US"; the Supreme Court developed the limits case by case (e.g. Schenck v. United States, 1919: clear and present danger; Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969: imminent lawless action).
  • In India the Constitution lists the grounds, which is why First Amendment 1951 was passed to add grounds quickly; Dr. Ambedkar and the framers "took advantage of American experience" by writing the restrictions into the text.

sections.title: 2.13 Questions asked by the professor in COLA 5 with model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. What does Article 19 say? For whom is it? Which Articles are only for citizens?

Model answer

Art 19(1) gives "all citizens" the right to (a) freedom of speech and expression, (b) assemble peaceably and without arms, (c) form associations or unions, (d) move freely, (e) reside and settle anywhere in India, and (g) practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business ((f) was repealed in 1978). It is available only to citizens. Arts 15, 16 and 19 (and 29, 30) are citizen-only; Art 14 and Art 21 apply to every person.

Question asked in class

Q2. Why did the Supreme Court strike down the Madras order in Romesh Thappar even though the Government allowed the paper to be printed?

Model answer

Because freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation; a paper which can be printed but not circulated has no practical freedom. And the ground of "law and order" (public order) was not in Art 19(2) at that time, so the Court could not uphold the ban. (Parliament then amended Art 19(2) in 1951 to add public order.)

Question asked in class

Q3. Distinguish law and order, public order and security of the State.

Model answer

See 2.7: three concentric circles. Law and order (individual quarrels) is widest and not a ground; public order (community-level disturbance of peace and tranquillity) is the middle circle, added in 1951; security of the State (rebellion, war, insurrection) is the innermost. A speech that disturbs only law and order cannot be restricted; one that disturbs public order can; one that threatens the State's security can be curbed more severely. (Ram Manohar Lohia, 1966.)

Question asked in class

Q4. A person abuses you and it is recorded on tape. Is it libel or slander?

Model answer

Libel, because the recording is a permanent form (words fixed in a durable medium that can be reproduced as evidence), even though the original utterance was spoken. Slander covers evanescent spoken words only. (Professor accepted "libel" and said the question should be debated in class.)

Question asked in class

Q5. What is the difference between a restriction and a reasonable restriction? Which case defines it?

Model answer

A restriction is any limit on the right; to be valid it must be reasonable. State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) defines the standard: restriction by law; on an Art 19(2) ground; real and proximate connection with the protected interest; not arbitrary or excessive; fair procedure and judicial review; judged objectively having regard to the nature of the right, the evil sought to be remedied, its extent and urgency, and the proportion between the two.

Question asked in class

Q6. Name the eight grounds of Art 19(2), and which amendments added which?

Model answer

Sovereignty and integrity of India (16th Amend., 1963 added "sovereignty and"); security of the State (original); friendly relations with foreign States (1st Amend., 1951); public order (1951); decency or morality (original); contempt of court (original); defamation (original); incitement to an offence (1951). The First Amendment also inserted "reasonable" and "in the interests of".

Question asked in class

Q7. Which case says pre-censorship of print media is not acceptable, and which case allows it for films?

Model answer

Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950) (print: not acceptable); K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970) (film: allowed because of its greater impact and the need for classification).

Question asked in class

Q8. Is freedom of speech absolute?

Model answer

No. Even Art 21 (right to life) can be taken away by procedure established by law (death penalty). Art 19(2) lists eight grounds on which reasonable restrictions can be imposed by law. The courts examine reasonableness.

Question asked in class

Q9. Which cases show that there is a fundamental right to give and receive information?

Model answer

Romesh Thappar (circulation), Odyssey v. Lokvidayan (telecast), LIC v. Manubhai Shah (reply), Cricket Association of Bengal (airwaves, right to receive). See Homework 2.1.

Question asked in class

Q10. What was the Hicklin test, and was it ever applied in India?

Model answer

English test of 1868: material is obscene if it tends to deprave and corrupt those open to such influences, judged by an isolated passage. The professor suggested it is not in India; in fact it was followed in India until the 1980s-1990s (e.g. Ranjit Udeshi, 1964) and was expressly replaced by the community standards test in Aveek Sarkar (2014).

Question asked in class

Q11. What is "slander" (spelt "slender" by a student)? Define the two kinds of defamation.

Model answer

Slander (not "slender" or "cylinder") = defamation by transient words; libel = defamation in permanent form; both are forms of defamation, an Art 19(2) ground.

Question asked in class

Q12. Why do Arts 15, 16 and 19 apply only to citizens when Art 14 applies to everyone?

Model answer

Because these are rights of membership of the political community (discrimination between citizens in public life/employment, political freedoms); the framers extended only the basic equality and life/liberty protections (Arts 14, 20, 21, 22) to all persons within India.

sections.title: 2.14 Homework and instructions in COLA 5
sections.html:
Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.3: Presentation schedule: the professor asked students to prepare a schedule for presentations ("from July") and bring presentations on Khushboo (next day) and Aveek Sarkar

Model answer

Model 2-minute presentation skeleton (works for any case): 1. Facts in 3 lines; 2. Issue; 3. Decision; 4. Ratio; 5. Why it matters today; 6. One criticism. The case cards in this file follow this pattern.

Khushboo (ready to present): In 2005 actress Khushboo told a magazine that pre-marital sex was not wrong if precautions were taken; 20+ criminal complaints were filed. The Supreme Court (2010) quashed them: expressing an unpopular view is protected by Art 19(1)(a), and there is no offence of discussing pre-marital sex; there was no obscenity, since nothing appealed to prurient interest, and no incitement. Aveek Sarkar (ready to present): see section 2.9: community standards test; nude photo of Becker and Feltus was an anti-racism statement, hence not obscene.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.4: Read the original judgments of Romesh Thappar and the debate on the First Constitutional Amendment (and Nehru's speeches); the professor said "I will not explain it, you must read it"

Model answer

Study map for the First Amendment debate (10 points to take away):

  • Passed 18 June 1951 by the Provisional Parliament (Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951).
  • Occasion: Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan, Master Tara Singh/Punjab HC decisions striking down curbs on speech; the Government's concern about communal propaganda and relations with Pakistan.
  • Nehru argued that the Constitution should not become a hindrance to social progress; he proposed new grounds. Critics (Syama Prasad Mookerjee, H.N. Kunzru, Kamath) objected that it was vague and curtailed civil liberties.
  • Outcome: Art 19(2) rewritten (see 2.6); Arts 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule were also added by the same Amendment (agrarian reforms); Art 15(4) was added to overcome State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) (reservation in educational institutions).
Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.5: Fill in the cases the professor named: Balaji Raghavan (titles), the Art 18 case

Model answer

See the case card in 2.1.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.6: Read Abbas the next day ("theory only; no adult material in it"), and be ready to explain why prior restraint is allowed on cinema

Model answer

See the case card in 2.10 and the table that compares print with cinema.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.7: Research Q: why the wife in the "blue drum" case was not given the death penalty, and the pregnant-woman rule

Model answer

See Homework 2.2.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 2.8: Class discipline instructions: attend regularly (the professor remarked attendance matters and that students who miss classes risk attendance shortage); submit presentation schedule; read news

exam.title: Applying Article 19(2): Citizenship Check, the Eight Grounds, "Law", Reasonableness and the Four-Fold Proportionality Test

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Checklist to solve any Art 19(1)(a) problem question (professor's sequence): (1) Is the claimant a citizen? If not, Art 19 is unavailable. (2) Is there a restriction/violation of the right? (3) Is it imposed by law (enacted by Parliament/State Legislature)? (4) Is it on one of the eight grounds (no other ground, e.g. "better administration", is allowed)? (5) Is it reasonable, which today means proportionate? Apply the four-fold test from Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020): legitimate aim, rational nexus, necessity, balancing (structural proportionality), plus judicial review.

"Legitimate" here is not the family-law meaning (legitimate child). It means a lawful and fair aim in the public interest such as national security, public safety, public order, public health, public morals, protection of the rights and reputation of others (ICCPR / European standards).

The professor wants all eight grounds written from memory; he said "I will come tomorrow, you will have them written; I will make you erase and rewrite".

Note on this lecture's content

COLA 6 contains a lot of campus administration and current-affairs commentary (student elections, university holidays, controversy over the Election Commission, party politics). That commentary is not law and has been left out. The legal substance is below. Where the professor used a real constitutional example (appointment of the Election Commission; the P.J. Thomas case), only the legal point is retained.
