sections.title: 3.1 Step 1: is the claimant a citizen? (the "Jantar Mantar" hypothetical)
sections.html:
Professor's problem question: A person wanted to give a speech at Jantar Mantar (Delhi) for or against the Chief Election Commissioner. Delhi Police refused permission. He files a case in the Delhi High Court saying that his freedom of speech has been violated by Delhi Police and appropriate action should be taken. "You are the Magistrate/Court; what will you do?" A student answered: Article 19 is only for citizens of India; if the petitioner is not an Indian citizen the freedom is not available. The professor applauded this as the first thing to check.

  • Step 1 answer: Art 19(1) says "all citizens". If the person is a foreigner, Art 19(1)(a) is not available (Hans Muller of Nuremberg v. Superintendent, Presidency Jail, 1955). He can still invoke Art 14 (equality), Art 21 (life and liberty) and Art 22; and, if applicable, Art 25 (freedom of religion, available to all persons).
  • If he is a citizen, go to the next steps: has the State restricted the right? On what ground? Under what law? Is the restriction reasonable? (Police refusal of permission for a public meeting would be tested under Art 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) (assembly) and the law on public meetings, e.g. Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018): Jantar Mantar protest regulations, where the Court said protest is a right but must be regulated reasonably, and the Ramlila Maidan case (2012).)
  • Professor's remark: "Do not trust me blindly; verify; the point is that checking citizenship is the first step."

sections.title: 3.2 Step 2 and 3: a violation, and the eight grounds (recitation)
sections.html:
A student read out the text. The professor asked her to say all grounds and then told the class: "Eight grounds. All eight must be on your tongue."

  1. Sovereignty and integrity of India
  2. Security of the State
  3. Friendly relations with foreign States
  4. Public order
  5. Decency or morality
  6. Contempt of court
  7. Defamation
  8. Incitement to an offence

Art 19(2) text for reading: "Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence."

Professor's reminders about the grounds:

  • "Restriction can be imposed only on these grounds. No other ground." Example: the Government cannot say "for better administration of the university/State we freeze your right to speak"; better administration is not a ground. (He conceded that for students inside an institution some additional discipline can be imposed under the institution's own rules, but generally a State law cannot rely on grounds outside Art 19(2).)
  • Public order was added later (1951); friendly relations with foreign States was originally explained with reference to Pakistan, and the lecture noted that the ground is not frequently used.

sections.title: 3.3 Step 4: the restriction must be by "law"
sections.html:
• Restriction must be imposed by law. The professor said: "law" here is not the wide definition in Art 13(3)(a) (which includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, custom or usage having the force of law).
  • "Law" = enacted law: an Act passed by Parliament or a State Legislature. (Subordinate legislation is valid only if it is made under a valid parent Act; mere executive orders or police instructions without statutory backing are not "law".) See Kharak Singh (1962) (regulation without statutory force) and Bijoe Emmanuel (1986).
  • This also protects citizens against restrictions improvised by officials. Example in the lecture: an officer cannot refuse permission or "freeze" speech on a ground not in the statute.

sections.title: 3.4 Step 5: the restriction must be reasonable, today meaning proportionate
sections.html:
The professor repeated what he taught the previous day (Lecture 2: State of Madras v. V.G. Row): the restriction must be "reasonable". He then added: "Reasonable has now become proportionate." He asked a student to find the four conditions laid down in Anuradha Bhasin.

Case

Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)

Citation / Court / Year

(2020) 3 SCC 637; decided 10 January 2020 (Supreme Court of India).

Bench / Author

N.V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy and B.R. Gavai JJ. (Justice Ramana authored the leading judgment).

Facts
  • After the abrogation of Art 370 (5 August 2019), the J&K administration imposed a communications blackout (mobile, landline and internet) and orders under s. 144 CrPC restricting movement and assembly. Anuradha Bhasin, editor of the Kashmir Times, challenged the shutdown as violating Art 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); Ghulam Nabi Azad intervened for the restrictions on movement.
  • The professor's illustration: restrictions on information flow (internet, TV, mobile, press) in Kashmir because of national-security concerns; is closing the information channel connected to the goal?
Issues
  • Does freedom of speech and the right to carry on trade or business through the internet enjoy constitutional protection?
  • Is an indefinite internet shutdown permissible? Are orders under s. 144 CrPC valid and must they be published?
Held (Decision)
  • Freedom of speech and expression and the right to practise any profession or carry on business over the internet are protected under Art 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); restrictions must meet the tests of Art 19(2)/(6) and proportionality.
  • Indefinite suspension of internet services is impermissible; shutdowns under the Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services Rules, 2017 must be temporary, limited in scope, reasoned, published and subject to periodic review (by a Review Committee, within a week).
  • s. 144 CrPC cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression or peaceful dissent; orders must state material facts, be proportionate, and are subject to judicial review.
  • The Court applied the four-fold proportionality test (below) borrowed from the German/Canadian line and Modern Dental College (2016) and K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).
Ratio decidendi

Any restriction on Art 19(1)(a) must satisfy proportionality: (1) legitimate goal, (2) suitability/rational nexus, (3) necessity (least restrictive alternative), (4) balancing (structural proportionality); the burden of justification lies on the State, and the order must be open to judicial review.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Professor: "Reasonable has become proportionate." Follow-up: Foundation for Media Professionals v. UT of J&K (2020) on 4G speed restrictions.
Use in the exam

Learn the four prongs as a mnemonic L-R-N-B (Legitimate aim, Rational nexus, Necessity, Balance), with judicial review as the procedural safeguard.

The four-fold proportionality test (as explained by the professor)

#ProngProfessor's explanationIllustration
1Legitimate aimThe action must pursue a legitimate purpose: legal and fair, serving public interest (not the interest of a politician or party). Not the family-law meaning of "legitimate" (legitimate child). Meaning is borrowed from ICCPR and European standards: national security, public safety, public order, public health, public morals, and protection of the rights and reputations of others.Maintaining peace and tranquillity in a hostel after violence is legitimate.
2Rational nexusThe restriction must be rationally connected to the aim. "Does shutting the internet bear a relationship to the flow of information that endangers national security?" There must be a direct nexus.If rumours spread through mobile networks and cause riots, curbing that medium has a nexus; blocking unrelated content does not.
3NecessityThe restriction must be necessary, and no less restrictive alternative must be available ("that alone, and nothing else, will do").If blocking a few URLs would stop the harm, a total shutdown is not necessary.
4Balance (structural proportionality / strict sense)The extent of the restriction must be balanced against the importance of the right and the benefit gained; the restriction must not be excessive. The professor said you may write it as "proportionality strict" or "balance" ("restricted").A month-long blackout to stop one day's rumour is disproportionate.
+Judicial review / procedural safeguardsThere must be a judicial review of the decision, and procedural safeguards (reasons, publication, periodic review).Review committee, written reasons.
  • Who must justify? The professor stressed: "the justification has to be given by the person who took the decision; the court cannot justify the decision for him." Example: a Vice-Chancellor who removes students from a hostel to restore peace should record that, "according to the present situation, this is the minimum action required to bring back tranquillity and peace"; if he has recorded this, the decision is valid; outsiders cannot say that "less would have done".
  • Who assesses necessity? It is the decision-maker's assessment, within the limits of reasonableness; the decision is subjective to an extent (some officials act early, some late), but the decision belongs to the authority and the court reviews whether the limits of proportionality were crossed (deference with review).
  • Proportionality in other contexts: Modern Dental College v. State of M.P. (2016) and K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017, 2018) adopted the same four-stage test for fundamental rights generally.

sections.title: 3.5 "Legitimate": what does it mean? (the in-class research)
sections.html:
The professor asked students to Google how "legitimate" has been defined by the ICCPR and the European Union. A student first offered "justification and rightfulness of exercising public authority"; a second student read out the ICCPR list.

SourceWhat it saysRemarks
ICCPR (International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 1966)Art 19(3): restrictions must be provided by law and necessary (a) for respect of the rights or reputations of others; (b) for the protection of national security, public order (ordre public), public health or morals. Arts 21 and 22 add public safety for assembly and association.The student's list: "national security, public safety, public order, public health, public morals, protection of rights and reputations" (combined from Arts 19, 21, 22).
European law (Art 10(2) ECHR; EU Charter Art 52(1))Restrictions must be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim (national security, territorial integrity, public safety, prevention of disorder or crime, protection of health or morals, protection of reputation or rights of others, preventing disclosure of confidential information, maintaining authority and impartiality of the judiciary) and be necessary in a democratic society.Source of the proportionality approach.
Professor's definition"Legitimate includes both legal and fair: legal, and for the work of society / public interest."Use this one-line definition in answers.
  • Legitimacy of children (professor's digression): under Indian family law, "all children are legitimate" in the sense of s. 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (children of void/voidable marriages are legitimate) and s. 112 of the Evidence Act (presumption of legitimacy; now s. 116 BSA 2023); a student answered "s. 16". That is a different concept and must not be used in constitutional proportionality.

sections.title: 3.6 A real-world application: the "appointment to constitutional bodies" discussion (legal points only)
sections.html:
A long part of the lecture used the Election Commission of India appointment controversy to illustrate the limits of protest and the value of reasoned objection. The legal points useful for the exam:

  • Art 324(2): the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and other Election Commissioners are appointed by the President, "subject to the provisions of any law made in that behalf by Parliament". For decades Parliament made no law, so the executive (PM) in practice chose the CEC; the professor said this was true under all governments.
  • Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023) (Constitution Bench): until Parliament makes a law, appointments are to be made by the President on the advice of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition (or leader of the largest opposition party) and the Chief Justice of India. Parliament then enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, which replaced the CJI in the committee with a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. The professor said "the Act can be challenged and the challenge should be decided quickly"; the executive is the appointing authority in most countries, and the real debate is whether an independent authority should appoint, a topic of general reform (collegium, governors).
  • Multi-member Commission: the professor said CEC and other ECs have equal powers; routine administrative decisions need no consultation; policy decisions are taken by majority of the three. (T.N. Seshan v. Union of India, 1995: the Commission is a multi-member body; the CEC is the chairman, and s. 10 of the 1991 Act says business shall be transacted unanimously as far as possible, otherwise by majority.) The professor said that two additional ECs were appointed once to dilute a strong CEC (T.N. Seshan); a student answered "1989". Check this: two ECs were appointed in October 1989 (and withdrawn in 1990); the two ECs aimed at Seshan were appointed in October 1993. For exams the safe point is simply that a multi-member Commission upheld in Seshan (1995).
  • Accountability: an official/commissioner is answerable through Parliament (questions to the Law Ministry), the Supreme Court (judicial review; the Court can call for records), RTI and the press; but only lawful, reasoned objection is acceptable. The professor said: "You cannot use illegal means to do legal work; rousing students to stop the country is not a remedy; if the commission has acted wrongly, impeachment/removal under Art 324(5) and judicial review exist."
  • Speech urging mob violence: statements such as "people will chase a named leader on the street" are discussed under the incitement to an offence / public order grounds and the imminent danger idea: mere words that nobody acts upon are not necessarily an offence; there must be proximate danger. (See Lecture 2, Rangarajan.)
Case

Centre for PIL v. Union of India (the P.J. Thomas case) (2011)

Citation / Court / Year

(2011) 4 SCC 1; decided 3 March 2011 (Supreme Court of India; 3-judge bench: S.H. Kapadia C.J., K.S. Radhakrishnan and Swatanter Kumar JJ.).

Facts
  • P.J. Thomas (Kerala-cadre IAS officer) was recommended by a High-Powered Committee (Prime Minister, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition) as Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC) in 2010. The Leader of the Opposition (Sushma Swaraj) dissented, noting that he was an accused in the Palmolein import corruption case in Kerala. The majority of the committee went ahead.
  • The professor said "in one line of objection, the whole appointment collapsed" and corrected a student: it is P.J. Thomas, not N.M. Thomas (State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas, 1976 is the reservation case).
Issues
  • Is an appointment valid when the appointing committee does not properly consider material bearing on the integrity of the candidate and overrides the dissent?
Held (Decision)
  • The Court quashed the appointment. The appointing committee must consider the institutional integrity of the office (CVC) and whether the candidate's appointment will undermine the institution; personal integrity alone is not the test.
  • The Leader of the Opposition's dissent, backed by relevant material, had to be properly considered; the committee's decision was vitiated by non-consideration of relevant facts (the pending Palmolein prosecution).
Ratio decidendi

Statutory appointments must be made on relevant considerations and with regard to the independence and integrity of the institution; courts can review the process.

Use in the exam

The professor used this to show that a single well-reasoned objection from the Leader of Opposition can invalidate an appointment, while a mere "I object" is not enough; the objector must show a valid defect.

Union of India (2023) (Constitution Bench): until Parliament makes a law, appointments are to be made by the President on the advice of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition (or leader of the largest opposition party) and the Chief Justice of India. Parliament then enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 , which replaced the CJI in the committee with a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the PM. The professor said "the Act can be challenged and the challenge should be decided quickly"; the executive is the appointing authority in most countries, and the real debate is whether an independent authority should appoint , a topic of general reform (collegium, governors). Multi-member Commission: the professor said CEC and other ECs have equal powers; routine administrative decisions need no consultation; policy decisions are taken by majority of the three . ( T.N. Seshan v. Union of India, 1995 : the Commission is a multi-member body; the CEC is the chairman, and s. 10 of the 1991 Act says business shall be transacted unanimously as far as possible, otherwise by majority.) The professor said that two additional ECs were appointed once to dilute a strong CEC (T.N. Seshan); a student answered "1989". Check this: two ECs were appointed in October 1989 (and withdrawn in 1990); the two ECs aimed at Seshan were appointed in October 1993 . For exams the safe point is simply that a multi-member Commission upheld in Seshan (1995) . Accountability: an official/commissioner is answerable through Parliament (questions to the Law Ministry), the Supreme Court (judicial review; the Court can call for records), RTI and the press ; but only lawful, reasoned objection is acceptable. The professor said: " You cannot use illegal means to do legal work ; rousing students to stop the country is not a remedy; if the commission has acted wrongly, impeachment/removal under Art 324(5) and judicial review exist." Speech urging mob violence: statements such as "people will chase a named leader on the street" are discussed under the incitement to an offence / public order grounds and the imminent danger idea: mere words that nobody acts upon are not necessarily an offence; there must be proximate danger . (See Lecture 2, Rangarajan .) Case Centre for PIL v. Union of India (the P.J. Thomas case) (2011) Citation / Court / Year (2011) 4 SCC 1; decided 3 March 2011 (Supreme Court of India; 3-judge bench: S.H. Kapadia C.J., K.S. Radhakrishnan and Swatanter Kumar JJ.). Facts P.J. Thomas (Kerala-cadre IAS officer) was recommended by a High-Powered Committee (Prime Minister, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition) as Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC) in 2010. The Leader of the Opposition (Sushma Swaraj) dissented , noting that he was an accused in the Palmolein import corruption case in Kerala. The majority of the committee went ahead. The professor said "in one line of objection, the whole appointment collapsed" and corrected a student: it is P.J. Thomas , not N.M. Thomas ( State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas , 1976 is the reservation case). Issues Is an appointment valid when the appointing committee does not properly consider material bearing on the integrity of the candidate and overrides the dissent? Held (Decision) The Court quashed the appointment . The appointing committee must consider the institutional integrity of the office (CVC) and whether the candidate's appointment will undermine the institution; personal integrity alone is not the test. The Leader of the Opposition's dissent, backed by relevant material, had to be properly considered ; the committee's decision was vitiated by non-consideration of relevant facts (the pending Palmolein prosecution). Ratio decidendi Statutory appointments must be made on relevant considerations and with regard to the independence and integrity of the institution ; courts can review the process. Use in the exam The professor used this to show that a single well-reasoned objection from the Leader of Opposition can invalidate an appointment , while a mere "I object" is not enough; the objector must show a valid defect .

sections.title: 3.7 Evidence obtained illegally (professor's digression)
sections.html:
The professor asked a student: "Evidence obtained by illegal means is not admissible in a court of law: in which case was this said?" The student answered an American case "… v. United States" (the exclusionary rule). The professor added: "that is an American case, not India."

United StatesIndia
RuleExclusionary rule: evidence obtained in violation of the Constitution (4th Amendment: unreasonable search and seizure) is inadmissible.Evidence is admissible if relevant, even if obtained by an illegal search, unless a statute or the Constitution bars it.
CasesWeeks v. United States (1914) (federal); Mapp v. Ohio (1961) (states); Wong Sun v. United States (1963) ("fruit of the poisonous tree").Pooran Mal v. Director of Inspection (1974); R.M. Malkani v. State of Maharashtra (1973); Yusufalli Esmail Nagree (1968).
ExceptionsGood-faith exception etc.Confessions: ss. 24-27 Evidence Act (now BSA 2023 ss. 22-23); Art 20(3) (compelled testimony): Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010).

Correction for the exam

Do not write that illegally obtained evidence is generally inadmissible in India. The professor correctly said the case he meant is American; the Indian position is the opposite (relevance test) (Pooran Mal, 1974), subject to constitutional and statutory exclusions (confessions, Art 20(3), and now privacy-based arguments after Puttaswamy).

sections.title: 3.8 Rules of the game cannot be changed midway (campus-election illustration)
sections.html:
The professor described a student election where the rule barred candidates with a pending disciplinary complaint; he refused to change the rule mid-election even though it looked unfair: "rules should not be changed in the middle of the game; change them for the next election." The legal analogue:

  • K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2008) 3 SCC 512: the criteria for selection cannot be altered after the process has begun; Tej Prakash Pathak v. Rajasthan High Court (2024) (Constitution Bench) confirmed that rules of the game cannot be changed midway unless the rules permit.
  • Link to Art 14: arbitrariness; legitimate expectation.

sections.title: 3.9 Questions asked by the professor in COLA 6, with model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. A person wanted to speak at Jantar Mantar for/against the CEC, Delhi Police refused, and he sues for violation of freedom of speech. As the court, what will you check first?

Model answer

Whether he is a citizen of India. Art 19(1) is confined to citizens (hence Arts 15, 16, 19 are citizen-only; Art 14 and 21 are for all persons). If he is a foreigner the Art 19(1)(a) claim fails; he can only invoke Arts 14, 21.

If he is a citizen, test the restriction: (i) by law; (ii) on an Art 19(2) ground; (iii) reasonable/proportionate.

Question asked in class

Q2. How many grounds are there in Art 19(2)? Recite them.

Model answer

Eight: sovereignty and integrity of India; security of the State; friendly relations with foreign States; public order; decency or morality; contempt of court; defamation; incitement to an offence. (See Lecture 2 for the amendments.)

Question asked in class

Q3. Can the State restrict speech for "better administration"?

Model answer

No. Restrictions are permitted only on the eight grounds in Art 19(2). "Better administration", "national interest", "economic development" are not grounds.

Question asked in class

Q4. What does "law" mean in Art 19(2)? Is it the same as in Art 13(3)?

Model answer

It means law duly enacted by Parliament or a State Legislature (and valid subordinate legislation derived from such an Act). It is not to be understood as widely as the Art 13(3)(a) definition (ordinances, orders, bye-laws, custom etc.). Executive instructions without a statutory basis are not "law".

Question asked in class

Q5. What is "reasonable" today? State the test.

Model answer

Reasonable has become proportionate. Under Anuradha Bhasin the four-fold test: legitimate aim; rational nexus; necessity; balancing (structural proportionality), with judicial review of the order.

Question asked in class

Q6. What does "legitimate" mean in the proportionality test? Is it the same as a legitimate child?

Model answer

No. It means legal and fair, in the public interest and pursuing recognised aims such as national security, public safety, public order, public health, public morals and protection of the rights and reputation of others (ICCPR Art 19(3), European standards). The family-law "legitimacy" of children (s. 16 HMA) is irrelevant.

Question asked in class

Q7. What is a "rational nexus"? Apply it to an internet shutdown.

Model answer

The restriction must have a direct connection with the legitimate aim. An internet shutdown can be rationally linked to stopping the spread of incitement or misinformation that may disturb public order or security, but only if the content spreads through that medium, and the restriction is temporary and targeted; a blanket, indefinite shutdown fails necessity and balance (Anuradha Bhasin).

Question asked in class

Q8. Who must justify a restriction, and can the court say a lesser action would have sufficed?

Model answer

The authority that took the decision must justify it, with recorded reasons ("this is the minimum necessary action in the present situation"). The court reviews proportionality but does not substitute its own policy view for that of the decision-maker, unless the restriction is clearly excessive or less restrictive means were obviously available.

Question asked in class

Q9. Which case says that evidence obtained by illegal means is inadmissible?

Model answer

In the United States, Weeks v. United States (1914) and Mapp v. Ohio (1961) (exclusionary rule). In India the rule is different: relevant evidence is admissible even if illegally obtained (Pooran Mal, 1974).

Question asked in class

Q10. Which case dealt with the appointment of the CVC which the Supreme Court quashed? What was the reasoning?

Model answer

Centre for PIL v. Union of India (2011) (P.J. Thomas). The committee ignored relevant material about the candidate's pending corruption case and the Leader of Opposition's dissent; the Court quashed the appointment, emphasising institutional integrity.

Question asked in class

Q11. Does the mere fact that a newspaper or a leader alleges wrongdoing prove it?

Model answer

No. A press report or allegation is not proof; it triggers a demand for inquiry by a competent authority (court, statutory body, RTI, Parliament), not a verdict by the accuser. This is why speech about public officials is protected but defamation and incitement remain grounds for restriction.

exam.title: Press Freedom and Indirect Suppression, Commercial Speech, and the Law of Obscenity (Hicklin → Miller → Aveek Sarkar → Tuljapurkar)

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Press freedom is part of Art 19(1)(a) (no separate clause). Indirect attacks (price-page schedules, newsprint quotas, taxes, denial of premises or power) are tested by their direct and inevitable effect, not their label: Sakal Papers (1962), Bennett Coleman (1972), Indian Express (1985).

Commercial speech: earlier not protected (Hamdard Dawakhana, 1960: magic-remedy advertisements); now protected if truthful and not misleading (Tata Press v. MTNL, 1995).

Obscenity (ground "decency or morality"): Hicklin (isolated passage, vulnerable reader) → community standards (average person, work as a whole, patently offensive, lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value) → Aveek Sarkar (2014) → Devidas Tuljapurkar (2015) adds a stricter, context-sensitive standard for historically respected figures (Mahatma Gandhi).

The professor has declared that he will set a fact-based question on Devidas Ramchandra Tuljapurkar v. State of Maharashtra. Read the original. A model answer structure is in 4.8.

sections.title: 4.1 Free speech has never been "free": the pattern of suppression
sections.html:
• Professor's thesis: "The life of free speech was never free; it was always burdened with restrictions." Those in power dislike criticism because adverse writing may cost them their position; so the State tries to suppress, first directly (Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan), and when the courts block that, indirectly by other economic and administrative means.
  • First Amendment (1951) came "even before the first Lok Sabha elections" and enlarged the grounds of restriction (public order, friendly relations with foreign States, incitement to an offence; "reasonable"), and the 16th Amendment (1963) added "sovereignty and". See Lecture 2.
  • Therefore the cases below are the Supreme Court's response to indirect suppression of the press.

sections.title: 4.2 Press freedom cases: the four classic decisions
sections.html:
The professor described them with Emergency-era colour (1975-77): the executive tried to control newspapers by (a) wages, (b) price-page schedules, (c) newsprint quotas, and (d) practical pressure (electricity and premises). Courts "came to the rescue" even though judges were then appointed by the Government.

Case

Express Newspapers (Private) Ltd. v. Union of India (the Working Journalists case) (1958)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1958 SC 578; 1959 SCR 12 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court).

Facts
  • The Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 and the wage board fixed minimum wages and conditions for journalists; newspaper owners said this burdened the press and violated Art 19(1)(a) and (g).
  • The professor's version: "the Government tried to raise journalists' pay; the press objected that it violates my right: if I pay 10 and you ask me to pay 20..."; the objection was rejected.
Issues
  • Does a general economic regulation (wages) that increases the cost of running a newspaper violate freedom of the press?
Held (Decision)
  • No. The Act regulates employment conditions; any effect on the press is remote and indirect and the press has no immunity from laws of general application. A law is bad if it directly curtails the freedom of speech, or if its real object is to restrict circulation or expression.
Ratio decidendi

The press is not exempt from general laws (wages, labour, tax). Only measures that single out the press or directly affect circulation and expression are invalid.

Use in the exam

Contrast with Sakal Papers: wages (valid, indirect) v. price-page (invalid, direct).

Case

Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India (1962)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1962 SC 305; (1962) 3 SCR 842 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India).

Facts
  • The Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspaper (Price and Page) Order, 1960 fixed the maximum number of pages a newspaper could publish for a given price (a price-page schedule), aimed at preventing unfair competition and making newspapers affordable.
Issues
  • Can the State regulate the price and number of pages to protect smaller papers? Does this violate Art 19(1)(a)? Can Art 19(1)(g) arguments save it?
Held (Decision)
  • The Order violated Art 19(1)(a): restricting the number of pages forces a newspaper to cut circulation or content, which directly affects freedom of speech and expression.
  • Art 19(2) is exhaustive: freedom of expression cannot be restricted on economic grounds (e.g. to protect small newspapers from competition). The State may not abridge the right "in the interest of the general public" unless the interest is in Art 19(2).
Ratio decidendi

A law that directly curtails circulation (and thereby speech) is invalid unless within Art 19(2); economic objectives are not grounds; the effect, not the form or intention, decides.

Case

Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (the Newsprint Policy case) (1972)

Citation / Court / Year

(1972) 2 SCC 788; AIR 1973 SC 106 (Supreme Court of India).

Facts
  • The Newsprint Policy 1972-73 (under the Newsprint Control Order, 1962 and Import Control orders) (i) capped the number of pages at 10; (ii) forbade increasing pages without reducing circulation; (iii) barred the starting of new newspapers/editions by established chains.
  • The Government justified it by the shortage of imported newsprint and foreign exchange. The professor said the Prime Minister (Indira Gandhi) disliked newspapers criticising her and used the policy as "colourable legislation": "We cannot give you the material, so you cannot print more pages."
Issues
  • Is the newsprint quota a valid regulation of an imported commodity or an invalid restriction on freedom of the press? What is the test: "pith and substance" (object) or "direct effect" (consequence)?
Held (Decision)
  • The policy was unconstitutional: it directly affected circulation and the volume of news and views, and thus violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 14 (discrimination between newspapers on page and circulation).
  • The test is the direct and inevitable effect of the impugned action on the right, not its object or the Government's motive ("pith and substance" was rejected for Art 19 cases). Shortage of foreign exchange is not a ground under Art 19(2).
  • Shareholders (citizens) of a company can claim Art 19 where the company's rights are affected, so the "company is not a citizen" objection did not defeat the petition.
Ratio decidendi

Restrictions on the material needed for publication (newsprint) are restrictions on speech if the effect is to curtail circulation or content; the Court looks at direct and inevitable consequence.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Followed in Indian Express (1985); affirms that the press is protected from indirect government pressure.
Use in the exam

Professor: "The Government said it cannot import more newsprint, so you must reduce pages; the Court rejected this as a disguised way to stop the press."

Case

Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1984/85)

Citation / Court / Year

(1985) 1 SCC 641; AIR 1986 SC 515 (Supreme Court of India; E.S. Venkataramiah, O. Chinnappa Reddy and A.P. Sen JJ.).

Facts
  • Customs duty and auxiliary duty were imposed on imported newsprint, which had been untaxed before; publishers claimed it raised prices, cut circulation and violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 14 (size-based classification of newspapers).
Issues
  • Can the State tax the press? Is a tax on newsprint a "restriction" on freedom of the press?
Held (Decision)
  • The press is not immune from taxation, but a tax on the press must be reasonable and not designed or likely to curtail circulation; the courts will scrutinise such taxes and the burden to justify lies on the State.
  • On the facts, the petitioners could not prove that circulation fell because of the duty, so the Court did not strike the duty down; it directed the Government to reconsider the tax policy. The size-based classification (to help small and medium papers) had a rational nexus, so Art 14 was not violated.
  • The Court affirmed that freedom of the press is "the heart of social and political intercourse" and that the press cannot be subjected to arbitrary or excessive taxation (no tax on knowledge).
Ratio decidendi

Fiscal measures affecting newsprint are valid if reasonable and not a device to restrict circulation; they are subject to judicial review.

Use in the exam

The professor mixed this with the Emergency stories of the Indian Express group (power cut to the printing press and cancellation of the lease of its Delhi building, which led to litigation in Delhi and Bombay where the courts gave relief). Safe to cite the case for "taxation of the press must be reasonable".

Indian Express (1985)Customs duty on newsprintNot struck; Government told to reconsiderPress can be taxed but reasonably; burden on State
  • The Emergency (1975-77): the professor narrated that the then Minister for Information and Broadcasting (I.K. Gujral) refused the Prime Minister's son's direction that news bulletins be cleared by him, and was replaced. Note: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla (1976) (habeas corpus case during the Emergency) is a separate decision, now regarded as wrongly decided and expressly overruled in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).
  • New mechanisms of indirect control (professor's point): after the courts secured the press against direct restraints, control can be exercised by other means: ownership and takeover of media houses, commercial pressure, advertising and "paid" party newspapers. The professor offered an example of ownership change of a TV network and of a free newspaper that turned out to be a party broadsheet (paid news / advertorial). Legally, the concern is addressed by (i) Press Council of India Act, 1978, (ii) cross-media ownership debates and (iii) the doctrine that the press must be free from indirect economic coercion (Sakal, Bennett Coleman). The professor's commentary on specific political parties and media owners is personal and is not examinable.
sections.text: The professor described them with Emergency-era colour (1975-77): the executive tried to control newspapers by (a) wages, (b) price-page schedules, (c) newsprint quotas, and (d) practical pressure (electricity and premises). Courts "came to the rescue" even though judges were then appointed by the Government. Case Express Newspapers (Private) Ltd. v. Union of India (the Working Journalists case) (1958) Citation / Court / Year AIR 1958 SC 578; 1959 SCR 12 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court). Facts The Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 and the wage board fixed minimum wages and conditions for journalists; newspaper owners said this burdened the press and violated Art 19(1)(a) and (g). The professor's version: "the Government tried to raise journalists' pay; the press objected that it violates my right: if I pay 10 and you ask me to pay 20..."; the objection was rejected. Issues Does a general economic regulation (wages) that increases the cost of running a newspaper violate freedom of the press? Held (Decision) No. The Act regulates employment conditions ; any effect on the press is remote and indirect and the press has no immunity from laws of general application . A law is bad if it directly curtails the freedom of speech, or if its real object is to restrict circulation or expression. Ratio decidendi The press is not exempt from general laws (wages, labour, tax). Only measures that single out the press or directly affect circulation and expression are invalid. Use in the exam Contrast with Sakal Papers : wages (valid, indirect) v. price-page (invalid, direct). Case Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India (1962) Citation / Court / Year AIR 1962 SC 305; (1962) 3 SCR 842 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India). Facts The Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspaper (Price and Page) Order, 1960 fixed the maximum number of pages a newspaper could publish for a given price (a price-page schedule), aimed at preventing unfair competition and making newspapers affordable. Issues Can the State regulate the price and number of pages to protect smaller papers? Does this violate Art 19(1)(a)? Can Art 19(1)(g) arguments save it? Held (Decision) The Order violated Art 19(1)(a) : restricting the number of pages forces a newspaper to cut circulation or content , which directly affects freedom of speech and expression. Art 19(2) is exhaustive : freedom of expression cannot be restricted on economic grounds (e.g. to protect small newspapers from competition). The State may not abridge the right "in the interest of the general public" unless the interest is in Art 19(2). Ratio decidendi A law that directly curtails circulation (and thereby speech) is invalid unless within Art 19(2); economic objectives are not grounds ; the effect , not the form or intention, decides. Case Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (the Newsprint Policy case) (1972) Citation / Court / Year (1972) 2 SCC 788; AIR 1973 SC 106 (Supreme Court of India). Facts The Newsprint Policy 1972-73 (under the Newsprint Control Order, 1962 and Import Control orders) (i) capped the number of pages at 10 ; (ii) forbade increasing pages without reducing circulation; (iii) barred the starting of new newspapers/editions by established chains . The Government justified it by the shortage of imported newsprint and foreign exchange . The professor said the Prime Minister (Indira Gandhi) disliked newspapers criticising her and used the policy as "colourable legislation": "We cannot give you the material, so you cannot print more pages." Issues Is the newsprint quota a valid regulation of an imported commodity or an invalid restriction on freedom of the press? What is the test: "pith and substance" (object) or "direct effect" (consequence)? Held (Decision) The policy was unconstitutional : it directly affected circulation and the volume of news and views , and thus violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 14 (discrimination between newspapers on page and circulation). The test is the direct and inevitable effect of the impugned action on the right, not its object or the Government's motive ("pith and substance" was rejected for Art 19 cases). Shortage of foreign exchange is not a ground under Art 19(2). Shareholders (citizens) of a company can claim Art 19 where the company's rights are affected, so the "company is not a citizen" objection did not defeat the petition. Ratio decidendi Restrictions on the material needed for publication (newsprint) are restrictions on speech if the effect is to curtail circulation or content ; the Court looks at direct and inevitable consequence . Significance / Later treatment Followed in Indian Express (1985) ; affirms that the press is protected from indirect government pressure. Use in the exam Professor: "The Government said it cannot import more newsprint, so you must reduce pages; the Court rejected this as a disguised way to stop the press." Case Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1984/85) Citation / Court / Year (1985) 1 SCC 641; AIR 1986 SC 515 (Supreme Court of India; E.S. Venkataramiah, O. Chinnappa Reddy and A.P. Sen JJ.). Facts Customs duty and auxiliary duty were imposed on imported newsprint , which had been untaxed before; publishers claimed it raised prices, cut circulation and violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 14 (size-based classification of newspapers). Issues Can the State tax the press? Is a tax on newsprint a "restriction" on freedom of the press? Held (Decision) The press is not immune from taxation , but a tax on the press must be reasonable and not designed or likely to curtail circulation ; the courts will scrutinise such taxes and the burden to justify lies on the State. On the facts, the petitioners could not prove that circulation fell because of the duty, so the Court did not strike the duty down ; it directed the Government to reconsider the tax policy. The size-based classification (to help small and medium papers) had a rational nexus , so Art 14 was not violated. The Court affirmed that freedom of the press is "the heart of social and political intercourse" and that the press cannot be subjected to arbitrary or excessive taxation (no tax on knowledge). Ratio decidendi Fiscal measures affecting newsprint are valid if reasonable and not a device to restrict circulation ; they are subject to judicial review . Use in the exam The professor mixed this with the Emergency stories of the Indian Express group (power cut to the printing press and cancellation of the lease of its Delhi building, which led to litigation in Delhi and Bombay where the courts gave relief). Safe to cite the case for "taxation of the press must be reasonable" . sections.title: 4.3 Misinformation: "we have enough freedom; we need protection from falsehood"
sections.html:
The professor's conclusion was: because of the Supreme Court's work and the efforts of political leaders, there is now enough freedom of speech in India; the real problem is misinformation (fake news, deepfake advertisements using celebrities and doctors, cyber-fraud such as fake ticket sites). He said society needs protection from misinformation and cited his own experience of being targeted by a fake ticketing scam, and of being misquoted in an international news story about alleged caste discrimination at his university. He asked students to verify before sharing. The legal tools he indicated:

  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019: misleading advertisement (s. 2(28)), deficiency in service, penalties and bans by the Central Consumer Protection Authority (the professor said: "you studied it in Consumer Protection last year: compensation for misleading ads").
  • Information Technology Act, 2000: s. 66D (cheating by personation using computer resource), s. 67 (obscene electronic material), Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021; s. 66A was struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015) as vague and overbroad. A 2023 amendment creating a government "fact check unit" for misinformation about the Government was struck down by the Bombay High Court in Kunal Kamra v. Union of India (2024) (verify current status).
  • IPC/BNS: cheating, defamation, incitement; BNS s. 353 (statements conducing to public mischief) replaces IPC s. 505.
  • Professor's personal view (not exam material): he suggested the Constitution should be amended to punish lying; the contrary view (for exam balance) is that truth cannot be fixed by the State and false speech has value within a free marketplace (Mill; Shreya Singhal).

sections.title: 4.4 Commercial speech (advertisements)
sections.html:
The professor said commercial speech is a major area ("learn it carefully; this section should also listen"). Early view: commercial speech is not protected, because the purpose of free speech is intellectual and political discourse, not business; this was the early position also in America. Then he developed the modern view.

Case

Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) Lal Kuan v. Union of India (1960)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1960 SC 554; (1960) 2 SCR 671 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India).

Facts
  • The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 prohibited advertisements that claimed cures for certain diseases (sexual disorders, venereal disease, leucoderma, cancer, etc.) by drugs or magic remedies. Hamdard Dawakhana (a traditional medicine firm) challenged it as a violation of free speech.
  • The professor described the background: "in our time Bengali dawakhanas and quacks promised cures for secret diseases; Nirmal Baba-type promises (eat jalebi on Sunday, wear a black shirt) mislead people; the Act was passed in 1954."
Issues
  • Is an advertisement "speech" under Art 19(1)(a), and can Parliament prohibit advertisements that promote harmful or false medical claims?
Held (Decision)
  • An advertisement is no doubt a form of speech, but its true character is determined by the product or business it promotes. When it propagates a trade or business (selling drugs), it is not "freedom of speech" within Art 19(1)(a); and the Act protects public health, so it was valid (also within 19(6) for the business aspect).
  • The professor read the Court's reasoning as: "the purpose of free speech is not to earn money; therefore commercial advertisement is not protected."
Ratio decidendi

A purely commercial advertisement promoting a trade is not protected speech, and harmful/misleading medical advertisements can be banned.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Departed from by Tata Press (1995), which holds that commercial speech is protected, but it still upholds bans on misleading or false advertisements; Hamdard's outcome (ban on magic-remedy advertisements) still stands.
Case

Tata Press Ltd. v. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. (MTNL) (1995)

Citation / Court / Year

(1995) 5 SCC 139 (Supreme Court of India).

Facts
  • Tata Press published "Tata Yellow Pages", a directory of classified business advertisements and telephone numbers. MTNL claimed an exclusive right under the Telegraph Act to publish telephone directories and asked it to stop. The professor's illustration: "a new book of constitutional law by Professor V.P. Tiwari has come out, but nobody knows; if it is advertised, people will buy it; the advertisement benefits the publisher and the reader."
Issues
  • Is commercial speech protected by Art 19(1)(a)? Can MTNL prevent publication of advertising directories?
Held (Decision)
  • Commercial speech/advertisements are protected under Art 19(1)(a): the public has a right to receive commercial information (price, availability, quality); an advertisement is not only for the advertiser; it benefits the consumer.
  • But the speech must not be misleading, deceptive or unfair, and false or misleading advertisements are not protected; they may be restricted under Art 19(2) (e.g. decency, morality, public order) and consumer protection laws.
  • MTNL's exclusive right extended to the telephone directory (subscribers' list), not to classified advertisements like the Yellow Pages.
Ratio decidendi

Commercial speech is part of freedom of speech and expression, subject to restrictions in Art 19(2) and to the requirement that advertisements be truthful and not misleading.

Use in the exam

Professor: "Commercial speech is also protected under Art 19(1)(a): provided the speech is not misleading." Also remember Hamdard (earlier, not protected) and the Consumer Protection link (misleading ads, deficiency of service).

sections.title: 4.5 Obscenity (decency or morality): the question of art, temples and standards
sections.html:
• Why obscenity is a restriction: Art 19(2) permits restrictions "in the interests of decency or morality". The criminal law: s. 292 IPC (now BNS s. 294) (sale, distribution, public exhibition of obscene material), s. 293 (sale to young persons; now BNS s. 295), the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986, and the IT Act, 2000 ss. 67, 67A, 67B.
  • Art and monuments are protected by statute: s. 292(2) IPC exempts works in the interest of science, literature, art or learning, and ancient monuments or temples (the professor mentioned Ajanta, Ellora, Konark (Sun Temple) and Khajuraho: "they have always existed, but they should not fall into the hands of adolescents who may be corrupted, and should not be located where such material is inappropriate").
  • Professor's point against Hicklin: if the test is the susceptibility of an impure mind, every literature falls: "even the Ramayana": a corrupt mind can read anything (Sita-Ram meeting in the garden, Mahabharata episodes) as erotic. "A mind that is already corrupt is not the standard."

Hicklin → Miller → Indian cases (timeline)

YearCase / SourceTest or holding
1868Regina v. Hicklin (England)Tendency to deprave and corrupt those open to immoral influences; judged by an isolated passage.
1964Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra (India)Applied Hicklin; bookseller convicted for Lady Chatterley's Lover; "contemporary mores" and art's social value must be weighed.
1973Miller v. California (US)Three-prong Miller/community standards test: (a) average person applying contemporary community standards, work as a whole appeals to prurient interest; (b) depicts patently offensive sexual conduct; (c) taken as a whole lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value (SLAPS).
1985Samaresh Bose v. Amal MitraBegan moving from Hicklin: judge from the viewpoint of a reasonable, strong-minded reader; distinguished obscenity from vulgarity.
1996Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (Bandit Queen)Context and message of the whole film; nudity/violence depicting a crime to show the victim's plight not obscene.
2010S. Khushboo v. KanniammalDiscussion of pre-marital sex is not obscenity.
2014Aveek Sarkar v. State of West BengalHicklin formally rejected; community standards test adopted for India.
2015Devidas Ramchandra Tuljapurkar v. State of MaharashtraCommunity standards + greater vigour where historically respected personalities are involved; test is contextual.
Case

Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (Bandit Queen) (1996)

Citation / Court / Year

(1996) 4 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India; Ahmadi C.J. and Bench).

Facts
  • The film Bandit Queen (directed by Shekhar Kapur) is based on the life of Phoolan Devi. The censors gave it an "A" certificate, with scenes of rape, frontal nudity and abusive language. The Delhi High Court (on a petition by Om Pal Singh Hoon) had set aside the censor's clearance and stopped its exhibition; the Supreme Court reversed that. (Phoolan Devi's own privacy challenge to the film was a separate matter: Phoolan Devi v. Shekhar Kapur.) The professor recalled: "Bandit Queen: a film challenged by Phoolan Devi against Shekhar Kapur".
Issues
  • Are the scenes obscene? How are nudity and violence judged in a serious film on social issues?
Held (Decision)
  • The Supreme Court upheld the film's release: the nude and rape scenes were not meant to arouse prurient interest but to show the brutality, humiliation and the social conditions that produced a bandit; the film must be viewed as a whole with its message. "Nudity does not necessarily arouse sexual feelings." The theme (a victim of social oppression) and the dignity of the scene matter.
Ratio decidendi

In judging obscenity, the whole work, theme, message and context are decisive; scenes of sexual violence meant to evoke revulsion and sympathy, not lust, are not obscene.

sections.title: 4.6 The Miller / community standards test explained (professor's explanation)
sections.html:
• Average person, not the hypersensitive: "not one who wants to become a pervert; the average person, generally what the people think". If most people regard the work as acceptable, it is acceptable.
  • Standards change with time and society: the professor's examples: formerly boys and girls sat separately and walking past a girls' group would draw comment; today 60-70% of students walk with an arm on a friend's shoulder and nobody notices; purdah among Muslim and Hindu women; a village where women did not speak to unknown men. So the community standard is relative to society and time.
  • "Work as a whole": not one passage. "You cannot ban the whole Ramcharitmanas for the garden scene where Sita and Ram look at each other; you cannot call the Mahabharata erotic because of one episode. You must see the whole story." One individual who is excited by romance cannot be the standard of the society.
  • Patently offensive way: the sexual conduct must be depicted in an obviously offensive manner as defined by law ("the word is used in such a way that you can see it is not acceptable").
  • Lacks serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value: if the work has such value it is not obscene. Example: medical and scientific images, e.g. pictures showing a young mother how to hold and breastfeed a baby (displayed at gynaecology wards), anatomy diagrams or cadavers used for medical teaching: "that is a medical requirement; you cannot treat it as an offence".
  • Exam rule given by the professor: if you write these three conditions (average person/contemporary community standards; patently offensive; lacks serious literary, artistic, political, scientific value), "I will be forced to give you 20 marks".

sections.title: 4.7 Compulsory cases: Aveek Sarkar and Tuljapurkar
sections.html:
Aveek Sarkar: see the case card in Lecture 2 (2.9): the Becker nude photograph; community standards; context (anti-racism). The professor said the line of development "started with Samaresh Bose, and then Aveek Sarkar" and told students to read it in the original ("it is compulsory reading").

Case

Devidas Ramchandra Tuljapurkar v. State of Maharashtra (2015)

Citation / Court / Year

(2015) 6 SCC 1; decided 14 May 2015 (Supreme Court of India; Dipak Misra and Prafulla C. Pant JJ.; judgment by Dipak Misra J.).

Facts
  • The Marathi poem "Gandhi Mala Bhetala" ("I met Gandhi") by Vasant Dattatraya Gurjar was published in 1994 in the Bulletin of the All India Bank Association Union (editor/publisher: Devidas Tuljapurkar). The poem used offensive, vulgar and obscene words about or attributed to Mahatma Gandhi, in a satire aimed at those who do not follow Gandhian values.
  • A complaint under s. 292 IPC (obscenity) and s. 34 followed. The Bombay High Court refused to quash. The poet did not appeal; the publisher/editor appealed to the Supreme Court.
  • Professor's summary: "Mahatma Gandhi was abused (the poem used his name to say obscene things)."
Issues
  • Is the poem obscene under s. 292 IPC? Which test applies? Does it matter that the words concern a historically respected figure? Is there a "poetic licence" defence?
Held (Decision)
  • The Court applied the contemporary community standards test (rejecting Hicklin, following Aveek Sarkar and Samaresh Bose). Where words are used about a historically respected person (Gandhi), the test is applied with greater vigour; the context and the purpose of the use of the person's name are examined. The Court rejected "poetic licence" as a defence.
  • The poem was found to cross the line (obscene), but because about twenty years had passed and the publisher had tendered an unconditional apology when readers objected, the Court discharged the appellant (the author was not before the Court).
Ratio decidendi

Freedom of speech does not allow obscene words about historically respected figures under cover of poetic licence; the community standards test applies more rigorously in such cases and the context is decisive.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Criticised as creating a "historically respected personalities" doctrine that may chill political satire and history writing (see the LiveLaw and The Wire commentaries). Criticism of a leader's policies or conduct is not the same as using obscene allusions to a revered figure.
Use in the exam

Declared by the professor as a compulsory exam question on facts.

sections.title: 4.8 Model answer structure for the declared fact-based question
sections.html:
The professor said: "If someone abuses Mr X (a living political leader), I will ask whether it is protected speech; if the student says "it is my fundamental right to abuse", I will give zero." Use IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion):

  • Issue: Is the abusive/obscene statement about (a living leader / a historical figure) protected by Art 19(1)(a), or can it be punished under s. 292 IPC (BNS s. 294), defamation (s. 499 IPC; BNS s. 356), or incitement?
  • Rule: (1) Art 19(1)(a) protects even offensive and unpopular speech; restrictions only under Art 19(2) by law, reasonable and proportionate. (2) Obscenity: contemporary community standards (average person; work as a whole; patently offensive; lacks serious value) (Aveek Sarkar). (3) Historically respected figures (Tuljapurkar): same test applied with greater vigour; context and purpose matter; no poetic-licence defence. (4) Defamation is separate; truth and public good are defences. (5) Incitement requires proximate danger (Rangarajan, Shreya Singhal).
  • Application: Ask: (i) Is the figure historically revered (Gandhi) or a current political functionary (criticism of whom is the heart of democracy)? (ii) Are the words sexually explicit/lascivious (obscenity) or merely abusive/insulting (not obscene, possibly defamatory; abuse alone is not obscenity)? (iii) Does the work as a whole have literary/political value? (iv) Is there imminent danger to public order?
  • Conclusion: (a) For merely abusive political criticism of a living leader: protected (or at most defamation, not obscenity). (b) For obscene allusions to a revered historical figure in a context lacking value: likely obscene per Tuljapurkar; but consider the poem's overall context, intention, time elapsed, apology. (c) No "fundamental right to abuse"; the protection of Art 19(1)(a) is for expression of ideas, subject to Art 19(2).

sections.title: 4.10 Questions asked by the professor in COLA 7, with model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. What was the new mechanism the Government adopted to suppress press freedom after the courts closed the direct route?

Model answer

After Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan, Sakal Papers and Bennett Coleman blocked direct restraints, the State used indirect pressures: newsprint, advertisements, taxation, power and premises, and (in the professor's analysis) the ownership of media houses. The law responds by testing direct and inevitable effect, not form.

Question asked in class

Q2. What were the earlier "grounds" such as libel and slander, and what were added in 1951 and 1963?

Model answer

Original Art 19(2): libel, slander, defamation, contempt of court, decency or morality, security of the State (undermining or tending to overthrow). 1951: public order, friendly relations with foreign States, incitement to an offence; "reasonable"; 1963: sovereignty and integrity.

Question asked in class

Q3. Is commercial advertisement protected speech? Which cases?

Model answer

Hamdard Dawakhana (1960): not protected when it merely promotes trade (magic remedies); Tata Press v. MTNL (1995): protected (public right to receive commercial information) provided it is not misleading; misleading ads are punishable (Consumer Protection Act, 2019).

Question asked in class

Q4. Why did Parliament pass the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954, and was it valid?

Model answer

To stop quackery and false claims of cure (sexual disorders, venereal disease, cancer etc.) that endanger public health. It was upheld in Hamdard Dawakhana (the advertisement of such remedies is not a protected exercise of Art 19(1)(a); it also falls within reasonable restrictions).

Question asked in class

Q5. Name the Hicklin case and explain the test.

Model answer

Regina v. Hicklin (1868): material is obscene if it tends to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences, judged by isolated passages. Rejected in India in Aveek Sarkar (2014); replaced by the community standards (Miller) test.

Question asked in class

Q6. State the three-part test that replaced Hicklin.

Model answer

(1) Would the average person applying contemporary community standards find that the work as a whole appeals to prurient interest? (2) Does the work depict sexual conduct in a patently offensive way (as defined by law)? (3) Does the work, taken as a whole, lack serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value? (Miller v. California, 1973; adopted in Aveek Sarkar).

Question asked in class

Q7. Why can nude depictions in medical textbooks or breastfeeding diagrams not be obscene?

Model answer

Because they have scientific/medical value and fail the third limb (the work as a whole is not lacking in serious scientific value); s. 292(2) IPC exempts material for science, art and learning; the context (instruction) negates prurient appeal.

Question asked in class

Q8. What additional factor did Tuljapurkar add, and was the poem held obscene?

Model answer

When a historically respected figure (Gandhi) is used as a vehicle for obscene allusions, the community standards test is applied with greater vigour and poetic licence is no defence; the poem was held obscene, but the editor/publisher was discharged because of the passage of time (20 years) and his unconditional apology.

Question asked in class

Q9. Name the case based on the film "Bandit Queen".

Model answer

Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996): the film was held not obscene, because the scenes had to be judged in the context of the film's message (social oppression, brutality).

Question asked in class

Q10. Give one example of how community standards differ between places and times.

Model answer

The professor's examples: segregated seating of boys and girls earlier vs students walking arm-in-arm now; purdah among women; a public kiss at an event in Jaipur (Gere-Shetty) judged by local standards. Standards are relative to society and time.

Question asked in class

Q11. Why did Parliament and the courts treat misleading advertisements differently from other speech?

Model answer

Because they cause economic harm and deceive consumers, they offer no contribution to the marketplace of ideas, and are covered by consumer protection law and Art 19(2) grounds; truthfulness is the condition for protection.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 4.1: Read the original Regina v. Hicklin ("read this case"; the professor said the meaning of the test is in the case itself)

Model answer

Key sentence (Cockburn C.J., 1868): "the test of obscenity is this, whether the tendency of the matter charged as obscenity is to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences, and into whose hands a publication of this sort may fall." Learn it as the "Hicklin test".

Model answer

See 4.7 and 4.8. Write a one-page answer and the IRAC structure.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 4.3: Read Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (Bandit Queen) (the professor asked "name of the case?"; students answered "Bobby Art, Om Pal Singh")

Model answer

See 4.5.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 4.4: Read Khushboo v. Kanniammal again ("this is also important; I will ask if I remember; I never cheat")

Model answer

See Lecture 2, 2.9.

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 4.5: Recall American cases on obscenity and the Miller test (professor: "and American cases")

Model answer

See the timeline table in 4.5: Hicklin (England), Miller v. California (US, 1973). Also read Roth v. United States (1957) (community standards, prurient interest) and Memoirs v. Massachusetts (1966).

Homework / instruction

Model answer

Practical rule: check source, date and a second reliable source; do not share unverified claims (risk of defamation, IT Act and BNS liability).

Homework / instruction

HOMEWORK 4.7: Google: which newspaper was closed down and its assets disputed (the professor asked "which newspaper?"; answer: National Herald, published by Associated Journals Ltd., founded by Jawaharlal Nehru in 1938)

Model answer

The professor's remarks on the pending case are political and are not exam material; the press-freedom lesson is that ownership, financial control and legal pressure are indirect channels of influence.

exam.title: Hate Speech, the Discussion-Advocacy-Incitement Test, and the Right to Silence (Bijoe Emmanuel, Nandini Satpathy, Miranda)

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Hate speech is not defined in the Constitution of India. It is defined in international instruments (UN) and discussed in the Law Commission's 267th Report (2017) and cases such as Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan (2014). Core idea: speech that attacks or incites hatred against a group based on religion, race, caste, ethnicity, gender, region etc., which leads to discrimination and violence.

Shreya Singhal (2015): every speech is Discussion, Advocacy or Incitement: the first two are constitutionally protected; only incitement (with a proximate, direct link to violence) can be an offence.

Right to silence: (i) in Art 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech includes freedom not to speak): Bijoe Emmanuel (1986); (ii) in Art 20(3)/21 (against self-incrimination): Nandini Satpathy (1978), Miranda warnings (US). The professor said Nandini Satpathy will be taught under Art 20.

Biggest question the professor says will be asked (but he will not teach): "Are the existing laws sufficient to control hate speech, or are new laws needed?" (Read the Law Commission 267th Report.) A full model answer is in 5.5.

What has been left out

This lecture opened with student-election administration, committee budgets, a rant on external speakers, and a long political and anecdotal digression (Indira Gandhi's era, party-political comments, a speculative history of the national anthem). Only the legal content is kept. Where the professor made a contested historical claim (the national anthem), the notes give the neutral legal point.

sections.title: 5.2 Hate speech: meaning, sources and why it is serious
sections.html:
• No constitutional definition: "Hate speech has been defined at several places, but not in the Constitution of India." The professor asked students to read the definition at two places (one is the United Nations). The UN's working definition (UN Strategy and Plan of Action on Hate Speech, 2019): "any kind of communication in speech, writing or behaviour, that attacks or uses pejorative or discriminatory language with reference to a person or a group on the basis of who they are, in other words, based on their religion, ethnicity, nationality, race, colour, descent, gender or other identity factor."
  • Why the UN? "When I say that hate speech has been defined by the United Nations, what does that mean? It means this is not only a national problem; it is an international problem." In the internet age "the world has become a small classroom": something posted on Instagram in America can be seen in India. Hence international co-operation and global platforms matter; Indian law can control only its own territory.
  • Professor's working definition: "When hate is created towards a particular group, that is hate speech; the group can be classified on any basis: gender (women), religious minority, race, caste, creed, geographical area." The result of creating hatred: people start discriminating against members of that group and sometimes become violent.
  • Illustrations the professor used: (1) statements portraying people of a particular locality as criminals can lead to discrimination, even in a job interview, and sometimes to violence against a person from that place; (2) inflammatory preachers abusing another religion; (3) remarks about people of a region ("all people from X are bad"); (4) fake news leading to riots and murders (he cited the Amravati and Udaipur killings of 2022, which followed communal controversy and social media posts).
  • Why it is worse than an ordinary crime: "When you commit murder, rape or dacoity it is against one person or one house. When you commit hate crime/speech, you brand lakhs of people at once (all Nagpurians, all people from Beed). If violence follows, whoever from that group is found is attacked, discriminated against, or deprived of rights." It therefore threatens Arts 14, 19, 21 and 25 for the whole group (and fraternity, Preamble).
  • Rise: with free speech and social media, "communication became easy", and hate speech cases, riots and killings increased, "especially on the basis of fake news".
  • Legal anchors for the exam: Preamble (fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation); Art 19(2) (public order; incitement to an offence; decency or morality; sovereignty and integrity of India; defamation); Art 25 (religion subject to public order, morality, health); Art 15 and Art 17; and ICCPR Art 20(2) ("any advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence shall be prohibited by law") and ICERD Art 4 (India is a party).

If violence follows, whoever from that group is found is attacked, discriminated against, or deprived of rights." It therefore threatens Arts 14, 19, 21 and 25 for the whole group (and fraternity , Preamble). Rise: with free speech and social media , "communication became easy", and hate speech cases, riots and killings increased, "especially on the basis of fake news ". Legal anchors for the exam: Preamble ( fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation ); Art 19(2) (public order; incitement to an offence; decency or morality; sovereignty and integrity of India; defamation); Art 25 (religion subject to public order, morality, health); Art 15 and Art 17 ; and ICCPR Art 20(2) ("any advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence shall be prohibited by law") and ICERD Art 4 (India is a party).

Case

Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India (2014)

Citation / Court / Year

(2014) 11 SCC 477; decided 12 March 2014 (Supreme Court of India; bench headed by B.S. Chauhan J.).

Facts
  • An NGO, Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan, filed a PIL seeking directions to stop inflammatory and hate speeches by politicians and religious leaders and to enforce existing law. The Election Commission told the Court that existing laws permit action.
  • The professor said that Justice Nariman wrote it ("a tight judge, generally anti-government"). The bench was headed by Justice B.S. Chauhan (not Nariman J.; Nariman J. wrote Shreya Singhal).
Issues
  • Should the Court frame guidelines to prevent hate speech? Is the existing law enough? Should hate speech be defined?
Held (Decision)
  • The Court declined to frame guidelines itself, observing that existing laws (ss. 153A, 153B, 295A, 505 IPC; RPA) are available, and directed the Law Commission to study whether it "deems proper to define hate speech" and to make recommendations to Parliament (including on strengthening the Election Commission to deal with hate speech).
  • The Court described hate speech as an effort to marginalise individuals based on their membership of a group, which undermines dignity and equality and threatens the fundamental values of the Constitution (fraternity). It also noted that it is a problem of enforcement as much as of definition.
Ratio decidendi

Hate speech damages dignity and equal citizenship; existing criminal provisions should be effectively enforced; legislative definition/reform was referred to the Law Commission.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Led to the 267th Law Commission Report (2017), whose chairman was Justice B.S. Chauhan (the same judge who headed the bench).
Use in the exam

The professor listed this case as the lead case on hate speech decided by the Supreme Court and asked students to read "one or two more" hate speech cases.

Case

Law Commission of India, Report No. 267: "Hate Speech" (2017)

Citation / Court / Year

Submitted to the Government on 23 March 2017 (Chairman: Justice B.S. Chauhan).

Held (Decision)
  • Recommended two new provisions in the IPC: s. 153C ("prohibition of incitement to hatred": punishing the incitement to hatred on grounds of race, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community, or any other ground) and s. 505A ("causing fear, alarm, or provocation of violence in certain cases").
  • Defined hate speech broadly as incitement to hatred primarily against a group of persons defined in terms of race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, religious belief and the like.
  • Factors to weigh before restricting speech: context, status of the victim, status of the speaker, potential to create discriminatory and disruptive circumstances (the likelihood of imminent harm); also non-penal measures such as sensitisation and public education on responsible speech.
Use in the exam

The professor: "Which Law Commission report? (a student: 2017; he said "267th, Justice B.S. Chauhan") and "this is a very important report; read it".
