sections.title: 5.4 Discussion, Advocacy, Incitement (Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, 2015)
sections.html:
Case

Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)

Citation / Court / Year

(2015) 5 SCC 1; decided 24 March 2015 (Supreme Court of India; Chelameswar and R.F. Nariman JJ.; judgment by Nariman J.).

Facts
  • In November 2012 two young women in Palghar (Maharashtra) were arrested under s. 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 for a Facebook post questioning the total shutdown of Mumbai after a political leader's death (and for "liking" it). Shreya Singhal, a law student, filed a PIL challenging s. 66A (punishing "grossly offensive", "annoying", "inconvenient" messages), s. 69A (blocking) and s. 79 (intermediary liability).
Issues
  • Is s. 66A within the Art 19(2) grounds? Is it vague/overbroad? Are ss. 69A and 79 valid?
Held (Decision)
  • s. 66A struck down as unconstitutional: vague and overbroad terms ("annoying", "inconvenient", "grossly offensive") are not among the eight Art 19(2) grounds, and they create a chilling effect.
  • The Court distinguished speech into (1) discussion, (2) advocacy and (3) incitement: "Mere discussion or even advocacy of a particular cause, however unpopular, is at the heart of Art 19(1)(a). It is only when such discussion or advocacy reaches the level of incitement that Art 19(2) kicks in." Incitement must have a proximate (direct) connection with a public order disturbance. Law and order, public order and security of State are distinguished again (Lohia).
  • s. 69A upheld (with procedural safeguards: written reasons, hearing, Review Committee, remedy by writ); s. 79(3)(b) read down (intermediary must act on actual knowledge through a court order or government notification relating to Art 19(2) subjects).
Ratio decidendi

Only incitement can be restricted; discussion and advocacy are constitutionally protected; vague speech laws that go beyond Art 19(2) are void.

Use in the exam

The professor said "Shreya Singhal: read it; speech is divided into three parts". Illustration he gave (re-told below).

The professor's illustration of the three stages (about a city called "Bharatpur")

StageExampleLegal status
1. Discussion"How is the city? Is it good or bad?": everyone may discuss.Protected
2. Advocacy"The city is wonderful; its people are hospitable; you must come and visit."Protected (even if unpopular or strongly worded)
3. Incitement"Whoever does not visit should be shot"; "whoever does not come will be cursed, will have a break-up, goddess will be angry": a call to violence/harm.Can be an offence if the other conditions are satisfied: immediate impact, direct and proximate connection (and, per the professor, the speech must have the potential for immediate harm).
  • Applied to religion: you can say "my religion is excellent" for 24 hours; you can say "Islam is so good that people should adopt it" or "Hindu dharma is so good that the whole world should adopt it": this is advocacy/propagation and not itself a crime. The offence arises when the promotion crosses into conversion by force, fraud or allurement (the anti-conversion statutes: the professor said "force, fraud, allurement; only after conversion happens by such means is there an offence, not before"). Authority: Rev. Stanislaus v. State of M.P. (1977) (the right to propagate in Art 25 does not include the right to convert; anti-conversion laws punishing force, fraud and inducement are valid). (Note: the transcript of this passage is garbled; this is the legally consistent reading.)
  • Conditions beyond incitement (professor): "Immediate impact; direct nexus": the speech must be of a kind that can actually produce violence now; compare Rangarajan ("spark in a powder keg") and Kedar Nath Singh (incitement to violence).

sections.title: 5.5 THE big question: are the existing laws enough to control hate speech? (model answer)
sections.html:
The professor said this is "the biggest question that will be asked from you, and I will not teach it; read the Law Commission report". Use this structure:

  • Introduction: hate speech = incitement to hatred against a group; it undermines dignity, equality and fraternity and can lead to violence (Pravasi Bhalai; Law Commission 267th Report); it is not defined in the Constitution or the IPC/BNS.
  • Existing law (adequate on paper): ss. 153A, 153B, 295A, 298, 505 IPC (now BNS ss. 196, 197, 299, 302, 353); RPA ss. 123(3), 123(3A); PCR Act; SC/ST Act; IT Act ss. 67, 69A and the 2021 Rules; CrPC ss. 95, 144 (BNSS ss. 98, 163). Judicial safeguards: Shreya Singhal (incitement), Ramji Lal Modi (295A upheld), Bilal Kaloo, Abhiram Singh.
  • Arguments that existing laws are sufficient: (i) the provisions already cover communal and caste-based enmity; (ii) the problem is enforcement (delays, prior-sanction requirements such as s. 196 CrPC / BNSS s. 217, selective prosecution, political pressure), not the absence of law (Pravasi Bhalai; Election Commission's stand); (iii) vague new offences risk the chilling effect struck down in Shreya Singhal; (iv) the Constitution uses Art 19(2) as the limit and no ground "hate speech" exists.
  • Arguments for new law: (i) the existing provisions are fragmented and old, focused on "public order" and "religious feelings", and do not squarely address group-targeted online hate, dehumanising speech or identity-based vilification (gender, sexual orientation); (ii) new media (virality, bots, cross-border posting) outpaces the law; (iii) Law Commission 267th Report proposes s. 153C and s. 505A; (iv) international obligations (ICCPR Art 20(2), ICERD Art 4).
  • Safeguards if new law is made: a clear definition tied to incitement and proximate harm; intent/knowledge; consider speaker's status, context, victim's status, reach; prior judicial scrutiny; non-penal measures (education, counter-speech, platform responsibility); and proportionality (Anuradha Bhasin).
  • Conclusion: a balanced reform: strengthen enforcement, adopt the narrowly drafted Law Commission provisions, and regulate platforms with due process, while preserving discussion and advocacy under Art 19(1)(a).

sections.title: 5.6 The right to silence (part of the freedom of speech)
sections.html:
The professor recalled that "the right to silence is also a fundamental right covered by Art 19(1)(a)" and asked which case, why, and the facts. Three different "rights to silence" must not be mixed up:

RightSourceCase
Freedom not to speak or sing (silence as expression)Art 19(1)(a) (and Art 25)Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)
Protection against self-incrimination (a person accused of an offence cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself)Art 20(3); also Art 21Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978); Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010)
Right to be told of the right to silence and to a lawyer on custodial interrogation ("Miranda warnings")US Fifth Amendment; in India Art 20(3), Art 21, Art 22(1)Miranda v. Arizona (1966) (US); D.K. Basu (1997)
Case

Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (the National Anthem case) (1986)

Citation / Court / Year

(1986) 3 SCC 615; AIR 1987 SC 748 (Supreme Court of India; O. Chinnappa Reddy and M.M. Dutt JJ.).

Facts
  • Three children (Bijoe, Binu Mol and Bindu Emmanuel) belonging to the Jehovah's Witnesses were expelled from school in Kerala because they stood respectfully during the national anthem "Jana Gana Mana" but did not sing: their religious faith permits prayer only to Jehovah. A Headmaster expelled them on the basis of a Kerala Education Department circular.
Issues
  • Can a person be compelled to sing the national anthem? Does freedom of speech include the right not to speak? Is there any law obliging singing? Is there an Art 25 claim?
Held (Decision)
  • The expulsion violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 25(1). No law obliges anyone to sing; the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 (s. 3) punishes preventing the singing or causing disturbance during the anthem, not refraining from singing.
  • Freedom of speech and expression includes the right to remain silent. Standing respectfully while the anthem is sung is enough; respect cannot be compelled. The Court cited the Indian tradition of tolerance and the American case West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943) (no compulsory flag salute).
Ratio decidendi

The right to freedom of speech and expression includes the right not to speak (to remain silent); no one can be compelled to sing the anthem if the person shows respect by standing and does not disturb.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India (2016, 2018): compulsory standing during the anthem in cinemas, ordered in 2016, was later made optional/diluted (2018); Bijoe Emmanuel remains good law.
Use in the exam

The professor: "Right to silence is also part of Art 19(1)(a): Vijay (Bijoe) Emmanuel; it was about the song Jana Gana Mana; the Court said you cannot compel anyone to sing; you only need to show respect by standing."

The anthem digression: what is exam-safe

The professor argued in class that "Jana Gana Mana" was composed to welcome King George V (1911) and criticised its text; some students pointed out that Rabindranath Tagore himself denied this in letters (1937, 1939), saying the "Bharat Bhagya Vidhata" is the eternal guide of the nation, not any monarch. This is a contested historical question, not examinable constitutional law. A PIL on the point (Sanjeev Bhatnagar v. Union of India, 2005) was dismissed by the Supreme Court (verify the report if you cite it).

Exam-safe principle: respect for national symbols cannot be compelled by singing; standing respectfully is sufficient (Bijoe Emmanuel). The same applies to "Vande Mataram": the professor said no one can be compelled; one must only not disrespect (a Bombay-based challenge, "B.D. Borkar v. Union", was mentioned as pending; no verification possible, so do not cite it).

Case

Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978)

Citation / Court / Year

(1978) 2 SCC 424; AIR 1978 SC 1025 (Supreme Court of India; V.R. Krishna Iyer J. for the Bench).

Facts
  • Nandini Satpathy, a former Chief Minister of Odisha, was summoned to the Vigilance Police Station (Cuttack) and given a long list of written questions in a corruption case. She refused to answer, claiming the right against self-incrimination. She was prosecuted under s. 179 IPC (refusing to answer a public servant authorised to question).
  • The professor: "She was held at the police station till 8, 9, 10, 11 at night; "we will not let you go till you speak". Can police compel? Can they detain for a long time if you don't reply?"
Issues
  • Does the protection in Art 20(3) (no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself) apply during police investigation and interrogation, or only at trial before the magistrate?
Held (Decision)
  • Art 20(3) is available at the stage of investigation, to a person who is an accused and also to a suspect who may be incriminated by the answers; the right is not confined to the court. A person may refuse to answer questions that may incriminate him (not all questions).
  • Police cannot compel answers; prolonged detention and pressure amount to torture and violate Art 20(3) and 21. Safeguards: the presence of a lawyer (or friend/relative) during interrogation; right to be informed of the right to silence (the Court considered the American Miranda warnings an aid to interpretation); questions to women to be asked in the presence of a woman/relative, and not at night at the police station (as suggested).
Ratio decidendi

The right to silence against self-incrimination extends to police interrogation; compulsion (physical or psychological) is barred; s. 161(2) CrPC (now BNSS s. 180(2)) gives a person the right to decline to answer incriminating questions.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010): narco-analysis, polygraph, BEAP tests without consent violate Art 20(3) and 21. D.K. Basu (1997): arrest and detention safeguards. Statements to police are not admissible in evidence against the accused (s. 162 CrPC / BNSS s. 181; ss. 25-26 Evidence Act / BSA ss. 23-24).
Use in the exam

Professor: "Nandini Satpathy is Art 20 (self-incrimination), not Art 19: that will be taught under Art 20; but this is what is called Miranda rights in India." He added: "earlier the protection was recognised only before the magistrate (statements before a judge can be used as evidence); Nandini Satpathy for the first time extended it to the stage of investigation by the police."

Case

Miranda v. Arizona (US Supreme Court, 1966)

Citation / Court / Year

384 U.S. 436 (1966) (Warren C.J.).

Facts
  • Ernesto Miranda was arrested for kidnapping and rape in Arizona, interrogated for two hours without being told he could remain silent or have a lawyer, and signed a confession.
Issues
  • Is a confession obtained in custodial interrogation without warnings admissible?
Held (Decision)
  • The Fifth and Sixth Amendments require that, before custodial interrogation, the police must warn the suspect: (1) you have the right to remain silent; (2) anything you say can and will be used against you in a court of law; (3) you have the right to talk to a lawyer and have him present while you are being questioned; (4) if you cannot afford a lawyer, one will be appointed for you. A statement taken without these warnings is inadmissible.
Ratio decidendi

Custodial interrogation is inherently coercive; procedural safeguards (warnings) are necessary to protect the privilege against self-incrimination.

Use in the exam

A student recited the four warnings in class (see the Miranda warning list above). Professor's explanation of why: "you are presumed innocent until guilt is proved; the other side must prove guilt; you need not help prove your own guilt; otherwise your freedom of being innocent would be diluted (the burden of proof)."

  • Professor's point on the "Miranda warning": the word "warning" does not mean the police warn you of consequences; it means the police must inform you that you are not bound to answer. "Every police interrogation, if it is done without this being said, would be illegal." Because many people are uneducated and do not know their rights, it is the police's duty to inform them.
  • Position in India (cautious): a full Miranda-type warning is not statutorily required at arrest, but Art 22(1) (to be informed of the grounds of arrest; right to consult and be defended by a lawyer), s. 41D CrPC (right to meet an advocate during interrogation) and D.K. Basu guidelines provide similar protection; s. 162 CrPC and Evidence Act ss. 24-27 limit the use of statements.
  • Physical violence by police is 100% illegal: "Police cannot hit you; punishment can be awarded only by a court." The professor compared military discipline: the punishments of admonition (mild warning) and reprimand (severe, formal, in writing) are recorded and imposed by the competent authority (the commanding officer); "likewise police cannot scold or beat; the judge also only records: you are being admonished, you are being reprimanded."
sections.text: The professor recalled that " the right to silence is also a fundamental right covered by Art 19(1)(a) " and asked which case, why, and the facts. Three different "rights to silence" must not be mixed up: Right Source Case Freedom not to speak or sing (silence as expression) Art 19(1)(a) (and Art 25) Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) Protection against self-incrimination (a person accused of an offence cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself) Art 20(3) ; also Art 21 Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978) ; Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) Right to be told of the right to silence and to a lawyer on custodial interrogation (" Miranda warnings") US Fifth Amendment; in India Art 20(3), Art 21, Art 22(1) Miranda v. Arizona (1966) (US); D.K. Basu (1997) Case Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (the National Anthem case) (1986) Citation / Court / Year (1986) 3 SCC 615; AIR 1987 SC 748 (Supreme Court of India; O. Chinnappa Reddy and M.M. Dutt JJ.). Facts Three children ( Bijoe, Binu Mol and Bindu Emmanuel ) belonging to the Jehovah's Witnesses were expelled from school in Kerala because they stood respectfully during the national anthem "Jana Gana Mana" but did not sing : their religious faith permits prayer only to Jehovah. A Headmaster expelled them on the basis of a Kerala Education Department circular. Issues Can a person be compelled to sing the national anthem? Does freedom of speech include the right not to speak ? Is there any law obliging singing? Is there an Art 25 claim? Held (Decision) The expulsion violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 25(1) . No law obliges anyone to sing; the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 (s. 3) punishes preventing the singing or causing disturbance during the anthem, not refraining from singing . Freedom of speech and expression includes the right to remain silent . Standing respectfully while the anthem is sung is enough; respect cannot be compelled . The Court cited the Indian tradition of tolerance and the American case West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943) (no compulsory flag salute). Ratio decidendi The right to freedom of speech and expression includes the right not to speak (to remain silent) ; no one can be compelled to sing the anthem if the person shows respect by standing and does not disturb. Significance / Later treatment Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India (2016, 2018): compulsory standing during the anthem in cinemas, ordered in 2016, was later made optional/diluted (2018); Bijoe Emmanuel remains good law . Use in the exam The professor: " Right to silence is also part of Art 19(1)(a) : Vijay (Bijoe) Emmanuel; it was about the song Jana Gana Mana; the Court said you cannot compel anyone to sing; you only need to show respect by standing ." The anthem digression: what is exam-safe The professor argued in class that "Jana Gana Mana" was composed to welcome King George V (1911) and criticised its text; some students pointed out that Rabindranath Tagore himself denied this in letters (1937, 1939), saying the "Bharat Bhagya Vidhata" is the eternal guide of the nation, not any monarch . This is a contested historical question , not examinable constitutional law. A PIL on the point ( Sanjeev Bhatnagar v. Union of India , 2005) was dismissed by the Supreme Court (verify the report if you cite it). Exam-safe principle: respect for national symbols cannot be compelled by singing ; standing respectfully is sufficient ( Bijoe Emmanuel ). The same applies to "Vande Mataram" : the professor said no one can be compelled; one must only not disrespect (a Bombay-based challenge, "B.D. Borkar v. Union", was mentioned as pending; no verification possible, so do not cite it). Case Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978) Citation / Court / Year (1978) 2 SCC 424; AIR 1978 SC 1025 (Supreme Court of India; V.R. Krishna Iyer J. for the Bench). Facts Nandini Satpathy , a former Chief Minister of Odisha, was summoned to the Vigilance Police Station (Cuttack) and given a long list of written questions in a corruption case . She refused to answer, claiming the right against self-incrimination . She was prosecuted under s. 179 IPC (refusing to answer a public servant authorised to question). The professor: "She was held at the police station till 8, 9, 10, 11 at night; "we will not let you go till you speak". Can police compel? Can they detain for a long time if you don't reply?" Issues Does the protection in Art 20(3) (no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself) apply during police investigation and interrogation , or only at trial before the magistrate? Held (Decision) Art 20(3) is available at the stage of investigation , to a person who is an accused and also to a suspect who may be incriminated by the answers; the right is not confined to the court . A person may refuse to answer questions that may incriminate him (not all questions). Police cannot compel answers ; prolonged detention and pressure amount to torture and violate Art 20(3) and 21 . Safeguards: the presence of a lawyer (or friend/relative) during interrogation; right to be informed of the right to silence (the Court considered the American Miranda warnings an aid to interpretation); questions to women to be asked in the presence of a woman/relative, and not at night at the police station (as suggested). Ratio decidendi The right to silence against self-incrimination extends to police interrogation ; compulsion (physical or psychological) is barred; s. 161(2) CrPC (now BNSS s. 180(2)) gives a person the right to decline to answer incriminating questions. Significance / Later treatment Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010): narco-analysis, polygraph, BEAP tests without consent violate Art 20(3) and 21 . D.K. Basu (1997): arrest and detention safeguards. Statements to police are not admissible in evidence against the accused (s. 162 CrPC / BNSS s. 181; ss. 25-26 Evidence Act / BSA ss. 23-24). Use in the exam Professor: " Nandini Satpathy is Art 20 (self-incrimination), not Art 19: that will be taught under Art 20; but this is what is called Miranda rights in India." He added: "earlier the protection was recognised only before the magistrate (statements before a judge can be used as evidence); Nandini Satpathy for the first time extended it to the stage of investigation by the police ." Case Miranda v. Arizona (US Supreme Court, 1966) Citation / Court / Year 384 U.S. 436 (1966) (Warren C.J.). Facts Ernesto Miranda was arrested for kidnapping and rape in Arizona, interrogated for two hours without being told he could remain silent or have a lawyer, and signed a confession. Issues Is a confession obtained in custodial interrogation without warnings admissible? Held (Decision) The Fifth and Sixth Amendments require that, before custodial interrogation , the police must warn the suspect: (1) you have the right to remain silent; (2) anything you say can and will be used against you in a court of law; (3) you have the right to talk to a lawyer and have him present while you are being questioned; (4) if you cannot afford a lawyer, one will be appointed for you. A statement taken without these warnings is inadmissible . Ratio decidendi Custodial interrogation is inherently coercive ; procedural safeguards (warnings) are necessary to protect the privilege against self-incrimination . Use in the exam A student recited the four warnings in class (see the Miranda warning list above). Professor's explanation of why : "you are presumed innocent until guilt is proved; the other side must prove guilt ; you need not help prove your own guilt; otherwise your freedom of being innocent would be diluted (the burden of proof )." Professor's point on the " Miranda warning": the word "warning" does not mean the police warn you of consequences; it means the police must inform you that you are not bound to answer . "Every police interrogation, if it is done without this being said, would be illegal ." Because many people are uneducated and do not know their rights , it is the police's duty to inform them. Position in India (cautious): a full Miranda -type warning is not statutorily required at arrest, but Art 22(1) (to be informed of the grounds of arrest; right to consult and be defended by a lawyer), s. 41D CrPC (right to meet an advocate during interrogation) and D.K. Basu guidelines provide similar protection; s. 162 CrPC and Evidence Act ss. 24-27 limit the use of statements. Physical violence by police is 100% illegal : "Police cannot hit you; punishment can be awarded only by a court ." The professor compared military discipline : the punishments of admonition (mild warning) and reprimand (severe, formal, in writing) are recorded and imposed by the competent authority (the commanding officer); "likewise police cannot scold or beat; the judge also only records: you are being admonished, you are being reprimanded."

sections.title: 5.7 Other legal asides in this lecture
sections.html:
AsideLegal point
Gender sensitisation / POSH: the professor objected to paying outside "experts" for awareness lectures and said the legal content is simple: no sexual harassment; if it happens, complain to the committee; know the remedies.Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) (guidelines, Arts 14, 15, 19(1)(g), 21); Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013: Internal Committee (s. 4; presiding officer a senior woman), Local Committee (s. 6), complaint within 3 months (extendable by 3), inquiry, penalties. (The professor said "POSH specialisation is not a recognised degree" and recommended using internal faculty and the Act itself.)
Free and fair elections / constitutionalism: "arbitrary power is unjust; even an elected representative must respect the Constitution."Constitutionalism: limited government, rule of law; free and fair elections are part of the basic structure (Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975). Note: in that case the Supreme Court (headed by A.N. Ray C.J., who was appointed after superseding three senior judges following Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) struck down clause (4) of Art 329A (which insulated the Prime Minister's election from judicial review) but allowed her election to stand on the basis of the amended Representation of the People law. It is therefore not accurate to say the Court simply ruled "against" her; the Allahabad High Court (Sinha J.) had set aside her election in State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (the election petition, 1975).
Action research (professor's preparation for a research methodology lecture)Not examinable.
Due process lecture anecdote: a senior advocate remarked he had never heard the professor's explanation of "process" elsewhere.Relevant to Lecture 8 (Art 21: procedure established by law v. due process).

sections.title: 5.8 Questions asked by the professor in COLA 9, with model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. How is hate speech defined? Where?

Model answer

Not in the Constitution of India. It has been defined by the UN (attack or pejorative/discriminatory language against a person or a group on the basis of religion, ethnicity, nationality, race, colour, descent, gender or other identity factor) and discussed by the Law Commission (267th Report: incitement to hatred against a group). Professor's one-liner: "hate created towards a particular group, which can be classified on any basis".

Question asked in class

Q2. Why is hate speech an international problem?

Model answer

Because internet and social media make content available across borders (a post on Instagram in America is seen in India); no State can control foreign platforms alone; hence the UN's concern and the need for international co-operation (ICCPR Art 20(2)).

Question asked in class

Q3. Why is hate speech more serious than an ordinary crime?

Model answer

An ordinary crime (murder, rape) harms one victim or household; hate speech brands an entire group (all people from a place, religion or caste), exposing every member to discrimination and violence; it undermines fraternity, dignity and equal citizenship.

Question asked in class

Q4. Is the existing law sufficient to control hate speech, or do we need new law? Which Law Commission report should be read?

Model answer

See 5.5. The report is the 267th Report, "Hate Speech" (2017) (Chairman: Justice B.S. Chauhan), which recommended ss. 153C and 505A IPC.

Question asked in class

Q5. Name the leading Supreme Court case on hate speech brought as a PIL by a "Pravasi" organisation.

Model answer

Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India (2014) 11 SCC 477: the Court directed the Law Commission to examine whether hate speech should be defined; existing laws to be enforced.

Question asked in class

Q6. How does Shreya Singhal classify speech? Which categories are protected?

Model answer

Discussion, advocacy, incitement. Discussion and advocacy (even of unpopular causes) are protected under Art 19(1)(a); incitement (with a proximate, direct link to harm) alone can be punished under Art 19(2).

Question asked in class

Q7. Is saying that "my religion is so good that the whole world should adopt it" an offence?

Model answer

No; it is advocacy/propagation (Art 25, Art 19(1)(a)); an offence arises only if there is force, fraud or allurement leading to conversion (anti-conversion statutes upheld in Rev. Stanislaus, 1977) or incitement to violence or hatred.

Question asked in class

Q8. Is the right to silence part of freedom of speech? Which case, and what were the facts?

Model answer

Yes. Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986): three Jehovah's Witness children stood respectfully but did not sing "Jana Gana Mana" and were expelled; the Court held that freedom of speech includes freedom of silence, and that no law compels singing; expulsion violated Arts 19(1)(a) and 25.

Question asked in class

Q9. What are "Miranda rights"? State the four warnings. What is the Indian counterpart?

Model answer

US warnings before custodial interrogation: (1) right to remain silent; (2) anything said can be used against you; (3) right to a lawyer present; (4) a lawyer will be appointed if you cannot afford one (Miranda v. Arizona, 1966). In India: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978) under Art 20(3)/Art 21, Art 22(1), D.K. Basu (1997).

Question asked in class

Q10. Why does the law give an accused the right to silence?

Model answer

Presumption of innocence: the prosecution must prove guilt; the accused cannot be forced to supply the evidence against himself; otherwise the burden of proof would be reversed. It also prevents custodial torture to extract confessions.

Question asked in class

Q11. Can the police hold a person at the station until she answers? Can they beat a suspect?

Model answer

No. Compelling answers by detention or pressure violates Art 20(3) and Art 21 (Nandini Satpathy). Physical violence is illegal; only a court can punish (D.K. Basu). Police may only ask questions; a person is not bound to answer incriminating ones.

Question asked in class

Q12. What is the difference between admonition and reprimand? (the Air Force illustration)

Model answer

Admonition is a mild warning; reprimand is a severe, formal and often recorded censure. Both are disciplinary measures imposed by the competent authority, not physical punishment; the professor used it to show that the police and even a judge may only record such censure and cannot beat or abuse.

Question asked in class

Q13. What are the three types of "silence" in constitutional law?

Model answer

(i) Art 19(1)(a): freedom not to speak (Bijoe Emmanuel); (ii) Art 20(3): privilege against self-incrimination (Nandini Satpathy); (iii) Custodial rights (Art 22(1), D.K. Basu; Miranda in the US).

exam.title: Right to Property - Art 19(1)(f), Art 31, Art 300A, Eminent Domain and the Compensation Story

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Original scheme (1950): property was protected twice - Art 19(1)(f) (a citizen's freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property) and Art 31 (protection of any person against deprivation/compulsory acquisition by the State). 44th Amendment (enacted 1978; in force 1979) deleted Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31 and inserted Art 300A in Part XII: "No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law." Property is now a constitutional (and human) right, not a Fundamental Right.

Eminent domain (Latin dominium eminens) = the sovereign power of the State to take private property for public use. Three conditions for a valid acquisition: (1) authority of law, (2) public purpose, (3) compensation.

Compensation saga: Bela Banerjee (1954) - "compensation" = just equivalent / market value → Fourth Amendment (1955) (adequacy non-justiciable) → R.C. Cooper (1970) → 25th Amendment (1971): "compensation" replaced by "amount" → Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld that change → 44th Amendment (1978) removed the whole thing from Part III → Art 300A. Modern law: LARR Act, 2013 (up to 4x market value in rural areas, 2x in urban areas).

Practical consequence of 44th Amendment: no writ under Art 32 for breach of property right alone (go to the High Court, Art 226); Art 13 no longer bites on property laws; the State needs only an ordinary law (not a constitutional amendment) to acquire property.

What has been left out of this lecture

The class began with an exam-paper discussion (marks, copies) and ran through long political commentary (party politics, a named politician's family, a security-cover digression) and an extended IPKF / Sri Lanka story used to illustrate "State suppressing the rights of citizens of another country". None of that is constitutional law that can be examined, and the political remarks are the professor's personal opinions; they are omitted. Only the legal content (and the questions asked) are kept.

Facts to double-check before quoting: the professor's statement that "the Supreme Court later struck down / dealt with" the amount amendment is garbled in the transcript. What is safe: the 25th Amendment's "amount" was upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973); the whole of Art 31 was then deleted in 1978.

sections.title: 6.1 Opening quiz: why does Art 19(1) jump from (e) to (g)?
sections.html:
The professor asked "A, B, C, D, E, F should come - why is it (g)? Whose mistake is it - mine, Dr Ambedkar's, or the typist's?" Answer: nobody's mistake. Art 19(1)(f) (right to acquire, hold and dispose of property) was omitted by the Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978; the lettering of the remaining clauses was not changed, so the list now reads (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (g).

ClauseFreedom (citizens only)Restriction clause
19(1)(a)Speech and expression19(2) - eight grounds
19(1)(b)Assemble peaceably and without arms19(3) - sovereignty and integrity of India; public order
19(1)(c)Form associations, unions or co-operative societies (words "co-operative societies" added by the 97th Amendment, 2011)19(4) - sovereignty and integrity; public order; morality

sections.title: 6.2 Is the university "State"? (the mobile-phone hypothetical)
sections.html:
To illustrate the point that property can be taken only by authority of law, the professor "confiscated" a student's mobile phone in class. A student objected: "Sir, the university is not State." The professor answered that the university is government-funded, on government land, and that he was acting as an instrumentality of the State.

  • Legal basis: Art 12 - "the State" includes the Government and Parliament, the Government and Legislature of each State, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. Statutory universities/institutions with State funding and control are "other authorities".
  • Tests: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority (1979) and Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi (1981) (functional test: financial resources of the State, deep and pervasive State control, functional character - public functions, State-conferred monopoly, department transferred to the body). Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (2002) (7 judges): the question is whether the body is "financially, functionally and administratively dominated by or under the control of the Government".
  • Application: the Maharashtra National Law University Act, 2014 (a State statute) creates MNLU, Nagpur; it is largely State-funded and State-controlled → it is "State" under Art 12 (a student's argument that it is "autonomous" does not change this). Consequently, Part III binds it and any taking of a student's property needs a law.
  • Result of the hypothetical: snatching the phone without any law is an act of the State without authority of law - violating Art 300A (and, if the phone were a student's "possession", natural justice/Art 14). Professor's punchline: "since the right to property is no longer a Fundamental Right, one cannot say Fundamental Right is violated - but Art 300A still protects it." (He then returned the phone.)

sections.title: 6.3 Why was the right to property in TWO places? (the professor's main question)
sections.html:
The professor repeatedly asked: "Art 31 had property, Art 19 also had property - why two places? Could Dr Ambedkar not have managed with one? And what difference did it make when both went and Art 300A came?" The framework below answers it completely.

AspectArt 19(1)(f) + 19(5)Art 31 (original)Art 300A (now)
Nature of rightA freedom - to acquire, hold and dispose of property; a continuing, positive freedom of citizensA protection against State power - the individual's shield when the State deprives or acquires; available to every person (citizen or not)A constitutional right (not Fundamental), also treated as a human right (Vidya Devi, 2020)
Who can claimCitizens only (like all of Art 19)Any personAny person
What it controlsRegulation/restriction of property use - must be a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public or for protection of Scheduled Tribes (Art 19(5))Deprivation (31(1): only "by authority of law") and compulsory acquisition/requisition (31(2): only for a public purpose and by a law providing compensation - the amount fixed or the principles specified)Deprivation only "by authority of law"; other conditions (public purpose; fair compensation) read in by the courts (K.T. Plantation, Vidya Devi, Bimal Kumar Shah)
RemedyArt 32 (Supreme Court) / Art 226Art 32 / Art 226Art 226 (High Court); Art 32 only if another Fundamental Right (Art 14, 21) is also breached
TestReasonableness (V.G. Row)Law + public purpose + compensationValid law + public purpose + fair compensation / procedural fairness
  • Professor's explanation (state this in the exam): Art 19(1)(f) gave citizens the right to hold property; Art 31 recognised the State's sovereign power to take it (eminent domain) subject to conditions. So "on one side the Constitution says you have the right to property; on the other it says the State has the power to take it" - a built-in tension that was hard to balance.
  • Technical precision: Art 31 is better described as a safeguard (deprivation only by law; acquisition only for a public purpose and on payment of compensation) than as a grant of power - the power itself (eminent domain) is inherent in sovereignty and would exist even if not written (compare: Parliament's power under Art 3 or the State's power to acquire property - the professor said "even if not written, the State can do it").
  • Why two clauses: one dealt with freedom of the owner (regulation) and one with the taking by the State (acquisition); the Court at first treated them as mutually exclusive (A.K. Gopalan reasoning: if Art 31 applies, Art 19(1)(f) does not), but R.C. Cooper (1970) held that the effect/impact of the law on the right matters - a law taking property must also satisfy Art 19(1)(f) reasonableness. This overlap caused endless litigation and repeated constitutional amendments.
  • What changed with Art 300A: the conflict was removed - the Government can now acquire property by ordinary legislation, without needing a constitutional amendment every time the Court insisted on compensation or reasonableness (Art 13 earlier invalidated any law that took away or abridged a Fundamental Right; after 1978 property laws are not tested against Part III on the ground of property).

sections.title: 6.4 Eminent domain - meaning and the three conditions
sections.html:
• Meaning (professor): "Eminent domain - the legal power of a government to seize private property" (Latin dominium eminens = supreme lordship; the term is associated with Hugo Grotius). It is a sovereign power: the State can acquire any property, anywhere, from anyone, because "the interest of the country is above our private interest". The professor told students to Google the term ("I don't know Latin; 80 per cent of teachers in India don't know it").
  • It is not an unlimited power. It is exercised only if all three conditions are met:
#ConditionExplanation (professor's words and law)
1Authority of lawA law enacted by the legislature - "law" here is not the wide Art 13(3)(a) "law" (ordinance, order, bye-law, custom or usage) but a valid Act of the legislature (or delegated legislation clearly authorised by such an Act). An executive order or a mere administrative act cannot deprive anyone of property (Bishambhar Dayal Chandra Mohan v. State of U.P. (1982) - verify citation). Example in class: "snatching a phone - no law - first mistake of the State."
2Public purposeProperty may be acquired only for a public purpose, never for a private purpose (not for a minister's farmhouse). Professor's examples: education/study, aviation and space, airports, railways, defence, roads. The class joke: "PP does not mean Pranjal Pandey; PP means Public Purpose."
3CompensationPayment for the property acquired. Its meaning changed over time (see 6.5): equivalent of market value (Bela Banerjee) → "amount" (25th Amendment) → statutory fair compensation (LARR Act 2013).

Class illustration (use as a problem-question template). A student ("Dikshaa from Mahendragarh") owns a beloved farmhouse. The Government wants it for an airport / railway / defence project. Can it take the farmhouse against her will? Yes, even forcibly - if (1) there is a valid law authorising acquisition, (2) the acquisition is for a public purpose (not a private farmhouse for someone else), and (3) she is paid compensation/fair compensation. Her love of the property, or the "evening sunset" memories, do not defeat the State's power; her remedy is to challenge any missing condition (no law, no public purpose, no or illusory compensation) before the High Court under Art 226.

sections.title: 6.5 The compensation controversy: from "compensation" to "amount" to Art 300A (timeline)
sections.html:
YearEventEffect on property / compensation
1950Constitution of IndiaArts 19(1)(f) and 31 (31(1) deprivation only by law; 31(2) compulsory acquisition only for a public purpose and on compensation); Art 31(4)/(6) protected pending/certain State laws; Art 31A, 31B came with the 1st Amendment.
1950-51Zamindari-abolition laws (Bihar, U.P., M.P.)The Patna High Court struck down the Bihar Land Reforms Act 1950 (Art 14); the others were upheld - which triggered the First Amendment.
1951Constitution (First Amendment) ActInserted Art 31A (laws on acquisition of estates etc. protected against Arts 14 and 19) and Art 31B + Ninth Schedule (laws placed in the Schedule protected from challenge as violating Part III).
1952State of Bihar v. Kameshwar SinghBihar Land Reforms Act 1950: validity decided on Arts 31(2), 31(4), 14 and 19(1)(f). The Act was upheld by a majority (with Art 31(4) protection) although two provisions were held discriminatory under Art 14.
1954State of W.B. v. Bela Banerjee"Compensation" in Art 31(2) means the just equivalent of what the owner has been deprived of (market value); the legislature cannot lay down arbitrary principles.
1955Constitution (Fourth Amendment) ActAmended Art 31(2) (and widened 31A): the adequacy of compensation cannot be questioned in court; distinguished deprivation (31(1)) from acquisition/requisition (31(2)); added laws to the Ninth Schedule.
1967Golak Nath v. State of PunjabParliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights (overruled in 1973).
1970R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (Bank Nationalisation)11 judges; compensation must be the money equivalent; Art 19(1)(f) also applies to a law of acquisition (rejects the "mutual exclusivity" idea).
1971Constitution (25th Amendment) Act (in force 20 April 1972)"compensation" replaced by "amount" in Art 31(2) - the amount may be fixed by law or by principles in the law and may be paid other than in cash; adequacy not justiciable; Art 19(1)(f) not to apply to such laws; Art 31C inserted (laws to implement Art 39(b) and (c) protected from challenge under Arts 14, 19, 31).
1973Kesavananda Bharati v. State of KeralaBasic-structure doctrine; "amount" substitution upheld; first part of Art 31C upheld, the "no judicial review" part struck down.
197642nd AmendmentExtended Art 31C to all Directive Principles (struck down in Minerva Mills, 1980).
1978Constitution (44th Amendment) Act (property provisions in force 20 June 1979)Repealed Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31; inserted Art 300A; added Art 30(1A) (compensation for acquisition of minority educational institutions' property must ensure the right under Art 30(1) is not restricted).
2011-13K.T. Plantation (2011); LARR Act 2013Public purpose is a pre-condition for Art 300A; new Act replaces the Land Acquisition Act 1894 (in force 1 Jan 2014).
2020Vidya Devi v. State of H.P.Property is a human right; the State cannot rely on adverse possession for land taken without due process.
2024Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar ShahArt 300A includes seven sub-rights (notice, hearing, reasoned decision, public purpose, fair compensation, efficient process, conclusion).

Professor's hyperbole vs law

The professor said that after "amount" replaced "compensation", the State could give "Re 1 for a Rs 1 crore property". That is a rhetorical illustration of the risk; it is not the law. The generally accepted position is that the amount must not be illusory or arbitrary (a fixed ₹1 would be open to challenge), and the post-1978 cases (K.T. Plantation; Vidya Devi) require public purpose and fair compensation to be justified. Use the hyperbole only with that qualification.

Case

State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee (1954)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1954 SC 170; 1954 SCR 558 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; judgment by S.R. Das J. - verify the author before quoting).

Facts
  • The West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948 provided for acquisition of land (mainly for rehabilitating refugees) and fixed compensation at the market value as on 31 December 1946, ignoring the rise in value after that date.
  • Bela Banerjee, whose land was acquired, argued that compensation fixed at the 1946 value was not "compensation" within Art 31(2).
Issues
  • What does "compensation" in Art 31(2) mean? May the legislature fix it arbitrarily? Is the adequacy of compensation justiciable?
Held (Decision)
  • The Court held that "compensation" means a just equivalent of what the owner has been deprived of. The legislature may lay down principles for determining compensation, but if the principle is arbitrary or results in a sum that is not the just equivalent, it is not "compensation" and the law is unconstitutional to that extent.
  • The provision fixing the 1946 market value (ignoring subsequent increase) was held invalid as not giving the owner a just equivalent.
Ratio decidendi

Compensation = just equivalent (market value) of the property taken; adequacy of compensation is justiciable where the principle laid down is not relevant to determining the value at the time of acquisition.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Provoked the Fourth Amendment (1955), which declared that the adequacy of compensation could not be questioned; later again diluted by the 25th Amendment (1971) ("amount").
  • The professor: "compensation means an amount equivalent to the market value - this was said in Bela Banerjee. Read the case; you will enjoy it."
Use in the exam

Cite for: "what does compensation mean?"; the move from compensation → amount; the argument that just equivalent is protected by the text.

Case

State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga (1952)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1952 SC 252; 1952 SCR 889 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court).

Facts
  • The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 abolished the zamindari system, vested estates in the State and provided for compensation under a statutory scheme. The Maharaja of Darbhanga challenged it. The Patna High Court had held it unconstitutional (discriminatory and violating Art 14). Meanwhile, Parliament passed the First Amendment (Art 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule).
Issues
  • Did the Act satisfy Art 31(2) (public purpose and compensation)? Was it protected by Art 31(4)? Did it violate Art 14 / 19(1)(f)?
Held (Decision)
  • By a majority, the Court upheld the Act as a whole: it was for a public purpose (agrarian reform) and was protected by Art 31(4) from the compensation challenge, so courts could not scrutinise the adequacy of compensation under that Act; two specific provisions were held discriminatory under Art 14 (3:2).
Ratio decidendi

Laws for abolition of intermediaries are for a public purpose; where Art 31(4) applies, the adequacy of compensation is not justiciable.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Professor's use: "the Court told the Bihar Government that compensation must be paid - but where was the money? Zamindars owned vast land - so Parliament amended the Constitution to say amount instead of compensation." (The professor mentioned "Kameshwar Prasad Singh etc." - the actual name is Kameshwar Singh; the holding on Art 31(4) was more nuanced than "compensation must be paid", so use the case for the background, and Bela Banerjee for the meaning of compensation.)
Use in the exam

Background case for zamindari abolition, Art 31A/31B, First Amendment and Art 31(4) protection. Verify details before quoting bench strengths.

Case

R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (Bank Nationalisation Case) (1970)

Citation / Court / Year

(1970) 1 SCC 248; AIR 1970 SC 564 (11-judge bench; majority 10:1, Ray J. dissenting).

Facts
  • Parliament nationalised 14 major banks by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969. A shareholder (R.C. Cooper) challenged it as violating Arts 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g) and 31(2).
Issues
  • Can a law of acquisition also be tested under Art 19? What does "compensation" mean? Is the Act discriminatory?
Held (Decision)
  • Parliament was competent, but the Act was struck down because the compensation principles in it were not the equivalent of the value of the banks' property and discriminated against the banks.
  • Rejected the A.K. Gopalan doctrine that the Fundamental Rights are mutually exclusive: the direct effect of a law on a right matters; a law of acquisition must also stand the test of Art 19(1)(f).
  • "Compensation" means the full money equivalent of the property taken; the legislature can lay down principles but not a colourable or illusory scheme.
Ratio decidendi

The object and effect of a law decide which Fundamental Rights are attracted; compensation means full market equivalent.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Parliament responded with the 25th Amendment ("amount") and Art 31C; the Government also issued the "privy purses" abolition move (Madhav Rao Scindia, 1970) - not covered in class.
Use in the exam

Cite for: rejection of the "mutual exclusivity" idea (why having both Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31 caused conflict) and for the meaning of compensation.

Case

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - the property angle

Citation / Court / Year

(1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge bench; 7:6 on the basic structure).

Facts
  • Challenge to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments, the Kerala Land Reforms Act and the Ninth Schedule additions (Kerala laws affecting a mutt's property).
Issues
  • Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights? Is the 25th Amendment valid?
Held (Decision)
  • Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure; Golak Nath overruled.
  • 25th Amendment: the substitution of "amount" for "compensation" and the removal of Art 19(1)(f) from acquisition laws were upheld; the first part of Art 31C was upheld; the second part (barring judicial review of the declaration that a law furthers Art 39(b)/(c)) was struck down.
Ratio decidendi

All constitutional amendments are subject to the basic-structure limit; property-related amendments of the 25th Amendment stood.

Significance / Later treatment
  • The professor's point: since Kesavananda allowed the Court to strike down an amendment that violates the basic structure, "the 44th Amendment was hardly necessary" - "most amendments are political". (His view; the textbook position is that the 44th Amendment removed the long-running conflict between property rights and socio-economic reform.)
  • Full treatment of Kesavananda in the lecture on Fundamental Rights v. Directive Principles.
Use in the exam

Cite as the case that finally upheld amount, and for "Parliament amends, Court tests for basic structure".

Case

K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011)

Citation / Court / Year

(2011) 9 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; K.S. Radhakrishnan J.).

Facts
  • Plantation owners challenged Karnataka legislation that took over their land holdings and argued that, with Art 31 gone, they were entitled to compensation under Art 300A.
Issues
  • After Art 31 was deleted, does Art 300A require (a) a public purpose and (b) compensation? Is there an inherent right to compensation in Entry 42 of List III?
Held (Decision)
  • Public purpose continues to be a pre-condition for deprivation of property under Art 300A.
  • There is no inherent or in-built right to compensation in Entry 42, List III (acquisition and requisitioning of property); the legislature has a margin to decide the quantum and manner.
  • However, a nil or illusory compensation must be justified on judicial standards and can be sustained only for measures that achieve greater social justice; the right to claim compensation can be inferred from Art 300A when the State's deprivation is arbitrary.
Ratio decidendi

Under Art 300A the State needs a law and a public purpose; compensation is not an absolute entitlement but the State must justify non-payment or illusory payment.

Use in the exam

Cite for "what remains of the right to property after the 44th Amendment?"

Case

Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020)

Citation / Court / Year

(2020) 2 SCC 569 (Supreme Court of India; Indu Malhotra and Ajay Rastogi JJ.; decided 8 January 2020).

Facts
  • In 1967-68 Himachal Pradesh took about 3.34 hectares of Vidya Devi's land to build a road without any acquisition proceeding or compensation. She learned of her entitlement only in 2010. The High Court dismissed her 2013 writ petition and left her to file a civil suit.
Issues
  • Can the State take land without following law and then claim ownership by adverse possession (over 42 years)? Is the right to property a human right?
Held (Decision)
  • The right to property, though no longer fundamental, is a human right and a constitutional right under Art 300A; the State can remove a person from property only under a procedure established by law.
  • The State cannot invoke adverse possession to defeat a citizen's title where it took the land without due acquisition; the Court inferred a duty to pay compensation and directed the State to pay compensation with solatium and interest.
Ratio decidendi

A welfare State cannot take private property without law and compensation; Art 300A protects against executive action unsupported by law.

Use in the exam

Use as the modern authority that Art 300A is a human right and for the "authority of law" requirement.

Case

Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah (2024)

Citation / Court / Year

2024 SCC OnLine SC 968 (2024 INSC 435); Supreme Court of India; P.S. Narasimha and Aravind Kumar JJ.; judgment dated 16 May 2024.

Facts
  • The Corporation sought to compulsorily acquire immovable property under s. 352 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980; the Calcutta High Court held that the Corporation did not have the power. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.
Issues
  • What does Art 300A's "authority of law" require beyond the existence of a statute?
Held (Decision)
  • Acquiring land without due procedure is outside the "authority of law". Art 300A contains seven sub-rights (the Court said the list is illustrative): (1) right to notice; (2) right to be heard; (3) right to a reasoned decision; (4) duty to acquire only for a public purpose; (5) right of restitution or fair compensation; (6) right to an efficient and expeditious process; (7) right of conclusion.
Ratio decidendi

Art 300A requires a fair, reasoned and procedurally sound acquisition process, not merely a statute.

Use in the exam

A short model line: "Post-44th Amendment, Art 300A is not a hollow right; Bimal Kumar Shah (2024) lists seven sub-rights which the State must respect."

Bela Banerjee "Compensation" in Art 31(2) means the just equivalent of what the owner has been deprived of (market value); the legislature cannot lay down arbitrary principles. 1955 Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act Amended Art 31(2) (and widened 31A): the adequacy of compensation cannot be questioned in court ; distinguished deprivation (31(1)) from acquisition/requisition (31(2)); added laws to the Ninth Schedule. 1967 Golak Nath v. State of Punjab Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights (overruled in 1973). 1970 R.C. Cooper v. Union of India ( Bank Nationalisation ) 11 judges; compensation must be the money equivalent ; Art 19(1)(f) also applies to a law of acquisition (rejects the "mutual exclusivity" idea). 1971 Constitution (25th Amendment) Act (in force 20 April 1972) "compensation" replaced by "amount" in Art 31(2) - the amount may be fixed by law or by principles in the law and may be paid other than in cash; adequacy not justiciable; Art 19(1)(f) not to apply to such laws; Art 31C inserted (laws to implement Art 39(b) and (c) protected from challenge under Arts 14, 19, 31). 1973 Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala Basic-structure doctrine; "amount" substitution upheld ; first part of Art 31C upheld, the "no judicial review" part struck down. 1976 42nd Amendment Extended Art 31C to all Directive Principles (struck down in Minerva Mills , 1980). 1978 Constitution (44th Amendment) Act (property provisions in force 20 June 1979) Repealed Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31; inserted Art 300A; added Art 30(1A) (compensation for acquisition of minority educational institutions' property must ensure the right under Art 30(1) is not restricted). 2011-13 K.T. Plantation (2011) ; LARR Act 2013 Public purpose is a pre-condition for Art 300A; new Act replaces the Land Acquisition Act 1894 (in force 1 Jan 2014). 2020 Vidya Devi v. State of H.P. Property is a human right ; the State cannot rely on adverse possession for land taken without due process. 2024 Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah Art 300A includes seven sub-rights (notice, hearing, reasoned decision, public purpose, fair compensation, efficient process, conclusion). Professor's hyperbole vs law The professor said that after "amount" replaced "compensation", the State could give " Re 1 for a Rs 1 crore property". That is a rhetorical illustration of the risk; it is not the law. The generally accepted position is that the amount must not be illusory or arbitrary (a fixed ₹1 would be open to challenge), and the post-1978 cases ( K.T. Plantation ; Vidya Devi ) require public purpose and fair compensation to be justified. Use the hyperbole only with that qualification. Case State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee (1954) Citation / Court / Year AIR 1954 SC 170; 1954 SCR 558 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; judgment by S.R. Das J. - verify the author before quoting ). Facts The West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948 provided for acquisition of land (mainly for rehabilitating refugees ) and fixed compensation at the market value as on 31 December 1946 , ignoring the rise in value after that date. Bela Banerjee , whose land was acquired, argued that compensation fixed at the 1946 value was not "compensation" within Art 31(2). Issues What does "compensation" in Art 31(2) mean? May the legislature fix it arbitrarily? Is the adequacy of compensation justiciable? Held (Decision) The Court held that " compensation " means a just equivalent of what the owner has been deprived of . The legislature may lay down principles for determining compensation, but if the principle is arbitrary or results in a sum that is not the just equivalent, it is not "compensation" and the law is unconstitutional to that extent. The provision fixing the 1946 market value (ignoring subsequent increase) was held invalid as not giving the owner a just equivalent. Ratio decidendi Compensation = just equivalent (market value) of the property taken ; adequacy of compensation is justiciable where the principle laid down is not relevant to determining the value at the time of acquisition. Significance / Later treatment Provoked the Fourth Amendment (1955) , which declared that the adequacy of compensation could not be questioned; later again diluted by the 25th Amendment (1971) ("amount"). The professor: " compensation means an amount equivalent to the market value - this was said in Bela Banerjee . Read the case; you will enjoy it." Use in the exam Cite for: "what does compensation mean?"; the move from compensation → amount ; the argument that just equivalent is protected by the text. Case State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga (1952) Citation / Court / Year AIR 1952 SC 252; 1952 SCR 889 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court). Facts The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 abolished the zamindari system, vested estates in the State and provided for compensation under a statutory scheme. The Maharaja of Darbhanga challenged it. The Patna High Court had held it unconstitutional (discriminatory and violating Art 14). Meanwhile, Parliament passed the First Amendment (Art 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule). Issues Did the Act satisfy Art 31(2) (public purpose and compensation)? Was it protected by Art 31(4)? Did it violate Art 14 / 19(1)(f)? Held (Decision) By a majority , the Court upheld the Act as a whole : it was for a public purpose (agrarian reform) and was protected by Art 31(4) from the compensation challenge, so courts could not scrutinise the adequacy of compensation under that Act; two specific provisions were held discriminatory under Art 14 (3:2). Ratio decidendi Laws for abolition of intermediaries are for a public purpose ; where Art 31(4) applies, the adequacy of compensation is not justiciable . Significance / Later treatment Professor's use: "the Court told the Bihar Government that compensation must be paid - but where was the money? Zamindars owned vast land - so Parliament amended the Constitution to say amount instead of compensation ." (The professor mentioned "Kameshwar Prasad Singh etc." - the actual name is Kameshwar Singh ; the holding on Art 31(4) was more nuanced than "compensation must be paid", so use the case for the background , and Bela Banerjee for the meaning of compensation.) Use in the exam Background case for zamindari abolition, Art 31A/31B, First Amendment and Art 31(4) protection. Verify details before quoting bench strengths. Case R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (Bank Nationalisation Case) (1970) Citation / Court / Year (1970) 1 SCC 248; AIR 1970 SC 564 (11-judge bench; majority 10:1, Ray J. dissenting). Facts Parliament nationalised 14 major banks by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969 . A shareholder ( R.C. Cooper ) challenged it as violating Arts 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g) and 31(2). Issues Can a law of acquisition also be tested under Art 19? What does "compensation" mean? Is the Act discriminatory? Held (Decision) Parliament was competent , but the Act was struck down because the compensation principles in it were not the equivalent of the value of the banks' property and discriminated against the banks. Rejected the A.K. Gopalan doctrine that the Fundamental Rights are mutually exclusive: the direct effect of a law on a right matters; a law of acquisition must also stand the test of Art 19(1)(f) . "Compensation" means the full money equivalent of the property taken; the legislature can lay down principles but not a colourable or illusory scheme. Ratio decidendi The object and effect of a law decide which Fundamental Rights are attracted; compensation means full market equivalent . Significance / Later treatment Parliament responded with the 25th Amendment ("amount") and Art 31C ; the Government also issued the "privy purses" abolition move (Madhav Rao Scindia, 1970) - not covered in class. Use in the exam Cite for: rejection of the "mutual exclusivity" idea (why having both Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31 caused conflict) and for the meaning of compensation. Case Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - the property angle Citation / Court / Year (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge bench; 7:6 on the basic structure). Facts Challenge to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments, the Kerala Land Reforms Act and the Ninth Schedule additions (Kerala laws affecting a mutt's property). Issues Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights? Is the 25th Amendment valid? Held (Decision) Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure ; Golak Nath overruled . 25th Amendment: the substitution of " amount " for "compensation" and the removal of Art 19(1)(f) from acquisition laws were upheld ; the first part of Art 31C was upheld; the second part (barring judicial review of the declaration that a law furthers Art 39(b)/(c)) was struck down . Ratio decidendi All constitutional amendments are subject to the basic-structure limit; property-related amendments of the 25th Amendment stood. Significance / Later treatment The professor's point: since Kesavananda allowed the Court to strike down an amendment that violates the basic structure, " the 44th Amendment was hardly necessary " - "most amendments are political". (His view; the textbook position is that the 44th Amendment removed the long-running conflict between property rights and socio-economic reform.) Full treatment of Kesavananda in the lecture on Fundamental Rights v. Directive Principles. Use in the exam Cite as the case that finally upheld amount , and for "Parliament amends, Court tests for basic structure". Case K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011) Citation / Court / Year (2011) 9 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; K.S. Radhakrishnan J.). Facts Plantation owners challenged Karnataka legislation that took over their land holdings and argued that, with Art 31 gone, they were entitled to compensation under Art 300A. Issues After Art 31 was deleted, does Art 300A require (a) a public purpose and (b) compensation? Is there an inherent right to compensation in Entry 42 of List III? Held (Decision) Public purpose continues to be a pre-condition for deprivation of property under Art 300A. There is no inherent or in-built right to compensation in Entry 42, List III (acquisition and requisitioning of property); the legislature has a margin to decide the quantum and manner . However, a nil or illusory compensation must be justified on judicial standards and can be sustained only for measures that achieve greater social justice ; the right to claim compensation can be inferred from Art 300A when the State's deprivation is arbitrary. Ratio decidendi Under Art 300A the State needs a law and a public purpose ; compensation is not an absolute entitlement but the State must justify non-payment or illusory payment. Use in the exam Cite for "what remains of the right to property after the 44th Amendment?" Case Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020) Citation / Court / Year (2020) 2 SCC 569 (Supreme Court of India; Indu Malhotra and Ajay Rastogi JJ.; decided 8 January 2020). Facts In 1967-68 Himachal Pradesh took about 3.34 hectares of Vidya Devi 's land to build a road without any acquisition proceeding or compensation . She learned of her entitlement only in 2010. The High Court dismissed her 2013 writ petition and left her to file a civil suit. Issues Can the State take land without following law and then claim ownership by adverse possession (over 42 years)? Is the right to property a human right? Held (Decision) The right to property, though no longer fundamental, is a human right and a constitutional right under Art 300A ; the State can remove a person from property only under a procedure established by law . The State cannot invoke adverse possession to defeat a citizen's title where it took the land without due acquisition; the Court inferred a duty to pay compensation and directed the State to pay compensation with solatium and interest. Ratio decidendi A welfare State cannot take private property without law and compensation ; Art 300A protects against executive action unsupported by law. Use in the exam Use as the modern authority that Art 300A is a human right and for the "authority of law" requirement. Case Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah (2024) Citation / Court / Year 2024 SCC OnLine SC 968 (2024 INSC 435); Supreme Court of India; P.S. Narasimha and Aravind Kumar JJ.; judgment dated 16 May 2024. Facts The Corporation sought to compulsorily acquire immovable property under s. 352 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980; the Calcutta High Court held that the Corporation did not have the power. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal. Issues What does Art 300A's "authority of law" require beyond the existence of a statute? Held (Decision) Acquiring land without due procedure is outside the "authority of law". Art 300A contains seven sub-rights (the Court said the list is illustrative): (1) right to notice; (2) right to be heard; (3) right to a reasoned decision; (4) duty to acquire only for a public purpose; (5) right of restitution or fair compensation; (6) right to an efficient and expeditious process; (7) right of conclusion. Ratio decidendi Art 300A requires a fair, reasoned and procedurally sound acquisition process, not merely a statute. Use in the exam A short model line: "Post-44th Amendment, Art 300A is not a hollow right; Bimal Kumar Shah (2024) lists seven sub-rights which the State must respect."

sections.title: 6.7 What difference did the 44th Amendment make? (the professor's question, fully answered)
sections.html:
• Student answer (professor: "yes, partly"): "We cannot go directly to the Supreme Court; Fundamental Right is gone." → Correct: Art 32 is for enforcement of Fundamental Rights; for Art 300A the remedy is a writ under Art 226 in the High Court (or a civil suit), with appeal to the Supreme Court. The professor: "it is no bad thing - you can go to the High Court locally; no need to go far."
  • The real difference - who can take property and how: Before 1978, if the State wanted property, an ordinary Act that violated Art 19(1)(f) or Art 31 was void under Art 13(2); the Government therefore resorted to constitutional amendments (First, Fourth, 17th, 25th...). After 1978, an Act does not need a constitutional amendment - it only needs to satisfy Art 300A; Art 13 is not invoked on a property ground.
  • Who can amend the Constitution? Only Parliament (Art 368) - subject to the basic-structure limit (Kesavananda); a State legislature cannot. So earlier, a State wanting to acquire property in a manner that violated Fundamental Rights could not do it by an Act; it needed Parliament to amend the Constitution.
  • Art 13 point: Art 13 speaks of "laws" violating Part III; since property is no longer in Part III, a property law cannot be struck down as a violation of a property Fundamental Right; it can still be challenged under Art 14 (arbitrariness), Art 21, Art 300A, or because it lacks a public purpose / procedural fairness.
  • Another change: the minority institutions safeguard (Art 30(1A)) and the agrarian reform shields (Arts 31A-31C, Ninth Schedule) remain.
  • Was the amendment necessary? The professor's view: "after Kesavananda, which allows challenge to every amendment on basic-structure grounds, the 44th Amendment was not really required". The textbook reasons: to end the conflict between property rights and social-welfare legislation; to stop repeated amendments (Janata Government's reform).

sections.title: 6.8 Modern statute: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (LARR)
sections.html:
• Replaced the colonial Land Acquisition Act, 1894; in force 1 January 2014.
  • Compensation: market value × a multiplier (1 to 2 in rural areas depending on distance from urban area) plus 100 per cent solatium → in practice up to four times the market value in rural areas and two times in urban areas (the professor: "four times in rural areas, two times in the city"). Compare "amount" under the 25th Amendment.
  • Other features: Social Impact Assessment; consent (80 per cent of affected families for private projects; 70 per cent for PPP projects); rehabilitation and resettlement entitlements; safeguards for irrigated multi-crop land.
  • Case: Indore Development Authority v. Manoharlal (2020) (5-judge bench) - interprets s. 24(2) (lapse of acquisition) of the 2013 Act (verify before citing).
  • Professor's political commentary about which party passed the Act and why is omitted.

sections.title: 6.9 Questions asked in COLA 12 - model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. Art 19(1) lists (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and then (g). Where is (f)? Whose mistake is it?

Model answer

No one's mistake. Art 19(1)(f) (right to acquire, hold and dispose of property) was repealed by the Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978; the remaining clauses were not re-lettered. The right to property was moved out of Part III into Art 300A.

Question asked in class

Q2. Dr Ambedkar put the right to property in two places - Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31. Why? Could one not suffice?

Model answer

They served different purposes: Art 19(1)(f) was a citizen's freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property, subject to reasonable restrictions (Art 19(5)); Art 31 governed the State's power of compulsory acquisition/deprivation, for any person - law, public purpose, compensation. In the professor's words, "19 gave us the right to keep property; 31 acknowledged the State's right to take it" - a built-in contradiction that produced decades of litigation and amendments, ending with deletion of both in 1978 and the insertion of Art 300A.

Question asked in class

Q3. What difference did it make when Arts 19(1)(f) and 31 were removed and Art 300A inserted? Do people now have no right to property?

Model answer

People do have the right - as a constitutional right under Art 300A and a human right, not as a Fundamental Right. Differences: (i) no direct Art 32 petition; remedy is the High Court under Art 226; (ii) property laws are no longer tested against Art 13 on the ground of property, so the State can acquire by ordinary law and does not need a constitutional amendment; (iii) the test is now authority of law + public purpose + fair compensation/procedure (K.T. Plantation; Vidya Devi; Bimal Kumar Shah).

Question asked in class

Q4. Can the State (or a Professor acting for the State) take a student's mobile phone?

Model answer

Only by authority of law. The university is "State" under Art 12 (statutory, State-funded and controlled - Ajay Hasia), so Part III and Art 300A bind it. Taking the phone without any law violates Art 300A; the State cannot rely on executive discretion (Vidya Devi).

Question asked in class

Q5. State the three conditions for compulsory acquisition of property.

Model answer

(1) Authority of law (a legislature-enacted statute - not the wide Art 13 "law" of orders and customs); (2) public purpose (never a purely private one); (3) compensation (market value → "amount" → fair compensation under LARR 2013).

Question asked in class

Q6. What is "eminent domain"?

Model answer

The sovereign power of the State to take private property for public use; Latin dominium eminens; inherent in sovereignty and exercised subject to law, public purpose and compensation.

Question asked in class

Q7. What does "law" mean in "authority of law"?

Model answer

A valid law enacted by the competent legislature (Parliament or State Legislature) - not a mere executive order or administrative decision. The professor: "law means not the Art 13 'law'; it is law enacted by the legislature."

Question asked in class

Q8. Can property be acquired for a private farmhouse of a politician?

Model answer

No. Only for a public purpose - education, airports, railways, defence, roads. Acquisition for a private purpose violates Art 300A.

Question asked in class

Q9. Which constitutional amendment replaced "compensation" with "amount"? What did "compensation" mean earlier?

Model answer

The 25th Amendment (1971) (in force 1972) - Parliament under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Earlier, "compensation" meant the just equivalent / market value of the property (State of W.B. v. Bela Banerjee, 1954; R.C. Cooper, 1970). The change was upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

Question asked in class

Q10. Which amendment removed the right to property from the Fundamental Rights?

Model answer

The 44th Amendment (1978) - it repealed Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31 and inserted Art 300A (and Art 30(1A)).

Question asked in class

Q11. Why were so many constitutional amendments needed on property? Who can amend the Constitution?

Model answer

Because Courts struck down acquisition laws that offended Arts 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 (via Art 13), the Government had to amend the Constitution (1st, 4th, 17th, 25th, 42nd); only Parliament can amend (Art 368), subject to the basic structure doctrine.

Question asked in class

Q12. What is the modern law on compensation for acquisition of land?

Model answer

LARR Act 2013: replaced the 1894 Act; market value with multiplier plus solatium (up to 4x in rural areas, 2x in urban areas), consent, SIA, R&R. Constitutional footing: Art 300A and Entry 42, List III.
