exam.title: Reasonable Restrictions on Art 19 - Grounds in Art 19(2) to 19(6), Assembly, Association, Movement, Profession, and Press/Broadcast/Voter Cases

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Rule of the lecture: the rights in Arts 14 and 19 are not absolute. Restrictions can be imposed only on the grounds listed in the Constitution (no fresh ground can be added - Kaushal Kishor, 2023), only by law, and they must be reasonable.

Grounds per clause (memorise): 19(2) speech - 8 grounds; 19(3) assembly - 2 (sovereignty and integrity of India, public order); 19(4) association - 3 (the same two + morality); 19(5) movement and residence - interests of the general public + protection of any Scheduled Tribe; 19(6) profession/trade - general public interest + professional or technical qualifications + State monopoly.

Cases to know from this lecture: Brij Bhushan (no pre-censorship of press) v. K.A. Abbas (pre-censorship of films valid); R. Rajagopal (1994); Express Newspapers / Sakal / Bennett Coleman / Indian Express (indirect control of press); Cricket Association of Bengal (airwaves are public property); 2G case (natural resources); Union of India v. ADR (voters' right to know); Ramlila Maidan (2012), Amit Sahni (2020), Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018) on protest; T.K. Rangarajan (no right to strike); Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) on passports; Kaushal Kishor (2023).

What has been left out of this lecture

The first part of the class (a political post about the Chief Justice; party-political jibes) and long stretches in the second half consisted of the professor's personal, unverified allegations about named political figures (including stories about private relationships, a suicide, a governor's residence, and criminal allegations against politicians), a drug-free-campus speech, a long IPKF-style political tangent, and anecdotes about students' hostels. These are not legal content, several are unverified allegations about identifiable people, and they have been omitted entirely. Only the constitutional law and the named cases are kept.

Transcript problems: the case the professor called "Sukhanand Swami" (a "criminal case" to be read on dissent) could not be identified from the garbled text - ask the professor before citing it. The case about a society that sells land only to members of one religion is probably Zoroastrian Co-operative Housing Society (2005) - the professor himself could not recall the name; verify before use.

sections.title: 7.1 Three rules for every restriction on Art 19
sections.html:
RuleContentAuthority
1. Only the listed groundsEach of Arts 19(2)-(6) lists exclusive grounds. "Those restrictions can be only on the grounds listed; no fresh ground can be added."Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023) (Art 19(2) grounds are exhaustive; no additional restrictions can be read in from Art 21 etc.).
2. By lawThe restriction must be imposed by "law" (statute, ordinance, rule made under a statute - Art 13(3)(a)); an executive/administrative order or mere departmental instruction is not enough.Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) (passport refusal without law); Anuradha Bhasin (2020); see Lecture 3.
3. ReasonableThe restriction must not be arbitrary or excessive; proportionality (legitimate aim, rational nexus, necessity, balancing).State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952); Chintaman Rao v. State of M.P. (1950); Anuradha Bhasin (2020).

sections.title: 7.3 Freedom of assembly - Art 19(1)(b) and 19(3)
sections.html:
• Text: "to assemble peaceably and without arms." An armed or violent assembly is outside the right at the threshold; a peaceful assembly may still be regulated for sovereignty and integrity or public order.
  • Professor's practical view (stated in class): a gathering is "peaceful" only if it can be controlled; if you bring "lakhs of people from all over the country and the world" to a capital that "cannot accommodate" them, there is no guarantee of peace. Hence regulation by time, place and number is reasonable: fix time slots (1-3 hours), designated spaces and limits on numbers. (This is his policy opinion; the law is in the cases below.)
  • Right to assemble ≠ right to occupy public roads indefinitely. Compare the tests: place (public road v. designated ground), duration (indefinite v. limited), effect on other citizens' rights (movement, livelihood, Art 21).
Case

In Re: Ramlila Maidan Incident dated 4/5.06.2011 v. Home Secretary, Union of India (2012)

Citation / Court / Year

(2012) 5 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India; B.S. Chauhan and Swatanter Kumar JJ.; suo motu; decided in 2012 - verify the date of judgment before citing).

Facts
  • On 4 June 2011 a yoga camp (permission granted for yoga) at Ramlila Maidan, New Delhi turned into an anti-corruption protest and hunger strike led by Baba Ramdev, with tens of thousands of participants. Section 144 CrPC was imposed; around midnight (4/5 June) the police used tear gas, lathi-charge and water cannons to evict the sleeping crowd. A woman participant (reported as Rajbala) later died of injuries and many people were injured (the professor said "about 80").
  • The Court took suo motu cognisance of the incident.
Issues
  • Whether the police action infringed the right to assemble peaceably and to express views (Art 19(1)(a),(b)) and Art 21; whether the s. 144 order and the midnight eviction were justified.
Held (Decision)
  • The right to assemble and to protest peacefully is a Fundamental Right, not absolute, and may be reasonably regulated in the interest of public order; restrictions must be proportionate.
  • The police action at midnight against a sleeping, peaceful crowd was excessive and unjustified; the State must facilitate peaceful assemblies, not stifle them, and excessive force is impermissible. (The judgment is also widely cited for treating the right to sleep as part of Art 21 - verify the wording before quoting.)
Ratio decidendi

Peaceful protest is protected by Arts 19(1)(a) and (b); police power under s. 144 CrPC / BNSS s. 163 must be exercised reasonably and proportionately.

Use in the exam

The professor: "a very important case on protest - read it." He compared it with Amit Sahni (roads cannot be occupied indefinitely).

Case

Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (the Shaheen Bagh case) (2020)

Citation / Court / Year

(2020) 10 SCC 439 (Supreme Court of India; bench of S.K. Kaul, Aniruddha Bose and Krishna Murari JJ.; decided 7 October 2020 - verify bench before quoting).

Facts
  • Protestors against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 occupied a public road at Shaheen Bagh (Delhi) for months, blocking commuters; a petition sought removal of the blockade.
Issues
  • Does the right to protest allow indefinite occupation of a public road at the cost of other citizens?
Held (Decision)
  • Public ways and public places cannot be occupied indefinitely; protest must be at designated places; the right to protest and the right to movement (and to livelihood) of others must be balanced; the administration must act to clear obstructions.
Ratio decidendi

The right to protest is not unlimited; it cannot be exercised by blocking public roads indefinitely.

Use in the exam

Professor: "the Supreme Court said public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely for protest at the expense of other citizens."

Case

Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018)

Citation / Court / Year

(2018) 17 SCC 324 (Supreme Court of India; A.K. Sikri J.; verify bench).

Facts
  • The National Green Tribunal had banned protests at Jantar Mantar, Delhi; the NGO challenged the order.
Held (Decision)
  • The right to protest peacefully is a Fundamental Right; a blanket ban was unreasonable. The State may regulate (time, place, manner) and designate protest sites, but must make a balanced arrangement for protest, with reasonable guidelines on noise, permissions and space.
Ratio decidendi

Regulation, not prohibition, of protest is permissible (proportionality).

Use in the exam

Pairs naturally with Anuradha Bhasin (proportionality) in a protest problem question; the lecture 3 hypothetical about Jantar Mantar is the same issue.

  • Himat Lal K. Shah v. Commissioner of Police, Ahmedabad (1973): a rule requiring prior permission for any public meeting on a street was struck down: the right to assemble cannot be left to the unguided discretion of the police; reasonable rules about time, place and manner are valid (verify citation: (1973) 1 SCC 227).
  • Section 144 CrPC → BNSS s. 163: powers to issue prohibitory orders; must be used for urgent prevention and cannot be a tool to suppress dissent (Anuradha Bhasin).

sections.title: 7.4 Association, unions, co-operative societies - Art 19(1)(c) and 19(4)
sections.html:
• Words: "to form associations or unions or co-operative societies" (the last words added by the 97th Amendment, 2011, along with Art 43B and Part IXB). Restrictions only on sovereignty and integrity of India, public order, morality - and reasonableness.
  • Scope: the right is to form an association; it does not include a right to recognition, to a collective bargaining outcome, or a right to strike.
Case

T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003)

Citation / Court / Year

(2003) 6 SCC 581 (Supreme Court of India; Banerjee and Lahoti JJ.; decided 6 August 2003).

Facts
  • The Tamil Nadu Government dismissed about 1.7 lakh employees who went on strike in July 2003 and invoked the Tamil Nadu Essential Services Maintenance Act (TESMA) ordinance. The employees' association challenged the dismissals.
Issues
  • Do government employees have a fundamental right to strike? Does the right to form associations include a right to strike?
Held (Decision)
  • Government employees have no fundamental, statutory or moral right to strike. The right to form an association under Art 19(1)(c) does not guarantee the effectiveness of the association or the right to resort to strike; strike is not a fundamental right.
  • The Court also said that the Government must be fair and that employees' remedies are negotiation, representation and legal remedies, but strike as a weapon is not a constitutional guarantee; society's interest in essential services prevails.
Ratio decidendi

No fundamental right to strike (for government employees) - Art 19(1)(c) protects forming unions, not striking.

Use in the exam

Professor's extension: "I can add that students of government universities also do not have a fundamental right to strike" (his opinion; cite Rangarajan for the principle and note that the Court has not ruled on student strikes specifically).

Case

Zoroastrian Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar, Co-operative Societies (2005) - (probable case)

Citation / Court / Year

(2005) 5 SCC 632 (Supreme Court of India; 3 judges) - verify; the professor could not name the case.

Facts
  • A co-operative housing society formed by Parsis adopted a bye-law that plots will be sold only to Zoroastrians (Parsis). The Registrar held the bye-law invalid.
Held (Decision)
  • The Court upheld the bye-law: a voluntary association has the right to decide who may be its members (Art 19(1)(c)); the Court distinguished a purely private society from public bodies and said this did not violate Arts 14, 15 or 29(2) as the Society was a private association of a small religious community with no State aid.
Use in the exam

The professor: "I do not quite understand this case - the Supreme Court allowed it, perhaps because the society was private." Use it for "can an association restrict membership?" and flag that the point is controversial.

sections.title: 7.5 Freedom of movement and residence - Art 19(1)(d),(e) and 19(5)
sections.html:
• Classroom illustration: "my hand hurts; can I move around while teaching?" → the freedom is real but not absolute: reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public (traffic, quarantine, security) and for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe.
  • Why Scheduled Tribes? Tribal communities are a homogeneous, vulnerable society with distinct language, culture and land relations; outsiders may exploit them or disturb their way of life, and some groups are isolated (the professor mentioned a foreign researcher killed by an isolated tribe on a closed island) - so entry itself may be controlled "for their protection and ours".
MechanismDetailsAuthority
Inner Line Permit (ILP)Travel permit required to enter Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland (and Manipur, from 2019-20) for Indian citizens from other parts of India; derived from the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873. The professor mentioned that he never needed one as he travelled as the State's guest, but that "police can ask for it any time; always carry it".Art 19(5) (protection of Scheduled Tribes); verify the current list.
Protected Area Permits (PAP)For foreigners in certain border areas (Foreigners (Protected Areas) Order, 1958).-
Restrictions on transfer of tribal landLand in Scheduled/tribal areas cannot be transferred to non-tribals; the professor noted that outsiders sometimes bypass this through long leases, benami arrangements or hotels built on tribal land. The Supreme Court has held that transfer of tribal land to non-tribals (and leases to private companies for mining) is void under the Fifth Schedule protections.Samatha v. State of A.P. (1997) 8 SCC 191 (verify); Fifth and Sixth Schedules.
SikkimSpecial protection (Art 371F); the professor said that Sikkimese women who marry outside lose certain property/status rights, "to preserve a homogeneous society". (Reported by the professor from conversation; verify before quoting - the legal position involves Sikkim Subject rules and recent court rulings.)Art 371F.
Passport / right to travel abroadBefore the Passport Act, 1967, passports were issued by executive discretion. In Satwant Singh Sawhney v. D. Ramarathnam (1967) the Supreme Court held that the right to travel abroad is part of "personal liberty" under Art 21 and cannot be denied except by procedure established by law; the Government then enacted the Passport Act 1967, which still left wide discretion (s. 10(3)). In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) that discretion was tested and Art 21 given a due-process reading (Lecture 8).Art 21; see Lecture 8.
SurveillanceKharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1962): domiciliary visits at night violated Art 21; shadowing and reporting movements did not violate Art 19(1)(d) because "freedom of movement" was not infringed by surveillance. Later overtaken by Puttaswamy (2017).Arts 19(1)(d), 21.

Mechanism Details Authority Inner Line Permit (ILP) Travel permit required to enter Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland (and Manipur , from 2019-20) for Indian citizens from other parts of India; derived from the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873 . The professor mentioned that he never needed one as he travelled as the State's guest, but that "police can ask for it any time; always carry it". Art 19(5) (protection of Scheduled Tribes); verify the current list. Protected Area Permits (PAP) For foreigners in certain border areas (Foreigners (Protected Areas) Order, 1958). - Restrictions on transfer of tribal land Land in Scheduled/tribal areas cannot be transferred to non-tribals; the professor noted that outsiders sometimes bypass this through long leases, benami arrangements or hotels built on tribal land . The Supreme Court has held that transfer of tribal land to non-tribals (and leases to private companies for mining) is void under the Fifth Schedule protections. Samatha v. State of A.P. (1997) 8 SCC 191 (verify); Fifth and Sixth Schedules. Sikkim Special protection (Art 371F); the professor said that Sikkimese women who marry outside lose certain property/status rights, "to preserve a homogeneous society". (Reported by the professor from conversation; verify before quoting - the legal position involves Sikkim Subject rules and recent court rulings.) Art 371F. Passport / right to travel abroad Before the Passport Act, 1967 , passports were issued by executive discretion. In Satwant Singh Sawhney v. D. Ramarathnam (1967) the Supreme Court held that the right to travel abroad is part of "personal liberty" under Art 21 and cannot be denied except by procedure established by law ; the Government then enacted the Passport Act 1967 , which still left wide discretion (s. 10(3)). In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) that discretion was tested and Art 21 given a due-process reading (Lecture 8). Art 21; see Lecture 8. Surveillance Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1962): domiciliary visits at night violated Art 21; shadowing and reporting movements did not violate Art 19(1)(d) because "freedom of movement" was not infringed by surveillance. Later overtaken by Puttaswamy (2017). Arts 19(1)(d), 21.

sections.title: 7.6 Freedom of profession, trade and business - Art 19(1)(g) and 19(6)
sections.html:
• Four words: "profession", "occupation", "trade", "business" - the Court interprets them widely; but the freedom is not unlimited.
  • (i) Professional or technical qualifications - Art 19(6)(i): to practise law you need an LL.B. degree and enrolment as an advocate (Advocates Act, 1961, ss. 29 and 33: only advocates may practise in courts); to perform heart surgery you need a medical degree and registration (National Medical Commission Act, 2019); to build a building you need a registered architect/engineer. A person can argue their own case but not another's unless enrolled; "the monopoly of the Bar in courts" is a qualification-based restriction. The professor's anecdote of a retired income-tax official appearing in tax matters illustrates that "knowing the subject" is not the same as "having the licence of the Bar". Bar Council of India v. A.K. Balaji (2018) 5 SCC 379: foreign lawyers/firms cannot practise Indian law in India (but may visit on a temporary fly-in/fly-out basis for international arbitration).
  • Interest rates: the professor mentioned that when the State caps interest rates or price, a trader cannot sell/buy above it - a general-public-interest regulation (Art 19(6)).
  • (ii) State monopoly - Art 19(6)(ii): the State (or a State corporation) may carry on a trade or business to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens. Professor's rationale: a welfare State must ensure availability of both profitable and non-profitable services; it therefore keeps some profit-making activities (e.g. railways) and uses the profit to fund services that make a loss; "many monopolies have been diluted since". Authority: Akadasi Padhan v. State of Orissa (1963) (State monopoly in kendu leaves valid; a law creating a monopoly under 19(6)(ii) need not separately satisfy the "reasonableness" test).
  • Important qualification: Chintaman Rao v. State of M.P. (1950) - restrictions must be reasonable, not arbitrary or excessive (a ban on bidi-manufacture workers during the agricultural season was struck down); Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978) - the right to carry on business includes the right to close it down (a law requiring government permission for closure struck down); Khoday Distilleries v. Sri Mahadeshwara Sahakara Sakkare Karkhane (1995) - there is no fundamental right to trade in liquor (a harmful trade, res extra commercium, which the State may prohibit or regulate heavily).

sections.title: 7.7 Press, broadcast and voters - the cases revised in this lecture
sections.html:
The professor revisited the Art 19(1)(a) cases of Lectures 2-4 and linked them with new ones. Revise the cards in Lectures 2 and 4 for the cases below and learn the new cards here.

Case / themeOne-line ruleWhere full card
Romesh Thappar (1950)Freedom of circulation is part of freedom of the press; restriction must fit Art 19(2).Lecture 2
Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950)Pre-censorship of a newspaper (an order that a journal's content be submitted for approval) is a restriction on the freedom of the press and invalid.Lecture 2
K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970)Pre-censorship of films is permissible (film = different medium with greater impact).Lecture 2
Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1958); Sakal Papers (1962); Bennett Coleman (1972)Indirect control of press (page limits, price-page schedules, newsprint quotas) is a restriction on speech and violates Art 19(1)(a).Lecture 4
Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985)Taxation affecting newspapers (customs duty on newsprint) must be considered in the light of press freedom; the Court did not strike it down but asked the Government to reconsider.Lecture 4
Tuljapurkar (2015)Obscenity and historically respected figures; "very important from the exam point of view".Lecture 4
Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)Airwaves are public property; the right to communicate and receive information is part of Art 19(1)(a); State monopoly over broadcasting is not protected.Lecture 2; plus Art 39 in 7.9 below
Case

R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (the "Auto Shankar" case) (1994)

Citation / Court / Year

(1994) 6 SCC 632 (Supreme Court of India; B.P. Jeevan Reddy J. for the Bench; decided 7 October 1994).

Facts
  • Auto Shankar (Gauri Shankar), a prisoner convicted of six murders and sentenced to death, wrote an autobiography in jail, which allegedly described his links with police and prison officials. He gave it to his wife to be published by the Tamil magazine "Nakkheeran". Prison authorities (the Inspector General of Prisons) asked the publisher not to publish and threatened action; the magazine petitioned.
  • The professor's retelling of this case included invented comic details; only the facts above are the case.
Issues
  • Can the State prevent publication in advance (prior restraint)? Is there a right to privacy in Art 21 against publication of one's life story? What may the press publish about public officials?
Held (Decision)
  • Right to privacy is implicit in Art 21; but no one can restrain publication of matters that are already public records (including court records).
  • Prior restraint is not permissible; the remedy of a person defamed or whose privacy is invaded is after publication (damages / action). Public officials have no right to privacy for their official acts and duties (except in matters under the Official Secrets Act); the press may criticise them. The State and its officials cannot seek to restrain the publication of material about their conduct.
  • The Court said the authorities could not stop the autobiography; whether it was defamatory could be tested after publication.
Ratio decidendi

No prior restraint on the press; privacy is protected by Art 21 but yields where the matter is in the public record or concerns the official conduct of public servants.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Landmark in press freedom v. privacy (links with Brij Bhushan). Professor: "read it in the original - I will not tell you more; you will enjoy it" (the case, not the stories)."
Use in the exam

Cite for: no pre-censorship of press; privacy/defamation after publication; public officials and their duties.

Case

Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (the 2G Spectrum case) (2012)

Citation / Court / Year

(2012) 3 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India; G.S. Singhvi and A.K. Ganguly JJ.; decided 2 February 2012). Follow-up: Special Reference No. 1 of 2012 (2012) 10 SCC 1.

Facts
  • In 2008 the Department of Telecommunications allotted licences and 2G spectrum at a low fixed price on a "first come, first served" basis to a few applicants, who then sold equity at high valuations. Public-interest petitioners challenged the allotments.
Issues
  • Can scarce natural resources be allotted without a transparent, competitive method? What constitutional principles bind the State in distributing them?
Held (Decision)
  • The first-come-first-served method as implemented was arbitrary and unconstitutional (Art 14); the licences were quashed. The Court treated natural resources, including spectrum, as public property held in trust by the State for the people, and said their distribution must serve the common good (Art 39(b)): "The State is a trustee."
  • Hence auction is the preferred method for maximising revenue; but in the Presidential Reference (2012) the Court clarified that auction is not the only constitutionally permissible method for all natural resources - a method must be fair, transparent and non-arbitrary, and the choice depends on the objective.
Ratio decidendi

The State must allocate natural resources fairly and transparently for the public good; resources like spectrum are public property (Art 14, Art 39(b)).

Use in the exam

The professor's link: the "air and spectrum" are "not anybody's father's property" and "belong to the people of India" - connect with Art 39(b) and (c) (material resources of the community to subserve the common good; concentration of wealth to be avoided) and with the Cricket Association reasoning that airwaves are public property. (His description of the political side of the 2G matter is omitted.)

Case

Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) and PUCL v. Union of India (2003)

Citation / Court / Year

(2002) 5 SCC 294 (Supreme Court of India; 3 judges; 2 May 2002) and (2003) 4 SCC 399 (13 March 2003).

Facts
  • The Association for Democratic Reforms sought directions that candidates for election disclose their criminal antecedents, assets and liabilities, and educational qualifications. The Election Commission issued disclosure directions after the Supreme Court's decision; Parliament then amended the Representation of the People Act (s. 33B) to dilute them.
Issues
  • Do voters have a fundamental right to know the background of candidates? Does this override a candidate's claim to privacy?
Held (Decision)
  • Voters have a fundamental right to information about candidates under Art 19(1)(a) (the right to know/receive information is part of freedom of speech and expression), because an informed vote is essential for free and fair elections (a basic feature).
  • The candidate's right to privacy is subordinate in the public interest. In PUCL (2003) the Court struck down s. 33B RPA (which tried to nullify the ADR directions) and upheld the voter's right to know.
Ratio decidendi

The right to know the antecedents of candidates is part of Art 19(1)(a); informed voters are essential for democracy.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024) (Constitution Bench, 15 February 2024): the Electoral Bond Scheme was held unconstitutional because it infringed the voter's right to information about political funding under Art 19(1)(a) (verify citation before use).
Use in the exam

Professor: "the voters' right to know... candidates argued that it is their privacy; the Supreme Court said, you must tell - and then people began to be exposed (the affidavit)."

Case

Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2023)

Citation / Court / Year

Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 113 of 2016; (2023) 4 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench: S.A. Nazeer, A.S. Bopanna, B.R. Gavai, V. Ramasubramanian and B.V. Nagarathna JJ.; majority by Ramasubramanian J.; Nagarathna J. concurring in part and separate; decided 3 January 2023).

Facts
  • After the 2016 gang-rape of a minor and her mother on a highway in Bulandshahr, a political leader (a former Minister) described the incident as a "political conspiracy and nothing else". The victims' family sought action and the Court referred larger questions to a Constitution Bench: restrictions on free speech by public functionaries; whether Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons; and vicarious liability of the Government for a Minister's statements.
Issues
  • (1) Can additional restrictions beyond Art 19(2) be imposed on a public functionary's free speech? (2) Can Fundamental Rights (Arts 19, 21) be claimed against non-State actors? (3) Does the State have a positive duty to protect liberty against private actors? (4) Is a Minister's statement attributable to the Government by collective responsibility (Art 75(3))?
Held (Decision)
  • No additional restrictions beyond Art 19(2) can be imposed on free speech (even for public functionaries); the grounds are exhaustive. (Nagarathna J. agreed.)
  • Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against persons other than the State or its instrumentalities (horizontal application, at least for Art 21 and in appropriate cases Art 19).
  • The State has a positive duty to protect the life and liberty of citizens even against threats from private persons (Nagarathna J. dissented: the duty is negative).
  • A Minister's statement cannot be vicariously attributed to the Government by invoking collective responsibility (even if it concerns State affairs); but if officials act on it and cause loss, the conduct may be actionable. Nagarathna J. held that a statement made as the Government's delegate can be attributed.
Ratio decidendi

Art 19(2) grounds are exhaustive; horizontal application of Arts 19 and 21; ministerial speech is not automatically government speech.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Nagarathna J.: public functionaries owe a duty of responsible speech (dignity, equality, fraternity); Parliament may legislate; political parties can regulate through codes of conduct.
Use in the exam

Listed by the professor as an exam-hint case ("Kaushal Kishor - horizontal application"). In the lecture it was used to say: "free speech and the obligations of public functionaries - political dissent and unpopular opinion are protected, subject only to the specific grounds." Art 75(3) (collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha) is the constitutional hook.

sections.title: 7.9 Art 39(b) and (c) - why airwaves and spectrum are "everyone's property"
sections.html:
• Art 39(b): the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good. Art 39(c): the operation of the economic system must not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment.
  • Application (professor): air and space (the electromagnetic spectrum) "belong to the people of India"; the State may license them, but must do so on terms that benefit the people, and cannot give a monopoly to anyone arbitrarily (Cricket Association; 2G).
  • Distinction: Art 39(b),(c) are Directive Principles (non-justiciable), but the Courts have used them to interpret Arts 14 and 19 (see Lecture on FR v. DPSP).

Art 39(c): the operation of the economic system must not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment. sections.title: 7.10 Professor's questions in COLA 13 - model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. Name the grounds on which the right to freedom of speech and expression can be restricted.

Model answer

Under Art 19(2): (1) sovereignty and integrity of India; (2) security of the State; (3) friendly relations with foreign States; (4) public order; (5) decency or morality; (6) contempt of court; (7) defamation; (8) incitement to an offence. There is no ground of "peace" or "tranquillity". (First Amendment 1951 added public order, friendly relations, incitement; 16th Amendment 1963 added sovereignty and integrity.)

Question asked in class

Q2. How many grounds restrict assembly (19(1)(b)) and association (19(1)(c))? Which is extra in association?

Model answer

Two for assembly (sovereignty and integrity of India; public order). Three for association - the same two plus morality (Art 19(4)).

Question asked in class

Q3. On what grounds can the right to move freely and to reside be restricted?

Model answer

Under Art 19(5): in the interests of the general public, or for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe (e.g. Inner Line Permit; restrictions on entry/land transfer in tribal areas).

Question asked in class

Q4. Why are outsiders required to take permits in tribal areas?

Model answer

To protect the land, culture, language and vulnerable communities of the tribes from exploitation and disturbance (and sometimes to protect outsiders from isolated tribes). The restriction is justified by Art 19(5). Legal tools: ILP (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation 1873), Fifth and Sixth Schedule land protections (Samatha, 1997).

Question asked in class

Q5. Can I practise law, medicine or architecture without the prescribed qualification? Which clause of Art 19 allows the restriction?

Model answer

No. Art 19(6)(i) allows the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications (Advocates Act 1961 ss. 29, 33 for advocates; NMC Act 2019 for doctors; Architects Act for architects). A person may argue their own case, but only enrolled advocates may represent others.

Question asked in class

Q6. Why does the Constitution allow State monopoly in trade and business?

Model answer

Art 19(6)(ii): the State or State-owned corporation may carry on a trade or business to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens. A welfare State needs to provide both profitable and unprofitable but essential services - monopolies like railways generate surplus to support unprofitable services. Upheld in Akadasi Padhan (1963).

Question asked in class

Q7. Is the pre-censorship of press valid? Of films? Why the difference?

Model answer

Press: pre-censorship invalid (Brij Bhushan, 1950); films: pre-censorship permissible (K.A. Abbas, 1970) because cinema has a more powerful, immediate impact and a different nature of exhibition; censorship must still be reasonable and limited to Art 19(2) grounds.

Question asked in class

Q8. Can the Government control newspapers indirectly (price, number of pages, taxes)?

Model answer

No. Control of circulation or content by price/page schedules or newsprint control is a restriction on press freedom (Express Newspapers, Sakal, Bennett Coleman); taxation affecting newspapers must be tested against press freedom (Indian Express, 1985).

Question asked in class

Q9. Who owns airwaves/spectrum? Can the Government give it to friends on first-come-first-served basis?

Model answer

Airwaves/spectrum are public property (Cricket Association of Bengal; Art 39(b)). The Government is a trustee and must allocate fairly and transparently; first-come-first-served as practised in 2008 was struck down in the 2G case (2012); auction is not the only method (Presidential Reference 2012).

Question asked in class

Q10. Do voters have a right to know the background of candidates?

Model answer

Yes. Union of India v. ADR (2002) and PUCL (2003): the right to know is part of Art 19(1)(a); candidates must disclose criminal antecedents, assets and qualifications; s. 33B RPA was struck down. (Extended in the Electoral Bonds judgment, 2024.)

Question asked in class

Q11. Do government employees (or students) have a fundamental right to strike?

Model answer

No. T.K. Rangarajan v. Govt of T.N. (2003) - no fundamental, statutory or moral right to strike; Art 19(1)(c) protects the right to form unions, not to strike.

Question asked in class

Q12. Can people protest anywhere and for as long as they like?

Model answer

No. Protest is protected by Art 19(1)(a),(b) but may be reasonably regulated - time, place, manner, and numbers (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, 2018); public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely (Amit Sahni, 2020); police action must be proportionate (Ramlila Maidan, 2012).

Question asked in class

Q13. Can a Minister's statement bind the Government? Are fundamental rights enforceable against private parties?

Model answer

Kaushal Kishor (2023): a Minister's personal statement is not vicariously attributable to the Government under Art 75(3); Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons in appropriate cases; no additional restrictions beyond Art 19(2) on free speech.

Question asked in class

Q14. Can the State stop publication of an autobiography written in jail?

Model answer

No prior restraint. R. Rajagopal (1994): the State cannot restrain publication in advance; remedies lie after publication; matters of public record and official conduct are open to publication.

exam.title: Art 19(1)(g) in Detail - Lawful Occupation, Education as Occupation, Hawkers, Dance Bars, Meat/Cattle Bans, and Religious Processions (Ramasamy Udayar)

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot - the professor's checklist for "write on Art 19(1)(g)"

The professor said: "If I ask a question on Art 19(1)(g), write only these points - anything else wastes time" (there are 200-300 cases on it). The checklist: (1) citizens only; (2) only a lawful profession; (3) includes the right to establish educational institutions (education = occupation, TMA Pai); (4) includes the right to close down a business; (5) right to trade does not mean a right to trade anywhere you like (hawkers - Sodan Singh / Olga Tellis); (6) no protection for illegal, immoral or inherently dangerous activities; (7) no protection for monopoly or arbitrary restriction (Chintaman Rao).

Cases to learn: TMA Pai Foundation (2002) and Islamic Academy (2003); Bijoe Emmanuel (right to silence); Olga Tellis (1985) and Sodan Singh (1989); State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel & Restaurants Association (dance bars, 2013); Quareshi (1958) → Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005); Hinsa Virodhak Sangh (2008); Om Prakash v. State of U.P. (2004); Ramasamy Udayar v. District Collector, Perambalur (Madras HC, 2021).

Declared exam hints: (a) the Supreme Court judgment of 15 October 2026 (sent on the previous evening at 8:07 pm) that converts to a non-Hindu religion cannot claim backward-class reservation - "this will come in the question"; (b) a question on Ramasamy Udayar and the difference between it and the Haridwar/Rishikesh meat-ban case (Om Prakash). The professor also said: "I do not ask questions about case names - even if you don't know the name or issue, if the facts come I should be able to tell the decision clearly. Fundamentals must be absolutely clear."

What has been left out

Roll-call and seating, a long exchange about students' backgrounds, a tangent on a student protest at Connaught Place (used to make the point "right to protest ≠ right to do it anywhere"), chocolates, and administrative remarks. Also omitted: personal remarks on named students and political jibes. Retained: the law, the cases, and the questions asked.

Transcript problems: "Colaba dealers / Colgate Tellis / Ogha Telis" = Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation; "Sodan/Sodhan Singh" = Sodan Singh v. NDMC; "Hanif Qureshi" = Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar. A student looking for "Kalyandas v. State of Tamil Nadu" and "an Imam Hussain case" was not on the right track; the professor pointed to Ramasamy Udayar.

sections.title: 8.1 Art 19(1)(g) - the checklist, with the law behind each point
sections.html:
#Point (professor)Law and authority
1Only citizens can claim it ("a non-citizen cannot claim this").Art 19(1) opens "All citizens shall have the right..."; non-citizens have Arts 14, 20, 21, 22, 25 etc.
2Only a lawful profession; one cannot claim the right to an illegal or immoral occupation ("a girl cannot claim it to sell ganja in the hostel").State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala (1957) (gambling is not "trade or business"); Khoday Distilleries v. Sri Mahadeshwara Sahakara Sakkare Karkhane (1995); NDPS Act 1985.
3Includes the right to establish an educational institution - education is an occupation, not charity and not "business".T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002) 8 SCC 481 (11 judges) - 8.3.
4Includes the right to close down a business ("like the right to open, there is a right to close; you cannot force a business to run" - taught again under Labour Law).Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978) 4 SCC 224 (a law requiring government permission for closure invalid); the later cases accept reasonable regulation of closure (Industrial Disputes Act).
5Right to trade ≠ right to trade anywhere (public property).Sodan Singh v. NDMC (1989) 4 SCC 155; Olga Tellis (1985) - 8.5.
6No protection for illegal / inherently dangerous activities - "no fundamental right to trade in intoxicating liquids, acid, ganja, cigarettes".Khoday Distilleries (1995) (no fundamental right to trade in liquor - State may prohibit or regulate heavily); Chamarbaugwala; Narendra Kumar v. Union of India (1960).
7Monopoly / arbitrary restriction not protected; restriction must be reasonable ("balance between the freedom guaranteed and the social control").Chintaman Rao v. State of M.P. (1950) - 8.6; Art 19(6)(ii) (State monopoly).

sections.title: 8.2 Lawful activity only - gambling, intoxicants and "immoral" trade
sections.html:
• Chamarbaugwala (1957): the Court held that the activities which are res extra commercium (gambling, lotteries as a business, trafficking in women, etc.) cannot be called "trade" or "business" under Art 19(1)(g) and are not protected; the legislature can prohibit them entirely.
  • Khoday Distilleries (1995): there is no fundamental right to trade in liquor; the State can prohibit, regulate or monopolise; but regulation must not be arbitrary (Art 14).
  • Professor's point: "when the Warden catches a student with ganja, do not argue that Dr Tiwari taught you that you have a fundamental right to sell cigarettes in the hostel - I did not teach that". (Cigarettes are lawful products but their sale in a hostel can be regulated by the rules; narcotic substances are illegal under the NDPS Act.)

sections.title: 8.3 Education as an occupation - TMA Pai (2002), Islamic Academy (2003)
sections.html:
The history (as told by the professor)

  • In ancient India, education was charity: gurukuls, ashrams, madrasas and Sanskrit universities charged no fee; students even received food, clothes or stipends; they did shramdaan and gave dakshina later. Education was therefore not seen as a business or occupation.
  • Around 1980s-90s, population growth overwhelmed government schools; private schools and colleges opened, charged arbitrary fees and exploited students. The State tried to regulate; the managements went to court saying "this is our business/occupation; you cannot impose restrictions".
  • Early position: the Supreme Court first said education is not a business or occupation - it is social service, so private institutions cannot charge arbitrary fees (Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka, 1992 - capitation fee violates the right to education under Art 21; Unni Krishnan J.P. v. State of A.P., 1993 - education is not a trade/business; fee and admission schemes regulated).
  • This continued till TMA Pai (2002), which is "a crucial point for all of us". Education investors, the professor said, threatened to set up institutions abroad (Maldives, Nepal, Bhutan) and "fees would go abroad" - after which the Government and the Court recalibrated.
Case

T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002)

Citation / Court / Year

(2002) 8 SCC 481 (11-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; B.N. Kirpal C.J. for the majority; decided 31 October 2002).

Facts
  • Several petitions by private professional colleges (medical, engineering) and minority institutions challenged State control over admissions, fee structure and the quota system after Unni Krishnan (1993), which had imposed a scheme (free and payment seats, State-set fees). The reference raised 11 questions on Arts 19(1)(g), 26, 29, 30.
Issues
  • Is there a fundamental right to establish and administer educational institutions? Is education a "business" or "occupation"? How far can the State regulate private unaided institutions' admission and fees? What is the unit for determining minority status?
Held (Decision)
  • Yes - the right to establish and administer educational institutions is protected as an "occupation" under Art 19(1)(g) (and, for minorities, under Art 30(1); for religious denominations, Art 26). It is not "trade" or "business" in the commercial sense: education is charitable in nature.
  • Consequence (professor): since it is an occupation, restrictions on it must be (i) reasonable, (ii) imposed by law, and (iii) in the public interest (Art 19(6)).
  • No capitation fee / no profiteering ("commercialisation" is not allowed); a reasonable surplus for the growth of the institution is permitted; admissions must be fair, transparent and merit-based; the State may regulate to ensure that, but cannot take over the administration of unaided private institutions (the scheme in Unni Krishnan was held to be unworkable and was set aside). Minority status is to be determined by reference to the State (not India) as the unit.
Ratio decidendi

Education is an occupation under Art 19(1)(g) but must be run on a non-profit basis (no capitation fee); reasonable regulation by law in the public interest is permitted.

Significance / Later treatment
  • The professor said the ratio was so unclear that "even the Supreme Court did not understand what it had decided, so another Constitution Bench was constituted to explain it": Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003) 6 SCC 697 (5 judges). In class a student named the year as 2018 - the professor accepted it (and said "I might be wrong") - the correct year is 2003.
  • Later: P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005) 6 SCC 537 (7 judges) held that the State cannot impose reservation / quota on unaided private institutions; Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) (RTE Act 25% quota upheld for unaided non-minority schools).
Use in the exam

Question for the exam: "Name the case which was decided to clarify the ratio of TMA Pai." → Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003). (Also note that TMA Pai was an 11-judge bench - "that is why it is a pillar case".)

Ratio decidendi Education is an occupation under Art 19(1)(g) but must be run on a non-profit basis (no capitation fee); reasonable regulation by law in the public interest is permitted. Significance / Later treatment The professor said the ratio was so unclear that "even the Supreme Court did not understand what it had decided, so another Constitution Bench was constituted to explain it": Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003) 6 SCC 697 (5 judges). In class a student named the year as 2018 - the professor accepted it (and said "I might be wrong") - the correct year is 2003 . Later: P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005) 6 SCC 537 (7 judges) held that the State cannot impose reservation / quota on unaided private institutions; Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) (RTE Act 25% quota upheld for unaided non-minority schools). Use in the exam Question for the exam: "Name the case which was decided to clarify the ratio of TMA Pai ." → Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003). (Also note that TMA Pai was an 11-judge bench - "that is why it is a pillar case".)

sections.title: 8.4 Positive and negative rights (silence) - Bijoe Emmanuel again
sections.html:
• The professor: "Other than Art 21, every Article has both a positive and a negative aspect" - e.g. Art 19(1)(a): right to speak and right to remain silent; Art 19(1)(c): right to form an association and (arguably) not to be forced to join one; Art 19(1)(g): right to carry on a business and to close it. sections.title: 8.5 Hawkers and pavement dwellers - Olga Tellis and Sodan Singh
sections.html:
Case

Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (the Pavement Dwellers case) (1985)

Citation / Court / Year

(1985) 3 SCC 545; AIR 1986 SC 180 (5-judge Constitution Bench; Y.V. Chandrachud C.J. for the Court).

Facts
  • Thousands of pavement and slum dwellers in Bombay (who worked as hawkers, domestic workers, casual labourers) lived on pavements and in slums near their workplaces. In July 1981 the Maharashtra Government and the Bombay Municipal Corporation announced that they would be evicted and deported to their places of origin; the Corporation began demolitions. The pavement dwellers (and the journalist Olga Tellis) petitioned.
  • Earlier, some had signed undertakings that they would vacate by a date; the State argued they had waived their rights.
Issues
  • Does the right to life (Art 21) include the right to livelihood? Can the State evict pavement dwellers? Can a person waive a Fundamental Right?
Held (Decision)
  • Right to life includes the right to livelihood: "no person can live without the means of living"; eviction deprives them of livelihood and therefore of life - unless done according to a procedure established by law that is just, fair and reasonable.
  • Pavements are meant for pedestrians; encroachments can be removed, but only after notice and a hearing (not summary eviction), and not during the monsoon; those enumerated in the 1976 census were entitled to alternative sites; slum dwellers' tenement improvement schemes were directed.
  • No waiver of Fundamental Rights: the undertakings the pavement dwellers had given to vacate by a date did not bind them; there can be no estoppel against the Constitution (the professor had earlier taught this under the doctrine of waiver - a student recalled it).
Ratio decidendi

Right to livelihood is part of Art 21; no waiver of Fundamental Rights; eviction must be by fair procedure.

Use in the exam

Professor: "This case I taught under doctrine of waiver." A student correctly connected it: "pavement dwellers were told to leave by a certain date and the agreement was held not binding."

Case

Sodan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1989)

Citation / Court / Year

(1989) 4 SCC 155 (5-judge Constitution Bench; also see Bombay Hawkers' Union v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) 3 SCC 528 and Gainda Ram v. M.C.D. (2010) 10 SCC 715).

Facts
  • Hawkers and small traders on the pavements of Delhi (including around Connaught Place) were removed by the NDMC; they claimed a fundamental right to hawk at their chosen places under Art 19(1)(g) and Art 21.
Issues
  • Does Art 19(1)(g) give hawkers a right to trade on public streets at a place of their choice?
Held (Decision)
  • Hawking is a trade protected by Art 19(1)(g) (it is the livelihood of the poor and serves the common man), but there is no fundamental right to carry on trade at a particular place of one's choice on public property; the State may regulate or prohibit hawking on safety, traffic and health grounds.
  • The authorities must frame a scheme with designated hawking zones and licensing; the State should not simply evict without an arrangement ("once they have a livelihood, they cannot be thrown out without an alternative remedy").
Ratio decidendi

The right to carry on trade is not a right to carry it on anywhere; public property cannot be taken by force; the State must provide regulated hawking zones.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Professor's comment: "This case corrected the mistake: if the Government can throw people out, then the right is hollow; hence the Court directed the creation of hawkers' zones - near railway stations, bus stands, metro stations - which benefits the common man who buys vegetables on his way home."
  • Statute: the Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014 now gives vendors a statutory right (town vending committees, survey, certificates).
  • Professor's example: a person has a right to hoist the national flag but not in the mouth of a fellow student or anywhere he pleases (compare Union of India v. Naveen Jindal, 2004 - flying the national flag is protected by Art 19(1)(a) but subject to the Flag Code and reasonable restrictions). The point: a right to do an activity is not a right to do it at any place.
Use in the exam

The professor: "When asked about trade rights on public places, write: right to hawk is protected, but not at a place of one's choice; the State must create hawking zones." A student pointed out that Sodan Singh said there is no fundamental right to a specific place - the professor agreed.

  • Legitimate economic activity v. illegal encroachment: the professor noted that long-established weekly markets (e.g. Sunday markets in Nagpur) have an "inherent right" created by decades of use; while a new person cannot set up a stall anywhere, traditional sites are treated differently - both Olga Tellis and Sodan Singh require the State to provide space instead of merely evicting.

sections.title: 8.6 "Monopoly is not protected" - Chintaman Rao (1950)
sections.html:
Case

Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1950)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1951 SC 118; 1950 SCR 759 (Supreme Court of India; Mahajan J.).

Facts
  • The Central Provinces and Berar Regulation of Manufacture of Bidis (Agricultural Purposes) Act, 1948 empowered the Deputy Commissioner to prohibit workers in villages from manufacturing bidis during the agricultural season, so that labour would be available for farming. Bidi manufacturers and workers challenged it under Art 19(1)(g).
Issues
  • When is a restriction on the freedom of trade "reasonable" under Art 19(6)?
Held (Decision)
  • The restriction was arbitrary and excessive - it extended to all bidi workers in the area, not only those engaged in agriculture; it was not a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public.
  • Test: "Reasonable implies intelligent care and deliberation, the choice of a course which reason dictates. Legislation which arbitrarily or excessively invades the right cannot be said to contain the quality of reasonableness... it must strike a proper balance between the freedom guaranteed and the social control permitted."
Ratio decidendi

A restriction on trade must be proportionate to the object; arbitrary or excessive restrictions are not reasonable.

Use in the exam

The professor referred to the case as "the Chintamani case about labour in bidi factories" - "monopoly is also not protected" (his point: neither unlimited freedom nor arbitrary State control is constitutional). Use it for the reasonableness test of Art 19(6).

sections.title: 8.7 Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 - what is and is not an offence
sections.html:
A student asked: "Is prostitution legal in India?" The professor: "Prostitution as such has never been declared illegal. The Act prohibits certain public and commercial acts - the police misuse the grey area." Read the Act (not "Chat GPT summaries"): "read the exact Act".

Section (ITPA 1956)OffenceNotes (professor and statute)
s. 3Punishment for keeping a brothel or allowing premises to be used as a brothelFirst conviction: rigorous imprisonment 1-3 years and fine up to ₹2,000; the professor: "the fine is very low; it should be revised". Read aloud by a student in class.
s. 4Living on the earnings of prostitutionMentioned by students ("living on the earnings"). Imprisonment up to 2 years (up to 7 years if a child is involved).
s. 5Procuring, inducing or taking a person for prostitutionProfessor: "pushing somebody into prostitution" is prohibited.
s. 7Prostitution in or in the vicinity of public placesProfessor: "running a brothel openly in a public place".
s. 8Seducing or soliciting for the purpose of prostitutionApplies where the act is in a public place or within sight of a public place. The professor's point: if a woman privately says "pay me ₹100" it is not an offence; "soliciting customers in a public place" is. Police nevertheless arrest women privately - "misuse". A student pointed out that police arrest sex workers standing alone even though s. 8 requires seducing or soliciting; the professor agreed this is wrong.
  • Classroom reading: students read "keeping, managing, acting or assisting in the keeping or management of a brothel" (s. 3(1)). The professor told them to read the Act itself (not secondary sources): "exact Act, not the summaries".
  • Related authorities (for completeness): Gaurav Jain v. Union of India (1997) (rehabilitation of children of sex workers); Budhadev Karmaskar v. State of W.B. (Supreme Court, 2011 and later orders) - sex workers have the right to a dignified life under Art 21, police should not harass adult voluntary sex workers (verify the order before citing). Under the BNS, trafficking is covered by s. 143.
Case

State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel & Restaurants Association (the Dance Bar case) (2013)

Citation / Court / Year

(2013) 8 SCC 519 (Supreme Court of India; Dipak Misra and Vikramajit Sen JJ.; decided 16 July 2013 - verify). Follow-up: (2019) 3 SCC 429.

Facts
  • The Bombay Police (Amendment) Act, 2005 inserted ss. 33A and 33B to ban dance performances in eating houses, permit rooms and beer bars (but exempted three-star and above hotels) on the ground that the dances were obscene and degrading to women's dignity, promoted drinking and exploitation. Thousands of women were bar dancers who supported their families; the closure threw them out of work.
  • The Bombay High Court struck the provisions down (2006). The State appealed.
Issues
  • Does the ban violate Art 19(1)(g) (and Arts 14 and 21)? Can the State ban rather than regulate? Is the classification (three-star hotels exempt) valid?
Held (Decision)
  • The ban was unconstitutional: it violated Art 19(1)(g) (the dancers' livelihood), Art 14 (arbitrary classification between dance bars and three-star hotels - "dignity" could not be protected only in some places) and the State had not shown that a total ban was necessary - regulation, not prohibition, was the proportionate answer.
  • The professor's retelling: the Court said that if the girls are denied this livelihood, you push them into prostitution - "they are not trained to work in factories nor to be software engineers" - which would violate their rights under Art 19(1)(g) and Art 21; if some customers behave wrongly, punish those persons - do not close the dancers' occupation. (This is the professor's paraphrase; check the judgment before quoting the exact words.)
Ratio decidendi

A total ban on a lawful livelihood based on a moral view that is not proved to be necessary is an unreasonable restriction; the State must adopt regulatory measures to protect dignity.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Professor: "This is a very important case - I have already asked a question on it, and I do not repeat cases in questions (there are so many cases)."
Use in the exam

Use for: protection of livelihood under Art 19(1)(g)/Art 21; proportionality; the idea that morality cannot be used to destroy women's livelihoods arbitrarily; the interface between dignity and occupation.

sections.title: 8.8 Meat, cattle and religious sentiments - Quareshi → Mirzapur Moti Kureshi, Hinsa Virodhak Sangh, Om Prakash
sections.html:
Case

Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar (1958) → State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1958 SC 731 (Constitution Bench; S.R. Das C.J.); (2005) 8 SCC 534 (7 judges; R.C. Lahoti C.J.).

Facts
  • State laws (Bihar, U.P., M.P.) banned the slaughter of cows and cow progeny (including bulls and bullocks) in the name of Art 48 (DPSP: prohibit slaughter of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle). Butchers (the Quareshi/Kureshi community) challenged them under Art 19(1)(g).
Held (Decision)
  • Quareshi (1958): a total ban on slaughter of cows and calves was valid; but a total ban on slaughter of bulls, bullocks and she-buffaloes that had ceased to be useful (milk/draught) was an unreasonable restriction - the professor described it as "the Court said: useless cattle may be slaughtered".
  • Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005): the 7-judge Bench overruled this part; it upheld a complete ban on slaughter of cow progeny of all ages, relying on Art 48, Art 51A(g) (compassion for living creatures), the usefulness of cattle (dung, urine, draught power) and the principle (from Minerva Mills, 1980) that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary and must be harmonised. The professor: "At that time Art 48 could not be given primacy because the Court had said Directive Principles are subsidiary; after Minerva Mills the Court was encouraged to give Art 48 more weight."
Ratio decidendi

A ban on cattle slaughter is a reasonable restriction under Art 19(6) when supported by Art 48 read with Art 51A(g); FR and DPSP are harmonised.

Use in the exam

The professor (affectionately): "I gave 50-50 [marks] to the student who knew that this case corrects the earlier one." Know both the 1958 and 2005 decisions and the reason for the change.

Case

Hinsa Virodhak Sangh v. Mirzapur Moti Kuresh Jamat (2008)

Citation / Court / Year

(2008) 5 SCC 33 (Supreme Court of India).

Facts
  • The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation closed its slaughterhouses (and meat shops) for nine days during Paryushan, the Jain festival of non-violence. The butchers' association challenged the order as violating Art 19(1)(g).
Held (Decision)
  • The closure for a few days in the year is a reasonable restriction in the public interest (to respect the sentiments of a significant community); it does not destroy the trade. The professor: "In 365 days, if meat is not sold for a few days in a municipal corporation, no mountain will fall". A long-term or city-wide ban would not be reasonable; in areas where the Jain community is in majority, a few days' closure is reasonable.
Ratio decidendi

A short, community-sensitive restriction is proportionate; a long ban would not be.

Use in the exam

Listed as "very important" by the professor.

Case

Om Prakash v. State of Uttar Pradesh (the Haridwar / Rishikesh meat-ban case) (2004)

Citation / Court / Year

(2004) 3 SCC 402 (Supreme Court of India) - verify bench.

Facts
  • The U.P. Government (and later Uttarakhand) banned the sale of meat, fish and eggs in Haridwar, Rishikesh (and Muni-ki-Reti), towns of great religious significance (Har ki Pauri). Traders (some challenging through employees' names, said the professor) argued that Art 19(1)(g) was violated because they had settled there for business and had been selling such items.
Held (Decision)
  • The ban was upheld: Hindu pilgrimage towns "maintain a clean, communal and predominantly vegetarian atmosphere"; the geographical situation and peculiar culture of these towns justify a complete restriction on public dealing in non-vegetarian items, including eggs; the restriction was not arbitrary and met Art 19(6). (The professor read the passage from the judgment aloud with a student.)
Ratio decidendi

A traditional, long-standing religious and cultural character of a locality can justify a location-specific ban on a trade.

Use in the exam

Question flagged by the professor: difference between Om Prakash and Ramasamy Udayar (8.9).

A long-term or city-wide ban would not be reasonable; in areas where the Jain community is in majority , a few days' closure is reasonable. Ratio decidendi A short, community-sensitive restriction is proportionate ; a long ban would not be. Use in the exam Listed as "very important" by the professor. Case Om Prakash v. State of Uttar Pradesh (the Haridwar / Rishikesh meat-ban case) (2004) Citation / Court / Year (2004) 3 SCC 402 (Supreme Court of India) - verify bench. Facts The U.P. Government (and later Uttarakhand) banned the sale of meat, fish and eggs in Haridwar, Rishikesh (and Muni-ki-Reti) , towns of great religious significance (Har ki Pauri). Traders (some challenging through employees' names, said the professor) argued that Art 19(1)(g) was violated because they had settled there for business and had been selling such items. Held (Decision) The ban was upheld : Hindu pilgrimage towns "maintain a clean, communal and predominantly vegetarian atmosphere"; the geographical situation and peculiar culture of these towns justify a complete restriction on public dealing in non-vegetarian items, including eggs; the restriction was not arbitrary and met Art 19(6). (The professor read the passage from the judgment aloud with a student.) Ratio decidendi A traditional, long-standing religious and cultural character of a locality can justify a location-specific ban on a trade. Use in the exam Question flagged by the professor: difference between Om Prakash and Ramasamy Udayar (8.9).

sections.title: 8.9 Ramasamy Udayar v. District Collector, Perambalur (Madras High Court, 2021) - and why it differs from Om Prakash
sections.html:
Case

Ramasamy Udayar v. District Collector, Perambalur District (2021)

Citation / Court / Year

2021 SCC OnLine Mad 1779 (Madras High Court; N. Kirubakaran and P. Velmurugan JJ.; decided 30 April 2021). (Judgment by Justice N. Kirubakaran: "people may be religious, men may be communal, but roads and streets are secular".)

Facts
  • In V. Kalathur village (Perambalur district, Tamil Nadu), both Hindus and Muslims live (on different sides). Hindu temple festivals and processions (the three-day Oorani Pongal festival) had been held through all the streets for decades. Around 2011-12, objections from the Muslim community (now the numerical majority in the area) began; the authorities granted permission with conditions in 2018, and a private respondent challenged the permission on the ground that the procession through a Muslim-dominated area would cause law-and-order problems.
Issues
  • Can a religious procession/festival be prohibited or restricted merely because another religion's followers are in majority in the area? Is there any right of free use of public streets?
Held (Decision)
  • No. "A procession - including a religious procession - cannot be prohibited or curtailed merely because another religious group predominantly lives or does business in the area." India is a secular country; the presence of a majority of one religion in an area is not a ground to disallow festivals/processions of another; roads and streets are secular (District Municipalities Act, 1920, s. 180-A: streets open to all).
  • The authorities may regulate (timing, route, noise, safety) but may not prohibit; each religious group has a Fundamental Right to take out processions provided it does not insult other religions, shout slogans against them, or disturb public order. The presence of a place of worship of another religion is not itself a ground for denying permission. The criminal cases against both parties were directed to be withdrawn.
Ratio decidendi

Secularism means that numerical dominance of one religion in an area cannot be used to exclude others' religious practices; the State's duty is to maintain law and order, not to yield to the heckler's veto.

Use in the exam

Declared exam question ("download and circulate to all - I will put a question on this case and on the difference"). Students had trouble finding it by name; the correct name is Ramasamy Udayar.

Verify before quoting

In class the professor and students also discussed whether the judgment protected ringing of temple bells / the manner of praying, and whether the ruling confined Muslims to the west side of the village. The published report of the case (verified) concerns festivals and processions through public streets; I could not verify the bell-ringing point. If you quote it, say "as discussed in class" rather than as a holding. Also note: the professor personally dislikes loud processions (any religion) and said that, as a policy maker, he would regulate loudspeakers and processions for all religions - this is his opinion, not the law.

The difference between Om Prakash and Ramasamy Udayar (model answer)

PointOm Prakash (Haridwar/Rishikesh) - ban upheldRamasamy Udayar (Perambalur) - ban not allowed
What was restrictedA trade (sale of meat, fish, eggs) - Art 19(1)(g)A religious festival/procession - Arts 25, 19(1)(a),(b), (d)
Who imposed itThe State by law (statutory/administrative notification with legislative backing)Local authority / opponents sought to bar it, without law, by invoking the objection of the local majority
History of the localityTowns traditionally and predominantly religious/vegetarian for centuries; outsiders came later to trade and the character of the town was at stakeHindu festival/processions had been held for decades; the objectors were new local majority who wanted to stop an old practice
ReasonablenessLocation-specific, non-discriminatory, preserves cultural/religious character - reasonable under Art 19(6)Prohibition based only on the religion of the local majority - arbitrary, contrary to secularism and Art 25; authorities may only regulate for public order
PrincipleProtect a long-standing tradition from commercial changeProtect minority/other religions' rights from the heckler's veto; "roads and streets are secular"

The professor's own explanation: "There are two or three reasons. In Om Prakash, the towns were traditionally religious and the new traders came later; in the Madras case, temple worship and festivals had been going on forever, and the objectors came later. So the common principle is: protect the long-standing practice/character; do not allow later arrivals to alter it by pressure." (The professor also made a policy comment: "if a Hindu majority village tried to stop a mosque's practices, the same rule would apply"; the logic is symmetrical.)

sections.title: 8.10 The conversion / backward-class judgment of 15 October 2026 (declared exam question)
sections.html:
The professor said he had sent the case the previous evening at 8:07 pm ("converts to a non-Hindu religion cannot claim backward-class status - will this come in the exam? - yes"). The details below are from the news report of the order; read the judgment text for the reasoning.

Case

Supreme Court ruling (15 October 2026) on backward-class reservation after conversion (State of Tamil Nadu appeal)

Citation / Court / Year

Supreme Court of India; bench of Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar JJ.; 15 October 2026 (the case title was not available in the source I checked; obtain it from the Supreme Court website or the professor's circulated copy).

Facts
  • The Tamil Nadu Government issued a Government Order in March 2024 seeking to extend reservation benefits to persons who had converted from Hinduism to other religions. The Madras High Court quashed the order; the State appealed.
Issues
  • Does a person who converts from Hinduism to Islam / another non-Hindu religion continue to be entitled to Backward Class reservation by virtue of the caste/backwardness they had before conversion?
Held (Decision)
  • The Supreme Court dismissed the State's appeal and upheld the High Court. It held that conversion from Hinduism to Islam or another non-Hindu religion does not automatically entitle a person to Backward Class reservation; backwardness from a former caste cannot carry over after conversion; statutory benefits under Art 16(4) cannot be extended merely on the basis of pre-conversion status.
  • Persons who profess a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism or Buddhism do not hold Scheduled Caste status (para 3 of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, as amended in 1956 and 1990); private religious bodies cannot determine statutory entitlements; reconversion to Hinduism needs independent, fact-specific verification by competent authorities.
Ratio decidendi

Reservation benefits (Arts 15(4), 16(4), 341) are tied to the social and educational backwardness recognised for the community within the religion; conversion to a non-Hindu religion ends SC status and does not automatically carry BC status.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Related: C. Selvarani v. Special Secretary-cum-District Collector (2024) - conversion solely to obtain reservation benefits is a "fraud on the Constitution" (verify the date/citation before relying on it); Soosai v. Union of India (1985) (SC status and Christian converts); K.P. Manu v. Scrutiny Committee (2015).
Use in the exam

Declared exam topic. Write: facts (TN GO, Madras HC), the question, the holding, Arts 15(4), 16(4), 341, 342, the SC Order of 1950, and a short critical note - arguments for (caste is a Hindu social structure; benefits are targeted) and against (backwardness may persist after conversion; Art 25 and Art 14 concerns; the Order itself has been challenged).

sections.title: 8.11 Questions asked in COLA 16 - model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. What are the main points to write if asked about Art 19(1)(g)?

Model answer

See the seven-point checklist in 8.1. Opening line: "Art 19(1)(g) guarantees citizens the right to practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business; it is subject to reasonable restrictions by law under Art 19(6) in the interests of the general public, including qualifications and State monopoly."

Question asked in class

Q2. Can a person claim Art 19(1)(g) to sell ganja or run an illegal business?

Model answer

No. Only lawful professions are protected; illegal, immoral or inherently dangerous activities (gambling, narcotics, trafficking, liquor trade as a right) are not (Chamarbaugwala, 1957; Khoday Distilleries, 1995).

Question asked in class

Q3. Is running a private school or college an occupation or a business? What does the classification achieve?

Model answer

TMA Pai (2002): an occupation (not trade/business in the commercial sense) - therefore (i) restrictions must be reasonable, (ii) by law, (iii) in the public interest; no capitation fee; reasonable surplus allowed; admissions transparent and merit-based.

Question asked in class

Q4. Name the case that was decided to clarify the ratio of TMA Pai.

Model answer

Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003) 6 SCC 697 (5 judges) - the year 2003, not 2018 (a student's slip in class).

Question asked in class

Q5. Which case recognises the right to silence under Art 19(1)(a)? Who wrote the judgment?

Model answer

Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) - the National Anthem case; judgment by O. Chinnappa Reddy J. (not B.P. Jeevan Reddy).

Question asked in class

Q6. Explain the rights of pavement dwellers and hawkers (Olga Tellis; Sodan Singh).

Model answer

Olga Tellis (1985): right to livelihood is part of Art 21; eviction only after fair procedure; no waiver of Fundamental Rights. Sodan Singh (1989): hawking is protected by Art 19(1)(g), but there is no right to trade at a place of one's choice on public property; the State must frame schemes and designate hawking zones; statute: Street Vendors Act 2014.

Question asked in class

Q7. Is there a right to close down a business?

Model answer

Yes - Art 19(1)(g) includes the right to close (Excel Wear, 1978); reasonable regulation (notice, compensation to workmen) is allowed.

Question asked in class

Q8. Is prostitution illegal in India? Which acts are prohibited?

Model answer

Prostitution per se is not an offence; the ITPA 1956 prohibits keeping a brothel (s. 3), living on its earnings (s. 4), procuring/inducing (s. 5), prostitution near public places (s. 7) and soliciting in a public place (s. 8). Private, voluntary activity is outside the Act; police misuse is a concern; sex workers have a right to dignity under Art 21.

Question asked in class

Q9. Was the ban on dance bars valid? Why?

Model answer

No - State of Maharashtra v. IHRA (2013): violated Art 19(1)(g) and Art 14; the ban deprived women of livelihood and the State had not shown that a total ban was necessary; regulate rather than ban.

Question asked in class

Q10. Explain the law on cattle slaughter and meat bans (Quareshi, Mirzapur, Hinsa Virodhak, Om Prakash).

Model answer

Quareshi (1958): cow/calf slaughter ban valid; ban on useless bulls/bullocks unreasonable. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005): overruled; complete ban on cow progeny valid (Art 48, Art 51A(g), harmonisation after Minerva Mills). Hinsa Virodhak (2008): 9-day closure during Paryushan reasonable. Om Prakash (2004): meat ban in Haridwar/Rishikesh upheld because of traditional religious character.

Question asked in class

Q11. State the difference between Om Prakash and Ramasamy Udayar.

Model answer

See the table in 8.9: trade ban upheld where the traditional religious character is preserved by law; a religious procession cannot be banned because another community is the local majority (the heckler's veto is not allowed; roads are secular).

Question asked in class

Q12. Can a person who converts from Hinduism to another religion claim backward-class reservation?

Model answer

Per the Supreme Court (15 October 2026, bench of P.K. Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar JJ.), conversion to a non-Hindu religion does not automatically entitle a person to BC benefits; SC status is lost on conversion to a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism; reconversion requires fact-specific verification. See 8.10.

Question asked in class

Q13. Does the Supreme Court hold that Directive Principles override Fundamental Rights (Art 48 v. Art 19(1)(g))?

Model answer

No. Since Minerva Mills (1980) the position is that FR and DPSP are complementary and must be harmonised; neither overrides the other. (Professor's warning from earlier lectures: writing that "Fundamental Rights override Directive Principles" earns zero marks.) Mirzapur Moti Kureshi shows harmonisation in action.
