exam.title: Fundamental Rights v. Directive Principles (Champakam → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills) and the Beginning of Art 21 (Life, Personal Liberty, Procedure Established by Law)

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

DANGER SENTENCE - never write it: "In certain cases Fundamental Rights are to be given priority over Directive Principles" (or the reverse). The professor: "the moment you write this sentence, your marks become zero." The correct modern position (Minerva Mills, 1980): Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary and supplementary to each other; the Constitution rests on the balance between Parts III and IV; the Court must adopt harmonious construction.

The story in one line: Champakam (1951: FR prevail, DPSP subsidiary) → First Amendment (1951: Art 15(4) reservation) → ... → 25th Amendment (1971: Art 31C) → Kesavananda (1973) upheld the first part of Art 31C and struck down the second (no judicial review) → 42nd Amendment (1976) extended 31C to all DPSPs → Minerva Mills (1980) struck that down and declared harmony.

Art 21 text: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Four things to know: who ("no person" - includes non-citizens), against whom (State, and now also private persons - Kaushal Kishor), meaning of life and personal liberty (A.K. Gopalan → Kharak Singh → Maneka Gandhi) and procedure established by law v. due process of law.

Declared exam hint: "I will create a question from Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P." - horizontal application of Arts 19 and 21; the judgment (and Nagarathna J.'s opinion) is to be read in the original by all.

What has been left out of this lecture

Attendance, scolding of late-comers, remarks on family law and demographics, party-political jibes (including about an Opposition leader and past governments), a long digression about a state minister's speech on organised crime, and personal comments on students. Retained: law, cases, and the professor's questions.

Factual slips corrected in these notes: the professor said the Magna Carta was signed in "2015" - it was 1215; he dated Lochner v. New York to "1903" - it was 1905; he said the 26th Amendment inserted Art 31C - it was the 25th (1971); he said eight judges sat on the US Supreme Court and Roosevelt threatened to add three - the Court had nine and the plan allowed up to six more; he described Kasab as not hanged in Bombay - the point is only that Art 21 protects even a convicted foreign terrorist, so the procedure of law had to be followed (Kasab was executed in 2012 at Yerwada, Pune).
sections.text: Exam snapshot DANGER SENTENCE - never write it: " In certain cases Fundamental Rights are to be given priority over Directive Principles " (or the reverse). The professor: " the moment you write this sentence, your marks become zero. " The correct modern position ( Minerva Mills , 1980): Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary and supplementary to each other; the Constitution rests on the balance between Parts III and IV; the Court must adopt harmonious construction . The story in one line: Champakam (1951: FR prevail, DPSP subsidiary) → First Amendment (1951: Art 15(4) reservation) → ... → 25th Amendment (1971: Art 31C) → Kesavananda (1973) upheld the first part of Art 31C and struck down the second (no judicial review) → 42nd Amendment (1976) extended 31C to all DPSPs → Minerva Mills (1980) struck that down and declared harmony . Art 21 text: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law ." Four things to know: who ("no person" - includes non-citizens), against whom (State, and now also private persons - Kaushal Kishor ), meaning of life and personal liberty (A.K. Gopalan → Kharak Singh → Maneka Gandhi ) and procedure established by law v. due process of law . Declared exam hint: "I will create a question from Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. " - horizontal application of Arts 19 and 21; the judgment (and Nagarathna J.'s opinion) is to be read in the original by all. What has been left out of this lecture Attendance, scolding of late-comers, remarks on family law and demographics, party-political jibes (including about an Opposition leader and past governments), a long digression about a state minister's speech on organised crime, and personal comments on students. Retained: law, cases, and the professor's questions. Factual slips corrected in these notes: the professor said the Magna Carta was signed in "2015" - it was 1215 ; he dated Lochner v. New York to "1903" - it was 1905 ; he said the 26th Amendment inserted Art 31C - it was the 25th (1971) ; he said eight judges sat on the US Supreme Court and Roosevelt threatened to add three - the Court had nine and the plan allowed up to six more; he described Kasab as not hanged in Bombay - the point is only that Art 21 protects even a convicted foreign terrorist, so the procedure of law had to be followed (Kasab was executed in 2012 at Yerwada, Pune).

sections.title: 9.1 Fundamental Rights v. Directive Principles - the full evolution
sections.html:
Step 1: why there was a conflict at all - Art 32 v. Art 37

  • Art 32: the right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights (itself a Fundamental Right) → Part III is justiciable.
  • Art 37: the Directive Principles in Part IV "shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country" → Part IV is non-justiciable.
  • Professor's explanation: "One Article says DPSPs cannot be enforced; the other says FRs can be enforced. If a matter comes to court, the court will naturally give the justiciable one its due and treat the non-justiciable as secondary - this is how the Court initially subordinated DPSPs to FRs."
Case

State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1951 SC 226; 1951 SCR 525 (Supreme Court of India; 7 judges; Das J.).

Facts
  • Madras Government's Communal G.O. reserved seats in State medical and engineering colleges by religion and caste (communal ratio). Champakam Dorairajan, a Brahmin woman, was denied admission despite higher marks and challenged it under Arts 15(1) and 29(2). The State defended the order as implementing Art 46 (DPSP: promote educational and economic interests of weaker sections).
Issues
  • Can a Directive Principle (Art 46) justify a violation of a Fundamental Right (Art 29(2)/15)?
Held (Decision)
  • The communal G.O. was unconstitutional (violated Art 29(2)). The Court held that the Directive Principles must conform to and run as subsidiary to the Chapter on Fundamental Rights; Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and cannot be overridden by Directive Principles.
Ratio decidendi

Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles; Part IV cannot override Part III (position in 1951).

Significance / Later treatment
  • Parliament responded with the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, inserting Art 15(4) (special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs). The professor: "After Champakam, the First Amendment brought the reservation clause." Reservation, not property, was the confusion that led to the amendment ("write that; do not write property").
Use in the exam

Professor's question: "What was the opinion of the Supreme Court on Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in the beginning of the Republic?" → FR prevail; DPSP subsidiary (Champakam); "that is wrong now" - that was only the 1950s position.

Step 2: the gradual shift - from subordination to balance

YearEventWhat it did
1951Champakam DorairajanFR prevail; DPSP subsidiary. → First Amendment (Art 15(4), 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule).
1958In re Kerala Education Bill (Art 143 reference)First clear attempt to harmonise: DPSPs should be given effect "as far as possible" in interpreting FRs.
1967Golak Nath v. State of PunjabParliament cannot amend Part III; DPSPs cannot override FRs.
197124th and 25th AmendmentsRestore Parliament's power to amend FRs; 25th Amendment inserts Art 31C (laws giving effect to Art 39(b) and (c) are not void for violating Arts 14, 19 or 31; no court can question such a law on the ground that it does not give effect to the policy).
1973Kesavananda Bharati v. State of KeralaBasic structure; 25th Amendment: the first part of Art 31C is valid; the second part (a law containing a declaration that it gives effect to the policy cannot be questioned in court) is struck down because judicial review is basic structure.
197642nd AmendmentExtends Art 31C to all Directive Principles (Part IV) - any law to implement any DPSP could override Arts 14, 19, 31; also adds Art 368(4),(5).
1980Minerva Mills v. Union of IndiaStruck down s. 55 (Art 368(4),(5)) and s. 4 (amended Art 31C) of the 42nd Amendment; held that FR and DPSP are complementary and must be harmonised; the Constitution is founded on the balance between Part III and Part IV.
Case

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - the Art 31C part (professor's version)

Citation / Court / Year

(1973) 4 SCC 225 (13-judge bench; 7:6). Full card on the property angle: Lecture 6.

Facts
  • The 25th Amendment inserted Art 31C protecting laws implementing Art 39(b)-(c) from challenge under Arts 14, 19, 31. It was challenged.
Held (Decision)
  • A student recited the answer in class (the professor corrected the mix-up of numbers - 24th, 25th, 26th - "it was the 25th that inserted 31C"): "the part protecting social and economic reforms was upheld; the second part, which barred judicial review, was struck down".
  • The professor: "Judicial review is basic structure. Clap for her." The first part of Art 31C therefore survived - so a law made to implement Art 39(b)/(c) was protected from FR challenge - but the Court retained its power to examine whether the law really relates to Art 39(b)/(c).
Use in the exam

Question asked in class: "In which case was the 25th Amendment (Art 31C) challenged?" → Kesavananda Bharati. "What happened?" → first part upheld, second part struck down (judicial review).

Case

Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)

Citation / Court / Year

(1980) 3 SCC 625; AIR 1980 SC 1789 (5-judge bench; 4:1; Y.V. Chandrachud C.J.; Bhagwati J. dissenting).

Facts
  • Minerva Mills, a sick textile mill, was taken over under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act 1974. The company challenged the take-over and the validity of ss. 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which (i) extended Art 31C to all Directive Principles and (ii) inserted Art 368(4) and (5) (no judicial review of constitutional amendments; unlimited power of Parliament).
Issues
  • Are ss. 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment valid? Can Directive Principles override Articles 14 and 19?
Held (Decision)
  • s. 55 (Art 368(4),(5)) struck down: Parliament's amending power is limited; a limited amending power is part of the basic structure; Parliament cannot enlarge it into absolute power.
  • s. 4 (amended Art 31C) struck down: giving all DPSPs the power to override Arts 14 and 19 would destroy the harmony and balance between Part III and Part IV; Part III cannot be subordinated to Part IV.
  • "The Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Parts III and IV. To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution." FR and DPSP are complementary and supplementary to each other. (The professor: "the Supreme Court said they are complementary, supplementary and must be harmonised.")
  • The 42nd Amendment, in these respects, was held "totally unconstitutional" (the professor's expression); Art 31C as it stood after Kesavananda (limited to Art 39(b),(c)) remained.
Ratio decidendi

Neither Part III nor Part IV has absolute primacy; they must be harmoniously construed.

Use in the exam
The one sentence to write

"Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary and supplementary; they must be harmonised; neither overrides the other." Never write "in certain cases FR have priority". A student began to say "in certain cases they have to be given priority" - the professor stopped her: "that is a wrong sentence; do not write it." (Examples used later to show harmony: Mirzapur Moti Kureshi 2005 - Art 48 with Art 19(1)(g); Lecture 8.)

Model essay (use in a long answer): "Fundamental Rights v. Directive Principles - relationship." (1) Part III is justiciable (Art 32); Part IV is non-justiciable (Art 37) yet "fundamental in governance". (2) Early view: Champakam - FRs prevail; DPSPs subsidiary; First Amendment (Art 15(4)). (3) Gradual harmonisation: Kerala Education Bill, 1958; Golak Nath; 24th-25th Amendments; Art 31C. (4) Kesavananda - first part of Art 31C valid, second part (judicial review) void; basic structure. (5) 42nd Amendment extended Art 31C to all DPSPs. (6) Minerva Mills - struck down; harmony and balance; complementary. (7) Later: DPSPs are used to give content to FRs (right to education, livelihood, environment). (8) Conclusion: balance, not primacy.

sections.title: 9.2 Art 21 - the structure of the lecture
sections.html:
Having finished Art 19, the professor skipped Art 20 ("I will take Art 20 later") and began Art 21 because "the Additional Advocate General of Madhya Pradesh had never heard it" - he stressed that "even in selection-committee interviews at professor level, people are rarely clear on this concept". He asked students to listen carefully; no writing; notes can be read later.

Words in Art 21IssueKey cases
"No person"Who is protected? Against whom?Foreigners protected (professor's Kasab example); human beings only; State and, increasingly, private actors - Rudul Sah (1983), Bodhisattwa Gautam (1996), Kaushal Kishor (2023).
"life"Narrow (mere existence) → broad (life with dignity)A.K. Gopalan (1950) → Kharak Singh (1962) → Maneka Gandhi (1978).
"personal liberty"Freedom from physical restraint → all liberties not in Art 19Gopalan → Maneka Gandhi.
"procedure established by law"Any procedure enacted by a legislature → procedure that is just, fair and reasonable (due process in substance)Gopalan → Maneka Gandhi; US: Lochner v. New York (1905).

sections.title: 9.3 "No person" - who can claim Art 21, and against whom?
sections.html:
• Available to every person, citizens and non-citizens: "Ajmal Kasab was not hanged anywhere he pleased; the procedure established by law was followed - because Art 21 is for everybody, including foreigners, even Pakistanis". (Professor's illustration; Kasab was convicted for the 26/11 attacks and executed in 2012.)
  • Only human beings, not corporations ("this right is available only to the human being, not for corporate or the like" - the professor's statement; the Court has applied the concept of "natural persons" for Art 21 though companies have other protections such as Art 14).
  • Against whom? The traditional view: Art 21 is a shield against the State - the State protects us from private wrongdoers; "if fire is lit by water, who will extinguish it?" - the professor's analogy: the State is like water that must put out fires; if the State itself becomes the fire, we need Art 21 to restrain the State, which has "money, ED, CBI, CID" and enormous power.
  • State's positive duty: "If someone attacks us, the State must protect us - even if it must put two-four cockroaches (criminals) behind bars" (the professor used a recent statement by a Deputy Chief Minister about firm action against organised crime as an example of the State's duty to protect life and liberty). Cross-reference: Kaushal Kishor (majority: State has a positive duty to protect against threats from non-State actors).
  • The new view - horizontal application: "a few days ago a case was decided in which some judges said it should have horizontal (not only vertical) application": the right to dignity (Art 21) and freedom of speech (Art 19) can be enforced against private persons (e.g. social media platforms such as X, LinkedIn, Facebook, or a private individual) – "they cannot violate my fundamental right to dignity". Case: Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2023) - see the full card in Lecture 7. The professor: "The original judgment is compulsory reading; I will create a question from it; the Class Representative should circulate the judgment to the whole batch with instructions that it has to be read by all." He noted that Nagarathna J. (who is to become Chief Justice of India in 2027 - verify) gave a separate opinion "with due respect to her", but the majority held horizontal application.

Remedy when a private person violates a Fundamental Right - the professor's hypothetical

A student ("Prateeksha") is falsely accused of election violence and rusticated for two years by the university; she wins in the High Court because the evidence was fabricated, but loses two months of classes - a loss that cannot be recouped. What remedy? The professor traced the development of compensation for violation of Fundamental Rights:

CaseRuleNotes
Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983)First case in which the Supreme Court awarded monetary compensation under Art 32 for violation of Art 21 (illegal detention for 14 years after acquittal).The professor called it "Rudal" and said the Court reasoned "money is not God - but it is not less than God" (a political quip he attributed to a leader). Compensation was against the State.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak) (1987)Absolute liability of hazardous enterprises; compensation correlated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise.The professor mentioned a compensation figure of lakhs; the case is cited for absolute liability (verify amounts).
Bodhisattwa Gautam v. Subhra Chakraborty (1996)The Supreme Court held that rape is a violation of Art 21 and awarded interim compensation to the victim, payable by the accused (a private person, a teacher/professor) - an early instance of horizontal application.Cited by the professor as the "old case" (he gave the name garbled as "Sura Chatterji"; the party names are Bodhisattwa Gautam v. Subhra Chakraborty) where the Court "for the first time" applied Art 21 against a private individual. The year is 1996.
  • Professor's opinion on the facts of a teacher-student relationship that later turns into an allegation: "my personal opinion is different; I have to read what the Act says" - not examinable. Law: consent obtained on a false promise of marriage; Art 21 protects against sexual violence; compensation awarded in public-law jurisdiction even against a private person.
  • Exam line: "Traditionally Art 21 operated vertically against the State; it is now being applied horizontally against private persons: Bodhisattwa Gautam (1996), Vishaka (1997), Kaushal Kishor (2023)."

sections.title: 9.4 Meaning of "life" - from Gopalan (1950) to Kharak Singh (1962)
sections.html:
Case

A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1950 SC 27; 1950 SCR 88 (Supreme Court of India; 6-judge bench; Kania C.J., Fazl Ali J. dissenting in part).

Facts
  • A.K. Gopalan, a Communist leader and member of the Provisional Parliament, was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (the Act was passed by the Indian Government soon after independence). He challenged the detention under Arts 19(1)(a),(b),(c),(d),(e),(g), 21 and 22. The professor: "Even such a big man was jailed by the Congress Government under preventive detention when the country was newly independent" (compare Emergency era; political point omitted).
Issues
  • What do "life", "personal liberty" and "procedure established by law" mean in Art 21? Are Arts 19 and 21 mutually exclusive? Is a preventive detention law subject to Art 19 tests?
Held (Decision)
  • "Life" and "personal liberty" were given a narrow meaning: personal liberty means physical liberty (freedom from arrest and detention); "life" = bare existence.
  • "Procedure established by law" meant any procedure laid down by a competent legislature - the Court would not examine whether the law was fair, just or reasonable (it rejected "due process" and read "law" as State-made law, not natural justice).
  • Arts 14, 19, 21 were mutually exclusive codes ("watertight compartments"): a preventive detention law needed only comply with Art 22 and the procedure it provided.
  • The Preventive Detention Act was upheld (except section 14, which barred courts from looking into grounds of detention).
Ratio decidendi

Art 21 protects only against arbitrary executive action, not against unreasonable laws; procedure = whatever the legislature prescribes.

Significance / Later treatment
  • The professor: "1950: the Supreme Court gave life a very restricted meaning - 'life' means do not kill me; I can be given little food, but must be kept alive." He said Gopalan was among the first cases the Court decided and "they were influenced - they gave very narrow meaning because the country was newly independent".
  • Overruled in effect by R.C. Cooper (1970) (rejecting watertight compartments) and Maneka Gandhi (1978) (procedure must be just, fair and reasonable).
Use in the exam

Professor: "First case you must read: A.K. Gopalan (1950)." He asked the class to identify the case; students said "A.K. Gopalan".

Case

Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1963 SC 1295; (1964) 1 SCR 332 (6-judge bench; judgment dated 18 December 1962; Ayyangar J. for the majority; Subba Rao J. dissenting in part).

Facts
  • Kharak Singh was accused of dacoity but released for lack of evidence. The U.P. Police Regulations (Chapter XX) authorised surveillance of "history-sheeters": (a) secret picketing of the house, (b) domiciliary visits at night, (c) periodic enquiries, (d) verification of movements, (e) reporting of movements, etc. Police visited his house at night to check whether he was at home or "out committing crimes" - waking his family.
Issues
  • Do these regulations violate Art 19(1)(d) (movement) and Art 21? Is privacy or sleep protected?
Held (Decision)
  • Domiciliary night visits (reg. 236(b)) violated "personal liberty" under Art 21 (they were invalid); the other forms of surveillance (shadowing, reports) did not infringe Art 19(1)(d) (surveillance of movements is not a restraint) and were upheld by the majority.
  • The Court said that "life" in Art 21 means more than mere animal existence - it includes the right to enjoy all faculties (quoting the American case Munn v. Illinois, 1877, per Field J.). Professor: "For the first time the Supreme Court said that sleeping also comes under Art 21" - his shorthand for the disturbance of sleep by night visits.
  • Subba Rao J. (dissent) held that all the surveillance measures violated Art 21 and recognised privacy as part of personal liberty.

"Life" means more than animal existence; "personal liberty" is more than physical restraint (privacy and dignity are protected); Gopalan was partly overruled.

  • Later: Govind v. State of M.P. (1975) and K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) (privacy as a Fundamental Right; Kharak Singh's majority on surveillance overruled).
Use in the exam

The class corrected the date: a student first said 1963 and then 1962 - the professor confirmed: "1962". "The professor: it is a case that expanded life and partially overruled Gopalan."

Facts A.K. Gopalan , a Communist leader and member of the Provisional Parliament , was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (the Act was passed by the Indian Government soon after independence). He challenged the detention under Arts 19(1)(a),(b),(c),(d),(e),(g), 21 and 22. The professor: " Even such a big man was jailed by the Congress Government under preventive detention when the country was newly independent " (compare Emergency era; political point omitted). sections.title: 9.5 "Personal liberty" - Maneka Gandhi (1978) and the expansion of Art 21
sections.html:
• The confusion: liberty is already protected in Art 19 (six freedoms) so what is "personal liberty" in Art 21? Gopalan: physical freedom from detention; "locomotion" (the professor asked students to explain: movement of the body).
  • Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): personal liberty includes "all those things that are not covered in Art 19" - the widest meaning; it protects the right to go abroad (Satwant Singh, 1967), privacy, dignity, shelter, livelihood etc. Professor's list of what has been read into Art 21: "reading newspapers and magazines, giving interviews to TV, not being handcuffed, sleeping, drinking water, roads..." ; and "what you wear, what you eat, where you go" ("Owaisi says: eating beef is part of personal liberty" - the professor gave this as an example of the breadth of liberty; the law on food laws and cow slaughter is in Lecture 8).
  • On dress codes (a heated exchange in class): the professor said that although students' choice of dress is part of their "personal liberty/privacy", he feels a professional dress norm is appropriate in a law school (court-room decorum); a student asked "since when did clothes decide what women can do?" - the professor said he only expresses a view and cannot point out students' attire. Exam-safe point: choice of dress is protected by Art 21 (privacy and dignity, Puttaswamy 2017) and Art 19(1)(a), but institutions may impose reasonable, uniform dress codes (litigated in the hijab cases, Aishat Shifa, Karnataka HC 2022 and a split verdict in the Supreme Court, October 2022 - verify before citing). This is not part of the professor's teaching.
Case

Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)

Citation / Court / Year

(1978) 1 SCC 248; AIR 1978 SC 597 (7-judge bench; M.H. Beg C.J., Y.V. Chandrachud, V.R. Krishna Iyer, P.N. Bhagwati, N.L. Untwalia, S. Murtaza Fazal Ali, P.S. Kailasam JJ.; Bhagwati J. wrote the main opinion).

Facts
  • Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded by the Government of India on 2 July 1977 under s. 10(3)(c) of the Passport Act, 1967 "in the interests of the general public", without giving reasons and without any prior notice or hearing (the Janata Government under Morarji Desai). The professor stressed the irony: "The Passport Act was made by Indira Gandhi's Government; it was used against her own daughter-in-law" - hence the moral "when you are in power, do not make bad laws - they may apply to you".
Issues
  • Does the right to travel abroad fall within "personal liberty"? Is "procedure established by law" satisfied by any procedure prescribed by law? What is the relationship between Arts 14, 19 and 21?
Held (Decision)
  • "Personal liberty" has the widest amplitude and includes the right to travel abroad (following Satwant Singh).
  • "Procedure established by law" must be "right, just and fair" and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; otherwise it is no procedure at all and Art 21 would be violated. The procedure must satisfy Art 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Art 19; Arts 14, 19, 21 are not mutually exclusive - the "golden triangle".
  • Section 10(3)(c) was upheld only by reading in the requirement of a fair hearing (audi alteram partem); the impounding order had been passed without any hearing, but because the Attorney General stated that the Government would give her an opportunity to be heard (and the Government gave her reasons later), the Court did not quash the order and the petition was disposed of. (The reported holding does not order the passport to be returned.)
Ratio decidendi

Procedure established by law must be just, fair and reasonable; Arts 14, 19 and 21 form a golden triangle and are read together.

Significance / Later treatment
  • The professor: "Before Maneka, the Court only asked: is there a procedure and was it followed? After Maneka, the Court asks: is the procedure itself fair? The moment it said 'we will see whether the law is fair', due process came in through the back door." "Sudden change: previously they did not say procedure is bad; suddenly Justice Bhagwati said so."
  • Opened the door to the vast expansion of Art 21: speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon), legal aid, bar on solitary confinement, right to livelihood (Olga Tellis), clean environment, privacy (Puttaswamy), dignity (Francis Coralie Mullin).
Use in the exam

The professor told students to read the original: "Maneka Gandhi; the name is spelt 'Maneka' in the law report - 'Menaka' is what we say in Hindi... I do not cut marks for spelling but 9 out of 10 becomes 10 out of 10." (A light comment about care in case names.)

sections.title: 9.6 "Procedure established by law" v. "due process of law"
sections.html:
• History (professor's account, corrected): The idea of "due process" goes back to Magna Carta, 1215 (clause 39: "no free man shall be seized... except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land"); the phrase "due process of law" appears in a statute of Edward III (1354). English kings were then bound by law; the jury (local people) decided facts; "due process" meant that the process used by the king was legally proper. After the Glorious Revolution of 1688 Parliament became supreme in England and the courts do not test the quality of Parliament's laws (the professor's example: "Parliament decided to join BRICS and decided to leave; the court did not check").
  • United States: "due process" is in the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments ("No person shall be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law"). American judges began to examine the quality of the law itself (substantive due process).
  • Lochner era: Courts struck down welfare legislation (maximum working hours, minimum wages, bans on child labour) as violating the "freedom of contract" - the owners and workers were treated as equals. See the Lochner case card below.
  • The Court-packing plan (1937): President Franklin D. Roosevelt (elected four times; the 22nd Amendment (1951) limited Presidents to two terms), frustrated by the Court striking down New Deal laws, proposed to appoint extra judges (the Judicial Procedures Reform Bill of 1937: up to six additional justices for each sitting justice over 70). The professor said: "he threatened the Court - if you strike down my Act, your judgment will be used only to sell groundnuts." The Court then changed course (West Coast Hotel v. Parrish, 1937 - the "switch in time that saved nine") and began to interpret due process more liberally.
  • India - the Constituent Assembly: the Drafting Committee had originally included "due process of law". The Constitutional Adviser B.N. Rau, on a visit to the US (1947), met Justice Felix Frankfurter, who advised: "Do not use this word; it will give excessive power to the judges; representatives of the people will be deprived of their power". Rau reported this, and the Assembly adopted "procedure established by law", a phrase taken from Art 31 of the Japanese Constitution (1946).
Case

Lochner v. New York (1905) - US Supreme Court

Citation / Court / Year

198 U.S. 45 (1905); 5:4; Peckham J. (the professor dated it "1903"; the correct year is 1905).

Facts
  • New York's Bakeshop Act (1895) limited bakers' working hours to 10 hours a day and 60 hours a week. Joseph Lochner, a bakery owner, was convicted for allowing an employee to work more than 60 hours.
Issues
  • Does the law violate the liberty of contract protected by the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause?
Held (Decision)
  • The Act was struck down as an unreasonable interference with the right of the baker and employees to contract; the labour regulation was not a valid health measure. Holmes J. dissented ("The Fourteenth Amendment does not enact Mr Herbert Spencer's Social Statics").
Ratio decidendi

Under substantive due process, courts may review the content of legislation; "freedom of contract" protected employers against welfare legislation (the "Lochner era", to 1937).

Significance / Later treatment
  • The professor: "owners exploiting the poor - 18 hours of work, no minimum wage, no working hour limits, no protection - and when the democratic Government made welfare laws, the Supreme Court struck them down. The Court was supreme over the legislature." This misuse is the reason the Indian framers preferred procedure established by law.
Use in the exam

The professor asked a student to present on Lochner the next day: "find the name of the case: L-O-C-H-N-E-R v. New York."

The difference - model answer

PointProcedure established by lawDue process of law
OriginJapanese Constitution (1946), adopted in India on the advice of B.N. Rau after consulting Justice FrankfurterEnglish concept (Magna Carta 1215; 1354 statute) developed in the US (5th and 14th Amendments)
What the court examinesOnly whether the procedure prescribed by a valid law has been followed by the implementing agencyWhether the law itself is fair, reasonable and valid (substantive) and the procedure is fair (procedural)
Role of the judiciaryLimited - Parliament has the upper handWide - the judiciary has the upper hand (judicial review of the quality of law)
Illustration (professor)A law lets me fail students after an examination; the court asks only: was the examination held?The court asks: was there due notice; was there adequate time (e.g. 10 questions in 3 minutes is unfair); is the law/procedure itself reasonable?
India todayAfter Maneka Gandhi (1978) the Supreme Court reads "procedure established by law" as requiring a just, fair and reasonable procedure - effectively due process (in substance) - while reasoning from Arts 14 and 19.The Court examines arbitrariness (Art 14), reasonableness (Art 19) and fairness (Art 21).

Professor's reason for preferring judicial review: "Every one of us - me, you, any politician - likes some power. When I come to power, I will favour those who belong to my party; I may make laws for our own people; what happens to the others, who did not vote for us? If the judiciary has the power to test the law, injustice is less likely. The judiciary does not contest elections; it only asks: is the law good or bad?" He added: "Due process and the basic structure - these two, I feel, are good checks (even if personally decided)."

sections.title: 9.7 Questions asked in COLA 19 - model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. What was the opinion of the Supreme Court on Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in the beginning of the Republic?

Model answer

In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Court held that Directive Principles are subsidiary to Fundamental Rights and cannot override them. That position has since changed: Minerva Mills (1980) - they are complementary and must be harmonised. (Do not write "in certain cases FR are to be given priority"; it fetches zero.)

Question asked in class

Q2. Why did the conflict between FR and DPSP arise? Which two Articles created the confusion?

Model answer

Art 32 (enforcement of FR by the Supreme Court) and Art 37 (DPSPs not enforceable by any court). One is justiciable and the other non-justiciable, so courts initially preferred the justiciable FR.

Question asked in class

Q3. What did Parliament do after Champakam? What did the 25th Amendment add?

Model answer

After Champakam Parliament enacted the First Amendment (1951) adding Art 15(4). The 25th Amendment (1971) added Art 31C: laws giving effect to Art 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged for violating Arts 14, 19, 31, and a declaration of such object cannot be questioned in court.

Question asked in class

Q4. In which case was Art 31C challenged? What happened?

Model answer

Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): the first part of Art 31C (protection for laws furthering Art 39(b),(c)) was upheld; the second part barring judicial review was struck down - judicial review is part of the basic structure.

Question asked in class

Q5. What did the 42nd Amendment do and what happened to it?

Model answer

It extended Art 31C to all Directive Principles (so a law implementing any DPSP could override Arts 14, 19 and 31) and added Art 368(4),(5). In Minerva Mills (1980) these provisions were struck down; FR and DPSP are complementary and supplementary, to be harmonised.

Question asked in class

Q6. Who can claim Art 21? Against whom? Does it apply to foreigners and corporations?

Model answer

"No person": all human beings, including foreigners (the procedure established by law must be followed even for a convicted terrorist); not corporations (classroom statement). Traditionally against the State; now also against private persons (horizontal application - Bodhisattwa Gautam 1996, Kaushal Kishor 2023).

Question asked in class

Q7. What is horizontal application of Fundamental Rights? Name the recent case.

Model answer

Enforcement of Fundamental Rights (here Arts 19 and 21) against non-State actors. Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023) - majority (Ramasubramanian J.) held Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons; Nagarathna J. concurring in part (see Lecture 7).

Question asked in class

Q8. What remedy is available if a Fundamental Right is violated and the loss cannot be recouped (e.g. classes lost because of wrongful rustication)?

Model answer

Monetary compensation under Art 32/226: Rudul Sah (1983) – compensation against the State; M.C. Mehta (1987) – absolute liability; Bodhisattwa Gautam (1996) – compensation payable even by a private individual.

Question asked in class

Q9. How did the Supreme Court interpret "life" in 1950 and in 1962?

Model answer

Gopalan (1950): narrow - bare existence/physical liberty. Kharak Singh (1962): "life" means more than animal existence; night-time domiciliary visits violate personal liberty (Art 21); privacy was recognised in Subba Rao J.'s minority opinion; Gopalan was partially overruled.

Question asked in class

Q10. What is "personal liberty" after Maneka Gandhi?

Model answer

It includes all liberties not covered by Art 19 and is of the widest amplitude (right to travel abroad, privacy, dignity, livelihood...).

Question asked in class

Q11. Explain "procedure established by law" and "due process of law". How did Maneka Gandhi change the position?

Model answer

See the table in 9.6. In Gopalan any procedure enacted by the legislature sufficed; in Maneka Gandhi the procedure must be just, fair and reasonable (non-arbitrary) - the Court reads Arts 14, 19 and 21 together (golden triangle), importing due process in substance.

Question asked in class

Q12. Why did the Constituent Assembly avoid "due process of law"? What was the Lochner problem?

Model answer

Because of Justice Frankfurter's advice to B.N. Rau and the American experience: the judiciary used due process to strike down welfare laws (maximum hours, child labour limits) as an infringement of "freedom of contract" - Lochner v. New York (1905); the Court was supreme over the legislature until the 1937 crisis (court-packing plan).

Question asked in class

Q13. Name the hotel case which was compulsory reading.

Model answer

State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel and Restaurants Association (2013) - the dance bar case (Lecture 8). (The transcript calls it "the hotel case"; this is the case assigned as compulsory reading in the previous lecture.)

The 25th Amendment (1971) added Art 31C : laws giving effect to Art 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged for violating Arts 14, 19, 31, and a declaration of such object cannot be questioned in court. Question asked in class Q4. In which case was Art 31C challenged? What happened? Model answer Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) : the first part of Art 31C (protection for laws furthering Art 39(b),(c)) was upheld ; the second part barring judicial review was struck down - judicial review is part of the basic structure. Question asked in class Q5. What did the 42nd Amendment do and what happened to it? Model answer It extended Art 31C to all Directive Principles (so a law implementing any DPSP could override Arts 14, 19 and 31) and added Art 368(4),(5). In Minerva Mills (1980) these provisions were struck down ; FR and DPSP are complementary and supplementary, to be harmonised. Question asked in class Q6. Who can claim Art 21? Against whom? Does it apply to foreigners and corporations? Model answer "No person": all human beings, including foreigners (the procedure established by law must be followed even for a convicted terrorist); not corporations (classroom statement). Traditionally against the State ; now also against private persons (horizontal application - Bodhisattwa Gautam 1996, Kaushal Kishor 2023). Question asked in class Q7. What is horizontal application of Fundamental Rights? Name the recent case. Model answer Enforcement of Fundamental Rights (here Arts 19 and 21) against non-State actors . Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023) - majority (Ramasubramanian J.) held Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons; Nagarathna J. concurring in part (see Lecture 7). Question asked in class Q8. What remedy is available if a Fundamental Right is violated and the loss cannot be recouped (e.g. classes lost because of wrongful rustication)? Model answer Monetary compensation under Art 32/226: Rudul Sah (1983) – compensation against the State; M.C. Mehta (1987) – absolute liability; Bodhisattwa Gautam (1996) – compensation payable even by a private individual. Question asked in class Q9. How did the Supreme Court interpret "life" in 1950 and in 1962? Model answer Gopalan (1950): narrow - bare existence/physical liberty. Kharak Singh (1962): "life" means more than animal existence; night-time domiciliary visits violate personal liberty (Art 21); privacy was recognised in Subba Rao J.'s minority opinion; Gopalan was partially overruled. Question asked in class Q10. What is "personal liberty" after Maneka Gandhi ? Model answer It includes all liberties not covered by Art 19 and is of the widest amplitude (right to travel abroad, privacy, dignity, livelihood...). Question asked in class Q11. Explain "procedure established by law" and "due process of law". How did Maneka Gandhi change the position? Model answer See the table in 9.6. In Gopalan any procedure enacted by the legislature sufficed; in Maneka Gandhi the procedure must be just, fair and reasonable (non-arbitrary) - the Court reads Arts 14, 19 and 21 together (golden triangle), importing due process in substance. Question asked in class Q12. Why did the Constituent Assembly avoid "due process of law"? What was the Lochner problem? Model answer Because of Justice Frankfurter's advice to B.N. Rau and the American experience: the judiciary used due process to strike down welfare laws (maximum hours, child labour limits) as an infringement of "freedom of contract" - Lochner v. New York (1905); the Court was supreme over the legislature until the 1937 crisis (court-packing plan). Question asked in class Q13. Name the hotel case which was compulsory reading. Model answer State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel and Restaurants Association (2013) - the dance bar case (Lecture 8). (The transcript calls it "the hotel case"; this is the case assigned as compulsory reading in the previous lecture.)

exam.title: Art 21 Continued - Procedure Established by Law v. Due Process of Law, Substantive v. Procedural Due Process, Expansion of Art 21 After Maneka Gandhi, Right to Die (Rathinam → Gian Kaur), D.K. Basu

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Procedure established by law (PEL): the court checks only whether the procedure laid down in the law was followed by the implementing authority. It does not ask whether the law itself is fair, and it does not ask whether Parliament followed its own law-making procedure.

DANGER SENTENCE - never write it: "Procedure established by law means the law was passed after following the proper procedure." The professor: "This makes my blood boil - zero marks." Reasons: Art 110(3) (Speaker's decision that a Bill is a Money Bill is final), Art 122 (proceedings in Parliament cannot be questioned in court on the ground of any irregularity of procedure), Art 118 (each House makes its own rules of procedure).

Due process of law (DPL) = two parts: (1) Substantive due process - the court examines the law itself: is it reasonable, fair, just? If not, the law is struck down. (2) Procedural due process - the court examines the procedure the law prescribes: is it fair, just, reasonable? If not, the procedure is corrected/improved (e.g. a fair hearing is read in - Maneka Gandhi).

Art 21 chain: Gopalan (1950, watertight compartments, PEL = any enacted procedure) → R.C. Cooper (1970, Gopalan's compartment theory overruled) → Maneka Gandhi (1978): Arts 14, 19 and 21 form the golden triangle; procedure must be just, fair and reasonable → flood of new rights (speedy trial, free legal aid, dignity, livelihood, environment, education, emergency medical aid).

Right to die: Rathinam (1994) said Art 21 includes the right not to live → s. 309 IPC void; Gian Kaur (1996) (5 judges) overruled it: right to life does not include the right to die; the unnatural extinction of life is incompatible with Art 21.

Homework announced: (1) Rights of arrested persons - D.K. Basu guidelines ("write tomorrow what the guidelines are"); (2) the Vishakha case "tomorrow"; (3) know the Lochner line of US cases that made Americans hate "due process".

What has been left out of this lecture

Personal anecdotes about the professor's career, past universities and colleagues, travel stories, comments on named students and on student-political figures, canteen/administration/TA-policy complaints, and the closing chatter about combined classes and schedules. Retained: the law, the cases and every question asked in class.

Corrections to remember: (a) the lecture says "Rati Ram" - the case is Rathi Ram v. Union of India (Delhi HC, 1985), and the Supreme Court case that followed is P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994); (b) the lecture's account of the High Court decisions is compressed - Delhi HC (Rathi Ram) and Bombay HC (Maruti Shripati Dubal, 1987) struck s. 309 down; Andhra Pradesh HC (Chenna Jagadeeswar, 1988) upheld it - so "different High Courts took different views" is correct; (c) the "environment" case mentioned as "Dharm Singh Mehta" is in all likelihood M.C. Mehta (and/or Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar) - verify the name before writing it.

Sensitive topic note: the discussion of suicide in this lecture is purely legal (constitutionality of s. 309 IPC, meaning of "life" in Art 21). The notes keep it at that level.

sections.title: 10.1 Procedure established by law v. Due process of law - the full comparison
sections.html:
PointProcedure Established by Law (India - text of Art 21)Due Process of Law (US 5th/14th Amendments)
MeaningAny deprivation of life/liberty is valid if done according to a procedure prescribed by a valid law (a law made by the competent legislature).Deprivation must be by law that is itself reasonable + a fair procedure. "Law" means just and fair law, not any enacted rule.
What the court examinesOnly whether the procedure in the law was actually followed by the implementing authority (police, officer, tribunal).(1) The quality/justice of the law itself (substantive); (2) the fairness of the procedure (procedural).
Can the court strike down the law for being unfair?Traditionally no (Gopalan). Court would only see that the executive followed the statute.Yes - under substantive due process the unreasonable law itself is struck down.
Does the court examine how Parliament passed the law?No. Arts 110(3), 118, 122 - internal proceedings of Parliament are not open to judicial scrutiny (except the limited cases of constitutional amendment/manner and form prescribed by the Constitution).No - due process is about the content/fairness, not the internal legislative process.
Example in the lectureA.K. Gopalan: detention under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 was done exactly as the Act prescribed → valid. A proctor debars a student: PEL checks only "did the university follow its own rule"; due process also asks "is the rule fair - was the student heard?".Maneka Gandhi (procedure improved: hearing read in); Mithu (s. 303 IPC itself unjust → struck down).
Source of the Indian phraseDrawn from Art 31 of the Japanese Constitution, suggested by B.N. Rau, preferred over "due process" (after meeting Justice Felix Frankfurter, who warned that "due process" makes judges super-legislators).US experience: Lochner v. New York (1905) and the Lochner era.
Position after Maneka Gandhi (1978)Text still says PEL, but the Supreme Court reads Art 21 with Arts 14 and 19: procedure must be "just, fair and reasonable" - not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive.India has therefore moved to a functional equivalent of due process (procedural fully; substantive through Arts 14, 19, 21 together).

Why "the law was made following proper procedure" earns zero

  • The expression "procedure established by law" refers to the procedure that the law prescribes for depriving a person of life or liberty - for example the procedure for arrest, remand, trial or detention in the CrPC/BNSS or the Preventive Detention Act.
  • It does not refer to the procedure by which Parliament passes the Bill. The courts cannot go into that: Art 110(3) - if a question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill, the Speaker's decision is final; Art 118 - each House frames its own rules; Art 122(1) - "the validity of any proceedings in Parliament shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure"; Art 122(2) - no officer or member is subject to court jurisdiction for regulating procedure.
  • Nuance for a high-scoring answer: the Aadhaar case (K.S. Puttaswamy (II), 2018) – the majority accepted the Speaker's Money Bill certification, but Chandrachud J. (dissent) held that certification is not immune from judicial review (a "fraud on the Constitution"); Rojer Mathew (2019) referred the question to a larger bench. So the safe line is: ordinarily the courts do not examine Parliament's internal procedure; the exact limits of review of Money-Bill certification are still being worked out.

sections.title: 10.2 Substantive and procedural due process - the professor's illustrations
sections.html:
(a) Procedural due process - Maneka Gandhi

  • Under procedure established by law, s. 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 (impounding a passport "in the interests of the general public") would simply have been valid: the Act allowed it, and the Government followed the Act.
  • Under due process, the Court asks: is the procedure fair? The Act had no hearing; the Court read in a fair hearing (audi alteram partem) and held the procedure must be just, fair and reasonable. Law not struck down; procedure improved.

(b) Substantive due process - Mithu v. State of Punjab

  • s. 303 IPC (murder by a life-convict) imposed a mandatory death sentence with no discretion. The Court asked not "was the procedure followed?" but "is the law itself just and fair?" - held unjust, unfair and unreasonable, hence void under Arts 14 and 21. This is substantive due process.

(c) Naz Foundation / s. 377 IPC (lecture example)

  • Naz Foundation v. Govt of NCT of Delhi (Delhi HC, 2009): s. 377 read down as to consensual sex between adults (Arts 14, 15, 21). Suresh Kumar Koushal (SC, 2013) reversed it. Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (SC, 2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct between adults: the law itself was tested against Arts 14, 15, 19 and 21 - a substantive review.
  • The professor's own remarks on the subject were sceptical and conversational; for the exam, treat it only as an example of a court examining the law's content, not just its procedure.
Case

Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983)

Citation / Court / Year

(1983) 2 SCC 277; AIR 1983 SC 473 (Supreme Court of India; 5 judges; Chandrachud C.J.).

Facts
  • Mithu, a life-convict, was convicted of murder under s. 302 and, because he was a life-convict who had committed murder, sentenced to death under s. 303 IPC, which provided that a person undergoing life imprisonment who commits murder "shall be punished with death" (no alternative).
Issues
  • Is a mandatory death sentence, which gives the court no discretion to consider circumstances, consistent with Arts 14 and 21?
Held (Decision)
  • s. 303 IPC is unconstitutional (violates Arts 14 and 21) and was struck down. A sentence of death imposed without any chance for the court to consider the circumstances of the offence and the offender is unjust, unfair and unreasonable.
Ratio decidendi

A law that prescribes a punishment (here, mandatory death) without allowing consideration of mitigating circumstances fails the test of just, fair and reasonable law under Arts 14 and 21. The substantive content of the law, not merely its procedure, is open to judicial review.

Reasoning
  • Following Maneka Gandhi, Art 21's "procedure" must be fair and reasonable; the Court extended that to the sentencing law itself: a mandatory sentence leaves no room for judicial discretion and treats unequal cases equally (Art 14).
  • The Court observed that a murder by a life-convict can range from a premeditated killing to a spur-of-the-moment act; s. 303 ignored the difference.
Significance / Later treatment
  • The classic Indian illustration of substantive due process.
  • Linked to Bachan Singh (1980): the death penalty is confined to the "rarest of rare" cases and requires judicial discretion.
Use in the exam

Use as the answer to "give an example where the law itself was struck down on the due process test". (Do not confuse with Maru Ram, which concerned remission and s. 433A CrPC.)

sections.title: 10.3 Expansion of Art 21 after Maneka Gandhi (1978) - the professor's list
sections.html:
The professor: "After 1978 there was a flood of cases. Every right of a human being that makes life worth living has been read into Art 21." Learn the case → right pairs below.

Right read into Art 21CaseOne-line holding
Speedy trial; free legal aid for the poorHussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1980) 1 SCC 81Thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar had been in jail longer than the maximum sentence for their offence. Held: speedy trial is part of Art 21; the State must provide free legal aid to the indigent (also Art 39A).
Humane treatment of prisoners; ban on fettersSunil Batra v. Delhi Administration (1978) 4 SCC 494Prisoners do not lose Art 21 on entering jail; bar fetters and solitary confinement unless justified; the Court has a continuing duty to protect prisoners.
Dignity in custody; protection against cruel punishmentFrancis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981) 1 SCC 608Bhagwati J.: the right to life is more than animal existence - it includes the right to live with human dignity (adequate nutrition, clothing, shelter, reading and writing, interviews with family and lawyer).
Right to livelihoodOlga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) 3 SCC 545The right to life includes the right to livelihood - pavement dwellers cannot be evicted without a fair hearing and notice (see Lecture 8 for the Art 19(1)(g) link).
Hawkers' zonesSodan Singh v. NDMC (1989) 4 SCC 155Hawkers have a right under 19(1)(g) subject to reasonable regulation (zoning); no right to occupy a particular place. (Detail: verify.)
Immediate medical aid in emergenciesParmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989) 4 SCC 286Every doctor, government or private, has a professional obligation to give immediate medical aid to a road-accident victim; police formalities cannot delay treatment. Art 21 imposes this duty on the State and the medical profession.
EducationMohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) 3 SCC 666 → Unni Krishnan J.P. v. State of A.P. (1993) 1 SCC 645Mohini Jain: right to education is part of Art 21. Unni Krishnan: right to education up to 14 years flows from Art 21; beyond that it is limited by the State's economic capacity. This led to the 86th Amendment (2002) - Art 21A.
Clean environmentSubhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) 1 SCC 598; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (series) - lecture name "Dharm Singh Mehta" is probably M.C. MehtaThe right to pollution-free water and air is part of the right to life (Art 21). M.C. Mehta (Oleum Gas Leak, 1987): absolute liability for hazardous industries.
Compensation for violationRudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983)Compensation under writ jurisdiction for illegal detention (see Lecture 9).
Privacy, reputation, and moreR. Rajagopal (1994); K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) (nine judges)Privacy is a Fundamental Right under Art 21 (and Part III as a whole).

Exam tip

For a "how has Art 21 expanded?" question: (1) text; (2) Gopalan - narrow; (3) Maneka Gandhi - broad, golden triangle; (4) list 5-6 rights with cases from the table; (5) conclude that Art 21 is now the most fertile Fundamental Right, the source of "unenumerated" rights.

Hussainara, Francis Coralie Mullin, Olga Tellis, Parmanand Katara, Unni Krishnan are the five the professor named; learn these first.

Case

Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1980)

Citation / Court / Year

(1980) 1 SCC 81; AIR 1979 SC 1369 (Supreme Court of India; Bhagwati J.).

Facts
  • A newspaper report exposed that thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar had been in jail for years, many for periods longer than the maximum sentence they could have got if convicted. Advocate Kapila Hingorani filed a writ petition under Art 32.
Issues
  • Does the right to life and personal liberty include a right to speedy trial and free legal aid?
Held (Decision)
  • Speedy trial is a Fundamental Right implicit in Art 21; the procedure that keeps a person in jail without trial for years is not "reasonable, fair and just". The State must provide free legal services to the poor accused. The Court ordered release of undertrials who had been in jail beyond the maximum possible sentence.
Ratio decidendi

A "just, fair and reasonable" procedure (Maneka Gandhi) requires speedy trial and free legal aid; Art 21 and Art 39A are read together.

Significance / Later treatment
  • First major public interest litigation (PIL) by the Supreme Court; bail and undertrial reform; legal-aid movement.
Use in the exam

Cite for "speedy trial under Art 21" and "free legal aid".

Case

Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981)

Citation / Court / Year

(1981) 1 SCC 608; AIR 1981 SC 746 (Supreme Court of India; Bhagwati J.).

Facts
  • Detenue Francis Coralie Mullin, detained under the COFEPOSA Act in Tihar Jail, complained that she was permitted only one interview a week with family/lawyer and was kept in unduly harsh conditions; she challenged these restrictions.
Issues
  • What does "life" in Art 21 mean? Do detenues have a right to meet family and lawyers freely?
Held (Decision)
  • "The right to life includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes along with it, namely the bare necessaries of life such as adequate nutrition, clothing and shelter and facilities for reading, writing and expressing oneself in diverse forms, freely moving about and mixing and commingling with fellow human beings." The restriction to one interview a week was struck down; cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment violates Art 21.
Ratio decidendi

"Life" in Art 21 = life with human dignity, not mere animal existence; any procedure that deprives a person of dignity must pass the Maneka Gandhi test.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Cited constantly for the dignity strand of Art 21; also linked to Munn v. Illinois / Kharak Singh dissent ("life is more than animal existence").
Use in the exam

Quote the "right to live with human dignity" passage in any Art 21 expansion answer.

Case

Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989)

Citation / Court / Year

(1989) 4 SCC 286; AIR 1989 SC 2039 (Supreme Court of India; Sabyasachi Mukharji J.).

Facts
  • A human-rights activist filed a PIL after a newspaper report of a scooterist injured in a road accident who was taken to a hospital but refused treatment because the case was a "medico-legal case" and the hospital said it should go to a hospital with jurisdiction for such cases; he died.
Issues
  • Is a doctor legally obliged to provide immediate medical aid to an accident victim before police formalities?
Held (Decision)
  • Preservation of life is of paramount importance; every doctor, whether at a Government hospital or otherwise, has a professional obligation to extend services to protect life. No law or procedure (including police formalities) can delay emergency treatment. Art 21 casts an obligation on the State to preserve life.
Ratio decidendi

The right to life includes the right to timely emergency medical care; the medico-legal formalities must follow, not precede, treatment.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Basis of the later "Good Samaritan" guidelines (SaveLIFE Foundation v. Union of India, 2016) protecting persons who help accident victims.
Use in the exam

Cite for "right to emergency medical aid".

Case

Unni Krishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) (with Mohini Jain, 1992)

Citation / Court / Year

(1993) 1 SCC 645 (Supreme Court of India; 5 judges; Jeevan Reddy J.); preceded by Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) 3 SCC 666 (2 judges).

Facts
  • Private medical and engineering colleges charged capitation fees. In Mohini Jain, a Karnataka rule allowing colleges to charge huge fees from non-State students was challenged. Unni Krishnan examined the whole scheme of private professional education.
Issues
  • Is there a fundamental right to education? Up to what level?
Held (Decision)
  • Mohini Jain: right to education is part of Art 21 (at all levels) and capitation fee is unconstitutional. Unni Krishnan: the right to education flows from Art 21 but is limited by Art 41 (economic capacity) - every citizen has a right to free education up to the age of 14; beyond that the right is subject to the limits of the State's economic capacity and development.
Ratio decidendi

The Fundamental Right to education exists up to 14 years; Arts 41, 45 and 46 define the scope beyond that.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Led to the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002): inserted Art 21A (free and compulsory education for children 6-14), changed Art 45 and added Art 51A(k); implemented by the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. The "scheme" of Unni Krishnan (regulation of private colleges) was later modified in TMA Pai (2002).
Use in the exam

Chain to write: Mohini Jain → Unni Krishnan → 86th Amendment → Art 21A → RTE Act, 2009.

sections.title: 10.4 Right to die? Section 309 IPC, Rathinam and Gian Kaur
sections.html:
Background: s. 309 IPC and the High Courts

  • s. 309 IPC punished "attempt to commit suicide" (simple imprisonment up to one year or fine). A completed suicide leaves no offender to punish; the law operated only where the attempt failed. Abetment of suicide (s. 306 IPC) is a separate offence against the abettor.
  • High Courts differed: Delhi HC (Rathi Ram, 1985) and Bombay HC (Maruti Shripati Dubal, 1987) held s. 309 unconstitutional (the right to life includes the right not to live, like freedom of speech includes freedom not to speak); the Andhra Pradesh HC (Chenna Jagadeeswar, 1988) upheld it.
  • The Supreme Court first sided with the strikers in P. Rathinam (1994) and then corrected itself in Gian Kaur (1996).
Case

P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994)

Citation / Court / Year

(1994) 3 SCC 394 (Supreme Court of India; 2 judges; R.M. Sahai and B.L. Hansaria JJ.).

Facts
  • Challenge to the constitutional validity of s. 309 IPC on Arts 14 and 21.
Issues
  • Does Art 21 include a right to die, so that s. 309 violates it?
Held (Decision)
  • s. 309 IPC is unconstitutional (violates Arts 14 and 21) and must be struck down. The Court reasoned that Art 21, like other rights, has a positive and a negative aspect: the right to life includes the right not to live a forced life.
Ratio decidendi

(Overruled) Art 21 includes the right to die - therefore punishing an attempt to commit suicide is unconstitutional.

Significance / Later treatment
  • Overruled in Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996).
Use in the exam

Treat as the "wrong turn" corrected by a larger bench.

Case

Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996)

Citation / Court / Year

(1996) 2 SCC 648; AIR 1996 SC 946 (Supreme Court of India; 5 judges; J.S. Verma J.).

Facts
  • Gian Kaur and her husband were convicted of abetment of suicide (s. 306 IPC) after a woman's death. They argued that if Rathinam held s. 309 void because Art 21 includes the right to die, then s. 306 (abetment) must also be void, since abetting the exercise of a fundamental right cannot be an offence.
Issues
  • Does the "right to life" under Art 21 include the "right to die"? Are ss. 306 and 309 IPC constitutional?
Held (Decision)
  • Rathinam overruled. The right to life under Art 21 does not include the right to die or to terminate one's life; "the right to life is a natural right embodied in Art 21 but suicide is an unnatural termination or extinction of life and, therefore, incompatible and inconsistent with the concept of right to life." Ss. 306 and 309 IPC are constitutionally valid. A distinction was drawn between suicide and the "right to die with dignity at the end of life" (a dying person, in a terminal state, hastening an already-commencing natural death process) - which is part of the right to live with dignity and was left open.
Ratio decidendi

The right to life is a natural right; "right to die" is unnatural and cannot be derived from Art 21. The positive/negative-aspect analogy with Art 19 does not hold because Art 19 rights are enumerated freedoms while the right to life is the right to be, not the right to end being.

Reasoning
  • Professor's gloss: "The right to life is a natural right. Just as we cannot create life in an unnatural way, we have no right to take it in an unnatural way."
  • Professor's policy reasoning (jurisprudential argument): life is full of failures ("90% of the time we fail"); if attempted suicide carried no consequence there would be no deterrence for people at their lowest moments - the law therefore discourages the act and encourages perseverance. (This is the lecture's rationale; the Court's own reasoning in Gian Kaur rests on the natural/unnatural distinction and on Art 21's scheme.)
Significance / Later treatment
  • Followed later by Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011) (passive euthanasia allowed in rare cases with High Court supervision) and Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) (five judges: right to die with dignity and living wills / advance directives recognised as part of Art 21, with safeguards).
  • Legislative change: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, s. 115 - a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and shall not be tried or punished; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does not re-enact s. 309 (attempt-to-suicide is no longer a general offence); abetment survives (BNS ss. 107-108, verify numbering); BNS s. 226 punishes an attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty.
Use in the exam

Two-line answer: "Rathinam (1994) held Art 21 includes the right to die; Gian Kaur (1996, 5 judges) overruled it - the right to life does not include the right to die; ss. 306 and 309 valid. Dying with dignity (passive euthanasia) was later recognised in Aruna Shanbaug and Common Cause."

sections.title: 10.5 Rights of arrested persons - D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
sections.html:
The professor: "D.K. Basu is a very important case; I have given it to you as work today - rights of arrested persons. Earlier, someone would be arrested and beaten; now there are guidelines."

Case

D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)

Citation / Court / Year

(1997) 1 SCC 416; AIR 1997 SC 610 (Supreme Court of India; Kuldip Singh and A.S. Anand JJ.).

Facts
  • D.K. Basu, Executive Chairman of Legal Aid Services, West Bengal, wrote a letter to the Chief Justice of India about deaths in police custody reported in newspapers; the Court treated the letter as a writ petition (PIL). The Court also dealt with a companion matter (Ashok Johri v. State of U.P.) on custodial death.
Issues
  • What safeguards must the police follow on arrest and detention to prevent custodial violence and death? Is compensation payable?
Held (Decision)
  • Custodial torture violates Art 21 (and Art 20(3), 22). The Court laid down 11 requirements/guidelines (below) to be followed in all cases of arrest/detention until legislative safeguards are enacted, and held that the State is liable to pay compensation (public-law remedy under Arts 32 and 226, over and above any private-law remedy) for custodial death/torture.
Ratio decidendi

Any form of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in custody - whether during investigation, interrogation or otherwise - is prohibited by Art 21; the police must follow the guidelines on arrest, and the State is vicariously liable in compensation.

Reasoning
  • A person in custody does not lose his Fundamental Rights; the greater the power of the police, the greater the need for accountability and transparency.
  • Transparency in arrest (identification, memo, witness, informing family) prevents "unrecorded" arrests, the main source of custodial violence.
Significance / Later treatment
  • Basis of the amendments to the CrPC (s. 41B - identification of police, memo of arrest; s. 41D - right to meet an advocate during interrogation; s. 50A - informing a nominated person; s. 54 - medical examination of arrested person); now in the BNSS, 2023 (verify section numbers).
  • Followed by Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) (guidelines on arrest in s. 498A cases).
Use in the exam

Learn the guidelines as a list and say that the guidelines have been legislated into the CrPC/BNSS.

The D.K. Basu requirements (learn as a list)

  1. Police personnel who carry out the arrest and handle interrogation must bear accurate, visible and clear identification and name tags with designations; particulars of all such personnel must be recorded in a register.
  2. The arresting officer shall prepare a memo of arrest at the time of arrest, attested by at least one witness (a family member or respectable member of the locality) and countersigned by the arrestee, showing the date and time of arrest.
  3. A person arrested/detained, held in a police station, interrogation centre or other lock-up, is entitled to have one friend or relative or other person known to him informed, as soon as practicable, that he has been arrested and where he is being held (unless the attesting witness is himself such a person).
  4. The time, place of arrest and venue of custody must be notified by the police within 8-12 hours after arrest, through the District Legal Aid Organisation and the local police station, if the next friend/relative lives outside the district or town.
  5. The arrestee must be made aware of his right to have someone informed of his arrest or detention as soon as he is put under arrest or detention.
  6. An entry must be made in the diary at the place of detention regarding the arrest, with the name of the person informed and the names/particulars of the police officials in whose custody the arrestee is.
  7. The arrestee should, where he so requests, be examined at the time of arrest for major and minor injuries; the "inspection memo" must be signed by both the arrestee and the arresting officer, and a copy given to the arrestee.
  8. The arrestee should be subjected to medical examination every 48 hours during detention by a trained doctor on the panel of approved doctors appointed by the Director of Health Services of the State/UT.
  9. Copies of all the documents, including the memo of arrest, should be sent to the Magistrate for his record.
  10. The arrestee may be permitted to meet his lawyer during interrogation, though not throughout the interrogation.
  11. A police control room should be provided at all district and State headquarters, where information regarding the arrest and the place of custody must be communicated by the arresting officer within 12 hours of effecting the arrest, and displayed on a conspicuous notice board at the control room.

The lecture's version (what the professor listed orally)

Name badge on police personnel; tell the arrestee why he is being arrested; inform his family; tell him he may take the help of a lawyer, and if he cannot afford one, free legal aid counsel must be provided; produce him before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Art 22(2)); and get a medical examination at the time of arrest.

The guidelines must be displayed in every police station. His instruction: "Next time you go to a police station, check whether the D.K. Basu guidelines are displayed. If not, call the SHO and ask why."

Why is a medical examination done at the time of arrest? (the professor's question)

The students answered "to check if he is healthy / diabetic / needs treatment". The professor rejected the "only medical care" answer and gave the real point:

  • The medical examination records the condition of the body at the time of arrest ("when you went in you had both legs intact and 32 teeth; if you come out with a broken leg and 16 teeth the record shows what happened in between").
  • If injuries occur during custody, the police are responsible - the report is evidence of custodial violence and fixes accountability.
  • So it protects against third-degree methods (custodial torture) - an issue of human rights and Art 21. Health care is only a secondary purpose.
  • Linked rules: Art 22(1) (informed of grounds of arrest, right to consult a lawyer), Art 22(2) (produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding travel time), Art 20(3) (no self-incrimination), s. 54 CrPC / BNSS (medical examination).

An entry must be made in the diary at the place of detention regarding the arrest, with the name of the person informed and the names/particulars of the police officials in whose custody the arrestee is. The arrestee should, where he so requests, be examined at the time of arrest for major and minor injuries ; the "inspection memo" must be signed by both the arrestee and the arresting officer, and a copy given to the arrestee. The arrestee should be subjected to medical examination every 48 hours during detention by a trained doctor on the panel of approved doctors appointed by the Director of Health Services of the State/UT. Copies of all the documents , including the memo of arrest, should be sent to the Magistrate for his record. The arrestee may be permitted to meet his lawyer during interrogation , though not throughout the interrogation. A police control room should be provided at all district and State headquarters, where information regarding the arrest and the place of custody must be communicated by the arresting officer within 12 hours of effecting the arrest, and displayed on a conspicuous notice board at the control room. The lecture's version (what the professor listed orally) Name badge on police personnel; tell the arrestee why he is being arrested; inform his family ; tell him he may take the help of a lawyer , and if he cannot afford one, free legal aid counsel must be provided; produce him before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Art 22(2)); and get a medical examination at the time of arrest . The guidelines must be displayed in every police station . His instruction: "Next time you go to a police station, check whether the D.K. Basu guidelines are displayed. If not, call the SHO and ask why." Why is a medical examination done at the time of arrest? (the professor's question) The students answered "to check if he is healthy / diabetic / needs treatment". The professor rejected the "only medical care" answer and gave the real point: The medical examination records the condition of the body at the time of arrest ("when you went in you had both legs intact and 32 teeth; if you come out with a broken leg and 16 teeth the record shows what happened in between"). If injuries occur during custody , the police are responsible - the report is evidence of custodial violence and fixes accountability . So it protects against third-degree methods (custodial torture) - an issue of human rights and Art 21 . Health care is only a secondary purpose. Linked rules: Art 22(1) (informed of grounds of arrest, right to consult a lawyer), Art 22(2) (produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours , excluding travel time), Art 20(3) (no self-incrimination), s. 54 CrPC / BNSS (medical examination).

sections.title: 10.6 Other points raised in this lecture
sections.html:
• Gopalan - "watertight compartments": each Fundamental Right is a separate code (Art 19 applies only to a free person; Art 21 only to detention). Overruled in R.C. Cooper (1970); final death in Maneka Gandhi (1978) (golden triangle of Arts 14, 19, 21).
  • Kharak Singh (1962) and Munn v. Illinois (1877): "life" means more than mere animal existence; the dissent of Subba Rao J. in Kharak Singh anticipated Maneka Gandhi on "personal liberty".
  • Arbitrary - the professor's rule on language: do not use "arbitrary" loosely; it has a definition. In constitutional law an action is arbitrary when it is done capriciously, irrationally or without adequate determining principle (E.P. Royappa, 1974; Shayara Bano, 2017 - "manifest arbitrariness"). Write "arbitrary" only after saying what made it so.
  • Money Bill: Art 110; Speaker's decision final (Art 110(3)).
  • Next class: the Vishakha case (sexual harassment at the workplace; Art 21 with Arts 14, 15, 19(1)(g); guidelines later converted into the POSH Act, 2013).
