sections.title: 10.7 Questions asked by the professor in this lecture - model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. What is the difference between "procedure established by law" and "due process of law"?

Model answer

PEL: the court only checks that the procedure prescribed in the law was followed by the authority implementing it; it does not test the fairness of the law or the procedure. DPL: the court checks both the law (substantive due process) and the procedure (procedural due process) for reasonableness, fairness and justness. Under PEL the proctor's order debarring a student is valid if the university rule was followed; under DPL the court also asks whether the rule is fair and the student was heard. Example: Gopalan (PEL - detention valid) v. Maneka Gandhi (hearing read in; fair procedure demanded).

Question asked in class

Q2. What do you mean by "procedure established by law"? (Why will you get zero if you write that the law was passed following the proper procedure?)

Model answer

It means the procedure laid down in the law for depriving a person of life or liberty (arrest, trial, detention), not Parliament's law-making procedure. Courts cannot inquire into the internal procedure of Parliament - Art 122 (proceedings not to be questioned on ground of irregularity), Art 110(3) (Speaker's Money-Bill decision final), Art 118 (rules of procedure). The correct answer: "the court will see whether the procedure prescribed in the law was followed while depriving the person."

Question asked in class

Q3. Define substantive due process and procedural due process.

Model answer

Substantive: the court examines whether the law itself is reasonable, fair and just; if not, it is struck down (Mithu - s. 303 IPC; Navtej Johar). Procedural: the court examines whether the procedure for implementing the law is just, fair and reasonable; if not, the procedure is corrected (Maneka Gandhi - hearing read in).

Question asked in class

Q4. Give an example of procedural due process.

Model answer

Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): s. 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act empowered the authority to impound a passport without a hearing. The Court did not strike the section but held the procedure must be fair and read in a right to be heard; the Attorney General undertook to give Maneka a hearing.

Question asked in class

Q5. Give an example of substantive due process.

Model answer

Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983): s. 303 IPC (mandatory death sentence for murder by a life-convict) was struck down as unjust, unfair and unreasonable under Arts 14 and 21. Another: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) (s. 377 IPC as applied to consensual adult same-sex acts).

Question asked in class

Q6. Why did Americans start hating "due process"? Which case?

Model answer

Lochner v. New York (1905), 198 U.S. 45: the US Supreme Court struck down a New York law limiting bakery employees to 60 hours a week as violating the liberty of contract under the 14th Amendment's due process clause. In the "Lochner era" the Court struck down many social-welfare laws on the ground that they were unreasonable, so "due process" became a tool for judges to impose their economic philosophy (the "super-legislature" charge). That is why Justice Frankfurter advised B.N. Rau not to use it and why the Indian Constitution says "procedure established by law".

Question asked in class

Q7. Why was Art 21 originally given a narrow meaning? Which case and which approach?

Model answer

A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950): Art 21's "law" meant any State-made (enacted) law; "procedure established by law" meant procedure prescribed by that law. The Court also adopted the watertight compartments approach - Arts 19, 21 and 22 were mutually exclusive codes. It was weakened by R.C. Cooper (1970) and overruled by Maneka Gandhi (1978).

Question asked in class

Q8. Name the post-1978 cases in which Art 21 was expanded and the rights recognised.

Model answer

Hussainara Khatoon (speedy trial, free legal aid); Sunil Batra (humane treatment in prison, no fetters); Francis Coralie Mullin (right to live with human dignity); Olga Tellis (livelihood); Sodan Singh (hawkers' trading zones); Parmanand Katara (immediate medical aid); Mohini Jain / Unni Krishnan (education up to 14 → Art 21A); Subhash Kumar / M.C. Mehta (clean environment); Rudul Sah (compensation); Puttaswamy (privacy).

Question asked in class

Q9. Is there a right to die under Art 21? What was the position in Rathinam and in Gian Kaur?

Model answer

No. In Rathinam (1994) a two-judge bench held that the right to life includes the right not to live and struck down s. 309 IPC. In Gian Kaur (1996) a five-judge bench overruled Rathinam: the right to life is a natural right; suicide is an unnatural extinction of life and inconsistent with Art 21; ss. 306 and 309 are valid. The "right to die with dignity" (passive euthanasia, living wills) was recognised later in Aruna Shanbaug (2011) and Common Cause (2018) within narrow limits.

Question asked in class

Q10. Why is suicide punished only when it is "attempted"? (professor's question on s. 309)

Model answer

A completed suicide leaves no offender to prosecute; the offence of attempt (s. 309 IPC) applied where the person survived. The rationale offered in the lecture: people face failure repeatedly; the law is to discourage the act and encourage perseverance, rather than leave attempts consequence-free. Present law: s. 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 presumes severe stress and bars prosecution; the BNS, 2023 omits the general offence of attempt; abetment of suicide remains an offence. (For the exam, mention that attempt-to-suicide is better treated as a health issue.)

Question asked in class

Q11. What are the rights of an arrested person? (D.K. Basu)

Model answer

Right to know grounds of arrest (Art 22(1)); to consult and be defended by a lawyer, with free legal aid if he cannot afford one (Art 22(1), Art 39A); to have a relative/friend informed; to be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Art 22(2)); to medical examination at the time of arrest and thereafter; identifiable police and a signed memo of arrest; protection from custodial torture (Art 21, Art 20(3)). D.K. Basu (1997) laid down 11 binding requirements (see 10.5).

Question asked in class

Q12. Why is a medical examination required at the time of arrest?

Model answer

To record the condition of the arrestee's body at the time he enters custody so that any injury later found can be traced to what happened in custody. It protects against third-degree methods and fixes police accountability; medical care for a disease such as diabetes is only a secondary purpose.

Question asked in class

Q13. Who was the lecturer's authority for "life is more than animal existence"?

Model answer

The phrase comes from Field J. in Munn v. Illinois (1877) (US), cited by Subba Rao J. (dissenting) in Kharak Singh (1962), adopted in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Francis Coralie Mullin (1981).

exam.title: Art 21 Revision - Due Process Already in Arts 14 and 19, the Lochner Problem, the Journey from Procedure Established by Law to Procedural and Substantive Due Process, Maneka Gandhi in Depth, Mithu, and the Birth of PIL (S.P. Gupta)

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Revision questions the professor opened with: To whom does Art 21 apply ("No person" - every person, not only citizens); vertical and horizontal application; expansion of "life"; expansion of "personal liberty"; PEL v. DPL.

Core thesis of the lecture: Due process was always present in Indian law - in Art 14 (reasonable classification) and Art 19 (reasonable restrictions) - the courts could always ask "is it reasonable?". Only Art 21 was closed to this question because the framers feared the Lochner-era American experience. Maneka Gandhi (1978) opened Art 21 to reasonableness (procedural due process); Mithu (1983) applied it to the law itself (substantive due process).

PEL v. DPL in one line (the professor's answer to "what is the difference?"): under due process the judiciary has more power (it tests the quality of the law); under procedure established by law the legislature is trusted more and the judiciary only checks that the prescribed procedure is there and was followed.

Three-step story of "fair": Gopalan (procedure = anything enacted) → Maneka Gandhi ("any procedure is no procedure"; must be just, fair and reasonable, not fanciful, arbitrary or oppressive) → Mithu (the law can be struck down for being unjust).

PIL arrives in the same era: seed in Bombay Kamgar Sabha (1976) → Hussainara Khatoon, Sunil Batra (1978-80) → first Constitution Bench acceptance in S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) - the Judges Transfer Case (lawyers have locus standi to challenge the transfer of judges).

What has been left out of this lecture

The opening banter about the professor's health and seating, repeated attendance and discipline remarks, comments on university fees and administration, personal anecdotes, and extended political commentary (on party leaders, the Emergency-era conduct of named individuals, motives attributed to persons in the Maneka Gandhi passport episode, voter-roll revision, nationality and currency controversies, press-conference remarks, animal-welfare remarks, and the conduct of a sitting High Court judge). Those are the lecturer's opinions or unproven allegations and are not exam material. The professor himself said: "Opinion and proven fact are different; an unproved allegation is only an allegation." Retained: law, cases and every question asked.

Corrections / flags: (1) Anwar Ali Sarkar was decided in 1952 (the West Bengal Special Courts Act is of 1950; the lecture says "struck down in 1950 itself" - the Act is 1950, the judgment 1952). (2) The lecture says the Government returned the passport and the Court dismissed the writ as infructuous - the reported judgment is generally summarised differently (the Court read in a fair hearing, took the Attorney General's undertaking to hear her, and did not quash the order); verify from the law report before stating that the passport was returned. (3) The lecture calls the Emergency-era executive action against the judiciary "arresting judges" - the documented episodes are the supersession of three senior judges in 1973 and the transfers of High Court judges (1976); do not write "judges were arrested" in the exam. (4) The 1981 circular on judges' transfers/consent is attributed in the lecture to "Gokhale"; H.R. Gokhale was Law Minister in the Emergency years, while the 1981 circular is generally attributed to Law Minister P. Shiv Shankar - verify. (5) The lecture's "Mithu v. Maru Ram" confusion is cleared in 11.5: the case is Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983).

sections.title: 11.1 Revision: who gets Art 21 and what it covers
sections.html:
• "No person" (Art 21) - the right is available to every person, citizen or foreigner. Contrast Art 19 ("all citizens"). The professor corrected himself in class: "Art 21 is not for every citizen; it is for every person."
  • Against whom? Originally only the State (Art 12) - vertical application. Now also against private persons in appropriate cases - horizontal application (Bodhisattwa Gautam, Kaushal Kishor (2023); see Lectures 7 and 9).
  • Expansion of "life" (more than animal existence - dignity, livelihood, health, shelter, environment) and expansion of "personal liberty" (everything not covered by Art 19 - Maneka Gandhi; the right to travel abroad - Satwant Singh). Case list: Lecture 10, 10.3.

sections.title: 11.2 Due process was always present in Arts 14 and 19
sections.html:
The professor's argument: many students (and "many teachers") think due process arrived only with Maneka Gandhi. Wrong. Under Art 14 and Art 19 the courts always had the power to ask whether a classification or restriction was reasonable; only in Art 21 the question was not asked until 1978.

ArticleQuestion the court could always askExample the professor gave
Art 14Is the classification reasonable (intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object)? If not, the law is quashed. Later also: is it arbitrary?State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952): the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 let the State direct that "offences or classes of offences or cases" be tried by Special Courts under a different procedure. Case

State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952)

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1952 SC 75; 1952 SCR 284 (Supreme Court of India; 7 judges; majority: Patanjali Sastri C.J., Mahajan, Mukherjea, Das, Chandrasekhara Aiyar JJ. in separate opinions; Bose J.; one judge, Das J., dissented on a part).

Facts
  • The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 empowered the State Government, by notification, to direct that "such offences or classes of offences or cases or classes of cases" as it thought fit be tried by a Special Court following a procedure that differed from the Criminal Procedure Code (for example, no committal proceedings, no jury, restricted right to cross-examine). Issues
  • Does a statute that allows the Government to pick cases for a more drastic procedure, without any guiding principle, violate equal protection of the laws?
Held (Decision)
  • s. 5(1) of the Act was struck down as violating Art 14. The classification of "offences or cases" for trial by special procedure was left to the unguided discretion of the executive and was not based on any intelligible differentia or relation to the object of the Act. The Act itself did not classify; it gave the executive a blank cheque to discriminate.
Ratio decidendi

Art 14 forbids class legislation, but permits reasonable classification: (1) intelligible differentia, (2) rational nexus with the object. A statute that leaves selection to the uncontrolled discretion of the executive, without a determining principle, offends Art 14.

  • Shows that the courts had the power to examine the reasonableness of a law under Art 14 from the start (the professor's point: "due process was already there in Art 14"). It also shows the Court acting within a year or two of Gopalan in a very different mode.
  • Extended later into the "manifest arbitrariness" doctrine (E.P. Royappa; Maneka Gandhi; Shayara Bano).
Use in the exam

Cite in answers on "due process before Maneka Gandhi" and on reasonable classification. Remember: decided 1952, Act of 1950.

sections.title: 11.3 Why was Art 21 kept closed? The Lochner-era problem (the professor's fuller account)
sections.html:
• Why Americans were afraid of government: they had lived under English rule; they did not want a strong federal government ("they trusted local leaders, not outsiders"). They agreed to ratify the 1787 Constitution only on the condition that fundamental rights be added - hence the first ten amendments (Bill of Rights, 1791), which are drafted in absolute language ("Congress shall make no law...") with no restriction clauses. Limits (restrictions) have therefore come only through judicial decisions, because "no absolute right is permissible."
  • Freedom of contract: the Court read "liberty" in the Due Process Clauses to include the liberty to contract. Employers and workers were treated as equals who were free to bargain.
  • The professor's extreme example: a mother with four children; a landlord says "I will kill one child, but I will feed three" - she may agree to save three. Can such a "contract" be allowed? No. Similarly, a worker who is promised one meal for a day's labour is not "freely" contracting. Such exploitation cannot be permitted in a rule-of-law, welfare-oriented State.
  • Yet the US Supreme Court, "by grabbing the power under due process of law", struck down protective legislation, saying the legislature was "interfering with the freedom of the people to contract" - the laissez-faire philosophy. Result: welfare legislation was held unconstitutional → the "Lochner era" (1905-1937).
  • The Indian lesson: The Bill of Rights was borrowed from America, and the framers first used "due process of law" in the draft. B.N. Rau, the Constitutional Adviser, travelled to many countries to show the draft ("as we show a house we build"). An American judge, Felix Frankfurter, warned him: if you write due process of law, "the whole power will come under five or six judges; however popular your leader, his word will not run" in a populous country. So the draft's "due process" was rejected and replaced - borrowed from Art 31 of the Japanese Constitution (1946) - by "procedure established by law".
  • Art 31 Japanese Constitution: "No person shall be deprived of life or liberty, nor shall any other criminal penalty be imposed, except according to procedure established by law." (The professor first said 33, then 39, and settled on 31; "here Art 21, there Art 31".)
Case

Lochner v. New York (1905)

Citation / Court / Year

198 U.S. 45 (1905) (US Supreme Court; 5-4; Peckham J.; Holmes J. dissenting).

Facts
  • A New York statute (the Bakeshop Act, 1895) limited bakery employees to ten hours a day / sixty hours a week. Joseph Lochner, a bakery owner, was convicted of letting an employee work longer and challenged the law.
Issues
  • Does the law violate the liberty of contract protected by the Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment?
Held (Decision)
  • The Act was struck down (5-4). The right to buy and sell labour is part of the liberty protected by the 14th Amendment; the maximum-hours law was not a genuine health measure but an unreasonable interference with freedom of contract.
Ratio decidendi

Substantive due process: courts may strike down legislation that interferes with "liberty of contract" if it is not a reasonable exercise of the State's police power.

Reasoning
  • Holmes J. (dissent): "The Fourteenth Amendment does not enact Mr. Herbert Spencer's Social Statics" - the Constitution does not embody a particular economic theory; the Court should not substitute its views for the legislature's.
Significance / Later treatment
  • Gave "due process" a bad name: judges as a "super-legislature" striking down welfare laws. Ended with the 1937 "switch in time" (West Coast Hotel v. Parrish) after Roosevelt's court-packing threat (see Lecture 9, 9.6).
  • Why it matters for India: because of Lochner, the framers (on the advice of Frankfurter and B.N. Rau) chose "procedure established by law" in Art 21.
Use in the exam

Keep it as a two-line case: year (1905, not 1903), bakers' hours, liberty of contract, Holmes's dissent, and its link to the Indian choice of words. The professor asked for a presentation on it (see Lecture 9).

sections.title: 11.4 Procedural due process - Maneka Gandhi explained by the professor
sections.html:
The meaning of "fair"

  • Under procedural due process the court must test whether the procedure is just, fair and reasonable - "not arbitrary, unjust, unfair". The professor's translation of fair: "ठीक-ठाक" (the procedure must be decent).
  • His illustration: a university rule says a student is "tested and passed/failed". The university holds the test but never checks the answer-books and declares results. Under PEL the court would only ask "was a test held?" - yes, so valid. Under procedural due process the court asks "was the procedure of testing fair?" - evaluation is part of fairness; the procedure is therefore bad. "Quality cannot be ensured by the judiciary under PEL."

The background to Maneka Gandhi

  • Before 1967 there was no passport statute; passports were issued or refused at the Government's discretion: "Government allowed some to go abroad and refused others - without giving a reason" (the lecture adds that corruption was possible).
  • Satwant Singh Sawhney v. D. Ramarathnam (1967): Satwant Singh was refused a passport without reasons. The Supreme Court (3:2) held that the right to travel abroad is part of "personal liberty" under Art 21 and cannot be denied except by a law (a procedure established by law); the executive cannot refuse a passport at its will. The case "forced the Government to enact a law" - the Passports Act, 1967.
  • Passports Act, 1967, s. 10: grounds on which a passport may be impounded/revoked; s. 10(3)(c): "if the passport authority deems it necessary so to do in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of India, friendly relations of India with any foreign country, or in the interests of the general public". s. 10(5): the authority shall furnish reasons "unless, in its opinion, it will not be in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India... or in the interests of the general public to furnish". The Government impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport and did not disclose the reasons.
  • The petition: under Art 32, she argued: (1) the order violates natural justice - nobody can be a judge in his own cause, nobody can be punished without notice and a hearing (audi alteram partem); (2) right to travel abroad is part of Art 21 (Satwant Singh) and Art 19(1)(a)/(g)/(d).
  • The Government's answer: Art 21 only requires "a procedure established by law" - and s. 10(3)(c) is the procedure; it does not provide for a hearing, so none can be demanded. (The text of Art 21, after Gopalan, supported this.)

The Court's answer - "any procedure is no procedure"

  • "Any procedure is no procedure." The procedure under Art 21 must be just, fair and reasonable; it cannot be fanciful, arbitrary or oppressive; it cannot depend on the whims and fancies of the authority. (Bhagwati J.; the professor: "very good English, Justice Bhagwati's... Krishna Iyer's too - those who feel weak in English should read the original judgments".)
  • Golden triangle: Arts 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive; a law depriving personal liberty must pass Art 21 + Art 14 + Art 19 tests.
  • Natural justice is part of Art 21: (a) nemo judex in causa sua (no one a judge in his own cause); (b) audi alteram partem (hear the other side); the fair procedure demands notice and hearing.

The Government's counter-argument and the post-decisional hearing doctrine

  • Government: "If we give her notice and time to reply, she may fly out of the country - the very purpose of impounding will be defeated. A notice may be dangerous."
  • The Court evolved (not the Government, as the professor stressed): the doctrine of post-decisional hearing. In a case of urgency or where a prior hearing might defeat the purpose, the authority may act first (impound the passport) and then give a hearing (a notice, an opportunity to explain, to file an affidavit or bond) - the hearing comes after the decision. The professor: "The administrative-law teacher will teach this in detail; I will not."
  • Result: s. 10(3)(c) is valid but must be read with a fair-hearing requirement; a non-communication of reasons is not permissible unless the authority has a recorded, valid ground. The Government, through the Attorney General, undertook to hear her. (Verify whether the passport was returned - see the flag above.)
  • Consequence for everyone: "Maneka Gandhi's case did not benefit only Maneka Gandhi; fair procedure now benefits all of us." The professor linked this to the later growth of rights - including rights regarding what we wear, eat and do (see Lecture 8, 8.8, and Lecture 9, 9.5).

sections.title: 11.5 Substantive due process - how it came to India
sections.html:
• In Maneka Gandhi the substantive law (the Passports Act) was not challenged - "the Passports Act continues to be there; only the procedure in s. 10 was refined".
  • What if the law itself is bad? The first such case: Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) - s. 303 IPC struck down. (The professor first recalled "Maru Ram" and "Mithu Ram" before settling on Mithu Singh v. State of Punjab; the professor said "1980 or 81" - the judgment is 1983. Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980) is a different case on remission and s. 433A CrPC.)
  • Why s. 303 was bad: Under s. 302, the court has a choice - death or life imprisonment (or a lesser term) - so it can see the gravity of the offence. Under s. 303, a person already undergoing a life sentence who commits murder must be hanged - "why he murders, how he murders, no discretion". The Court: this is arbitrary; the judge has no discretion to value the merits; so it is unconstitutional.
  • First time that "due process" was applied to Art 21 itself (the substantive law); "you should not be confused: Anwar Ali Sarkar and many such cases had already applied due process under Arts 14 and 19". The professor's comment: "Dr Ambedkar could have said, we are already applying it in Art 14, so what is the problem in Art 21?"
  • Examples of laws struck down on the substantive test (professor's list): s. 377 IPC (as applied to consensual adults; Navtej Johar, 2018) and adultery (s. 497 IPC; Joseph Shine v. Union of India, 2018) - "possible only because we have due process of law; had it been PEL, the Court would only have checked whether someone had been punished under 377".
  • Around the same period: Minerva Mills (1980) - FR/DPSP "complementary and supplementary".
StageCase / yearWhat the court examines
1. Narrow PELA.K. Gopalan (1950)Is there a law? Was the procedure in it followed? (No test of fairness.)
2. Due process via Art 14Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) and later casesIs the classification reasonable? Is the law arbitrary?
3. Due process via Art 19Romesh Thappar, Chintaman Rao, V.G. Row etc.Is the restriction reasonable?
4. Gopalan weakenedR.C. Cooper (1970)Arts 19 and 21 not watertight; effect of the law, not its object, matters.
5. Procedural due processManeka Gandhi (1978)Procedure must be just, fair, reasonable; natural justice read in.
6. Substantive due processMithu (1983); later Navtej (2018), Joseph Shine (2018)Is the law itself just, fair and reasonable?
7. Rights explosionHussainara, Sunil Batra, Francis Coralie, Olga Tellis, Parmanand Katara, Unni Krishnan, Subhash Kumar, Puttaswamy ...Art 21 as source of unenumerated rights.

sections.title: 11.6 Public Interest Litigation (PIL) - origin and the Judges Transfer Case
sections.html:
Why PIL arose

  • Before the 1980s the Supreme Court was "for powerful people with money" - big lawyers and high-class cases; ordinary people got no relief.
  • The seed: Bombay Kamgar Sabha v. Abdulbhai Faizullabhai (1976) - a union (representative body) was allowed to carry the cause of the whole body of labour before the Court.
  • 1977-79 onward: many cases in which the Court relaxed locus standi - Hussainara Khatoon (letter/newspaper report about undertrials), Sunil Batra (letter from a prisoner treated as a writ petition) and others.
  • First Constitution Bench acceptance of PIL: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981), the Judges Transfer Case.
Case

S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) - the First Judges Case

Citation / Court / Year

AIR 1982 SC 149; 1981 Supp SCC 87 (Supreme Court of India; 7 judges; Bhagwati J. delivered the leading opinion).

Facts
  • A Law Ministry circular (1981) asked the Chief Justices to obtain the consent of additional judges to be appointed to other High Courts and to follow a policy of appointing/transferring judges between States (outsiders in each High Court); non-continuation of an additional judge of the Delhi High Court and the transfer of High Court Chief Justices were also challenged. The stated reasons were to promote impartiality and national integration (the "outsider judge" idea); the professor's concern was that transfers could be used to control the judiciary (punishment postings).
  • Petitioners: a group of lawyers led by S.P. Gupta, advocate of the Allahabad High Court, who filed writ petitions challenging the circular and the transfers. The Government objected: lawyers have no locus standi - they have no personal interest in the transfers; the judges concerned were the persons aggrieved, and judges cannot sue because they depend on the Government for postings.
Issues
  • Do advocates have locus standi to challenge the transfer / non-appointment of judges? (the PIL question)
  • Is the transfer of a High Court judge/Chief Justice without consent valid? What is the role of the Chief Justice of India in appointments and transfers under Arts 124, 217, 222?
Held (Decision)
  • Locus standi liberalised: where a legal wrong or injury is caused to a person or class of persons who, by reason of poverty, disability or socially or economically disadvantaged position, cannot approach the court, any member of the public acting bona fide can move the court (Art 226/32). Advocates have a sufficient interest in the independence of the judiciary - they are "officers of the court" and justice cannot be delivered without the Bar. The professor: "The judge alone cannot do justice; without the help of lawyers there is no justice; so lawyers also have an interest."
  • On the merits, the majority upheld the transfers and held that "consultation" with the Chief Justice of India under Arts 124(2), 217 and 222 does not mean concurrence; the Executive's view could prevail (the "primacy of the Executive"). A transfer of a judge in public interest was held valid (verify the finer holdings on additional judges and consent).
Ratio decidendi

The doctrine of locus standi is relaxed in public interest litigation: a bona fide member of the public (and, in appropriate cases, the Bar) may enforce the legal rights of those unable to approach the court. The independence of the judiciary is a basic feature, and the Bar is a stakeholder in it.

Reasoning
  • Bhagwati J.: the Court's role in a developing society is to make access to justice meaningful for the poor; a procedural technicality should not defeat a substantive right. The professor: "Again Justice Bhagwati - he did many good things."
  • Practical point: judges cannot sue for their own transfers; if no one else could, executive control of the judiciary (punishment postings) would go unchallenged. The professor warned: "if the judiciary is under the executive it becomes like the IAS officers... justice will not be there".
Significance / Later treatment
  • Established PIL as part of constitutional adjudication.
  • The "consultation, not concurrence" holding was overruled by the Second Judges Case - Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993) (primacy of the CJI) - and the collegium system was reaffirmed in the Third Judges Case (1998, presidential reference). The 99th Amendment / NJAC Act (2014) was struck down in the Fourth Judges Case (2015).
  • Related: Union of India v. Sankalchand Himatlal Sheth (1977) (transfer of a High Court judge without consent held invalid; verify details).
Use in the exam

Write: "S.P. Gupta (1981) - the Judges Transfer Case - the first Constitution Bench acceptance of PIL; liberalised locus standi (including for lawyers); also decided 'consultation' ≠ 'concurrence' (later overruled in 1993)."

sections.title: 11.7 Model long answer: "Trace the development of due process in Indian constitutional law"
sections.html:
1. Text of Art 21: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." The Constituent Assembly rejected "due process of law" (B.N. Rau, after speaking to Justice Frankfurter, feared a super-legislature; the phrase "procedure established by law" was taken from Art 31 of the Japanese Constitution).
  2. Lochner background: in America the Due Process Clause was used (Lochner, 1905) to strike down welfare laws in the name of freedom of contract.
  3. A.K. Gopalan (1950): "law" = enacted law; "procedure" = any procedure prescribed; each Article a watertight compartment. The Court checked only whether the prescribed procedure was followed.
  4. Due process through Arts 14 and 19: reasonable classification (Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952) and reasonable restrictions (Art 19(2)-(6)) gave the Court power to review the quality of laws, except in Art 21.
  5. R.C. Cooper (1970): the compartment theory was overruled; the effect of State action on rights matters.
  6. Maneka Gandhi (1978): the Passports Act s. 10(3)(c) allowed impounding without a hearing; the Court held "procedure" must be just, fair and reasonable (Arts 14, 19, 21 - the golden triangle); natural justice is part of Art 21; post-decisional hearing allowed in cases of urgency. → procedural due process.
  7. Mithu (1983): s. 303 IPC (mandatory death) struck down as arbitrary - the law itself must be fair → substantive due process.
  8. Result: Art 21 has become the source of numerous unenumerated rights (Hussainara, Francis Coralie, Olga Tellis, Puttaswamy), PIL has made them accessible (S.P. Gupta), and Navtej Johar / Joseph Shine (2018) show substantive review of penal laws. Conclusion: though the words are "procedure established by law", the Indian position is now functionally the same as due process of law.

sections.title: 11.8 Questions asked by the professor in this lecture - model answers
sections.html:
Question asked in class

Q1. To whom does Article 21 apply - to every citizen or every person?

Model answer

To every person ("No person shall be deprived..."), including foreigners and non-citizens. Art 19 applies to citizens only. (The professor deliberately tested this: the correct word is "person".)

Question asked in class

Q2. What was discussed under Art 21 in the last class? (vertical and horizontal application, expansion of life, expansion of personal liberty, PEL v. DPL)

Model answer

Vertical = Art 21 against the State; horizontal = against private persons (Kaushal Kishor, 2023; Bodhisattwa Gautam). Expansion of life = life with dignity, livelihood, health, environment, education. Expansion of personal liberty = everything not in Art 19 (travel abroad, privacy, choice of dress/food). PEL v. DPL = see Q 3.

Question asked in class

Q3. What is the difference between procedure established by law and due process of law?

Model answer

Under PEL the legislature is trusted more and the court only sees whether the prescribed procedure exists and has been followed. Under DPL the judiciary has more power: it tests the quality of the law (substantive due process) and the fairness of the procedure (procedural due process). Example: s. 377 IPC and adultery could be struck down only because of due process; under PEL the Court would only have checked whether someone had been punished under s. 377.

Question asked in class

Q4. Was there any element of due process in the Constitution before Maneka Gandhi? Give a case.

Model answer

Yes - in Art 14 (reasonable classification) and Art 19 (reasonable restrictions). State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) struck down s. 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 because the classification of cases for special trial was not a valid classification. Only Art 21 had no such test until 1978.

Question asked in class

Q5. Why was due process not available under Art 21 earlier? (the Lochner-era problem)

Model answer

Because the framers feared the American experience: in the Lochner era the US Supreme Court used due process to strike down social-welfare laws on the basis of "freedom of contract". On Frankfurter's advice to B.N. Rau, "due process of law" was dropped and "procedure established by law" (from Art 31 of the Japanese Constitution) was adopted.

Question asked in class

Q6. Which article of the Japanese Constitution has "procedure established by law"?

Model answer

Article 31 (not 33 or 39).

Question asked in class

Q7. Who was the Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly, and what did he do about "due process"?

Model answer

Sir B.N. Rau; he consulted jurists abroad including Justice Felix Frankfurter, who warned that "due process" would give a few judges excessive power over legislation. The phrase was replaced by "procedure established by law".

Question asked in class

Q8. Why did the American framers/people have "absolute" rights in the Bill of Rights, and how did restrictions come in?

Model answer

The first ten amendments (1791) were demanded as the condition of ratifying the Constitution and are drafted in absolute terms. No right can be absolute in practice, so restrictions came through judicial decisions, unlike India where they are in the text (Art 19(2)-(6)).

Question asked in class

Q9. What is "fair" in "procedural due process"? Give the professor's example.

Model answer

Fair = just and reasonable, not arbitrary, unjust or unfair. Example: a university holds a test but never checks the answer-books and declares pass/fail. Under PEL the Court would say "a test was conducted"; under procedural due process it would say the procedure is not fair because evaluation is part of fairness.

Question asked in class

Q10. What are the facts of Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and what did the Court hold?

Model answer

Her passport was impounded under s. 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 in the interest of the general public, without reasons or a hearing. She argued that natural justice was violated. The Government said Art 21 only requires a procedure prescribed by law. The Court held: right to go abroad is part of personal liberty (Satwant Singh, 1967); procedure must be just, fair and reasonable - "any procedure is no procedure"; natural justice is part of Art 21; Arts 14, 19, 21 form a golden triangle; s. 10(3)(c) is valid only if a fair (post-decisional) hearing is provided.

Question asked in class

Q11. What was Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) and what was its consequence?

Model answer

The Supreme Court held that the right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Art 21 and the executive cannot refuse a passport arbitrarily; a law is needed. Parliament enacted the Passports Act, 1967.

Question asked in class

Q12. The Government said: if we give notice she will flee. What doctrine did the Court evolve?

Model answer

The doctrine of post-decisional hearing: in a case of urgency (where a prior hearing would defeat the object) the authority can act first and then give the person a hearing; the hearing comes after the decision, but it must be real and meaningful.

Question asked in class

Q13. When did substantive due process come to India? Name the case and the provision struck down.

Model answer

Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983): s. 303 IPC (mandatory death sentence for a murder committed by a life-convict) was struck down under Arts 14 and 21 because it gave the court no discretion and was arbitrary. (Not Maru Ram.)

Question asked in class

Q14. Why is the Court's power over the "quality" of a law a feature of due process but not of PEL? Give two examples of laws struck down on that ground.

Model answer

Because only under due process does the court ask whether the law itself is fair. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) struck down s. 377 IPC as applied to consensual adults, and Joseph Shine (2018) struck down adultery (s. 497 IPC); Mithu (1983) struck down s. 303 IPC.

Question asked in class

Q15. How did Public Interest Litigation begin in India? Name the first Constitution Bench case that accepted PIL.

Model answer

Seed: Bombay Kamgar Sabha (1976) (representative standing). Then Hussainara Khatoon and Sunil Batra (letter petitions). The first Constitution Bench acceptance: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) - the Judges Transfer Case, where advocates were held to have locus standi.

Question asked in class

Q16. Why did lawyers have locus standi in the Judges Transfer Case?

Model answer

Judges cannot challenge their own transfers (they depend on the Government for postings) and the poor/ignorant are not the aggrieved class here. The Court held that advocates are officers of the court and justice cannot be delivered without the Bar; hence the Bar has a sufficient interest in the independence of the judiciary and can sue in public interest.

Question asked in class

Q17. Why is it dangerous if the judiciary is under the control of the executive (the professor's point on judge transfers)?

Model answer

Because transfers (e.g. "punishment postings") can be used to pressurise judges; if judges work "under" the executive like administrative officers, justice (especially against the State) will not be available. Independence of the judiciary is part of the basic structure.

sections.title: A. The professor's "danger sentences" and standing exam rules
sections.html:
Never write these - marks lost

"In certain cases Fundamental Rights have priority over Directive Principles" (or vice versa) → zero. Write: FR and DPSP are complementary and supplementary; the Constitution rests on the balance between Parts III and IV; harmonious construction (Minerva Mills, 1980). (Lecture 9)

"Procedure established by law means the law was passed after following proper procedure" → zero ("my blood boils"). It means the procedure prescribed in the law for depriving a person of life/liberty; courts cannot go into Parliament's internal procedure (Arts 110(3), 118, 122). (Lecture 10)

"The restriction is arbitrary" without saying what made it arbitrary - the word has a definition (capricious, irrational, without adequate determining principle). (Lecture 10)

Never write that a Fundamental Right is "absolute" - all rights are subject to restrictions (Art 19(2)-(6) or judicial limits). (Lectures 2, 11)

Do not copy-paste or write "personal opinion" as fact - the professor repeatedly separated opinion / allegation / proved fact. In constitutional law cite the case.

Things the professor said will come in the exam

Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023) - horizontal application of Arts 19 and 21; the whole batch must read it ("I will create a question from it"). (Lectures 7 and 9)

Tuljapurkar / obscenity (Gandhi, Hicklin → Miller → Aveek Sarkar) - community standards, contemporary community standards test, Gandhi-Godse literary context. (Lecture 4)

The eight grounds of Art 19(2) - memorise the list and one case each (table C below). (Lectures 2-3)

Ramasamy Udayar (Madras HC, 2021) - religious procession through a street and Art 19(1)(g)/25/26; plus the 15 Oct 2026 Supreme Court ruling on conversion and backward-class status. (Lecture 8)

The dance-bar (hotel) case - State of Maharashtra v. IHRA (2013) - compulsory reading. (Lectures 8, 9)

Maneka Gandhi / PEL v. DPL / substantive and procedural due process - an essay question in practically any year. (Lectures 9-11)

Right to property: Art 31 → 300A; "amount" v. "compensation"; Kesavananda; Bimal Kumar Shah (2024) (Lecture 6)

sections.title: C. Art 19(2) - the eight grounds and one case each
sections.html:
#GroundKey case(s) from the lectures / standard authorityMemory hook
1Sovereignty and integrity of India (added 16th Amend., 1963)Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995) - mere slogans without incitement are not an offence (verify); sedition-related line of thinking."S-I"
2Security of the StateRomesh Thappar (1950) - security of State = grave, aggravated forms of public disorder (war, rebellion); Brij Bhushan (1950)."Security"
3Friendly relations with foreign States (1st Amend., 1951)Statutes against propaganda harming relations with foreign States; rarely litigated."Friends"
4Public order (1st Amend., 1951)Superintendent, Central Prison v. Ram Manohar Lohia (1960) - "proximate" connection; S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989) - the spark in a powder keg; Shreya Singhal (2015) - incitement test; Ramlila Maidan (2012)."Order"
5Decency or moralityHicklin → Ranjit Udeshi (1965) → Aveek Sarkar (2014) (community standards) → Tuljapurkar (2015)."Morals"
6Contempt of courtContempt of Courts Act, 1971; "truth as a defence" 2006 amendment."Contempt"
7DefamationSubramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) - criminal defamation (s. 499 IPC) upheld."Defame"
8Incitement to an offence (1st Amend., 1951)Shreya Singhal (2015) - discussion / advocacy / incitement; Pravasi Bhalai (2014) - hate speech."Incite"

Memory line for the eight grounds: Sovereignty - Security - Friendly relations - Public order - Decency/morality - Contempt - Defamation - Incitement (S-S-F-P-D-C-D-I). Art 19(3): sovereignty and integrity, public order (assembly); 19(4): the same two + morality (association); 19(5): general public interest and protection of Scheduled Tribes (movement/residence); 19(6): general public interest, qualifications, State monopoly (profession).

sections.title: G. How to answer an exam question on a case (template)
sections.html:
1. Name, year, court (and bench strength if a Constitution Bench).
  2. Two-line facts - only the facts that matter to the issue.
  3. Issue - phrase as a question under a specific Article.
  4. Held / ratio - the principle in one sentence; quote the key phrase only if you are sure of it.
  5. Why it matters - what changed afterwards (an Amendment, an Act, a later case that followed or overruled it).
  6. Link - connect to the question's Article and one other case from the notes (the examiner rewards a chain: Gopalan → Cooper → Maneka → Mithu).

Verification note

Items marked "verify" in the chapters should be checked against a law report before being quoted verbatim - they rest either on the lecturer's recollection or on details the public sources did not settle (for example the Sodan Singh holdings, Samatha, Bishambhar Dayal, Himat Lal Shah, the Zoroastrian Co-operative case, C. Selvarani, the Sikkim women's-rights claim, the Ramlila Maidan date, and the Maneka Gandhi passport outcome).

Political commentary, personal anecdotes and unproven allegations in the lectures about named individuals have been deliberately left out of the notes; where relevant, each chapter says so in its "What has been left out" box.

sections.html:
These notes consolidate every document in the four classnotes files — raw lecture transcripts, structured lecture notes, the verbatim class record, worksheet problems and the two study companions — into one day-wise, exam-ready compendium. The course ran from 15 July 2026 to 7 October 2026 across twenty-one recorded sessions. Q&A; blocks answer the questions actually asked in the lectures, including the full twenty-one-problem Article 14 workshop. Flowcharts summarise the doctrines that decide examination answers.

day.title: Article 13, Personal Laws & the Road to the First Amendment
day.trail: Personal law vs fundamental rights · Shah Bano · Shayara Bano · Goolrokh · Talaq-e-biddat vs talaq-e-ahsan · Kameshwar Singh & the Ninth Schedule · Shankari Prasad homework

sections.title: Overview
sections.html: This session (recorded verbatim, without a printed date) sits immediately before the 16 July lecture on Shankari Prasad: it closes by assigning precisely that case. The professor uses Article 13(2) to open the deepest question of the early course — can personal laws be declared void when they violate fundamental rights?
sections.text: This session (recorded verbatim, without a printed date) sits immediately before the 16 July lecture on Shankari Prasad : it closes by assigning precisely that case. The professor uses Article 13(2) to open the deepest question of the early course — can personal laws be declared void when they violate fundamental rights?

sections.title: Personal Laws versus Fundamental Rights
sections.html:
The professor frames the problem through marriage. Islamic law does not permit a Hindu to marry a Muslim girl unless she converts — and conversion, he asks, why should she want to convert? Article 21, read broadly, says a person may marry anybody. The personal law therefore violates a citizen's fundamental right, and the violation is doubly suspect because it is gender-based: a Muslim boy may marry anybody, including a Hindu girl, but a Muslim girl cannot marry outside her religion without converting. The question for inquiry: can such a Koranic practice, violating Article 21, be declared void under Article 13(2)?

A parallel problem comes from constitutional history: by constitutional amendment some fundamental rights have been taken away — above all the right to property. Whether those amendments are valid is studied under Article 13(3).

sections.title: The Reform Record of Parliament — and the POCSO Digression
sections.html:
Parliament, the professor argues, has been discriminatory in its reform energy. Starting from the very first Parliament, every manner of reform was introduced among Hindus. In Hindu tradition marriage was a Kanya Daan given before puberty; in Muslim law too the age of puberty was the age of marriage. The age of marriage was later raised to eighteen while the age of consent stood at sixteen — and the professor recounts joining a mild protest against the resulting incoherence: “What is this? Do you want to keep our daughters in adulterous relationships? They cannot marry, but they can have sex? Raise the age of consent to eighteen as well.” Under POCSO the age of consent became eighteen (following the Justice Verma Committee — Verma being originally from Satna, near Indore), and the Supreme Court had remarked only days earlier that such strict laws on the sexuality of girls aged sixteen to eighteen have sent thousands of boys — and girls, the law being gender-neutral — to jail.

Professor'S Aside

A chachi fell in love with her sixteen-or-seventeen-year-old nephew, conceived from him, and now compels the nephew to marry her. The family pleaded: abort the child, leave the relationship. She refused — “Now I shall marry only him” — an FIR followed, and the chachi is in jail, delivering a child. POCSO is a very strict law; Google it if you do not believe me. Why are you so worried? Worry about the chacha if you must — the chacha falls outside POCSO; it is the chachi who falls within our field of study.

sections.title: How the Court Approaches Personal Law
sections.html:
A Hindu cannot marry more than once; a Hindu cannot marry a Muslim girl; and among Muslims too personal law frequently violates their own members' fundamental rights. The professor poses the classification question: shall we treat personal law as “custom” — and is there not a significant difference between custom and personal law? For Hindus considerable reform was enacted; for Muslims it was not. Jawaharlal Nehru's stated reason was that they were “not yet sufficiently educated to accept reforms” — and, the professor notes, seventy-five or eighty years later exactly the same thing is still said.

The Supreme Court's technique is studied through three assigned cases. In Shah Bano, the question was maintenance beyond the iddat period, which Islamic law does not extend; the Court, “with a certain cleverness,” granted relief from the side without commenting upon the personal law itself. Even when it declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional it did so in a roundabout manner, avoiding a direct attack. In Shayara Bano the same pattern appears. And a Parsi lady — educated at an NLU — who married a Hindu (a Gupta) was barred by Parsi personal law from performing her father's funeral rites; the Supreme Court granted her permission, again without ruling on the personal law. A student supplies the citation: Goolrokh M. Gupta v. Valsad Parsi Anjuman (2017); the professor directs the class to read both that and the connected Pardiwala rulings. A Christian case is added: Christian mothers lacked guardianship over their own children — the father's name was necessary even to open a bank account — and again the Court granted relief while sidestepping the personal law. For Hindus, the starting case is Narsu Appa Mali.

Professor'S Aside

A court remains a court only so long as society obeys its orders. Have you observed what happened in Pakistan — how the people burned down the Supreme Court? Read the case of Asia Bibi.

On codification of Muslim law, the professor is blunt: it is about vote bank. Many Muslims do not adhere strictly to the faith's practices; the government lacks the courage to reform. Around sixty Islamic countries exist, and in nearly all of them — including Pakistan — polygamy is prohibited; but the All India Muslim Personal Law Board resists, and in politics everyone wants votes. “Modi also wants votes.”

sections.title: Talaq Clarified — the Classroom Exchange
sections.html:
A hypothetical is put: a prominent Nagpur advocate's Muslim friend wishes to give talaq to his wife — will the petition lie in the High Court or the District Court? The professor makes the class work through it, then corrects the vocabulary: talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) has been declared unconstitutional; talaq-e-ahsan is the only permissible method — one pronouncement in the first month, the second in the second month, the third in the third month, pronounced especially when the wife is not menstruating. Proceedings now lie before the District Court, not by writ petition in the High Court — a distinction the professor says he now tests even in faculty selection interviews.

Professor'S Aside

Until you say “instant” triple talaq, triple talaq has not been declared unconstitutional — the word “instant” must be added. And are you educated or uneducated? Then why do you not speak in legal language? She is explaining as though she has gone to some village for a legal aid camp. Buy a newspaper sometimes. Why are newspapers printed? To be read — not to eat peanuts with.

Professor'S Aside

Do not study from Chat G-P-T. It gives wrong answers. Today, coming here, I asked it what arguments had been advanced in the case I am about to teach — it gave me entirely wrong answers. I said, “Have you not yet come down from your intoxication?” I asked it what Dr. Ambedkar said at Sholapur, and it fetched his Delhi speech. We professors know the context, so we are rarely cheated — you all will be cheated. Depend on original sources.

sections.title: The First Amendment — Kameshwar Singh and Article 31B
sections.html:
Asked why the First Constitutional Amendment came about, a student (Kanishk) answers correctly: Champakam Dorairajan. The professor confirms it was one reason — but the most important was property. He recalls Dr. Ambedkar's final Constituent Assembly speech (assigned as compulsory reading): “Today we are going to start a life of contradictions.” After working the class through the answer, the doctrine emerges: political equality has arrived — one person, one vote; one vote, one value — but a huge gulf persists in the economic and social dimensions of society, and that disparity must be dismantled by the fastest path if the country is to remain united.

Professor'S Aside

There is a character in our Ramayana — Bali. Whoever fought him, half their power came to him. When even the foolish students of NLU stand up in moot court, the students of traditional colleges think, “Oh dear, this person is from NLU, he will certainly speak well” — half of them fall into depression and their performance deteriorates. That is what economic disparity does to confidence. I have lived outside the village for forty years, and still, sometimes, confidence fails me.

Land being a State subject, every State enacted zamindari abolition laws, taking the landlords' land and giving it to the tenants who worked it. The rajas and maharajas — whose rights the professor illustrates with the full style of the complainant in the leading case: “Maharajadhiraj Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga” — challenged the Bihar Act, and the Patna High Court declared it unconstitutional under Article 13(2): property was a fundamental right, and the Act took it away. Nehru, greatly distressed, brought the First Amendment, inserting Article 31A and Article 31B and creating the Ninth Schedule.

A student (Sanika) reads Article 31B aloud. Its effect: any Act placed in the Ninth Schedule is deemed never to have become void for violating Part III, notwithstanding any judgment of any court. The original Constitution had eight schedules (which the class was told to memorise on day one); the Ninth was added by the First Amendment. With it, the Kameshwar Singh judgment was reduced to zero — the Bihar Act sailed through.

Professor'S Aside

If any act is placed in the Ninth Schedule, that act will become like Duryodhan after Gandhari opened her eyes — his body became like a thunderbolt; he could not be killed. The act gains judicial immunity: the judiciary will not be able to review it, even if it violates fundamental rights, and even if the Kameshwar judgment were to apply.

The professor confirms it was one reason — but the most important was property . sections.title: Homework — Shankari Prasad
sections.html:
Key Point

Three small things to read in Shankari Prasad v. Union of India: (1) the petitioners' arguments — one will certainly be that Parliament is a “State” under Article 12, so an amendment violating fundamental rights is void under Article 13(2); find the other grounds, and the name of the top-class advocate who filed the petition — in today's era, as Hanuman ji holds value in the Ramayana, that advocate holds value in the Constitution of India; (2) the respondents' (Attorney General's) grounds; (3) the name of the judge who delivered the judgment, and on what grounds. Two further tasks: the three or four personal-law cases from every religion, and the meanings of order, rule, by-law and ordinance.

Professor'S Aside

There was a girl in the fourth or fifth year whose boyfriend was from this section. She would come and stand five minutes before the break, chat for a minute, and then walk with me — “Sir, I have come to receive you; you are my dearest teacher.” A simple man, I believed she had come to receive me. Many days later I discovered she came for someone else. She is seen running every day.

Schedules of the Indian Constitution

The Ninth Schedule mechanism: (i) Parliament places specific Acts in the Schedule; (ii) such Acts become immune from judicial review for violation of Fundamental Rights; (iii) Article 13(2) ceases to apply to them; (iv) even if they violate Articles 14, 19 and 31, they remain valid. The Schedule itself is not immune from review — the Acts placed within it are. The professor's image: “The Constituent Assembly made an umbrella where rainwater would not go. Call that umbrella the 9th Schedule.”

Article 368 requires passage by both Houses — under Article 79, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha). The Provisional Parliament problem of 1951: elections were held only in 1951–52, so the Rajya Sabha did not yet exist when the First Amendment was passed. Article 379 (now repealed) gave the provisional Parliament all the powers of a regular Parliament; the President could make rules to remove difficulties. “If Rajya Sabha was not there, should the country have been locked up? Or should there be some mechanism for improvement?”

sections.title: Ambedkar's Three Contradictions
sections.html: In his final speech Dr. Ambedkar identified: (1) political equality — “one man, one vote, one vote, one value”; (2) social inequality — hierarchies of caste and class persisting; (3) economic inequality — disparities in wealth and land. The First Amendment's purpose was to remove the economic contradiction by enabling land reform; the constitutional goal is an egalitarian society — justice, social, economic and political.

sections.title: Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India (1951)
sections.html:
Case

Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India

5-judge bench · unanimous (5:0) · judgment by M. Patanjali Sastri J. · P.R. Das for petitioners · M.C. Setalvad (first Attorney General

Facts
Zamindars of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh challenged land reform laws as violating Part III. Parliament responded with the First Amendment (Articles 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule). Blocked from attacking the Acts directly, the zamindars challenged the Amendment itself — strategic logic: if the tree falls, the branch falls anyway.
Held
The First Constitutional Amendment is valid. (1) Article 368 confers constituent power, distinct from ordinary legislative power under Articles 245–246; Article 13(2) applies only to the latter. (2) The definition of “law” in Article 13(3) deliberately omits “constitutional amendment.” (3) Article 368 contains no exception for Part III — the framers could have written “except Part III” and did not.
Principle
Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights; an amendment is not “law” under Article 13(2).

The six petitioner arguments — and the lesson in over-pleading

#Petitioners' argumentCourt's response
1Only a proper two-House Parliament can amend; the one-house provisional Parliament lacked competenceArticle 379 empowered the provisional Parliament
2The President wrongly modified Article 368 to permit single-House amendmentConsidered weak — over-pleading weakens a case: when one ground is found false, the judge may view the entire petition with suspicion
3An amendment is “law” under Article 13(2) — Parliament is “State” under Article 12Rejected — see ratio
4State ratification was necessary (Arts 31A/31B affected court powers)Only direct, not indirect, effects on courts trigger ratification
#Petitioners' argumentCourt's response
5The Bill was changed after introductionParliament is master of its own procedure — “slave only to the Constitution”
6Parliament cannot legislate on land (State subject)Conflates legislative power with constituent power

The petitioners' case, argument by argument

The respondents' two textual pillars: Article 13(3) enumerates ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages — not constitutional amendments; and Article 368 speaks of amending “any provision of this Constitution” without carving out Part III. Both omissions are deliberate. Under constituent power, “Parliament becomes as powerful as the Constituent Assembly itself was. Just as there were no restrictions on the Constituent Assembly, similarly no restrictions will remain with Parliament either, because restrictions are not written anywhere.”

Ordinary legislative powerConstituent power
Derived from Articles 245–246Derived from Article 368
Subject to Article 13(2)Not subject to Article 13(2)
Limited by the Seventh ScheduleAs powerful as the Constituent Assembly itself
Makes ordinary lawsMakes and amends the Constitution

The two powers of Parliament distinguished

Doctrine of harmonious construction

Two apparently conflicting provisions are interpreted so that both survive: Article 13 governs legislative power; Article 368 governs constituent power; each operates in its own sphere. Reading Article 13 broadly would render Article 368 “dead” for Part III — an interpretation courts must avoid. “Harmony means making a balance between both, keeping both alive. Lest one dies. Both survive.”

sections.title: Sajjan Singh (1965) — the Seeds of Doubt
sections.html:
The Seventeenth Amendment (1964), expanding the Ninth Schedule and amending Article 31A, was challenged. The majority (Gajendragadkar C.J., Wanchoo and Raghubar Dayal JJ.) reaffirmed Shankari Prasad. But two judges — both with Nagpur connections, the professor notes — wrote separate opinions that planted the Basic Structure seed.

  • Justice Hidayatullah: Fundamental Rights are “primordial sacrosanct” rights; Article 13(2) does not expressly exclude amendments; rights of such significance cannot be abrogated in the same manner as ordinary provisions; certain rights are inalienable — recognised by the Constitution, not created by it.
  • Justice Mudholkar: the comparative argument. At a Banaras Hindu University conference a German professor had described the Basic Law's eternity clause — Article 79(3) entrenches the federal structure, the democratic and social state and the inviolability of human dignity against all amendment. A Pakistan Supreme Court judgment (likely Fazlul Quader Chowdhury, 1963) had similarly limited amending power. And the U.S. Constitution's Article V contains two unamendable matters: the slave-trade clause (temporarily, until 1808) and equal suffrage in the Senate (permanently — no State, without its consent, may be deprived of its equal suffrage). If other constitutions entrench cores, the Indian Constitution too must have essential features beyond the amending power's reach; a constitution has a soul and an identity that cannot be destroyed while claiming the same constitution survives.
Professor'S Aside

Think of the scholarship of that era: no internet; Supreme Court Reports not easily available; no interns — the very concept of an intern was unknown in India until the Clinton–Lewinsky scandal brought it into headlines; judgments typed on manual typewriters, where an error on the 21st line of a page meant retyping the whole page. Justice Mudholkar was not in line to become Chief Justice. He had nothing personal to gain. He could simply have signed the majority opinion — yet he undertook the research, because he believed the Constitution and the people of India deserved it.

sections.title: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967)
sections.html:
Case

Golak Nath v. State of Punjab

11-judge bench · 6:5 · majority led by K. Subba Rao C.J.

Facts
The validity of the Seventeenth Amendment's protection of land reform laws was again in issue; the Court reconsidered Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh.
Held
Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. Article 368 (its marginal heading then reading “Procedure for amendment”) supplies only procedure, not power; the power flows from the residuary legislative power — Entry 97, List I read with Article 248 — making an amendment an exercise of legislative power, hence “law” under Article 13(2), hence void insofar as it abridges Part III.
Principle
Fundamental Rights placed beyond the amending power; the doctrine of prospective overruling introduced — the ruling operates only from the judgment date, so all earlier amendments survived.
Professor'S Aside

That poor guy won the case, but he didn't get any relief — the property already taken remained taken.

sections.title: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — the Middle Path
sections.html:
Thirteen judges — the largest bench in Indian history — tested the 24th Amendment. Between Shankari Prasad's unlimited power and Golaknath's no power over Part III, the Court took the middle path: Parliament can amend any provision, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot destroy or abrogate the Constitution's basic structure or essential identity. The 24th Amendment was upheld, but the amending power it confirmed is a limited power. (The case is taught in full detail on 22 July — Day 3.)

sections.title: Comparative and Historical References
sections.html:
U.S. Article V offers a four-way amendment process (Congress proposes with State legislatures ratifying — the common route; Congress proposes with State conventions ratifying — used once, for the 21st Amendment repealing Prohibition; two-thirds of State legislatures demand a convention — never used; and convention-plus-convention). In the United States amendment is treated as a political question: no judicially enforced basic structure exists there. The German Basic Law (1949), Article 79(3), expressly entrenches the division into Länder, the Länder's participation in legislation, and the principles of human dignity (Article 1) and the democratic, social federal state (Article 20).

Case

Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)

U.S. Supreme Court · 7:2

Facts
Dred Scott, enslaved, sued for freedom having lived with his owner in a free State and territory.
Held
African Americans, enslaved or free, were not citizens and could not sue; the Missouri Compromise was unconstitutional. “Once a slave, always a slave — you can never become a free citizen.”
Principle
Widely regarded as the worst U.S. Supreme Court decision; it inflamed public opinion and catalysed the Civil War (1861–65).

The Civil War connection to Article 356: Lincoln — a self-educated man of humble origins, early a shoemaker, who had lost almost every election before winning the presidency — sent the military to prevent secession at the cost of roughly 800,000 casualties in a country of 31 million, and was assassinated shortly after. The Indian framers, aware of that bloodshed, designed President's Rule as a constitutional safety valve — a Centre may take over a State's administration when constitutional machinery fails, without armed conflict. (The Second Amendment's right to bear arms, the lecture noted, itself grew from the States' desire to maintain militias against federal overreach.)

Homework

Assigned reading (three days): Shankari Prasad in full (harmonious construction); Sajjan Singh — only Hidayatullah and Mudholkar JJ., identifying the difference in their reasoning; Golaknath — Subba Rao C.J.'s majority; Kesavananda — Sikri C.J. and Mathew J., and the difference between them. Memorise 4–6 significant sentences from each leading judgment (descriptions of Fundamental Rights as “sacrosanct”; the limits of parliamentary power; definitions of the basic structure). Presentation assignments: the doctrine of prospective overruling with every case applying it, and K.S. Puttaswamy (9 judges) on privacy.

Professor'S Aside

Look beyond grades and CGPA. Amitabh Bachchan, despite his stature, reaches the set first — often before the sweepers — and never performs without rehearsal. True achievement lies not in transient accolades but in the lasting impact of one's work and the integrity with which one performs it.

sections.title: Preliminary Remarks — Conduct and the BCI
sections.html:
• Collective responsibility: if classroom property is damaged and no student is identified, the replacement cost (e.g. Rs. 60,000 for a device) is recovered equally from the whole class — a written rule in the university manual.
  • Proxy attendance: calling “Present” for absent peers' roll numbers leads to deduction; fraudulent claims undermine trust.
  • Medical leave abuse: a student broke his leg playing football and demanded leave on the ground that the university “gave permission to play.” Rejected: “Who asked you to play? Is it compulsory from our side?” — personal responsibility is not to be shifted onto the institution.
  • Bar Council of India directions: faculty must be addressed as Sir/Ma'am; posting on social media about protests (or anything attracting legal action) is prohibited; the Internship Committee is to conduct an orientation on the BCI letter; violations are reportable to the BCI for disciplinary action.

sections.title: The Original Constitution — Art and Symbolism
sections.html:
Students are directed to examine the original hand-written Constitution, illuminated by artists: calligraphy by Prem Behari Narain Raizada; depictions of Lord Ram; Lord Krishna imparting the Bhagavad Gita on a chariot — placed in the Directive Principles section to symbolise Raj Dharma; and figures from Islamic history, including Akbar, in Part 8. The artwork is a deliberate choice of the framers to represent India's diverse cultural and religious heritage, directly connected to the constitutional value of secularism.

Western secularismIndian secularism (Sarva Dharma Sambhava)
Strict separation — “distance” — between State and religion; born of the Church–Ruler conflictEqual respect for all religions; the State engages with every faith equally
Often excludes religious expression from the public sphereActively acknowledges the positive teachings of all religions
Western secularismIndian secularism (Sarva Dharma Sambhava)
—“Destroy India's ancient culture” appears nowhere in the Constitution — those who wrote it wrote it down themselves

sections.title: Universal Teachings — the Gita and the Quran
sections.html:
Uddhared atmanatmanam natmanam avasadayet · Atmaiva hy atmano bandhur atmaiva ripur atmanah

— Bhagavad Gita — recited and expounded in class

Three lessons drawn: (1) self-elevation — a human being must elevate themselves through intellect, willpower and good deeds; nobody else can do it for you; external privileges are irrelevant without personal effort; (2) avoiding despair — one must not sink into laziness and bad thoughts (the anecdote: a colleague who would feign illness moments before class out of lack of confidence); (3) mastery of the mind — the mind is one's greatest friend or, uncontrolled, one's greatest enemy (the cautionary tale: a woman in Meerut who conspired with her driver to murder her husband).

Professor'S Aside

Now tell me, where in the Gita is it written that only Hindus have to control the mind? How did this become “non-secular”? This is for every human being! Do people who follow Islam never go into depression? If they are going into depression, to elevate them, we can tell them from the Quran as well. No, no — tell them from the Gita too!

From the Quran: a Pakistan case in which the court praised the Quran for identifying the two pillars of Islam as tolerance and forgiveness. “If Islam says Tolerance and Forgiveness, why shouldn't this be taught to all Hindu children as well? ... See, our religions are one and the same in these aspects! They also say tolerance, we also say tolerance. They also say forgiveness, we also say forgiveness. This is what the Constitution wanted!” The professor also criticised figures like Ramdev for commercialising spirituality — the scriptures teach that everything must be left behind, so true adherence precludes becoming a wealthy businessman.

sections.title: The Case
sections.html:
Case

His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala

AIR 1973 SC 1461 · 13 judges — the largest Constitution Bench in Supreme Court history · decided 24 April 1973 · a deeply

Facts
Kesavananda Bharati, chief of a Kerala religious sect (matha) which owned significant land, petitioned under Article 32 to enforce rights under Articles 25, 26, 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 against the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 and its 1969 Amendment. While the petition was pending, the Indira Gandhi government passed the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments (partly to overcome Golaknath), and the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1971 was placed in the Ninth Schedule. The petition was amended to challenge the amendments themselves.
Held
By 7:6 — Parliament may amend any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot abrogate or destroy the Constitution's basic structure or identity.
Principle
The Basic Structure Doctrine. Key advocates: for the petitioners, Nani A. Palkhivala (leader) with Daphtary, Chagla, Soli Sorabjee, Deewan and Harindranath; for the State, H.M. Seervai, Advocate General of Maharashtra — “the world's greatest constitutional jurist,” not to be “limited” to a state role.

fragmented 7:6 verdict — “a 6.5 to 6.5 judgment” pulled to a majority by the Chief Justice · 66 days of hearing (the longest until the

Ayodhya hearings, at about 63)

The central issue and the Preamble

What is the extent of the amending power under Article 368? Is it absolute, or subject to inherent or implied limitations? Can Fundamental Rights be abrogated by amendment — was Golaknath correctly decided, and what does “amendment” mean? On the Preamble: it was debated, discussed and passed by the Constituent Assembly in the same manner as all other provisions; adopted, enacted and given to ourselves with the rest; expressly declared by the framers to be part of the Constitution. It is not a mere guiding philosophy external to the document — it is an integral part of it.

Petitioners (Palkhivala)Respondents (the State)
The power to amend is limited and restricted — it is not a power to destroyThe amending power is absolute, unlimited and unfettered
The Constitution was granted to secure freedom from tyranny; an unlimited amending power can be used to become tyrannical and take away all rightsUnfettered parliamentary supremacy is a basic principle of the Indian legal system
The features of freedom are at risk if not constitutionally protected from the whims of a transient majoritySocio-economic obligations may require amending property rights and other FRs
A restrictive competence was already voiced by Hidayatullah and Mudholkar JJ. in Sajjan Singh — continuation, not innovationEven a democracy can be turned into one-party rule if power is not checked (noted in class with irony: an argument made by a State itself trending toward one-party rule)

The competing arguments

Professor'S Aside

The biggest servants of Indira Gandhi were these two: Dwivedi and Beg. Dwivedi's case is understandable; he was related to a Cabinet Minister who was Indira Gandhi's right hand... What about Beg? Beg tried to be even more loyal than Dwivedi to Indira Gandhi, and later became Chief Justice too, because Indira Gandhi made him one!

“With the Constitution” (majority)Non-committed / pivotal“With the Government” (minority)
C.J. S.M. Sikri; Justices Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, Reddy — the amending power cannot destroy the basic structure; their loyalty was to constitutional identityJustice H.R. Khanna — the decisive, non-aligned voteJustices S.N. Dwivedi and M.H. Beg (the “servants” of the government); A.N. Ray relatively more neutral among the six

Judicial alignments on the 13-judge bench (as described in the lecture)

sections.title: The Majority — Ratio by Ratio
sections.html:
The students were made to read the ratios aloud in class. Each majority judge emphasised a different formulation:

Judge(s)Core ratioEssential features identified
C.J. S.M. Sikri“Amendment of this Constitution” does not enable Parliament to abrogate Fundamental Rights or completely change the fundamental features so as to destroy its identitySupremacy of the Constitution; republican and democratic form; secular character; separation of powers; federal character
Judge(s)Core ratioEssential features identified
Shelat & Grover JJ.The power extends to all articles but is not unlimited so as to abrogate or change the identity of the Constitution and its basic featuresAdds: sovereignty of India; dignity of the individual; unity and integrity of the country
Hegde & Mukherjea JJ.The power is very wide but does not include the power to destroy or emasculate the basic elements or fundamental featuresBasic elements / fundamental features
P.J. Reddy J.Power is wide, but not wide enough to totally abrogate or emasculate Fundamental Rights or essential elements of the basic structure or destroy the identityAbrogate / emasculate; identity; essential elements

The “identity” judges — four formulations of one idea

The decisive opinion — Justice H.R. Khanna

Khanna J. began by rejecting implied limitations: Parliament's power is wide, with no inherent restriction — which initially delighted the government. The turn came from the word “amendment” itself: “The question has been posed ... whether the power to amend under the above article includes the power to completely abrogate the Constitution and replace it by an entirely new Constitution. The answer ... should be in the negative ... The word ‘amendment’ postulates that the old Constitution survives without loss of identity despite the change and continues even though it has been subjected to alterations.” A mere retention of trivial provisions while the basic structure is destroyed is no amendment: it is not permissible to touch the foundation or alter the basic institutional pattern. The power is not inherently limited, but “amendment” necessarily excludes “destruction” — change everything, but you cannot destroy the Basic Structure. His vote created the 7:6.
