sections.title: Philosophy, Tyranny and the Emergency
sections.html:
The professor connected the doctrine to social contract theory: government was formed for convenience, given limited power; by giving up freedom we took guaranteed rights; if rulers misbehave, we remove them — “Locke was proved wrong by Indira Gandhi!” The Indian design rejected both absolute parliamentary sovereignty (the British model) and absolute unrestricted rights (the early American model): rights are guaranteed but subject to reasonable restrictions (Articles 19(2)–(6)); Parliament is supreme but not sovereign to the point of destroying constitutional identity.

Professor'S Aside

What did Indira Gandhi say? “I am absolute! I have unlimited power, unfettered power!” ... If such a restriction of Basic Structure hadn't been put on Parliament's power, who knows — today Indira Gandhi might have brought another amendment stating, “Even after I die, my descendants shall be Prime Ministers!” ... Today we can say with assurance: there are certain basic things that no matter what majority you get, you cannot change. (The professor attributes the force of this point to a debate with Professor Faizan Mustafa.)

The Emergency (1975–77) illustrated unchecked power. Inder Kumar Gujral, then I&B; Minister, was dismissed for refusing to censor news and submit it for prior approval to Sanjay Gandhi — “Do you want to stay a minister or not?” The electricity of the Indian Express was cut off to prevent printing, generating the line of Indian Express cases vital to Article 19 jurisprudence. The principle of Romesh Thappar was invoked: circulation of a newspaper and dissemination of information are included within the right to speech and expression — the State cannot circumvent free speech by allowing printing but banning distribution.

Key Point

Self-reliance reiterated at close: all political parties — BJP, Congress, Owaisi — act in their own interest, not for students. “That is why Lord Krishna said what I told you: You will have to elevate yourself! Nobody is going to elevate you.” And on federalism: C.J. Sikri declared the federal character a basic feature in 1973, yet academics still persist in calling the Constitution “quasi-federal” — a label the professor dismisses as incorrect and outdated.

Judge(s)Core ratioKey terminology
C.J. S.M. SikriPower to amend does not include power to completely change fundamental features so as to destroy identityIdentity; supremacy; republican/democratic form; secularism; separation of powers; federal character
Shelat & Grover JJ.Power not unlimited; cannot abrogate or change identity and basic featuresIdentity & basic features; sovereignty; dignity of individual; unity & integrity
Hegde & Mukherjea JJ.Power very wide but does not include power to destroy or emasculate basic elementsDestroy / emasculate basic elements
P.J. Reddy J.Not wide enough to totally abrogate or emasculate FRs or essential elements of basic structureAbrogate / emasculate; identity; essential elements

day.title: Article 13 Doctrines — Eclipse, Severability, Waiver
day.trail: Two facets of Article 13 · Doctrine of Eclipse + decision map · Severability — the RMDC eight rules · Waiver — Basheshar Nath · Waiver vs estoppel

sections.title: The Text and Its Two Facets
sections.html:
Article 13(1) addresses laws in force before 26 January 1950: inconsistent pre-constitutional laws are void “to the extent of such inconsistency.” Article 13(2) is a prospective prohibition: “The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void.” Article 13(3) defines “law” expansively — ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law; Article 13(4) (added by the 24th Amendment, 1971) exempts amendments under Article 368.

AspectArticle 13(1) — pre-Constitution lawsArticle 13(2) — post-Constitution laws
Competence at inceptionPlenary — the enacting legislature was sovereign or fully competent; the law was born validLimited — the Constitution is the source of power; a Part III-violating law is made without jurisdiction, born void
The defectSupervening inconsistency — an external event (the Constitution) creates inconsistency with an otherwise valid lawInherent nullity — breach of a constitutional prohibition; a jurisdictional vice
AspectArticle 13(1) — pre-Constitution lawsArticle 13(2) — post-Constitution laws
Status on 26-01-1950Eclipsed / dormant for citizens; enforceable for non-citizens and pre-Constitution matters; voidable, not void ab initio“Still-born,” void ab initio — a nullity from inception for all purposes
Effect of FR amendmentAutomatic revival — the shadow lifts; no re-enactment neededNo revival — a dead law cannot be vitalised by amendment; it must be re-enacted
Jurisprudential basisPower existed; enforcement against citizens was temporarily suspendedUltra vires / want of jurisdiction
Theoretical outcomeDoctrine of revivalDoctrine of re-enactment

The fundamental dichotomy — the most tested distinction in the topic

sections.title: Doctrine of Eclipse
sections.html:
The metaphor is astronomical: an eclipse does not destroy the celestial body, it merely obscures it. The Sun is the pre-constitutional law radiating legal force; the Moon is the inconsistent Fundamental Right; the shadow is Article 13(1); the Earth is the affected population — for citizens the law is in shadow, for non-citizens it shines fully. When the Moon moves away (the Fundamental Right is amended), the Sun automatically becomes visible again. The problem the doctrine solves: declaring all inconsistent pre-constitutional laws dead would destroy vested rights, past transactions and completed decrees, creating legal chaos.

Decision map for the Doctrine of Eclipse — and its post-Constitutional boundary

The four simultaneous states of an inconsistent pre-Constitutional law: (1) as against citizens — dormant or moribund, unenforceable; (2) as against non-citizens — fully operative, since Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are citizens' rights (Keshav Madhav Menon); (3) for pre-Constitution transactions — fully effective, Article 13(1) not being retrospective (Bhikaji Narain); (4) potential for revival — automatic when the inconsistency is removed.

Case

Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955)

5-judge bench · AIR 1955 SC 781 · locus classicus of eclipse

Facts
The C.P. and Berar Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1948 — enacted under the Government of India Act, 1935 by a legislature with plenary powers — created a State monopoly in motor transport, clashing with Article 19(1)(g) as it then stood. The First Amendment (1951) added the state-monopoly clause to Article 19(6).
Held
Per B.K. Mukherjea J., unanimously: the impugned law “became, as it were, eclipsed, for the time being, by the fundamental right... Such laws were not dead for all purposes... It is only as against the citizens that they remained in a dormant or moribund condition.” The amendment “removed the shadow”; the 1948 Act revived automatically — no re-enactment required.
Principle
Pre-constitutional laws are void only quoad citizens; supervening inconsistency is curable retrospectively by constitutional amendment.
Case

Keshav Madhav Menon v. State of Bombay (1951)

AIR 1951 SC 128 · per S.R. Das J.

Facts
Prosecution under the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931 for publishing a pamphlet without prior authorisation; proceedings had begun before the Constitution.
Held
Article 13(1) operates prospectively from the Constitution's commencement; it does not invalidate past transactions or pending proceedings under laws valid when the act was done. “The voidness of the law is from the date of the commencement of the Constitution and not from an earlier date.”
Principle
The distinction between void ab initio and void from a future date is the very foundation of the eclipse doctrine.
Case

Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959)

AIR 1959 SC 648 · 4:1 · per S.K. Das J.

Facts
The U.P. State Road Transport Act, 1951 — a post-Constitutional state monopoly — was challenged under Article 19(1)(g); the State invoked Bhikaji Narain's revival logic.
Held
Article 13(2) imposes a constitutional prohibition; the State legislature “had no power to make the impugned law.” A post-Constitutional inconsistent law is “still-born” and void ab initio — “A dead law cannot be revived by any constitutional amendment... it must be re-enacted.”
Principle
Eclipse applies exclusively to pre-Constitutional laws under Article 13(1).
Case

Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1955)

AIR 1955 SC 728

Facts
The U.P. Road Transport Act, 1951 (post-Constitutional) was challenged while the First Amendment's Article 19(6) change was in force.
Held
Applying Thomas Cooley's American doctrine: “A statute void for unconstitutionality is dead and cannot be vitalized by a subsequent amendment of the Constitution removing the constitutional objection but must be re-enacted.”
Principle
The critical difference between pre- and post-Constitutional laws: a constitutional amendment does not retroactively confer jurisdiction on the legislature that passed the void law.
Case

State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974)

AIR 1974 SC 1300 · per H.R. Khanna J.

Facts
The Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1953 (post-Constitutional) required employers' contributions; provisions were challenged under Articles 19(1)(f) and 14 by a company (a citizen).
Held
A post-Constitutional law void for violating Articles 14 or 19 is void only quoad citizens — the contravention exists only in relation to those entitled to the right. The law remains valid and enforceable against non-citizens.
Principle
Modifies the “still-born” theory by making it person-specific: void in personam for citizens, not void in rem against the world.

Revival through the Ninth Schedule — and the Dularey Lodh anomaly

Article 31B is the one great exception to the re-enactment rule: it deems a listed Act never to have been void — an absolute constitutional fiction applying to pre- and post-Constitutional laws alike. But its limits were later drawn: Waman Rao (1981) held laws added to the Ninth Schedule before Kesavananda (24 April 1973) to be beyond review, while post-1973 insertions remain challengeable; I.R. Coelho (2007, 9 judges) confirmed that any law placed in the Schedule after 24 April 1973 is open to review on the twin grounds of Part III violation and basic structure. Dularey Lodh v. III Additional District Judge, Kanpur (1984) is the anomaly — applying eclipse language to a post-Constitutional statutory bar blocking a decree: once the 1972 Act's bar was removed, “by virtue of the doctrine of eclipse the decree will revive and become at once operative and executable.” It has not been followed as a general principle. The four arguments for extending eclipse to post-Constitutional laws: (1) legislative incompetence is relative to the Fundamental Right, not absolute — the law should not be treated as non-est; (2) Articles 200–201 and 213(3) contemplate laws of doubtful vires, implying some existence; (3) Parliament's power to repeal State laws (Article 252) presupposes their valid existence; (4) practical sense — re-enactment for a cured inconsistency is formalistic waste. The settled position nonetheless remains Deep Chand's: eclipse is for pre-Constitutional laws only.
sections.text: The metaphor is astronomical: an eclipse does not destroy the celestial body, it merely obscures it. The Sun is the pre-constitutional law radiating legal force; the Moon is the inconsistent Fundamental Right; the shadow is Article 13(1); the Earth is the affected population — for citizens the law is in shadow, for non-citizens it shines fully. When the Moon moves away (the Fundamental Right is amended), the Sun automatically becomes visible again. The problem the doctrine solves: declaring all inconsistent pre-constitutional laws dead would destroy vested rights, past transactions and completed decrees, creating legal chaos. Decision map for the Doctrine of Eclipse — and its post-Constitutional boundary The four simultaneous states of an inconsistent pre-Constitutional law: (1) as against citizens — dormant or moribund, unenforceable; (2) as against non-citizens — fully operative, since Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are citizens' rights ( Keshav Madhav Menon ); (3) for pre-Constitution transactions — fully effective, Article 13(1) not being retrospective ( Bhikaji Narain ); (4) potential for revival — automatic when the inconsistency is removed. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) 5-judge bench · AIR 1955 SC 781 · locus classicus of eclipse Facts The C.P. and Berar Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1948 — enacted under the Government of India Act, 1935 by a legislature with plenary powers — created a State monopoly in motor transport, clashing with Article 19(1)(g) as it then stood. The First Amendment (1951) added the state-monopoly clause to Article 19(6). Held Per B.K. Mukherjea J., unanimously : the impugned law “became, as it were, eclipsed, for the time being, by the fundamental right... Such laws were not dead for all purposes... It is only as against the citizens that they remained in a dormant or moribund condition.” The amendment “removed the shadow”; the 1948 Act revived automatically — no re-enactment required. State of Bombay (1951) AIR 1951 SC 128 · per S.R. Das J. Facts Prosecution under the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931 for publishing a pamphlet without prior authorisation; proceedings had begun before the Constitution. Held Article 13(1) operates prospectively from the Constitution's commencement; it does not invalidate past transactions or pending proceedings under laws valid when the act was done. “The voidness of the law is from the date of the commencement of the Constitution and not from an earlier date.” Principle The distinction between void ab initio and void from a future date is the very foundation of the eclipse doctrine. Case Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) AIR 1959 SC 648 · 4:1 · per S.K. Das J. Facts The U.P. State Road Transport Act, 1951 — a post-Constitutional state monopoly — was challenged under Article 19(1)(g); the State invoked Bhikaji Narain's revival logic. Road Transport Act, 1951 (post-Constitutional) was challenged while the First Amendment's Article 19(6) change was in force. sections.title: Doctrine of Severability
sections.html:
Severability is embedded in the text — “to the extent of such inconsistency” — in both 13(1) and 13(2). Borrowed from American law (the “Doctrine of Separability”), the judicial function is to excise the malignant portion, not kill the organism; but if malignant and healthy tissue are inextricably interwoven, the entire statute falls. The twin test: (1) separability in fact — the valid and invalid parts must be physically and notionally separable; (2) separability in intent — would the legislature have enacted the valid part without the invalid? If either answer is negative, the whole Act falls.

RuleContent (R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla, 1957)
1The intention of the legislature is determinative — the master rule: would it have passed the valid portion knowing the infirmity?
2Where valid and invalid provisions are inextricably mixed, the invalidity of a part fails the whole
3Where provisions are distinct and severable, the valid portion survives as a self-contained code
4Even distinct sections forming a single integrated scheme may fall together — substance over form
5If the remainder is “so thin and truncated” as to be materially different legislation, all falls
6Judicial legislation prohibited — if severance would require rewriting, the court strikes down the whole; courts delete, never amend
RuleContent (R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla, 1957)
7Substance over form — arrangement in the statute book is irrelevant; functional interconnection decides
8External aids — legislative history, Statement of Objects and Reasons, title, preamble, scheme — may prove the hypothetical intent

The eight governing rules of severability

Case

R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957)

AIR 1957 SC 628 · 5-judge bench · locus classicus

Facts
The Prize Competitions Act, 1955 defined “prize competition” broadly enough to cover both skill competitions (crosswords, essays — protected business under 19(1)(g)) and gambling (lotteries, lucky draws — res extra commercium, outside 19(1)(g)).
Held
The Act was unconstitutional as applied to skill competitions but valid as to gambling; the distinction was “clear-cut and well-recognized,” and Parliament's primary object was the gambling evil. The Court read down the definition: the Act applies only to gambling competitions.
Principle
Severability by restricting application — the classic instance of saving an Act by confining it to the valid class.
Case

Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)

AIR 1950 SC 124 · 6 judges

Facts
Section 9(1-A), Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 — banning entry and circulation of journals “for securing the public safety or the maintenance of public order.” “Public safety” was not a ground in Article 19(2) as it then stood.
Held
The provision fell entirely: the distinction between “public safety” and “public order” was “not precise”; severing the words would leave a power still capable of unconstitutional application — danger of misuse is the decisive factor.
Principle
Inseverability where permissible and impermissible applications cannot be cleanly separated.
Case

State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)

AIR 1951 SC 318

Facts
The Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949, challenged on multiple grounds.
Held
Eight specific unconstitutional sections were severed; the core Prohibition Act survived as a complete, workable code.
Principle
Rule 3 in action — distinct invalid parts removed, the rest upheld.
Case

A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)

AIR 1950 SC 27

Facts
Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 barred detainees from disclosing grounds of detention to a court.
Held
Only Section 14 violated Articles 19(1)(a) and 21; the rest of the Act was a complete code without it.
Principle
“Save as much of an Act as can be saved” — declare void only what must be void.
Case

Mithu Singh v. State of Punjab (1983)

AIR 1983 SC 473 · 5-judge bench

Facts
Section 303 IPC mandated the death penalty for murder by a life convict — no judicial discretion.
Held
The classification (life convicts versus other murderers) lacked intelligible differentia, and mandatory death excluded judicial consideration of mitigating circumstances, violating Articles 14 and 21. Section 303 was a standalone provision, cleanly severable from the IPC's sentencing scheme (Section 302 continues to govern).
Principle
A penal provision excised cleanly; the rest of the Code operates normally.

The reconciliation came in Superintendent, Central Prison, Fatehgarh v. Ram Manohar Lohia (1960), per Subba Rao J.: in RMDC the two activities were conceptually distinct with no confusion risk; in Romesh Thappar the two purposes overlapped imprecisely, with a real danger the power granted for the constitutional purpose would be used for the unconstitutional one. The decisive factor is the danger of misuse — essentially a test of overbreadth.

sections.title: Doctrine of Waiver
sections.html:
Waiver is the intentional, voluntary relinquishment of a known right. Its elements: (1) knowledge of the right; (2) intention to abandon it; (3) voluntariness — no coercion or duress. Can a citizen waive a fundamental right? The answer is a resounding no.

Case

Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959)

AIR 1959 SC 149 · 5-judge bench · majority of C.J. S.R. Das, Kapur and Subba Rao JJ.; N.H. Bhagwati J. concurring more broadly;

Facts
Basheshar Nath, a wealthy businessman, settled under Section 8A of the Taxation of Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, agreeing to pay about Rs. 4.5 lakh in instalments. When Section 5(1) of that Act was held unconstitutional in Suraj Mall Mohta (1955), he stopped paying; the Department sought recovery as arrears of land revenue, arguing he had waived his Article 14 right by settling.
Held
Fundamental rights cannot be waived. Article 14 is a principle of public policy, the foundation of the Constitution — not a private right to be bartered away.
Principle
Justice Subba Rao's rationale: rights are limitations on State power, not gifts; “The large majority of our people are economically poor, educationally backward, and politically not yet conscious of their rights... They may, without understanding the consequences, agree to waive their rights. It would be the duty of the Court to protect them against themselves.” Waiver assumes equal bargaining power — a fiction in India.

S.K. Das J. dissenting

Bhagwati J. went further: no fundamental right in Part III can be waived. The dissenter S.K. Das J. distinguished rights for the public benefit (Articles 15, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, 24 — non-waivable) from rights for individual advantage (Articles 16, 19, and the Article 14 right at issue — waivable); the settlement falling in the second category, the petitioner had validly waived. The deep rationales of the majority: Part III is a charter of public policy (jus publicum), not a contract; allowing waiver would let the State extract rights-surrenders for licenses and settlements, making rights negotiable commodities; the Indian reality of unequal bargaining power imposes a paternalistic duty; and constitutional morality binds the State even where the individual does not insist.

The modern critique

Arvind Datar's critique: every right necessarily includes the right not to exercise it — the right to speech includes the right to remain silent; post-Puttaswamy decisional autonomy recognises informed choices to forgo rights (the reality-show contract; the voluntarily posted photograph). Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978) held that the right to carry on business includes the right not to carry it on — a choice inherent in the right. And Olga Tellis: estoppel cannot stand against fundamental rights; no individual act can validate a void law.

AspectWaiverEstoppel
SourceContract law — an agreement to release a rightEvidence law (s. 115, Evidence Act) — a rule preventing contradiction of one's own representation
NatureSubstantive and contractual — extinguishes a rightProcedural and evidentiary — bars the remedy, not the right
BasisIntention of the right-holderConduct, reliance and detriment; intention to deceive unnecessary
MaximQuilibet potest renuntiare juri pro se inducto — inapplicable to fundamental rightsAllegans contraria non est audiendus
Application to FRsCannot apply — a fundamental right cannot be waivedCannot apply — there is no estoppel against the Constitution

Waiver distinguished from estoppel

DoctrineSourceKey casesCore principle
EclipseArticle 13(1) — pre-Constitutional lawsBhikaji Narain (1955); Keshav Madhav Menon (1951); Deep Chand (1959); Ambica Mills (1974); Waman Rao (1981); I.R. Coelho (2007)An inconsistent pre-Constitutional law is dormant for citizens, operative for non-citizens and past transactions, and revives automatically when the FR is amended
Severability“To the extent of” in 13(1) & 13(2) — both classes of lawRMDC (1957); Romesh Thappar (1950); Gopalan (1950); Balsara (1951); Mithu Singh (1983); Lohia (1960)Only the offending part falls if distinct and separable; if inseparable or misuse-prone, the whole falls; the test is legislative intent
WaiverJudge-made limit from the nature of FRs as public rightsBasheshar Nath (1959); Olga Tellis (1986); Excel Wear (1978)A citizen cannot voluntarily relinquish fundamental rights; no estoppel against the Constitution

The three doctrines of Article 13 — comprehensive comparison

Appendix

Full case list with citations as distributed: Eclipse — Bhikaji Narain AIR 1955 SC 781; Keshav Madhav Menon AIR 1951 SC 128; Deep Chand AIR 1959 SC 648; Saghir Ahmad AIR 1955 SC 728; Ambica Mills AIR 1974 SC 1300; Dularey Lodh AIR 1984 SC 1260; Waman Rao AIR 1981 SC 271; I.R. sections.title: Overview
sections.html: This session (undated; it recaps Kesavananda and sets up the Article 14 sequence) begins with the text of the amended Article 368. The 24th Amendment's Article 368(3) — “Nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article” — and the consequential Article 13(4) were designed as a watertight separation between amending power and fundamental rights: Parliament's direct legislative answer to Golaknath.

The 24th Amendment's Article 368(3) — “Nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article” — and the consequential Article 13(4) were designed as a watertight separation between amending power and fundamental rights: Parliament's direct legislative answer to Golaknath .

sections.title: From Kesavananda to Minerva Mills
sections.html:
Kesavananda (7:6) overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment, but on the implied-limitation reasoning of constitutional identity: the Constitution possesses a fundamental identity, an essential character constituting its core; Article 368 grants the power to amend, not to destroy. Illustrative constituents of the basic structure identified across the judgments: supremacy of the Constitution; the republican and democratic form of government (one cannot amend in a monarchy or a foreign ruler); secularism; federalism and the distribution of powers; separation of powers; the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Articles 32, 136, 141 and 142; and Fundamental Rights — while not all FRs are per se basic structure, some are so foundational that their destruction would violate it; the essence of Part III is protected.

The executive's retort was the 42nd Amendment (1976), the Emergency-era “Mini-Constitution.” Article 368(4): “No amendment of this Constitution (including the provisions of Part III) made or purporting to have been made under this article whether before or after the commencement of section 55 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 shall be called in question in any court on any ground.” Article 368(5) declared that there shall be “no limitation whatever” on the constituent power. The first clause was a direct ouster of the judiciary's Kesavananda jurisdiction; the second an assertion of unlimited power.

Case

Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)

Y.V. Chandrachud and P.N. Bhagwati JJ. prominent · suo motu cognizance of sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment

Facts
The immediate issue was a challenge under Article 31C, but the Court took up the validity of the 42nd Amendment's clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 on its own motion.
Held
Twin holdings: (1) the Indian scheme vests supremacy in the Constitution, not in Parliament — Parliament is a creature of the Constitution; (2) judicial review of constitutional amendments is an integral basic feature. Article 368(4) was struck down as violative of basic structure; so was 368(5), which sought to destroy the limited nature of the amending power — itself part of the basic structure.
Principle
The final synthesis: Parliament may amend under Article 368; Article 13 does not bar amendments; but any amendment destroying the basic structure is void.
Case

I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)

9-judge bench · unanimous

Facts
Post-Kesavananda legislatures kept adding laws to the Ninth Schedule — some allegedly arbitrary, even near-100% reservation destroying equality.
Held
The cut-off is 24 April 1973, the date Kesavananda was decided. Any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule after that date is not immune from judicial review, and can be tested on the twin grounds of Part III violation and basic structure violation; if it fails, it is struck down.
Principle
Unchecked post-1973 insertion would render the Basic Structure Doctrine a dead letter. Open research question left to the class: does the doctrine apply only to amendments, or directly to any ordinary legislation (beyond the Ninth Schedule route)?

Held Twin holdings: (1) the Indian scheme vests supremacy in the Constitution, not in Parliament — Parliament is a creature of the Constitution; (2) judicial review of constitutional amendments is an integral basic feature. Article 368(4) was struck down as violative of basic structure; so was 368(5), which sought to destroy the limited nature of the amending power — itself part of the basic structure. Principle The final synthesis: Parliament may amend under Article 368; Article 13 does not bar amendments; but any amendment destroying the basic structure is void. Case I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) 9-judge bench · unanimous Facts Post- Kesavananda legislatures kept adding laws to the Ninth Schedule — some allegedly arbitrary, even near-100% reservation destroying equality. Held The cut-off is 24 April 1973, the date Kesavananda was decided. Any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule after that date is not immune from judicial review, and can be tested on the twin grounds of Part III violation and basic structure violation; if it fails, it is struck down. Principle Unchecked post-1973 insertion would render the Basic Structure Doctrine a dead letter. Open research question left to the class: does the doctrine apply only to amendments, or directly to any ordinary legislation (beyond the Ninth Schedule route)?

sections.title: Article 14 — Dissecting the Text
sections.html:
“The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.”

— Article 14

ElementAnalysis
“The State” — the duty-bearerA vertical right enforceable against the State; Article 12 defines it. Test — Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. IICB (2002): financial, functional and administrative domination, or deep and pervasive government control. Even private universities (e.g. SRM, per the Chennai case) have been held to be “State”; a fortiori a National Law University established by State Act, with the Chief Justice as Chancellor and Secretaries (Finance, Law, Education) on its governing board, receiving substantial state funding — “500% State”
“Any person” — the right-holderThe word “citizen” is conspicuously absent, unlike Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29. The right extends to non-citizens, aliens, even artificial legal persons (companies)
“Within the territory of India”The guarantee operates within the Republic's geographical boundaries — it prohibits discrimination even against a foreign national on Indian soil

Three foundational elements of the Article

sections.title: The Salma and Prapti Hypothetical — Deconstructing the Textualist Argument
sections.html:
Facts: MNLU Nagpur's admission policy (eligibility for CLAT: “Citizen of India”). Prapti, an Indian citizen with CLAT rank 300, gains admission. Salma, a Pakistani citizen with rank 290 — higher merit — is denied solely for not being an Indian citizen. She petitions under Article 32. Her purely textualist argument: (a) Article 14 says “any person,” not “any citizen”; (b) I am a person; (c) the State (MNLU, through admission committee head Dr. Disha Kher) has denied me equality before the law; (d) the policy discriminates between persons — one citizen, one non-citizen — treating my higher marks as inferior; (e) the policy is unconstitutional on the face of Article 14.

The Socratic demolition of the intuitive responses: (1) “The University's bye-law says so” — but the Constitution is supreme (Article 13(2)); a bye-law is tested against the constitutional standard, not on its own terms. (2) “She is not a citizen, so she has no right” — a legislative addition; the framers consciously used “any person” in Article 14 and “citizen” in Article 19; the interpreter cannot insert a word deliberately omitted. (3) “Article 29 (or 15) applies only to citizens” — a non sequitur; a challenge under Article 14 must be answered on the anvil of Article 14: “You cannot defeat a claim for khichdi (Article 14) by serving chicken (Article 29).” (4) “Equality before law differs from equal protection” — a semantic trap; the combined effect is a comprehensive mandate of non-arbitrariness. (5) “There are reasonable restrictions” — unlike Article 19, Article 14 enumerates none; the classification must pass the twin test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus, with the burden on the State.

The Open Question

The unresolved suspense — the threshold question for the next class: if Article 14's text is taken to its logical extreme, every law preferring citizens over non-citizens in state benefits would be unconstitutional — yet such laws are ubiquitous. Find the principle that harmonises the inclusive text of Article 14 with the sovereign right of a State to prefer its own citizens, without importing the word “citizen” into the text.

day.title: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification & the Nexus Test
day.trail: Treating unequals equally · The two-fold command · Anwar Ali Sarkar — the dacoit case · Kathi Raning — the contrast · Chiranjit Lal — one person, one class

sections.title: The Core Principle — Why Classification Is Essential
sections.html:
The right to equality is not a mandate for absolute, mechanical, rigid equality. To treat everyone identically regardless of differing circumstances, needs and conditions is not equality — it is injustice. The foundational maxim: “Equals must be treated equally, and unequals must be treated unequally.” God and nature have created human beings with infinite variety — in upbringing, age, education, income, background and needs — so the law must classify persons and things into groups based on relevant similarities, applying appropriate rules to each.

  • Illustration 1 — dietary needs: one person observes a religious fast (sabudana, fruits), another is non-vegetarian. If the mess serves chicken biryani to everyone and compels the fasting student to eat it “in the name of equality,” that violates her rights; equally, forcing the non-vegetarian to eat only khichdi every day because another is fasting is injustice.
  • Illustration 2 — regional habits: a person from Uttar Pradesh may eat four or five parathas for breakfast; a person from Maharashtra is satisfied with poha. A uniform “poha only” rule leaves the first hungry — a failure to account for different needs.
  • Illustration 3 — age: a sixty-year-old has different physical, medical and dietary requirements from a twenty-year-old; applying the same standard to both is not equal treatment.

Hence the two-fold command of Article 14: (1) persons similarly situated (the same class) must be treated alike — if Niyati and Manaswi both fast but Niyati gets plain sabudana worth Rs. 15 while Manaswi gets sabudana vada with raisins and cashews worth Rs. 500, that is discrimination within a class; (2) persons differently situated may — indeed must — be treated differently. The critical question: how do we decide who falls into one class? That is the function of the Doctrine of Reasonable Classification and the Nexus Test.

Article 14 does not forbid classification; it forbids class legislation — discrimination against a class without any reasonable basis — while permitting reasonable classification. A legislature that cannot classify cannot govern. The burden of proving unreasonableness lies in the first instance on the challenger, though once a prima facie case of discrimination is made out it may shift to the State.

The two-limb test — the analytical spine of every Article 14 answer

sections.title: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) — the “Dacoit Case”
sections.html:
Case

State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar

AIR 1952 SC 75 · 7-judge Constitutional Bench · 6:1 majority · Patanjali Sastri C.J. dissenting

Facts
The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 provided for speedier trial of certain offences. Section 5(1) empowered the State Government, by notification, to direct that any particular case or class of cases be tried by a Special Court — with no guidelines, criteria or standards governing the selection. The special procedure was more stringent than the CrPC: ordinary procedural safeguards were withdrawn. Anwar Ali Sarkar and 49 co-accused, caught in an armed dacoity raid, were notified into a Special Court, tried, convicted and sentenced; he challenged Section 5(1) under Article 14.
Held
Section 5(1) unconstitutional. Limb 1 failed — no basis or criterion for classifying which cases go to speedier trial; selection rested on the subjective opinion of executive officers; change the officers and different cases would be picked: not “intelligible,” but arbitrary and capricious. Limb 2 failed — how does unguided discretion serve speedier trial? The means (absolute discretion) are not rationally related to the end. Illustration: dacoities in five districts, two dacoits caught in each; District A's pair notified to the harsher Special Court while Districts B–E enjoy ordinary protections — discrimination within a single class (all dacoity accused), with no justifiable answer to “why these two?”
Principle
A law conferring absolute, unguided, unfettered discretion on the executive to classify persons or cases, without criteria or standards, violates Article 14.

sections.title: Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra (1952) — the Contrast Case
sections.html:
Case

Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra

AIR 1952 SC 123 · text of the impugned section virtually identical to the West Bengal Act

Facts
A Saurashtra State Ordinance empowered the government to send cases to Special Courts — but its preamble recited the exceptional law-and-order situation: widespread communal violence, dacoity, breakdown of the ordinary criminal justice system in named disturbed regions.
Held
Upheld. In context, the discretion was not unguided: the preamble itself channelled it — cases connected with the breakdown of public order were the legitimate target. The discretion was bounded by the statute's stated objective.
Principle
A provision identical in text may be valid or invalid depending on context, purpose, and the presence of guiding principles — in the statute or its surrounding circumstances. Noteworthy: Patanjali Sastri C.J. was a judge in both cases — dissenting in Anwar Ali Sarkar (to uphold) and in the majority in Kathi Raning (upholding).
Anwar Ali Sarkar (struck down)Kathi Raning (upheld)
Act specified no categories of offencesOrdinance specified the categories — in the preamble and the disturbed regions
Uncontrolled discretion with the State GovernmentClear guidance to Executive Magistrates
Failed the intelligible differentia testPassed the intelligible differentia test

Two virtually identical provisions, two opposite outcomes

sections.title: Can a Single Person Constitute a Class?
sections.html:
Case

Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India (1950)

AIR 1950 SC 41

Facts
A single “sick” industrial undertaking — a textile mill threatening the livelihood of over 1,30,000 people — was taken over by the government for better management; shareholders objected to being singled out.
Held
Yes — a single person or entity can constitute a valid class where it possesses unique characteristics distinguishing it from all others, and the law addresses that unique situation. Illustration offered in class: if one company causes 90% of an industry's pollution, a law addressing that company may be a valid classification.
Principle
The test remains the same: intelligible differentia plus rational nexus — even for a class of one.

sections.title: Other Authorities and a Note on Judicial Fallibility
sections.html:
• Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar (1958) — the consolidating authority: several propositions summarising the law on Article 14 and reasonable classification.
  • In re: Special Courts Act — further elucidation of the limits of special courts and Article 14.
  • Ex-Services Association v. Union of India (2006) — cut-off date (1997) for retired servicemen's medical benefits: those retired before paid nothing, those after paid. The reasoning has been debated; students are encouraged to examine it critically and form their own views, with reasons.
Professor'S Aside

Judges, like all human beings, can err in reasoning. A judgment is not divine law. Justice Endlaw of the Delhi High Court, in the Delhi University photocopying case brought by Oxford University Press, delivered a celebrated judgment: “Copyright is not divine law” — a critique of the colonial mindset of blindly copying Western copyright laws, in a case where the library photocopied expensive textbooks for students who could not afford them. The principle may be right even where a given application is debatable.

sections.title: Questions for Reflection — Answered
sections.html:
Question

Why is classification necessary for the application of Article 14?

Answer

Because equality is not identical treatment: treating unequals equally is itself a violation of equality. Without classification the State could not legislate for specific groups or problems; the power to classify is an essential incident of legislative power. Article 14 forbids only class legislation, not reasonable classification.

Question

What are the two tests for a valid classification? Explain with reference to Anwar Ali Sarkar.

Answer

(1) Intelligible differentia — a clear, real, substantial basis distinguishing those grouped in from those left out; (2) rational nexus between that differentia and the statute's object. In Anwar Ali Sarkar, Section 5(1) supplied no differentia at all — the executive's unguided pick-and-choose — and the conferral of absolute discretion had no rational connection with speedier trial. Both limbs failing, the provision was void.

Question

Why did Anwar Ali Sarkar succeed while a similar provision was upheld in Kathi Raning Rawat?

Answer

Context and guidance. The Saurashtra Ordinance's preamble supplied the criteria — offences connected with an exceptional breakdown of public order in named regions — channelling the executive's discretion toward a constitutional object. The West Bengal Act had no such internal or contextual guide, leaving naked discretion. Same text, different legal fate.

Question

Why is Article 14 placed before Articles 19 and 21 in the Constitution?

Answer

The lecture leaves this as the question for the next class: is equality more important than life (Article 21) and freedom (Article 19)? The placement is a conscious constitutional choice — the framework for answering it (equality as the first among the rights, and later the Golden Triangle that makes them co-equal) develops over the following sessions.

Homework

Reading list: Anwar Ali Sarkar; Kathi Raning Rawat; Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri; Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Tendolkar; In re: Special Courts Act; Ex-Services Association (2006, critically).

day.title: Equality Before Law vs Equal Protection of Laws
day.trail: Scope of “person” · E.P. Royappa introduced · Historical disabilities · The basketball and IAS illustrations · Ten valid and five invalid classes

sections.title: Foundations
sections.html: Article 14's dual mandate: equality before law, a negative concept prohibiting special privileges and disabilities, of English origin; and equal protection of the laws, a positive concept requiring the State to treat equals equally and unequals unequally — justifying affirmative action and reasonable classification — drawn from the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The term “person” includes citizens, aliens (Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka nationals alike) and companies, ensuring the protection against discrimination extends to every individual within Indian territory.

sections.title: Reasonable Classification — The Working Cases
sections.html:
Case

E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)

(1974) 4 SCC 3

Facts
E.P. Royappa, a senior IAS officer serving as Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu — the highest State-level IAS post — was moved out and made Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission Board (a post declared equivalent in rank and salary), then OSD. He challenged the removal as arbitrary.
Held
Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness: a decision that is arbitrary is inherently unequal — a significant expansion beyond the traditional classification test. (The doctrine is taught in full on Day 10.)
Principle
The “New Doctrine of Equality”: arbitrariness read as a facet of Article 14.

Anwar Ali Sarkar and Kathi Raning Rawat were revisited in compressed form with the comparison table (Day 6), and Federation of Armed Forces v. Union of India was added: a policy requiring retired armed forces personnel to make a one-time payment for lifetime medical facilities while active personnel received free treatment — the cut-off discriminating between similarly situated groups without a reasonable nexus may be unconstitutional.

sections.title: Equality Before Law — The Negative Concept in History
sections.html:
The lecture illuminated the disabilities and privileges this concept abolishes through four historical episodes:

  • Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa — thrown out of a first-class compartment at Pietermaritzburg despite a valid ticket, solely on race; the turning point of his life.
  • The Travancore breast tax — lower-caste women prohibited from wearing upper garments unless they paid it; the tragic protest of Nangeli, who cut off her breasts.
  • “No peon, no water” — Dalits denied access to public water sources; Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's own experience of not being allowed to drink water without a peon's assistance.
  • Karna's exclusion — denied participation in Draupadi's swayamvar as a Suta-putra, not of royal lineage.

Equality before law abolishes these historical disabilities and privileges, creating a level playing field for all.

sections.title: Equal Protection — The Positive Concept
sections.html:
Two illustrations anchored the positive dimension. The basketball example: two players, one six-and-a-half feet tall, one three feet; a uniform twelve-foot hoop advantages the taller — that is merely equality before law. True equal protection may adjust conditions to make the contest fair. The IAS examination example: Person A, born into affluence — optimal nutrition, top-tier education, coaching from infancy, social capital of judges and ministers acquired by daily osmosis; Person B, born into rural poverty — nutritional deficits, late schooling, no social capital. Applying an identical standard (same examination, same age limit, same cut-off) guarantees B's perpetual ineligibility: the competition is rigged not by individual malice but by historically accumulated structural advantage.

CriterionEquality Before LawEqual Protection of Laws
OriginBritish legal traditionAmerican legal tradition (14th Amendment)
NatureNegative conceptPositive concept
CommandThe State shall not deny equalityThe State shall afford equal protection
FunctionAbolition of special, discriminatory privilegesReasonable classification and positive discrimination to remedy structural disadvantage
Concept of equalityFormal — treating all alikeSubstantive — treating unequals differently to achieve genuine equality
IllustrationFirst-class ticket: anyone holding it may travelReservation / quota system in education and employment

The two facets of Article 14 compared

Homework

Homework: create 10 valid classifications satisfying both the intelligible-differentia and nexus tests, and 5 invalid ones failing them; support each with case law where possible; keep the classes diverse (avoid multiple variations of “committees”). Also read: E.P. Royappa (1974) 4 SCC 3; Anwar Ali Sarkar AIR 1952 SC 75; Kathi Raning Rawat AIR 1952 SC 123; Federation of Armed Forces; and the historical incidents — Travancore Breast Tax, No Peon No Water — for the context of Article 14.

Applying an identical standard (same examination, same age limit, same cut-off) guarantees B's perpetual ineligibility: the competition is rigged not by individual malice but by historically accumulated structural advantage. Criterion Equality Before Law Equal Protection of Laws Origin British legal tradition American legal tradition (14th Amendment) Nature Negative concept Positive concept Command The State shall not deny equality The State shall afford equal protection Function Abolition of special, discriminatory privileges Reasonable classification and positive discrimination to remedy structural disadvantage Concept of equality Formal — treating all alike Substantive — treating unequals differently to achieve genuine equality Illustration First-class ticket: anyone holding it may travel Reservation / quota system in education and employment The two facets of Article 14 compared Homework Homework: create 10 valid classifications satisfying both the intelligible-differentia and nexus tests, and 5 invalid ones failing them; support each with case law where possible; keep the classes diverse (avoid multiple variations of “committees”). Also read: E.P. Royappa (1974) 4 SCC 3; Anwar Ali Sarkar AIR 1952 SC 75; Kathi Raning Rawat AIR 1952 SC 123; Federation of Armed Forces; and the historical incidents — Travancore Breast Tax, No Peon No Water — for the context of Article 14.

day.title: Positive Discrimination & Social Justice
day.trail: Discrimination as a global phenomenon · Code Noir & the French Declaration · Loving v. Virginia · Forms of affirmative action · Nivedita Jain · Individual exploitation vs social discrimination

sections.title: The Universality of Discrimination
sections.html:
A common and erroneous criticism holds that social discrimination — particularly caste and untouchability — was uniquely Indian. Historically, systemic, legally sanctioned discrimination was near-universal. Japan's Burakumin (“hamlet people”) suffered ostracism analogous to untouchability — residential segregation and restrictions on social intercourse — the existence of the very word evidencing institutionalisation. Ancient Mesopotamia, Greece and Rome divided society into rigid classes — free persons, slaves, citizens, non-citizens — with rights to property, contract and courts apportioned by status; law functioned as an instrument of exclusion.

The Code Noir (1685), promulgated by Louis XIV for the French colonies, systematised exploitation in 60 articles: it defined the legal conditions of slavery with precision, classified human beings as movable property (meubles) stripping them of juridical personality, mandated Catholicism and ordered the expulsion of Jews — remaining in force long after France's revolutionary declarations of universal rights. The heritability principle partus sequitur ventrem — the child follows the mother's condition — created the doctrine of “once a slave, always a slave.” A comparative caution: India's bonded labour (prohibited by Article 23, including begar) is brutal, but the bonded labourer retains residual legal personality, unlike the chattel slave who was a res — a thing.

The French Declaration of 1789 is celebrated as liberalism's foundational text, yet women were not entitled to citizenship, and property qualifications confined the vote to citoyens actifs; the poor and all women were citoyens passifs — civil rights without political rights. The most vaunted proclamation of equality in the Western canon was, at inception, a document for propertied white males. Racial discrimination in the United States persisted into living memory: until Loving v. Virginia (1967), anti-miscegenation laws were valid — Richard Loving (white) and Mildred Jeter (Black), married in the District of Columbia, were convicted on returning to Virginia under the Racial Integrity Act, before a unanimous Supreme Court held the statutes violative of equal protection and due process. The Nazi Nuremberg Laws (1935) — protecting “German or related blood” (Blutschutzgesetz) — were the most extreme expression of state-sanctioned social discrimination; the lecture also referred to recent conflict reports of checking sexual organs to determine religious identity before execution.

Key Point

Key takeaway: discrimination on grounds of race, caste, religion and sex was a global phenomenon. Indian society has — and continues to have — profound shortcomings requiring rectification; but the portrayal of discrimination as an exclusively Indian pathology is historically false and intellectually dishonest. Every society must confront its own legacy; the Indian constitutional project is a conscious, ongoing effort to dismantle inherited structures of injustice.

sections.title: The Two Dimensions — and the Impossibility of Formal Competition
sections.html:
Equality before law is fundamentally prohibitory: post-independence, the sole criterion for a first-class railway compartment is a valid first-class ticket — whether the passenger is Black, White, Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh or Parsi, of any caste or sex. Equal protection, by contrast, authorises and sometimes requires preferential treatment for the historically disadvantaged. The lecture's centrepiece contrast: Child A (the child of privilege — optimal nutrition and healthcare, top-tier resources from infancy, social capital: connections with judges and ministers, knowledge of institutions acquired by osmosis) against Child B (the child of disadvantage — poverty, health deficits, late schooling, informational deficits, systemic barriers). A purely formal, identical standard of competition guarantees B's perpetual exclusion from power, influence and advancement — the competition is inherently rigged by historically accumulated structural advantage.

Professor'S Aside

The early Indian Civil Services examination is the paradigm. For years no Indian succeeded — not for want of intellect, but because the examination tested a universe of knowledge centred on Christian theology and the Bible, entirely alien to the Indian experience. Questions like “Who gave the apple to whom?” were incomprehensible to a candidate not steeped in scripture. That was structural exclusion — and it shows why the professor says NEET has never operated on a purely meritocratic basis.

sections.title: Forms of Affirmative Action
sections.html:
FormMechanismExample
Preferential treatment (tie-breaker)Equal marks, different social groups — the disadvantaged candidate (e.g. a Scheduled Tribe woman) is selected, equal achievement against greater disadvantage being greater meritTwo candidates at identical scores
Augmented scoring (bonus marks)Marks added to raw scores by categoryOBC +5; SC +10; ST +15; woman +10; woman with disability +5 — a disabled ST woman scoring 580 reaches 610
Quota system (reservation)A fixed percentage of seats reserved; a reserved candidate may be selected with lower absolute marks, subject to any minimum thresholdIndia's chosen, “more robust” mechanism under Article 15(4) / 16(4)

Three modalities of positive discrimination

Case

State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kumari Nivedita Jain

The limits of reservation

Facts
To fill backward-class medical seats, MP progressively lowered the qualifying marks from 50 to 45 to 35 to 30 — then removed the minimum entirely, permitting admission regardless of entrance score, even zero or negative.
Held
The Supreme Court upheld the State's action.
Principle
The extremity of compensatory discrimination — and, as the professor notes, evidence that medical admissions have grappled with the merit-versus-social-justice tension from the outset; NEET has never been purely meritocratic.
Case

State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)

The trigger for Article 15(4)

Facts
Madras's Communal G.O. allocated medical and engineering seats by caste and community.
Held
Struck down under Article 15(1): discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste. Consequence: the First Constitutional Amendment (1951) inserted Article 15(4), empowering special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.
Principle
The case that constitutionalised affirmative action in education.

sections.title: The Taxonomy — Individual Exploitation vs Social Discrimination
sections.html:
Individual exploitation arises from personal relationships and private enmities — the abuse of personal power. The case studies from contemporary India: Madhumita Shukla, the poetess murdered by Uttar Pradesh's Amarmani Tripathi when she pressed for marriage after seeking his patronage; Geetika Sharma, the air hostess allegedly coerced into servicing the business clients of Haryana minister Gopal Kanda, who died by suicide leaving a detailed note; Shivani Bhatnagar, the journalist murdered through her entanglement with IPS officer R.K. Sharma in pursuit of access to the Prime Minister's Office; Naina Sahni, the tandoor murder victim of Congress politician Sushil Sharma. “As long as the sun and moon exist, individual exploitation will persist” — rooted in the ineradicable human capacity for passion, jealousy, greed and vengeance; law can punish it, not prevent it.

Social discrimination is categorically different: not personal enmity but membership of a targeted group — the victim harmed not for who they are but for what they are within the discriminatory structure. The archetype is Dr. Ambedkar: no personal enmity with anyone (his father was a respected Subedar); forced to sit outside the classroom and denied water by peons — social boycott by caste. Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad of Baroda sponsored his studies abroad on merit. The grounds: sex (Sabarimala entry restrictions, litigated in Indian Young Lawyers' Association; historical denial of property rights, remedied only by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005); caste (hierarchy by birth imposing civil and religious disabilities); race (Jim Crow, apartheid); religion (assertion of one faith's supremacy; extremist interpretations denying the very right to life of others; the Nazi persecution as the extreme); and economic status (the Marxist critique of law as superstructural exploitation; Shakespeare's line — “The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers,” Henry VI Part 2 — a critique of law used to oppress the poor).

CriterionIndividual exploitationSocial discrimination
BasisPersonal enmity, private relationships, individual passionMembership in a targeted group (caste, race, religion, sex)
ScopeInterpersonalSystemic and structural
TargetThe victim as an individualThe victim as a representative of a group
RemedyCriminal prosecution and civil action for specific wrongsConstitutional and legislative group measures — affirmative action, reservations, social justice
PersistenceIneradicable so long as human passions existDismantlable through sustained legal and social reform

The taxonomy applied to remedies

Key Point

Social justice is the telos — the ultimate purpose — of equal protection: the set of positive measures by which the State dismantles structures of social discrimination, recognising that formal equality is an insufficient guarantee of a dignified life for those subjected to centuries of systemic subordination. It demands conditions in which the historically disadvantaged participate in the life of the nation on terms of genuine, substantive equality.

sections.title: The Hypothetical — West Bengal Prohibition Ordinance
sections.html:
A newly elected West Bengal government issues an ordinance imposing prohibition — a total ban on the manufacture, transportation, storage, sale, purchase and consumption of alcoholic liquor. Section 3's proviso exempts: (A) military personnel; (B) foreigners; (C) consumption within 5-star hotels. A citizen — “Niyati,” in the classroom's casting — petitions under Article 14. Her arguments: (1) military personnel are citizens too, and she is “an army in herself, all alone”; (2) is she “any less than a foreigner”?; (3) the 5-star exception is discrimination purely by economic class — if the rich may drink in luxury, why not the person of modest means at home or in a 3-star hotel?

Step one — identify the true legislative objective

The ban is a means, not an end. The deeper objectives are grounded in the Directive Principles: public health (Article 47) — the State shall endeavour to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks injurious to health; public order and safety — prevention of alcohol-related crime and nuisance (the vivid illustration: a rickshaw-puller earning Rs. 300 a day who spends Rs. 500 on a bottle — the cascade of demanding money from and beating his wife, chain-snatching to finance the addiction, further crime under influence); and protection of the vulnerable — a paternalistic, welfarist rationale: the government is not opposed to drinking by those who can “afford and reconcile” it, but is deeply concerned for the poor.

Step two — test each exception

ExceptionIntelligible differentiaNexus analysis
A — Military personnelA fundamentally distinct class: separate regulated society (cantonments), military discipline, unique stresses and sacrificesClear: they are not the vulnerable socio-economic class the Act protects; stable state-provided income; “trained enough” to know how much and when to drink. Precedent — upheld in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (AIR 1951 SC 318)
B — ForeignersA distinct juridical class: non-citizens, transient, not subjects of the State's socio-economic reformNot offending international sensibilities; facilitating commerce and tourism; in colder-climate cultures (the Sikkim example — universal drinking as thermoregulatory norm) alcohol is integral to meals; the object of protecting the Indian poor does not rationally extend to foreign visitors' cultural habits
C — 5-star hotelsEconomic elite — the clientele is a proxy for socio-economic statusFor validity: a person spending Rs. 10,000–20,000 is definitionally outside the protected class — his drinking does not produce the theft and domestic violence over a Rs. 200 shortfall the Act targets; the classification perfectly serves the object. For invalidity: facially discriminatory by economic capacity — “it promotes inequality”; if the object were public health per se, the classification fails, for alcohol is equally harmful to the rich liver and the poor

Testing the three exceptions against the twin limbs

A classroom vote followed: an overwhelming majority held the classification invalid (for the petitioner); a small minority for validity. The lecture's conclusion: both sides are arguable — the outcome depends on which objective the court prioritises. F.N. Balsara is the seminal authority grappling with these precise questions.

Research Task

Research assignment: in Bihar a prohibition law was challenged and initially declared unconstitutional; a subsequent ordinance, its flaws rectified, was upheld. Identify the first ordinance and the flaw in its classification scheme; then the second, and the legislative improvements that satisfied the intelligible-differentia and rational-nexus tests.

sections.title: Hypothetical — Age Concession for Rural NEET Candidates
sections.html: A Maharashtra ordinance grants a five-year age concession to students of rural (village) background appearing for NEET; city students get none. For validity: rural and urban students are distinct classes — documented lack of access to quality schools, coaching and infrastructure. For invalidity (a student's counter-argument): the classification is over-inclusive and outdated — a village child may attend a school superior to an urban slum's municipal school; a rich landlord's village child has every facility while the urban domestic worker's child in Dharavi has none; the classification fails to distinguish the rural rich from the urban poor. The Supreme Court's view (per the lecture): a blanket “rural” classification is unreasonable — it ignores the disparities within the urban category, particularly the uniquely disadvantaged urban slum-dweller, whose condition is often worse than the rural poor (who may retain community support and access to food). In the same judgment the Court upheld a classification based on mountainous or hilly terrain (the Uttarakhand example): the geographical hardship, sparse population and severe lack of accessible schools place all residents of that terrain at a fundamental disadvantage.

sections.title: The Case Compendium — and the R.D. Shetty Lesson
sections.html:
CaseBasis of classification / key principle
State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952)Foundational two-limb test; unguided discretion to send cases to special courts struck down
State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)Prohibition-law exemptions for military personnel and foreigners upheld as reasonable
Chiranjit Lal Chowdhury v. Union of India (1950)A single “sick” industrial undertaking — a class in itself; 1,30,000 livelihoods at stake
Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra (1952)Special courts for named disturbed regions upheld — objective situation of public order
Air India v. Nergesh Meerza (1981)Service regulation retiring air hostesses on first pregnancy examined — classification by sex and pregnancy
R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority (1979)A tender requiring “5 years' experience in a 3-Star Hotel”; the contract awarded to a person with 10 years' experience running a tea-stall (tapri). Struck down: the class “3-star hotel management” is fundamentally different from “tea-stall management” — the authority failed to respect its own intelligible differentia

Landmark cases on reasonable classification

Professor'S Aside

Read case facts with meticulous care. A colleague preparing to teach R.D. Shetty repeatedly missed the critical detail that the eligibility criterion was specifically “5 years of experience in a 3-Star Hotel.” Because she skipped over the qualifier “3-Star,” she never saw the legal problem — the authority had equated a 3-star hotel manager's experience with a tea-stall owner's. Without grasping the fact, the intelligible differentia at the heart of the case becomes invisible. The lesson: read facts with precision.

sections.title: The Method for Solving Article 14 Problems
sections.html:
StepQuestion
1. Identify the classificationExactly what groups has the law created? Who is included, who excluded?
StepQuestion
2. Determine the legislative objectiveWhy was the law passed — what social evil, policy goal or constitutional directive (DPSPs)? The most critical step: a prohibition law's objective is not “to ban alcohol” but public health and public order
3. Test intelligible differentiaIs the distinction real, substantial, non-arbitrary? Is a rural student always differently situated from an urban one — or does the distinction fail between rich rural and poor urban?
4. Test rational nexusDoes that specific difference connect directly to the objective? Military personnel are different — but is their differentness connected to preventing alcohol-induced destitution? If the objective is public health, all consumption is harmful, and every exception's nexus fails

sections.title: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1973)
sections.html:
Case

E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu

AIR 1974 SC 555 · bench including P.N. Bhagwati and Y.V. Chandrachud JJ.

Facts
Royappa, IAS, Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu — the highest State-level IAS post — was removed and appointed Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission Board (the Chairman being the Chief Minister; the Deputy Chairman therefore the post immediately below), then made OSD. An official order declared the posts equivalent in rank and salary to Chief Secretary.
Held
He lost — he could not prove arbitrariness — but the principle was established. The petitioner's argument: equality is not determined solely by salary; power, position, prestige, status and respect are essential components (the classroom example: a professor given Rs. 5 lakh but assigned housekeeping duties is not made Vice-Chancellor). The State's answer — equal salary, equivalent posts, no discrimination — missed the point. Bhagwati J.: “Mala fide and arbitrariness are easy to claim, but hardest to prove.”
Principle
The flaw in the old law: where there is no comparator class (a person uniquely targeted), discrimination cannot be proven and Article 14 lies dormant. The new perspective: whether or not discrimination exists, if the State has absolute discretionary power or acts arbitrarily, Article 14 is violated. “Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be ‘cribbed, cabined and confined’ within the traditional limits of classification.”

What is arbitrariness?

A decision based on whims and fancies — without reason, logic or justification; the opposite of a judicious decision. Its characteristics: (1) absence of reason; (2) whims and fancies — “I liked it, so I did it”; (3) lack of evidentiary support; (4) no consideration of relevant factors. Why absolute discretion breeds arbitrariness: every human being has preferences — someone likes chicken, someone biryani — and unfettered power lets personal preference govern. Discretion cannot be eliminated (governance requires it — if a fire breaks out, the teacher must evacuate the class; everything cannot be pre-written), but it must be structured, guided, reasonable. Proving arbitrariness is extremely difficult — “as tough as proving the existence of oxygen without instruments.”

sections.title: The Three Pillars Before Maneka Gandhi
sections.html:
Case

Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962)

first Indian citation of Munn v. Illinois

Facts
Police surveillance of a citizen, challenged under Article 21.
Held
“Life does not mean mere animal existence. It includes all those things which make life meaningful and beautiful. It includes the right to develop all our faculties.”
Principle
The expansive reading of Article 21 from which the rights to privacy, to choose one's partner, and to live with dignity all descend — without this sentence, the constitutional protection for love marriages, personal relationships and individual autonomy would not exist. (Contemporary application: the Allahabad High Court recently scolded police for investigating a married couple's private life — protected under Article 21.)
Case

R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) — Bank Nationalisation

11-judge bench — one of only a handful in history

Facts
Indira Gandhi nationalised several banks. The petitioner was not a bank but a director and shareholder — because the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) belongs only to citizens, and a company is not a citizen; the bank could not sue, its shareholder-director could.
Held
The government argued it need comply only with Article 31, not Article 19. Rejected: “Nothing doing! They cannot be separated. While acting under Article 31, you must also comply with Article 19(1)(f).”
Principle
Fundamental rights are not watertight compartments — the foundation stone of the Golden Triangle, expressly acknowledged by Bhagwati J. in Maneka Gandhi.
Case

Satwant Singh v. Union of India — the Passport Precedent

Facts
Before 1967 India had no Passport Act; issuance was executive discretion. Satwant Singh's passport was refused — “We denied it because we chose to deny it.”
Held
The Court directed the government: if you want to deny passports, make a law; write down the reasons. Result: the Passports Act, 1967 — whose Section 10(3) authorised impounding “without assigning any reason, in public interest”: absolute, arbitrary power.
Principle
The statutory hook that Maneka Gandhi would strike.

sections.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
sections.html:
Case

Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India

AIR 1978 SC 597

Facts
Two constables arrived at her residence: “Ministry of External Affairs — please surrender your passport.” On asking why: “Orders from above. We don't know why.” The government invoked Section 10(3) — impounding without assigning any reason — and defended it: “If we tell her the reason, she will run away!”
Held
The doctrine of post-decisional hearing evolved: in urgency the State may impound first, but must immediately (1) issue a notice stating the grounds; (2) afford a hearing; (3) continue the impounding only if justified, else return the passport. Section 10(3)'s absolute unguided discretion was arbitrary power, violating Article 14; and Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive — any law depriving personal liberty must satisfy non-arbitrariness (14) and reasonableness (19) as well as Article 21. The Golden Triangle was formally established.
Principle
Outcome: Maneka Gandhi did not get her passport back — the case was dismissed on other grounds, continuing the pattern: Marbury (no relief), Kesavananda (no relief), Royappa (no relief), Maneka (no relief). Landmark cases create principles; they do not always grant relief to the petitioner.

sections.title: Marbury v. Madison (1803) — the Origin of Judicial Review
sections.html:
Case

Marbury v. Madison

5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803) · Chief Justice John Marshall

Facts
The Constitution was 14–15 years old; no article mentioned judicial review. In the lame-duck period after John Adams lost the 1800 election, his party appointed 40 judges; commissions were signed and sealed, but some undelivered when Jefferson took office at midnight. Jefferson: “Throw these undelivered commissions away!” Marbury sought mandamus against Secretary of State Madison.
Held
Three issues: (1) Does Marbury have a right to the commission? Yes — the right vested when signed and sealed; “where there is a right, there is a remedy” (ubi jus ibi remedium). (2) Can the Court issue mandamus to the executive? Yes — in the most famous sentence of American constitutional law: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” (3) Does mandamus lie in the Court's original jurisdiction? No — Article III, Section 2 does not cover it; Section 13 of the Judiciary Act 1789, which purported to grant it, was unconstitutional and void — the first federal statute ever struck down.
Principle
The political genius: the Court asserted the massive power of judicial review yet ordered no relief against the President, avoiding a confrontation Jefferson would likely have defied. “We will show our power, but we will not use it in this case.” Marbury did not get his commission.

sections.title: Applying the Tests — the Bearer Bonds Problem
sections.html:
Question

The government, to bring black money into the mainstream and fund new medical colleges, issues Bearer Bonds purchasable by anyone without questions about the money's source; after ten years the investment becomes white. A PIL challenges the Act under Article 14: it is an injustice to honest taxpayers who paid full income tax; it rewards dishonesty and encourages hoarding in expectation of future amnesty schemes. Decide.

Answer

(1) Presumption of constitutionality: courts presume a parliamentary statute valid; the burden is on the challenger. (2) Judicial deference to economic policy: courts do not intervene in policy, especially economic policy, unless it is manifestly arbitrary. (3) The two tests: intelligible differentia — is there a clear distinction between holders of black money and others? Yes, the classification is clear. Rational nexus — the object is to surface black money, fund medical colleges, improve the doctor-patient ratio; allowing investment without declaring the source directly furthers that object. Nexus exists. (4) Conclusion: the Act is constitutionally valid — it satisfies both limbs and, as an economic policy measure, deserves deference. (This is the pattern of R.K. Garg v. Union of India, the recommended original reading.)

Exam Tips

Examination tips: structure the answer Introduction → Facts (brief) → Legal Provisions → Tests Applied → Case Laws → Conclusion; use headings (“Intelligible Differentia,” “Rational Nexus,” “Non-Arbitrariness,” “Presumption of Constitutionality”); cite cases with name, year and principle; quote judicial observations for weight; do NOT invoke “colourable legislation” unless genuinely applicable — misapplied doctrines cost marks; distinguish “arbitrary” from “mala fide”; always remember the Golden Triangle (cite Maneka Gandhi and R.C. Cooper).

“Arbitrariness and equality are sworn enemies. Equality cannot be crippled, cabined, cribbed, or imprisoned in some doctrinal limitations.”

— E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu

day.title: Rule of Law I — Dicey & the Glorious Revolution
day.trail: Meaning and definition · Dicey's book and its three parts · The Glorious Revolution 1688-89 · The three components · How to answer a Rule of Law question

sections.title: Meaning and Definition
sections.html:
Rule of Law means that no man is above law and every person is subject to the jurisdiction of ordinary courts of law, irrespective of position and rank.

— The working definition

The phrase originates in the French La Principe de Legalite — the principle of legality: governance according to law, not according to the whims and fancies of any person. Black's Law Dictionary defines it as governance according to law; the Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary provides a similar definition. Rule of Law is a foundational concept of constitutional jurisprudence ensuring that everything runs by law.

sections.title: Dicey and His Book
sections.html: Professor Albert Venn Dicey systematically articulated the concept in An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885), observing and documenting the prevailing circumstances in England after the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89: the powers of the monarchy curtailed, governance increasingly in the hands of the House of Commons — the common people. Dicey did not create the Rule of Law; he observed and documented it. His book was divided into three parts: (1) The Sovereignty of Parliament — which Dicey took to be fundamental, total and beyond challenge; (2) The Rule of Law; (3) the constitutional conventions. When Irish home rule returned to Parliament's agenda some three decades later, Dicey changed his mind about parliamentary omnipotence: in the final edition of The Law of the Constitution (1915) he lamented that parliamentary sovereignty had fallen prey to the party system.
