sections.title: The Glorious Revolution of 1688-89
sections.html:
A watershed in British constitutional history establishing the supremacy of Parliament over the monarchy. It began on 5 November 1688 when William of Orange, backed by a 21,000-strong army, invaded England; uprisings in the north followed; by the end of 1688 James II had fled to France, where Louis XIV offered the king-in-exile his protection. The revolution was driven by a deep-seated fear of Catholicism and the belief that Catholics were plotting the overthrow of church and state — a conspiracy theory given credibility by genuine Catholic subterfuge, most notably the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. James II's authority had appeared secure on his accession in February 1685, but support ebbed as it became clear he wished not only freedom of worship for Catholics but removal of the Test and Corporation Acts so they could occupy public office.

In the months after James's flight, a Convention Parliament decided he had effectively abdicated; William and his wife Mary were declared joint monarchs — a minor Dutch prince became King of England. The Bill of Rights (1689) determined the monarch must be Protestant; the Act of Settlement (1701) went further, demanding that whoever inherited the Crown must “joyn in communion with the Church of England as by law established.” The revolution established parliamentary supremacy — though the events of 1688 constituted a foreign invasion by the Dutch Republic; bloodshed in England was limited, but the settlement was secured in Ireland and Scotland by force and much loss of life. The revolution also fostered the growth of slavery by ending the Royal African Company's monopoly on the trade in 1698 — for the non-white inhabitants of the British Atlantic empire it represented not the broadening of freedom but the expansion of servitude.

sections.title: The Three Components
sections.html:
Dicey's three components — the architecture of the Rule of Law

1. Supremacy of Law

“No man shall be punished or made to suffer in body or goods except for the violation of the law, and such violation must be established in an ordinary court of the land and in an ordinary legal manner.” Key elements: no punishment without law; punishment only through the ordinary legal manner; no arbitrary power — government cannot punish by its own fiat; no wide discretionary powers — persons in authority in Britain do not enjoy wide, arbitrary or discretionary powers; and wherever there is discretion, there is room for arbitrariness. The concept was necessary because before its establishment people acted according to their own will. The Anwar Ali Sarkar case exemplifies the violation: unguided State discretion to send cases for speedy trial without rational basis — one Collector might send a rape case for speedy trial because it received good publicity while another ignores a similar case. The law itself should specify what kind of cases go to speedy trial.

Professor'S Aside

If a student expresses an opinion I disagree with, I cannot throw her out of class simply because I didn't like what she said. That would be acting on individual whims and fancies. The law gives everyone the liberty to hold independent opinions based on their own choice, conviction and thinking. If someone is to be punished, it must be in accordance with the law, not personal preference.

2. Equality before Law

“No man is above the law and everyone, whatever his condition or rank, is subject to the ordinary laws of the land. Every person can sue or be sued in a court of law.” Dicey was not concerned with equality in a general sense but with limiting official power in favour of individual legal rights. His two specific ideas: (1) officials as such enjoy no special protection — an official who abuses power is personally liable to anyone whose rights he violates, just as if he were a private citizen; (2) disputes between government and citizen are settled in the ordinary courts according to ordinary law, not in special governmental courts. The framers incorporated this into Article 14: “The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.” Equality before Law (the negative aspect — no special privilege will be created; no untouchability, no caste restrictions, no prohibition on wearing clothes on the upper body, no denial of access to ponds) was borrowed from the British tradition; Equal Protection of Laws (the positive aspect — no discriminatory and depressive status will be created) from the American.

3. Predominance of Legal Spirit

“The general principles of the British Constitution and especially the liberties of the individual are judge-made — the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons in particular cases brought before the courts from time to time.” Peculiar to Britain: the rights of individuals form part of and pervade the Constitution because they are secured by the courts. British Constitutional Law is not the source but the consequence of the rights of individuals as defined by courts. Referring to the Habeas Corpus Act, Dicey said it was “worth a hundred Constitutional articles guaranteeing individual liberty.” He accepted there was Rule of Law in the U.S.A. because the rights declared in the Constitution could be enforced, the Constitution giving legal security to the rights declared.

The classroom explanation is the lecture's philosophical centre. Think of the hundred people you have known since childhood: how many would you have enmity with? A student estimates 80-20; the professor suggests closer to 90-95 neutral, 5-10 hostile. With most people we do not fight — we do not violate their rights, nor they ours. Even without a teacher or State present, peace prevails, because human beings are usually peaceful. Even before the State or formal law existed, people lived in an orderly, non-volatile manner. The famous maxim: “Your right ends where my nose begins” — possibly originating in France, later used by Abraham Lincoln and others: you may practice punching all you want, but it must not hit someone else's nose. This theory governed society even when there was no sovereign, no State, no king, no Prime Minister — a natural, self-regulating order.

Professor'S Aside

The State might have made a few laws, but as human society evolved, some laws kept forming along with us. When the State came into existence, there were already existing laws. At the very least, the right to life, the right to food, the right to marry and the right to procreation were certainly already there. These rights were not given by any king or any State. Generally people respected each other and took care of each other — and such practices which became customs were, in essence, laws. The State came later to make it even better.

Generally people respected each other and took care of each other — and such practices which became customs were, in essence, laws. The State came later to make it even better.

sections.title: Rule of Law vs Rule by Law
sections.html:
AspectRule by LawRule of Law
MeaningWork happens according to whatever law existsThe law itself must be just, fair and reasonable
QualityNo concern for justice or quality of the lawLaw must have inherent quality, respect fundamental rights and human dignity
AspectRule by LawRule of Law
ExamplesA dictator's orders; oppressive lawsLaws respecting fundamental rights and promoting justice

The critical distinction

  • North Korea: when the father of the “missile man” died, the new ruler ordered all subjects to weep, with tears in their eyes — anyone without tears would be killed. Not illegal, because the sovereign ordered it; but no fairness, no justice, no reasonableness — Rule by Law. (When dictators die, the professor observes, people actually celebrate.)
  • Taliban: girls cannot study under existing laws — order without justice.
  • Women's rights: in some interpretations Indian girls from Muslim households are given fewer rights, told not to get educated, married off early, made to wear a burqa — contrasted with Iranian girls who protested against the burqa by coming onto the streets and being shot at, some agitating that if forced to wear it they would wear nothing at all.

sections.title: How to Answer a Question on the Rule of Law
sections.html: The ideal structure, displayed on the PPT: (1) Meaning — the general definition; (2) Dictionary definition — Black's Law Dictionary, Oxford; (3) Jurist's view — the historical perspective. Sir Edward Coke, Chief Justice in James I's reign, was the originator of the doctrine in England; but Greek philosophers — Aristotle, Plato and Cicero — first wrote about it. Aristotle notably said that “law should govern and those who are in power should be servants of law.” This introduction pattern (general meaning, dictionary definition, jurist's view) works for any topic — Rule of Law or Natural Justice alike.

sections.title: Significance and Application
sections.html: Dicey's thesis has been criticised from various angles, but his basic tenet stands: power is derived from, and is to be exercised according to, law — the absence of arbitrary and discretionary power, equality before law, legal protection of basic rights. In India the Supreme Court has read Article 14 to encompass non-arbitrariness: E.P. Royappa — arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality. In Kesavananda Bharati, the Court enunciated the Rule of Law as one of the most important aspects of the basic structure doctrine. The broad emphasis: absence of any centre of unlimited or arbitrary power, proper structuration and control of power. Government intervention in citizens' daily activities is ever-increasing, creating possibility of arbitrariness in State action — Rule of Law is the counter, because its basic emphasis is the exclusion of arbitrariness. Lawlessness and unreasonableness in government are its antithesis.

sections.title: Classroom Interaction — the Honesty Principle
sections.html:
Professor'S Aside

I am not as stupid as students think — I remember faces and names even when students lie. One student claims her attendance is fine; it is actually fifteen percent — fifteen out of thirty-five classes. Lying and saying “I do come” will not help the situation improve; accept the truth so the problem can be addressed. I ask about attendance only for your betterment — I even help students at risk of being debarred, because a full year back is a serious consequence. I am not as cruel as students think; if someone genuinely cannot wake in the morning, I will jokingly arrange for a bucket of water to be poured over them. The rules exist and cannot be bypassed — but there is room for empathy if students are honest about their difficulties.

sections.title: The NLU System — and the Quasi-Federal Warning
sections.html:
Key Point

The professor does not teach by reading from a book: whatever he teaches is what he expects in the examination. He has taught that the Constitution of India is not quasi-federal. Every book and article will say “quasi-federal” — the moment a student writes that word in an exam, they receive a zero and fail; he will not entertain a book brought to argue otherwise. The correct position, as taught: Dr. Ambedkar first said the Constitution is federal; the Supreme Court repeatedly said it is federal; later the Court declared federation part of the basic structure. “Anyone writing quasi-federal is merely acting as a follower of a Western country. I am not Western. I am Indian.”

Professor'S Aside

A student from Nagpur — a local girl — is threatened, humorously, that eight to ten of us will come to her house for tea and to lodge a complaint about her attendance. In my local rustic language, “abusing” actually means criticism. When I taught IPS officers, criticising corruption — if the SSP is not corrupt, a traffic inspector does not have the courage to take money at a crossroad; the topic was the Prevention of Corruption Act — a huge complaint was made against me for taunting and abusing the very officers who had paid my airfare. And if we eat your salt, we cannot abuse you — but I still promise to visit; Symbiosis often hosts my lectures, so a visit is not impossible.

sections.title: Rule of Law — Its True Origins in Ancient India
sections.html:
Since Equality before Law is drawn from the Rule of Law, the professor returns to its deeper origins. The Rule of Law is a concept very difficult to explain but very easy to understand. Books trace it only to Western countries; the professor asserts emphatically that the Rule of Law has always been there in our country — read any story from ancient India and you will find it. Natural justice can be considered part of the Rule of Law:

Case

Lord Rama and Ravana — natural justice in the Ramayana

Classroom authority for the ancient Indian Rule of Law

Facts
Rama sent messages to Ravana not once but twice, warning him to return Mother Sita and avoid a destructive war; even during the war he gave repeated warnings.
Held
—
Principle
Rama told Ravana that he was a great and knowledgeable saint, and needed only to return Sita to be excused — notice and opportunity to amend before force: natural justice.
Case

Yudhishthira's exile — the Mahabharata example

Facts
Yudhishthira lost the game of gambling; the condition was twelve years of exile and one year in an unknown place. Lord Krishna knew a war would take place — yet did not stop it.
Held
—
Principle
He insisted that the rule be followed: even the contemplated catastrophe did not justify setting aside the agreed condition.
Case

Shravan Kumar — the devoted son

Facts
Shravan Kumar was carrying his blind parents; Lord Dasharatha accidentally killed him.
Held
—
Principle
The Rule of Law demanded that the king take responsibility for the care and protection of the dead boy's parents. King Dasharatha went to them and served them water; they ultimately cursed him to die of the same grief of losing a son. Dasharatha was a king — he could have avoided this, but the Rule of Law bound him. This is the true spirit of the ancient Indian Rule of Law.

sections.title: The Colonial Erasure of Indian Legal Heritage
sections.html:
Why are these hundreds and thousands of ancient Indian examples ignored? Because of the British need to show dominance: had the British acknowledged that Indians had good things of their own, the Indian people would never have accepted their superiority. The narrative pushed was that Indians were inferior — “snake charmers.” The professor dislikes the term intensely: charm actually means something good (a charming friend); the real satisfaction comes from the Hindi word sapera. Did the British come all the way to India just to see snakes? If they liked India so much — why didn't they want to go back even after independence?

The historical footnote: the British eventually folded their hands before people like Dr. Ambedkar and pleaded — with democracy, the public would elect representatives, but the British had fallen in love with India and were not going back. Since they would not win elections, they asked for representation without elections. Dr. Ambedkar granted the Anglo-Indian community two MPs in Parliament for ten years under Article 331; the professor criticises the Congress Party for repeatedly extending the provision until its removal by the 104th Constitutional Amendment. If India was not good, no one would have wanted to settle here — from the Mughals to the British, everyone who came stayed. Even Mark Tully, the BBC reporter, came to report and stayed — the professor recommends him as an excellent writer.

Exam Directive

Examination directive: if asked about the Rule of Law, write a little bit about India. The professor states candidly that no matter how hard the “cockroach” tries, he thinks Modi will remain in power another three years and only Modi sympathisers would evaluate their answer sheets — but regardless of who is in power, he will be evaluating their papers. If a student writes that the Rule of Law came from Western countries, three marks will be deducted automatically. Search for and find references to the Rule of Law in ancient Indian literature — even new Indian literature is still older than Western sources. Decolonise your legal thinking.

sections.title: ADM Jabalpur — the Darkest Hour of the Rule of Law
sections.html:
ADM Jabalpur and its correction — the timeline that must be memorised

Case

ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla

The Emergency case · habeas corpus during MISA detentions

Facts
During the Emergency, MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) was applied and everyone was arrested under it; Fundamental Rights stood suspended. Detainees petitioned that they were wrongly detained and should be released. The Supreme Court then had very good judges — at least three beyond doubt: Justice Khanna, a very upright judge; Justice Bhagwati, who called himself the pioneer of human rights; Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, a very good judge — along with Justice Beg (whom the professor harshly calls Indira Gandhi's “peon”) and Chief Justice A.N. Ray (made Chief Justice by Indira Gandhi, later changing his allegiance). It seemed the decision would be 4:1 for liberty.
Held
The shocking judgment came — the professor states bluntly that Indira Gandhi bought everyone; the only man who was not sold was Justice H.R. Khanna. The judges held: “The entire repository of the right to liberty is the Constitution. If the Constitution has not given the right, then you do not have the right at all. Since the Constitution and rights were suspended, there was no Right to Life left to protect.”
Principle
The core: all rights come only from the Constitution — suspend the Constitution and you have no rights at all.

Nani Palkhivala's argument (appearing for the detainees) posed a terrifying hypothetical: suppose a girl committed a crime and the police went to arrest “Ishita,” but by mistake caught an innocent girl, “Aarya,” who protests she is not Ishita — and the police answer, “To hell with it, you are in our hands now.” The darker question: during an Emergency, if a policeman, out of personal enmity or after drinking, simply shoots an innocent person without any crime — is there any remedy? Justice Chandrachud's devastating response: “I am sorry, but the present law does not allow any relief.” A station house officer could come, shoot you, and you would have no legal recourse whatsoever. The professor tells students to read the case themselves — “you will feel like abusing the judges even more” — and recounts visiting Justice Bhagwati's home and bluntly asking him what had happened, whether he had consumed something.

The overruling — the 44th Amendment

Because it was a manifestly wrong decision, immediately after the Morarji Desai government came to power the 44th Constitutional Amendment was passed: the Right to Life can never be suspended, even during an Emergency. Two articles cannot be suspended — Articles 20 and 21. The professor made the class chant “twenty and twenty-one” five times to memorise it: this is explicitly written in Article 359, which now reads “except 20 and 21.” Thus ADM Jabalpur stands overruled by the 44th Amendment.

The emotional correction — Justice D.Y. Chandrachud

Justice D.Y. Chandrachud — son of Justice Y.V. Chandrachud — felt a deep sense of guilt over his father's betrayal. In the landmark Privacy case he wrote a powerful passage, read aloud in class: “Neither life nor liberty are bounties conferred by the State, nor does the Constitution create these rights.” Our life and liberty are not a bounty (a gift) of the State or the Constitution; they are given by Nature or God, and the Constitution has merely accepted this fact — it is not the sole repository of these rights, which existed even before its advent. The exact opposite of what his father had written.

Professor'S Aside

The parable of the naughty father and the good son: a very naughty father abused everyone in the village his whole life. On his deathbed he told his decent son that everyone would abuse him after his death, and asked the son to do something to make people praise him. The son realised that if he did even dirtier work than his father, people would say the father was better — so while the father only abused, the son started throwing mud and dung at people. After a few days the villagers began saying, “His father was better!” D.Y. Chandrachud did something similar: to make his father look better, he wrote this profound passage — though it was not legally necessary, the 44th Amendment having already fixed the problem — explicitly writing that ADM Jabalpur is overruled, washing away his father's sin.

sections.title: The Visit of Justice Sanjiv Khanna — Reading Cases Pays
sections.html:
Professor'S Aside

Justice Sanjiv Khanna — nephew of Justice H.R. Khanna — visited the university for convocation. Students, having been taught ADM Jabalpur, were eager for photos with him because of the heroic legacy: for his courageous dissent, H.R. Khanna was not made Chief Justice. I told Justice Khanna he had a huge fan following; he was surprised — Chief Justice for only five or six months, who would know him? I explained: he had converted the injustice done to his uncle into justice by rising to Chief Justice himself. He was pleased immensely and took photos with students for a long time.

Professor'S Aside

A PhD scholar, on her honeymoon in Kashmir, recognised Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul at her hotel and called me for advice on what to say. I told her: quickly read two or three of his judgments, then tell him how much you appreciated his explanation of proportionality in the Privacy judgment. She did — and it led to a meaningful conversation. When Justice S.K. Krishna — a popular judge, Chairman of the Pay Commission — visited, I could engage him by recollecting his judgments and commission reports. The moral: when students read cases and judgments, they have something substantial to talk about with eminent people. Otherwise they will just come, eat food, leave — and not have a good life.

sections.title: Indian Heritage, Exports and Traditional Knowledge
sections.html:
The professor opens with a reflection on how Indian traditions and products were systematically neglected after independence. If sarees had been exported to the world, India could have become economically strong much earlier — Aishwarya Rai once draped a saree for a European actress, demonstrating the global appeal of Indian attire; girls who do not feel like studying could, he jokes, go to Europe and open a business draping sarees at weddings and functions. The larger point: Nehru focused heavily on imports and neglected exports, believing there was nothing in India worth exporting — a fundamental flaw. A student counters that Nehru himself wore kurta-pajama and khadi; the professor replies that he is not asking Nehru to wear a saree.

  • Sanskrit — “the most scientific language in the world”; research on Sanskrit is happening at NASA, yet Nehru stopped its teaching in India, insisting English was essential for progress.
  • Pilgrimage and tourism — Ayodhya, a place of immense faith for crores, had no railway station while Faizabad, fifteen kilometres away, was developed with all trains stopping; Chitrakoot was ignored in favour of Karwi. When students suggest this avoided Hindu-Muslim conflict, the professor counters that no Muslim ever said a railway station should not be built at a Hindu place; those who objected should have been sent to Pakistan — India was divided on the basis of religion, and Hindus in Hindustan must have the right to live as Hindus.
  • Somnath — the temple had been broken seventeen times; after independence Sardar Patel decided to rebuild it. There was a mosque at the site, but Patel requested the local Muslims to agree, noting the place had no specific Islamic significance like a visit from the Prophet; they agreed — today there is no conflict over Somnath. Nehru, by contrast, refused to allow similar temple construction in Uttar Pradesh — a political calculation, the professor argues, to secure votes by maintaining Hindu-Muslim tension; the ongoing disputes over Ayodhya and Mathura are the direct result.
  • Traditional medicine — the professor's father prepared a medicine for cataract from the juice of a white bush which could cure even the highest level of cataract; Ayurveda was demoted, not promoted, and curing someone at home with it can today lead to jail. Turmeric, tulsi and neem are being patented by America, though Indian mothers have used tulsi water for sick children for generations. Had lakhs of such remedies been patented and exported, the economic gains would have been enormous. He is not against Western medicine or clothing — people can wear pants and suits, but Indian products should have been marketed too. Modi popularised the Indian jacket, and now ninety percent of people wear it: proof that promotion works.
Question

A student argues: government priorities after independence were different — first feed the hungry during the Bengal famine, build ISRO, DRDO and the IITs, then turn to traditional knowledge. The professor's response?

Answer

“Tell me one institute opened to promote Ayurvedic medicine.” When a student mentions AIIMS, he dismisses it as having only a neglected Ayurveda department — no dedicated government institute for Ayurveda was ever established. Even today millets and Indian generic foods have become globally popular — why was this importance not recognised earlier? Seventy years have passed, and the neglect continued throughout. A second student then makes the thoughtful point that those in power can only act on what they know: Nehru and Gandhi were educated abroad, absorbed Western philosophies of freedom and liberty, and naturally implemented what they had learned. The professor acknowledges the argument but, needing to move forward with the syllabus, humorously declares the student has “won for now,” inviting a dedicated debate another day.
sections.text: The professor opens with a reflection on how Indian traditions and products were systematically neglected after independence. If sarees had been exported to the world, India could have become economically strong much earlier — Aishwarya Rai once draped a saree for a European actress, demonstrating the global appeal of Indian attire; girls who do not feel like studying could, he jokes, go to Europe and open a business draping sarees at weddings and functions. The larger point: Nehru focused heavily on imports and neglected exports, believing there was nothing in India worth exporting — a fundamental flaw. A student counters that Nehru himself wore kurta-pajama and khadi; the professor replies that he is not asking Nehru to wear a saree. Sanskrit — “the most scientific language in the world”; research on Sanskrit is happening at NASA, yet Nehru stopped its teaching in India, insisting English was essential for progress. Pilgrimage and tourism — Ayodhya, a place of immense faith for crores, had no railway station while Faizabad, fifteen kilometres away, was developed with all trains stopping; Chitrakoot was ignored in favour of Karwi. When students suggest this avoided Hindu-Muslim conflict, the professor counters that no Muslim ever said a railway station should not be built at a Hindu place; those who objected should have been sent to Pakistan — India was divided on the basis of religion, and Hindus in Hindustan must have the right to live as Hindus. Somnath — the temple had been broken seventeen times; after independence Sardar Patel decided to rebuild it. There was a mosque at the site, but Patel requested the local Muslims to agree, noting the place had no specific Islamic significance like a visit from the Prophet; they agreed — today there is no conflict over Somnath. Nehru, by contrast, refused to allow similar temple construction in Uttar Pradesh — a political calculation, the professor argues, to secure votes by maintaining Hindu-Muslim tension; the ongoing disputes over Ayodhya and Mathura are the direct result. Traditional medicine — the professor's father prepared a medicine for cataract from the juice of a white bush which could cure even the highest level of cataract; Ayurveda was demoted, not promoted, and curing someone at home with it can today lead to jail. Turmeric, tulsi and neem are being patented by America, though Indian mothers have used tulsi water for sick children for generations. Had lakhs of such remedies been patented and exported, the economic gains would have been enormous. He is not against Western medicine or clothing — people can wear pants and suits, but Indian products should have been marketed too. Modi popularised the Indian jacket, and now ninety percent of people wear it: proof that promotion works. sections.title: Rule of Law — Recap and Deeper Exploration
sections.html:
Why study the Rule of Law? One of its components, Equality before Law, is part of Article 14. Supremacy of Law means two things: no punishment except for violation of law, and no governance by individual whims and fancies (the classroom example of the opinion-expressing student). Equality before Law — all are equal, but all cannot be equal, which is why the theory of classification exists in both England and India. Predominance of Legal Spirit receives the interactive treatment: the most naughty student in class (Isha, self-certified) considers the hundred people she has known since childhood — her estimate of enmity is 80-20, corrected to 90-95 neutral, 5-10 hostile. With most people we do not fight: rights go unviolated on both sides; peace prevails even without teacher or State, because human beings are usually peaceful. Even before the State or formal law existed, people lived in an orderly, non-volatile manner.

Find Out

Homework attached to the maxim: find out who said “Your right ends where my nose begins” — it may have originated in France and was later used by Abraham Lincoln and others. The idea: you can practice punching all you want, but it should not hit someone else's nose; as long as there is distance, people do not interfere. This theory governed society even when there was no sovereign, no State, no king, no Prime Minister — no Nehru, no Modi. It is a natural, self-regulating order. Students are also directed to read the International Commission of Jurists' modern expansion of the concept.

sections.title: Magna Carta (1215)
sections.html:
The professor traces the Rule of Law in England to 1215. Magna Carta was one of the first official documents about human rights — the first written promise by a King not to do certain things. In older times kings levied taxes on the public for personal whims: to fight wars for a princess; to build grand monuments for a deceased wife; simply to display power. The common people's blood was sucked through arbitrary taxation; there was no curb on the king's power. The Barons of England — not the common man, but middle-class people — confronted the king and threatened revolt; the king was compelled to accept: no taxation without consultation. This was the first time a king acknowledged that some people had some rights.

  • Magna Carta was not for the common man initially.
  • It was signed not once but on several occasions — each new king signed the charter afresh.
  • The first version may have had only fifteen items; later versions expanded to thirty-nine.
  • The words “due process” were used for the first time in Magna Carta — likely in Article 39 of a later version.

sections.title: Rule of Law in India — Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh
sections.html:
Case

Dr. Subramanian Swamy v. Dr. Manmohan Singh

Modern application of the Rule of Law

Facts
A government servant can be prosecuted for corruption only with the government's sanction. If a minister in Manmohan Singh's government was corrupt, permission to prosecute had to come from Manmohan Singh himself — naturally, it was not granted.
Held
The Supreme Court held that refusing sanction for the prosecution of a corrupt official is a violation of the Rule of Law.
Principle
The professor is criticising on the basis of this judicial pronouncement, not personal whims. Reading the case is compulsory — anyone who does not read it will fail the mid-term (though he later admits he has never actually framed a question on it).

sections.title: The World Justice Project — Measuring the Rule of Law
sections.html:
The WJP attempts a new definition and annually audits countries. India is currently ranked around 76th — lower, the professor feels, than deserved. His methodological critique: Scandinavian countries like Norway have smaller, more homogeneous populations and sufficient money, hence fewer problems; India's immense diversity brings unique challenges — “many arrangements for anger”: give reservation, the General category gets angry; don't give it, the rest get angry; permit Tazia processions, the idol-immersers get angry; permit idol immersion, the Tazia processors get angry.

WJP componentWhat it includes
Accountability · Open Government · Just Law · Accessible and Impartial JusticeThe WJP's four main components (its restated pillars)
Constraints on government powersLimited by the legislature, the judiciary, independent audit, and non-governmental checks
Absence of corruptionIn the executive, judicial and legislative branches
Open governmentPublished laws, Right to Information, civic participation, complaint mechanisms — weakened in India because no matter how good a law Modi makes, Rahul Gandhi will never support it, and vice versa; party interest over national interest
Fundamental rightsEqual treatment, right to life, due process, freedom of opinion, belief, privacy, assembly, labour rights
Order and securityCrime control, limited civil conflict, no resort to violence for personal grievances
Regulatory enforcementEffective enforcement without improper influence, no unreasonable delay, due process in administrative proceedings, no expropriation without lawful process and compensation
Civil justiceAccess and affordability; freedom from discrimination, corruption and improper government influence; no unreasonable delay; effective enforcement; accessible ADR
WJP componentWhat it includes
Criminal justiceEffective investigation, timely adjudication, effective correctional system, impartiality, freedom from corruption and improper influence, due process rights of the accused — the professor humorously references an incident where a former Home Minister was beaten up, suggesting such things affect this parameter

The WJP conceptual framework, as read out in class

Where the Rule of Law is stronger, the economy is stronger (hard work rewarded, looting less); countries are more peaceful; people are more educated; people live longer. The Bihar example: it became poor because Jungle Raj replaced the Rule of Law — no one sets up a factory where they must pay bribes or risk kidnapping. And the Rule of Law can be applied anywhere, practically: students can measure it in their own university — do classes start on time; are syllabus and reading material provided; do teachers come on time; do exams and results happen on time — broken down into Academic, Hostel Management, Mess Management and Placement Cell parameters for NLU Nagpur.

sections.title: Homework — Legitimate Expectation and American Equality
sections.html: Legitimate Expectation: read what it is, where it started, how it developed, when it travelled to India, and two to four cases. The class votes to read the American equality cases before Article 15: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) — “separate but equal” upheld, on the reasoning that “legislation is powerless to eradicate racial instincts or abolish distinctions based upon physical differences”; and Brown v. Board of Education (1954) — separate is inherently unequal, the reversal. Asked how he remembers exact dates, the professor answers: “First love is never forgotten” — a BBC London article reported that people who tried to find their first love after many years married them eighty percent of the time; for him the Constitution is his first and last love.

sections.title: Personal Anecdotes — Capability and the Scholarship Issue
sections.html:
Professor'S Aside

In 2012 a gentleman approached me to teach CLAT coaching. I refused; when he persisted, I demanded three thousand rupees per lecture — fifteen thousand in today's money. He asked me to first give a demo class, because the students were “very naughty” and had chased away three teachers. I replied: “Throw your approval in the dustbin. I don't have time to give a test. If you bring lousy teachers, kids will do this only.” I refused to negotiate and insisted on payment for all thirty classes upfront — joking that the director should not instigate the kids to chase me away after twenty-eight classes to avoid paying. My confidence came from knowing my subject thoroughly. Nidhi Mugreja, a good teacher, earns around six to seven lakh rupees a month teaching at Rahul IAS — possibly ten. In India there is no lack of employment; there is a lack of capable people.

Professor'S Aside

I belong to the General category, with no reservation, and have changed many government jobs, always thriving because of competence. I chose to stay in Nagpur because Delhi's pollution gave me respiratory problems and black spots on my heart — doctors said it looked as if I smoked twenty cigarettes a day, though I have never even seen a cigarette up close. Nagpur, especially the Mihan area, offers morning and evening walks and a peaceful life.

The scholarship saga: Merit-cum-Means had been interpreted by the Vice Chancellor for seven years as “Merit separate, Means separate,” with scholarships given under two heads. Becoming Chairman of the committee, the professor argued that Merit-cum-Means means Merit in Means — just as a “Drawing-cum-Dining room” does not mean the dining room and drawing room are separate. After a world-class research effort and a trip to the Executive Council, a judge ruled in his favour. New rules: only students with family income up to Rs. 8 lakh (the government's means criterion) are eligible, and within that group the toppers receive the scholarship; families with one crore rupees are not eligible at all. “This is Rule of Law in action — and that is why people get angry with me. But if one keeps reading and building capability, one will always find work elsewhere.”

sections.title: The Problems and Answers
sections.html:
Question

1 · Prohibition with exemptions. A State bans liquor entirely in the interest of public health and temperance, but exempts soldiers and sailors consuming foreign liquor in military messes, canteens, warships and troopships, and foreign tourists possessing liquor under a special permit. Ordinary residents get no permit route. Is the exemption of defence personnel (separate service conditions, functional needs aboard ships) and foreign visitors (transient status, different customs) valid, even though allowing them to drink seems to work against the very purpose of temperance among the general population?

Answer

OFFICIAL SECTION B ANSWER: Defence personnel and vessels were already recognised as a distinct legal category under separate service and discipline laws, and foreigners were distinguished by their transient status and different customs — both real, non-fanciful differentia. The Supreme Court held that special treatment of a class already treated as distinct under other statutes has a rational nexus to practical governance — even though the High Court had earlier found no such nexus and struck the exemption down. (This is the pattern of State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, taught on 30 July.)

Question

2 · The rent-control cut-off. A rent law permanently frees all buildings constructed after a cut-off date from rent control, to encourage fresh construction. Decades later, the “new” buildings are over twenty-five years old, yet their landlords still enjoy total freedom, while equally old pre-cutoff buildings remain regulated forever. The classification made sense when passed — is it still valid to keep exempting them forever, with no time limit?

Answer

OFFICIAL SECTION B ANSWER (as far as the source preserves it): the classification — date of construction — was valid when first made, a genuine, verifiable distinction with a real incentive-based nexus. But a classification's validity is not frozen... [the source text breaks off here]. COMPLETION ON THE COURSE FRAMEWORK: ...at the date of enactment. The rational nexus between “newness” and the incentive object evaporates once the exempted buildings age into the regulated class's condition; perpetuating the distinction indefinitely, with no sunset, is a continuing failure of the nexus limb as applied today. The better view: the exemption was valid when made but is open to challenge as arbitrary in its continuing operation — the legislature must re-examine the cut-off.

Question

3 · The labour welfare fund. A law requires “establishments” — all factories, plus tramway and motor-bus businesses — to deposit unclaimed wages and bonuses in a welfare fund, but excludes businesses with fewer than fifty employees and government establishments other than factories. Is it valid to regulate only larger establishments and specific sectors, leaving out smaller trade businesses and most government bodies, on the reasoning that the legislature may tackle a widespread problem in phases?

Answer

VALID. The differentia is intelligible: large factories and public transport undertakings concentrate wage labour and unpaid dues; small trading businesses and non-factory offices present a smaller, more diffuse administrative problem. The nexus with the object — recovering unclaimed dues for workers' welfare where the problem is administratively concentrated — is rational, and the legislature may legitimately attack a widespread evil in phases, beginning where the concern is greatest (the pattern of the phased-approach reasoning taught with this problem).

Question

4 · The flat land tax. A State imposes a single flat rate per acre on “all lands,” so the owner of fertile, income-generating farmland pays the same as the owner of unproductive forest yielding barely any income — one owner earned only a small annual income from roughly 25,000 acres of forest yet faced a tax demand many times his earnings. The law also lets government exempt “any land or class of lands” at its own discretion, with no guidelines. Is a flat rate on wildly unequal land valid, and is the unguided discretionary exemption valid?

Answer

INVALID ON BOTH COUNTS. First, imposing identical burden on admittedly unequal subjects — fertile versus barren land — is the very “equal treatment of unequals” that Article 14 forbids (the positive concept of equal protection, 27 July lecture): a rational tax would classify by productivity or income. Second, the unguided power to exempt “any land” is Anwar Ali Sarkar's vice in reverse — absolute, unguided executive discretion with no criteria, which fails the intelligible differentia limb and breeds arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa).

Question

5 · The pension line. The government liberalises the pension formula but applies it only to employees retiring on or after a fixed date; employees retired even a day earlier, with identical service of the same kind, quality and length, remain on the old, less generous formula for life. All served the same employer — is a line drawn purely on the date of retirement valid when the object was simply better financial security in old age?

Answer

INVALID. Cut-off dates are not per se unconstitutional, but the differentia must have a rational nexus with the object. Here the object — old-age financial security for those who rendered comparable service — is indifferent to the day of retirement; the classification neither identifies a class needing different treatment nor serves economy or transition (no such justification appears). Same-service pensioners are similarly situated; the day's difference is arbitrary in effect — the pattern of the cut-off analysis in Ex-Services Association (taught 24–25 July), where a cut-off discriminating between similarly situated groups without reasonable nexus was condemned.

Question

6 · The air hostesses (three sub-questions). An airline has two cabin-crew cadres: male flight pursers and female air hostesses. Air hostesses must retire at 35, or earlier on marriage within the first four years of service, or immediately upon first pregnancy — whichever first; pursers serve until 58. Extension beyond these conditions lies purely in the Managing Director's unguided discretion. (a) Are two separate cadres with different rules valid, given different recruitment sources and historical service conditions? (b) Is termination upon first pregnancy valid, on the theory that pregnancy affects ability to do the job? (c) Is it valid to let one official decide, with no written standard, whose service is extended?

Answer

(a) VALID — separate cadres recruited from different sources with different historical conditions can constitute an intelligible differentia; that much is not per se objectionable. (b) INVALID — a rule terminating a woman upon first pregnancy draws the line on sex and pregnancy alone. The “ability to do the job” rationale is over-broad: pregnancy is a temporary condition, not a permanent incapacity, and the rule spares the employer any individualised inquiry while visiting the entire burden on women alone — the classification fails the nexus limb and is sex-based discrimination of the kind Articles 14–15 target (Air India v. Nergesh Meerza was the course's designated case for exactly this regulation). (c) INVALID — the Managing Director's unguided discretion to extend service is Anwar Ali Sarkar's absolute, standardless pick-and-choose: wherever there is discretion without criteria, there is room for arbitrariness.

Question

7 · The degree-and-diploma split. Degree-holder and diploma-holder Assistant Engineers had formed one integrated cadre — equal pay, equal promotion prospects. New rules give degree-holders a higher pay scale and reserve promotion to Executive Engineer for degree-holders alone; diploma-holders, however senior, are no longer eligible. Is re-splitting a merged cadre valid, on the reasoning that a degree involves deeper theoretical training better equipping a person for the senior post's technical and managerial responsibility?

Answer

VALID. The differentia — formal engineering degree versus diploma — is real, verifiable and non-fanciful; the nexus — the senior post's greater technical and managerial responsibility requiring deeper theoretical training — is rational. The prior integration of the cadres is a fact of history, not a constitutional bar: the State may re-classify when the qualification genuinely correlates with the demands of the post. (The answer would flip if the degree bore no rational relation to the post's functions — then the split would be arbitrary.)

Question

8 · The black-money bonds. To pull undisclosed wealth into productive investment, government issues special bonds buyable with black money, granting immunity from questions about its source, protection from tax proceedings and certain exemptions — while honest taxpayers who declared and paid tax on everything receive nothing comparable. Is giving immunities specifically to holders of undisclosed wealth, where the stated aim is productive investment of black money, valid — or does it reward tax evasion at the expense of the honest?

Answer

VALID — this is the Bearer Bonds problem solved in class (c.31 July) and read as R.K. Garg v. Union of India. (1) Presumption of constitutionality; the burden lies on the challenger. (2) Judicial deference to economic policy unless manifestly arbitrary. (3) Intelligible differentia: holders of undisclosed wealth are a clearly distinct class. (4) Rational nexus: allowing them to invest without declaring the source directly furthers the object — surfacing black money, funding development. The emotional claim of “rewarding dishonesty” does not supply a constitutional ground; the hardship of honest taxpayers is not a listed vice in the classification.

Question

9 · The SC/ST test exemption. Departmental tests must be passed for promotion to a higher clerical grade, but the government may temporarily exempt in-service SC/ST employees for a limited period. A batch of promotions goes largely to exempted employees by seniority, ahead of a general-category employee who passed the tests. Is the temporary exemption valid, where the object is adequate representation of historically disadvantaged communities?

Answer

VALID. The differentia is intelligible — Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are historically disadvantaged and under-represented communities, the very class the Constitution's scheme of compensatory discrimination addresses (Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are facets of equality, not exceptions — the 13 August lecture). The nexus — securing adequate representation in public service — is direct. That some promoted employees had not passed the test while a general candidate had is within the logic of substantive equality: the Court has upheld even the removal of minimum qualifying marks for reserved candidates (Kumari Nivedita Jain). The exemption is temporary and targeted, not a permanent lowering of standards.

Question

10 · The single-company law. After a special inquiry into one textile mill in financial and managerial trouble threatening the supply of an essential commodity (cloth), Parliament passes a law naming that company alone — removing its managing agents and directors, letting government appoint new ones, curtailing shareholders' voting rights. No other company, even similarly troubled, is touched. Can a law targeting a single named entity be a valid classification, given that a “class” normally means a group of more than one?

Answer

VALID — a single person or entity can constitute a class where its situation is unique: the special inquiry established this company's specific financial and managerial crisis threatening an essential commodity's supply and a vast workforce's livelihoods — characteristics not shared by “similarly troubled” companies in the abstract. Chiranjit Lal Chowdhury settles that a class of one is permissible if the differentia is intelligible and the nexus rational. The shareholder's “hostile discrimination” argument is the strongest counter, but it fails because the law responds to demonstrated, unique facts, not hostility toward the named entity.

Question

11 · The pick-and-choose special courts. After communal riots, a State law allows Special Courts with a faster procedure dropping safeguards like jury trial and committal, but does not specify which offences, areas or cases go to them — government may by notification pick any individual “case” or “offence,” with no guiding standard. Is free, case-by-case executive selection of who gets the harsher procedure valid?

Answer

INVALID — this is Anwar Ali Sarkar itself. Both limbs fail: no intelligible differentia (no criteria at all; the selection rests on executive whim — change the officer, change the cases), and no rational nexus (unguided discretion bears no connection to speedy trial). Persons accused of the same offence may face radically different procedures with no justifiable answer to “why me?”

Question

12 · The ordinance with built-in criteria. After integration of princely states, regions of the new State see organised armed robbery, dacoity, looting and murder; an ordinance itself names the disturbed regions and lists the serious violent offences (murder, dacoity, robbery and related) to be tried by a faster special procedure. A convict argues being tried differently from accused persons elsewhere is discriminatory. Does building the criteria into the law, rather than leaving unguided choice, make the classification valid?

Answer

VALID — this is Kathi Raning Rawat. The differentia is intelligible (named regions suffering an exceptional breakdown of law and order; named grave offences), and the nexus — a speedier, tougher procedure precisely where the ordinary system has broken down — is rational. Contrast Anwar Ali Sarkar: the guidance here is in the law itself, so no standardless discretion exists.

Question

13 · The custody-statement rule. Confessions to police are generally inadmissible, but a person in custody who gives information leading to a fact's discovery (say, a hidden weapon) may have the discovery-related portion of his statement proved — while a person not in custody making a full voluntary confession is governed by ordinary rules instead. Is treating custody statements differently valid?

Answer

VALID. The differentia is intelligible — persons in police custody face a materially higher risk of police pressure, inducement and fabrication, so their statements warrant a distinct, more restrictive admissibility rule. The nexus is rational: admitting only the discovery-related portion, verified by the actual discovery of the object, is a safeguard precisely calibrated to that risk — the corroboration of the fact guarantees reliability in a way a free-floating confession does not. Differential treatment keyed to a real difference in vulnerability satisfies both limbs.

Question

14 · The two tobaccos. A sales-tax law taxes one premium, largely export-oriented, cigarette-grade variety of tobacco while exempting the more common “country” variety used for chewing and bidi-making. Traders in the taxed variety argue there is no fair reason to single out their product while a competing product goes untaxed. Is taxing one commercial variety while exempting another variety of the same broad category valid?

Answer

VALID. The two varieties are genuinely different commodities — grown, cured, marketed and used differently; one is a distinct, higher-value, export-oriented product, the other locally consumed. The differentia is real and commercial, not fanciful; the nexus — taxing the higher-value commodity (and, implicitly, sparing the local consumption of the common variety) — is a rational revenue measure. A “same broad category” does not make sub-varieties a single class for all purposes.

Question

15 · The seventeen-month year. On a district's transfer into a newly formed State, a transitional provision fixes the “previous year” for agricultural income tax in that district as seventeen months (instead of twelve), with the rate computed on an adjusted average-annual-income formula; taxpayers elsewhere in the State use the standard year. The transferred district's taxpayers say the result is harsher and discriminatory. Is a temporary, one-time transitional computation valid?

Answer

VALID. Transitional provisions classify by a real and temporary necessity: reconciling two different accounting-year systems at the merger. The differentia — the transferred district — is intelligible and self-evident; the nexus — an adjusted computation period and averaging formula to bridge the systems — is directly rational. Genuine administrative difficulty at a one-time transition is a classic reasonable classification; it is neither permanent nor capricious.

Question

16 · The adultery exemption. An offence punishes a man for sexual relations with another man's wife without the husband's consent, but expressly exempts the wife — not even as abettor — however great her role. Is criminalising only men while completely exempting women valid, given that special treatment favourable to women is separately and expressly permitted by the Constitution?

Answer

VALID on the course's framework. The differentia is sex-based, but it operates favourably to women; the Constitution expressly contemplates special provisions for women (Article 15(3) — the “injection” against historically entrenched discrimination, taught 10–11 August). The legislature proceeded on the protective assumption that in the marital context the wife is the victim, not the perpetrator, and therefore withdrew her from criminal liability even as an abettor. A sex-based classification is not per se invalid; what Article 15(1) forbids is discrimination — hostile or prejudicial treatment — not protective differentiation.

Question

17 · The blanket bar on women in liquor premises. An excise law bans the employment of any woman — and any man under twenty-five — anywhere liquor is consumed by the public: bars, hotel restaurants, room service. The stated purpose is protecting women (and young men) from the environment's risks; trained hospitality professionals who are women are completely barred regardless of individual skill, experience or actual workplace safety. Is a blanket protective ban valid, or does it fail because narrower measures (workplace safety rules) could address the same concerns?

Answer

INVALID. Protective legislation for women is constitutionally contemplated, but the ban is over-inclusive and the nexus fails: the object — safety in the working environment — can be achieved by narrower, individualised means (safety regulations, conditions of service), so a total exclusion from an entire profession based purely on sex and age is disproportionate to the object. The classification assumes what it should prove — that every woman, whatever her training and whatever the actual conditions of a specific workplace, is endangered — and therefore treats the protected class as incapable of choice. The course's test: where a less restrictive measure serves the object equally, the blanket ban is arbitrary.

Question

18 · The fifteen-percent interview. A college admits students by written test plus interview, with more than fifteen percent of total marks allotted to the interview; each interview lasts two to three minutes and consists of formal questions about parentage and residence — nothing that tests merit. Some high-scoring written candidates are kept out while lower scorers enter on unexplained interview marks. Though every candidate passed through the same process, can the weightage be struck down as unfair and arbitrary in effect, even without a “classification” in the traditional sense?

Answer

INVALID. This is the E.P. Royappa extension: equality is violated not only by bad classifications but by arbitrary process. A component worth fifteen percent of the admission that, by its own design (two-to-three minutes, formal questions on parentage and residence), cannot assess merit, is irrational — the mechanism bears no relation to the object (selecting on merit). The identical application of an irrational process is still arbitrary; unexplained interview marks functioning as an unreviewable discretion fail non-arbitrariness even where every candidate was “treated alike.”

Question

19 · The EWS quota's exclusion. A constitutional amendment allows up to 10% reservation for “economically weaker sections” — but only for those who do not belong to SCs, STs or OBCs (who already have their own separate reservation). It is argued that since poverty exists in every community, excluding the poor of already-reserved communities from the new quota discriminates against the poorest of the poor. Is treating “economically weak general-category citizens” as a distinct class from “economically weak persons from already-reserved communities” valid?

Answer

VALID — the position of Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, as taught on 10 August. The class “economically weaker sections of citizens not already covered by reservation” is coherent: the excluded communities already possess separate, older reservation benefits rooted in social and educational backwardness, so the new, purely economic quota reaches precisely those whom the existing scheme leaves out. The classification identifies two genuinely different positions, not one class arbitrarily halved.

Question

20 · The 27% with creamy layer. A government order grants 27% reservation for socially and educationally “backward classes,” identified substantially using caste as an indicator — while excluding the more advanced “creamy layer” within those communities so the benefit reaches the genuinely disadvantaged. Critics say using caste at all, then sub-dividing the backward class, is irrational and that economic status alone should have been the test. Is caste as an indicator (not the sole test) plus creamy-layer exclusion valid?

Answer

VALID — the position of Indra Sawhney. (1) Caste may be a starting point for identifying social and educational backwardness — in Indian conditions caste is a very real component of social position — but it cannot be the sole criterion; the identification here uses caste as an indicator within a broader assessment. (2) Excluding the creamy layer keeps the benefit targeted at those genuinely, not merely nominally, disadvantaged — the advanced members of a backward class have already escaped the disadvantage the measure targets. Both limbs satisfied: intelligible differentia (genuinely backward versus advanced members) and rational nexus (advancement of the actually disadvantaged).

Question

21 · The juvenile's date. An accused was a minor on the date of the alleged offence but had crossed the juvenile age by the time of investigation or production before the court. One view fixes juvenile status by age on the date of production; the other by age on the date of the offence. Which is more consistent with treating similarly-placed young offenders equally?

Answer

The date of the offence. The protective juvenile-justice procedure attaches to the person's condition when the act was done — that is the morally and legally relevant moment, common to all young offenders in like circumstances. The date of production is an accident of procedure: it varies enormously with how quickly or slowly a case moves, so two offenders identically situated at the offence would receive different treatment according to docket speed alone. Equality among similarly-placed offenders therefore requires fixing status by age on the date of the offence — the certain, rational basis; the production-date rule creates an arbitrary, litigation-driven lottery.
sections.text: Question 1 · Prohibition with exemptions. A State bans liquor entirely in the interest of public health and temperance, but exempts soldiers and sailors consuming foreign liquor in military messes, canteens, warships and troopships, and foreign tourists possessing liquor under a special permit. Ordinary residents get no permit route. Is the exemption of defence personnel (separate service conditions, functional needs aboard ships) and foreign visitors (transient status, different customs) valid, even though allowing them to drink seems to work against the very purpose of temperance among the general population? Answer OFFICIAL SECTION B ANSWER: Defence personnel and vessels were already recognised as a distinct legal category under separate service and discipline laws, and foreigners were distinguished by their transient status and different customs — both real, non-fanciful differentia. The Supreme Court held that special treatment of a class already treated as distinct under other statutes has a rational nexus to practical governance — even though the High Court had earlier found no such nexus and struck the exemption down. (This is the pattern of State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara , taught on 30 July.) Question 2 · The rent-control cut-off. A rent law permanently frees all buildings constructed after a cut-off date from rent control, to encourage fresh construction. Decades later, the “new” buildings are over twenty-five years old, yet their landlords still enjoy total freedom, while equally old pre-cutoff buildings remain regulated forever. The classification made sense when passed — is it still valid to keep exempting them forever, with no time limit? Answer OFFICIAL SECTION B ANSWER (as far as the source preserves it): the classification — date of construction — was valid when first made, a genuine, verifiable distinction with a real incentive-based nexus. But a classification's validity is not frozen... [the source text breaks off here]. COMPLETION ON THE COURSE FRAMEWORK: ...at the date of enactment. The rational nexus between “newness” and the incentive object evaporates once the exempted buildings age into the regulated class's condition; perpetuating the distinction indefinitely, with no sunset, is a continuing failure of the nexus limb as applied today. The better view: the exemption was valid when made but is open to challenge as arbitrary in its continuing operation — the legislature must re-examine the cut-off. Question 3 · The labour welfare fund. A law requires “establishments” — all factories, plus tramway and motor-bus businesses — to deposit unclaimed wages and bonuses in a welfare fund, but excludes businesses with fewer than fifty employees and government establishments other than factories. Is it valid to regulate only larger establishments and specific sectors, leaving out smaller trade businesses and most government bodies, on the reasoning that the legislature may tackle a widespread problem in phases? Answer VALID. The differentia is intelligible: large factories and public transport undertakings concentrate wage labour and unpaid dues; small trading businesses and non-factory offices present a smaller, more diffuse administrative problem. The nexus with the object — recovering unclaimed dues for workers' welfare where the problem is administratively concentrated — is rational, and the legislature may legitimately attack a widespread evil in phases, beginning where the concern is greatest (the pattern of the phased-approach reasoning taught with this problem). Question 4 · The flat land tax. A State imposes a single flat rate per acre on “all lands,” so the owner of fertile, income-generating farmland pays the same as the owner of unproductive forest yielding barely any income — one owner earned only a small annual income from roughly 25,000 acres of forest yet faced a tax demand many times his earnings. The law also lets government exempt “any land or class of lands” at its own discretion, with no guidelines. Is a flat rate on wildly unequal land valid, and is the unguided discretionary exemption valid? Answer INVALID ON BOTH COUNTS. First, imposing identical burden on admittedly unequal subjects — fertile versus barren land — is the very “equal treatment of unequals” that Article 14 forbids (the positive concept of equal protection, 27 July lecture): a rational tax would classify by productivity or income. Second, the unguided power to exempt “any land” is Anwar Ali Sarkar's vice in reverse — absolute, unguided executive discretion with no criteria, which fails the intelligible differentia limb and breeds arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa ). Question 5 · The pension line. The government liberalises the pension formula but applies it only to employees retiring on or after a fixed date; employees retired even a day earlier, with identical service of the same kind, quality and length, remain on the old, less generous formula for life. All served the same employer — is a line drawn purely on the date of retirement valid when the object was simply better financial security in old age? Answer INVALID. Cut-off dates are not per se unconstitutional, but the differentia must have a rational nexus with the object. Here the object — old-age financial security for those who rendered comparable service — is indifferent to the day of retirement; the classification neither identifies a class needing different treatment nor serves economy or transition (no such justification appears). Same-service pensioners are similarly situated; the day's difference is arbitrary in effect — the pattern of the cut-off analysis in Ex-Services Association (taught 24–25 July), where a cut-off discriminating between similarly situated groups without reasonable nexus was condemned. Question 6 · The air hostesses (three sub-questions). An airline has two cabin-crew cadres: male flight pursers and female air hostesses. Air hostesses must retire at 35, or earlier on marriage within the first four years of service, or immediately upon first pregnancy — whichever first; pursers serve until 58. Extension beyond these conditions lies purely in the Managing Director's unguided discretion. (a) Are two separate cadres with different rules valid, given different recruitment sources and historical service conditions? (b) Is termination upon first pregnancy valid, on the theory that pregnancy affects ability to do the job? (c) Is it valid to let one official decide, with no written standard, whose service is extended? Answer (a) VALID — separate cadres recruited from different sources with different historical conditions can constitute an intelligible differentia; that much is not per se objectionable. (b) INVALID — a rule terminating a woman upon first pregnancy draws the line on sex and pregnancy alone. The “ability to do the job” rationale is over-broad: pregnancy is a temporary condition, not a permanent incapacity, and the rule spares the employer any individualised inquiry while visiting the entire burden on women alone — the classification fails the nexus limb and is sex-based discrimination of the kind Articles 14–15 target (Air India v. Nergesh Meerza was the course's designated case for exactly this regulation). (c) INVALID — the Managing Director's unguided discretion to extend service is Anwar Ali Sarkar's absolute, standardless pick-and-choose: wherever there is discretion without criteria, there is room for arbitrariness. Question 7 · The degree-and-diploma split. Degree-holder and diploma-holder Assistant Engineers had formed one integrated cadre — equal pay, equal promotion prospects. New rules give degree-holders a higher pay scale and reserve promotion to Executive Engineer for degree-holders alone; diploma-holders, however senior, are no longer eligible. Is re-splitting a merged cadre valid, on the reasoning that a degree involves deeper theoretical training better equipping a person for the senior post's technical and managerial responsibility? Answer VALID. The differentia — formal engineering degree versus diploma — is real, verifiable and non-fanciful; the nexus — the senior post's greater technical and managerial responsibility requiring deeper theoretical training — is rational. The prior integration of the cadres is a fact of history, not a constitutional bar: the State may re-classify when the qualification genuinely correlates with the demands of the post. (The answer would flip if the degree bore no rational relation to the post's functions — then the split would be arbitrary.) Question 8 · The black-money bonds. To pull undisclosed wealth into productive investment, government issues special bonds buyable with black money, granting immunity from questions about its source, protection from tax proceedings and certain exemptions — while honest taxpayers who declared and paid tax on everything receive nothing comparable. Is giving immunities specifically to holders of undisclosed wealth, where the stated aim is productive investment of black money, valid — or does it reward tax evasion at the expense of the honest? Answer VALID — this is the Bearer Bonds problem solved in class (c.31 July) and read as R.K. Garg v. Union of India. (1) Presumption of constitutionality; the burden lies on the challenger. (2) Judicial deference to economic policy unless manifestly arbitrary. (3) Intelligible differentia: holders of undisclosed wealth are a clearly distinct class. (4) Rational nexus: allowing them to invest without declaring the source directly furthers the object — surfacing black money, funding development. The emotional claim of “rewarding dishonesty” does not supply a constitutional ground; the hardship of honest taxpayers is not a listed vice in the classification. The lecture opens with the professor inquiring about the assignment: students confirm they have copied material up to the 93rd Constitutional Amendment and completed the objective section and Article 15. Professor'S Aside

When Prince reports that his result shows the classification as “valid,” I strongly disagree. If the result shows valid, it means either you have not given the proper command to the analytical tool, or you are being a slave to the Supreme Court without critical thinking, or you are simply not reading the material properly.

sections.title: The 93rd Amendment's Minority Exemption — the Nexus Critique
sections.html:
The professor's substantive critique (framed as his critique of the Congress party's approach, which he terms placing one community above everything — above the country, above any law): the objective of the RTE Act and the 93rd Amendment is that poor children receive good education in good schools. His rhetorical question is the crux of the nexus analysis: Where is it written that they shouldn't get an education in minority schools? What problem is there with minority schools? Properly analysed (he confirms he ran the exercise in another class that day and knew the outcome independently), the classification fails: poor children are one category needing assistance; private schools are a category separate from government schools; children fundamentally need to study. The minority-institution exclusion introduces an extraneous classification with no logical connection to the stated objective — where is the classification for minority coming in? The point is whether it's a school or not a school.

The Supreme Court in Ashok Kumar Thakur held minority institutions exempt because they are “specially protected by Article 30.” The professor challenges this: are the rest of the people protected by the Constitution of Pakistan? The other schools operate under the Indian Constitution — Article 19(1)(g), the freedom of trade and business, protects all citizens, including those running non-minority private schools. And he articulates the hierarchy principle: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are superior to other Articles in the constitutional scheme. Article 30's protection cannot be elevated above Article 19. He characterises the failure to recognise this as “foolishness” and Ashok Kumar Thakur as “among all the terrible decisions,” attributing the exemption to Congress's vote-bank politics. The practical reality check: who will educate a child in a Muslim madrasa? Would the students' own parents educate them there? Muslims have very few schools besides Jamia Millia Islamia and Aligarh Muslim University — where even now, he asserts, “Islamisation” is occurring.

sections.title: The Constitutional Hierarchy — and the Loudspeaker Example
sections.html: Students are directed to examine Article 25: it opens “Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part” — the critical phrase “other provisions of this Part” makes Article 25 subject to the rest of Part III, including Articles 14, 19 and 21. The contemporary illustration: the Supreme Court's ruling on loudspeakers in mosques — used at very high volumes creating noise disturbance, the practice was restricted because Article 21 (the right to life, read to include peaceful living without noise pollution) is superior to Article 25. If anyone's Article 21 rights are disturbed, Article 25 must yield. By the same reasoning, if Article 30 protection for minority institutions conflicts with Article 19(1)(g) rights or the equality framework, Article 30 must yield. Rahul Gandhi, the professor adds, now alleges judges engage in sycophancy for Modi as well — a pattern of judicial deference to political power across administrations.

sections.title: State of Rajasthan v. Thakur Pratap Singh — Religion-Based Tax
sections.html:
Case

State of Rajasthan v. Thakur Pratap Singh (or Sampratap Singh)

Taught as the Article 15 authority on religious discrimination

Facts
In a village plagued by dacoity, villagers requested the Congress Chief Minister to post additional police. He replied the government was “very poor” — the villagers would have to contribute for the extra personnel. The wealthy villagers agreed. But back in Jaipur, after consulting Rahul Gandhi, instructions came: do not collect money from Muslims. An Act followed, requiring villagers to pay the additional police tax — with an express exemption for Muslims.
Held
Such discrimination on the basis of religion violates Article 15(1), which prohibits discrimination solely on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
Principle
The professor's ongoing bewilderment: when dacoity affects the entire village and everyone should contribute to the solution, why should Muslims alone be exempted? “Even today I do not understand the rationale.” The case is taught as part of Article 15: discrimination in the name of religion is constitutionally prohibited.

sections.title: Sukanya Samriddhi v. Union of India — Caste Discrimination in Prisons
sections.html:
Case

Sukanya Samriddhi v. Union of India (2023/24)

CJI Dhananjaya Chandrachud · argued by Justice Muralidhar (former Chief Justice, Orissa High Court, engaged by the petitioner)

Facts
Sukanya — “a very dynamic journalist” — researched and revealed that caste-based discrimination persisted in Indian prisons decades after independence: work assignments were made by caste, Dalit prisoners assigned to dig drains and clean bathrooms, Brahmin prisoners assigned to cook. This despite Congress having amended the Constitution to declare India “Socialist Secular.” Disturbed, she filed a PIL.
Held
Counsel argued that Article 15 explicitly prohibits caste discrimination, yet the prison system was recording prisoners' castes and assigning work on that basis. CJI Chandrachud made a landmark observation: there is no need to record caste anywhere, as recording facilitates discrimination. The Court directed that the caste column and references to caste in the registers of undertrial and convict prisoners “shall be deleted.”
Principle
The judgment connects to Ambedkar's vision of a casteless society. The professor contrasts Rahul Gandhi's persistent four-year demand for a caste census as moving in the opposite direction, notes the BJP initially opposed it on the principled ground of a casteless society (consistent with both Ambedkar and the judgment) before political pressures forced a relent, and asks the class how many agree with the judgment — calling it “a great judgment.” The underlying logic: if caste is not recorded, discrimination becomes harder; recording it facilitates discrimination.
