sections.title: The Caste Census Debate
sections.html:
The professor's critique of the caste census, in layers. Rahul Gandhi's formula: “Jitni jiski sankhya, uski utni hissedari” — as is the population, so is the share. The implied strategy: Dalits plus OBCs — together roughly ninety percent of the population (some add Muslims) — promised seventy to eighty percent reservation would secure their votes. The professor's challenge: is the government distributing stolen goods that must be divided proportionally among thieves? The constitutional anchors: the primary focus of the Constitution is equality; Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination of any kind; Article 16(4) provides reservation only where adequate representation is lacking, read with Article 335's requirement of efficiency of administration — together yielding the Supreme Court's principle that reservation cannot exceed fifty percent.

When a student raises the EWS reservation's breach of the fifty percent cap (upheld as part of the basic structure), the professor clarifies: EWS is fundamentally different — not caste-based, and specifically unavailable to those already receiving reservation benefits; it brings in people from other castes previously excluded rather than increasing benefits for the same castes. The dangers of the census: groups learning their exact percentages would demand proportional power — Dalits seeking the Prime Ministership where concentrated, Yadavas their strongholds — precisely the dynamic that led to Partition (Jinnah's argument that Muslims, a minority in a Hindu-majority country, would never genuinely come to power). Proportional reservation demands would bring violent protests, police firing — he predicts at least fifty to a hundred deaths. Vote bank politics is “the biggest evil of democracy”: parties manipulating caste and religious identities, making groups fight while politicians secure votes. Even if seventy to eighty percent of the population belongs to certain castes, giving seventy to eighty percent reservation effectively ends the constitutional commitment to equality; since proportional reservation cannot constitutionally be given, there is no positive gain from determining exact percentages. He acknowledges the current government has also compromised on this principle for votes — but the ideal remains a casteless society.

sections.title: The True Purpose of Reservation — Ending the Ruler-Ruled Divide
sections.html:
The professor's philosophical account opens with Manthara's couplet from the Ramayana, in Awadhi: “Koi hoi Ram hame ka hani, cheri chhod na hoi bai rani” — whoever becomes king, I lose nothing; I remain a servant. Under the old order, whoever ruled, the servants remained servants: the line between ruling class and ruled class was absolutely fixed. In monarchical systems no servant, however capable, could become king. Reservation was designed to break this permanent divide. By opening government positions to Dalits and backward classes, it aimed to erase the psychology of “I am the ruler and these are the ruled.” Based on competence, anyone — Dalit or general caste — can become a Collector through the IAS examination, or a representative through votes.

Initially Dalits could not pass the IAS examination, necessitating modest reservation to provide the opportunity. The goal was to bridge the gulf so Dalits would not feel disconnected — not “what do we have to do with this country; we are peons anyway” — but rather: “This country is ours too, and we are rulers of this country, and we are protectors of this country, and we have to do good for this country.” Reservation was to transform the psychology of the ruled class, lifting them from inferiority complex into patriotism and ownership — to make the ruled class part of the ruler class. Economic empowerment was never the primary purpose. The professor cites his own son, who never prepared an hour for a government job: a Chief Secretary earns perhaps Rs. 1.5–2 lakh monthly with privileges while in office, but afterward “they'll die of hunger” — one could earn more selling samosas. The craze for government jobs exists because of corruption; the day corruption ends, no child will aspire to government employment. His friend and NLU Jodhpur classmate, now a Group General Counsel, earns Rs. 4 crore annually — far more than any government position — talented people increasingly choose the private sector.

sections.title: The Creamy Layer — Tina Dabi and Davinder Singh
sections.html: Tina Dabi, IAS: her father is a General Manager in BSNL, her mother herself an IAS officer. With both parents high-ranking government officers for twenty-five years, what legitimate need remained for reservation benefits? If her children also avail reservation, the cycle perpetuates without addressing genuine disadvantage. The professor references Dr. Mahatme (nominated Rajya Sabha member, eye surgeon from Nagpur) who discussed this with him two or three times and compiled a list demonstrating the problem. The judiciary has now acted through State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, permitting sub-classification within SC/ST categories — but Justice Gavai, himself a Dalit, faced significant criticism and abuse for supporting it, and the Modi government, seeking votes, filed an affidavit declining to implement it: vote bank politics again.

sections.title: The Delhi Judicial Service Association Case (1991) — the Judge and the Police
sections.html:
Case

Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat (1991)

Facts
A Gujarat judge, very strict with police officers over investigation quality (“Haven't done investigation, what are you doing?”), generated resentment in an understaffed, overworked force — running between crime scenes (a rape investigation interrupted by a truck-car collision with eight dead). The officers devised a plan: invited to the police station for dinner and inspection, the judge was pressed to drink — “I don't take it... but since you are pressing, I'll take it” — until inebriated. Then they beat him severely, shaved his head, placed him on a donkey, and paraded him: “Look, he's a judge, drinks alcohol and is unconscious — what judgment must he be giving!” The incident terrorised the entire judiciary; even IPS officers possibly involved were protected by fear — no one filed complaints.
Held
News reached Delhi; the judicial establishment was outraged. The Supreme Court held that even if the judge had consumed alcohol, the appropriate response was to put him in a car, take him home, and let him sleep — alcohol's effects dissipate naturally. The IPS officer involved was suspended; the Court issued guidelines on when and how a Magistrate may be arrested, providing procedural protections for judicial officers.
Principle
The life lesson drawn in class: one should not misbehave excessively with anyone. The professor admits his own mistakes — losing his temper, scolding people, having recently thrown someone out of his office for leaving mid-studies to watch a movie and sit in a bar (the theatre had a bar inside; second-year students bought alcohol elsewhere after the honest bar owner, checking identification, refused to serve minors under Maharashtra's age of twenty-one).

sections.title: The Arrest Warrant Against the President
sections.html:
Professor'S Aside

Two men were drinking at 8 PM — a good time — debating judicial corruption. One insisted that with contacts — even just a judge's clerk — one could get anyone jailed; the other, honest like me, disagreed. A bet: Rs. 500 to get an arrest warrant against anyone named. The second man gave Rs. 5,000 and named the President of India, the Chief Justice of India, and the Governor of Gujarat. A “3rd class” magistrate actually issued the warrants. The winner had them published in a first-class newspaper: “THE HIGHEST LEVEL OF CORRUPTION IN JUDICIARY! Arrest warrant against the President of India!” — this in Ahmedabad; the judge was presumably suspended. The constitutional impossibility: arrest warrants cannot be issued against the President and Governor, who enjoy immunity under Article 361. Problems in the country have existed throughout history and continue to; none of it is unique to any political era.

sections.title: Political Dynamics — the Evolution of the BJP's Approach
sections.html:
The BJP initially positioned itself as different — leaders like Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Murli Manohar Joshi maintained that while others might engage in dishonesty, they would not. Losing power changed the approach: Vajpayee's government fell by a single vote — cast by the Chief Minister of Orissa, who was not even supposed to vote in Parliament. A complete absence of morality, with enormous cost: an unstable government under a Prime Minister without real authority, then re-elections. The lesson absorbed: “diamond cuts diamond” — until one is willing to be somewhat dishonest, one cannot come to power. The professor expresses nostalgia for the earlier generation — Sushma Swaraj, Arun Jaitley, Pramod Mahajan, “top-class leaders” who could not secure power because they missed out on a little dishonesty, losing by a single improperly obtained vote.

Amit Shah's tit-for-tat response to political attacks and released videos: “You got me beaten up for 10 hours, now I'll make it 50 hours for you. My video got released, now his will be released — get him beaten up in front of TV people!” The professor showed the class a video of P. Chidambaram subjected to such treatment, criticising the cycle — a female student rightly observed that retaliation is wrong: removing corrupt leaders is appropriate, but adopting their methods undermines the moral justification. The same with scandal-whataboutery: “In our time paper leaked” — “So BJP's spokesperson says, ‘In your time it leaked 10 times!'” The appropriate response should be: “It leaked 10 times in your time — that's why we removed you. Now do something different.” The failure to break this cycle is a significant problem in Indian politics.

sections.title: Article 15 — The Structure and the Five Grounds
sections.html:
In the Draft Constitution, Article 15 was numbered Article 9: “The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on ground only of religion, race, caste, sex, or any of them. In particular, no citizen shall on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or any of them be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition...” The historical context ties to Article 14's treatment of disabilities — Nangeli, denied upper garments; communities denied water and education — the disabilities Articles 14, 15, 16 and 17 were designed to eliminate. Article 15 now contains six clauses: 1, 2 and 3 from the original Constitution; 4 (First Amendment, 1951); 5 (93rd Amendment, 2005); 6 (103rd Amendment — 10% EWS).

Article 15's six clauses — three original, three added by amendment

The tablet-versus-injection analogy

Article 14 is a tablet — general medicine working slowly, its application requiring interpretation (is the classification reasonable? does it pass the nexus test?), with the risk that courts, following flawed reasoning like Plessy v. Ferguson, reach wrong conclusions under the guise of formal equality. Articles 15, 16, 17 and 18 are injections — immediate, specific prohibitions of the particular discriminations that have historically plagued Indian society. Dr. Ambedkar, understanding how deeply entrenched these practices were, did not want their elimination to depend on the chances of judicial interpretation: he wanted the existing problems eradicated instantly, hence the specific provisions despite the general guarantee.

GroundNotes from the lecture
ReligionPersecution pervades history — European Catholic–Protestant conflicts above all. Laws cannot be made on religion alone; the professor questions how the Haj subsidy (8–10 years ago, benefiting only Muslims going on Haj) was constitutionally justified — possibly as “poor Muslims” (religion plus another factor)
RaceEthnic origin and physical features — Nepalis, Afghans, Chinese, Koreans. India's millennia of migration: Jews arrived in the 6th century BCE, before Christianity or Islam existed. Contemporary discrimination against people from the Northeast (“Seven Sisters”) in Bangalore, Noida and elsewhere — based on physical features, i.e. race
CasteThe word “caste” is Portuguese, not Indian. Origins traced to occupational divisions — iron-smiths, gold-smiths — skills transmitted hereditarily in the absence of institutions like IITs. In the Mahabharata, characters carry no caste surnames: Shri Krishna is not “Shri Krishna Yadav,” Arjun not “Arjun Singh,” Duryodhan not “Duryodhan Singh.” Rigid caste surnames developed later. The system may have begun on a convenience basis — occupational groups developing their own customs, like the protected Andaman tribes (the film Tejas depicts a pilot crashing in such an area). Yet caste discrimination remains a severe problem — murders still occur on its basis
SexKanishk answers the distinction: sex is biological; gender is a social construct and identity. Gender stereotypes examined: NLU graduates of five years, same mess food, same education, both working at Amar Chand Mangaldas till midnight — yet after marriage the kitchen belongs exclusively to the wife. The professor calls the modern double burden — full-time job plus all household management — “harassment,” applauds the reversal (the wife calling from the stadium to have her husband make tea), discusses housewives' isolation and depression in nuclear families, and recommends women maintain professional engagement even at modest financial return, for connection and purpose
Place of birthThe British practice of declaring communities “Criminal Tribes” — in Saurashtra, people born into certain communities designated criminals by birth, under special surveillance. Today: suspicion attaching even to innocents born in certain countries or regions (Syria)

The five prohibited grounds of Article 15(1)

Origins traced to occupational divisions — iron-smiths, gold-smiths — skills transmitted hereditarily in the absence of institutions like IITs. In the Mahabharata, characters carry no caste surnames: Shri Krishna is not “Shri Krishna Yadav,” Arjun not “Arjun Singh,” Duryodhan not “Duryodhan Singh.” Rigid caste surnames developed later. The system may have begun on a convenience basis — occupational groups developing their own customs, like the protected Andaman tribes (the film Tejas depicts a pilot crashing in such an area). Yet caste discrimination remains a severe problem — murders still occur on its basis Sex Kanishk answers the distinction: sex is biological; gender is a social construct and identity. Gender stereotypes examined: NLU graduates of five years, same mess food, same education, both working at Amar Chand Mangaldas till midnight — yet after marriage the kitchen belongs exclusively to the wife. The professor calls the modern double burden — full-time job plus all household management — “harassment,” applauds the reversal (the wife calling from the stadium to have her husband make tea), discusses housewives' isolation and depression in nuclear families, and recommends women maintain professional engagement even at modest financial return, for connection and purpose Place of birth The British practice of declaring communities “Criminal Tribes” — in Saurashtra, people born into certain communities designated criminals by birth, under special surveillance. Today: suspicion attaching even to innocents born in certain countries or regions (Syria) The five prohibited grounds of Article 15(1)

sections.title: The Added Clauses — 15(4), 15(5), 15(6)
sections.html:
15(4): added by the First Amendment after Champakam Dorairajan struck down the Communal G.O.'s caste-based educational reservations under 15(1) — empowering special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs. The professor stresses the beneficiaries are identified as “socially and educationally backward” — the word “economically” is conspicuously absent, a distinction later crucial in Indra Sawhney and the EWS debate.

15(5): added by the 93rd Amendment (2005, Congress-led UPA) — special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs regarding admission to educational institutions, including private unaided ones, but excluding minority institutions under Article 30(1). The professor's reiterated critique: the amendment's object is poor children in good schools; minority institutions — Christian convent schools like St. Stephen's, St. Mary's, St. Joseph's — are among the country's best, so exempting them undermines the objective. Muslim minority institutions of comparable quality are very few (Jamia — where his son studied English Honours — and AMU, both facing “Islamisation”):

the exemption's practical effect protects numerous Christian institutions while offering Muslims a symbolic gesture with no real educational purpose. He is not speaking against any community — he is critiquing a policy that fails the constitutional nexus test.

sections.title: 15(6), the 103rd Amendment and Janhit Abhiyan
sections.html:
Article 15(6) — 10% EWS reservation — was brought by the Modi government in January 2019, just before the April elections; the timing suggests electoral motivation. The parallel: the Congress government under P.V. Narasimha Rao had also tried 10% reservation for the economically poor — struck down in Indra Sawhney, because Articles 15(4) and 16(4) envision reservation for the “socially and educationally” backward; the conjunction is crucial, and economic backwardness alone was not a valid basis. The practical difficulty with economic criteria: false certificates are easy to obtain — two students (Shreya Pandey from Bhopal and Ayesha, two years senior) from families owning multiple factories held “below poverty line” certificates and drew scholarships; confronted, Shreya claimed she had not obtained the certificate herself. Then the satirical essay: a student describing her father's “poverty” — so poor he could afford only one driver for his BMW; when the driver took leave, the father had to drive himself in Delhi traffic, unable to read the newspaper, missing tenders worth crores. Given the difficulty of reliably determining economic status, Ambedkar focused on social and educational backwardness — more identifiable, less fraud-prone. When the 103rd Amendment wrote EWS into Articles 15(6) and 16(6) explicitly, it overcame the Indra Sawhney objection — the Court had said economic reservation was unconstitutional because the Constitution did not provide for it; the government responded by amending the Constitution to provide for it.

Case

Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022/23)

Validity of the 103rd Amendment

Facts
The 10% EWS reservation under Articles 15(6) and 16(6) challenged as violating the equality code and the fifty percent ceiling.
Held
Upheld. Assigned reading: determine the bench strength, the issues framed, the decision on each, any dissents, the ratio decidendi and supporting reasoning — a one-page written summary is required.
Principle
EWS reservation differs in character: not caste-based, and unavailable to those already receiving reservation benefits.

sections.html:
Homework

Reading for the three-day break (Friday night through Sunday night): (1) Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India — bench composition, issues, decisions, dissents, ratio; one-page summary. Union of India — Justice Jeevan Reddy's judgment, all issues (8–9 distinct issues, studied issue-wise, not just the final ratio). (4) Bonus: State of Madras v. sections.title: Article 15 — The Clauses
sections.html:
ClauseContent
15(1)State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
15(2)No discrimination in access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment; wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, places of public resort — society cannot discriminate against potential buyers or tenants by religion, caste or sex
15(3)Special provisions for women and children — formal equality may not achieve substantive equality; protective discrimination addresses historical disadvantage

sections.title: Article 16 — Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment
sections.html:
ClauseContent
16(1)“There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State.”
16(2)No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible or discriminated against in respect of any employment or office under the State
16(3)Parliament (alone) may prescribe residence requirements for employment in a State or UT — reinforced by Article 35's exclusive parliamentary power, ensuring uniformity and preventing parochialism
16(4)Reservation of appointments or posts for any backward class of citizens not adequately represented in the State's services
16(4A)77th Amendment (1995) — reservation in promotion for SCs and STs
16(4B)81st Amendment (2000) — carry-forward of unfilled reserved vacancies
16(5)Religious or denominational institutions may require their office-holders to profess the concerned religion
16(6)103rd Amendment — up to 10% EWS reservation in employment, in addition to existing reservations

The eight clauses of Article 16

The distinctive grounds: descent (preventing hereditary appointments — the feudal practice of reserving positions for particular families) and residence (reflecting federal balance — citizens' mobility rights against States' local interests, with Article 16(3) as the sole exception, exercisable only by Parliament).

sections.title: Dr. Ambedkar's Vision
sections.html:
The ultimate aim is to have equality. Reservations are a means to achieve that equality, not an end in themselves.

— Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly debates on Article 16

Four points from the debates: (1) equality as the ultimate goal — reservations a temporary measure toward a society where they are unnecessary; (2) backwardness as a recognizable, measurable condition requiring state intervention; (3) balancing competing interests while the overall objective survives; (4) reservations as transitional — a mechanism to lift disadvantaged communities to a level where they compete on equal terms.

sections.title: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951
sections.html:
A watershed enacted in response to Supreme Court decisions striking down progressive measures. The primary trigger: Champakam Dorairajan — the Communal G.O., first introduced in 1926-27, allocating educational seats communally (illustratively: Brahmins 3, Harijans 2, Muslims 1, other communities variously), struck down under Article 15(1). The Court's reasoning: the State may make special provisions for backward classes, but they must rest on backwardness, not merely religion or caste — the Communal G.O. did not adequately distinguish the two. The amendment added Article 15(4) to overturn this effect.

Three speeches from the Provisional Parliament: Nehru argued passionately that the Constitution must not become an obstacle to social reform; Ambedkar defended the amendment as necessary to the constitutional goal of equality — the Court's interpretation had made upliftment measures impossible; Syama Prasad Mookerjee raised serious objections: the Article 19(2) speech restrictions were being broadened excessively, threatening the democratic fabric; property rights were being eroded; judicial review's scope might shrink, undermining checks and balances. Despite the objections, the amendment passed.

sections.title: Landmark Cases
sections.html:
Case

E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu

Under Articles 14 and 16

Facts
The Chief Secretary's removal and appointment as OSD.
Held
Article 14 (and through it, Article 16) strikes at arbitrariness: “Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be ‘cribbed, cabined and confined’ within the traditional limits of classification.” Administrative discretion is necessary for governance but must rest on relevant considerations, not whims.
Principle
The high evidentiary burden of proving arbitrariness — “easy to claim, hardest to prove.”
Case

Zoroastrian Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar Cooperative Societies (2005)

Facts
A cooperative housing society restricted membership to Zoroastrians (Parsis) only.
Held
Upheld: housing societies are not “places of public resort” under Article 15(2); a society may restrict membership by religion or community.
Principle
The professor's concern: “I feel in the long run this won't be right, because we want a plural society. If everyone makes pockets — Muslims here, Hindus here, Yadavs here, Dalits here — our unity will be destroyed.” The reasoning rests on a literal reading of 15(2); the broader constitutional vision of a secular, egalitarian society might require a more expansive interpretation.
Case

State of Rajasthan v. Pratap Singh

Facts
Additional tax and police force imposed on a particular area, allegedly discriminating against a community.
Held
The word “only” in Article 15(1): discrimination based solely on enumerated grounds is prohibited — if the State shows additional, rational reasons for its action, it stands.
Principle
“Only” is the hinge of Article 15(1).
Case

Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration

Facts
Routine hand-cuffing of undertrial prisoners challenged.
Held
Hand-cuffing is degrading treatment, violating dignity; permissible only exceptionally where genuine risk of escape or violence exists, justified case by case.
Principle
Referenced when the professor invoked it to argue for removing hand-cuffs from a young boy who had eloped with a girl.

sections.title: The Law-Society Interface
sections.html:
Does law change society, or society change law? Both. Law changing society: Article 17 abolished untouchability — attitudes have not wholly changed, but the legal prohibition created the framework for challenge and gradually shifted norms; the Domestic Violence Act 2005 and the Criminal Law Amendment 2013 changed attitudes toward violence against women. Society changing law: the recognition of live-in relationships reflects evolved attitudes; Navtej Singh Johar's decriminalisation of Section 377 reflects the Court recognising changed society.

The professor's ambivalence on Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): the U.S. Supreme Court held that “legislation is powerless to eradicate racial instincts, or abolish distinctions based upon physical differences” — a philosophy of law's limited power to change deep-seated attitudes, with which he expresses some sympathy (social change takes time). Yet Plessy was reversed in Brown v. Board of Education (1954) — separate but equal is inherently unequal — showing that while law may not instantly change society, it can set a normative framework that eventually transforms it.

Two stories of social change through innovation

  • Babu Jagjivan Ram's railway water booths: as Railway Minister, he appointed Dalit women at station water booths — travellers needing water had to drink from their hands or go without. The forced interaction broke down caste prejudice over time.
  • The Punjabrao Deshmukh experiment: at a function, Dalit women dressed elegantly cooked and served; guests did not realise their caste until informed after the meal. Initial discomfort gave way to the realisation that the food was no different and the women no lesser. “It takes hard work to change society. Saying ‘Accept it' doesn't work.”
Professor'S Aside

A personal story: I spent years mentally preparing myself to accept the possibility of my son marrying a Kashmiri Muslim girl. It is difficult; the prejudices are deeply ingrained. I consulted a sociology teacher, Deepmala, who said: “This we have to change slowly. Stigma remains, but slowly...” Social change — including acceptance of diverse communities and relationships — is a gradual process.

sections.title: Procedural Fairness — Hostel Allocation and the Amravati Analogy
sections.html:
The hostel allocation anecdote: four beds; four sections (BA, Justicing, BBA and one other); one bed per section by chit-picking, decided in consultation with students; six medical-ground applications (epilepsy, PCOD and other genuine conditions) against four beds. Why the decision was not arbitrary: (1) a reasonable basis — equal sectional access; (2) precedent — the same process was used in December, and objections then could have produced discussion and better options; (3) consultation, not unilateral action; (4) no partiality — “what will we get by doing partiality?”; (5) openness to better alternatives.

The Amravati analogy for discretion versus arbitrariness: travelling to Amravati, three routes — the super-fast Gadkari highway at Rs. 3,000 toll; a partially developed highway at Rs. 1,500, slightly harder; a toll-free route, longer and slower. The driver (administrator) may choose any, with reasons: the fast highway — “we arrive half an hour early; Rs. 3,000 is worth it”; the free route — “we save Rs. 3,000; the extra time does not matter for a wedding.” Arbitrariness occurs only when there is no reason at all — “I am saying, that's why.” When a relevant reason is given, the decision is not arbitrary, even if another option was better. On the medical applications: “I am having full sympathy with my students. But my limitations are there” — the tension between individual rights and resource constraints in administrative decision-making.

sections.title: Critical Analysis — and the Homework
sections.html:
For the current frameworkAgainst
Historical justice — 15(4) and 16(4) address historical injustice and uplift disadvantaged communitiesReverse discrimination against non-reserved categories
Substantive equality — formal equality is insufficient without addressing structural disadvantageInefficiency — merit and efficiency in services and education compromised
Constitutional balancing — individual rights against collective welfare, equality against diversityPolitical manipulation for electoral ends rather than genuine upliftment

Articles 15–16: the balanced assessment

Homework

Homework: (1) Constituent Assembly Debates on Article 16 — Ambedkar's statements on equality as the primary and ultimate aim; prepare a presentation of the key arguments. (2) The First Amendment speeches of Nehru, Ambedkar and Mookerjee — focus on Mookerjee's critique of the Article 19(2) restrictions and Article 15(4). (3) Read and analyse: Zoroastrian Housing (is a housing society a “place of public resort”? does property include the right to associate with co-religionists? implications for pluralism?); Rajasthan v. Pratap Singh (the meaning of “only”; when additional burden constitutes discrimination); Champakam Dorairajan (why the G.O. fell; the political response); E.P. Royappa (arbitrariness under 14 and 16; the evidentiary burden); Prem Shankar Shukla (routine hand-cuffing). (4) Read at least 10 cases on arbitrariness: E.P. Royappa; Maneka Gandhi; Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib; DTC v. DTC Mazdoor Congress; N. Nagendra Rao v. State of A.P.; Indian Railway Construction Co. v. Ajay Kumar; Central Inland Water Transport v. Brojo Nath Ganguly; Olga Tellis; K.S. Puttaswamy (both citations). (5) Comparative questions: Article 15 vs 16 (scope; why “residence” and “descent” appear only in 16(2)); Article 16(3) with Article 35. (6) Prepare for the coming classes on 15(4), 15(5), 15(6), 16(4), 16(5), 16(6) — key case: Janhit Abhiyan.

Puttaswamy (both citations). (5) Comparative questions: Article 15 vs 16 (scope; why “residence” and “descent” appear only in 16(2)); Article 16(3) with Article 35. sections.title: Overview
sections.html: The day reconstructs the Constituent Assembly's debate of 30 November 1948 on Draft Article 10 (equality of opportunity in public employment — now Article 16), presided over by the Vice-President (Dr. H.C. Mookherjee). The core issue: guaranteeing equality of opportunity while addressing the historical exclusion of certain communities from government service.

sections.title: Preliminary — the Death Penalty Amendment (Draft Article 11-B)
sections.html:
• Shri Amiyo Kumar Ghosh (Bihar) opposed constitutionalising abolition of capital punishment: the State must retain grave penalties for crisis; fettering it “for all time” is unwise — changes should come through the IPC, amendable as circumstances change. He supported the principle but rejected the constitutional form.
  • Shri K. Hanumanthaiya (Mysore) opposed from the State's perspective: citing Shaw's play about Joan of Arc — who preferred death to a “dead life” in prison — convicts may prefer death; society rests not only on reformation but on the “fear instinct”; without the death penalty deterrence is lost; early release after seven or eight years would “encourage the method of revenge.” His reference to the Godse case was interrupted and ruled out of order by the Chair.
  • Dr. Ambedkar: “I do not accept the amendment.” The amendment was negatived.

sections.title: The Backward Classes Debate
sections.html:
Ambedkar identified three conflicting viewpoints to reconcile: (1) equality of opportunity for all — every qualified person free to apply and be tested; (2) no reservations of any kind — all qualified citizens on the same footing; (3) guaranteed entry for communities historically outside the administration. The Drafting Committee's formula: sub-clause (1) embodies the generic principle; sub-clause (3) satisfies the third view, qualified by the word “backward.”

Supporters of reservationTheir positions
Ari Bahadur Gurung (W. Bengal)Gurkhas domiciled in India owe allegiance to India, not Nepal; fought in Kashmir and Hyderabad; deserve equal civil-service opportunity
R.M. Nalavade (Bombay)Supported for the depressed classes; “backward classes” too vague — might exclude Scheduled Castes; even provincial reservations were not producing adequate representation
Dr. Dharam Prakash (U.P.)Substitute “Scheduled Castes” for “backward”; administration still communally biased; reservation only for the “real depressed classes” until they “reach the same level”
Chandrika Ram (Bihar)Cited the 1921 and 1931 censuses; three sections of society — highest (caste Hindus), middle (backward classes), lowest (SCs/Harijans); backward classes denied political rights deserve legislature reservation too; criticised the Socialists for opposing
P. Kakkan (Madras)For “poor Harijan candidates”: higher officers select “only their own people”; special steps for police and military, citing Harijan bravery in Kashmir
V.I. Muniswami Pillay (Madras)Confused by “backward”; quoted Sardar Patel — “Not only justice must be done to the Harijans, but their case must be treated with generosity”; “not the object of any leaders of the Harijan community to perpetuate the communal bogey”
T. Channiah (Mysore)South Indian understanding: socially and educationally backward; Mysore's “A Class” (open) and “B Class” (reserved) vacancies; opposed Kunzru's ten-year limit — reservation should run “150 years,” the period opportunities were denied
Supporters of reservationTheir positions
H.J. Khandekar (C.P. & Berar)Wanted Scheduled Castes explicit: candidates “ordinarily ignored” despite qualifications; even 12.5% (higher) and 16.5% (lower) service reservations yielded under 1% recruitment; sought Public Service Commission representation and relaxed qualifications
Sardar Hukam Singh (East Punjab)Conflict between Article 10 and Article 296: open competition takes “the topmost men,” but minority claims must also be considered — does Article 10 override 296?
Mohamed Ismail Sahib (Madras)In Madras “backward” had technical meaning — 150+ Hindu communities; would minority communities (Muslims, Christians, SCs) also backward and under-represented be included? Opposed Kunzru's limit — “the measure should not be period of time” but whether the community has advanced; countered the communalism charge: “Communalism comes when people are denied rights... reservation creates contentment and harmony”

The case for reservation, member by member

CriticsTheir positions
Damodar Swarup Seth (U.P.)Delete clause (3): reservation is “the very negation of efficiency and good Government”; “backward” not easy to define; would “give rise to castism and favouritism”; give facilities and concessions to improve education, appoint solely on merit
Pandit H.N. Kunzru (U.P.)Ten-year time limit — three arguments: “backward” undefined; special provisions should not operate “indefinitely”; legislative representation is limited to ten years (Art. 305), so service reservation should be too. Warned of “fissiparous tendencies” — classes claiming backwardness for protection
Prof. K.T. ShahAdd “managing” in clause (4) — “in connection with” is too broad, catching honorary positions and donations
T.T. Krishnamachari (Madras)The sharp critique: a “paradise for lawyers” (quoting Prof. Ivor Jennings on the fundamental rights chapter); what does equality of opportunity mean for illiterates? Blamed the residence amendment for all the problems; “loose drafting”; “I cannot congratulate the Drafting Committee on putting this particular word in”; “backward” definable by caste, community, religion, literacy, economic status — no one knows

sections.title: Dr. Ambedkar's Concluding Speech
sections.html:
• On “paradise for lawyers”: he would ask Krishnamachari to point to any constitution in the world that is not one — the vast storehouses of American, Canadian and other law reports say so. He is “not ashamed at all” if this Constitution must be taken to the Federal Court for interpretation: that is the fate of every constitution and every drafting committee.
  • On residence: common citizenship implies residence is no qualification — making it one subtracts from common citizenship's value. Yet people cannot be allowed to fly about “as mere birds of passage without any roots,” taking “the plums and walking away.” Provinces already had varying qualifying periods (domicile, ten years, seven); the amendment's purpose: the qualifying period should be uniform throughout India, achievable only by giving the power to Parliament, not the local units.
  • On “backward”: the three viewpoints had to be reconciled in a workable formula. The danger of over-reservation: supposing reservations for communities totalling seventy percent of posts, leaving thirty percent open — could anyone say equality of opportunity survives? “Therefore the seats to be reserved... must be confined to a minority of seats. It is then only that the first principle could find its place in the Constitution and effective in operation.” Without a qualifying phrase like “backward,” the exception “will ultimately eat up the rule altogether. Nothing of the rule will remain.” The Drafting Committee inserted “backward” on its own shoulders — it did not appear in the fundamental right as passed by the Assembly — to prevent the exception from devouring the rule.
  • On definition and justiciability: “A backward community is a community which is backward in the opinion of the Government.” On whether the rule is justiciable: difficult to answer dogmatically — personally he thought it would be; a State reserving so many seats that equality was destroyed could be taken to the Federal Court and Supreme Court, which would decide whether the government acted “in a reasonable and prudent manner.” To Krishnamachari's “who is a reasonable man?”: the words are used in many laws — the Transfer of Property Act among them — and courts will not find difficulty.

sections.title: The Final Article and Its Afterlife
sections.html:
Article 10 as amended: (1) equality of opportunity in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State; (2) no ineligibility or discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence; (2a) Parliament's residence-requirement power; (3) reservation for backward classes not adequately represented; (4) religious institutions' office-holders. Post-Constitution, the “exception” theory (reservation as exception to equality) governed for years — until N.M. Thomas and Indra Sawhney recharacterised Article 16(4) as a facet of equality, a means of achieving it, creating a level playing field: backward classes are a separate class under reasonable classification. The residence philosophy connects to Article 301: trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India shall be free — India as one economic and social unit; as goods flow freely, citizens should move and work freely.

Earlier viewLater view (N.M. Thomas / Indra Sawhney)
Equality is the ruleEquality is the rule
Reservation is an exception to equalityReservation is a means to achieve equality
Reservation deviates from meritReservation creates a level playing field
Backward classes are like othersBackward classes are a separate class

The shift in the understanding of Article 16(4)

Quotes

Key quotes to remember: Ambedkar — “Equality is a general rule, while reservation is an exception”; “Unless you use some such qualifying phrase as ‘backward,' the exception made in favour of reservation will ultimately eat up the rule altogether”; “A backward community is a community which is backward in the opinion of the Government”; “The seats to be reserved must be confined to a minority of seats.” Mohamed Ismail Sahib — “Communalism does not come in because people want their rights...” Hukam Singh — “What would be the fate of the minorities?” Khandekar — “Though there are commissions... our candidates will not be able to compete with the candidates of the Brahmin community or the so-called Savarna Hindus.” Kunzru — “It is not desirable that... any special provisions laid down for [backward classes] should operate indefinitely.” Krishnamachari — “This chapter of fundamental rights is a paradise for lawyers. And, as a piece of loose drafting, article 10 takes the palm.”

sections.title: Student Presentation — Are 15(4) and 16(4) Fundamental Rights or Exceptions?
sections.html:
Diksha of Haryana (Mahendragarh) presents. The professor's clarification: Articles 12 to 35 are Part III — so the real doubt is not whether 15(4) and 16(4) are fundamental rights, but whether they are exceptions to 15(1) and 16(1) or facets of equality itself.

Case

State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976)

7-judge bench · 5:2 · (1976) 2 SCC 310

Facts
The constitutionality of special treatment for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Kerala government service was at issue before the largest bench then assembled for the question.
Held
Five judges held Article 16(4) is NOT an exception to Article 16: it is within the purview of Article 16 as a facet of equality, providing equality of opportunity in line with clause (1), giving positive support and content to 16(1). The Court envisaged not formal or legal equality but proportional equality — the progressive elimination of pronounced inequality.
Principle
Justice Chinnappa Reddy repeated the position in A.B.S.K. Sangh (Akhil Bharatiya Shoshit Karmachari Sangh) v. Union of India — a demonstration of the power of Public Interest Litigation.

The same logic extends to 15(4): both rest on Article 14's equality. The theoretical footing is Ronald Dworkin's distinction: the right to equal treatment (formal equality — an equal distribution) versus the right to treatment as an equal (substantive — the fundamental right to be treated with equal concern and respect). Unequal treatment of equals violates equality; so does equal treatment of unequals. Article 15(4) rests not on prejudice, contempt or insult toward forward classes — it promotes equality by requiring affirmative action to remove discrimination.

Supporting arguments: (1) constitutional practice — 15(4) and 16(4) have been implemented through executive orders without separate legislation, and courts have consistently upheld this; a fundamental right cannot be taken away without authority of law, so treating these as exceptions would render the executive actions unconstitutional; (2) DPSP harmony — fundamental rights and Directive Principles are read in harmony (itself basic structure): Article 38 (social order for the people's welfare) and Article 46 (promoting the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections) — the pattern of Article 21A's derivation from Article 21 read with Articles 41, 45 and 46; (3) Article 335 — SC/ST claims must be considered “consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration,” a positive obligation, not a device to avoid reservation; (4) Hohfeldian analysis — rights as claims, privileges, powers and immunities: a positive State duty creates a corresponding claim, enforceable under Articles 32 and 226 (mandamus); (5) international recognition — the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights recognises positive rights; (6) comparison — Articles 17, 23 and 24 equally require positive State action, yet are unquestionably fundamental rights: requiring state action does not stop a right from being one.

sections.title: The Birth of Reservation Jurisprudence — Mandal
sections.html:
The Mandal Commission was appointed by Prime Minister Morarji Desai on 20 December 1978, chaired by Justice B.P. Mandal, tasked to: (1) determine criteria for identifying socially and educationally backward classes; (2) recommend steps for their advancement; (3) examine the desirability of reservation in appointments and posts; (4) report to the President. The birth story: Dr. Ambedkar did not define “backward class” — when asked, he left it to the government of the day, a strategic avoidance of a politically impossible definition.

The report was submitted on 31 December 1980 — and left untouched, gathering dust. The turning point: V.P. Singh's 1990 political crisis, his chair “shaking.” Someone suggested the 50-52% backward classes could save him: he implemented 27% OBC reservation through an executive order — crucial because he lacked parliamentary majority. The 52% thesis: the OBC population was estimated at 52%, hence 27% (within the 50% ceiling). The protests: students preparing for UPSC for three-plus years saw their chances drastically cut — with 500 seats, reservations taking 300 left 200 for the general category. 60-70 people died by self-immolation; around 200 died of burns. The government remained “deaf and blind”; with limited media (no social media, few mobile phones), the government provided incomplete data. The students went to the Supreme Court.

sections.title: The Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953) — the First Attempt
sections.html: Established 1953 under Kaka Kalelkar; report 1955-56 — the first attempt to identify backward classes. Criteria: (1) traditional apathy for education from social and environmental conditions; (2) occupational handicap; (3) poverty and lack of educational institutions in rural areas; (4) living in inaccessible areas. The failure: no unanimous report — five members recorded minutes of dissent against linking caste with backwardness; even Chairman Kalelkar himself opposed caste as the basis. The Union Government's 1961 memorandum: “It cannot be denied that the caste system is the greatest hindrance in the way of our progress towards an egalitarian society, and the recognition of the specified castes as backward may serve to maintain and even perpetuate the existing distinctions on the basis of caste” — concluding that “some positive and workable criteria should be devised.” No all-India OBC list was drawn; States chose their own criteria; the Centre preferred economic tests.

sections.title: The Mandal Commission's Methodology
sections.html:
An empirical survey of 405 of the 406 districts then existing — two villages and one urban area per district — a genuine effort at objectivity. Eleven criteria in three categories:

CategoryCriteriaWeight
Social (3 points each)Considered socially backward by others; dependent mainly on manual labour; early marriage (25% of females, 10% of males marrying above the State average at a very young age); female work participation at least 25% above the State average (economic compulsion)12
Educational (2 points each)Children aged 5-15 never attending school at least 25% above State average; dropout rate at least 25% above; matriculates at least 25% below6
Economic (1 point each)Average family assets at least 25% below State average; families in kutcha houses at least 25% above; drinking water source beyond half a kilometre; landless families or only “khasra” land at least 25% above4

The eleven indicators of backwardness

Castes scoring 11 points (50%) or above were listed as socially and educationally backward; households below 20 for any caste were excluded as too small a sample. The evaluation offered in class: this cannot be called the best method, but it was the best effort — not arbitrary, suited to the task, with economic indicators flowing directly from social and educational backwardness.

sections.title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) — the Mandal Case
sections.html:
Case

Indra Sawhney v. Union of India

9-judge bench — the largest for reservation matters · Justice P.B. Jeevan Reddy's judgment is the assigned reading

Facts
Challenge to the 27% OBC reservation implemented by executive order in 1990, and the consolidated questions on Article 16(4).
Held
See the issue-wise holdings below.
Principle
Reservation jurisprudence's organising case.
IssueHolding
Can reservation be given by executive order?Yes — Article 16(4) uses “provision,” not “law”; the constitutional mandate exists; crucial for V.P. Singh, who lacked a parliamentary majority
IssueHolding
Is 16(4) an exception to 16(1)?No — following N.M. Thomas, it is a facet of equality, a form of reasonable classification
Who are the “backward class of citizens”?Caste alone cannot determine it (following Balaji); but caste can be a starting point for identifying social backwardness
The creamy layerExcluded — when a member of a backward class reaches an “advanced social level or status,” they “would no longer belong to the backward class and would have to be weeded out” (Jeevan Reddy J.), preventing the privileged within backward classes from monopolising benefits
Reservation in promotionsInitially rejected — but prospective overruling (the doctrine first established in Golaknath) allowed continuation for five years
Sub-classificationLeft open at this stage (backward vs. more backward)
The 50% ceilingReservation cannot ordinarily exceed 50% — a rule of caution, not absolute (following N.M. Thomas); relaxation possible in rural and remote areas
Carry-forward ruleUnfilled reserved vacancies may be carried forward — subject to the 50% ceiling (later addressed by the 81st Amendment's Article 16(4B))

Indra Sawhney, issue by issue

Case

M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963)

The earlier framework

Facts
Mysore's 68% reservation challenged.
Held
Caste cannot be the sole criterion — poverty or place of residence can also indicate backwardness; 68% struck down as excessive; reservation should generally not exceed 50%. Article 15(4) was then viewed as an exception to 15(1). The Court made clear its judgment did not affect SC/ST reservations.
Principle
The source of the 50% ceiling that Indra Sawhney adopted as a rule of caution.

day.title: Backward Classes — Four Advocates Argue Indra Sawhney
day.trail: The social-backwardness thesis · Palkhivala · Jethmalani · Parasaran · Venugopal · The Court's holdings · The EWS inconsistency · Quotes to memorise

sections.title: The Core Thesis — All Backwardness Is Rooted in Social Backwardness
sections.html:
The Court's causal chain: (1) social backwardness (the caste system's discrimination, stigma and exclusion) is the root cause; (2) it produces educational backwardness (exclusion from access); (3) which produces economic backwardness (no education, no employment) — which in turn reinforces social backwardness. “They feed upon each other, constituting a vicious circle.” The quotes to remember: “Social hierarchy and economic position exhibit an indisputable mutual relationship”; “The lower the caste, the poorer its members. The poorer the members of the caste, the lower the caste.” It is therefore logically flawed to find a person “socially backward but educationally forward” and use that to deny reservation — the categories are intertwined, and the root is social status determined by caste.

Why pure economic criteria are rejected: “mere poverty” cannot be the criterion — the vast majority of India is poor, and among the poor are many socially and educationally forward (the professor's example: himself — a “forward community” member, not wealthy, but a PhD professor, certainly not educationally backward). Reservation based on income alone would benefit poor individuals from forward castes, which is not Article 16(4)'s object: correcting a specific historical injustice rooted in caste. From this logic grows the creamy layer: within a backward class, members who have “progressed far enough and far ahead so as to compare favourably with the leading forward class economically, socially and educationally” should not take the benefit — an upper income ceiling secures it “only for such of those members who are still behind, who really deserve.”

sections.title: The Purpose — Sharing State Power, Not Poverty Alleviation
sections.html: Reservation was not designed to make anyone wealthy — a government job cannot do that. The object is to dismantle the historical dominance of certain castes in the State apparatus and enable backward classes to share state power. The pre-independence reality — “It is a well known fact that till Independence, the administrative apparatus was manned almost exclusively by members of the upper caste” — excluded Shudras, SCs, STs and backward groups among Muslims and Christians from any administrative role, leaving them perpetually “ruled.” The goal is empowerment and dignity: moving a community from the feeling of being ruled to being part of the ruling class — bringing pratishtha (prestige), samman (respect) and garv (pride). The textual distinction matters: Article 15(4) reserves in education for classes “socially and educationally backward” (it would be pointless to reserve educational seats for a class educationally forward); Article 16(4) reserves employment for the “backward class of citizens” — where, per Indra Sawhney, social backwardness is the main criterion, and it is incorrect to require the class to be both socially and educationally backward for jobs.

sections.title: The Supreme Court's Holdings
sections.html:
On identification: the Court rejected Palkhivala's extreme (caste irrelevant) and Jethmalani's restriction (only Shudras). Caste is “a very very important component of our country” — “If reservation is made in favour of backward class of citizens, the bar contained in clause 2 is not attracted, even if backward classes are identified with reference to caste.” But caste cannot be the sole factor: reservation for all Muslims simpliciter (religion alone) is unconstitutional; “Muslims + poverty” (a specific backward class) is permissible. The four principal factors of social backwardness — poverty, caste, occupation, habitation: “Poverty, caste, occupation, and habitation are the principal factors which contributed to rank a class as socially backward.” The primary accent of 16(4) is social backwardness; educational backwardness is a requirement of 15(4), not 16(4).

#QuestionRuling
1Is a law required for reservation?No — executive order suffices: 16(4) says “provision,” not “law”
2Is 16(4) an exception to 16(1)?No — a facet, an elaboration of reasonable classification
3Is 16(4) exhaustive?No — reservation can also be made under 16(1) itself in “very exceptional situations” and “public interest,” not for vote-bank politics
4Can caste be a starting point?Yes — relevant, but never the sole criterion
5Economic criteria alone?No — reservation under 16(4) cannot rest purely on economics (the later 10% EWS came by constitutional amendment and remains contested)
6Sub-categories (“backward” and “more backward”)?Yes — States may sub-classify so benefits reach the most marginalised
7The limit?Normally 50%; extraordinary circumstances may justify exception
8Carry-forward?Valid, subject to the 50% ceiling — later addressed by the 81st Amendment (16(4B))
9Reservation in promotion?No — but prospective overruling allowed five years' continuation; nullified later by the 77th Amendment (16(4A))
#QuestionRuling
10Judicial review?Yes — identifying backwardness is primarily for the executive, subject to review for flawed exercise
11Oversight?A permanent commission should periodically review the backward-class list

sections.title: The EWS Inconsistency — the Professor's Critique
sections.html:
Professor'S Aside

The Court in Indra Sawhney said reservation cannot be based on economic criteria, and that the 50% limit is a general rule. It also said 16(4) is not exhaustive, and reservation can be made under 16(1) in “exceptional situations.” Then a 10% EWS reservation arrives — and is upheld. My question: if reservation can be given under Article 16(1) for any exceptional situation, why was the EWS reservation not simply accommodated under 16(1)? Kitne peg pee ke aate hain Supreme Court ke judges? — How many pegs do Supreme Court judges drink before coming to court?

sections.title: Part 1 — The Constitutional Text
sections.html:
Article 19(1) guarantees all citizens the rights to (a) freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout India; (e) to reside and settle anywhere in India; and (g) to practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business. Sub-clause (f) — acquire, hold and dispose of property — was omitted by the Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978. The words “or co-operative societies” in (c) were added by the Ninety-seventh Amendment, 2011. Each freedom has its own restriction clause: (a) is limited by clause (2), (b) by (3), (c) by (4), (d) and (e) by (5), (g) by (6). The word “press” does not appear — press freedom is read into (a): Brij Bhushan, Sakal Papers, Indian Express Newspapers.

The eight grounds — an exhaustive list

A restriction “in the interest of the general public” is allowed for trade under clause (6) but not for speech: Sakal Papers; reaffirmed in Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023).

The 1950 text and the First Amendment

As enacted, clause (2) allowed restrictions only relating to libel, slander, defamation, contempt of court, matters offending decency or morality, or which undermined “the security of, or tend[ed] to overthrow, the State.” Two gaps drove the early litigation: no “reasonable,” and no “public order.” Three lines of cases mattered: (1) Romesh Thappar and Brij Bhushan (both 26 May 1950) invalidated provincial public-safety provisions — the Punjab High Court then struck down sedition (section 124A) in Tara Singh Gopi Chand (1950); (2) the Organiser order in Brij Bhushan targeted “news and views about Pakistan” — the government wanted power to curb war-talk after the Nehru–Liaquat Pact of April 1950; (3) the Patna High Court in the Bharati Press case (In re Shailabala Devi, 1950) held even incitement to murder not covered unless it threatened the State — the “Bihar” case the lecturer recalled.

The First Amendment (1951) added three grounds — public order, friendly relations with foreign States, incitement to an offence; inserted the word “reasonable,” opening every restriction to judicial review; replaced “libel, slander, defamation” with “defamation” alone and dropped “tends to overthrow the State”; and operated retrospectively — Section 3 deemed the new clause “always to have been enacted,” reviving struck-down laws. The same Act added Article 15(4) (answering Champakam Dorairajan), amended 19(6) for nationalisation, and added Articles 31A and 31B with the Ninth Schedule. The Supreme Court reversed the Patna view in State of Bihar v. Shailabala Devi (AIR 1952 SC 329) a year later — part of the stated need having disappeared, though the text stayed. The Sixteenth Amendment (1963) added “the sovereignty and integrity of India” to clauses (2), (3) and (4), following the November 1962 Committee on National Integration and Regionalism report amid secessionist demands and the war with China; it also changed Articles 84 and 173 and the Third Schedule oaths — candidates, legislators, ministers and judges now swear to uphold sovereignty and integrity.

Why Article 19 belongs only to citizens

ArticleSubjectWho can claim
14Equality before lawAny person, citizen or not
15No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birthCitizens
16Equal opportunity in public employmentCitizens
19The six freedomsCitizens
20, 21, 22Criminal process protections, life and liberty, arrestAny person

The constitutional scheme of right-holders

Consequences: a foreign national cannot found a claim on Article 19 (Hans Muller of Nuremberg, AIR 1955 SC 367); a company is not a citizen (State Trading Corporation, AIR 1963 SC 1811) but its shareholders and editors can sue for their own rights (Bennett Coleman); in Cricket Association of Bengal the government argued a foreign broadcaster was using an Indian body to claim 19(1)(a) — the majority answered that the citizen-organiser was exercising its own right through an agent.

Articles 17 and 18 in brief

Article 17 abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice in any form, and makes enforcement of any disability arising from it an offence — enforced through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989; it binds private persons as well as the State (PUDR, 1982). The lecturer's hygiene-based account of untouchability's origins was expressly his personal view — not a legal proposition; Article 17 treats untouchability as exclusion based on birth, as Dr. Ambedkar described his own experience. Article 18: the State shall confer no title other than military or academic distinction (clause 1); no citizen shall accept a foreign title (clause 2); non-citizen office-holders of profit or trust need the President's consent for foreign titles (clause 3), and no such office-holder may accept presents, emoluments or offices from a foreign State without consent (clause 4). No penalty is prescribed; Parliament may legislate for breach but has not.

Permitted — military distinctionParam Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra; military ranksExpress exception, clause (1)
