sections.title: Part 2 — The Landmark Cases
sections.html:
Case

Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)

AIR 1950 SC 124 · 6 judges · majority per Patanjali Sastri J.; Fazl Ali J. dissenting

Facts
Cross Roads, an English weekly printed in Bombay; on 1 March 1950 Madras banned its entry, circulation, sale and distribution under section 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 “for securing the public safety and the maintenance of public order.” Thappar went straight to the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Held
Petition allowed; section 9(1-A) void. Article 32 is itself a fundamental right — the Court cannot turn a petitioner away. Freedom of speech includes freedom to propagate ideas, and propagation is secured by circulation: “Liberty of circulation is as essential to that freedom as the liberty of publication.” “Public order” is a wide expression covering every breach of tranquillity from affray to rebellion — but the 1950 clause (2) spoke only of the security of the State; only aggravated disorder endangering the State's foundations could justify curbing speech. A provision whose language authorises both valid and invalid restrictions cannot be severed — void as a whole. Fazl Ali J.: serious disorder does undermine the State's security, as sedition does.
Principle
The first free-speech ruling: circulation is part of speech; the 19(2) grounds are exhaustive and read narrowly; the seed of the overbreadth doctrine. It caused the First Amendment.
Case

Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950)

AIR 1950 SC 129 · the same six judges, the same day · Fazl Ali J. dissenting

Facts
The Chief Commissioner of Delhi required the weekly Organiser to submit for pre-publication scrutiny “all communal matter and news and views about Pakistan including photographs and cartoons” under section 7(1)(c), East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949.
Held
Pre-censorship is a restriction on the liberty of the press, which is an essential part of 19(1)(a); the majority applied Romesh Thappar — public safety/public order is not the security of the State, so clause (2) did not save it. Fazl Ali J. read “public safety” as the security of the State and would have dismissed. Blackstone, quoted: the press's liberty “consists in laying no previous restraint upon publications.”
Principle
Press freedom lives inside 19(1)(a) though the Article never says “press”; prior restraint demands justification under clause (2). It does NOT hold all print pre-censorship void — Virendra v. State of Punjab (1957) upheld a time-limited power with a right of representation and struck down one without safeguards.
Case

State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952)

AIR 1952 SC 196 · 5 judges · Patanjali Sastri C.J.

Facts
The People's Education Society declared an unlawful association under the 1908 Act's section 15(2)(b) (financing the banned Communist Party); the Madras amendment required stated grounds, allowed representation, and made an Advisory Board's finding bind the government — but the declaration was Gazette-only and membership itself became an offence.
Held
Restriction struck down. Reasonableness covers substance and procedure; the test is statute-by-statute — “no abstract standard, or general pattern, of reasonableness.” The factors: the nature of the right, the purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil, the disproportion of the imposition, and prevailing conditions. Shutting out judicial inquiry in favour of executive satisfaction is reasonable only in very exceptional circumstances; the absence of personal notice when membership was criminalised was a serious defect. The Court is “a sentinel on the qui vive.”
Principle
The foundational reasonableness test for all of Article 19; the “disproportion” factor is the root of modern proportionality (Modern Dental College 2016; Anuradha Bhasin 2020). Limit noted: it arose under 19(1)(c)/(4) — a ruling on one freedom is weak authority on another.
Case

K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970)

(1970) 2 SCC 780 · 5 judges · Hidayatullah C.J.

Facts
Abbas, journalist and film-maker (on the Khosla Committee), made the 16-minute documentary A Tale of Four Cities with a brief blurred red-light-district shot; offered a “U” certificate only with cuts, he challenged pre-censorship itself and the vagueness of the Cinematograph Act's section 5-B(2) directions.
Held
Censorship of films including prior restraint is justified; U/A classification is reasonable; directions not void for vagueness but must be supplemented to protect artistic and social value. Film is treated differently from print — instant appeal, realism, combined effect on eye and ear, strong effect on children. American decisions are not decisive: the First Amendment is absolute in form, Article 19(2) expressly permits reasonable restrictions. A law leaving censors “in a boundless sea of uncertainty” would be struck, but courts first construe sensibly. The flaw in the directions: treating artistic and inartistic work alike — censors judge the handling of a theme, not the theme. The Solicitor-General conceded time limits and court- or tribunal-level appeals.
Principle
The print-film distinction. Key lines: “The motion picture is able to stir up emotions more deeply than any other product of art”; “our standards must be so framed that we are not reduced to a level where the protection of the least capable and the most depraved amongst us determines what the morally healthy cannot view or read”; “Sex and obscenity are not always synonymous.”
Case

Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana (1988)

(1988) 3 SCC 410 · per Venkataramiah J.

Facts
Doordarshan was showing Honi-Anhoni; two organisations obtained a Bombay High Court injunction against episodes 12 and 13 in a public interest petition alleging superstition and fright to children — the producer added as a party only the day before the order.
Held
Injunction set aside. The right to exhibit a film on Doordarshan, on Doordarshan's terms, is part of 19(1)(a) — like publishing through a newspaper, subject to the medium owner's terms; an interim injunction infringes the producer's right where petitioners show no legal right and no material of real harm; “It spreads superstition” is not a 19(2) ground. The Court expressly left open whether a citizen may set up a private broadcasting station.
Principle
Dissemination extends to television; courts must not impose prior restraint by injunction on non-listed grounds. The reserved question was taken up in Cricket Association of Bengal.
Case

LIC v. Prof. Manubhai D. Shah (1992)

(1992) 3 SCC 637 · two appeals together · per Ahmadi J.

Facts
Shah's study paper arguing LIC premiums were unduly high; a member's counter reprinted in LIC's magazine Yogakshema; Shah's rejoinder refused (“in-house publication”). Separately, Doordarshan refused to telecast Beyond Genocide, the Golden Lotus-winning Bhopal documentary holding a “U” certificate, calling it outdated and sub judice.
Held
Both appeals dismissed — LIC must print the rejoinder with explanation and apology for delay; Doordarshan must telecast. “Speech is God's gift to mankind.” Freedom includes circulating views through print, radio and television and using the medium to answer criticism. LIC is “State” under Article 12; its publicly funded magazine, open to outside subscribers, must be fair — printing one side and refusing the other violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(a). Once the film-maker's right is recognised, the refusing party bears the burden of showing a 19(2) ground — criticism of government is not one. Ruling confined to “the peculiar facts”: no absolute duty to print whatever any citizen sends.
Principle
Right of reply against State-controlled media; burden of justification on the State. It does not create such a right against a private publisher.
Case

Secretary, Ministry of I&B; v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)

(1995) 2 SCC 161 · Sawant and Mohan JJ. jointly; Jeevan Reddy J. concurring

Facts
CAB's 1993 Hero Cup: Doordarshan offered Rs. 1 crore; CAB sold worldwide rights to Trans World International for a guaranteed US$550,000 plus 70% of excess; the Telecom Department told VSNL to refuse the uplink and customs detained TWI's equipment; interim orders let both telecast. The 1994 BCCI–ESPN dispute recurred.
Held
(para 124) Airwaves are public property; a public authority must regulate their use in the public interest. The right to impart and receive information is part of freedom of speech; a citizen has access to telecasting subject to public-property limits. The Central Government must set up an independent, autonomous public authority to control the airwaves. Sports telecast by a non-profit body has a speech element — earning revenue incidentally does not convert expression into trade. 19(2) permits no monopoly over speech (unlike 19(6) for business). Jeevan Reddy J.'s limits: no citizen has a fundamental right to set up a private broadcasting station — that is for Parliament; “From the standpoint of Article 19(1)(a), what is paramount is the right of the listeners and viewers and not the right of the broadcaster.” Both opinions found the Telegraph Act, 1885 unsuited to broadcasting; the Prasar Bharati Act, 1990 was brought into force in 1997.
Principle
The right to receive information; airwaves public property; no broadcasting monopoly. The lecture's version — that the rights-holder must give the feed to Doordarshan — is not in the judgment: that rule comes from the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007.
Case

S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010)

(2010) 5 SCC 600 · per Chauhan J.

Facts
In a 2005 India Today survey the actress endorsed pre-marital sex within committed relationships and girls' self-protection; twenty-three criminal complaints (defamation, obscenity, insult to modesty) followed, mostly from one political party's functionaries.
Held
All quashed. A reference to sex is not per se obscene; the standard is contemporary community tolerance as of an average reasonable person; no identifiable person or definite group was defamed, so the complainants were not “persons aggrieved”; pre-marital sex between consenting adults is no offence, so advocating its acceptance cannot be incitement; the complaints were mala fide, for political mileage. “It is not the task of the criminal law to punish individuals merely for expressing unpopular views”; “Morality and Criminality are not co-extensive”; the law must not have a “chilling effect.”
Principle
Unpopular social opinion protected from morality-based prosecution; lays down no new obscenity test (that came in Aveek Sarkar, which cites it).
Case

Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014)

(2014) 4 SCC 257 · per Radhakrishnan J.

Facts
Stern's photograph of Boris Becker nude with his fiancée Barbara Feltus (her father took it), reproduced by Sports World and Anandabazar Patrika in May 1993; an Alipore lawyer's complaint under section 292 IPC; summons issued; the High Court refused to quash.
Held
Hicklin is “not the correct test.” Obscenity is judged from the average person's viewpoint applying contemporary community standards, the work as a whole, in its context and for its message; nudity is not obscene per se — only material tending to excite lustful thoughts. The photograph's message was against racism; prosecution quashed.
Principle
Hicklin (followed since Ranjit Udeshi 1965) replaced by the community standard test. Note: a two-judge bench displaced a five-judge bench's retention of Hicklin; the judgment reads Udeshi as itself recognising changing standards.
Case

Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996)

(1996) 1 SCC 361 · 5-judge Constitution Bench · per Ahmadi C.J., Kuldip Singh J. concurring

Facts
Petitions in Kerala and Madhya Pradesh, transferred to the Supreme Court, challenged the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards as “titles” under Article 18(1).
Held
The awards are valid — not titles — but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes; a user should forfeit the award; a high-level committee should set selection criteria. “The theory of equality does not mandate that merit should not be recognized.”
Principle
Article 18 targets ranks of nobility and colonial loyal-subject creation; honours recognising work done are compatible with equality.

Two cases raised by students

Case

Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) — the Tamas case

(1988) 1 SCC 668

Facts
A petition to stop Doordarshan showing Tamas, the serial from Bhisham Sahni's Partition novel, alleging it would inflame communal feeling.
Held
Refused: two High Court judges had watched it and found a message of peace; the work is judged as a whole by the standard of reasonable, strong-minded people — not of those who sense danger in every hostile view.
Principle
Depicting violence is not inciting it.
Case

S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989)

(1989) 2 SCC 574 — the case a student named “Shankar Asrani v. Jagjivan Ram”

Facts
The Tamil film Ore Oru Gramathile criticised caste-based reservation; after agitation threats the High Court revoked its “U” certificate.
Held
Certificate restored. Open criticism of policy is not a restriction ground; the State cannot plead inability to control a hostile audience — freedom “cannot be held to ransom by an intolerant group of people”; the anticipated danger must be “a spark in a powder keg,” justified “on the anvil of necessity and not the quicksand of convenience or expediency.”
Principle
The Indian proximity test; the State's duty to protect speech against hostile audiences.

What speech includes

Form of expressionAuthority
Oral and written speech; publication and circulation (including volume of circulation)Romesh Thappar; Sakal Papers
Press freedomBrij Bhushan; Bennett Coleman; Indian Express Newspapers (1985)
Political criticismKedar Nath Singh; S. Rangarajan
Artistic and literary expressionRanjit D. Udeshi; Samaresh Bose v. Amal Mitra (1985)
FilmsK.A. Abbas; Rangarajan; Bobby Art International (1996)
Television and broadcastingOdyssey; LIC; Cricket Association of Bengal
Academic and research expressionLIC (a research study paper)
Peaceful advocacy and demonstrationKameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar (1962)
Digital and internet communicationShreya Singhal (2015); Anuradha Bhasin (2020)
Symbols and symbolic acts — flying the flagUnion of India v. Naveen Jindal (2004)
Photographs and cartoonsBrij Bhushan; Aveek Sarkar
SilenceBijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)
Advertisements — commercial speechTata Press v. MTNL (1995), qualifying Hamdard Dawakhana (1960)
Entertainment and sportCricket Association of Bengal
Replying to criticismLIC v. Manubhai Shah
Receiving informationRaj Narain (1975); Cricket Association of Bengal

The scope of “speech and expression”

Circulation and the right to receive

An idea that cannot be disseminated has not been expressed in any useful sense. Romesh Thappar: a journal's entry ban restricts speech; Sakal Papers: price-by-page laws restrict speech by cutting circulation — the State cannot curb speech to regulate business; Bennett Coleman: newsprint quotas capping pages restrict speech; Odyssey: stopping a telecast restricts the producer; LIC: refusing a reply restricts the critic. Article 19(1)(a) also protects the listener and viewer: Raj Narain — the people's right to know every public act of their functionaries; Indian Express Newspapers — press freedom exists for the public's right to know; CAB — the viewers' interest is paramount; Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) — voters' right to know candidates' antecedents. The Right to Information Act, 2005 is the statutory vehicle.

Reasonable restriction — the five-step checklist

The five-step checklist for any restriction on speech

Points examiners look for: “Law” — the lecturer said only an Act of the legislature; the usual formulation is wider: a statute or a rule made under statutory power qualifies, bare executive instructions do not (the High Court rejected Doordarshan's norms on this basis in LIC). Burden — once the citizen shows a restriction, the State must justify it (LIC; CAB para 46). Proportionality today — legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity, balance (Modern Dental College; Anuradha Bhasin). “In the interests of” — wider than “for the maintenance of” (Ramji Lal Modi, 1957), but the 1960 Lohia case keeps it within proximity.

The three tiers of disorder

Three concentric circles — Hidayatullah J. in Ram Manohar Lohia (1966)

Romesh Thappar supplies the first half of the analysis — public order is wider than the security of the State, and in 1950 only the latter was a ground. The test is the act's effect on the community, not its nature (Arun Ghosh v. State of West Bengal, 1970). Proximate and reasonable nexus: a remote, hypothetical or far-fetched connection will not do (Lohia, 1960).

Obscenity — from Hicklin to community standards

YearCaseContribution
1868R. v. Hicklin (England)Tendency to deprave and corrupt those open to immoral influences; isolated passages; the most susceptible reader
1965Ranjit D. UdeshiHicklin adopted with modifications; sex and nudity in art not obscene without more; conviction for selling Lady Chatterley's Lover upheld
1970K.A. AbbasUdeshi principles applied to film; standards not set by the most depraved
1985Samaresh Bose v. Amal MitraVulgarity is not obscenity; judge reads from the author's and reader's positions
1996Bobby Art International (Bandit Queen)Nudity judged in the work's context and message
2010KhushbooOpinion on sexual morality not obscene; contemporary community standards
2014Aveek SarkarHicklin rejected; community standard test adopted

The fifty-year arc of the obscenity test

Under the community standard test, ask three things: would an average person, applying contemporary standards, find the material tends to excite lust? Is it taken as a whole? What is its context and message?

Pre-censorship: print and film

PrintFilm
Leading case Brij Bhushan (1950)K.A. Abbas (1970)
Result Pre-censorship order struck downPrior certification upheld
Reason No ground in Article 19(2) supported itFilm's stronger impact on a mass audience, including children
Limits Can survive only with narrow scope, a time limit and a right of representation (Virendra, 1957)Needs definite standards, room for art, a time limit and an independent appeal
Later authority R. Rajagopal v. State of T.N. (1994): no prior restraint on publishing about public officialsS. Rangarajan: certification must be reasonable, judged by an ordinary person of common sense

Prior restraint across media

Incitement, proximity and the remaining grounds

Speech becomes punishable when it incites, not when it merely discusses or advocates. United States: Schenck (1919) — clear and present danger from anti-draft leaflets; Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) — advocacy protected unless directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it. India: Kedar Nath Singh (1962) saved section 124A by confining sedition to words with a tendency or intention to create disorder or incite violence — strong criticism of government is protected; Rangarajan (1989) — danger not “remote, conjectural or far-fetched,” a spark in a powder keg; Shreya Singhal (2015) — discussion, advocacy and incitement distinguished; only incitement can be restricted. A caution: Arup Bhuyan v. State of Assam (2011) adopted Brandenburg for membership of banned organisations; a larger bench overruled that holding in 2023, warning against importing American doctrine without regard to 19(2)–(4). A fiery speech nobody acts on is rhetoric, not incitement.

Sovereignty and integrity: restricting advocacy of secession or cession of territory; Parliament used it to enact UAPA, 1967; section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 now penalises acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity. A student asked how violation is “quantified” — it is not measured: the State points to a law, shows the speech falls within it, and shows a proximate link to the harm. Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995): raising separatist slogans a few times, with no response and no disorder, is not an offence. Contempt: Articles 129 and 215 and the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; fair criticism of a judgment is permitted (E.M.S. Namboodiripad). Defamation: tort and crime (sections 499–500 IPC, now section 356 BNS); Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) upheld criminal defamation, treating reputation as part of Article 21; Khushboo shows the limit — only a person actually aggrieved may complain. Decency or morality: wider than obscenity, not confined to sexual morality (Ramesh Yeshwant Prabhoo, 1996). Friendly relations: added 1951, rarely litigated — targets propaganda damaging relations with another country, not criticism of its policies. Security of the State: rebellion, waging war — the innermost circle.
sections.text: Case Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) AIR 1950 SC 124 · 6 judges · majority per Patanjali Sastri J.; Fazl Ali J. dissenting Facts Cross Roads, an English weekly printed in Bombay; on 1 March 1950 Madras banned its entry, circulation, sale and distribution under section 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 “for securing the public safety and the maintenance of public order.” Thappar went straight to the Supreme Court under Article 32. Held Petition allowed; section 9(1-A) void. Article 32 is itself a fundamental right — the Court cannot turn a petitioner away. Freedom of speech includes freedom to propagate ideas, and propagation is secured by circulation: “Liberty of circulation is as essential to that freedom as the liberty of publication.” “Public order” is a wide expression covering every breach of tranquillity from affray to rebellion — but the 1950 clause (2) spoke only of the security of the State; only aggravated disorder endangering the State's foundations could justify curbing speech. A provision whose language authorises both valid and invalid restrictions cannot be severed — void as a whole. Fazl Ali J.: serious disorder does undermine the State's security, as sedition does. Principle The first free-speech ruling: circulation is part of speech; the 19(2) grounds are exhaustive and read narrowly; the seed of the overbreadth doctrine. It caused the First Amendment. Case Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950) AIR 1950 SC 129 · the same six judges, the same day · Fazl Ali J. dissenting Facts The Chief Commissioner of Delhi required the weekly Organiser to submit for pre-publication scrutiny “all communal matter and news and views about Pakistan including photographs and cartoons” under section 7(1)(c), East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949. Held Pre-censorship is a restriction on the liberty of the press, which is an essential part of 19(1)(a); the majority applied Romesh Thappar — public safety/public order is not the security of the State, so clause (2) did not save it. Fazl Ali J. read “public safety” as the security of the State and would have dismissed. Blackstone, quoted: the press's liberty “consists in laying no previous restraint upon publications.” Principle Press freedom lives inside 19(1)(a) though the Article never says “press”; prior restraint demands justification under clause (2). It does NOT hold all print pre-censorship void — Virendra v. State of Punjab (1957) upheld a time-limited power with a right of representation and struck down one without safeguards. Case State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) AIR 1952 SC 196 · 5 judges · Patanjali Sastri C.J. Facts The People's Education Society declared an unlawful association under the 1908 Act's section 15(2)(b) (financing the banned Communist Party); the Madras amendment required stated grounds, allowed representation, and made an Advisory Board's finding bind the government — but the declaration was Gazette-only and membership itself became an offence. Held Restriction struck down. Reasonableness covers substance and procedure; the test is statute-by-statute — “no abstract standard, or general pattern, of reasonableness.” The factors: the nature of the right, the purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil, the disproportion of the imposition, and prevailing conditions. Shutting out judicial inquiry in favour of executive satisfaction is reasonable only in very exceptional circumstances; the absence of personal notice when membership was criminalised was a serious defect. The Court is “a sentinel on the qui vive.” Principle The foundational reasonableness test for all of Article 19; the “disproportion” factor is the root of modern proportionality (Modern Dental College 2016; Anuradha Bhasin 2020). Limit noted: it arose under 19(1)(c)/(4) — a ruling on one freedom is weak authority on another. Case K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970) (1970) 2 SCC 780 · 5 judges · Hidayatullah C.J. Facts Abbas, journalist and film-maker (on the Khosla Committee), made the 16-minute documentary A Tale of Four Cities with a brief blurred red-light-district shot; offered a “U” certificate only with cuts, he challenged pre-censorship itself and the vagueness of the Cinematograph Act's section 5-B(2) directions. Held Censorship of films including prior restraint is justified; U/A classification is reasonable; directions not void for vagueness but must be supplemented to protect artistic and social value. Film is treated differently from print — instant appeal, realism, combined effect on eye and ear, strong effect on children. American decisions are not decisive: the First Amendment is absolute in form, Article 19(2) expressly permits reasonable restrictions. A law leaving censors “in a boundless sea of uncertainty” would be struck, but courts first construe sensibly. The flaw in the directions: treating artistic and inartistic work alike — censors judge the handling of a theme, not the theme. The Solicitor-General conceded time limits and court- or tribunal-level appeals. Principle The print-film distinction. Key lines: “The motion picture is able to stir up emotions more deeply than any other product of art”; “our standards must be so framed that we are not reduced to a level where the protection of the least capable and the most depraved amongst us determines what the morally healthy cannot view or read”; “Sex and obscenity are not always synonymous.” Case Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana (1988) (1988) 3 SCC 410 · per Venkataramiah J. Facts Doordarshan was showing Honi-Anhoni; two organisations obtained a Bombay High Court injunction against episodes 12 and 13 in a public interest petition alleging superstition and fright to children — the producer added as a party only the day before the order. Held Injunction set aside. The right to exhibit a film on Doordarshan, on Doordarshan's terms, is part of 19(1)(a) — like publishing through a newspaper, subject to the medium owner's terms; an interim injunction infringes the producer's right where petitioners show no legal right and no material of real harm; “It spreads superstition” is not a 19(2) ground. The Court expressly left open whether a citizen may set up a private broadcasting station. Principle Dissemination extends to television; courts must not impose prior restraint by injunction on non-listed grounds. The reserved question was taken up in Cricket Association of Bengal . Case LIC v. Prof. Manubhai D. Shah (1992) (1992) 3 SCC 637 · two appeals together · per Ahmadi J. Facts Shah's study paper arguing LIC premiums were unduly high; a member's counter reprinted in LIC's magazine Yogakshema; Shah's rejoinder refused (“in-house publication”). Separately, Doordarshan refused to telecast Beyond Genocide, the Golden Lotus-winning Bhopal documentary holding a “U” certificate, calling it outdated and sub judice. Held Both appeals dismissed — LIC must print the rejoinder with explanation and apology for delay; Doordarshan must telecast. “Speech is God's gift to mankind.” Freedom includes circulating views through print, radio and television and using the medium to answer criticism. LIC is “State” under Article 12; its publicly funded magazine, open to outside subscribers, must be fair — printing one side and refusing the other violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(a). Once the film-maker's right is recognised, the refusing party bears the burden of showing a 19(2) ground — criticism of government is not one. Ruling confined to “the peculiar facts”: no absolute duty to print whatever any citizen sends. Principle Right of reply against State-controlled media; burden of justification on the State. It does not create such a right against a private publisher. Case Secretary, Ministry of I&B; v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995) (1995) 2 SCC 161 · Sawant and Mohan JJ. jointly; Jeevan Reddy J. concurring Facts CAB's 1993 Hero Cup: Doordarshan offered Rs. 1 crore; CAB sold worldwide rights to Trans World International for a guaranteed US$550,000 plus 70% of excess; the Telecom Department told VSNL to refuse the uplink and customs detained TWI's equipment; interim orders let both telecast. The 1994 BCCI–ESPN dispute recurred. Held (para 124) Airwaves are public property; a public authority must regulate their use in the public interest. The right to impart and receive information is part of freedom of speech; a citizen has access to telecasting subject to public-property limits. The Central Government must set up an independent, autonomous public authority to control the airwaves. Sports telecast by a non-profit body has a speech element — earning revenue incidentally does not convert expression into trade. 19(2) permits no monopoly over speech (unlike 19(6) for business). Jeevan Reddy J.'s limits: no citizen has a fundamental right to set up a private broadcasting station — that is for Parliament; “From the standpoint of Article 19(1)(a), what is paramount is the right of the listeners and viewers and not the right of the broadcaster.” Both opinions found the Telegraph Act, 1885 unsuited to broadcasting; the Prasar Bharati Act, 1990 was brought into force in 1997. Principle The right to receive information; airwaves public property; no broadcasting monopoly. The lecture's version — that the rights-holder must give the feed to Doordarshan — is not in the judgment: that rule comes from the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007. Case S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010) (2010) 5 SCC 600 · per Chauhan J. Facts In a 2005 India Today survey the actress endorsed pre-marital sex within committed relationships and girls' self-protection; twenty-three criminal complaints (defamation, obscenity, insult to modesty) followed, mostly from one political party's functionaries. Held All quashed. A reference to sex is not per se obscene; the standard is contemporary community tolerance as of an average reasonable person; no identifiable person or definite group was defamed, so the complainants were not “persons aggrieved”; pre-marital sex between consenting adults is no offence, so advocating its acceptance cannot be incitement; the complaints were mala fide, for political mileage. “It is not the task of the criminal law to punish individuals merely for expressing unpopular views”; “Morality and Criminality are not co-extensive”; the law must not have a “chilling effect.” Principle Unpopular social opinion protected from morality-based prosecution; lays down no new obscenity test (that came in Aveek Sarkar , which cites it). Case Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014) (2014) 4 SCC 257 · per Radhakrishnan J. Facts Stern's photograph of Boris Becker nude with his fiancée Barbara Feltus (her father took it), reproduced by Sports World and Anandabazar Patrika in May 1993; an Alipore lawyer's complaint under section 292 IPC; summons issued; the High Court refused to quash. Held Hicklin is “not the correct test.” Obscenity is judged from the average person's viewpoint applying contemporary community standards, the work as a whole, in its context and for its message; nudity is not obscene per se — only material tending to excite lustful thoughts. The photograph's message was against racism; prosecution quashed. Principle Hicklin (followed since Ranjit Udeshi 1965) replaced by the community standard test. Note: a two-judge bench displaced a five-judge bench's retention of Hicklin; the judgment reads Udeshi as itself recognising changing standards. Case Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) (1996) 1 SCC 361 · 5-judge Constitution Bench · per Ahmadi C.J., Kuldip Singh J. concurring Facts Petitions in Kerala and Madhya Pradesh, transferred to the Supreme Court, challenged the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards as “titles” under Article 18(1). Held The awards are valid — not titles — but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes; a user should forfeit the award; a high-level committee should set selection criteria. “The theory of equality does not mandate that merit should not be recognized.” Principle Article 18 targets ranks of nobility and colonial loyal-subject creation; honours recognising work done are compatible with equality. Two cases raised by students Case Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) — the Tamas case (1988) 1 SCC 668 Facts A petition to stop Doordarshan showing Tamas , the serial from Bhisham Sahni's Partition novel, alleging it would inflame communal feeling. Held Refused: two High Court judges had watched it and found a message of peace; the work is judged as a whole by the standard of reasonable, strong-minded people — not of those who sense danger in every hostile view. Principle Depicting violence is not inciting it. Case S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989) (1989) 2 SCC 574 — the case a student named “Shankar Asrani v. Jagjivan Ram ” Facts The Tamil film Ore Oru Gramathile criticised caste-based reservation; after agitation threats the High Court revoked its “U” certificate. Held Certificate restored. Open criticism of policy is not a restriction ground; the State cannot plead inability to control a hostile audience — freedom “cannot be held to ransom by an intolerant group of people”; the anticipated danger must be “a spark in a powder keg,” justified “on the anvil of necessity and not the quicksand of convenience or expediency.” Principle The Indian proximity test; the State's duty to protect speech against hostile audiences. What speech includes Form of expression Authority Oral and written speech; publication and circulation (including volume of circulation) Romesh Thappar ; Sakal Papers Press freedom Brij Bhushan ; Bennett Coleman ; Indian Express Newspapers (1985) Political criticism Kedar Nath Singh ; S. Rangarajan Artistic and literary expression Ranjit D. Udeshi ; Samaresh Bose v. Amal Mitra (1985) Films K.A. Abbas ; Rangarajan; Bobby Art International (1996) Television and broadcasting Odyssey; LIC; Cricket Association of Bengal Academic and research expression LIC (a research study paper) Peaceful advocacy and demonstration Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar (1962) Digital and internet communication Shreya Singhal (2015); Anuradha Bhasin (2020) Symbols and symbolic acts — flying the flag Union of India v. Naveen Jindal (2004) Photographs and cartoons Brij Bhushan ; Aveek Sarkar Silence Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) Advertisements — commercial speech Tata Press v. MTNL (1995), qualifying Hamdard Dawakhana (1960) Entertainment and sport Cricket Association of Bengal Replying to criticism LIC v. Manubhai Shah Receiving information Raj Narain (1975); Cricket Association of Bengal The scope of “speech and expression” Circulation and the right to receive An idea that cannot be disseminated has not been expressed in any useful sense. Romesh Thappar : a journal's entry ban restricts speech; Sakal Papers : price-by-page laws restrict speech by cutting circulation — the State cannot curb speech to regulate business; Bennett Coleman : newsprint quotas capping pages restrict speech; Odyssey: stopping a telecast restricts the producer; LIC: refusing a reply restricts the critic. Article 19(1)(a) also protects the listener and viewer: Raj Narain — the people's right to know every public act of their functionaries; Indian Express Newspapers — press freedom exists for the public's right to know; CAB — the viewers' interest is paramount; Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) — voters' right to know candidates' antecedents. The Right to Information Act, 2005 is the statutory vehicle. Reasonable restriction — the five-step checklist The five-step checklist for any restriction on speech Points examiners look for: “Law” — the lecturer said only an Act of the legislature; the usual formulation is wider: a statute or a rule made under statutory power qualifies, bare executive instructions do not (the High Court rejected Doordarshan's norms on this basis in LIC). Burden — once the citizen shows a restriction, the State must justify it (LIC; CAB para 46). Proportionality today — legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity, balance (Modern Dental College; Anuradha Bhasin ). “In the interests of” — wider than “for the maintenance of” (Ramji Lal Modi, 1957), but the 1960 Lohia case keeps it within proximity. The three tiers of disorder Three concentric circles — Hidayatullah J. in Ram Manohar Lohia (1966) Romesh Thappar supplies the first half of the analysis — public order is wider than the security of the State, and in 1950 only the latter was a ground. The test is the act's effect on the community, not its nature ( Arun Ghosh v. State of West Bengal, 1970). Proximate and reasonable nexus: a remote, hypothetical or far-fetched connection will not do ( Lohia , 1960). Obscenity — from Hicklin to community standards Year Case Contribution 1868 R. v. Hicklin (England) Tendency to deprave and corrupt those open to immoral influences; isolated passages; the most susceptible reader 1965 Ranjit D. Udeshi Hicklin adopted with modifications; sex and nudity in art not obscene without more; conviction for selling Lady Chatterley's Lover upheld 1970 K.A. Abbas Udeshi principles applied to film; standards not set by the most depraved 1985 Samaresh Bose v. Amal Mitra Vulgarity is not obscenity; judge reads from the author's and reader's positions 1996 Bobby Art International (Bandit Queen) Nudity judged in the work's context and message 2010 Khushboo Opinion on sexual morality not obscene; contemporary community standards 2014 Aveek Sarkar Hicklin rejected; community standard test adopted The fifty-year arc of the obscenity test Under the community standard test, ask three things: would an average person, applying contemporary standards, find the material tends to excite lust? Is it taken as a whole? What is its context and message? Pre-censorship: print and film Print Film Leading case Brij Bhushan (1950) K.A. Abbas (1970) Result Pre-censorship order struck down Prior certification upheld Reason No ground in Article 19(2) supported it Film's stronger impact on a mass audience, including children Limits Can survive only with narrow scope, a time limit and a right of representation (Virendra, 1957) Needs definite standards, room for art, a time limit and an independent appeal Later authority R. Rajagopal v. State of T.N. (1994): no prior restraint on publishing about public officials S. Rangarajan: certification must be reasonable, judged by an ordinary person of common sense Prior restraint across media Incitement, proximity and the remaining grounds Speech becomes punishable when it incites, not when it merely discusses or advocates. United States: Schenck (1919) — clear and present danger from anti-draft leaflets; Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) — advocacy protected unless directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it. India: Kedar Nath Singh (1962) saved section 124A by confining sedition to words with a tendency or intention to create disorder or incite violence — strong criticism of government is protected; Rangarajan (1989) — danger not “remote, conjectural or far-fetched,” a spark in a powder keg; Shreya Singhal (2015) — discussion, advocacy and incitement distinguished; only incitement can be restricted. A caution: Arup Bhuyan v. State of Assam (2011) adopted Brandenburg for membership of banned organisations; a larger bench overruled that holding in 2023, warning against importing American doctrine without regard to 19(2)–(4). A fiery speech nobody acts on is rhetoric, not incitement. Sovereignty and integrity: restricting advocacy of secession or cession of territory; Parliament used it to enact UAPA, 1967; section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 now penalises acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity. A student asked how violation is “quantified” — it is not measured: the State points to a law, shows the speech falls within it, and shows a proximate link to the harm. Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995): raising separatist slogans a few times, with no response and no disorder, is not an offence. Contempt: Articles 129 and 215 and the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; fair criticism of a judgment is permitted (E.M.S. Namboodiripad ). Defamation: tort and crime (sections 499–500 IPC, now section 356 BNS); Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) upheld criminal defamation, treating reputation as part of Article 21; Khushboo shows the limit — only a person actually aggrieved may complain. Decency or morality: wider than obscenity, not confined to sexual morality (Ramesh Yeshwant Prabhoo, 1996). Friendly relations: added 1951, rarely litigated — targets propaganda damaging relations with another country, not criticism of its policies. Security of the State: rebellion, waging war — the innermost circle.

sections.title: Part 4 — Comparative Constitutional Law
sections.html:
India writes its limits into the constitutional text; the United States leaves them to the courts; the international instruments follow the Indian pattern of right plus limitation clause.

PointIndiaUnited States
TextRight in 19(1)(a); eight grounds in 19(2)Absolute wording; no restriction clause
PointIndiaUnited States
HolderCitizens“The people”; the bar is on government
Source of limitsLegislation tested by courts for reasonablenessJudicial doctrine
PressNot named; read into 19(1)(a)Named expressly
IncitementProximity — spark in a powder keg (Rangarajan); incitement stage (Shreya Singhal)Imminent lawless action (Brandenburg)
Prior restraint of filmsUpheld (K.A. Abbas)Allowed only with strict procedural safeguards
ObscenityCommunity standard test (Aveek Sarkar), borrowed from RothRoth, refined in Miller v. California (1973)
Criminal defamationUpheld (Subramanian Swamy)Largely displaced by New York Times v. Sullivan (1964)

India and the United States compared

How Indian courts use American cases: persuasive on the guarantee's purpose, not its limits — K.A. Abbas and Rangarajan both say the First Amendment's absolute wording makes its case law an unsafe guide; Abbas quotes Douglas J. conceding that a “reasonable regulation” clause like India's leaves room for censorship; CAB borrowed the viewers' rights idea from Red Lion but rejected the scarcity argument on the facts. The framers learned from American experience: Dr. Ambedkar defended the limitation clauses in the Constituent Assembly by citing American decisions holding free speech not absolute. “Marketplace of ideas” traces to Holmes J.'s dissent in Abrams v. United States (1919). The U.S. case ladder: Schenck (1919); Whitney v. California (1927, Brandeis J. concurring — the remedy for bad speech is more speech); Brandenburg (1969); Near v. Minnesota (1931) and New York Times v. United States (1971) — prior restraint's heavy presumption of invalidity; Roth (1957); Joseph Burstyn v. Wilson (1952) — motion pictures protected; Sullivan (1964) — public officials must prove actual malice; Red Lion Broadcasting (1969) — viewers' and listeners' rights paramount.

InstrumentProvisionWhat it protectsLimitsUsed in
Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948Article 19Opinion and expression; to seek, receive and impart information through any mediaGeneral clause in Article 29LIC v. Manubhai Shah
ICCPR, 1966Articles 19, 20Opinion without interference; expression in any mediumProvided by law and necessary for rights or reputations, national security, public order, public health or morals; Article 20 bars war propaganda and incitement to hatredIndia acceded 1979
European Convention, 1950Article 10To hold opinions and receive and impart informationPrescribed by law and necessary in a democratic society; broadcasting may be licensedCAB, paras 37 and 163
French Declaration, 1789Articles 11, 4Free communication of thoughts and opinionsResponsibility for abuse defined by lawCAB, para 167

The international instruments

The First Amendment debate and Nehru's speech

Nehru's case: the courts had read Article 19 so widely that Parliament could not legislate for public order. The Bill was introduced 12 May 1951, referred to a Select Committee on 16 May, passed 2 June 1951 by 228 votes to 20. His argument, in paraphrase: the Constitution had been “kidnapped and purloined by lawyers”; judicial readings were blocking social and economic policy; the amendment was enabling only — it restricted no speech itself and restored Parliament's lawmaking power, still subject to judicial review; he criticised the press's tone — freedom carries responsibility; on sedition he called section 124A “highly objectionable and obnoxious” — yet the new public order ground later saved that section in Kedar Nath Singh. The Statement of Objects and Reasons cited courts holding a person not culpable “even if he advocates murder and other crimes of violence” — the Patna ruling. The opposition, led by Syama Prasad Mookerjee, argued a provisional Parliament chosen before the first general election should not cut back fundamental rights — though he accepted that adding “reasonable” was an improvement. For the verbatim speech: Parliamentary Debates of the Provisional Parliament, 16 May to 2 June 1951; book-length accounts: Granville Austin, Working a Democratic Constitution (1999); Tripurdaman Singh, Sixteen Stormy Days (2020).

Article 21 and the death penalty — why no right is absolute

Article 21's exception is in its text: no deprivation of life or liberty “except according to procedure established by law.” If even life may be taken by law, speech cannot be absolute. Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) upheld the death penalty but confined it to the “rarest of rare”; Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) requires a balance sheet of aggravating and mitigating circumstances for each accused. The “blue drum” case, corrected: the class was told the lover received death and the wife twenty years — that does not match the record as of 5 October 2026. Saurabh Rajput was killed in Meerut in March 2025, his body found in a cement-filled blue drum; on 30 September 2026 the Meerut district court convicted his wife Muskan Rastogi and Sahil Shukla of murder; sentencing is listed for 14 October 2026, the prosecution seeking death for both. Points of law for the discussion: (1) conspiracy and abetment carry the same punishment as the offence — a student's claim that conspiracy does not attract death is incorrect (Kehar Singh, 1988); (2) sentencing is individual — same murder, different sentences for different roles and mitigating circumstances; (3) murder has only two punishments — death or life; a trial court cannot impose “twenty years”; only the High Court or Supreme Court may fix a term without remission as a death alternative (Swamy Shraddananda, 2008); (4) motherhood is a mitigating factor, not a bar — no rule exempts a mother. The Shabnam case (Amroha): April 2008 — Shabnam and Saleem killed seven members of her family; she was pregnant at arrest, delivered in jail in December 2008, the child fostered at about six; death sentences 2010, confirmed in Shabnam v. State of U.P. (2015), review dismissed January 2020, mercy petitions rejected — a student's claim that she “was hanged” is wrong: the latest reports (2021) record a sentence awaiting a death warrant and no execution. Shabnam v. Union of India (2015) separately holds a death warrant cannot issue until legal remedies are exhausted. Pregnant women: the High Court must commute a pregnant woman's death sentence to life (section 416 CrPC, now section 456 BNSS); before a 2009 amendment it could only postpone execution; Article 6(5) ICCPR likewise forbids execution of pregnant women — the rule protects a woman pregnant when the sentence falls due, which did not help Shabnam, whose child was born before trial ended.

sections.title: Part 6 — The Twenty-Five Study Questions, Answered
sections.html:
#Question (compressed)Answer: the case and the proposition
1Why did Romesh Thappar refuse to sever section 9(1-A)?Language wide enough for both valid and invalid applications is void as a whole — the overbreadth idea; post-1951 the same ban would be tested for reasonableness and proximity on the public order ground
#Question (compressed)Answer: the case and the proposition
2Does the First Amendment vindicate Fazl Ali J.'s dissent?Both: it vindicates his view that serious disorder endangers the State — and confirms the majority's reading of the 1950 text (public order genuinely was not listed)
3What does Brij Bhushan decide about pre-censorship as such?That it is a restriction needing a 19(2) ground — not that all print pre-censorship is void; the Organiser order would today be tested under public order plus Virendra safeguards
4Which V.G. Row factors did the Madras law fail?Procedural fairness above all — no personal notice though membership was criminalised, and judicial inquiry shut out; a binding Advisory Board cannot cure that except in very exceptional circumstances
5Abbas's stage-difference vs Blackstone's no-prior-restraintBoth hold for different media: prior restraint is permissible only with a legal basis, standards, time limits and appeal — Blackstone's absolute rule belongs to print's history, not Indian law
6LIC hypotheticals: not “State”; no counter printed; private funding(a) No Article 12 duty — the ruling collapses; (b) no right of reply arises absent the one-sided publication; (c) the public-funds rationale fails — the ruling was confined to its peculiar facts
7Sawant J. vs Jeevan Reddy J. on private broadcastingSawant: airwaves public property, independent regulator; Jeevan Reddy: no citizen's right to a station — Parliament decides; a would-be broadcaster must look to legislation
8Khushboo had she advocated an offenceAdvocacy is protected until incitement (Shreya Singhal); urging an offence with proximity could be restricted — the reasoning would move from obscenity to incitement analysis
9Should the message matter in obscenity?Yes — Bobby Art and Aveek Sarkar read depictions with their message; the same photograph in a perfume advertisement, stripped of the anti-racist context, would likely fail
10Padma awardee prints “Padma Shri” on a posterBalaji Raghavan: awards are not titles but must not be used as prefix or suffix — he should forfeit the award
11Reconciling Brij Bhushan with AbbasThe distinction rests on medium and safeguards together; a streamed film belongs with film (sight, sound, mass reach), while the transmission platform engages Sakal's direct-effect test
12The dissemination chainThappar: circulation is speech; Sakal: price-page laws cut circulation; Odyssey: telecast is expression; LIC: the reply; CAB: the right to receive and the airwaves
13Odyssey's reserved question after CABAnswered in part: the organiser may telecast through an agency of its choice; a private station remains for Parliament (Jeevan Reddy J.)
14Would Udeshi survive Aveek Sarkar?Possibly not on the merits — community standards, the whole work and its context might exonerate the novel — though Udeshi's strict liability for sellers and modified-Hicklin method would be gone
15V.G. Row's “disproportion” vs modern proportionalityThe same idea in looser form: one factor among five, now a structured four-part review (aim, suitability, necessity, balance)
16Two-month State-wide ban citing “likelihood of communal tension”Test the five steps: statutory basis (yes, PSA); public order (listed); proximate link (likelihood must be real, not conjectural — Lohia); proportionality (two months, whole State — overbroad); procedure (notice, reasons) — likely fails steps 3–5
17DM circular, no statutory backing, clearing college magazinesFails step 1 — “law” means statute or statutory rule; bare executive instructions cannot restrict speech (Beg J. in Bennett Coleman; LIC)
#Question (compressed)Answer: the case and the proposition
18Speaker A (thin crowd, break-up-the-country) vs Speaker B (armed crowd, burn the police station now)A: Balwant Singh — slogans without response or disorder are not an offence; B: Rangarajan's spark in a powder keg and Shreya Singhal's incitement stage — punishable
19University journal refuses a student's rejoinder (Dongargaon)If publicly funded, the university is “State” and LIC applies; if private, LIC does not — its right-of-reply reasoning rests on State action and public funds
20Federation sells exclusive rights; public broadcaster demands the feedCAB helps both sides — viewers' rights paramount, no monopoly; but the feed-sharing rule itself comes from the Sports Broadcasting Signals Act, 2007
21News portal publishes A calling B a thief — libel or slander?A recording is permanent form — libel; but Indian criminal law treats spoken and written defamation alike, so the classification matters little here
22Injunction against a Partition serialRefuse: Ramesh (message of peace, strong-minded viewer), Rangarajan (State must protect speech from hostile audiences), Odyssey (no injunction on non-listed grounds)
23Spark in a powder keg vs imminent lawless actionComparable stringency; the difference is textual — “in the interests of public order” plus reasonableness lets Indian courts weigh proximity case by case against a listed ground
24Why India upholds film pre-certification and criminal defamation when America would notBecause Article 19(2) lists grounds and permits “reasonable restrictions” — the First Amendment's absolute text forces judge-made exceptions (Abbas; Subramanian Swamy)
25Did the First Amendment narrow or strengthen the right?Both: it added grounds (narrowing) and the word “reasonable” (strengthening) — every restriction now faces judicial review (V.G. Row), as the 1950 cases could not ensure

The reading list (the lecturer first said “N.M. Thomas” and corrected himself to P.J. Thomas — N.M. Thomas being a reservation case)

Corrections

Where the lecture and the judgments differ — seven points to correct before writing them in an exam: (1) The community standard test is not from Ranjit Udeshi — Udeshi expressly refused to discard Hicklin and only qualified it; Aveek Sarkar (2014) is the authority. (2) The ten-page limit is Bennett Coleman, not Sakal — Sakal (1961) struck down the price-to-pages schedule; Bennett Coleman (1972) struck down the flat ten-page ceiling; the chain the lecturer described (fewer advertisements, higher price, lower circulation, closure) is Sakal's reasoning, repeated in Bennett Coleman. (3) The “Indian Express” lease was never cancelled — Express Newspapers (1985) quashed two show-cause notices (re-entry on the lease; demolition); the other Indian Express case concerns newsprint duty. (4) Tata Press did not overrule Hamdard Dawakhana — a three-judge bench cannot overrule five; it read Hamdard as confined to advertisements of prohibited drugs, relying on Indian Express (1985). (5) This Lohia case is a preventive detention case — the concentric circles come from Hidayatullah J. reading “public order” in rule 30(1)(b) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, while Article 19 stood suspended; the distinction is now used to read “public order” in 19(2), and Anuradha Bhasin repeats the circles when judging section 144 orders. (6) “Law” need not itself be an Act of the legislature — the tested restrictions came through statutory orders and rules (the Price and Page Order 1960 in Sakal; rule 458 of the Telegraph Rules in Tata Press; the Suspension Rules 2017 in Anuradha Bhasin); what fails is bare executive policy with no statute behind it — Beg J.'s ground in Bennett Coleman. (7) Proportionality has more than one formulation — the class's four steps (aim, rational connection, necessity, balancing) are the earlier cases' statement; Columbia's analysis of Anuradha Bhasin reports the Court's own five-point summary (legitimate goal, necessity, alternatives considered, least restrictive measure, judicial review) — the student who added judicial review was right about this case. Two points the lecture got exactly right: “better administration” is not a ground (Sakal — no “interests of the general public” head); and the two-drunks example is Hidayatullah J.'s own illustration in Lohia.

sections.title: The Briefs
sections.html:
Case

Hans Muller v. Superintendent, Presidency Jail, Calcutta (1955)

AIR 1955 SC 367 · per Bose J. — closing pages only required

Facts
Hans Muller, a West German subject, arrested 18 September 1954 and detained under section 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 with a view to expulsion; his passport endorsed for return only; a German fraud warrant and extradition request pending; the Centre's signed expulsion order held back once he moved the High Court.
Held
(1) Competence: Entries 9–10, Union List — preventive detention connected with foreign affairs; the Foreigners Act, 1946 supported. (2) Articles 21 and 22 protect “citizen and foreigner alike.” (3) Detention to arrange expulsion is genuinely preventive — preventing evasion. (4) A State may act in anticipation of the Centre's order. (5) Excluding certain British subjects from “foreigner” is a reasonable classification. (6) Article 19's rights to move and reside have “no corresponding” foreigner rights — all a foreigner is guaranteed is life and liberty under Article 21. (7) Expulsion power is “absolute and unfettered.” (8) Expulsion is not extradition — the expelled person leaves a free man; government may choose the Foreigners Act route even where extradition is requested. (9) Bad faith not shown.
Principle
Cite for: Article 19 is confined to citizens. Be precise — the Court spoke of the rights to move and reside, in an expulsion case; free speech by a foreigner was not in issue. The same visitor still has Articles 14 and 21.
Case

Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1965)

AIR 1966 SC 740 · Sarkar, Hidayatullah, Raghubar Dayal, Mudholkar, Bachawat JJ. · Lohia argued in person · released 4:1

Facts
The 1962 Chinese-attack Emergency; the Defence of India Rules' rule 30(1)(b) permitting detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “public safety” and “maintenance of public order” — not “law and order.” On 9 August 1965 the Patna District Magistrate ordered Lohia's detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “the public safety and the maintenance of law and order”; served 1.40 a.m.; Hazaribagh Central Jail by 3.30 p.m.; Lohia's Hindi letter from jail became the writ petition.
Held
(1) The petition was entertainable: the Article 359 order bars petitions only where liberty was taken “under” the Act — whether it was so taken must itself be examined; the President's order “did not make lawless actions lawful.” (2) Sarkar J.: the order is the only warrant and must be strictly in the rule's terms; “public order” in an emergency law means disorder of a grave nature, “law and order” lesser local disorder (rowdiness at Holi); the State cannot use an affidavit to show the order meant what it does not say; one valid and one invalid ground (public safety valid; law and order not) — under Shibban Lal Saksena the whole order falls. (3) Hidayatullah J. (with Bachawat J.): disorder is a spectrum; two drunkards quarrelling cause disorder, not public disorder — if the two belong to rival communities and one stirs communal passion, public disorder is “apprehended”; the circles — “Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State”; by writing “law and order” the Magistrate “was adding a clause to the Defence of India Rules.” (4) Mudholkar J.: the words made the order ambiguous on its face. Dissent (Raghubar Dayal J.): actual satisfaction, not form, controls; the file note showed public order satisfaction.
Principle
The three concentric circles; for Article 19(2) only the inner two circles are grounds — a mere law and order problem is not.

(Raghubar Dayal J. dissenting)

Case

Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India (1961)

AIR 1962 SC 305 · unanimous Constitution Bench · per Mudholkar J. · G.S. Pathak for petitioners; M.C. Setalvad, Attorney-General,

Facts
Sakal, the Marathi daily from Poona (circulation ~52,000 weekdays, 56,000 Sundays; six pages at 7 naye paise, Sunday ten at 12), and two readers' petitions, against the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Order, 1960 — a schedule fixing maximum pages per price; supplements only on 26 January, 15 August, once a quarter, else by permission.
Held
Section 3(1) unconstitutional. (1) Press freedom is within 19(1)(a) — Brij Bhushan. (2) Circulation is part of the right — “not merely to the matter which he is entitled to circulate, but also to the volume of circulation.” (3) The real purpose was to cut circulation — a minimum price for pages makes papers too costly for a class of readers. (4) Price affects circulation (the Press Commission's findings: Free Press Journal's price cut doubled circulation; two Tamil dailies' price rise lost 33,000 readers). (5) Cutting pages compels restricting news; cutting advertisements forces prices up — “no remote, but a direct consequence,” a vicious cycle ending in closure. (6) Supplement control leaves issues to government's “sweet will and pleasure.” (7) 19(2) is exhaustive — nothing allows restriction for the general public or a section. (8) 19(6) cannot be borrowed — each freedom has its own clause; the State cannot regulate the business side “by directly and immediately curtailing” speech. (9) The test is direct effect: a law capping a named paper's subscribers would be void; achieving it through a rate schedule makes no difference. (10) A good object (checking monopoly) does not save bad means — “a dangerous weapon which is capable of being used against democracy itself.” The Article 14 point and the readers' standing were left undecided.
Principle
Indirect restrictions on the press: the State cannot do through price, pages or advertisements what it cannot do directly.

for the Union

Case

Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1972)

(1972) 2 SCC 788 · Sikri C.J., Ray, Jaganmohan Reddy, Mathew, Beg JJ. · 4:1 (Mathew J. dissenting) · Palkhivala, Daphtary,

Facts
Four groups — Bennett Coleman (Times of India), Hindustan Times, Express Newspapers, The Hindu — against the Newsprint Policy 1972-73: a 10-page quota ceiling (Remark V); circulation growth 10% for dailies under 1,00,000 but 3% for larger (VII(a)); a 20% page increase for under-10-page dailies usable only for pages (VII(c)); no page increases by cutting circulation, no quota shifting within common ownership units (VIII); no new newspaper or edition even within quota (X).
Held
Two preliminary objections rejected: a company is not a citizen — but under R.C. Cooper shareholders do not lose rights by incorporating; Article 358 (1971 Emergency) does not protect executive action lacking legislative authority. The majority (Ray J.): rationing scarce newsprint is allowed — but “shortage of newsprint can stop with allotment”; the test is direct effect, not pith and substance; the policy directly controlled page growth, circulation and advertisement space. The ten-page ceiling: the three Times editions averaged 13.13, 13.99 and 17.83 pages — cuts of 23.8%, 28.4%, 43.8% against a 4.5% newsprint fall; The Hindu faced 16 to 10. Unequals treated as equals — Article 14 violated. Estimated losses: Rs. 39 lakh (Bennett Coleman), Rs. 44 lakh (Hindustan Times), Rs. 38 lakh (The Hindu). Remarks V, VII(a), VII(c), VIII struck down under Articles 14 and 19(1)(a); X under 19(1)(a). Press liberty is “an Ark of the Covenant.” Beg J. concurring: the conditions had no authority of law at all. Mathew J. dissenting: “an abridgment of speech, but not an abridgment of the freedom of speech”; Article 19(1)(a) is not “the guardian of unlimited talkativeness”; the community's right to hear supports maximum circulation; Article 39(b) validates the small-dailies' classification.
Principle
The effect test — judge a measure by its direct effect on the right, not its label or purpose; shareholders and editors can enforce 19(1)(a) through the company.

Nambyar for petitioners; F.S. Nariman for the Union

Case

Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1985)

(1986) 1 SCC 133 · A.P. Sen, Venkataramiah, Misra JJ. · F.S. Nariman for petitioners

Facts
The press enclave on Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg; Express Newspapers' plots leased from 1954; building only east of a diagonal sewer under the 1957 agreement; 1977 request to divert and build with double basement; DDA and Ministry approvals (1978); Rs. 1.30 crore spent by February 1980. Then: 17 February 1980 — Jagmohan takes office as Lieutenant-Governor and that Sunday evening calls for the municipal files; 29 February — the Zonal Engineer's locks broken to remove the file; 1 March — press conference announcing an inquiry by three subordinates in three days and a demolition warning, broadcast on radio and television; 1 March — a show-cause notice for demolition; 10 March — a notice to show cause on lease re-entry; 12 March — the committee's report released at another press conference. The Indian Express had published on Jagmohan's role in the Turkman Gate demolitions during the Emergency.
Held
Both notices quashed. The Lieutenant-Governor confused power over Union property (Entry 32, Union List) with his Article 239 powers — nearness to the Centre gave him no authority over its property. A.P. Sen J.: the notices “are intended and meant to silence the voice of the Indian Express” — a direct and immediate threat to press freedom, violating 19(1)(a) read with 14; a writ lies though the matter looks contractual; the re-entry notice was real, not exploratory; summary eviction was unavailable; mala fides — power used for an alien purpose is bad faith; the specific allegations were met only with bare denials; nothing was contemplated before 17 February; promissory estoppel binds the successor government. Venkataramiah J.: arbitrary, without independent application of mind — Article 14. Misra J.: the land rights spring from contract and planning law, not 19(1)(a) — a matter for a civil suit.
Principle
Administrative harassment of a newspaper as an indirect attack on press freedom (Sen J.); the model of proving mala fides from a detailed chronology. Do not write that the lease was cancelled — two show-cause notices issued, both quashed.
Case

Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) Lal Kuan v. Union of India (1959)

AIR 1960 SC 554 · per Kapur J. · K.M. Munshi and N.C. Chatterjee for petitioners; C.K. Daphtary, Solicitor-General, for the Union

Facts
The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954: “advertisement” defined widely (labels, cartons, leaflets); “magic remedy” includes talisman, mantra, kavacha; section 3 barred advertisements suggesting drugs for miscarriage, contraception, sexual capacity or venereal disease “or any other disease... specified in rules”; section 8 allowed seizure. Hamdard, the Delhi Unani house, was stopped from advertising forty products; the Poona branch of Sadhana Ausadhalaya was raided without warrant.
Held
Method: find the law's true nature and character — history, mischief, remedy; presumption of constitutionality. History: the 1927 Council of State resolution, the Chopra Committee, the Drugs Act 1940, the Bhatia Committee 1953, English statutes. The evil: self-medication driven by extravagant advertising to a credulous public. Article 19(1)(a): “An advertisement is no doubt a form of speech but its true character is reflected by the object for the promotion of which it is employed” — a commercial advertisement does not propagate social, political or economic ideas; advertising prohibited drugs is not speech (relying on Valentine v. Chrestensen). 19(1)(f)/(g): reasonable in the general public's interest. But: section 3(d)'s delegation — naming further diseases by rule with no criteria — “uncanalised and uncontrolled power,” void; the Rules' Schedule fell with it (severable). Section 8's seizure power went far beyond the Act's purpose and lacked safeguards — void; mandamus to return seized goods.
Principle
The starting point of the commercial speech story (1959: purely commercial advertising outside 19(1)(a)) — and a leading case on excessive delegation. Confined by later cases to its facts.
Case

Tata Press Ltd. v. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. (1995)

(1995) 5 SCC 139 · per Kuldip Singh J. · Dr. Abhishek Singhvi for Tata Press; K.K. Venugopal and Arun Jaitley for the Nigam

Facts
MTNL (80% government-held, licensee under the Telegraph Act 1885) gave directory publishing to contractors earning from Yellow Pages advertising; Tata Press published its own Yellow Pages buyers' guide (Bombay editions 1992-94); rule 458 of the Telegraph Rules, 1951 bars publishing “any list of telephone subscribers” without permission; the City Court dismissed MTNL's suit, the Single Judge and Division Bench of Bombay reversed and enjoined.
Held
Appeal allowed. Hamdard rested on Valentine v. Chrestensen — but American law moved: Sullivan (1964), Bigelow v. Virginia (1975), Virginia State Board of Pharmacy (1976 — a free flow of commercial information is indispensable), Bates v. State Bar of Arizona (lawyer advertising allowed; false and misleading advertising restrainable). The Indian text differs: Article 19(2) itself lists the restrictions — deceptive, unfair, misleading and untruthful commercial speech is hit by 19(2). Hamdard confined: it dealt with prohibited drugs; Indian Express (1985) had already called its wider observations too broad. Advertising pays most of the media's cost (60-80% of newspaper revenue) — Sakal and Bennett Coleman show curbing advertisements hits circulation. The receiver's right: the recipient may have a deeper interest than the advertiser (the life-saving drug example). Holding: “Commercial speech” is part of 19(1)(a). Application: a telephone directory is a public utility the authority may regulate; paid Yellow Pages advertising is not that service; a 19(1)(a) right cannot be denied by creating a government monopoly; Tata's guide is compiled by trade, not by subscription — not a “list of subscribers.” Rule 458 remains mandatory for white-pages entries.
Principle
Commercial advertisements are protected speech; listeners and readers have their own right to receive. Limits: false, misleading or deceptive advertising may be restrained (the judgment does not say which 19(2) head covers it — a gap for critical answers). It did not overrule Hamdard.
Case

Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra (1964)

AIR 1965 SC 881 · Gajendragadkar C.J., Wanchoo, Hidayatullah, Shah, Rajagopala Ayyangar JJ. · per Hidayatullah J. · R.K. Garg

Facts
Four partners of Bombay's Happy Book Stall found with unexpurgated Lady Chatterley's Lover; one sold a copy to a decoy customer; all convicted under section 292 IPC (fines of Rs. 20); Mulk Raj Anand testified to the novel's literary merit.
Held
(1) Section 292 valid — a reasonable restriction in the interests of decency or morality; obscenity has “extremely poor value” in spreading ideas, though where ideas of public interest are conveyed (the medical textbook) the balance tilts toward speech. (2) Knowledge of obscenity is not an ingredient — no “knowingly” in the section; liability is strict, though absence of knowledge may mitigate sentence. (3) The test: Hicklin set out (tendency to deprave and corrupt susceptible minds), “uniformly applied in India”; mere treatment of sex and nudity in art is not obscenity “without something more” — Michelangelo's angels need not wear breeches; but “We do not think that it should be discarded.” Three qualifications: not stray words — the whole work viewed overall; yet the obscene matter also considered “by itself and separately”; art must so preponderate as to throw obscenity into shadow. Obscenity “without a preponderating social purpose or profit” has no protection — judged “by our national standards.” (4) The novel: Lawrence's sincerity accepted, but the sexual descriptions were its only attraction for the common reader; the law protects “not those who can protect themselves”; the impugned portions passed permissible limits; no preponderating social gain shown. Appeal dismissed. (Contrast: the English Central Criminal Court in R. v. Penguin Books had held the same novel not obscene.)
Principle
Cite for “Hicklin as modified,” not for the community standard test; and for the seller's strict liability.
