Case

Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014) — the brief

Facts
Stern's Becker-Feltus photograph (taken by her father), reproduced by Sports World (cover story, 5 May 1993) and Anandabazar Patrika (6 May 1993); the Alipore lawyer's complaint under section 292 IPC and section 4 of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986; summons 10 May 1993; the High Court refusing to quash. (An earlier lecture called the fiancée South African; the judgment calls her a dark-skinned film actress, the complainant a German film actress.)
Held
Standards change (paras 12-19) — Udeshi, Kakodkar, Samaresh Bose, Khushboo each stressed contemporary values; the yardstick (para 19): “contemporary mores and national standards,” not the susceptible group. Hicklin judged by isolated passages and the most susceptible readers; Roth (1957) moved to the average person; Canada followed in Towne Cinema and Butler. Para 24: “We are also of the view that Hicklin test is not the correct test” — the community standard test applies; nudity is not obscenity per se — only material exciting lustful thoughts; the message and context (paras 25-26, following Bobby Art; Ajay Goswami). The photograph: standing close, Becker's arm covering her breast, taken by her own father; the message — skin colour matters little, love prevails; no tendency to deprave. Proceedings quashed.
Principle
Three working rules: the average person, not the most susceptible; the work as a whole; context and message. The standard is national and contemporary. For criticism: a two-judge bench declared Hicklin incorrect although the five-judge bench in Udeshi had declined to discard it.
Case

Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996)

(1996) 4 SCC 1 · Ahmadi C.J., Bharucha, Kirpal JJ. · per Bharucha J.

Facts
Bandit Queen, from Mala Sen's book (on sale since 1991 without objection): Phoolan Devi married as a child, raped, humiliated by police, gang-raped, stripped and paraded naked, turning dacoit and to revenge. The Tribunal (Lentin J., retired Bombay High Court, and three women members) allowed the coarse language (ordinary speech in the Chambal), kept the police-beating scene (it explains her turning), cut the second of three rape sequences and trimmed the first and third, kept the naked parade whole — cutting it “would be a sacrilege,” comparing Schindler's List's frontal nudity. The Delhi High Court quashed the certificate. The petitioner: a Gujjar claiming the film slurred his community (the rapist named Babu Gujjar) and Indian womanhood.
Held
'A' certificate restored. The guidelines are broad standards, not a statute — clause 2's sub-clauses cannot outweigh clauses 1 and 3. Where the theme is of social relevance it must prevail; this film “is not a pretty story” — it accuses the society that tormented her. The naked parade: those who stripped her meant to demean her; showing it conveys exactly that — sympathy for the victim, disgust for the perpetrators; “Nakedness does not always arouse the baser instinct.” The High Court's error: the revulsion the Tribunal spoke of was at the sadism of the strippers, not her nudity. Rape is shown for its terrifying effect, not glorified. The test: for a serious film, ask of each scene — does it advance the message? If so, leave it alone, with an 'A' certificate. A film illustrating a social evil must necessarily show the evil; a film extolling it is impermissible; the depiction must be just sufficient. Deference to the expert multi-member Tribunal (three of four members women); the writ court ought not to have entertained a petition resting on a community slur.
Principle
Nudity is not obscene by itself — context and purpose decide; the “advance the message” test that Aveek Sarkar later applied to a photograph.
Case

Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)

(2020) 3 SCC 637 · N.V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy, B.R. Gavai JJ. · (brief written from Columbia's case analysis plus four

Facts
2 August 2019 — J&K; Home Department advises tourists and Amarnath pilgrims to leave; schools and offices closed. 4 August — mobile networks, internet and landlines shut; District Magistrates impose section 144 CrPC. 5 August — the constitutional order ending Article 370's special status. Anuradha Bhasin, editor of the Kashmir Times (Srinagar), unable to publish since 6 August; Ghulam Nabi Azad M.P.; an intervenor noting restrictions described as temporary had lasted over 100 days. The State: cross-border terrorism history (similar steps in 2016); the internet never restricted in Jammu and Ladakh; social media's one-to-many reach; selective blocking not technically possible; newspaper standards do not carry over to the internet.
Held
(1) Orders must be produced and published — Article 32 remedies and the right to information require it; no law affecting rights should be passed in secret. (2) The internet: the most used and accessible medium of information; trade and commerce through it are protected under 19(1)(g) subject to 19(6); expression through it is integral to 19(1)(a), restrictable only under 19(2) — but no fundamental right of access to the internet was declared (no party argued for one). (3) A restriction may in a proper case amount to complete prohibition, but the government must explain why lesser measures would not do. (4) Proportionality: whether the least restrictive choice was made (para 53), drawing on Modern Dental College; the Court's own five points — legitimate goal, necessity, alternatives considered, least restrictive measure, judicial review; the restriction's degree, scope, territory and duration must match necessity (para 71). (5) Shutdowns: governed by the 2017 Suspension Rules under the Telegraph Act — only the Union or State Home Secretary (or a Joint Secretary in unavoidable circumstances, confirmed within 24 hours); reasons recorded; Review Committee; section 5(2) requires “public emergency” or “public safety” of a serious nature; orders must be published for challenge; complete suspension is drastic — only if necessary and unavoidable after assessing alternatives (para 99); indefinite suspension impermissible. (6) Section 144: only where danger exists or is apprehended, in the nature of an emergency; cannot suppress legitimate expression; orders must state material facts — mechanical or cryptic orders unlawful; repetitive orders are abuse; the concentric circles repeated (para 120). (7) Press freedom valuable under 19(1)(a), but no evidence publication was actually stopped — no sword of Damocles may “hang over the press indefinitely” (para 151). Order: the Government to review all suspension and section 144 orders, publish them, and withdraw those unnecessary or without time limits.
Principle
Proportionality as the present meaning of “reasonable”; the internet as protected medium (without overstating access as a right); restriction orders must be published and reasoned. Critics note: principles laid down, no immediate relief given.

Superintendent, Presidency Jail, Calcutta (1955) AIR 1955 SC 367 · per Bose J. — closing pages only required Facts Hans Muller , a West German subject, arrested 18 September 1954 and detained under section 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 with a view to expulsion; his passport endorsed for return only; a German fraud warrant and extradition request pending; the Centre's signed expulsion order held back once he moved the High Court. Held (1) Competence: Entries 9–10, Union List — preventive detention connected with foreign affairs; the Foreigners Act, 1946 supported. (2) Articles 21 and 22 protect “citizen and foreigner alike.” (3) Detention to arrange expulsion is genuinely preventive — preventing evasion. (4) A State may act in anticipation of the Centre's order. (5) Excluding certain British subjects from “foreigner” is a reasonable classification. (6) Article 19's rights to move and reside have “no corresponding” foreigner rights — all a foreigner is guaranteed is life and liberty under Article 21. (7) Expulsion power is “absolute and unfettered.” (8) Expulsion is not extradition — the expelled person leaves a free man; government may choose the Foreigners Act route even where extradition is requested. (9) Bad faith not shown. Principle Cite for: Article 19 is confined to citizens. Be precise — the Court spoke of the rights to move and reside, in an expulsion case; free speech by a foreigner was not in issue. The same visitor still has Articles 14 and 21. Case Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1965) AIR 1966 SC 740 · Sarkar, Hidayatullah, Raghubar Dayal, Mudholkar, Bachawat JJ. · Lohia argued in person · released 4:1 Facts The 1962 Chinese-attack Emergency; the Defence of India Rules' rule 30(1)(b) permitting detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “public safety” and “maintenance of public order” — not “law and order.” On 9 August 1965 the Patna District Magistrate ordered Lohia 's detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “the public safety and the maintenance of law and order”; served 1.40 a.m.; Hazaribagh Central Jail by 3.30 p.m.; Lohia 's Hindi letter from jail became the writ petition. Held (1) The petition was entertainable: the Article 359 order bars petitions only where liberty was taken “under” the Act — whether it was so taken must itself be examined; the President's order “did not make lawless actions lawful.” (2) Sarkar J.: the order is the only warrant and must be strictly in the rule's terms; “public order” in an emergency law means disorder of a grave nature, “law and order” lesser local disorder (rowdiness at Holi); the State cannot use an affidavit to show the order meant what it does not say; one valid and one invalid ground (public safety valid; law and order not) — under Shibban Lal Saksena the whole order falls. (3) Hidayatullah J. (with Bachawat J.): disorder is a spectrum; two drunkards quarrelling cause disorder, not public disorder — if the two belong to rival communities and one stirs communal passion, public disorder is “apprehended”; the circles — “Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State”; by writing “law and order” the Magistrate “was adding a clause to the Defence of India Rules.” (4) Mudholkar J.: the words made the order ambiguous on its face. Dissent (Raghubar Dayal J.): actual satisfaction, not form, controls; the file note showed public order satisfaction. Principle The three concentric circles; for Article 19(2) only the inner two circles are grounds — a mere law and order problem is not. (Raghubar Dayal J. dissenting) Case Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India (1961) AIR 1962 SC 305 · unanimous Constitution Bench · per Mudholkar J. · G.S. Pathak for petitioners; M.C. Setalvad, Attorney-General, Facts Sakal, the Marathi daily from Poona (circulation ~52,000 weekdays, 56,000 Sundays; six pages at 7 naye paise, Sunday ten at 12), and two readers' petitions, against the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Order, 1960 — a schedule fixing maximum pages per price; supplements only on 26 January, 15 August, once a quarter, else by permission. Held Section 3(1) unconstitutional. (1) Press freedom is within 19(1)(a) — Brij Bhushan . (2) Circulation is part of the right — “not merely to the matter which he is entitled to circulate, but also to the volume of circulation.” (3) The real purpose was to cut circulation — a minimum price for pages makes papers too costly for a class of readers. (4) Price affects circulation (the Press Commission's findings: Free Press Journal's price cut doubled circulation; two Tamil dailies' price rise lost 33,000 readers). (5) Cutting pages compels restricting news; cutting advertisements forces prices up — “no remote, but a direct consequence,” a vicious cycle ending in closure. (6) Supplement control leaves issues to government's “sweet will and pleasure.” (7) 19(2) is exhaustive — nothing allows restriction for the general public or a section. (8) 19(6) cannot be borrowed — each freedom has its own clause; the State cannot regulate the business side “by directly and immediately curtailing” speech. (9) The test is direct effect: a law capping a named paper's subscribers would be void; achieving it through a rate schedule makes no difference. (10) A good object (checking monopoly) does not save bad means — “a dangerous weapon which is capable of being used against democracy itself.” The Article 14 point and the readers' standing were left undecided. Principle Indirect restrictions on the press: the State cannot do through price, pages or advertisements what it cannot do directly. for the Union Case Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1972) (1972) 2 SCC 788 · Sikri C.J., Ray, Jaganmohan Reddy, Mathew, Beg JJ. · 4:1 (Mathew J. dissenting) · Palkhivala, Daphtary, Facts Four groups — Bennett Coleman (Times of India), Hindustan Times, Express Newspapers, The Hindu — against the Newsprint Policy 1972-73: a 10-page quota ceiling (Remark V); circulation growth 10% for dailies under 1,00,000 but 3% for larger (VII(a)); a 20% page increase for under-10-page dailies usable only for pages (VII(c)); no page increases by cutting circulation, no quota shifting within common ownership units (VIII); no new newspaper or edition even within quota (X). Held Two preliminary objections rejected: a company is not a citizen — but under R.C. Cooper shareholders do not lose rights by incorporating; Article 358 (1971 Emergency) does not protect executive action lacking legislative authority. The majority (Ray J.): rationing scarce newsprint is allowed — but “shortage of newsprint can stop with allotment”; the test is direct effect, not pith and substance; the policy directly controlled page growth, circulation and advertisement space. The ten-page ceiling: the three Times editions averaged 13.13, 13.99 and 17.83 pages — cuts of 23.8%, 28.4%, 43.8% against a 4.5% newsprint fall; The Hindu faced 16 to 10. Unequals treated as equals — Article 14 violated. Estimated losses: Rs. 39 lakh ( Bennett Coleman ), Rs. 44 lakh (Hindustan Times), Rs. 38 lakh (The Hindu). Remarks V, VII(a), VII(c), VIII struck down under Articles 14 and 19(1)(a); X under 19(1)(a). Press liberty is “an Ark of the Covenant.” Beg J. concurring: the conditions had no authority of law at all. Mathew J. dissenting: “an abridgment of speech, but not an abridgment of the freedom of speech”; Article 19(1)(a) is not “the guardian of unlimited talkativeness”; the community's right to hear supports maximum circulation; Article 39(b) validates the small-dailies' classification. Principle The effect test — judge a measure by its direct effect on the right, not its label or purpose; shareholders and editors can enforce 19(1)(a) through the company. Nambyar for petitioners; F.S. Nariman for the Union Case Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1985) (1986) 1 SCC 133 · A.P. Sen, Venkataramiah, Misra JJ. · F.S. Nariman for petitioners Facts The press enclave on Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg; Express Newspapers' plots leased from 1954; building only east of a diagonal sewer under the 1957 agreement; 1977 request to divert and build with double basement; DDA and Ministry approvals (1978); Rs. 1.30 crore spent by February 1980. Then: 17 February 1980 — Jagmohan takes office as Lieutenant-Governor and that Sunday evening calls for the municipal files; 29 February — the Zonal Engineer's locks broken to remove the file; 1 March — press conference announcing an inquiry by three subordinates in three days and a demolition warning, broadcast on radio and television; 1 March — a show-cause notice for demolition; 10 March — a notice to show cause on lease re-entry; 12 March — the committee's report released at another press conference. The Indian Express had published on Jagmohan's role in the Turkman Gate demolitions during the Emergency. Held Both notices quashed. The Lieutenant-Governor confused power over Union property (Entry 32, Union List) with his Article 239 powers — nearness to the Centre gave him no authority over its property. A.P. Sen J.: the notices “are intended and meant to silence the voice of the Indian Express” — a direct and immediate threat to press freedom, violating 19(1)(a) read with 14; a writ lies though the matter looks contractual; the re-entry notice was real, not exploratory; summary eviction was unavailable; mala fides — power used for an alien purpose is bad faith; the specific allegations were met only with bare denials; nothing was contemplated before 17 February; promissory estoppel binds the successor government. Venkataramiah J.: arbitrary, without independent application of mind — Article 14. Misra J.: the land rights spring from contract and planning law, not 19(1)(a) — a matter for a civil suit. Principle Administrative harassment of a newspaper as an indirect attack on press freedom (Sen J.); the model of proving mala fides from a detailed chronology. Do not write that the lease was cancelled — two show-cause notices issued, both quashed. Case Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) Lal Kuan v. Union of India (1959) AIR 1960 SC 554 · per Kapur J. · K.M. Held Method: find the law's true nature and character — history, mischief, remedy; presumption of constitutionality. History: the 1927 Council of State resolution, the Chopra Committee, the Drugs Act 1940, the Bhatia Committee 1953, English statutes. The evil: self-medication driven by extravagant advertising to a credulous public. Article 19(1)(a): “An advertisement is no doubt a form of speech but its true character is reflected by the object for the promotion of which it is employed” — a commercial advertisement does not propagate social, political or economic ideas; advertising prohibited drugs is not speech (relying on Valentine v. Chrestensen). 19(1)(f)/(g): reasonable in the general public's interest. But: section 3(d)'s delegation — naming further diseases by rule with no criteria — “uncanalised and uncontrolled power,” void; the Rules' Schedule fell with it (severable). Section 8's seizure power went far beyond the Act's purpose and lacked safeguards — void; mandamus to return seized goods. Principle The starting point of the commercial speech story (1959: purely commercial advertising outside 19(1)(a)) — and a leading case on excessive delegation. Confined by later cases to its facts. (5) Shutdowns: governed by the 2017 Suspension Rules under the Telegraph Act — only the Union or State Home Secretary (or a Joint Secretary in unavoidable circumstances, confirmed within 24 hours); reasons recorded; Review Committee; section 5(2) requires “public emergency” or “public safety” of a serious nature; orders must be published for challenge; complete suspension is drastic — only if necessary and unavoidable after assessing alternatives (para 99); indefinite suspension impermissible. (6) Section 144: only where danger exists or is apprehended, in the nature of an emergency; cannot suppress legitimate expression; orders must state material facts — mechanical or cryptic orders unlawful; repetitive orders are abuse; the concentric circles repeated (para 120). (7) Press freedom valuable under 19(1)(a), but no evidence publication was actually stopped — no sword of Damocles may “hang over the press indefinitely” (para 151). Order: the Government to review all suspension and section 144 orders, publish them, and withdraw those unnecessary or without time limits. Principle Proportionality as the present meaning of “reasonable”; the internet as protected medium (without overstating access as a right); restriction orders must be published and reasoned. Critics note: principles laid down, no immediate relief given. readable paragraphs — check quotations against the judgment)

sections.title: Doctrines at a Glance
sections.html:
DoctrineOne-line statementAnchor
Basic structureParliament may amend any provision but cannot destroy the Constitution's identityKesavananda (1973)
Harmonious constructionConflicting provisions are read so both survive in their spheresShankari Prasad (1951)
Prospective overrulingA new rule operates from the judgment date; past transactions standGolaknath (1967)
EclipseA pre-Constitutional inconsistent law is dormant for citizens, alive for others, and revives when the FR changesBhikaji Narain (1955)
SeverabilityVoid only “to the extent” — unless the parts are inseparable or misuse-proneRMDC (1957)
Waiver (no waiver)Fundamental rights are public rights; they cannot be surrenderedBasheshar Nath (1959)
Two-limb classificationIntelligible differentia + rational nexus with the objectAnwar Ali Sarkar (1952)
Non-arbitrarinessArbitrariness is the antithesis of equality — no comparator neededE.P. Royappa (1973)
Golden triangleArticles 14, 19 and 21 are read togetherManeka Gandhi (1978)
Post-decisional hearingUrgent action first; notice and hearing immediately afterManeka Gandhi (1978)
ReasonablenessSubstance and procedure; no abstract standard — weigh right, purpose, urgency, disproportion, conditionsV.G. Row (1952)
ProportionalityLegitimate aim; rational connection; necessity; balance — plus judicial reviewAnuradha Bhasin (2020)
Three circlesLaw and order ⊃ public order ⊃ security of the State — only the inner two ground speech restrictionsLohia (1966)
Community standard testObscenity by the average person, contemporary standards, whole work, context and messageAveek Sarkar (2014)
Creamy layerThe advanced within a backward class are weeded outIndra Sawhney (1992)
50% ceilingReservation ordinarily cannot exceed half — a rule of cautionBalaji (1963) → Indra Sawhney
Rule of Law vs Rule by LawThe law itself must be just, fair and reasonableDicey; North Korea v. India

sections.title: The Professor's Standing Directives
sections.html:
Exam Directives

(1) If asked about the Rule of Law, write a little about India — writing that it came from Western countries costs three marks automatically. (2) Never write “quasi-federal” — the Constitution is federal; federation is basic structure. (3) Chant it five times: Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended — Article 359 now reads “except 20 and 21.” (4) Reading Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh is compulsory — “anyone who does not read it will fail the mid-term” (he has never actually framed a question on it). (5) Do not study from ChatGPT — it fetches the wrong speech and invents arguments; depend on original sources. (6) In answers, use the structure: meaning → dictionary definition → jurist's view. (7) Use simple language in presentations — “repeated,” not “reiterated.” (8) Cite each case only for the point it proves, and read the facts with precision — skip one qualifier (“3-Star”) and the differentia becomes invisible. (9) The law-and-order / public-order / security distinction will be asked in the exam. (10) Read the advocates' arguments — Palkhivala, Jethmalani, Parasaran, Venugopal — and the judges' reasoning: that is how one becomes an expert in law.

day.title: Article 14 worksheet — case map
day.trail: Which decided case each of the 21 worksheet problems is modelled on

sections.title: Case map for the 21 problems
sections.html:
Here is the complete case law mapping for each of the 21 questions in your Article 14 Worksheet:

1. State Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)

  • Principle: Reasonable classification under Article 14.

  • Key Holding: The Supreme Court upheld the exemption granted to military personnel and foreign visitors from the prohibition law (Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949), holding that defence personnel (due to discipline and service conditions) and tourists (due to transient status) form distinct, valid classes with an intelligible differentia having a rational nexus to the law.

2. Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1984)

  • Principle: Lapses of time making an initially valid classification arbitrary.

  • Key Holding: The Supreme Court held that while exempting new buildings from rent control to encourage construction is initially valid, continuing that exemption indefinitely without a time limit becomes discriminatory and unreasonable over time, as older post-cutoff buildings no longer differ from pre-cutoff buildings.

3. Jalan Trading Co. (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Mill Mazdoor Sabha (1967)

  • Principle: Step-by-step or phased implementation of welfare legislation.

  • Key Holding: The legislature is not bound to extend a law to all establishments at once. It can classify based on size (e.g., 50+ workers) or sector (factories, transport) to address problems in phases based on administrative feasibility without violating Article 14.

4. K.T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala (1961)

  • Principle: Equal treatment of unequals (Equality in Taxation) & Unguided Discretion.

  • Key Holding: Imposing a uniform flat tax per acre without considering the productivity/income of the land treats unequally situated landowners as equal, resulting in discrimination. Furthermore, conferring unguided, unchanneled power to exempt "any land" grants arbitrary administrative power.

5. D.S. Nakara v. Union of India (1983)

  • Principle: Cut-off dates creating arbitrary sub-classification within a homogeneous class.

  • Key Holding: All retired government servants form a single homogeneous class. Creating an arbitrary cut-off date to deny revised, liberalized pension benefits to those who retired before that date violates Article 14, as there is no rational nexus to the objective of providing social security.

6. Air India v. Nergesh Meerza (1981)

  • Principle: Gender discrimination, arbitrary service rules, and unguided discretion.

  • Key Holding:

    • Q6a: Maintaining separate cadres for male pursers and female hostesses was valid due to different recruitment sources/conditions.

    • Q6b: Terminating service upon first pregnancy was struck down as arbitrary, offensive, and an insult to Indian womanhood.

    • Q6c: Unbridled power vested in the Managing Director to extend service without standard criteria was held to be arbitrary and violative of Article 14.

7. T. Devadasan v. Union of India (1964) / State of J&K v. Triloki Nath Khosa (1974)

  • Principle: Classification based on educational qualifications within an integrated cadre for promotion.

  • Key Holding: Even if degree-holders and diploma-holders were integrated into a single cadre, the state can subsequently re-classify them for higher promotional avenues based on educational qualifications (degree vs. diploma), as higher academic standards are relevant to higher managerial/technical duties.

8. R.K. Garg v. Union of India (1981)

  • Principle: Economic legislation and latitude given to the legislature (Special Bearer Bonds Act).

  • Key Holding: The Supreme Court upheld immunities for black money holders, holding that economic laws require greater judicial restraint and flexibility. The distinction aimed to unearth black money for national economic revival, providing an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the state's objective.

9. State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976)

  • Principle: Affirmative action, test exemptions, and substantive equality.

  • Key Holding: Granting temporary exemptions from qualifying tests to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to ensure adequate representation in public service is a valid classification under Article 14 (and Article 16(1)), promoting real, substantive equality.

10. Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India (1950)

  • Principle: "Single Person Class" / Single Entity Legislation.

  • Key Holding: A law targeting a single named company (Sholapur Spinning and Weaving Company) can be a valid classification if that single entity exhibits extraordinary circumstances (e.g., severe mismanagement affecting essential supply) that place it in a class by itself.

11. State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952)

  • Principle: Bare administrative discretion to choose trial procedure.

  • Key Holding: Section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act was struck down because it gave the executive unguided, arbitrary power to refer any individual "case" or "offence" to a Special Court with a harsher/speedier procedure without laying down statutory criteria or policy guidelines.

12. Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra (1952)

  • Principle: Statutory classification specifying offences and areas for Special Courts.

  • Key Holding: Distinguished from Anwar Ali Sarkar. Where the statute/ordinance itself identifies specific disturbed regions and specific violent offences to be tried by Special Courts, it lays down a valid legislative policy and does not confer arbitrary executive choice.

13. State of Uttar Pradesh v. Deoman Upadhyaya (1960)

  • Principle: Classification under Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act.

  • Key Holding: Securing information leading to discovery from a person in police custody differs rationally from statements by a person not in custody. The inherent pressure of police custody justifies restricting admissibility only to the part of the statement that leads directly to discovery.

14. East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1962)

  • Principle: Legislative discretion in tax classification across product varieties.

  • Key Holding: The state has broad latitude in choosing what to tax. Taxing Virginia tobacco (higher value, export quality) while exempting country tobacco (chewing, local bidi) is a valid commercial classification.

15. Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar (1958) / State of M.P. v. Bhopal Sugar Industries (1964)

  • Principle: Transitional administrative classifications during state reorganisation.

  • Key Holding: Temporary differential tax or procedural rules applied to newly merged territories during transitional phases following state boundary reorganisations are valid due to practical administrative necessity.

16. Yusuf Abdul Aziz v. State of Bombay (1954)

  • Principle: Validity of Section 497 IPC (Adultery exemption for women) via Article 15(3).

  • Key Holding: Non-prosecution of women for adultery under Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code was upheld as a special protective provision for women permitted under Article 15(3) of the Constitution (Note: Later struck down in Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018) under modern non-arbitrariness jurisprudence).

17. Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2007)

  • Principle: Protective discrimination vs. Romantic Paternalism (Gender equality).

  • Key Holding: A blanket ban prohibiting women from working in liquor-serving premises under the guise of security/protection violates Article 14 and Article 15. The state must provide protection rather than curtailing women's employment opportunities.

18. Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi (1981)

  • Principle: Doctrine of Arbitrariness (New Dimension of Article 14) in interview weightage.

  • Key Holding: Allocating disproportionately high marks (e.g., over 15%) to a brief, 2–3 minute interview leads to arbitrary selection. High oral weightage combined with superficial assessment violates Article 14 due to manifest arbitrariness.

19. Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022)

  • Principle: Constitutionality of 103rd Amendment (EWS Reservation).

  • Key Holding: The Supreme Court upheld the exclusion of SC/ST/OBC communities from the 10% EWS quota, ruling that since SC/ST/OBCs already enjoy separate affirmative action benefits under Articles 15(4) and 16(4), excluding them from EWS prevents double benefits and forms a reasonable classification.

20. Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)

  • Principle: Mandal Commission Case — Caste as an indicator and the Creamy Layer doctrine.

  • Key Holding: Caste can be used as a primary indicator to identify social and educational backwardness. However, to ensure benefits reach the truly disadvantaged, the advanced members ("creamy layer") within a backward class must be excluded.

21. Pratap Singh v. State of Jharkhand (2005)

  • Principle: Determination of juvenility under Juvenile Justice Act.

  • Key Holding: The relevant date for determining whether an accused is a juvenile entitled to the protection of the Juvenile Justice Act is the date of the commission of the offence, not the date of production before the court/authority.

cases.name: Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India
cases.holding: First Amendment upheld: "law" in Art 13(2) means ordinary legislation, not a constitutional amendment made under Art 368; FRs can be amended.

cases.name: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan
cases.holding: 17th Amendment upheld following Shankari Prasad (majority of three); Hidayatullah and Mudholkar JJ., concurring, doubted whether FRs could be abridged — the seed of the basic structure idea.

cases.name: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
cases.holding: 11 judges, 6:5: an amendment is "law" under Art 13(2), so Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights; doctrine of prospective overruling applied.

cases.name: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
cases.holding: 13 judges, 7:6: Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot destroy its basic structure; Golak Nath overruled; 24th Amendment and first part of Art 31C upheld.

cases.name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.holding: Struck down ss. 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment (Art 31C extension and Art 368(4)-(5)): limited amending power, judicial review and the FR–DPSP balance are basic features.

cases.name: Waman Rao v. Union of India
cases.holding: Ninth Schedule laws inserted after 24 April 1973 (the Kesavananda date) are open to basic-structure review. Decided 9 May 1980 (reported (1981) 2 SCC 362).

cases.name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
cases.holding: 9 judges, unanimous: laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be tested against Part III and the basic structure.

cases.name: State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga
cases.holding: Bihar Land Reforms Act largely upheld (protected by Arts 31(4), 31A–31B); certain provisions on arrears and compensation struck down.

cases.name: Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay
cases.holding: Art 13(1) is prospective: a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with FRs is void only from 26 January 1950; past acts and pending prosecutions are not affected.

cases.name: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.holding: Doctrine of eclipse: a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a FR is not dead but eclipsed; it revives when the FR is amended (here, by the First Amendment). Judgment of S.R. Das, Acting C.J.

cases.name: Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.holding: A post-Constitution law that violates a FR is void from inception (still-born); the doctrine of eclipse does not apply to it.

cases.name: Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P.
cases.holding: A post-Constitution law void for violating Art 19(1)(g) is not revived by a later constitutional amendment; it must be re-enacted (Cooley).

cases.name: State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd.
cases.holding: A post-Constitution law that violates a citizens-only right is void only against citizens and remains operative against non-citizens and companies. Judgment of Mathew J.

cases.name: Dularey Lodh v. III Addl. District Judge, Kanpur
cases.holding: Applied eclipse-type reasoning to a post-Constitution provision — cited as an anomaly in the doctrine.

cases.name: R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India
cases.holding: Doctrine of severability: the Prize Competitions Act was read down to apply only to gambling competitions; the valid part was severed from the invalid.

cases.name: Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income-Tax
cases.holding: Fundamental rights cannot be waived; at least the Art 14 right rests on public policy and cannot be bargained away. Decided 19 November 1958 (AIR 1959 SC 149).

cases.name: Suraj Mall Mohta & Co. v. A.V. Visvanatha Sastri
cases.holding: s. 5(1) of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947 violated Art 14 (a harsher procedure for a class indistinguishable from others).

cases.name: Mithu v. State of Punjab
cases.holding: s. 303 IPC (mandatory death sentence for murder by a life convict) struck down as violating Arts 14 and 21.

cases.name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
cases.holding: Preventive Detention Act, 1950 upheld except s. 14, which was severed; "procedure established by law" read as enacted procedure; Arts 19, 21, 22 treated as separate codes (later rejected in R.C. Cooper and Maneka Gandhi).

cases.name: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara
cases.holding: Bombay Prohibition Act largely upheld; exemptions for the armed forces and foreign visitors held a reasonable classification; specific provisions severed.

cases.name: Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India
cases.holding: A law aimed at a single company (Sholapur Spinning & Weaving Co.) upheld: even one person or entity can form a class if special circumstances justify it. Reported AIR 1951 SC 41.

cases.name: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
cases.holding: 7 judges, 6:1 (Patanjali Sastri C.J. dissenting): s. 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 void — uncontrolled discretion to send any "case" to a special court; no intelligible differentia.

cases.name: Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra
cases.holding: Special courts ordinance with almost identical wording upheld: its preamble and context (specified disturbed areas and offences) guided the discretion.

cases.name: Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar
cases.holding: Classic statement of the reasonable-classification test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus) and the presumption of constitutionality.

cases.name: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
cases.holding: "Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies": Art 14 strikes at arbitrary State action (Bhagwati J.); petitioner failed on facts. Decided 23 November 1973; reported (1974) 4 SCC 3.

cases.name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
cases.holding: 7 judges: "procedure established by law" must be fair, just and reasonable; Arts 14, 19 and 21 are interlinked (the golden triangle); right to travel abroad part of Art 21; hearing (even post-decisional) required. s. 10(3)(c) Passports Act was not struck down.

cases.name: Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India
cases.holding: The State must follow the standards it sets for itself (tender for a restaurant/snack bar); arbitrary departure violates Art 14; IAAI is "State".

cases.name: R.K. Garg v. Union of India
cases.holding: Special Bearer Bonds (Immunities and Exemptions) Act, 1981 upheld: economic legislation gets greater latitude.

cases.name: Air India v. Nergesh Meerza
cases.holding: Separate cadres upheld, but termination of air hostesses on first pregnancy struck down as arbitrary, and the MD's unguided power to extend service held invalid.

cases.name: D.S. Nakara v. Union of India
cases.holding: An arbitrary cut-off date dividing a homogeneous class of pensioners for liberalised pension violated Art 14.

cases.name: Delhi Transport Corporation v. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress
cases.holding: Regulation permitting termination of permanent employees on notice without reasons held arbitrary and void.

cases.name: N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P.
cases.holding: State liability for negligence of its officers in exercise of statutory functions; sovereign immunity narrowly confined.

cases.name: Indian Railway Construction Co. Ltd. v. Ajay Kumar
cases.holding: On judicial review of administrative action: illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety; Wednesbury and proportionality.

cases.name: State of U.P. v. Deoman Upadhyaya
cases.holding: s. 27 of the Evidence Act (discovery statements by persons in custody) does not violate Art 14.

cases.name: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
cases.holding: 7 judges: a body is "State" under Art 12 if it is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by or under the control of the Government (deep and pervasive control); CSIR held to be State.

cases.name: Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.holding: A rent-control exemption for new buildings, valid when made, became discriminatory when continued indefinitely — a classification can lose its nexus with time. Decided 26 October 1983 ((1984) 1 SCC 222).

cases.name: Kunnathat Thathunni Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala
cases.holding: Flat land tax per acre regardless of productivity treated unequals equally, and the unguided power to exempt was arbitrary — Travancore-Cochin Land Tax Act struck down. Decided 9 December 1960 (AIR 1961 SC 552).

cases.name: State of Jammu & Kashmir v. Triloki Nath Khosa
cases.holding: Even within an integrated cadre, promotion may be restricted to degree-holders: educational qualification is a valid basis of classification for promotion. Decided 26 September 1973 ((1974) 1 SCC 19).

cases.name: East India Tobacco Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.holding: Taxing Virginia tobacco while exempting country tobacco upheld — the legislature has wide latitude in selecting objects of taxation.

cases.name: Khandige Sham Bhat v. Agricultural Income Tax Officer
cases.holding: A 17-month "previous year" for the Malabar area transferred to Kerala (s. 2A, Kerala Agricultural Income-tax Act) upheld as a reasonable transitional classification (Subba Rao J.).

cases.name: Yusuf Abdul Aziz v. State of Bombay
cases.holding: s. 497 IPC (adultery), which exempted the wife from punishment, upheld as a special provision for women under Art 15(3); later struck down in Joseph Shine (2018).

cases.name: Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India
cases.holding: s. 30 of the Punjab Excise Act, 1914 (no employment of women or men under 25 in liquor premises) struck down: protective discrimination must not become romantic paternalism.

cases.name: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi
cases.holding: A society running a regional engineering college is "State"; allocating one-third of marks to a 2-3 minute interview was arbitrary (interview weight should not exceed about 15%). Decided 13 November 1980 ((1981) 1 SCC 722).

cases.name: Pratap Singh v. State of Jharkhand
cases.holding: 5 judges: juvenility is determined by the age on the date of the offence, not the date of production before the authority.

cases.name: Jalan Trading Co. (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Mill Mazdoor Union
cases.holding: Payment of Bonus Act, 1965: s. 37 struck down as excessive delegation; other provisions upheld. (Not the case for the welfare-fund worksheet problem — see Ambica Mills.)

cases.name: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
cases.holding: Communal G.O. allotting seats by religion/caste violated Art 29(2); DPSPs cannot override FRs. Led to Art 15(4) by the First Amendment.

cases.name: State of Rajasthan v. Thakur Pratap Singh
cases.holding: Notification exempting Harijan and Muslim inhabitants from a punitive police tax discriminated on grounds of caste and religion — void under Arts 14 and 15(1).

cases.name: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
cases.holding: 68% reservation struck down; caste may be relevant but cannot be the sole test of backwardness; reservations should generally stay below 50%. Decided 28 September 1962 (AIR 1963 SC 649).

cases.name: General Manager, Southern Railway v. Rangachari
cases.holding: Art 16(4) "appointments or posts" covers reservation in promotions as well (later overruled on this point in Indra Sawhney).

cases.name: T. Devadasan v. Union of India
cases.holding: The carry-forward rule that led to over 50% reservation in a year was struck down. Decided 29 August 1963 (AIR 1964 SC 179). It is not a case on degree v. diploma holders — that is Triloki Nath Khosa (1974).

cases.name: State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas
cases.holding: 7 judges, 5:2: temporary exemption of SC/ST employees from departmental tests upheld; Art 16(4) is a facet of Art 16(1), not an exception. Decided 19 September 1975; reported (1976) 2 SCC 310.

cases.name: Akhil Bharatiya Soshit Karamchari Sangh (Railway) v. Union of India
cases.holding: Reservation in promotions for SC/ST in the Railways upheld; an unregistered association can maintain an Art 32 petition. Decided 14 November 1980 (reported (1981) 1 SCC 246).

cases.name: State of M.P. v. Kumari Nivedita Jain
cases.holding: Complete relaxation of minimum qualifying marks for SC/ST candidates in medical admissions upheld.

cases.name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
cases.holding: 9 judges: 27% OBC reservation upheld subject to exclusion of the creamy layer; 50% ceiling as a rule; no reservation in promotions under Art 16(4) (prospectively, for five years); backward class can be identified by caste.

cases.name: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
cases.holding: 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments upheld; States must show backwardness, inadequacy of representation and administrative efficiency before reserving in promotions.

cases.name: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
cases.holding: 5 judges: Nagaraj need not be referred to a larger bench, but the requirement to collect data on backwardness of SC/ST was held contrary to Indra Sawhney; creamy layer applies to SC/ST in promotions.

cases.name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
cases.holding: 5 judges, 3:2 (7 November 2022): the 103rd Amendment (10% EWS reservation, Arts 15(6), 16(6)) upheld, including exclusion of SC/ST/OBC from the EWS quota.

cases.name: Sukanya Shantha v. Union of India
cases.holding: 3 October 2024 (Chandrachud C.J., Pardiwala and Manoj Misra JJ.): caste-based segregation and work allocation in prison manuals violate Arts 14, 15, 17, 21 and 23; manuals to be revised; caste column in prison registers to be deleted.

cases.name: Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat
cases.holding: The Nadiad CJM assault case: police officers punished for contempt; guidelines for arrest of judicial officers laid down.

cases.name: Zoroastrian Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar, Co-operative Societies
cases.holding: A bye-law restricting membership of a co-operative society to Parsis upheld; a society is not "State" and members may contractually limit membership.

cases.name: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
cases.holding: Routine handcuffing of undertrials violates Art 21; permissible only in exceptional cases with recorded reasons.

cases.name: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivakant Shukla
cases.holding: 4:1 (H.R. Khanna J. dissenting): during the Emergency no habeas corpus petition could be maintained to enforce Art 21. Effectively undone by the 44th Amendment (Art 359: Arts 20-21 cannot be suspended) and expressly overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).

cases.name: Dr. Subramanian Swamy v. Dr. Manmohan Singh
cases.holding: A citizen may seek sanction to prosecute a public servant; the competent authority must decide the request within a time-bound period (three months, extendable by one).

cases.name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
cases.holding: 9 judges: privacy is a fundamental right under Art 21 and Part III; M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh overruled to that extent; ADM Jabalpur overruled.

cases.name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
cases.holding: Ban on entry of the journal Cross Roads struck down: freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation; "public order/safety" was not a ground in the original Art 19(2); a law capable of invalid application is void as a whole.

cases.name: Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi
cases.holding: Pre-censorship order on the Organizer struck down as an unconstitutional restriction on press freedom (decided with Romesh Thappar).

cases.name: State of Madras v. V.G. Row
cases.holding: Test of reasonableness: no abstract standard; consider the nature of the right, purpose, extent and urgency of the evil, and proportion. s. 15(2)(b) Criminal Law Amendment Act (Madras) struck down.

cases.name: Express Newspapers (Private) Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.holding: Working Journalists Act upheld in principle (laws of general application with only incidental effect on the press are valid), but the Wage Board decision was set aside.

cases.name: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.holding: Price-page schedule struck down: the State cannot restrict circulation (a 19(1)(a) right) in the interest of the general public under 19(6).

cases.name: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India
cases.holding: Newsprint policy restricting pages struck down; direct-effect test; shareholders may challenge (4:1, Mathew J. dissenting).

cases.name: Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.holding: Import duty on newsprint: the press is not immune from tax, but taxation must not cripple circulation; matter remitted for re-examination. Decided 6 December 1984 ((1985) 1 SCC 641).

cases.name: Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India
cases.holding: Notices of re-entry and demolition against the Express building quashed as without authority and mala fide.

cases.name: Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) Lal Kuan v. Union of India
cases.holding: Commercial advertisement of drugs is not protected speech under 19(1)(a); s. 3(d) of the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act struck down for excessive delegation. Decided 18 December 1959 (AIR 1960 SC 554).

cases.name: Tata Press Ltd. v. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd.
cases.holding: Commercial speech is protected by Art 19(1)(a); Hamdard confined; public has a right to receive commercial information.

cases.name: Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: s. 292 IPC upheld; Hicklin test applied with modifications; Lady Chatterley's Lover held obscene.

cases.name: Samaresh Bose v. Amal Mitra
cases.holding: Vulgarity is not obscenity; the novel Prajapati judged as a whole was not obscene.

cases.name: Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal
cases.holding: Hicklin test discarded; obscenity judged by contemporary community standards from the view of an average person, the work as a whole (Boris Becker photo not obscene).

cases.name: Devidas Ramachandra Tuljapurkar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: Poetic licence does not extend to obscene words put in the mouth of a historically respected personality (Mahatma Gandhi); community-standards test applies.

cases.name: Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon
cases.holding: Bandit Queen: nudity and rape scenes in context, to convey the message of the film, are not obscene; 'A' certificate restored.

cases.name: K.A. Abbas v. Union of India
cases.holding: Pre-censorship of films is valid under Art 19(2) because of the medium's impact; film may be treated differently from other forms of expression.

cases.name: Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana
cases.holding: Right to exhibit a film on Doordarshan is part of 19(1)(a); an injunction cannot be based on grounds outside Art 19(2).

cases.name: LIC of India v. Prof. Manubhai D. Shah
cases.holding: A State instrumentality (LIC; Doordarshan) cannot refuse to publish a reply / telecast a film on arbitrary grounds; right of reply.

cases.name: Secretary, Ministry of I&B v. Cricket Association of Bengal
cases.holding: Airwaves are public property; the right to telecast and to receive information is part of 19(1)(a); no State monopoly over broadcasting.

cases.name: S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram
cases.holding: Film Ore Oru Gramathiley: anticipated danger must be proximate ("spark in a powder keg"); the State cannot plead inability to handle a hostile audience.

cases.name: Ramesh s/o Chotalal Dalal v. Union of India
cases.holding: Tamas TV serial: effect judged by the standards of reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous persons; telecast allowed.

cases.name: Superintendent, Central Prison, Fatehgarh v. Ram Manohar Lohia
cases.holding: "In the interests of public order" requires a proximate, not remote or far-fetched, connection; s. 3 of the U.P. Special Powers Act struck down.

cases.name: Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar
cases.holding: Three concentric circles: law and order (largest), public order, security of the State (smallest); detention to maintain "law and order" under a rule permitting it for "public order" quashed. Reported AIR 1966 SC 740.

cases.name: Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar
cases.holding: s. 124A IPC (sedition) upheld but confined to acts with a tendency to incite violence or public disorder.

cases.name: Arun Ghosh v. State of West Bengal
cases.holding: Public order v. law and order turns on the degree of disturbance to the life of the community (the effect of the act).

cases.name: E.M. Sankaran Namboodiripad v. T. Narayanan Nambiar
cases.holding: Conviction for contempt upheld for statements that judges were guided by class interests; fair criticism is permitted but not scandalising the court.

cases.name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
cases.holding: s. 66A IT Act struck down as vague and overbroad; only "incitement" (not discussion or advocacy) may be restricted; s. 79 read down.

cases.name: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
cases.holding: Expulsion of Jehovah's Witness children who stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem violated Arts 19(1)(a) and 25.

cases.name: Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India
cases.holding: National awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma) are not "titles" under Art 18, but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes. Decided 15 December 1995 ((1996) 1 SCC 361).

cases.name: Hans Muller of Nurenburg v. Superintendent, Presidency Jail, Calcutta
cases.holding: Art 19 is for citizens; the power to expel foreigners is unfettered; Arts 21 and 22 protect foreigners too.

cases.name: S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal
cases.holding: Criminal complaints over remarks on pre-marital sex quashed; unpopular views are protected; no obscenity or defamation of an identifiable group. Judgment of B.S. Chauhan J., 28 April 2010.

cases.name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
cases.holding: Speech and trade over the internet are protected by Arts 19(1)(a) and (g); internet shutdown and s. 144 orders must be published, proportionate and periodically reviewed.

cases.name: Centre for PIL v. Union of India (P.J. Thomas)
cases.holding: Appointment of the Central Vigilance Commissioner quashed: institutional integrity must be considered by the High-Powered Committee.

cases.name: Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India
cases.holding: Court declined to frame hate-speech guidelines; referred the issue to the Law Commission (leading to Report No. 267).

cases.name: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani
cases.holding: Art 20(3) applies at the stage of police interrogation; right to silence against self-incriminating questions; s. 161(2) CrPC read with it.

cases.name: Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.holding: 5 judges (4:1): Art 19(2) grounds are exhaustive; no additional restrictions on ministers' speech; FRs under Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against non-State actors (horizontal application).

cases.name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
cases.holding: Criminal defamation (ss. 499-500 IPC) upheld; reputation is part of Art 21.

cases.name: In Re: Ramlila Maidan Incident v. Home Secretary
cases.holding: Right to peaceful assembly is a FR; the midnight police action on sleeping protestors (4/5 June 2011) was unreasonable; State and protestors held liable.

cases.name: Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police
cases.holding: Shaheen Bagh: public ways cannot be occupied indefinitely; protests must be in designated places.

cases.name: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India
cases.holding: A blanket ban on protests at Jantar Mantar and Boat Club is unreasonable; police to frame guidelines for regulated use.

cases.name: T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu
cases.holding: Government employees have no fundamental, legal, moral or equitable right to strike.

cases.name: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu
cases.holding: Auto Shankar: right to privacy implicit in Art 21; no prior restraint on publication based on public records; public officials and defamation.

cases.name: Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2G Spectrum)
cases.holding: 122 telecom licences quashed: the first-come-first-served allocation was arbitrary; natural resources must be distributed fairly (public trust).

cases.name: Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms
cases.holding: Voters have a right to know candidates' criminal antecedents, assets and qualifications (Art 19(1)(a)).

cases.name: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds)
cases.holding: 5 judges, unanimous (15 February 2024): the Electoral Bond Scheme and the related amendments struck down — voters' right to information about political funding under Art 19(1)(a).

cases.name: People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India
cases.holding: s. 33B of the Representation of the People Act (inserted to dilute ADR) struck down.

cases.name: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India
cases.holding: Asiad workers: payment below minimum wage is "forced labour" under Art 23; Arts 17, 23, 24 are enforceable against private persons; PIL standing.

cases.name: Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.holding: A blanket ban on bidi-making during the agricultural season was excessive — a restriction must not be arbitrary or beyond what the object requires.

cases.name: Excel Wear v. Union of India
cases.holding: The right to carry on business includes the right to close it; s. 25-O of the Industrial Disputes Act struck down.

cases.name: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
cases.holding: 11 judges: establishing and running educational institutions is an "occupation" under 19(1)(g); minority rights under Art 30; no capitation fees.

cases.name: Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka
cases.holding: Clarified TMA Pai: fee-regulation and admission committees for unaided institutions.

cases.name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
cases.holding: Right to livelihood is part of the right to life (Art 21); pavement dwellers entitled to notice before eviction; no estoppel against FRs. Decided 10 July 1985 (AIR 1986 SC 180).

cases.name: Sodan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee
cases.holding: Street hawking is a trade under 19(1)(g), subject to reasonable regulation; no right to a particular place.

cases.name: State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel & Restaurants Association
cases.holding: Ban on dancing in bars (exempting three-star hotels) struck down under Arts 14 and 19(1)(g). Bench: Altamas Kabir C.J. and S.S. Nijjar J. (judgment by Nijjar J.), 16 July 2013.

cases.name: Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar
cases.holding: Total ban on slaughter of cows and calves upheld; ban on slaughter of useless bulls, bullocks and she-buffaloes struck down.

cases.name: State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat
cases.holding: 7 judges (6:1): total ban on slaughter of cow progeny upheld, overruling Quareshi on that point; DPSPs (Arts 48, 48A, 51A(g)) inform reasonableness.

cases.name: Hinsa Virodhak Sangh v. Mirzapur Moti Kuresh Jamat
cases.holding: Closure of municipal slaughterhouses for nine days during the Paryushan festival is a reasonable restriction.

cases.name: Om Prakash v. State of U.P.
cases.holding: Ban on sale of meat, fish and eggs within Haridwar, Rishikesh and Muni-ki-Reti municipal limits upheld as a reasonable restriction.

cases.name: Ramasamy Udayar v. District Collector, Perambalur (Madras HC)
cases.holding: A religious procession cannot be prohibited on public roads merely because another religious group lives predominantly in the area.

cases.name: The Secretary to Government v. Sameer Ahamed N.
cases.holding: 15 October 2026 (Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar JJ.): conversion from Hinduism does not carry pre-conversion backwardness into a notified Muslim backward class; Tamil Nadu's G.O. of 9 March 2024 rightly quashed.

cases.name: State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee
cases.holding: "Compensation" in Art 31(2) means a just equivalent of what the owner is deprived of. Judgment of Patanjali Sastri C.J., 11 December 1953 (AIR 1954 SC 170).

cases.name: Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India
cases.holding: Bank Nationalisation Act struck down (10:1): compensation principles were not relevant; Arts 19 and 31 are not mutually exclusive (Gopalan's compartment theory rejected); shareholders can sue.

cases.name: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: 9 judges, 5 November 2024: Art 31C survives in the form upheld in Kesavananda (the original text revived when the 42nd Amendment change was struck down in Minerva Mills); by 8:1 (7 + Nagarathna J. partly concurring; Dhulia J. dissenting) not every item of private property is a "material resource of the community" under Art 39(b).

cases.name: K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka
cases.holding: Art 300A requires public purpose and a law; no in-built right to compensation, but the law must be just, fair and reasonable.

cases.name: Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh
cases.holding: Right to property is a constitutional and human right; State cannot take land without due process; compensation ordered.

cases.name: Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah
cases.holding: Art 300A contains seven sub-rights (notice, hearing, reasoned decision, public purpose, compensation, efficient process, conclusion).

cases.name: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.holding: Domiciliary night visits under U.P. Police Regulation 236(b) violated personal liberty; other surveillance upheld (Subba Rao J. dissenting on privacy). "Life" means more than animal existence (quoting Field J. in Munn v. Illinois).

cases.name: Satwant Singh Sawhney v. D. Ramarathnam, Assistant Passport Officer
cases.holding: The right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Art 21; passport refusal without law was invalid — prompted the Passports Act, 1967.

cases.name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
cases.holding: Speedy trial is part of Art 21; release of undertrials detained beyond the maximum sentence; free legal aid.

cases.name: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
cases.holding: Right to life includes the right to live with human dignity; detenu's right to meet family and lawyer.

cases.name: Pt. Parmanand Katara v. Union of India
cases.holding: Every doctor must give emergency medical aid to preserve life without waiting for police formalities.

cases.name: Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka
cases.holding: Right to education flows from Art 21; capitation fees arbitrary.

cases.name: Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh
cases.holding: Right to free education up to 14 years is a FR under Art 21 (later Art 21A); beyond that, subject to the State's economic capacity.

cases.name: P. Rathinam v. Union of India
cases.holding: s. 309 IPC (attempt to suicide) held unconstitutional under Art 21 — overruled by Gian Kaur (1996).

cases.name: Smt. Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab
cases.holding: 5 judges: the right to life does not include the right to die; ss. 306 and 309 IPC valid; Rathinam overruled.

cases.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.holding: 11 requirements for arrest and detention to prevent custodial violence; compensation for violation of Art 21. Decided 18 December 1996 ((1997) 1 SCC 416).

cases.name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
cases.holding: First Judges Case: liberalised locus standi for PIL; executive primacy in judicial appointments (later overruled in 1993).

cases.name: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.holding: Death penalty for murder upheld but confined to the "rarest of rare" cases, with special reasons.

cases.name: Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.holding: Rarest-of-rare test elaborated: balance-sheet of aggravating and mitigating circumstances.

cases.name: Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Admn.)
cases.holding: Indira Gandhi assassination conspiracy: conviction and death sentence of Kehar Singh upheld.

cases.name: Swamy Shraddananda v. State of Karnataka
cases.holding: Constitutional courts may substitute death with life imprisonment without remission for a fixed term or for the rest of life.

cases.name: Shabnam v. Union of India
cases.holding: Death warrant issued before the convicts exhausted their remedies was quashed: execution only after all remedies are exhausted.

cases.name: Pooran Mal v. Director of Inspection (Investigation), Income-tax
cases.holding: Evidence obtained by an illegal search is not inadmissible merely for that reason (no exclusionary rule in India).

cases.name: State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali (Bombay HC)
cases.holding: Uncodified personal laws are not "laws in force" under Art 13 and cannot be tested against Part III; Bombay Prevention of Hindu Bigamous Marriages Act upheld.

cases.name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
cases.holding: s. 125 CrPC maintenance available to a divorced Muslim wife beyond iddat if she cannot maintain herself.

cases.name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
cases.holding: 3:2: instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) set aside (Nariman and Lalit JJ. as manifestly arbitrary under Art 14; Kurian Joseph J. as un-Islamic).

cases.name: Marbury v. Madison
cases.holding: Judicial review: "it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is."

cases.name: Dred Scott v. Sandford
cases.holding: Persons of African descent were not US citizens; Congress could not ban slavery in the territories (Missouri Compromise void). Overturned by the 13th and 14th Amendments.

cases.name: Plessy v. Ferguson
cases.holding: "Separate but equal" upheld.

cases.name: Brown v. Board of Education
cases.holding: Racial segregation in public schools is inherently unequal; Plessy overruled in education.

cases.name: Loving v. Virginia
cases.holding: Laws banning interracial marriage violate equal protection and due process.

cases.name: Lochner v. New York
cases.holding: 5:4: maximum-hours law for bakers struck down as violating liberty of contract (substantive due process); Holmes J. dissenting.

cases.name: Miranda v. Arizona
cases.holding: Custodial interrogation requires warnings: right to silence and to counsel.

cases.name: Brandenburg v. Ohio
cases.holding: Advocacy is protected unless directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it.

cases.name: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke
cases.holding: Rigid racial quotas invalid, but race may be one factor in admissions.

cases.name: Munn v. Illinois
cases.holding: Upheld State regulation of grain elevators; Field J.'s dissent on "life" meaning more than mere animal existence was quoted in Kharak Singh.

cases.name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
cases.holding: In the absence of legislation, the Court laid down binding guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace, drawing on CEDAW and Arts 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21.

cases.name: Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of U.P.
cases.holding: A post-Constitution law that contravenes Part III is void ab initio under Art 13(2); the doctrine of eclipse does not apply, and a later non-retrospective amendment cannot revive it.

cases.name: State of West Bengal v. Union of India
cases.holding: Seven judges (6:1) held that Parliament may legislate to acquire property vested in a State; the States are not sovereign units.

cases.name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
cases.holding: Nine judges: federalism and secularism are basic features; the President's satisfaction under Art 356 is open to judicial review.

cases.name: K.K. Kochunni v. State of Madras
cases.holding: An Art 32 petition cannot be refused merely because it raises disputed questions of fact; a law depriving persons of property rights could be challenged directly under Art 32.

cases.name: Tilokchand Motichand v. H.B. Munshi
cases.holding: Even under Art 32, the Court may refuse relief to a petitioner guilty of unreasonable delay (laches).

cases.name: Dr. M. Ismail Faruqui v. Union of India
cases.holding: The Court declined to answer the Art 143 reference on the Ayodhya site and upheld most of the Acquisition of Certain Area at Ayodhya Act, 1993.

cases.name: Anant Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat
cases.holding: Courts should not decide constitutional validity on presumed or hypothetical facts; property-tax provisions of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act upheld.

cases.name: D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar
cases.holding: Repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution.

cases.name: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu
cases.holding: The Tenth Schedule is valid, but para 7 (ouster of courts) needed ratification under Art 368(2) and was invalid; the Speaker's decision is subject to judicial review.

cases.name: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa
cases.holding: Monetary compensation can be awarded under Arts 32 and 226 for violation of Art 21 (custodial death); sovereign immunity is no defence in public law.

cases.name: Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha
cases.holding: Expulsion of MPs for the cash-for-query scandal upheld; parliamentary privileges are subject to judicial review for gross illegality or violation of constitutional provisions.

cases.name: N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer, Namakkal
cases.holding: Art 329(b) bars challenges to the election process except by an election petition after the election.

cases.name: Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v. State of Bombay
cases.holding: A declaration that a law is void under Art 13 operates, by force of Art 141, as binding law: courts must ignore the void part and the accused bears no onus to prove its invalidity again.

cases.name: Managing Director, ECIL v. B. Karunakar
cases.holding: The inquiry report must be given to the delinquent employee before the disciplinary decision; the ruling was made prospective.

cases.name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
cases.holding: Art 329A(4), inserted by the 39th Amendment to validate the Prime Minister's election, was struck down as violating the basic structure (free and fair elections, judicial review).

cases.name: Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara v. Central Provinces Syndicate Ltd.
cases.holding: A legislature may change the law retrospectively but cannot declare a court's judgment ineffective or say the law shall be interpreted otherwise than as declared.

cases.name: Sadasib Prakash Brahmachari v. State of Orissa
cases.holding: A new law may deem schemes framed under a provision struck down to have been settled under the new, valid law (s 79A, Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act).

cases.name: State of Mysore v. D. Achiah Chetty
cases.holding: Where acquisition was discriminatory because two procedures existed, the legislature could retrospectively leave one procedure and validate past acquisitions.

cases.name: Linkletter v. Walker
cases.holding: The Constitution neither requires nor prohibits retrospective effect; Mapp v. Ohio was not applied to convictions final before it — the origin of prospective overruling in constitutional cases.

cases.name: Antill Ranger & Co. Pty Ltd v. Commissioner for Motor Transport
cases.holding: Neither prospectively nor retrospectively can a State law make lawful what the Constitution says is unlawful; a law barring recovery of charges void under s 92 of the Australian Constitution was invalid.

cards.name: Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1996 SC 770 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Petitions challenged the National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri) as "titles" prohibited by Art 18(1).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Are national awards "titles" within Art 18(1)?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • No. They are awards/distinctions, not titles; they do not create a class of hereditary or social superiority, and Art 18 does not forbid recognising merit. But they must not be used as a prefix or suffix to the name; misuse can lead to forfeiture (Awards Rules).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Art 18 prohibits titles that denote nobility or social hierarchy; honours conferred for merit without privileges are consistent with equality.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor mentioned this case ("there is a case on this, see it") as the authority on awards vs titles.

cards.name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1950 SC 124; 1950 SCR 594 (Supreme Court; decided 26 May 1950, 4 months after the Constitution came into force).

fields.label: Bench / Author
fields.html: Patanjali Sastri J. wrote the majority opinion; Fazl Ali J. dissented (the professor noted that Fazl Ali J. wanted "public order" and "security of the State" read liberally because disorder can lead to threats to the State).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• Romesh Thappar printed and published Cross Roads, an English weekly, in Bombay (printed in Madras). The Madras Government, under s. 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949, banned the entry and circulation of the journal in Madras State.
  • The professor's framing: "Nehru's Government gave permission to *print* but banned *circulation*. Who prints a paper to keep it in his room?"

fields.label: Issues
fields.html:
• Does the freedom of speech and expression include freedom of circulation?
  • Is a law that restricts a publication to prevent disturbance of "public order"/"law and order" valid under the then Art 19(2) (which allowed restrictions only for matters affecting the security of, or tending to overthrow, the State)?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, and that freedom is ensured by the freedom of circulation. Without circulation the right is empty.
  • Because Art 19(2) (before 1951) did not list "public order"/"law and order" as a ground, s. 9(1-A) could not be saved. The section was void.
  • The Court distinguished "public order" from "law and order" and from "security of the State": the last is the narrowest; not every disturbance of public order endangers the State.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation; a restriction must fall within the grounds listed in Art 19(2); "law and order" is not a ground (the Court said that Art 19(2) as then worded could not support curbs for mere public disorder).

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Together with Brij Bhushan it triggered the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951, which added "public order", "friendly relations with foreign States" and "incitement to an offence" and made restrictions "reasonable" and applicable retrospectively.
  • The three concentric circles are later described in Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1966): law and order (widest), public order, security of State (narrowest).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor repeatedly asked: "What did the Supreme Court say?" Two things: (1) law and order is not a ground; (2) circulation is covered by Art 19(1)(a). He asked students to read the original judgment, which explains the three terms well.

cards.name: Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana (1988)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1988) 3 SCC 410 (Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• Odyssey produced the Doordarshan TV serial "Honi Anhoni". A public-interest organisation, Lokvidayan Sanghatana, objected that the serial promoted superstition and sought to stop its telecast.
  • The professor recalled the case as "Doordarshan denied permission to telecast a serial" and said the Court recognised a right to telecast. (Exam-safe version: the dispute was about stopping a telecast, and the Court upheld the producer's right to exhibit it.)

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the right to telecast a film/serial on the national broadcaster form part of Art 19(1)(a)? Can it be stopped at a third party's instance?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • A citizen's right to exhibit films on Doordarshan, subject to the terms and conditions of the broadcaster and the restrictions in Art 19(2), is part of freedom of speech and expression. The challenge to the serial failed because no Art 19(2) ground was made out.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The right to disseminate by television is part of Art 19(1)(a), and the right cannot be defeated except on grounds in Art 19(2).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "Read the case; the right to telecast was held to be a fundamental right and it cannot be denied (except on Art 19(2) grounds)". A student pointed to Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) (telecast of the serial Tamas, based on Bhisham Sahni's novel on Partition), where the Court refused to ban the serial; effect of a work must be judged from the standpoint of reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous persons, not of those with weak and vacillating minds.

cards.name: LIC of India v. Manubhai D. Shah (1992)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1992) 3 SCC 637 (Supreme Court of India). Also reported as Life Insurance Corporation v. Professor Manubhai D. Shah.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• Prof. Manubhai Shah (Consumer Education and Research Centre, Ahmedabad) wrote a study criticising LIC's policies/premiums. LIC's in-house magazine, Yogakshema, published a rebuttal and defence of the policies. When Shah asked to publish his reply in the same magazine, LIC refused.
  • Professor's analogy: "If the university magazine praised the university and a student wrote a criticism and the Registrar refused to print it, the student can say: I want to publish my account too."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the freedom of speech include the right of reply and the right to publish a counter-view in the organ of a body that has published criticism?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Refusal to publish the reply violated Art 19(1)(a). A one-sided presentation by a State instrumentality, which refuses an opposing view, denies fair debate.
  • LIC, as a statutory corporation (State within Art 12), was bound by Art 19 and had to give space to the reply; it could not rely on its "proprietary" rights over the magazine.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Free speech includes the right to reply / the right to a fair and balanced presentation when the State or its instrumentality uses its own platform to put forward a view.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Professor's summary: "publish, because that is also public"; he added the example of a private institution. (Caution: the holding is about LIC as State, not about every private publisher; horizontal application of Art 19 is addressed separately in Kaushal Kishor, see Lecture 19.)

cards.name: Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1995) 2 SCC 161 (Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Bench / Author
fields.html: Sawant J. (for himself and Kuldip Singh J.), with Jeevan Reddy J. concurring.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The Cricket Association of Bengal hosted the Hero Cup one-day international matches (1993) at Eden Gardens and gave telecast rights to a foreign production company (Trans World International, TWI). The Government and Doordarshan (state broadcaster with a monopoly on terrestrial telecasting) insisted that only Doordarshan could telecast/uplink the matches within India.
