  • The professor's version (BCCI contract of "thousands of crores" to a foreign company; Doordarshan could not afford it): the simplified point is that the State monopoly over broadcasting was challenged.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Are airwaves public property? Can the State claim a monopoly over broadcasting? Is there a fundamental right to telecast and to receive information?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Airwaves/frequencies are public property, to be used for public good and in line with Art 39(b) and (c) (distribution of material resources of the community).
  • The right to impart and receive information (through any medium: print, electronic, audio-visual) is part of Art 19(1)(a); a State monopoly over broadcasting is not mandated by the Constitution.
  • The right to broadcast is not unlimited: licensing and regulation are permitted if they fall within Art 19(2) (and 19(1)(g)).
  • The Court recommended an independent, autonomous public authority representing all sections of society to control and regulate the airwaves.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Freedom of speech includes the right to receive and impart information through electronic media; airwaves are public property and cannot be monopolised by the Government.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor wanted the full name: Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting v. Cricket Association of Bengal (not "of India": "आपने इंडिया कह दिया तो ... यही सब गड़बड़ हो जाता है"). Remember the proposition: right to receive information.

cards.name: State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1952 SC 196; 1952 SCR 597 (Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Bench / Author
fields.html: Patanjali Sastri C.J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • V.G. Row, an office-bearer of the People's Education Society, Madras, challenged a Madras notification declaring the Society an unlawful association under the Indian Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1908 (s. 15(2)(b)), claiming violation of Art 19(1)(c) (right to form associations).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • What is a reasonable restriction under Art 19(2)-(6), and who decides reasonableness?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Court held that the Act (as it existed) was unreasonable: it allowed the executive to declare an association unlawful on its own opinion, with no judicial review, no hearing and no objective standard.
  • The Court laid down the factors for reasonableness (applied to all restrictions in Art 19(2)-(6)): the restriction must be in the interest of the general public; the Court looks at both substantive and procedural aspects: nature of the right, underlying purpose of the restriction, extent and urgency of the evil, disproportion of the imposition, prevailing conditions; the standard is objective, not subjective, and not what the legislature thinks.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A restriction is reasonable only if it is not arbitrary or excessive, bears a real and direct connection with the object, and is accompanied by fair procedure (including judicial review).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor listed what a valid restriction needs: (1) imposed by law (Act of Parliament/State Legislature); (2) only for a ground mentioned in Art 19(2): no other ground can be used; (3) a real, approximate connection between the speech and the protected interest (a "rational nexus"); (4) reasonable (nowadays tested as proportionate); (5) fair procedure. He asked students to cite State of Madras v. V.G. Row for the definition of reasonable restriction.

cards.name: Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2014) 4 SCC 257 (Supreme Court of India, two-Judge bench: K.S. Radhakrishnan and A.K. Sikri JJ.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The German magazine Stern (1993) carried a photograph of tennis star Boris Becker posing naked with his fiancée Barbara Feltus, a Black Afro-German model, as a statement against racial discrimination (apartheid). The photograph was reprinted in the Kolkata-based magazine Sports World and in Anand Bazar Patrika (publisher/editor Aveek Sarkar). A complaint under s. 292 IPC (obscenity) followed.
  • The professor: "A German tennis player's girlfriend from South Africa, a Black woman; he said skin colour makes no difference to love, and published their nude photograph; an Indian magazine reprinted it."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is the publication obscene under s. 292 IPC? Which test governs: the old Hicklin test or a community standards test?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Court rejected the Hicklin test and adopted the community standards test: the work must be judged as a whole, from the standpoint of an average, reasonable person applying contemporary community standards, not by looking at a single isolated passage and not from the viewpoint of a hypersensitive or the most susceptible reader.
  • The photograph, in context (a message against racial prejudice), did not appeal to prurient interest; hence not obscene; the proceedings were quashed.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Obscenity is judged by contemporary community standards and the whole work and its context; nudity is not obscene per se.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Followed Ranjit D. Udeshi (1964) (which had applied Hicklin) → Samaresh Bose v. Amal Mitra (1985) (moved away) → Bobby Art International (1996) → Aveek Sarkar (2014) (formally buried Hicklin).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor asked a student to present this case. Know the test sentence above by heart.

cards.name: S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2010) 5 SCC 600 (Supreme Court of India; K.G. Balakrishnan C.J., Deepak Verma and B.S. Chauhan JJ.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• In a 2005 magazine interview, the South Indian film actress Khushboo said that pre-marital sex is not wrong in itself but that girls should be careful about sexually transmitted diseases and pregnancy. About 22-23 criminal complaints (obscenity, defamation, Indecent Representation of Women Act, s. 292, 499, 500, 504, 505 IPC etc.) were filed across Tamil Nadu alleging that she corrupted Indian culture.
  • Professor: "She was asked whether physical relations before marriage are right or wrong; she said there is no harm but be careful; a case was filed that she is corrupting our girls."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Do these remarks constitute an offence (obscenity, defamation, incitement)? Where is the line between expression of views and criminal liability?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Court quashed the complaints. Expressing a view on pre-marital sex, even if unpopular, is protected speech; a mere discussion or even advocacy of a popular or unpopular cause is the heart of Art 19(1)(a) and is not a crime unless it is an incitement to commit an offence.
  • Living together / pre-marital sex is not an offence in itself; no obscenity (no appeal to prurient interest; no incitement); the complaints amounted to harassment. The Court also stressed that multiple complaints in different places for one statement is an abuse of process.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Unpopular opinions on morality are protected by Art 19(1)(a); obscenity requires material that is lascivious / appeals to prurient interest; mere advocacy is not criminal.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor said "Khushboo was a very interesting case; presentation tomorrow". He added that no new principle of obscenity was laid down in Khushboo; the test comes from Aveek Sarkar.

cards.name: Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1950 SC 129; 1950 SCR 605 (Supreme Court of India; decided 26 May 1950 on the same day as Romesh Thappar).

fields.label: Bench / Author
fields.html: Patanjali Sastri J. for the majority (6-judge bench; Fazl Ali J. dissented).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• Brij Bhushan was the printer/publisher of The Organiser, an English weekly (RSS-affiliated) in Delhi. Under s. 7(1)(c) of the East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949 (applicable in Delhi), the Chief Commissioner ordered the weekly to submit for scrutiny, before publication, all communal matter and news and views about Pakistan, including photographs and cartoons.
  • The professor: "After Partition many things could be said abusing Pakistan; Nehru said you cannot abuse Pakistan, and imposed press censorship: check with us first."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is pre-censorship of a newspaper a valid restriction on Art 19(1)(a), particularly when "public order" was not a ground in Art 19(2) (before 1951)?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The order was unconstitutional. Pre-censorship of a journal is a restraint on the liberty of the press and is not saved by Art 19(2) as then worded (only matters undermining the security of, or tending to overthrow, the State).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Prior restraint on the press is a direct restriction of freedom of speech and expression and is invalid unless within Art 19(2). "Pre-censorship in print media is not acceptable."

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • First Amendment (1951) overruled the result by adding "public order" and "friendly relations with foreign States". Pre-censorship remains disfavoured: Kharak Singh, Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1959), Sakal Papers (1962).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor: "name the case on pre-censorship of print media: Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi." He said a student wrongly named a case on incitement to an offence (a different matter) and asked to keep them apart.

cards.name: K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1971 SC 481; (1970) 2 SCC 780 (Supreme Court of India; Hidayatullah C.J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• K.A. Abbas (film-maker and journalist) challenged the censorship provisions of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 after the Censor Board gave his documentary "A Tale of Four Cities" an "A" certificate (adults only), objecting to pre-censorship and to the classification into "U" and "A".
  • Professor: "Brij Bhushan said prior restraint is bad for print; films are certified before release; Abbas asked how can you impose prior restraint?"

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is pre-censorship of films consistent with Art 19(1)(a), given Brij Bhushan?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Pre-censorship of films is valid under Art 19(2): the cinema has a unique impact on the audience (sight and sound together; emotional power; audience sits in the dark, absorbed, with a lasting effect), so it can be treated differently from the press.
  • Classification into U (universal) and A (adults) is a reasonable restriction.
  • The standard of the censor must be that of an ordinary person with common sense and not one who is over-sensitive or prudish; guidelines must be specific and applied with freedom for artistic expression.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Prior restraint on films is permissible because motion pictures are a different medium with greater impact than the printed word; the classification system is valid.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Statutory system today: Cinematograph Act, 1952 as amended in 2023: certificates U, UA 7+, UA 13+, UA 16+, A, S. Certification by the CBFC (Central Board of Film Certification, the "Film Censor Board" whose office the professor said he visited).
  • S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989): the State cannot ban a certified film because of the threat of violence by objectors (heckler's veto); danger must be like a "spark in a powder keg", proximate and direct.
  • Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (Bandit Queen) (1996): scenes of nudity and violence must be judged in the context of the film's message.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor: "Broadcasting things need prior sanction because the impact is larger; people see and hear; reading takes effort. Telecast reaches lakhs at once and influences the mind more." He asked students to read Abbas (theory only) the next day.

cards.name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2020) 3 SCC 637; decided 10 January 2020 (Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Bench / Author
fields.html: N.V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy and B.R. Gavai JJ. (Justice Ramana authored the leading judgment).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• After the abrogation of Art 370 (5 August 2019), the J&K administration imposed a communications blackout (mobile, landline and internet) and orders under s. 144 CrPC restricting movement and assembly. Anuradha Bhasin, editor of the Kashmir Times, challenged the shutdown as violating Art 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); Ghulam Nabi Azad intervened for the restrictions on movement.
  • The professor's illustration: restrictions on information flow (internet, TV, mobile, press) in Kashmir because of national-security concerns; is closing the information channel connected to the goal?

fields.label: Issues
fields.html:
• Does freedom of speech and the right to carry on trade or business through the internet enjoy constitutional protection?
  • Is an indefinite internet shutdown permissible? Are orders under s. 144 CrPC valid and must they be published?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Freedom of speech and expression and the right to practise any profession or carry on business over the internet are protected under Art 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); restrictions must meet the tests of Art 19(2)/(6) and proportionality.
  • Indefinite suspension of internet services is impermissible; shutdowns under the Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services Rules, 2017 must be temporary, limited in scope, reasoned, published and subject to periodic review (by a Review Committee, within a week).
  • s. 144 CrPC cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression or peaceful dissent; orders must state material facts, be proportionate, and are subject to judicial review.
  • The Court applied the four-fold proportionality test (below) borrowed from the German/Canadian line and Modern Dental College (2016) and K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Any restriction on Art 19(1)(a) must satisfy proportionality: (1) legitimate goal, (2) suitability/rational nexus, (3) necessity (least restrictive alternative), (4) balancing (structural proportionality); the burden of justification lies on the State, and the order must be open to judicial review.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Professor: "Reasonable has become proportionate." Follow-up: Foundation for Media Professionals v. UT of J&K (2020) on 4G speed restrictions.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Learn the four prongs as a mnemonic L-R-N-B (Legitimate aim, Rational nexus, Necessity, Balance), with judicial review as the procedural safeguard.

cards.name: Centre for PIL v. Union of India (the P.J. Thomas case) (2011)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2011) 4 SCC 1; decided 3 March 2011 (Supreme Court of India; 3-judge bench: S.H. Kapadia C.J., K.S. Radhakrishnan and Swatanter Kumar JJ.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• P.J. Thomas (Kerala-cadre IAS officer) was recommended by a High-Powered Committee (Prime Minister, Home Minister, Leader of Opposition) as Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC) in 2010. The Leader of the Opposition (Sushma Swaraj) dissented, noting that he was an accused in the Palmolein import corruption case in Kerala. The majority of the committee went ahead.
  • The professor said "in one line of objection, the whole appointment collapsed" and corrected a student: it is P.J. Thomas, not N.M. Thomas (State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas, 1976 is the reservation case).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is an appointment valid when the appointing committee does not properly consider material bearing on the integrity of the candidate and overrides the dissent?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Court quashed the appointment. The appointing committee must consider the institutional integrity of the office (CVC) and whether the candidate's appointment will undermine the institution; personal integrity alone is not the test.
  • The Leader of the Opposition's dissent, backed by relevant material, had to be properly considered; the committee's decision was vitiated by non-consideration of relevant facts (the pending Palmolein prosecution).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Statutory appointments must be made on relevant considerations and with regard to the independence and integrity of the institution; courts can review the process.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor used this to show that a single well-reasoned objection from the Leader of Opposition can invalidate an appointment, while a mere "I object" is not enough; the objector must show a valid defect.

cards.name: Express Newspapers (Private) Ltd. v. Union of India (the Working Journalists case) (1958)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1958 SC 578; 1959 SCR 12 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 and the wage board fixed minimum wages and conditions for journalists; newspaper owners said this burdened the press and violated Art 19(1)(a) and (g).
  • The professor's version: "the Government tried to raise journalists' pay; the press objected that it violates my right: if I pay 10 and you ask me to pay 20..."; the objection was rejected.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does a general economic regulation (wages) that increases the cost of running a newspaper violate freedom of the press?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • No. The Act regulates employment conditions; any effect on the press is remote and indirect and the press has no immunity from laws of general application. A law is bad if it directly curtails the freedom of speech, or if its real object is to restrict circulation or expression.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The press is not exempt from general laws (wages, labour, tax). Only measures that single out the press or directly affect circulation and expression are invalid.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Contrast with Sakal Papers: wages (valid, indirect) v. price-page (invalid, direct).

cards.name: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India (1962)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1962 SC 305; (1962) 3 SCR 842 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspaper (Price and Page) Order, 1960 fixed the maximum number of pages a newspaper could publish for a given price (a price-page schedule), aimed at preventing unfair competition and making newspapers affordable.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can the State regulate the price and number of pages to protect smaller papers? Does this violate Art 19(1)(a)? Can Art 19(1)(g) arguments save it?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Order violated Art 19(1)(a): restricting the number of pages forces a newspaper to cut circulation or content, which directly affects freedom of speech and expression.
  • Art 19(2) is exhaustive: freedom of expression cannot be restricted on economic grounds (e.g. to protect small newspapers from competition). The State may not abridge the right "in the interest of the general public" unless the interest is in Art 19(2).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A law that directly curtails circulation (and thereby speech) is invalid unless within Art 19(2); economic objectives are not grounds; the effect, not the form or intention, decides.

cards.name: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (the Newsprint Policy case) (1972)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1972) 2 SCC 788; AIR 1973 SC 106 (Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The Newsprint Policy 1972-73 (under the Newsprint Control Order, 1962 and Import Control orders) (i) capped the number of pages at 10; (ii) forbade increasing pages without reducing circulation; (iii) barred the starting of new newspapers/editions by established chains.
  • The Government justified it by the shortage of imported newsprint and foreign exchange. The professor said the Prime Minister (Indira Gandhi) disliked newspapers criticising her and used the policy as "colourable legislation": "We cannot give you the material, so you cannot print more pages."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is the newsprint quota a valid regulation of an imported commodity or an invalid restriction on freedom of the press? What is the test: "pith and substance" (object) or "direct effect" (consequence)?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The policy was unconstitutional: it directly affected circulation and the volume of news and views, and thus violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 14 (discrimination between newspapers on page and circulation).
  • The test is the direct and inevitable effect of the impugned action on the right, not its object or the Government's motive ("pith and substance" was rejected for Art 19 cases). Shortage of foreign exchange is not a ground under Art 19(2).
  • Shareholders (citizens) of a company can claim Art 19 where the company's rights are affected, so the "company is not a citizen" objection did not defeat the petition.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Restrictions on the material needed for publication (newsprint) are restrictions on speech if the effect is to curtail circulation or content; the Court looks at direct and inevitable consequence.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Followed in Indian Express (1985); affirms that the press is protected from indirect government pressure.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "The Government said it cannot import more newsprint, so you must reduce pages; the Court rejected this as a disguised way to stop the press."

cards.name: Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1984/85)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1985) 1 SCC 641; AIR 1986 SC 515 (Supreme Court of India; E.S. Venkataramiah, O. Chinnappa Reddy and A.P. Sen JJ.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Customs duty and auxiliary duty were imposed on imported newsprint, which had been untaxed before; publishers claimed it raised prices, cut circulation and violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 14 (size-based classification of newspapers).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can the State tax the press? Is a tax on newsprint a "restriction" on freedom of the press?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The press is not immune from taxation, but a tax on the press must be reasonable and not designed or likely to curtail circulation; the courts will scrutinise such taxes and the burden to justify lies on the State.
  • On the facts, the petitioners could not prove that circulation fell because of the duty, so the Court did not strike the duty down; it directed the Government to reconsider the tax policy. The size-based classification (to help small and medium papers) had a rational nexus, so Art 14 was not violated.
  • The Court affirmed that freedom of the press is "the heart of social and political intercourse" and that the press cannot be subjected to arbitrary or excessive taxation (no tax on knowledge).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Fiscal measures affecting newsprint are valid if reasonable and not a device to restrict circulation; they are subject to judicial review.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor mixed this with the Emergency stories of the Indian Express group (power cut to the printing press and cancellation of the lease of its Delhi building, which led to litigation in Delhi and Bombay where the courts gave relief). Safe to cite the case for "taxation of the press must be reasonable".

cards.name: Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) Lal Kuan v. Union of India (1960)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1960 SC 554; (1960) 2 SCR 671 (Constitution Bench, Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 prohibited advertisements that claimed cures for certain diseases (sexual disorders, venereal disease, leucoderma, cancer, etc.) by drugs or magic remedies. Hamdard Dawakhana (a traditional medicine firm) challenged it as a violation of free speech.
  • The professor described the background: "in our time Bengali dawakhanas and quacks promised cures for secret diseases; Nirmal Baba-type promises (eat jalebi on Sunday, wear a black shirt) mislead people; the Act was passed in 1954."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is an advertisement "speech" under Art 19(1)(a), and can Parliament prohibit advertisements that promote harmful or false medical claims?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• An advertisement is no doubt a form of speech, but its true character is determined by the product or business it promotes. When it propagates a trade or business (selling drugs), it is not "freedom of speech" within Art 19(1)(a); and the Act protects public health, so it was valid (also within 19(6) for the business aspect).
  • The professor read the Court's reasoning as: "the purpose of free speech is not to earn money; therefore commercial advertisement is not protected."

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A purely commercial advertisement promoting a trade is not protected speech, and harmful/misleading medical advertisements can be banned.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Departed from by Tata Press (1995), which holds that commercial speech is protected, but it still upholds bans on misleading or false advertisements; Hamdard's outcome (ban on magic-remedy advertisements) still stands.

cards.name: Tata Press Ltd. v. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. (MTNL) (1995)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1995) 5 SCC 139 (Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Tata Press published "Tata Yellow Pages", a directory of classified business advertisements and telephone numbers. MTNL claimed an exclusive right under the Telegraph Act to publish telephone directories and asked it to stop. The professor's illustration: "a new book of constitutional law by Professor V.P. Tiwari has come out, but nobody knows; if it is advertised, people will buy it; the advertisement benefits the publisher and the reader."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is commercial speech protected by Art 19(1)(a)? Can MTNL prevent publication of advertising directories?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Commercial speech/advertisements are protected under Art 19(1)(a): the public has a right to receive commercial information (price, availability, quality); an advertisement is not only for the advertiser; it benefits the consumer.
  • But the speech must not be misleading, deceptive or unfair, and false or misleading advertisements are not protected; they may be restricted under Art 19(2) (e.g. decency, morality, public order) and consumer protection laws.
  • MTNL's exclusive right extended to the telephone directory (subscribers' list), not to classified advertisements like the Yellow Pages.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Commercial speech is part of freedom of speech and expression, subject to restrictions in Art 19(2) and to the requirement that advertisements be truthful and not misleading.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "Commercial speech is also protected under Art 19(1)(a): provided the speech is not misleading." Also remember Hamdard (earlier, not protected) and the Consumer Protection link (misleading ads, deficiency of service).

cards.name: Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (Bandit Queen) (1996)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1996) 4 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India; Ahmadi C.J. and Bench).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The film Bandit Queen (directed by Shekhar Kapur) is based on the life of Phoolan Devi. The censors gave it an "A" certificate, with scenes of rape, frontal nudity and abusive language. The Delhi High Court (on a petition by Om Pal Singh Hoon) had set aside the censor's clearance and stopped its exhibition; the Supreme Court reversed that. (Phoolan Devi's own privacy challenge to the film was a separate matter: Phoolan Devi v. Shekhar Kapur.) The professor recalled: "Bandit Queen: a film challenged by Phoolan Devi against Shekhar Kapur".

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Are the scenes obscene? How are nudity and violence judged in a serious film on social issues?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The Supreme Court upheld the film's release: the nude and rape scenes were not meant to arouse prurient interest but to show the brutality, humiliation and the social conditions that produced a bandit; the film must be viewed as a whole with its message. "Nudity does not necessarily arouse sexual feelings." The theme (a victim of social oppression) and the dignity of the scene matter.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: In judging obscenity, the whole work, theme, message and context are decisive; scenes of sexual violence meant to evoke revulsion and sympathy, not lust, are not obscene.

cards.name: Devidas Ramchandra Tuljapurkar v. State of Maharashtra (2015)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2015) 6 SCC 1; decided 14 May 2015 (Supreme Court of India; Dipak Misra and Prafulla C. Pant JJ.; judgment by Dipak Misra J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The Marathi poem "Gandhi Mala Bhetala" ("I met Gandhi") by Vasant Dattatraya Gurjar was published in 1994 in the Bulletin of the All India Bank Association Union (editor/publisher: Devidas Tuljapurkar). The poem used offensive, vulgar and obscene words about or attributed to Mahatma Gandhi, in a satire aimed at those who do not follow Gandhian values.
  • A complaint under s. 292 IPC (obscenity) and s. 34 followed. The Bombay High Court refused to quash. The poet did not appeal; the publisher/editor appealed to the Supreme Court.
  • Professor's summary: "Mahatma Gandhi was abused (the poem used his name to say obscene things)."

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is the poem obscene under s. 292 IPC? Which test applies? Does it matter that the words concern a historically respected figure? Is there a "poetic licence" defence?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Court applied the contemporary community standards test (rejecting Hicklin, following Aveek Sarkar and Samaresh Bose). Where words are used about a historically respected person (Gandhi), the test is applied with greater vigour; the context and the purpose of the use of the person's name are examined. The Court rejected "poetic licence" as a defence.
  • The poem was found to cross the line (obscene), but because about twenty years had passed and the publisher had tendered an unconditional apology when readers objected, the Court discharged the appellant (the author was not before the Court).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Freedom of speech does not allow obscene words about historically respected figures under cover of poetic licence; the community standards test applies more rigorously in such cases and the context is decisive.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Criticised as creating a "historically respected personalities" doctrine that may chill political satire and history writing (see the LiveLaw and The Wire commentaries). Criticism of a leader's policies or conduct is not the same as using obscene allusions to a revered figure.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Declared by the professor as a compulsory exam question on facts.

cards.name: Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India (2014)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2014) 11 SCC 477; decided 12 March 2014 (Supreme Court of India; bench headed by B.S. Chauhan J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• An NGO, Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan, filed a PIL seeking directions to stop inflammatory and hate speeches by politicians and religious leaders and to enforce existing law. The Election Commission told the Court that existing laws permit action.
  • The professor said that Justice Nariman wrote it ("a tight judge, generally anti-government"). The bench was headed by Justice B.S. Chauhan (not Nariman J.; Nariman J. wrote Shreya Singhal).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Should the Court frame guidelines to prevent hate speech? Is the existing law enough? Should hate speech be defined?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Court declined to frame guidelines itself, observing that existing laws (ss. 153A, 153B, 295A, 505 IPC; RPA) are available, and directed the Law Commission to study whether it "deems proper to define hate speech" and to make recommendations to Parliament (including on strengthening the Election Commission to deal with hate speech).
  • The Court described hate speech as an effort to marginalise individuals based on their membership of a group, which undermines dignity and equality and threatens the fundamental values of the Constitution (fraternity). It also noted that it is a problem of enforcement as much as of definition.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Hate speech damages dignity and equal citizenship; existing criminal provisions should be effectively enforced; legislative definition/reform was referred to the Law Commission.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Led to the 267th Law Commission Report (2017), whose chairman was Justice B.S. Chauhan (the same judge who headed the bench).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor listed this case as the lead case on hate speech decided by the Supreme Court and asked students to read "one or two more" hate speech cases.

cards.name: Law Commission of India, Report No. 267: "Hate Speech" (2017)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: Submitted to the Government on 23 March 2017 (Chairman: Justice B.S. Chauhan).

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Recommended two new provisions in the IPC: s. 153C ("prohibition of incitement to hatred": punishing the incitement to hatred on grounds of race, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, place of birth, residence, language, caste or community, or any other ground) and s. 505A ("causing fear, alarm, or provocation of violence in certain cases").
  • Defined hate speech broadly as incitement to hatred primarily against a group of persons defined in terms of race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, religious belief and the like.
  • Factors to weigh before restricting speech: context, status of the victim, status of the speaker, potential to create discriminatory and disruptive circumstances (the likelihood of imminent harm); also non-penal measures such as sensitisation and public education on responsible speech.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor: "Which Law Commission report? (a student: 2017; he said "267th, Justice B.S. Chauhan") and "this is a very important report; read it".

cards.name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2015) 5 SCC 1; decided 24 March 2015 (Supreme Court of India; Chelameswar and R.F. Nariman JJ.; judgment by Nariman J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • In November 2012 two young women in Palghar (Maharashtra) were arrested under s. 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 for a Facebook post questioning the total shutdown of Mumbai after a political leader's death (and for "liking" it). Shreya Singhal, a law student, filed a PIL challenging s. 66A (punishing "grossly offensive", "annoying", "inconvenient" messages), s. 69A (blocking) and s. 79 (intermediary liability).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is s. 66A within the Art 19(2) grounds? Is it vague/overbroad? Are ss. 69A and 79 valid?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• s. 66A struck down as unconstitutional: vague and overbroad terms ("annoying", "inconvenient", "grossly offensive") are not among the eight Art 19(2) grounds, and they create a chilling effect.
  • The Court distinguished speech into (1) discussion, (2) advocacy and (3) incitement: "Mere discussion or even advocacy of a particular cause, however unpopular, is at the heart of Art 19(1)(a). It is only when such discussion or advocacy reaches the level of incitement that Art 19(2) kicks in." Incitement must have a proximate (direct) connection with a public order disturbance. Law and order, public order and security of State are distinguished again (Lohia).
  • s. 69A upheld (with procedural safeguards: written reasons, hearing, Review Committee, remedy by writ); s. 79(3)(b) read down (intermediary must act on actual knowledge through a court order or government notification relating to Art 19(2) subjects).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Only incitement can be restricted; discussion and advocacy are constitutionally protected; vague speech laws that go beyond Art 19(2) are void.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor said "Shreya Singhal: read it; speech is divided into three parts". Illustration he gave (re-told below).

cards.name: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (the National Anthem case) (1986)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1986) 3 SCC 615; AIR 1987 SC 748 (Supreme Court of India; O. Chinnappa Reddy and M.M. Dutt JJ.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Three children (Bijoe, Binu Mol and Bindu Emmanuel) belonging to the Jehovah's Witnesses were expelled from school in Kerala because they stood respectfully during the national anthem "Jana Gana Mana" but did not sing: their religious faith permits prayer only to Jehovah. A Headmaster expelled them on the basis of a Kerala Education Department circular.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can a person be compelled to sing the national anthem? Does freedom of speech include the right not to speak? Is there any law obliging singing? Is there an Art 25 claim?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The expulsion violated Art 19(1)(a) and Art 25(1). No law obliges anyone to sing; the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 (s. 3) punishes preventing the singing or causing disturbance during the anthem, not refraining from singing.
  • Freedom of speech and expression includes the right to remain silent. Standing respectfully while the anthem is sung is enough; respect cannot be compelled. The Court cited the Indian tradition of tolerance and the American case West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette (1943) (no compulsory flag salute).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The right to freedom of speech and expression includes the right not to speak (to remain silent); no one can be compelled to sing the anthem if the person shows respect by standing and does not disturb.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Shyam Narayan Chouksey v. Union of India (2016, 2018): compulsory standing during the anthem in cinemas, ordered in 2016, was later made optional/diluted (2018); Bijoe Emmanuel remains good law.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor: "Right to silence is also part of Art 19(1)(a): Vijay (Bijoe) Emmanuel; it was about the song Jana Gana Mana; the Court said you cannot compel anyone to sing; you only need to show respect by standing."

cards.name: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1978) 2 SCC 424; AIR 1978 SC 1025 (Supreme Court of India; V.R. Krishna Iyer J. for the Bench).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• Nandini Satpathy, a former Chief Minister of Odisha, was summoned to the Vigilance Police Station (Cuttack) and given a long list of written questions in a corruption case. She refused to answer, claiming the right against self-incrimination. She was prosecuted under s. 179 IPC (refusing to answer a public servant authorised to question).
  • The professor: "She was held at the police station till 8, 9, 10, 11 at night; "we will not let you go till you speak". Can police compel? Can they detain for a long time if you don't reply?"

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the protection in Art 20(3) (no person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself) apply during police investigation and interrogation, or only at trial before the magistrate?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Art 20(3) is available at the stage of investigation, to a person who is an accused and also to a suspect who may be incriminated by the answers; the right is not confined to the court. A person may refuse to answer questions that may incriminate him (not all questions).
  • Police cannot compel answers; prolonged detention and pressure amount to torture and violate Art 20(3) and 21. Safeguards: the presence of a lawyer (or friend/relative) during interrogation; right to be informed of the right to silence (the Court considered the American Miranda warnings an aid to interpretation); questions to women to be asked in the presence of a woman/relative, and not at night at the police station (as suggested).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The right to silence against self-incrimination extends to police interrogation; compulsion (physical or psychological) is barred; s. 161(2) CrPC (now BNSS s. 180(2)) gives a person the right to decline to answer incriminating questions.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010): narco-analysis, polygraph, BEAP tests without consent violate Art 20(3) and 21. D.K. Basu (1997): arrest and detention safeguards. Statements to police are not admissible in evidence against the accused (s. 162 CrPC / BNSS s. 181; ss. 25-26 Evidence Act / BSA ss. 23-24).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "Nandini Satpathy is Art 20 (self-incrimination), not Art 19: that will be taught under Art 20; but this is what is called Miranda rights in India." He added: "earlier the protection was recognised only before the magistrate (statements before a judge can be used as evidence); Nandini Satpathy for the first time extended it to the stage of investigation by the police."

cards.name: Miranda v. Arizona (US Supreme Court, 1966)

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Ernesto Miranda was arrested for kidnapping and rape in Arizona, interrogated for two hours without being told he could remain silent or have a lawyer, and signed a confession.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is a confession obtained in custodial interrogation without warnings admissible?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The Fifth and Sixth Amendments require that, before custodial interrogation, the police must warn the suspect: (1) you have the right to remain silent; (2) anything you say can and will be used against you in a court of law; (3) you have the right to talk to a lawyer and have him present while you are being questioned; (4) if you cannot afford a lawyer, one will be appointed for you. A statement taken without these warnings is inadmissible.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Custodial interrogation is inherently coercive; procedural safeguards (warnings) are necessary to protect the privilege against self-incrimination.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: A student recited the four warnings in class (see the Miranda warning list above). Professor's explanation of why: "you are presumed innocent until guilt is proved; the other side must prove guilt; you need not help prove your own guilt; otherwise your freedom of being innocent would be diluted (the burden of proof)."

cards.name: State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee (1954)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1954 SC 170; 1954 SCR 558 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; judgment by S.R. Das J. - verify the author before quoting).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948 provided for acquisition of land (mainly for rehabilitating refugees) and fixed compensation at the market value as on 31 December 1946, ignoring the rise in value after that date.
  • Bela Banerjee, whose land was acquired, argued that compensation fixed at the 1946 value was not "compensation" within Art 31(2).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • What does "compensation" in Art 31(2) mean? May the legislature fix it arbitrarily? Is the adequacy of compensation justiciable?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Court held that "compensation" means a just equivalent of what the owner has been deprived of. The legislature may lay down principles for determining compensation, but if the principle is arbitrary or results in a sum that is not the just equivalent, it is not "compensation" and the law is unconstitutional to that extent.
  • The provision fixing the 1946 market value (ignoring subsequent increase) was held invalid as not giving the owner a just equivalent.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Compensation = just equivalent (market value) of the property taken; adequacy of compensation is justiciable where the principle laid down is not relevant to determining the value at the time of acquisition.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Provoked the Fourth Amendment (1955), which declared that the adequacy of compensation could not be questioned; later again diluted by the 25th Amendment (1971) ("amount").
  • The professor: "compensation means an amount equivalent to the market value - this was said in Bela Banerjee. Read the case; you will enjoy it."

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite for: "what does compensation mean?"; the move from compensation → amount; the argument that just equivalent is protected by the text.

cards.name: State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga (1952)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1952 SC 252; 1952 SCR 889 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 abolished the zamindari system, vested estates in the State and provided for compensation under a statutory scheme. The Maharaja of Darbhanga challenged it. The Patna High Court had held it unconstitutional (discriminatory and violating Art 14). Meanwhile, Parliament passed the First Amendment (Art 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Did the Act satisfy Art 31(2) (public purpose and compensation)? Was it protected by Art 31(4)? Did it violate Art 14 / 19(1)(f)?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • By a majority, the Court upheld the Act as a whole: it was for a public purpose (agrarian reform) and was protected by Art 31(4) from the compensation challenge, so courts could not scrutinise the adequacy of compensation under that Act; two specific provisions were held discriminatory under Art 14 (3:2).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Laws for abolition of intermediaries are for a public purpose; where Art 31(4) applies, the adequacy of compensation is not justiciable.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Professor's use: "the Court told the Bihar Government that compensation must be paid - but where was the money? Zamindars owned vast land - so Parliament amended the Constitution to say amount instead of compensation." (The professor mentioned "Kameshwar Prasad Singh etc." - the actual name is Kameshwar Singh; the holding on Art 31(4) was more nuanced than "compensation must be paid", so use the case for the background, and Bela Banerjee for the meaning of compensation.)

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Background case for zamindari abolition, Art 31A/31B, First Amendment and Art 31(4) protection. Verify details before quoting bench strengths.

cards.name: R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (Bank Nationalisation Case) (1970)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1970) 1 SCC 248; AIR 1970 SC 564 (11-judge bench; majority 10:1, Ray J. dissenting).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Parliament nationalised 14 major banks by the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969. A shareholder (R.C. Cooper) challenged it as violating Arts 14, 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g) and 31(2).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can a law of acquisition also be tested under Art 19? What does "compensation" mean? Is the Act discriminatory?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Parliament was competent, but the Act was struck down because the compensation principles in it were not the equivalent of the value of the banks' property and discriminated against the banks.
  • Rejected the A.K. Gopalan doctrine that the Fundamental Rights are mutually exclusive: the direct effect of a law on a right matters; a law of acquisition must also stand the test of Art 19(1)(f).
  • "Compensation" means the full money equivalent of the property taken; the legislature can lay down principles but not a colourable or illusory scheme.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The object and effect of a law decide which Fundamental Rights are attracted; compensation means full market equivalent.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Parliament responded with the 25th Amendment ("amount") and Art 31C; the Government also issued the "privy purses" abolition move (Madhav Rao Scindia, 1970) - not covered in class.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite for: rejection of the "mutual exclusivity" idea (why having both Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31 caused conflict) and for the meaning of compensation.

cards.name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - the property angle

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge bench; 7:6 on the basic structure).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Challenge to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments, the Kerala Land Reforms Act and the Ninth Schedule additions (Kerala laws affecting a mutt's property).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights? Is the 25th Amendment valid?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure; Golak Nath overruled.
  • 25th Amendment: the substitution of "amount" for "compensation" and the removal of Art 19(1)(f) from acquisition laws were upheld; the first part of Art 31C was upheld; the second part (barring judicial review of the declaration that a law furthers Art 39(b)/(c)) was struck down.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: All constitutional amendments are subject to the basic-structure limit; property-related amendments of the 25th Amendment stood.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• The professor's point: since Kesavananda allowed the Court to strike down an amendment that violates the basic structure, "the 44th Amendment was hardly necessary" - "most amendments are political". (His view; the textbook position is that the 44th Amendment removed the long-running conflict between property rights and socio-economic reform.)
  • Full treatment of Kesavananda in the lecture on Fundamental Rights v. Directive Principles.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite as the case that finally upheld amount, and for "Parliament amends, Court tests for basic structure".

cards.name: K.T. Plantation Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Karnataka (2011)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2011) 9 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; K.S. Radhakrishnan J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Plantation owners challenged Karnataka legislation that took over their land holdings and argued that, with Art 31 gone, they were entitled to compensation under Art 300A.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • After Art 31 was deleted, does Art 300A require (a) a public purpose and (b) compensation? Is there an inherent right to compensation in Entry 42 of List III?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Public purpose continues to be a pre-condition for deprivation of property under Art 300A.
  • There is no inherent or in-built right to compensation in Entry 42, List III (acquisition and requisitioning of property); the legislature has a margin to decide the quantum and manner.
  • However, a nil or illusory compensation must be justified on judicial standards and can be sustained only for measures that achieve greater social justice; the right to claim compensation can be inferred from Art 300A when the State's deprivation is arbitrary.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Under Art 300A the State needs a law and a public purpose; compensation is not an absolute entitlement but the State must justify non-payment or illusory payment.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite for "what remains of the right to property after the 44th Amendment?"

cards.name: Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2020) 2 SCC 569 (Supreme Court of India; Indu Malhotra and Ajay Rastogi JJ.; decided 8 January 2020).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • In 1967-68 Himachal Pradesh took about 3.34 hectares of Vidya Devi's land to build a road without any acquisition proceeding or compensation. She learned of her entitlement only in 2010. The High Court dismissed her 2013 writ petition and left her to file a civil suit.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can the State take land without following law and then claim ownership by adverse possession (over 42 years)? Is the right to property a human right?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The right to property, though no longer fundamental, is a human right and a constitutional right under Art 300A; the State can remove a person from property only under a procedure established by law.
  • The State cannot invoke adverse possession to defeat a citizen's title where it took the land without due acquisition; the Court inferred a duty to pay compensation and directed the State to pay compensation with solatium and interest.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A welfare State cannot take private property without law and compensation; Art 300A protects against executive action unsupported by law.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Use as the modern authority that Art 300A is a human right and for the "authority of law" requirement.

cards.name: Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar Shah (2024)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: 2024 SCC OnLine SC 968 (2024 INSC 435); Supreme Court of India; P.S. Narasimha and Aravind Kumar JJ.; judgment dated 16 May 2024.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Corporation sought to compulsorily acquire immovable property under s. 352 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980; the Calcutta High Court held that the Corporation did not have the power. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • What does Art 300A's "authority of law" require beyond the existence of a statute?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • Acquiring land without due procedure is outside the "authority of law". Art 300A contains seven sub-rights (the Court said the list is illustrative): (1) right to notice; (2) right to be heard; (3) right to a reasoned decision; (4) duty to acquire only for a public purpose; (5) right of restitution or fair compensation; (6) right to an efficient and expeditious process; (7) right of conclusion.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Art 300A requires a fair, reasoned and procedurally sound acquisition process, not merely a statute.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: A short model line: "Post-44th Amendment, Art 300A is not a hollow right; Bimal Kumar Shah (2024) lists seven sub-rights which the State must respect."

cards.name: In Re: Ramlila Maidan Incident dated 4/5.06.2011 v. Home Secretary, Union of India (2012)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2012) 5 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India; B.S. Chauhan and Swatanter Kumar JJ.; suo motu; decided in 2012 - verify the date of judgment before citing).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• On 4 June 2011 a yoga camp (permission granted for yoga) at Ramlila Maidan, New Delhi turned into an anti-corruption protest and hunger strike led by Baba Ramdev, with tens of thousands of participants. Section 144 CrPC was imposed; around midnight (4/5 June) the police used tear gas, lathi-charge and water cannons to evict the sleeping crowd. A woman participant (reported as Rajbala) later died of injuries and many people were injured (the professor said "about 80").
  • The Court took suo motu cognisance of the incident.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Whether the police action infringed the right to assemble peaceably and to express views (Art 19(1)(a),(b)) and Art 21; whether the s. 144 order and the midnight eviction were justified.

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The right to assemble and to protest peacefully is a Fundamental Right, not absolute, and may be reasonably regulated in the interest of public order; restrictions must be proportionate.
  • The police action at midnight against a sleeping, peaceful crowd was excessive and unjustified; the State must facilitate peaceful assemblies, not stifle them, and excessive force is impermissible. (The judgment is also widely cited for treating the right to sleep as part of Art 21 - verify the wording before quoting.)

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Peaceful protest is protected by Arts 19(1)(a) and (b); police power under s. 144 CrPC / BNSS s. 163 must be exercised reasonably and proportionately.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor: "a very important case on protest - read it." He compared it with Amit Sahni (roads cannot be occupied indefinitely).

cards.name: Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (the Shaheen Bagh case) (2020)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2020) 10 SCC 439 (Supreme Court of India; bench of S.K. Kaul, Aniruddha Bose and Krishna Murari JJ.; decided 7 October 2020 - verify bench before quoting).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Protestors against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 occupied a public road at Shaheen Bagh (Delhi) for months, blocking commuters; a petition sought removal of the blockade.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the right to protest allow indefinite occupation of a public road at the cost of other citizens?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • Public ways and public places cannot be occupied indefinitely; protest must be at designated places; the right to protest and the right to movement (and to livelihood) of others must be balanced; the administration must act to clear obstructions.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The right to protest is not unlimited; it cannot be exercised by blocking public roads indefinitely.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "the Supreme Court said public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely for protest at the expense of other citizens."

cards.name: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2018) 17 SCC 324 (Supreme Court of India; A.K. Sikri J.; verify bench).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The National Green Tribunal had banned protests at Jantar Mantar, Delhi; the NGO challenged the order.

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The right to protest peacefully is a Fundamental Right; a blanket ban was unreasonable. The State may regulate (time, place, manner) and designate protest sites, but must make a balanced arrangement for protest, with reasonable guidelines on noise, permissions and space.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Regulation, not prohibition, of protest is permissible (proportionality).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Pairs naturally with Anuradha Bhasin (proportionality) in a protest problem question; the lecture 3 hypothetical about Jantar Mantar is the same issue.

cards.name: T.K. Rangarajan v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2003)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2003) 6 SCC 581 (Supreme Court of India; Banerjee and Lahoti JJ.; decided 6 August 2003).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Tamil Nadu Government dismissed about 1.7 lakh employees who went on strike in July 2003 and invoked the Tamil Nadu Essential Services Maintenance Act (TESMA) ordinance. The employees' association challenged the dismissals.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Do government employees have a fundamental right to strike? Does the right to form associations include a right to strike?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Government employees have no fundamental, statutory or moral right to strike. The right to form an association under Art 19(1)(c) does not guarantee the effectiveness of the association or the right to resort to strike; strike is not a fundamental right.
  • The Court also said that the Government must be fair and that employees' remedies are negotiation, representation and legal remedies, but strike as a weapon is not a constitutional guarantee; society's interest in essential services prevails.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: No fundamental right to strike (for government employees) - Art 19(1)(c) protects forming unions, not striking.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor's extension: "I can add that students of government universities also do not have a fundamental right to strike" (his opinion; cite Rangarajan for the principle and note that the Court has not ruled on student strikes specifically).

cards.name: Zoroastrian Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar, Co-operative Societies (2005) - (probable case)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2005) 5 SCC 632 (Supreme Court of India; 3 judges) - verify; the professor could not name the case.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • A co-operative housing society formed by Parsis adopted a bye-law that plots will be sold only to Zoroastrians (Parsis). The Registrar held the bye-law invalid.

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The Court upheld the bye-law: a voluntary association has the right to decide who may be its members (Art 19(1)(c)); the Court distinguished a purely private society from public bodies and said this did not violate Arts 14, 15 or 29(2) as the Society was a private association of a small religious community with no State aid.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor: "I do not quite understand this case - the Supreme Court allowed it, perhaps because the society was private." Use it for "can an association restrict membership?" and flag that the point is controversial.

cards.name: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (the "Auto Shankar" case) (1994)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1994) 6 SCC 632 (Supreme Court of India; B.P. Jeevan Reddy J. for the Bench; decided 7 October 1994).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• Auto Shankar (Gauri Shankar), a prisoner convicted of six murders and sentenced to death, wrote an autobiography in jail, which allegedly described his links with police and prison officials. He gave it to his wife to be published by the Tamil magazine "Nakkheeran". Prison authorities (the Inspector General of Prisons) asked the publisher not to publish and threatened action; the magazine petitioned.
  • The professor's retelling of this case included invented comic details; only the facts above are the case.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can the State prevent publication in advance (prior restraint)? Is there a right to privacy in Art 21 against publication of one's life story? What may the press publish about public officials?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Right to privacy is implicit in Art 21; but no one can restrain publication of matters that are already public records (including court records).
  • Prior restraint is not permissible; the remedy of a person defamed or whose privacy is invaded is after publication (damages / action). Public officials have no right to privacy for their official acts and duties (except in matters under the Official Secrets Act); the press may criticise them. The State and its officials cannot seek to restrain the publication of material about their conduct.
  • The Court said the authorities could not stop the autobiography; whether it was defamatory could be tested after publication.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: No prior restraint on the press; privacy is protected by Art 21 but yields where the matter is in the public record or concerns the official conduct of public servants.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Landmark in press freedom v. privacy (links with Brij Bhushan). Professor: "read it in the original - I will not tell you more; you will enjoy it" (the case, not the stories)."

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite for: no pre-censorship of press; privacy/defamation after publication; public officials and their duties.

cards.name: Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (the 2G Spectrum case) (2012)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2012) 3 SCC 1 (Supreme Court of India; G.S. Singhvi and A.K. Ganguly JJ.; decided 2 February 2012). Follow-up: Special Reference No. 1 of 2012 (2012) 10 SCC 1.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • In 2008 the Department of Telecommunications allotted licences and 2G spectrum at a low fixed price on a "first come, first served" basis to a few applicants, who then sold equity at high valuations. Public-interest petitioners challenged the allotments.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can scarce natural resources be allotted without a transparent, competitive method? What constitutional principles bind the State in distributing them?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The first-come-first-served method as implemented was arbitrary and unconstitutional (Art 14); the licences were quashed. The Court treated natural resources, including spectrum, as public property held in trust by the State for the people, and said their distribution must serve the common good (Art 39(b)): "The State is a trustee."
  • Hence auction is the preferred method for maximising revenue; but in the Presidential Reference (2012) the Court clarified that auction is not the only constitutionally permissible method for all natural resources - a method must be fair, transparent and non-arbitrary, and the choice depends on the objective.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The State must allocate natural resources fairly and transparently for the public good; resources like spectrum are public property (Art 14, Art 39(b)).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor's link: the "air and spectrum" are "not anybody's father's property" and "belong to the people of India" - connect with Art 39(b) and (c) (material resources of the community to subserve the common good; concentration of wealth to be avoided) and with the Cricket Association reasoning that airwaves are public property. (His description of the political side of the 2G matter is omitted.)

cards.name: Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) and PUCL v. Union of India (2003)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2002) 5 SCC 294 (Supreme Court of India; 3 judges; 2 May 2002) and (2003) 4 SCC 399 (13 March 2003).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Association for Democratic Reforms sought directions that candidates for election disclose their criminal antecedents, assets and liabilities, and educational qualifications. The Election Commission issued disclosure directions after the Supreme Court's decision; Parliament then amended the Representation of the People Act (s. 33B) to dilute them.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Do voters have a fundamental right to know the background of candidates? Does this override a candidate's claim to privacy?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Voters have a fundamental right to information about candidates under Art 19(1)(a) (the right to know/receive information is part of freedom of speech and expression), because an informed vote is essential for free and fair elections (a basic feature).
  • The candidate's right to privacy is subordinate in the public interest. In PUCL (2003) the Court struck down s. 33B RPA (which tried to nullify the ADR directions) and upheld the voter's right to know.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The right to know the antecedents of candidates is part of Art 19(1)(a); informed voters are essential for democracy.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (2024) (Constitution Bench, 15 February 2024): the Electoral Bond Scheme was held unconstitutional because it infringed the voter's right to information about political funding under Art 19(1)(a) (verify citation before use).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "the voters' right to know... candidates argued that it is their privacy; the Supreme Court said, you must tell - and then people began to be exposed (the affidavit)."

cards.name: Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2023)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 113 of 2016; (2023) 4 SCC 1 (Constitution Bench: S.A. Nazeer, A.S. Bopanna, B.R. Gavai, V. Ramasubramanian and B.V. Nagarathna JJ.; majority by Ramasubramanian J.; Nagarathna J. concurring in part and separate; decided 3 January 2023).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • After the 2016 gang-rape of a minor and her mother on a highway in Bulandshahr, a political leader (a former Minister) described the incident as a "political conspiracy and nothing else". The victims' family sought action and the Court referred larger questions to a Constitution Bench: restrictions on free speech by public functionaries; whether Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons; and vicarious liability of the Government for a Minister's statements.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • (1) Can additional restrictions beyond Art 19(2) be imposed on a public functionary's free speech? (2) Can Fundamental Rights (Arts 19, 21) be claimed against non-State actors? (3) Does the State have a positive duty to protect liberty against private actors? (4) Is a Minister's statement attributable to the Government by collective responsibility (Art 75(3))?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• No additional restrictions beyond Art 19(2) can be imposed on free speech (even for public functionaries); the grounds are exhaustive. (Nagarathna J. agreed.)
  • Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against persons other than the State or its instrumentalities (horizontal application, at least for Art 21 and in appropriate cases Art 19).
  • The State has a positive duty to protect the life and liberty of citizens even against threats from private persons (Nagarathna J. dissented: the duty is negative).
  • A Minister's statement cannot be vicariously attributed to the Government by invoking collective responsibility (even if it concerns State affairs); but if officials act on it and cause loss, the conduct may be actionable. Nagarathna J. held that a statement made as the Government's delegate can be attributed.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Art 19(2) grounds are exhaustive; horizontal application of Arts 19 and 21; ministerial speech is not automatically government speech.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Nagarathna J.: public functionaries owe a duty of responsible speech (dignity, equality, fraternity); Parliament may legislate; political parties can regulate through codes of conduct.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Listed by the professor as an exam-hint case ("Kaushal Kishor - horizontal application"). In the lecture it was used to say: "free speech and the obligations of public functionaries - political dissent and unpopular opinion are protected, subject only to the specific grounds." Art 75(3) (collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha) is the constitutional hook.

cards.name: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2002) 8 SCC 481 (11-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court; B.N. Kirpal C.J. for the majority; decided 31 October 2002).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Several petitions by private professional colleges (medical, engineering) and minority institutions challenged State control over admissions, fee structure and the quota system after Unni Krishnan (1993), which had imposed a scheme (free and payment seats, State-set fees). The reference raised 11 questions on Arts 19(1)(g), 26, 29, 30.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is there a fundamental right to establish and administer educational institutions? Is education a "business" or "occupation"? How far can the State regulate private unaided institutions' admission and fees? What is the unit for determining minority status?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Yes - the right to establish and administer educational institutions is protected as an "occupation" under Art 19(1)(g) (and, for minorities, under Art 30(1); for religious denominations, Art 26). It is not "trade" or "business" in the commercial sense: education is charitable in nature.
  • Consequence (professor): since it is an occupation, restrictions on it must be (i) reasonable, (ii) imposed by law, and (iii) in the public interest (Art 19(6)).
  • No capitation fee / no profiteering ("commercialisation" is not allowed); a reasonable surplus for the growth of the institution is permitted; admissions must be fair, transparent and merit-based; the State may regulate to ensure that, but cannot take over the administration of unaided private institutions (the scheme in Unni Krishnan was held to be unworkable and was set aside). Minority status is to be determined by reference to the State (not India) as the unit.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Education is an occupation under Art 19(1)(g) but must be run on a non-profit basis (no capitation fee); reasonable regulation by law in the public interest is permitted.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• The professor said the ratio was so unclear that "even the Supreme Court did not understand what it had decided, so another Constitution Bench was constituted to explain it": Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003) 6 SCC 697 (5 judges). In class a student named the year as 2018 - the professor accepted it (and said "I might be wrong") - the correct year is 2003.
  • Later: P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra (2005) 6 SCC 537 (7 judges) held that the State cannot impose reservation / quota on unaided private institutions; Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012) (RTE Act 25% quota upheld for unaided non-minority schools).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Question for the exam: "Name the case which was decided to clarify the ratio of TMA Pai." → Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003). (Also note that TMA Pai was an 11-judge bench - "that is why it is a pillar case".)

cards.name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (the Pavement Dwellers case) (1985)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1985) 3 SCC 545; AIR 1986 SC 180 (5-judge Constitution Bench; Y.V. Chandrachud C.J. for the Court).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• Thousands of pavement and slum dwellers in Bombay (who worked as hawkers, domestic workers, casual labourers) lived on pavements and in slums near their workplaces. In July 1981 the Maharashtra Government and the Bombay Municipal Corporation announced that they would be evicted and deported to their places of origin; the Corporation began demolitions. The pavement dwellers (and the journalist Olga Tellis) petitioned.
  • Earlier, some had signed undertakings that they would vacate by a date; the State argued they had waived their rights.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the right to life (Art 21) include the right to livelihood? Can the State evict pavement dwellers? Can a person waive a Fundamental Right?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Right to life includes the right to livelihood: "no person can live without the means of living"; eviction deprives them of livelihood and therefore of life - unless done according to a procedure established by law that is just, fair and reasonable.
  • Pavements are meant for pedestrians; encroachments can be removed, but only after notice and a hearing (not summary eviction), and not during the monsoon; those enumerated in the 1976 census were entitled to alternative sites; slum dwellers' tenement improvement schemes were directed.
  • No waiver of Fundamental Rights: the undertakings the pavement dwellers had given to vacate by a date did not bind them; there can be no estoppel against the Constitution (the professor had earlier taught this under the doctrine of waiver - a student recalled it).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Right to livelihood is part of Art 21; no waiver of Fundamental Rights; eviction must be by fair procedure.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "This case I taught under doctrine of waiver." A student correctly connected it: "pavement dwellers were told to leave by a certain date and the agreement was held not binding."

cards.name: Sodan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee (1989)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1989) 4 SCC 155 (5-judge Constitution Bench; also see Bombay Hawkers' Union v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985) 3 SCC 528 and Gainda Ram v. M.C.D. (2010) 10 SCC 715).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Hawkers and small traders on the pavements of Delhi (including around Connaught Place) were removed by the NDMC; they claimed a fundamental right to hawk at their chosen places under Art 19(1)(g) and Art 21.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does Art 19(1)(g) give hawkers a right to trade on public streets at a place of their choice?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Hawking is a trade protected by Art 19(1)(g) (it is the livelihood of the poor and serves the common man), but there is no fundamental right to carry on trade at a particular place of one's choice on public property; the State may regulate or prohibit hawking on safety, traffic and health grounds.
  • The authorities must frame a scheme with designated hawking zones and licensing; the State should not simply evict without an arrangement ("once they have a livelihood, they cannot be thrown out without an alternative remedy").

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
