fields.html: The right to carry on trade is not a right to carry it on anywhere; public property cannot be taken by force; the State must provide regulated hawking zones.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Professor's comment: "This case corrected the mistake: if the Government can throw people out, then the right is hollow; hence the Court directed the creation of hawkers' zones - near railway stations, bus stands, metro stations - which benefits the common man who buys vegetables on his way home."
  • Statute: the Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act, 2014 now gives vendors a statutory right (town vending committees, survey, certificates).
  • Professor's example: a person has a right to hoist the national flag but not in the mouth of a fellow student or anywhere he pleases (compare Union of India v. Naveen Jindal, 2004 - flying the national flag is protected by Art 19(1)(a) but subject to the Flag Code and reasonable restrictions). The point: a right to do an activity is not a right to do it at any place.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor: "When asked about trade rights on public places, write: right to hawk is protected, but not at a place of one's choice; the State must create hawking zones." A student pointed out that Sodan Singh said there is no fundamental right to a specific place - the professor agreed.

cards.name: Chintaman Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1950)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1951 SC 118; 1950 SCR 759 (Supreme Court of India; Mahajan J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Central Provinces and Berar Regulation of Manufacture of Bidis (Agricultural Purposes) Act, 1948 empowered the Deputy Commissioner to prohibit workers in villages from manufacturing bidis during the agricultural season, so that labour would be available for farming. Bidi manufacturers and workers challenged it under Art 19(1)(g).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • When is a restriction on the freedom of trade "reasonable" under Art 19(6)?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The restriction was arbitrary and excessive - it extended to all bidi workers in the area, not only those engaged in agriculture; it was not a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public.
  • Test: "Reasonable implies intelligent care and deliberation, the choice of a course which reason dictates. Legislation which arbitrarily or excessively invades the right cannot be said to contain the quality of reasonableness... it must strike a proper balance between the freedom guaranteed and the social control permitted."

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A restriction on trade must be proportionate to the object; arbitrary or excessive restrictions are not reasonable.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor referred to the case as "the Chintamani case about labour in bidi factories" - "monopoly is also not protected" (his point: neither unlimited freedom nor arbitrary State control is constitutional). Use it for the reasonableness test of Art 19(6).

cards.name: State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel & Restaurants Association (the Dance Bar case) (2013)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2013) 8 SCC 519 (Supreme Court of India; Dipak Misra and Vikramajit Sen JJ.; decided 16 July 2013 - verify). Follow-up: (2019) 3 SCC 429.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• The Bombay Police (Amendment) Act, 2005 inserted ss. 33A and 33B to ban dance performances in eating houses, permit rooms and beer bars (but exempted three-star and above hotels) on the ground that the dances were obscene and degrading to women's dignity, promoted drinking and exploitation. Thousands of women were bar dancers who supported their families; the closure threw them out of work.
  • The Bombay High Court struck the provisions down (2006). The State appealed.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the ban violate Art 19(1)(g) (and Arts 14 and 21)? Can the State ban rather than regulate? Is the classification (three-star hotels exempt) valid?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The ban was unconstitutional: it violated Art 19(1)(g) (the dancers' livelihood), Art 14 (arbitrary classification between dance bars and three-star hotels - "dignity" could not be protected only in some places) and the State had not shown that a total ban was necessary - regulation, not prohibition, was the proportionate answer.
  • The professor's retelling: the Court said that if the girls are denied this livelihood, you push them into prostitution - "they are not trained to work in factories nor to be software engineers" - which would violate their rights under Art 19(1)(g) and Art 21; if some customers behave wrongly, punish those persons - do not close the dancers' occupation. (This is the professor's paraphrase; check the judgment before quoting the exact words.)

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A total ban on a lawful livelihood based on a moral view that is not proved to be necessary is an unreasonable restriction; the State must adopt regulatory measures to protect dignity.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Professor: "This is a very important case - I have already asked a question on it, and I do not repeat cases in questions (there are so many cases)."

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Use for: protection of livelihood under Art 19(1)(g)/Art 21; proportionality; the idea that morality cannot be used to destroy women's livelihoods arbitrarily; the interface between dignity and occupation.

cards.name: Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar (1958) → State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1958 SC 731 (Constitution Bench; S.R. Das C.J.); (2005) 8 SCC 534 (7 judges; R.C. Lahoti C.J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • State laws (Bihar, U.P., M.P.) banned the slaughter of cows and cow progeny (including bulls and bullocks) in the name of Art 48 (DPSP: prohibit slaughter of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle). Butchers (the Quareshi/Kureshi community) challenged them under Art 19(1)(g).

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Quareshi (1958): a total ban on slaughter of cows and calves was valid; but a total ban on slaughter of bulls, bullocks and she-buffaloes that had ceased to be useful (milk/draught) was an unreasonable restriction - the professor described it as "the Court said: useless cattle may be slaughtered".
  • Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005): the 7-judge Bench overruled this part; it upheld a complete ban on slaughter of cow progeny of all ages, relying on Art 48, Art 51A(g) (compassion for living creatures), the usefulness of cattle (dung, urine, draught power) and the principle (from Minerva Mills, 1980) that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary and must be harmonised. The professor: "At that time Art 48 could not be given primacy because the Court had said Directive Principles are subsidiary; after Minerva Mills the Court was encouraged to give Art 48 more weight."

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A ban on cattle slaughter is a reasonable restriction under Art 19(6) when supported by Art 48 read with Art 51A(g); FR and DPSP are harmonised.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor (affectionately): "I gave 50-50 [marks] to the student who knew that this case corrects the earlier one." Know both the 1958 and 2005 decisions and the reason for the change.

cards.name: Hinsa Virodhak Sangh v. Mirzapur Moti Kuresh Jamat (2008)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2008) 5 SCC 33 (Supreme Court of India).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation closed its slaughterhouses (and meat shops) for nine days during Paryushan, the Jain festival of non-violence. The butchers' association challenged the order as violating Art 19(1)(g).

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The closure for a few days in the year is a reasonable restriction in the public interest (to respect the sentiments of a significant community); it does not destroy the trade. The professor: "In 365 days, if meat is not sold for a few days in a municipal corporation, no mountain will fall". A long-term or city-wide ban would not be reasonable; in areas where the Jain community is in majority, a few days' closure is reasonable.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A short, community-sensitive restriction is proportionate; a long ban would not be.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Listed as "very important" by the professor.

cards.name: Om Prakash v. State of Uttar Pradesh (the Haridwar / Rishikesh meat-ban case) (2004)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (2004) 3 SCC 402 (Supreme Court of India) - verify bench.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The U.P. Government (and later Uttarakhand) banned the sale of meat, fish and eggs in Haridwar, Rishikesh (and Muni-ki-Reti), towns of great religious significance (Har ki Pauri). Traders (some challenging through employees' names, said the professor) argued that Art 19(1)(g) was violated because they had settled there for business and had been selling such items.

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The ban was upheld: Hindu pilgrimage towns "maintain a clean, communal and predominantly vegetarian atmosphere"; the geographical situation and peculiar culture of these towns justify a complete restriction on public dealing in non-vegetarian items, including eggs; the restriction was not arbitrary and met Art 19(6). (The professor read the passage from the judgment aloud with a student.)

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A traditional, long-standing religious and cultural character of a locality can justify a location-specific ban on a trade.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Question flagged by the professor: difference between Om Prakash and Ramasamy Udayar (8.9).

cards.name: Ramasamy Udayar v. District Collector, Perambalur District (2021)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: 2021 SCC OnLine Mad 1779 (Madras High Court; N. Kirubakaran and P. Velmurugan JJ.; decided 30 April 2021). (Judgment by Justice N. Kirubakaran: "people may be religious, men may be communal, but roads and streets are secular".)

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • In V. Kalathur village (Perambalur district, Tamil Nadu), both Hindus and Muslims live (on different sides). Hindu temple festivals and processions (the three-day Oorani Pongal festival) had been held through all the streets for decades. Around 2011-12, objections from the Muslim community (now the numerical majority in the area) began; the authorities granted permission with conditions in 2018, and a private respondent challenged the permission on the ground that the procession through a Muslim-dominated area would cause law-and-order problems.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can a religious procession/festival be prohibited or restricted merely because another religion's followers are in majority in the area? Is there any right of free use of public streets?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• No. "A procession - including a religious procession - cannot be prohibited or curtailed merely because another religious group predominantly lives or does business in the area." India is a secular country; the presence of a majority of one religion in an area is not a ground to disallow festivals/processions of another; roads and streets are secular (District Municipalities Act, 1920, s. 180-A: streets open to all).
  • The authorities may regulate (timing, route, noise, safety) but may not prohibit; each religious group has a Fundamental Right to take out processions provided it does not insult other religions, shout slogans against them, or disturb public order. The presence of a place of worship of another religion is not itself a ground for denying permission. The criminal cases against both parties were directed to be withdrawn.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Secularism means that numerical dominance of one religion in an area cannot be used to exclude others' religious practices; the State's duty is to maintain law and order, not to yield to the heckler's veto.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Declared exam question ("download and circulate to all - I will put a question on this case and on the difference"). Students had trouble finding it by name; the correct name is Ramasamy Udayar.

cards.name: Supreme Court ruling (15 October 2026) on backward-class reservation after conversion (State of Tamil Nadu appeal)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: Supreme Court of India; bench of Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar JJ.; 15 October 2026 (the case title was not available in the source I checked; obtain it from the Supreme Court website or the professor's circulated copy).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The Tamil Nadu Government issued a Government Order in March 2024 seeking to extend reservation benefits to persons who had converted from Hinduism to other religions. The Madras High Court quashed the order; the State appealed.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does a person who converts from Hinduism to Islam / another non-Hindu religion continue to be entitled to Backward Class reservation by virtue of the caste/backwardness they had before conversion?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• The Supreme Court dismissed the State's appeal and upheld the High Court. It held that conversion from Hinduism to Islam or another non-Hindu religion does not automatically entitle a person to Backward Class reservation; backwardness from a former caste cannot carry over after conversion; statutory benefits under Art 16(4) cannot be extended merely on the basis of pre-conversion status.
  • Persons who profess a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism or Buddhism do not hold Scheduled Caste status (para 3 of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, as amended in 1956 and 1990); private religious bodies cannot determine statutory entitlements; reconversion to Hinduism needs independent, fact-specific verification by competent authorities.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Reservation benefits (Arts 15(4), 16(4), 341) are tied to the social and educational backwardness recognised for the community within the religion; conversion to a non-Hindu religion ends SC status and does not automatically carry BC status.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Related: C. Selvarani v. Special Secretary-cum-District Collector (2024) - conversion solely to obtain reservation benefits is a "fraud on the Constitution" (verify the date/citation before relying on it); Soosai v. Union of India (1985) (SC status and Christian converts); K.P. Manu v. Scrutiny Committee (2015).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Declared exam topic. Write: facts (TN GO, Madras HC), the question, the holding, Arts 15(4), 16(4), 341, 342, the SC Order of 1950, and a short critical note - arguments for (caste is a Hindu social structure; benefits are targeted) and against (backwardness may persist after conversion; Art 25 and Art 14 concerns; the Order itself has been challenged).

cards.name: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1951 SC 226; 1951 SCR 525 (Supreme Court of India; 7 judges; Das J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Madras Government's Communal G.O. reserved seats in State medical and engineering colleges by religion and caste (communal ratio). Champakam Dorairajan, a Brahmin woman, was denied admission despite higher marks and challenged it under Arts 15(1) and 29(2). The State defended the order as implementing Art 46 (DPSP: promote educational and economic interests of weaker sections).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Can a Directive Principle (Art 46) justify a violation of a Fundamental Right (Art 29(2)/15)?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The communal G.O. was unconstitutional (violated Art 29(2)). The Court held that the Directive Principles must conform to and run as subsidiary to the Chapter on Fundamental Rights; Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and cannot be overridden by Directive Principles.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles; Part IV cannot override Part III (position in 1951).

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Parliament responded with the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, inserting Art 15(4) (special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs). The professor: "After Champakam, the First Amendment brought the reservation clause." Reservation, not property, was the confusion that led to the amendment ("write that; do not write property").

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor's question: "What was the opinion of the Supreme Court on Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in the beginning of the Republic?" → FR prevail; DPSP subsidiary (Champakam); "that is wrong now" - that was only the 1950s position.

cards.name: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - the Art 31C part (professor's version)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1973) 4 SCC 225 (13-judge bench; 7:6). Full card on the property angle: Lecture 6.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The 25th Amendment inserted Art 31C protecting laws implementing Art 39(b)-(c) from challenge under Arts 14, 19, 31. It was challenged.

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• A student recited the answer in class (the professor corrected the mix-up of numbers - 24th, 25th, 26th - "it was the 25th that inserted 31C"): "the part protecting social and economic reforms was upheld; the second part, which barred judicial review, was struck down".
  • The professor: "Judicial review is basic structure. Clap for her." The first part of Art 31C therefore survived - so a law made to implement Art 39(b)/(c) was protected from FR challenge - but the Court retained its power to examine whether the law really relates to Art 39(b)/(c).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Question asked in class: "In which case was the 25th Amendment (Art 31C) challenged?" → Kesavananda Bharati. "What happened?" → first part upheld, second part struck down (judicial review).

cards.name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1980) 3 SCC 625; AIR 1980 SC 1789 (5-judge bench; 4:1; Y.V. Chandrachud C.J.; Bhagwati J. dissenting).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Minerva Mills, a sick textile mill, was taken over under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act 1974. The company challenged the take-over and the validity of ss. 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which (i) extended Art 31C to all Directive Principles and (ii) inserted Art 368(4) and (5) (no judicial review of constitutional amendments; unlimited power of Parliament).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Are ss. 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment valid? Can Directive Principles override Articles 14 and 19?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• s. 55 (Art 368(4),(5)) struck down: Parliament's amending power is limited; a limited amending power is part of the basic structure; Parliament cannot enlarge it into absolute power.
  • s. 4 (amended Art 31C) struck down: giving all DPSPs the power to override Arts 14 and 19 would destroy the harmony and balance between Part III and Part IV; Part III cannot be subordinated to Part IV.
  • "The Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Parts III and IV. To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution." FR and DPSP are complementary and supplementary to each other. (The professor: "the Supreme Court said they are complementary, supplementary and must be harmonised.")
  • The 42nd Amendment, in these respects, was held "totally unconstitutional" (the professor's expression); Art 31C as it stood after Kesavananda (limited to Art 39(b),(c)) remained.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Neither Part III nor Part IV has absolute primacy; they must be harmoniously construed.

fields.label: The one sentence to write
fields.html: "Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary and supplementary; they must be harmonised; neither overrides the other." Never write "in certain cases FR have priority". A student began to say "in certain cases they have to be given priority" - the professor stopped her: "that is a wrong sentence; do not write it." (Examples used later to show harmony: Mirzapur Moti Kureshi 2005 - Art 48 with Art 19(1)(g); Lecture 8.)

cards.name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1950 SC 27; 1950 SCR 88 (Supreme Court of India; 6-judge bench; Kania C.J., Fazl Ali J. dissenting in part).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • A.K. Gopalan, a Communist leader and member of the Provisional Parliament, was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 (the Act was passed by the Indian Government soon after independence). He challenged the detention under Arts 19(1)(a),(b),(c),(d),(e),(g), 21 and 22. The professor: "Even such a big man was jailed by the Congress Government under preventive detention when the country was newly independent" (compare Emergency era; political point omitted).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • What do "life", "personal liberty" and "procedure established by law" mean in Art 21? Are Arts 19 and 21 mutually exclusive? Is a preventive detention law subject to Art 19 tests?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• "Life" and "personal liberty" were given a narrow meaning: personal liberty means physical liberty (freedom from arrest and detention); "life" = bare existence.
  • "Procedure established by law" meant any procedure laid down by a competent legislature - the Court would not examine whether the law was fair, just or reasonable (it rejected "due process" and read "law" as State-made law, not natural justice).
  • Arts 14, 19, 21 were mutually exclusive codes ("watertight compartments"): a preventive detention law needed only comply with Art 22 and the procedure it provided.
  • The Preventive Detention Act was upheld (except section 14, which barred courts from looking into grounds of detention).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Art 21 protects only against arbitrary executive action, not against unreasonable laws; procedure = whatever the legislature prescribes.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• The professor: "1950: the Supreme Court gave life a very restricted meaning - 'life' means do not kill me; I can be given little food, but must be kept alive." He said Gopalan was among the first cases the Court decided and "they were influenced - they gave very narrow meaning because the country was newly independent".
  • Overruled in effect by R.C. Cooper (1970) (rejecting watertight compartments) and Maneka Gandhi (1978) (procedure must be just, fair and reasonable).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Professor: "First case you must read: A.K. Gopalan (1950)." He asked the class to identify the case; students said "A.K. Gopalan".

cards.name: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1963 SC 1295; (1964) 1 SCR 332 (6-judge bench; judgment dated 18 December 1962; Ayyangar J. for the majority; Subba Rao J. dissenting in part).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Kharak Singh was accused of dacoity but released for lack of evidence. The U.P. Police Regulations (Chapter XX) authorised surveillance of "history-sheeters": (a) secret picketing of the house, (b) domiciliary visits at night, (c) periodic enquiries, (d) verification of movements, (e) reporting of movements, etc. Police visited his house at night to check whether he was at home or "out committing crimes" - waking his family.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Do these regulations violate Art 19(1)(d) (movement) and Art 21? Is privacy or sleep protected?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Domiciliary night visits (reg. 236(b)) violated "personal liberty" under Art 21 (they were invalid); the other forms of surveillance (shadowing, reports) did not infringe Art 19(1)(d) (surveillance of movements is not a restraint) and were upheld by the majority.
  • The Court said that "life" in Art 21 means more than mere animal existence - it includes the right to enjoy all faculties (quoting the American case Munn v. Illinois, 1877, per Field J.). Professor: "For the first time the Supreme Court said that sleeping also comes under Art 21" - his shorthand for the disturbance of sleep by night visits.
  • Subba Rao J. (dissent) held that all the surveillance measures violated Art 21 and recognised privacy as part of personal liberty.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: "Life" means more than animal existence; "personal liberty" is more than physical restraint (privacy and dignity are protected); Gopalan was partly overruled.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Later: Govind v. State of M.P. (1975) and K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) (privacy as a Fundamental Right; Kharak Singh's majority on surveillance overruled).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The class corrected the date: a student first said 1963 and then 1962 - the professor confirmed: "1962". "The professor: it is a case that expanded life and partially overruled Gopalan."

cards.name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1978) 1 SCC 248; AIR 1978 SC 597 (7-judge bench; M.H. Beg C.J., Y.V. Chandrachud, V.R. Krishna Iyer, P.N. Bhagwati, N.L. Untwalia, S. Murtaza Fazal Ali, P.S. Kailasam JJ.; Bhagwati J. wrote the main opinion).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded by the Government of India on 2 July 1977 under s. 10(3)(c) of the Passport Act, 1967 "in the interests of the general public", without giving reasons and without any prior notice or hearing (the Janata Government under Morarji Desai). The professor stressed the irony: "The Passport Act was made by Indira Gandhi's Government; it was used against her own daughter-in-law" - hence the moral "when you are in power, do not make bad laws - they may apply to you".

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the right to travel abroad fall within "personal liberty"? Is "procedure established by law" satisfied by any procedure prescribed by law? What is the relationship between Arts 14, 19 and 21?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• "Personal liberty" has the widest amplitude and includes the right to travel abroad (following Satwant Singh).
  • "Procedure established by law" must be "right, just and fair" and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive; otherwise it is no procedure at all and Art 21 would be violated. The procedure must satisfy Art 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Art 19; Arts 14, 19, 21 are not mutually exclusive - the "golden triangle".
  • Section 10(3)(c) was upheld only by reading in the requirement of a fair hearing (audi alteram partem); the impounding order had been passed without any hearing, but because the Attorney General stated that the Government would give her an opportunity to be heard (and the Government gave her reasons later), the Court did not quash the order and the petition was disposed of. (The reported holding does not order the passport to be returned.)

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Procedure established by law must be just, fair and reasonable; Arts 14, 19 and 21 form a golden triangle and are read together.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• The professor: "Before Maneka, the Court only asked: is there a procedure and was it followed? After Maneka, the Court asks: is the procedure itself fair? The moment it said 'we will see whether the law is fair', due process came in through the back door." "Sudden change: previously they did not say procedure is bad; suddenly Justice Bhagwati said so."
  • Opened the door to the vast expansion of Art 21: speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon), legal aid, bar on solitary confinement, right to livelihood (Olga Tellis), clean environment, privacy (Puttaswamy), dignity (Francis Coralie Mullin).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor told students to read the original: "Maneka Gandhi; the name is spelt 'Maneka' in the law report - 'Menaka' is what we say in Hindi... I do not cut marks for spelling but 9 out of 10 becomes 10 out of 10." (A light comment about care in case names.)

cards.name: Lochner v. New York (1905) - US Supreme Court

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: 198 U.S. 45 (1905); 5:4; Peckham J. (the professor dated it "1903"; the correct year is 1905).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • New York's Bakeshop Act (1895) limited bakers' working hours to 10 hours a day and 60 hours a week. Joseph Lochner, a bakery owner, was convicted for allowing an employee to work more than 60 hours.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the law violate the liberty of contract protected by the Fourteenth Amendment's due process clause?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The Act was struck down as an unreasonable interference with the right of the baker and employees to contract; the labour regulation was not a valid health measure. Holmes J. dissented ("The Fourteenth Amendment does not enact Mr Herbert Spencer's Social Statics").

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Under substantive due process, courts may review the content of legislation; "freedom of contract" protected employers against welfare legislation (the "Lochner era", to 1937).

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • The professor: "owners exploiting the poor - 18 hours of work, no minimum wage, no working hour limits, no protection - and when the democratic Government made welfare laws, the Supreme Court struck them down. The Court was supreme over the legislature." This misuse is the reason the Indian framers preferred procedure established by law.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: The professor asked a student to present on Lochner the next day: "find the name of the case: L-O-C-H-N-E-R v. New York."

cards.name: Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1983) 2 SCC 277; AIR 1983 SC 473 (Supreme Court of India; 5 judges; Chandrachud C.J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Mithu, a life-convict, was convicted of murder under s. 302 and, because he was a life-convict who had committed murder, sentenced to death under s. 303 IPC, which provided that a person undergoing life imprisonment who commits murder "shall be punished with death" (no alternative).

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is a mandatory death sentence, which gives the court no discretion to consider circumstances, consistent with Arts 14 and 21?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • s. 303 IPC is unconstitutional (violates Arts 14 and 21) and was struck down. A sentence of death imposed without any chance for the court to consider the circumstances of the offence and the offender is unjust, unfair and unreasonable.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A law that prescribes a punishment (here, mandatory death) without allowing consideration of mitigating circumstances fails the test of just, fair and reasonable law under Arts 14 and 21. The substantive content of the law, not merely its procedure, is open to judicial review.

fields.label: Reasoning
fields.html:
• Following Maneka Gandhi, Art 21's "procedure" must be fair and reasonable; the Court extended that to the sentencing law itself: a mandatory sentence leaves no room for judicial discretion and treats unequal cases equally (Art 14).
  • The Court observed that a murder by a life-convict can range from a premeditated killing to a spur-of-the-moment act; s. 303 ignored the difference.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• The classic Indian illustration of substantive due process.
  • Linked to Bachan Singh (1980): the death penalty is confined to the "rarest of rare" cases and requires judicial discretion.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Use as the answer to "give an example where the law itself was struck down on the due process test". (Do not confuse with Maru Ram, which concerned remission and s. 433A CrPC.)

cards.name: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1980)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1980) 1 SCC 81; AIR 1979 SC 1369 (Supreme Court of India; Bhagwati J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • A newspaper report exposed that thousands of undertrial prisoners in Bihar had been in jail for years, many for periods longer than the maximum sentence they could have got if convicted. Advocate Kapila Hingorani filed a writ petition under Art 32.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the right to life and personal liberty include a right to speedy trial and free legal aid?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • Speedy trial is a Fundamental Right implicit in Art 21; the procedure that keeps a person in jail without trial for years is not "reasonable, fair and just". The State must provide free legal services to the poor accused. The Court ordered release of undertrials who had been in jail beyond the maximum possible sentence.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: A "just, fair and reasonable" procedure (Maneka Gandhi) requires speedy trial and free legal aid; Art 21 and Art 39A are read together.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • First major public interest litigation (PIL) by the Supreme Court; bail and undertrial reform; legal-aid movement.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite for "speedy trial under Art 21" and "free legal aid".

cards.name: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1981) 1 SCC 608; AIR 1981 SC 746 (Supreme Court of India; Bhagwati J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Detenue Francis Coralie Mullin, detained under the COFEPOSA Act in Tihar Jail, complained that she was permitted only one interview a week with family/lawyer and was kept in unduly harsh conditions; she challenged these restrictions.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • What does "life" in Art 21 mean? Do detenues have a right to meet family and lawyers freely?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • "The right to life includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes along with it, namely the bare necessaries of life such as adequate nutrition, clothing and shelter and facilities for reading, writing and expressing oneself in diverse forms, freely moving about and mixing and commingling with fellow human beings." The restriction to one interview a week was struck down; cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment violates Art 21.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: "Life" in Art 21 = life with human dignity, not mere animal existence; any procedure that deprives a person of dignity must pass the Maneka Gandhi test.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Cited constantly for the dignity strand of Art 21; also linked to Munn v. Illinois / Kharak Singh dissent ("life is more than animal existence").

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Quote the "right to live with human dignity" passage in any Art 21 expansion answer.

cards.name: Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1989) 4 SCC 286; AIR 1989 SC 2039 (Supreme Court of India; Sabyasachi Mukharji J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • A human-rights activist filed a PIL after a newspaper report of a scooterist injured in a road accident who was taken to a hospital but refused treatment because the case was a "medico-legal case" and the hospital said it should go to a hospital with jurisdiction for such cases; he died.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is a doctor legally obliged to provide immediate medical aid to an accident victim before police formalities?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • Preservation of life is of paramount importance; every doctor, whether at a Government hospital or otherwise, has a professional obligation to extend services to protect life. No law or procedure (including police formalities) can delay emergency treatment. Art 21 casts an obligation on the State to preserve life.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The right to life includes the right to timely emergency medical care; the medico-legal formalities must follow, not precede, treatment.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Basis of the later "Good Samaritan" guidelines (SaveLIFE Foundation v. Union of India, 2016) protecting persons who help accident victims.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite for "right to emergency medical aid".

cards.name: Unni Krishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) (with Mohini Jain, 1992)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1993) 1 SCC 645 (Supreme Court of India; 5 judges; Jeevan Reddy J.); preceded by Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) 3 SCC 666 (2 judges).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Private medical and engineering colleges charged capitation fees. In Mohini Jain, a Karnataka rule allowing colleges to charge huge fees from non-State students was challenged. Unni Krishnan examined the whole scheme of private professional education.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Is there a fundamental right to education? Up to what level?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • Mohini Jain: right to education is part of Art 21 (at all levels) and capitation fee is unconstitutional. Unni Krishnan: the right to education flows from Art 21 but is limited by Art 41 (economic capacity) - every citizen has a right to free education up to the age of 14; beyond that the right is subject to the limits of the State's economic capacity and development.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The Fundamental Right to education exists up to 14 years; Arts 41, 45 and 46 define the scope beyond that.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Led to the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002): inserted Art 21A (free and compulsory education for children 6-14), changed Art 45 and added Art 51A(k); implemented by the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. The "scheme" of Unni Krishnan (regulation of private colleges) was later modified in TMA Pai (2002).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Chain to write: Mohini Jain → Unni Krishnan → 86th Amendment → Art 21A → RTE Act, 2009.

cards.name: P. Rathinam v. Union of India (1994)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1994) 3 SCC 394 (Supreme Court of India; 2 judges; R.M. Sahai and B.L. Hansaria JJ.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Challenge to the constitutional validity of s. 309 IPC on Arts 14 and 21.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does Art 21 include a right to die, so that s. 309 violates it?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • s. 309 IPC is unconstitutional (violates Arts 14 and 21) and must be struck down. The Court reasoned that Art 21, like other rights, has a positive and a negative aspect: the right to life includes the right not to live a forced life.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: (Overruled) Art 21 includes the right to die - therefore punishing an attempt to commit suicide is unconstitutional.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html: • Overruled in Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Treat as the "wrong turn" corrected by a larger bench.

cards.name: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1996) 2 SCC 648; AIR 1996 SC 946 (Supreme Court of India; 5 judges; J.S. Verma J.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • Gian Kaur and her husband were convicted of abetment of suicide (s. 306 IPC) after a woman's death. They argued that if Rathinam held s. 309 void because Art 21 includes the right to die, then s. 306 (abetment) must also be void, since abetting the exercise of a fundamental right cannot be an offence.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the "right to life" under Art 21 include the "right to die"? Are ss. 306 and 309 IPC constitutional?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • Rathinam overruled. The right to life under Art 21 does not include the right to die or to terminate one's life; "the right to life is a natural right embodied in Art 21 but suicide is an unnatural termination or extinction of life and, therefore, incompatible and inconsistent with the concept of right to life." Ss. 306 and 309 IPC are constitutionally valid. A distinction was drawn between suicide and the "right to die with dignity at the end of life" (a dying person, in a terminal state, hastening an already-commencing natural death process) - which is part of the right to live with dignity and was left open.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The right to life is a natural right; "right to die" is unnatural and cannot be derived from Art 21. The positive/negative-aspect analogy with Art 19 does not hold because Art 19 rights are enumerated freedoms while the right to life is the right to be, not the right to end being.

fields.label: Reasoning
fields.html:
• Professor's gloss: "The right to life is a natural right. Just as we cannot create life in an unnatural way, we have no right to take it in an unnatural way."
  • Professor's policy reasoning (jurisprudential argument): life is full of failures ("90% of the time we fail"); if attempted suicide carried no consequence there would be no deterrence for people at their lowest moments - the law therefore discourages the act and encourages perseverance. (This is the lecture's rationale; the Court's own reasoning in Gian Kaur rests on the natural/unnatural distinction and on Art 21's scheme.)

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Followed later by Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011) (passive euthanasia allowed in rare cases with High Court supervision) and Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) (five judges: right to die with dignity and living wills / advance directives recognised as part of Art 21, with safeguards).
  • Legislative change: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, s. 115 - a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and shall not be tried or punished; the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does not re-enact s. 309 (attempt-to-suicide is no longer a general offence); abetment survives (BNS ss. 107-108, verify numbering); BNS s. 226 punishes an attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Two-line answer: "Rathinam (1994) held Art 21 includes the right to die; Gian Kaur (1996, 5 judges) overruled it - the right to life does not include the right to die; ss. 306 and 309 valid. Dying with dignity (passive euthanasia) was later recognised in Aruna Shanbaug and Common Cause."

cards.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: (1997) 1 SCC 416; AIR 1997 SC 610 (Supreme Court of India; Kuldip Singh and A.S. Anand JJ.).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • D.K. Basu, Executive Chairman of Legal Aid Services, West Bengal, wrote a letter to the Chief Justice of India about deaths in police custody reported in newspapers; the Court treated the letter as a writ petition (PIL). The Court also dealt with a companion matter (Ashok Johri v. State of U.P.) on custodial death.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • What safeguards must the police follow on arrest and detention to prevent custodial violence and death? Is compensation payable?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • Custodial torture violates Art 21 (and Art 20(3), 22). The Court laid down 11 requirements/guidelines (below) to be followed in all cases of arrest/detention until legislative safeguards are enacted, and held that the State is liable to pay compensation (public-law remedy under Arts 32 and 226, over and above any private-law remedy) for custodial death/torture.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Any form of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in custody - whether during investigation, interrogation or otherwise - is prohibited by Art 21; the police must follow the guidelines on arrest, and the State is vicariously liable in compensation.

fields.label: Reasoning
fields.html:
• A person in custody does not lose his Fundamental Rights; the greater the power of the police, the greater the need for accountability and transparency.
  • Transparency in arrest (identification, memo, witness, informing family) prevents "unrecorded" arrests, the main source of custodial violence.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Basis of the amendments to the CrPC (s. 41B - identification of police, memo of arrest; s. 41D - right to meet an advocate during interrogation; s. 50A - informing a nominated person; s. 54 - medical examination of arrested person); now in the BNSS, 2023 (verify section numbers).
  • Followed by Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) (guidelines on arrest in s. 498A cases).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Learn the guidelines as a list and say that the guidelines have been legislated into the CrPC/BNSS.

cards.name: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1952 SC 75; 1952 SCR 284 (Supreme Court of India; 7 judges; majority: Patanjali Sastri C.J., Mahajan, Mukherjea, Das, Chandrasekhara Aiyar JJ. in separate opinions; Bose J.; one judge, Das J., dissented on a part).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 empowered the State Government, by notification, to direct that "such offences or classes of offences or cases or classes of cases" as it thought fit be tried by a Special Court following a procedure that differed from the Criminal Procedure Code (for example, no committal proceedings, no jury, restricted right to cross-examine). Anwar Ali Sarkar was one of the accused sent for trial before a Special Court, and challenged the section under Art 14.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does a statute that allows the Government to pick cases for a more drastic procedure, without any guiding principle, violate equal protection of the laws?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • s. 5(1) of the Act was struck down as violating Art 14. The classification of "offences or cases" for trial by special procedure was left to the unguided discretion of the executive and was not based on any intelligible differentia or relation to the object of the Act. The Act itself did not classify; it gave the executive a blank cheque to discriminate.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Art 14 forbids class legislation, but permits reasonable classification: (1) intelligible differentia, (2) rational nexus with the object. A statute that leaves selection to the uncontrolled discretion of the executive, without a determining principle, offends Art 14.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Shows that the courts had the power to examine the reasonableness of a law under Art 14 from the start (the professor's point: "due process was already there in Art 14"). It also shows the Court acting within a year or two of Gopalan in a very different mode.
  • Extended later into the "manifest arbitrariness" doctrine (E.P. Royappa; Maneka Gandhi; Shayara Bano).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Cite in answers on "due process before Maneka Gandhi" and on reasonable classification. Remember: decided 1952, Act of 1950.

cards.name: Lochner v. New York (1905)

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: 198 U.S. 45 (1905) (US Supreme Court; 5-4; Peckham J.; Holmes J. dissenting).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: • A New York statute (the Bakeshop Act, 1895) limited bakery employees to ten hours a day / sixty hours a week. Joseph Lochner, a bakery owner, was convicted of letting an employee work longer and challenged the law.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html: • Does the law violate the liberty of contract protected by the Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html: • The Act was struck down (5-4). The right to buy and sell labour is part of the liberty protected by the 14th Amendment; the maximum-hours law was not a genuine health measure but an unreasonable interference with freedom of contract.

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: Substantive due process: courts may strike down legislation that interferes with "liberty of contract" if it is not a reasonable exercise of the State's police power.

fields.label: Reasoning
fields.html: • Holmes J. (dissent): "The Fourteenth Amendment does not enact Mr. Herbert Spencer's Social Statics" - the Constitution does not embody a particular economic theory; the Court should not substitute its views for the legislature's.

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Gave "due process" a bad name: judges as a "super-legislature" striking down welfare laws. Ended with the 1937 "switch in time" (West Coast Hotel v. Parrish) after Roosevelt's court-packing threat (see Lecture 9, 9.6).
  • Why it matters for India: because of Lochner, the framers (on the advice of Frankfurter and B.N. Rau) chose "procedure established by law" in Art 21.

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Keep it as a two-line case: year (1905, not 1903), bakers' hours, liberty of contract, Holmes's dissent, and its link to the Indian choice of words. The professor asked for a presentation on it (see Lecture 9).

cards.name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) - the First Judges Case

fields.label: Citation / Court / Year
fields.html: AIR 1982 SC 149; 1981 Supp SCC 87 (Supreme Court of India; 7 judges; Bhagwati J. delivered the leading opinion).

fields.label: Facts
fields.html:
• A Law Ministry circular (1981) asked the Chief Justices to obtain the consent of additional judges to be appointed to other High Courts and to follow a policy of appointing/transferring judges between States (outsiders in each High Court); non-continuation of an additional judge of the Delhi High Court and the transfer of High Court Chief Justices were also challenged. The stated reasons were to promote impartiality and national integration (the "outsider judge" idea); the professor's concern was that transfers could be used to control the judiciary (punishment postings).
  • Petitioners: a group of lawyers led by S.P. Gupta, advocate of the Allahabad High Court, who filed writ petitions challenging the circular and the transfers. The Government objected: lawyers have no locus standi - they have no personal interest in the transfers; the judges concerned were the persons aggrieved, and judges cannot sue because they depend on the Government for postings.

fields.label: Issues
fields.html:
• Do advocates have locus standi to challenge the transfer / non-appointment of judges? (the PIL question)
  • Is the transfer of a High Court judge/Chief Justice without consent valid? What is the role of the Chief Justice of India in appointments and transfers under Arts 124, 217, 222?

fields.label: Held (Decision)
fields.html:
• Locus standi liberalised: where a legal wrong or injury is caused to a person or class of persons who, by reason of poverty, disability or socially or economically disadvantaged position, cannot approach the court, any member of the public acting bona fide can move the court (Art 226/32). Advocates have a sufficient interest in the independence of the judiciary - they are "officers of the court" and justice cannot be delivered without the Bar. The professor: "The judge alone cannot do justice; without the help of lawyers there is no justice; so lawyers also have an interest."
  • On the merits, the majority upheld the transfers and held that "consultation" with the Chief Justice of India under Arts 124(2), 217 and 222 does not mean concurrence; the Executive's view could prevail (the "primacy of the Executive"). A transfer of a judge in public interest was held valid (verify the finer holdings on additional judges and consent).

fields.label: Ratio decidendi
fields.html: The doctrine of locus standi is relaxed in public interest litigation: a bona fide member of the public (and, in appropriate cases, the Bar) may enforce the legal rights of those unable to approach the court. The independence of the judiciary is a basic feature, and the Bar is a stakeholder in it.

fields.label: Reasoning
fields.html:
• Bhagwati J.: the Court's role in a developing society is to make access to justice meaningful for the poor; a procedural technicality should not defeat a substantive right. The professor: "Again Justice Bhagwati - he did many good things."
  • Practical point: judges cannot sue for their own transfers; if no one else could, executive control of the judiciary (punishment postings) would go unchallenged. The professor warned: "if the judiciary is under the executive it becomes like the IAS officers... justice will not be there".

fields.label: Significance / Later treatment
fields.html:
• Established PIL as part of constitutional adjudication.
  • The "consultation, not concurrence" holding was overruled by the Second Judges Case - Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (1993) (primacy of the CJI) - and the collegium system was reaffirmed in the Third Judges Case (1998, presidential reference). The 99th Amendment / NJAC Act (2014) was struck down in the Fourth Judges Case (2015).
  • Related: Union of India v. Sankalchand Himatlal Sheth (1977) (transfer of a High Court judge without consent held invalid; verify details).

fields.label: Use in the exam
fields.html: Write: "S.P. Gupta (1981) - the Judges Transfer Case - the first Constitution Bench acceptance of PIL; liberalised locus standi (including for lawyers); also decided 'consultation' ≠ 'concurrence' (later overruled in 1993)."

cards.name: Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India
cards.sub: 5-judge bench · unanimous (5:0) · judgment by M. Patanjali Sastri J. · P.R. Das for petitioners · M.C. Setalvad (first Attorney General

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Zamindars of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh challenged land reform laws as violating Part III. Parliament responded with the First Amendment (Articles 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule). Blocked from attacking the Acts directly, the zamindars challenged the Amendment itself — strategic logic: if the tree falls, the branch falls anyway.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The First Constitutional Amendment is valid. (1) Article 368 confers constituent power, distinct from ordinary legislative power under Articles 245–246; Article 13(2) applies only to the latter. (2) The definition of “law” in Article 13(3) deliberately omits “constitutional amendment.” (3) Article 368 contains no exception for Part III — the framers could have written “except Part III” and did not.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights; an amendment is not “law” under Article 13(2).

cards.name: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
cards.sub: 11-judge bench · 6:5 · majority led by K. Subba Rao C.J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The validity of the Seventeenth Amendment's protection of land reform laws was again in issue; the Court reconsidered Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. Article 368 (its marginal heading then reading “Procedure for amendment”) supplies only procedure, not power; the power flows from the residuary legislative power — Entry 97, List I read with Article 248 — making an amendment an exercise of legislative power, hence “law” under Article 13(2), hence void insofar as it abridges Part III.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Fundamental Rights placed beyond the amending power; the doctrine of prospective overruling introduced — the ruling operates only from the judgment date, so all earlier amendments survived.

cards.name: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
cards.sub: U.S. Supreme Court · 7:2

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Dred Scott, enslaved, sued for freedom having lived with his owner in a free State and territory.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: African Americans, enslaved or free, were not citizens and could not sue; the Missouri Compromise was unconstitutional. “Once a slave, always a slave — you can never become a free citizen.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Widely regarded as the worst U.S. Supreme Court decision; it inflamed public opinion and catalysed the Civil War (1861–65).

cards.name: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
cards.sub: AIR 1973 SC 1461 · 13 judges — the largest Constitution Bench in Supreme Court history · decided 24 April 1973 · a deeply

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Kesavananda Bharati, chief of a Kerala religious sect (matha) which owned significant land, petitioned under Article 32 to enforce rights under Articles 25, 26, 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 against the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 and its 1969 Amendment. While the petition was pending, the Indira Gandhi government passed the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments (partly to overcome Golaknath), and the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1971 was placed in the Ninth Schedule. The petition was amended to challenge the amendments themselves.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: By 7:6 — Parliament may amend any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot abrogate or destroy the Constitution's basic structure or identity.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The Basic Structure Doctrine. Key advocates: for the petitioners, Nani A. Palkhivala (leader) with Daphtary, Chagla, Soli Sorabjee, Deewan and Harindranath; for the State, H.M. Seervai, Advocate General of Maharashtra — “the world's greatest constitutional jurist,” not to be “limited” to a state role.

cards.name: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955)
cards.sub: 5-judge bench · AIR 1955 SC 781 · locus classicus of eclipse

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The C.P. and Berar Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1948 — enacted under the Government of India Act, 1935 by a legislature with plenary powers — created a State monopoly in motor transport, clashing with Article 19(1)(g) as it then stood. The First Amendment (1951) added the state-monopoly clause to Article 19(6).

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Per B.K. Mukherjea J., unanimously: the impugned law “became, as it were, eclipsed, for the time being, by the fundamental right... Such laws were not dead for all purposes... It is only as against the citizens that they remained in a dormant or moribund condition.” The amendment “removed the shadow”; the 1948 Act revived automatically — no re-enactment required.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Pre-constitutional laws are void only quoad citizens; supervening inconsistency is curable retrospectively by constitutional amendment.

cards.name: Keshav Madhav Menon v. State of Bombay (1951)
cards.sub: AIR 1951 SC 128 · per S.R. Das J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Prosecution under the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931 for publishing a pamphlet without prior authorisation; proceedings had begun before the Constitution.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Article 13(1) operates prospectively from the Constitution's commencement; it does not invalidate past transactions or pending proceedings under laws valid when the act was done. “The voidness of the law is from the date of the commencement of the Constitution and not from an earlier date.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The distinction between void ab initio and void from a future date is the very foundation of the eclipse doctrine.

cards.name: Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959)
cards.sub: AIR 1959 SC 648 · 4:1 · per S.K. Das J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The U.P. State Road Transport Act, 1951 — a post-Constitutional state monopoly — was challenged under Article 19(1)(g); the State invoked Bhikaji Narain's revival logic.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Article 13(2) imposes a constitutional prohibition; the State legislature “had no power to make the impugned law.” A post-Constitutional inconsistent law is “still-born” and void ab initio — “A dead law cannot be revived by any constitutional amendment... it must be re-enacted.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Eclipse applies exclusively to pre-Constitutional laws under Article 13(1).

cards.name: Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1955)
cards.sub: AIR 1955 SC 728

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The U.P. Road Transport Act, 1951 (post-Constitutional) was challenged while the First Amendment's Article 19(6) change was in force.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Applying Thomas Cooley's American doctrine: “A statute void for unconstitutionality is dead and cannot be vitalized by a subsequent amendment of the Constitution removing the constitutional objection but must be re-enacted.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The critical difference between pre- and post-Constitutional laws: a constitutional amendment does not retroactively confer jurisdiction on the legislature that passed the void law.

cards.name: State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974)
cards.sub: AIR 1974 SC 1300 · per H.R. Khanna J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1953 (post-Constitutional) required employers' contributions; provisions were challenged under Articles 19(1)(f) and 14 by a company (a citizen).

fields.label: Held
fields.html: A post-Constitutional law void for violating Articles 14 or 19 is void only quoad citizens — the contravention exists only in relation to those entitled to the right. The law remains valid and enforceable against non-citizens.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Modifies the “still-born” theory by making it person-specific: void in personam for citizens, not void in rem against the world.

cards.name: R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. Union of India (1957)
cards.sub: AIR 1957 SC 628 · 5-judge bench · locus classicus

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Prize Competitions Act, 1955 defined “prize competition” broadly enough to cover both skill competitions (crosswords, essays — protected business under 19(1)(g)) and gambling (lotteries, lucky draws — res extra commercium, outside 19(1)(g)).

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The Act was unconstitutional as applied to skill competitions but valid as to gambling; the distinction was “clear-cut and well-recognized,” and Parliament's primary object was the gambling evil. The Court read down the definition: the Act applies only to gambling competitions.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Severability by restricting application — the classic instance of saving an Act by confining it to the valid class.

cards.name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)
cards.sub: AIR 1950 SC 124 · 6 judges

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Section 9(1-A), Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 — banning entry and circulation of journals “for securing the public safety or the maintenance of public order.” “Public safety” was not a ground in Article 19(2) as it then stood.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The provision fell entirely: the distinction between “public safety” and “public order” was “not precise”; severing the words would leave a power still capable of unconstitutional application — danger of misuse is the decisive factor.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Inseverability where permissible and impermissible applications cannot be cleanly separated.

cards.name: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)
cards.sub: AIR 1951 SC 318

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949, challenged on multiple grounds.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Eight specific unconstitutional sections were severed; the core Prohibition Act survived as a complete, workable code.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Rule 3 in action — distinct invalid parts removed, the rest upheld.

cards.name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
cards.sub: AIR 1950 SC 27

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 barred detainees from disclosing grounds of detention to a court.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Only Section 14 violated Articles 19(1)(a) and 21; the rest of the Act was a complete code without it.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: “Save as much of an Act as can be saved” — declare void only what must be void.

cards.name: Mithu Singh v. State of Punjab (1983)
cards.sub: AIR 1983 SC 473 · 5-judge bench

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Section 303 IPC mandated the death penalty for murder by a life convict — no judicial discretion.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The classification (life convicts versus other murderers) lacked intelligible differentia, and mandatory death excluded judicial consideration of mitigating circumstances, violating Articles 14 and 21. Section 303 was a standalone provision, cleanly severable from the IPC's sentencing scheme (Section 302 continues to govern).

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: A penal provision excised cleanly; the rest of the Code operates normally.

cards.name: Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959)
cards.sub: AIR 1959 SC 149 · 5-judge bench · majority of C.J. S.R. Das, Kapur and Subba Rao JJ.; N.H. Bhagwati J. concurring more broadly;

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Basheshar Nath, a wealthy businessman, settled under Section 8A of the Taxation of Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, agreeing to pay about Rs. 4.5 lakh in instalments. When Section 5(1) of that Act was held unconstitutional in Suraj Mall Mohta (1955), he stopped paying; the Department sought recovery as arrears of land revenue, arguing he had waived his Article 14 right by settling.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Fundamental rights cannot be waived. Article 14 is a principle of public policy, the foundation of the Constitution — not a private right to be bartered away.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Justice Subba Rao's rationale: rights are limitations on State power, not gifts; “The large majority of our people are economically poor, educationally backward, and politically not yet conscious of their rights... They may, without understanding the consequences, agree to waive their rights. It would be the duty of the Court to protect them against themselves.” Waiver assumes equal bargaining power — a fiction in India.

cards.name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
cards.sub: Y.V. Chandrachud and P.N. Bhagwati JJ. prominent · suo motu cognizance of sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The immediate issue was a challenge under Article 31C, but the Court took up the validity of the 42nd Amendment's clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 on its own motion.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Twin holdings: (1) the Indian scheme vests supremacy in the Constitution, not in Parliament — Parliament is a creature of the Constitution; (2) judicial review of constitutional amendments is an integral basic feature. Article 368(4) was struck down as violative of basic structure; so was 368(5), which sought to destroy the limited nature of the amending power — itself part of the basic structure.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The final synthesis: Parliament may amend under Article 368; Article 13 does not bar amendments; but any amendment destroying the basic structure is void.

cards.name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)
cards.sub: 9-judge bench · unanimous

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Post-Kesavananda legislatures kept adding laws to the Ninth Schedule — some allegedly arbitrary, even near-100% reservation destroying equality.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The cut-off is 24 April 1973, the date Kesavananda was decided. Any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule after that date is not immune from judicial review, and can be tested on the twin grounds of Part III violation and basic structure violation; if it fails, it is struck down.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Unchecked post-1973 insertion would render the Basic Structure Doctrine a dead letter. Open research question left to the class: does the doctrine apply only to amendments, or directly to any ordinary legislation (beyond the Ninth Schedule route)?

cards.name: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
cards.sub: AIR 1952 SC 75 · 7-judge Constitutional Bench · 6:1 majority · Patanjali Sastri C.J. dissenting

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 provided for speedier trial of certain offences. Section 5(1) empowered the State Government, by notification, to direct that any particular case or class of cases be tried by a Special Court — with no guidelines, criteria or standards governing the selection. The special procedure was more stringent than the CrPC: ordinary procedural safeguards were withdrawn. Anwar Ali Sarkar and 49 co-accused, caught in an armed dacoity raid, were notified into a Special Court, tried, convicted and sentenced; he challenged Section 5(1) under Article 14.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Section 5(1) unconstitutional. Limb 1 failed — no basis or criterion for classifying which cases go to speedier trial; selection rested on the subjective opinion of executive officers; change the officers and different cases would be picked: not “intelligible,” but arbitrary and capricious. Limb 2 failed — how does unguided discretion serve speedier trial? The means (absolute discretion) are not rationally related to the end. Illustration: dacoities in five districts, two dacoits caught in each; District A's pair notified to the harsher Special Court while Districts B–E enjoy ordinary protections — discrimination within a single class (all dacoity accused), with no justifiable answer to “why these two?”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: A law conferring absolute, unguided, unfettered discretion on the executive to classify persons or cases, without criteria or standards, violates Article 14.

cards.name: Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra
cards.sub: AIR 1952 SC 123 · text of the impugned section virtually identical to the West Bengal Act

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: A Saurashtra State Ordinance empowered the government to send cases to Special Courts — but its preamble recited the exceptional law-and-order situation: widespread communal violence, dacoity, breakdown of the ordinary criminal justice system in named disturbed regions.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Upheld. In context, the discretion was not unguided: the preamble itself channelled it — cases connected with the breakdown of public order were the legitimate target. The discretion was bounded by the statute's stated objective.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: A provision identical in text may be valid or invalid depending on context, purpose, and the presence of guiding principles — in the statute or its surrounding circumstances. Noteworthy: Patanjali Sastri C.J. was a judge in both cases — dissenting in Anwar Ali Sarkar (to uphold) and in the majority in Kathi Raning (upholding).

cards.name: Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India (1950)
cards.sub: AIR 1950 SC 41

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: A single “sick” industrial undertaking — a textile mill threatening the livelihood of over 1,30,000 people — was taken over by the government for better management; shareholders objected to being singled out.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Yes — a single person or entity can constitute a valid class where it possesses unique characteristics distinguishing it from all others, and the law addresses that unique situation. Illustration offered in class: if one company causes 90% of an industry's pollution, a law addressing that company may be a valid classification.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The test remains the same: intelligible differentia plus rational nexus — even for a class of one.

cards.name: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974)

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: E.P. Royappa, a senior IAS officer serving as Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu — the highest State-level IAS post — was moved out and made Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission Board (a post declared equivalent in rank and salary), then OSD. He challenged the removal as arbitrary.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness: a decision that is arbitrary is inherently unequal — a significant expansion beyond the traditional classification test. (The doctrine is taught in full on Day 10.)

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The “New Doctrine of Equality”: arbitrariness read as a facet of Article 14.

cards.name: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kumari Nivedita Jain
cards.sub: The limits of reservation

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: To fill backward-class medical seats, MP progressively lowered the qualifying marks from 50 to 45 to 35 to 30 — then removed the minimum entirely, permitting admission regardless of entrance score, even zero or negative.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The Supreme Court upheld the State's action.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The extremity of compensatory discrimination — and, as the professor notes, evidence that medical admissions have grappled with the merit-versus-social-justice tension from the outset; NEET has never been purely meritocratic.

cards.name: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
cards.sub: The trigger for Article 15(4)

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Madras's Communal G.O. allocated medical and engineering seats by caste and community.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Struck down under Article 15(1): discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste. Consequence: the First Constitutional Amendment (1951) inserted Article 15(4), empowering special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The case that constitutionalised affirmative action in education.

cards.name: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
cards.sub: AIR 1974 SC 555 · bench including P.N. Bhagwati and Y.V. Chandrachud JJ.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Royappa, IAS, Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu — the highest State-level IAS post — was removed and appointed Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission Board (the Chairman being the Chief Minister; the Deputy Chairman therefore the post immediately below), then made OSD. An official order declared the posts equivalent in rank and salary to Chief Secretary.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: He lost — he could not prove arbitrariness — but the principle was established. The petitioner's argument: equality is not determined solely by salary; power, position, prestige, status and respect are essential components (the classroom example: a professor given Rs. 5 lakh but assigned housekeeping duties is not made Vice-Chancellor). The State's answer — equal salary, equivalent posts, no discrimination — missed the point. Bhagwati J.: “Mala fide and arbitrariness are easy to claim, but hardest to prove.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The flaw in the old law: where there is no comparator class (a person uniquely targeted), discrimination cannot be proven and Article 14 lies dormant. The new perspective: whether or not discrimination exists, if the State has absolute discretionary power or acts arbitrarily, Article 14 is violated. “Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be ‘cribbed, cabined and confined’ within the traditional limits of classification.”

cards.name: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962)
cards.sub: first Indian citation of Munn v. Illinois

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Police surveillance of a citizen, challenged under Article 21.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: “Life does not mean mere animal existence. It includes all those things which make life meaningful and beautiful. It includes the right to develop all our faculties.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The expansive reading of Article 21 from which the rights to privacy, to choose one's partner, and to live with dignity all descend — without this sentence, the constitutional protection for love marriages, personal relationships and individual autonomy would not exist. (Contemporary application: the Allahabad High Court recently scolded police for investigating a married couple's private life — protected under Article 21.)

cards.name: R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) — Bank Nationalisation
cards.sub: 11-judge bench — one of only a handful in history

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Indira Gandhi nationalised several banks. The petitioner was not a bank but a director and shareholder — because the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) belongs only to citizens, and a company is not a citizen; the bank could not sue, its shareholder-director could.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The government argued it need comply only with Article 31, not Article 19. Rejected: “Nothing doing! They cannot be separated. While acting under Article 31, you must also comply with Article 19(1)(f).”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Fundamental rights are not watertight compartments — the foundation stone of the Golden Triangle, expressly acknowledged by Bhagwati J. in Maneka Gandhi.

cards.name: Satwant Singh v. Union of India — the Passport Precedent

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Before 1967 India had no Passport Act; issuance was executive discretion. Satwant Singh's passport was refused — “We denied it because we chose to deny it.”

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The Court directed the government: if you want to deny passports, make a law; write down the reasons. Result: the Passports Act, 1967 — whose Section 10(3) authorised impounding “without assigning any reason, in public interest”: absolute, arbitrary power.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The statutory hook that Maneka Gandhi would strike.

cards.name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
cards.sub: AIR 1978 SC 597

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Two constables arrived at her residence: “Ministry of External Affairs — please surrender your passport.” On asking why: “Orders from above. We don't know why.” The government invoked Section 10(3) — impounding without assigning any reason — and defended it: “If we tell her the reason, she will run away!”

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The doctrine of post-decisional hearing evolved: in urgency the State may impound first, but must immediately (1) issue a notice stating the grounds; (2) afford a hearing; (3) continue the impounding only if justified, else return the passport. Section 10(3)'s absolute unguided discretion was arbitrary power, violating Article 14; and Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive — any law depriving personal liberty must satisfy non-arbitrariness (14) and reasonableness (19) as well as Article 21. The Golden Triangle was formally established.

fields.label: Principle
