fields.html: Outcome: Maneka Gandhi did not get her passport back — the case was dismissed on other grounds, continuing the pattern: Marbury (no relief), Kesavananda (no relief), Royappa (no relief), Maneka (no relief). Landmark cases create principles; they do not always grant relief to the petitioner.

cards.name: Marbury v. Madison
cards.sub: 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803) · Chief Justice John Marshall

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Constitution was 14–15 years old; no article mentioned judicial review. In the lame-duck period after John Adams lost the 1800 election, his party appointed 40 judges; commissions were signed and sealed, but some undelivered when Jefferson took office at midnight. Jefferson: “Throw these undelivered commissions away!” Marbury sought mandamus against Secretary of State Madison.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Three issues: (1) Does Marbury have a right to the commission? Yes — the right vested when signed and sealed; “where there is a right, there is a remedy” (ubi jus ibi remedium). (2) Can the Court issue mandamus to the executive? Yes — in the most famous sentence of American constitutional law: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” (3) Does mandamus lie in the Court's original jurisdiction? No — Article III, Section 2 does not cover it; Section 13 of the Judiciary Act 1789, which purported to grant it, was unconstitutional and void — the first federal statute ever struck down.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The political genius: the Court asserted the massive power of judicial review yet ordered no relief against the President, avoiding a confrontation Jefferson would likely have defied. “We will show our power, but we will not use it in this case.” Marbury did not get his commission.

cards.name: Lord Rama and Ravana — natural justice in the Ramayana
cards.sub: Classroom authority for the ancient Indian Rule of Law

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Rama sent messages to Ravana not once but twice, warning him to return Mother Sita and avoid a destructive war; even during the war he gave repeated warnings.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Rama told Ravana that he was a great and knowledgeable saint, and needed only to return Sita to be excused — notice and opportunity to amend before force: natural justice.

cards.name: Yudhishthira's exile — the Mahabharata example

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Yudhishthira lost the game of gambling; the condition was twelve years of exile and one year in an unknown place. Lord Krishna knew a war would take place — yet did not stop it.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: He insisted that the rule be followed: even the contemplated catastrophe did not justify setting aside the agreed condition.

cards.name: Shravan Kumar — the devoted son

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Shravan Kumar was carrying his blind parents; Lord Dasharatha accidentally killed him.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The Rule of Law demanded that the king take responsibility for the care and protection of the dead boy's parents. King Dasharatha went to them and served them water; they ultimately cursed him to die of the same grief of losing a son. Dasharatha was a king — he could have avoided this, but the Rule of Law bound him. This is the true spirit of the ancient Indian Rule of Law.

cards.name: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
cards.sub: The Emergency case · habeas corpus during MISA detentions

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: During the Emergency, MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) was applied and everyone was arrested under it; Fundamental Rights stood suspended. Detainees petitioned that they were wrongly detained and should be released. The Supreme Court then had very good judges — at least three beyond doubt: Justice Khanna, a very upright judge; Justice Bhagwati, who called himself the pioneer of human rights; Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, a very good judge — along with Justice Beg (whom the professor harshly calls Indira Gandhi's “peon”) and Chief Justice A.N. Ray (made Chief Justice by Indira Gandhi, later changing his allegiance). It seemed the decision would be 4:1 for liberty.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The shocking judgment came — the professor states bluntly that Indira Gandhi bought everyone; the only man who was not sold was Justice H.R. Khanna. The judges held: “The entire repository of the right to liberty is the Constitution. If the Constitution has not given the right, then you do not have the right at all. Since the Constitution and rights were suspended, there was no Right to Life left to protect.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The core: all rights come only from the Constitution — suspend the Constitution and you have no rights at all.

cards.name: Dr. Subramanian Swamy v. Dr. Manmohan Singh
cards.sub: Modern application of the Rule of Law

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: A government servant can be prosecuted for corruption only with the government's sanction. If a minister in Manmohan Singh's government was corrupt, permission to prosecute had to come from Manmohan Singh himself — naturally, it was not granted.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The Supreme Court held that refusing sanction for the prosecution of a corrupt official is a violation of the Rule of Law.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The professor is criticising on the basis of this judicial pronouncement, not personal whims. Reading the case is compulsory — anyone who does not read it will fail the mid-term (though he later admits he has never actually framed a question on it).

cards.name: State of Rajasthan v. Thakur Pratap Singh (or Sampratap Singh)
cards.sub: Taught as the Article 15 authority on religious discrimination

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: In a village plagued by dacoity, villagers requested the Congress Chief Minister to post additional police. He replied the government was “very poor” — the villagers would have to contribute for the extra personnel. The wealthy villagers agreed. But back in Jaipur, after consulting Rahul Gandhi, instructions came: do not collect money from Muslims. An Act followed, requiring villagers to pay the additional police tax — with an express exemption for Muslims.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Such discrimination on the basis of religion violates Article 15(1), which prohibits discrimination solely on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The professor's ongoing bewilderment: when dacoity affects the entire village and everyone should contribute to the solution, why should Muslims alone be exempted? “Even today I do not understand the rationale.” The case is taught as part of Article 15: discrimination in the name of religion is constitutionally prohibited.

cards.name: Sukanya Samriddhi v. Union of India (2023/24)
cards.sub: CJI Dhananjaya Chandrachud · argued by Justice Muralidhar (former Chief Justice, Orissa High Court, engaged by the petitioner)

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Sukanya — “a very dynamic journalist” — researched and revealed that caste-based discrimination persisted in Indian prisons decades after independence: work assignments were made by caste, Dalit prisoners assigned to dig drains and clean bathrooms, Brahmin prisoners assigned to cook. This despite Congress having amended the Constitution to declare India “Socialist Secular.” Disturbed, she filed a PIL.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Counsel argued that Article 15 explicitly prohibits caste discrimination, yet the prison system was recording prisoners' castes and assigning work on that basis. CJI Chandrachud made a landmark observation: there is no need to record caste anywhere, as recording facilitates discrimination. The Court directed that the caste column and references to caste in the registers of undertrial and convict prisoners “shall be deleted.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The judgment connects to Ambedkar's vision of a casteless society. The professor contrasts Rahul Gandhi's persistent four-year demand for a caste census as moving in the opposite direction, notes the BJP initially opposed it on the principled ground of a casteless society (consistent with both Ambedkar and the judgment) before political pressures forced a relent, and asks the class how many agree with the judgment — calling it “a great judgment.” The underlying logic: if caste is not recorded, discrimination becomes harder; recording it facilitates discrimination.

cards.name: Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat (1991)

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: A Gujarat judge, very strict with police officers over investigation quality (“Haven't done investigation, what are you doing?”), generated resentment in an understaffed, overworked force — running between crime scenes (a rape investigation interrupted by a truck-car collision with eight dead). The officers devised a plan: invited to the police station for dinner and inspection, the judge was pressed to drink — “I don't take it... but since you are pressing, I'll take it” — until inebriated. Then they beat him severely, shaved his head, placed him on a donkey, and paraded him: “Look, he's a judge, drinks alcohol and is unconscious — what judgment must he be giving!” The incident terrorised the entire judiciary; even IPS officers possibly involved were protected by fear — no one filed complaints.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: News reached Delhi; the judicial establishment was outraged. The Supreme Court held that even if the judge had consumed alcohol, the appropriate response was to put him in a car, take him home, and let him sleep — alcohol's effects dissipate naturally. The IPS officer involved was suspended; the Court issued guidelines on when and how a Magistrate may be arrested, providing procedural protections for judicial officers.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The life lesson drawn in class: one should not misbehave excessively with anyone. The professor admits his own mistakes — losing his temper, scolding people, having recently thrown someone out of his office for leaving mid-studies to watch a movie and sit in a bar (the theatre had a bar inside; second-year students bought alcohol elsewhere after the honest bar owner, checking identification, refused to serve minors under Maharashtra's age of twenty-one).

cards.name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022/23)
cards.sub: Validity of the 103rd Amendment

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The 10% EWS reservation under Articles 15(6) and 16(6) challenged as violating the equality code and the fifty percent ceiling.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Upheld. Assigned reading: determine the bench strength, the issues framed, the decision on each, any dissents, the ratio decidendi and supporting reasoning — a one-page written summary is required.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: EWS reservation differs in character: not caste-based, and unavailable to those already receiving reservation benefits.

cards.name: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
cards.sub: Under Articles 14 and 16

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Chief Secretary's removal and appointment as OSD.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Article 14 (and through it, Article 16) strikes at arbitrariness: “Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be ‘cribbed, cabined and confined’ within the traditional limits of classification.” Administrative discretion is necessary for governance but must rest on relevant considerations, not whims.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The high evidentiary burden of proving arbitrariness — “easy to claim, hardest to prove.”

cards.name: Zoroastrian Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar Cooperative Societies (2005)

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: A cooperative housing society restricted membership to Zoroastrians (Parsis) only.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Upheld: housing societies are not “places of public resort” under Article 15(2); a society may restrict membership by religion or community.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The professor's concern: “I feel in the long run this won't be right, because we want a plural society. If everyone makes pockets — Muslims here, Hindus here, Yadavs here, Dalits here — our unity will be destroyed.” The reasoning rests on a literal reading of 15(2); the broader constitutional vision of a secular, egalitarian society might require a more expansive interpretation.

cards.name: State of Rajasthan v. Pratap Singh

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Additional tax and police force imposed on a particular area, allegedly discriminating against a community.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The word “only” in Article 15(1): discrimination based solely on enumerated grounds is prohibited — if the State shows additional, rational reasons for its action, it stands.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: “Only” is the hinge of Article 15(1).

cards.name: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Routine hand-cuffing of undertrial prisoners challenged.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Hand-cuffing is degrading treatment, violating dignity; permissible only exceptionally where genuine risk of escape or violence exists, justified case by case.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Referenced when the professor invoked it to argue for removing hand-cuffs from a young boy who had eloped with a girl.

cards.name: State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976)
cards.sub: 7-judge bench · 5:2 · (1976) 2 SCC 310

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The constitutionality of special treatment for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Kerala government service was at issue before the largest bench then assembled for the question.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Five judges held Article 16(4) is NOT an exception to Article 16: it is within the purview of Article 16 as a facet of equality, providing equality of opportunity in line with clause (1), giving positive support and content to 16(1). The Court envisaged not formal or legal equality but proportional equality — the progressive elimination of pronounced inequality.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Justice Chinnappa Reddy repeated the position in A.B.S.K. Sangh (Akhil Bharatiya Shoshit Karmachari Sangh) v. Union of India — a demonstration of the power of Public Interest Litigation.

cards.name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
cards.sub: 9-judge bench — the largest for reservation matters · Justice P.B. Jeevan Reddy's judgment is the assigned reading

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Challenge to the 27% OBC reservation implemented by executive order in 1990, and the consolidated questions on Article 16(4).

fields.label: Held
fields.html: See the issue-wise holdings below.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Reservation jurisprudence's organising case.

cards.name: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963)
cards.sub: The earlier framework

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Mysore's 68% reservation challenged.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Caste cannot be the sole criterion — poverty or place of residence can also indicate backwardness; 68% struck down as excessive; reservation should generally not exceed 50%. Article 15(4) was then viewed as an exception to 15(1). The Court made clear its judgment did not affect SC/ST reservations.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The source of the 50% ceiling that Indra Sawhney adopted as a rule of caution.

cards.name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950)
cards.sub: AIR 1950 SC 124 · 6 judges · majority per Patanjali Sastri J.; Fazl Ali J. dissenting

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Cross Roads, an English weekly printed in Bombay; on 1 March 1950 Madras banned its entry, circulation, sale and distribution under section 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 “for securing the public safety and the maintenance of public order.” Thappar went straight to the Supreme Court under Article 32.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Petition allowed; section 9(1-A) void. Article 32 is itself a fundamental right — the Court cannot turn a petitioner away. Freedom of speech includes freedom to propagate ideas, and propagation is secured by circulation: “Liberty of circulation is as essential to that freedom as the liberty of publication.” “Public order” is a wide expression covering every breach of tranquillity from affray to rebellion — but the 1950 clause (2) spoke only of the security of the State; only aggravated disorder endangering the State's foundations could justify curbing speech. A provision whose language authorises both valid and invalid restrictions cannot be severed — void as a whole. Fazl Ali J.: serious disorder does undermine the State's security, as sedition does.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The first free-speech ruling: circulation is part of speech; the 19(2) grounds are exhaustive and read narrowly; the seed of the overbreadth doctrine. It caused the First Amendment.

cards.name: Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950)
cards.sub: AIR 1950 SC 129 · the same six judges, the same day · Fazl Ali J. dissenting

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Chief Commissioner of Delhi required the weekly Organiser to submit for pre-publication scrutiny “all communal matter and news and views about Pakistan including photographs and cartoons” under section 7(1)(c), East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Pre-censorship is a restriction on the liberty of the press, which is an essential part of 19(1)(a); the majority applied Romesh Thappar — public safety/public order is not the security of the State, so clause (2) did not save it. Fazl Ali J. read “public safety” as the security of the State and would have dismissed. Blackstone, quoted: the press's liberty “consists in laying no previous restraint upon publications.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Press freedom lives inside 19(1)(a) though the Article never says “press”; prior restraint demands justification under clause (2). It does NOT hold all print pre-censorship void — Virendra v. State of Punjab (1957) upheld a time-limited power with a right of representation and struck down one without safeguards.

cards.name: State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952)
cards.sub: AIR 1952 SC 196 · 5 judges · Patanjali Sastri C.J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The People's Education Society declared an unlawful association under the 1908 Act's section 15(2)(b) (financing the banned Communist Party); the Madras amendment required stated grounds, allowed representation, and made an Advisory Board's finding bind the government — but the declaration was Gazette-only and membership itself became an offence.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Restriction struck down. Reasonableness covers substance and procedure; the test is statute-by-statute — “no abstract standard, or general pattern, of reasonableness.” The factors: the nature of the right, the purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil, the disproportion of the imposition, and prevailing conditions. Shutting out judicial inquiry in favour of executive satisfaction is reasonable only in very exceptional circumstances; the absence of personal notice when membership was criminalised was a serious defect. The Court is “a sentinel on the qui vive.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The foundational reasonableness test for all of Article 19; the “disproportion” factor is the root of modern proportionality (Modern Dental College 2016; Anuradha Bhasin 2020). Limit noted: it arose under 19(1)(c)/(4) — a ruling on one freedom is weak authority on another.

cards.name: K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970)
cards.sub: (1970) 2 SCC 780 · 5 judges · Hidayatullah C.J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Abbas, journalist and film-maker (on the Khosla Committee), made the 16-minute documentary A Tale of Four Cities with a brief blurred red-light-district shot; offered a “U” certificate only with cuts, he challenged pre-censorship itself and the vagueness of the Cinematograph Act's section 5-B(2) directions.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Censorship of films including prior restraint is justified; U/A classification is reasonable; directions not void for vagueness but must be supplemented to protect artistic and social value. Film is treated differently from print — instant appeal, realism, combined effect on eye and ear, strong effect on children. American decisions are not decisive: the First Amendment is absolute in form, Article 19(2) expressly permits reasonable restrictions. A law leaving censors “in a boundless sea of uncertainty” would be struck, but courts first construe sensibly. The flaw in the directions: treating artistic and inartistic work alike — censors judge the handling of a theme, not the theme. The Solicitor-General conceded time limits and court- or tribunal-level appeals.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The print-film distinction. Key lines: “The motion picture is able to stir up emotions more deeply than any other product of art”; “our standards must be so framed that we are not reduced to a level where the protection of the least capable and the most depraved amongst us determines what the morally healthy cannot view or read”; “Sex and obscenity are not always synonymous.”

cards.name: Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana (1988)
cards.sub: (1988) 3 SCC 410 · per Venkataramiah J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Doordarshan was showing Honi-Anhoni; two organisations obtained a Bombay High Court injunction against episodes 12 and 13 in a public interest petition alleging superstition and fright to children — the producer added as a party only the day before the order.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Injunction set aside. The right to exhibit a film on Doordarshan, on Doordarshan's terms, is part of 19(1)(a) — like publishing through a newspaper, subject to the medium owner's terms; an interim injunction infringes the producer's right where petitioners show no legal right and no material of real harm; “It spreads superstition” is not a 19(2) ground. The Court expressly left open whether a citizen may set up a private broadcasting station.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Dissemination extends to television; courts must not impose prior restraint by injunction on non-listed grounds. The reserved question was taken up in Cricket Association of Bengal.

cards.name: LIC v. Prof. Manubhai D. Shah (1992)
cards.sub: (1992) 3 SCC 637 · two appeals together · per Ahmadi J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Shah's study paper arguing LIC premiums were unduly high; a member's counter reprinted in LIC's magazine Yogakshema; Shah's rejoinder refused (“in-house publication”). Separately, Doordarshan refused to telecast Beyond Genocide, the Golden Lotus-winning Bhopal documentary holding a “U” certificate, calling it outdated and sub judice.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Both appeals dismissed — LIC must print the rejoinder with explanation and apology for delay; Doordarshan must telecast. “Speech is God's gift to mankind.” Freedom includes circulating views through print, radio and television and using the medium to answer criticism. LIC is “State” under Article 12; its publicly funded magazine, open to outside subscribers, must be fair — printing one side and refusing the other violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(a). Once the film-maker's right is recognised, the refusing party bears the burden of showing a 19(2) ground — criticism of government is not one. Ruling confined to “the peculiar facts”: no absolute duty to print whatever any citizen sends.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Right of reply against State-controlled media; burden of justification on the State. It does not create such a right against a private publisher.

cards.name: Secretary, Ministry of I&B; v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)
cards.sub: (1995) 2 SCC 161 · Sawant and Mohan JJ. jointly; Jeevan Reddy J. concurring

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: CAB's 1993 Hero Cup: Doordarshan offered Rs. 1 crore; CAB sold worldwide rights to Trans World International for a guaranteed US$550,000 plus 70% of excess; the Telecom Department told VSNL to refuse the uplink and customs detained TWI's equipment; interim orders let both telecast. The 1994 BCCI–ESPN dispute recurred.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: (para 124) Airwaves are public property; a public authority must regulate their use in the public interest. The right to impart and receive information is part of freedom of speech; a citizen has access to telecasting subject to public-property limits. The Central Government must set up an independent, autonomous public authority to control the airwaves. Sports telecast by a non-profit body has a speech element — earning revenue incidentally does not convert expression into trade. 19(2) permits no monopoly over speech (unlike 19(6) for business). Jeevan Reddy J.'s limits: no citizen has a fundamental right to set up a private broadcasting station — that is for Parliament; “From the standpoint of Article 19(1)(a), what is paramount is the right of the listeners and viewers and not the right of the broadcaster.” Both opinions found the Telegraph Act, 1885 unsuited to broadcasting; the Prasar Bharati Act, 1990 was brought into force in 1997.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The right to receive information; airwaves public property; no broadcasting monopoly. The lecture's version — that the rights-holder must give the feed to Doordarshan — is not in the judgment: that rule comes from the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007.

cards.name: S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010)
cards.sub: (2010) 5 SCC 600 · per Chauhan J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: In a 2005 India Today survey the actress endorsed pre-marital sex within committed relationships and girls' self-protection; twenty-three criminal complaints (defamation, obscenity, insult to modesty) followed, mostly from one political party's functionaries.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: All quashed. A reference to sex is not per se obscene; the standard is contemporary community tolerance as of an average reasonable person; no identifiable person or definite group was defamed, so the complainants were not “persons aggrieved”; pre-marital sex between consenting adults is no offence, so advocating its acceptance cannot be incitement; the complaints were mala fide, for political mileage. “It is not the task of the criminal law to punish individuals merely for expressing unpopular views”; “Morality and Criminality are not co-extensive”; the law must not have a “chilling effect.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Unpopular social opinion protected from morality-based prosecution; lays down no new obscenity test (that came in Aveek Sarkar, which cites it).

cards.name: Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014)
cards.sub: (2014) 4 SCC 257 · per Radhakrishnan J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Stern's photograph of Boris Becker nude with his fiancée Barbara Feltus (her father took it), reproduced by Sports World and Anandabazar Patrika in May 1993; an Alipore lawyer's complaint under section 292 IPC; summons issued; the High Court refused to quash.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Hicklin is “not the correct test.” Obscenity is judged from the average person's viewpoint applying contemporary community standards, the work as a whole, in its context and for its message; nudity is not obscene per se — only material tending to excite lustful thoughts. The photograph's message was against racism; prosecution quashed.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Hicklin (followed since Ranjit Udeshi 1965) replaced by the community standard test. Note: a two-judge bench displaced a five-judge bench's retention of Hicklin; the judgment reads Udeshi as itself recognising changing standards.

cards.name: Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996)
cards.sub: (1996) 1 SCC 361 · 5-judge Constitution Bench · per Ahmadi C.J., Kuldip Singh J. concurring

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Petitions in Kerala and Madhya Pradesh, transferred to the Supreme Court, challenged the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards as “titles” under Article 18(1).

fields.label: Held
fields.html: The awards are valid — not titles — but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes; a user should forfeit the award; a high-level committee should set selection criteria. “The theory of equality does not mandate that merit should not be recognized.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Article 18 targets ranks of nobility and colonial loyal-subject creation; honours recognising work done are compatible with equality.

cards.name: Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) — the Tamas case

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: A petition to stop Doordarshan showing Tamas, the serial from Bhisham Sahni's Partition novel, alleging it would inflame communal feeling.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Refused: two High Court judges had watched it and found a message of peace; the work is judged as a whole by the standard of reasonable, strong-minded people — not of those who sense danger in every hostile view.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Depicting violence is not inciting it.

cards.name: S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989)
cards.sub: (1989) 2 SCC 574 — the case a student named “Shankar Asrani v. Jagjivan Ram”

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Tamil film Ore Oru Gramathile criticised caste-based reservation; after agitation threats the High Court revoked its “U” certificate.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Certificate restored. Open criticism of policy is not a restriction ground; the State cannot plead inability to control a hostile audience — freedom “cannot be held to ransom by an intolerant group of people”; the anticipated danger must be “a spark in a powder keg,” justified “on the anvil of necessity and not the quicksand of convenience or expediency.”

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The Indian proximity test; the State's duty to protect speech against hostile audiences.

cards.name: Hans Muller v. Superintendent, Presidency Jail, Calcutta (1955)
cards.sub: AIR 1955 SC 367 · per Bose J. — closing pages only required

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Hans Muller, a West German subject, arrested 18 September 1954 and detained under section 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 with a view to expulsion; his passport endorsed for return only; a German fraud warrant and extradition request pending; the Centre's signed expulsion order held back once he moved the High Court.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: (1) Competence: Entries 9–10, Union List — preventive detention connected with foreign affairs; the Foreigners Act, 1946 supported. (2) Articles 21 and 22 protect “citizen and foreigner alike.” (3) Detention to arrange expulsion is genuinely preventive — preventing evasion. (4) A State may act in anticipation of the Centre's order. (5) Excluding certain British subjects from “foreigner” is a reasonable classification. (6) Article 19's rights to move and reside have “no corresponding” foreigner rights — all a foreigner is guaranteed is life and liberty under Article 21. (7) Expulsion power is “absolute and unfettered.” (8) Expulsion is not extradition — the expelled person leaves a free man; government may choose the Foreigners Act route even where extradition is requested. (9) Bad faith not shown.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Cite for: Article 19 is confined to citizens. Be precise — the Court spoke of the rights to move and reside, in an expulsion case; free speech by a foreigner was not in issue. The same visitor still has Articles 14 and 21.

cards.name: Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1965)
cards.sub: AIR 1966 SC 740 · Sarkar, Hidayatullah, Raghubar Dayal, Mudholkar, Bachawat JJ. · Lohia argued in person · released 4:1

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The 1962 Chinese-attack Emergency; the Defence of India Rules' rule 30(1)(b) permitting detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “public safety” and “maintenance of public order” — not “law and order.” On 9 August 1965 the Patna District Magistrate ordered Lohia's detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “the public safety and the maintenance of law and order”; served 1.40 a.m.; Hazaribagh Central Jail by 3.30 p.m.; Lohia's Hindi letter from jail became the writ petition.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: (1) The petition was entertainable: the Article 359 order bars petitions only where liberty was taken “under” the Act — whether it was so taken must itself be examined; the President's order “did not make lawless actions lawful.” (2) Sarkar J.: the order is the only warrant and must be strictly in the rule's terms; “public order” in an emergency law means disorder of a grave nature, “law and order” lesser local disorder (rowdiness at Holi); the State cannot use an affidavit to show the order meant what it does not say; one valid and one invalid ground (public safety valid; law and order not) — under Shibban Lal Saksena the whole order falls. (3) Hidayatullah J. (with Bachawat J.): disorder is a spectrum; two drunkards quarrelling cause disorder, not public disorder — if the two belong to rival communities and one stirs communal passion, public disorder is “apprehended”; the circles — “Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State”; by writing “law and order” the Magistrate “was adding a clause to the Defence of India Rules.” (4) Mudholkar J.: the words made the order ambiguous on its face. Dissent (Raghubar Dayal J.): actual satisfaction, not form, controls; the file note showed public order satisfaction.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The three concentric circles; for Article 19(2) only the inner two circles are grounds — a mere law and order problem is not.

cards.name: Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India (1961)
cards.sub: AIR 1962 SC 305 · unanimous Constitution Bench · per Mudholkar J. · G.S. Pathak for petitioners; M.C. Setalvad, Attorney-General,

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Sakal, the Marathi daily from Poona (circulation ~52,000 weekdays, 56,000 Sundays; six pages at 7 naye paise, Sunday ten at 12), and two readers' petitions, against the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Order, 1960 — a schedule fixing maximum pages per price; supplements only on 26 January, 15 August, once a quarter, else by permission.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Section 3(1) unconstitutional. (1) Press freedom is within 19(1)(a) — Brij Bhushan. (2) Circulation is part of the right — “not merely to the matter which he is entitled to circulate, but also to the volume of circulation.” (3) The real purpose was to cut circulation — a minimum price for pages makes papers too costly for a class of readers. (4) Price affects circulation (the Press Commission's findings: Free Press Journal's price cut doubled circulation; two Tamil dailies' price rise lost 33,000 readers). (5) Cutting pages compels restricting news; cutting advertisements forces prices up — “no remote, but a direct consequence,” a vicious cycle ending in closure. (6) Supplement control leaves issues to government's “sweet will and pleasure.” (7) 19(2) is exhaustive — nothing allows restriction for the general public or a section. (8) 19(6) cannot be borrowed — each freedom has its own clause; the State cannot regulate the business side “by directly and immediately curtailing” speech. (9) The test is direct effect: a law capping a named paper's subscribers would be void; achieving it through a rate schedule makes no difference. (10) A good object (checking monopoly) does not save bad means — “a dangerous weapon which is capable of being used against democracy itself.” The Article 14 point and the readers' standing were left undecided.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Indirect restrictions on the press: the State cannot do through price, pages or advertisements what it cannot do directly.

cards.name: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1972)
cards.sub: (1972) 2 SCC 788 · Sikri C.J., Ray, Jaganmohan Reddy, Mathew, Beg JJ. · 4:1 (Mathew J. dissenting) · Palkhivala, Daphtary,

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Four groups — Bennett Coleman (Times of India), Hindustan Times, Express Newspapers, The Hindu — against the Newsprint Policy 1972-73: a 10-page quota ceiling (Remark V); circulation growth 10% for dailies under 1,00,000 but 3% for larger (VII(a)); a 20% page increase for under-10-page dailies usable only for pages (VII(c)); no page increases by cutting circulation, no quota shifting within common ownership units (VIII); no new newspaper or edition even within quota (X).

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Two preliminary objections rejected: a company is not a citizen — but under R.C. Cooper shareholders do not lose rights by incorporating; Article 358 (1971 Emergency) does not protect executive action lacking legislative authority. The majority (Ray J.): rationing scarce newsprint is allowed — but “shortage of newsprint can stop with allotment”; the test is direct effect, not pith and substance; the policy directly controlled page growth, circulation and advertisement space. The ten-page ceiling: the three Times editions averaged 13.13, 13.99 and 17.83 pages — cuts of 23.8%, 28.4%, 43.8% against a 4.5% newsprint fall; The Hindu faced 16 to 10. Unequals treated as equals — Article 14 violated. Estimated losses: Rs. 39 lakh (Bennett Coleman), Rs. 44 lakh (Hindustan Times), Rs. 38 lakh (The Hindu). Remarks V, VII(a), VII(c), VIII struck down under Articles 14 and 19(1)(a); X under 19(1)(a). Press liberty is “an Ark of the Covenant.” Beg J. concurring: the conditions had no authority of law at all. Mathew J. dissenting: “an abridgment of speech, but not an abridgment of the freedom of speech”; Article 19(1)(a) is not “the guardian of unlimited talkativeness”; the community's right to hear supports maximum circulation; Article 39(b) validates the small-dailies' classification.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The effect test — judge a measure by its direct effect on the right, not its label or purpose; shareholders and editors can enforce 19(1)(a) through the company.

cards.name: Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1985)
cards.sub: (1986) 1 SCC 133 · A.P. Sen, Venkataramiah, Misra JJ. · F.S. Nariman for petitioners

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The press enclave on Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg; Express Newspapers' plots leased from 1954; building only east of a diagonal sewer under the 1957 agreement; 1977 request to divert and build with double basement; DDA and Ministry approvals (1978); Rs. 1.30 crore spent by February 1980. Then: 17 February 1980 — Jagmohan takes office as Lieutenant-Governor and that Sunday evening calls for the municipal files; 29 February — the Zonal Engineer's locks broken to remove the file; 1 March — press conference announcing an inquiry by three subordinates in three days and a demolition warning, broadcast on radio and television; 1 March — a show-cause notice for demolition; 10 March — a notice to show cause on lease re-entry; 12 March — the committee's report released at another press conference. The Indian Express had published on Jagmohan's role in the Turkman Gate demolitions during the Emergency.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Both notices quashed. The Lieutenant-Governor confused power over Union property (Entry 32, Union List) with his Article 239 powers — nearness to the Centre gave him no authority over its property. A.P. Sen J.: the notices “are intended and meant to silence the voice of the Indian Express” — a direct and immediate threat to press freedom, violating 19(1)(a) read with 14; a writ lies though the matter looks contractual; the re-entry notice was real, not exploratory; summary eviction was unavailable; mala fides — power used for an alien purpose is bad faith; the specific allegations were met only with bare denials; nothing was contemplated before 17 February; promissory estoppel binds the successor government. Venkataramiah J.: arbitrary, without independent application of mind — Article 14. Misra J.: the land rights spring from contract and planning law, not 19(1)(a) — a matter for a civil suit.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Administrative harassment of a newspaper as an indirect attack on press freedom (Sen J.); the model of proving mala fides from a detailed chronology. Do not write that the lease was cancelled — two show-cause notices issued, both quashed.

cards.name: Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) Lal Kuan v. Union of India (1959)
cards.sub: AIR 1960 SC 554 · per Kapur J. · K.M. Munshi and N.C. Chatterjee for petitioners; C.K. Daphtary, Solicitor-General, for the Union

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954: “advertisement” defined widely (labels, cartons, leaflets); “magic remedy” includes talisman, mantra, kavacha; section 3 barred advertisements suggesting drugs for miscarriage, contraception, sexual capacity or venereal disease “or any other disease... specified in rules”; section 8 allowed seizure. Hamdard, the Delhi Unani house, was stopped from advertising forty products; the Poona branch of Sadhana Ausadhalaya was raided without warrant.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Method: find the law's true nature and character — history, mischief, remedy; presumption of constitutionality. History: the 1927 Council of State resolution, the Chopra Committee, the Drugs Act 1940, the Bhatia Committee 1953, English statutes. The evil: self-medication driven by extravagant advertising to a credulous public. Article 19(1)(a): “An advertisement is no doubt a form of speech but its true character is reflected by the object for the promotion of which it is employed” — a commercial advertisement does not propagate social, political or economic ideas; advertising prohibited drugs is not speech (relying on Valentine v. Chrestensen). 19(1)(f)/(g): reasonable in the general public's interest. But: section 3(d)'s delegation — naming further diseases by rule with no criteria — “uncanalised and uncontrolled power,” void; the Rules' Schedule fell with it (severable). Section 8's seizure power went far beyond the Act's purpose and lacked safeguards — void; mandamus to return seized goods.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: The starting point of the commercial speech story (1959: purely commercial advertising outside 19(1)(a)) — and a leading case on excessive delegation. Confined by later cases to its facts.

cards.name: Tata Press Ltd. v. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. (1995)
cards.sub: (1995) 5 SCC 139 · per Kuldip Singh J. · Dr. Abhishek Singhvi for Tata Press; K.K. Venugopal and Arun Jaitley for the Nigam

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: MTNL (80% government-held, licensee under the Telegraph Act 1885) gave directory publishing to contractors earning from Yellow Pages advertising; Tata Press published its own Yellow Pages buyers' guide (Bombay editions 1992-94); rule 458 of the Telegraph Rules, 1951 bars publishing “any list of telephone subscribers” without permission; the City Court dismissed MTNL's suit, the Single Judge and Division Bench of Bombay reversed and enjoined.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Appeal allowed. Hamdard rested on Valentine v. Chrestensen — but American law moved: Sullivan (1964), Bigelow v. Virginia (1975), Virginia State Board of Pharmacy (1976 — a free flow of commercial information is indispensable), Bates v. State Bar of Arizona (lawyer advertising allowed; false and misleading advertising restrainable). The Indian text differs: Article 19(2) itself lists the restrictions — deceptive, unfair, misleading and untruthful commercial speech is hit by 19(2). Hamdard confined: it dealt with prohibited drugs; Indian Express (1985) had already called its wider observations too broad. Advertising pays most of the media's cost (60-80% of newspaper revenue) — Sakal and Bennett Coleman show curbing advertisements hits circulation. The receiver's right: the recipient may have a deeper interest than the advertiser (the life-saving drug example). Holding: “Commercial speech” is part of 19(1)(a). Application: a telephone directory is a public utility the authority may regulate; paid Yellow Pages advertising is not that service; a 19(1)(a) right cannot be denied by creating a government monopoly; Tata's guide is compiled by trade, not by subscription — not a “list of subscribers.” Rule 458 remains mandatory for white-pages entries.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Commercial advertisements are protected speech; listeners and readers have their own right to receive. Limits: false, misleading or deceptive advertising may be restrained (the judgment does not say which 19(2) head covers it — a gap for critical answers). It did not overrule Hamdard.

cards.name: Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra (1964)
cards.sub: AIR 1965 SC 881 · Gajendragadkar C.J., Wanchoo, Hidayatullah, Shah, Rajagopala Ayyangar JJ. · per Hidayatullah J. · R.K. Garg

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Four partners of Bombay's Happy Book Stall found with unexpurgated Lady Chatterley's Lover; one sold a copy to a decoy customer; all convicted under section 292 IPC (fines of Rs. 20); Mulk Raj Anand testified to the novel's literary merit.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: (1) Section 292 valid — a reasonable restriction in the interests of decency or morality; obscenity has “extremely poor value” in spreading ideas, though where ideas of public interest are conveyed (the medical textbook) the balance tilts toward speech. (2) Knowledge of obscenity is not an ingredient — no “knowingly” in the section; liability is strict, though absence of knowledge may mitigate sentence. (3) The test: Hicklin set out (tendency to deprave and corrupt susceptible minds), “uniformly applied in India”; mere treatment of sex and nudity in art is not obscenity “without something more” — Michelangelo's angels need not wear breeches; but “We do not think that it should be discarded.” Three qualifications: not stray words — the whole work viewed overall; yet the obscene matter also considered “by itself and separately”; art must so preponderate as to throw obscenity into shadow. Obscenity “without a preponderating social purpose or profit” has no protection — judged “by our national standards.” (4) The novel: Lawrence's sincerity accepted, but the sexual descriptions were its only attraction for the common reader; the law protects “not those who can protect themselves”; the impugned portions passed permissible limits; no preponderating social gain shown. Appeal dismissed. (Contrast: the English Central Criminal Court in R. v. Penguin Books had held the same novel not obscene.)

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Cite for “Hicklin as modified,” not for the community standard test; and for the seller's strict liability.

cards.name: Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014) — the brief

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Stern's Becker-Feltus photograph (taken by her father), reproduced by Sports World (cover story, 5 May 1993) and Anandabazar Patrika (6 May 1993); the Alipore lawyer's complaint under section 292 IPC and section 4 of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986; summons 10 May 1993; the High Court refusing to quash. (An earlier lecture called the fiancée South African; the judgment calls her a dark-skinned film actress, the complainant a German film actress.)

fields.label: Held
fields.html: Standards change (paras 12-19) — Udeshi, Kakodkar, Samaresh Bose, Khushboo each stressed contemporary values; the yardstick (para 19): “contemporary mores and national standards,” not the susceptible group. Hicklin judged by isolated passages and the most susceptible readers; Roth (1957) moved to the average person; Canada followed in Towne Cinema and Butler. Para 24: “We are also of the view that Hicklin test is not the correct test” — the community standard test applies; nudity is not obscenity per se — only material exciting lustful thoughts; the message and context (paras 25-26, following Bobby Art; Ajay Goswami). The photograph: standing close, Becker's arm covering her breast, taken by her own father; the message — skin colour matters little, love prevails; no tendency to deprave. Proceedings quashed.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Three working rules: the average person, not the most susceptible; the work as a whole; context and message. The standard is national and contemporary. For criticism: a two-judge bench declared Hicklin incorrect although the five-judge bench in Udeshi had declined to discard it.

cards.name: Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996)
cards.sub: (1996) 4 SCC 1 · Ahmadi C.J., Bharucha, Kirpal JJ. · per Bharucha J.

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: Bandit Queen, from Mala Sen's book (on sale since 1991 without objection): Phoolan Devi married as a child, raped, humiliated by police, gang-raped, stripped and paraded naked, turning dacoit and to revenge. The Tribunal (Lentin J., retired Bombay High Court, and three women members) allowed the coarse language (ordinary speech in the Chambal), kept the police-beating scene (it explains her turning), cut the second of three rape sequences and trimmed the first and third, kept the naked parade whole — cutting it “would be a sacrilege,” comparing Schindler's List's frontal nudity. The Delhi High Court quashed the certificate. The petitioner: a Gujjar claiming the film slurred his community (the rapist named Babu Gujjar) and Indian womanhood.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: 'A' certificate restored. The guidelines are broad standards, not a statute — clause 2's sub-clauses cannot outweigh clauses 1 and 3. Where the theme is of social relevance it must prevail; this film “is not a pretty story” — it accuses the society that tormented her. The naked parade: those who stripped her meant to demean her; showing it conveys exactly that — sympathy for the victim, disgust for the perpetrators; “Nakedness does not always arouse the baser instinct.” The High Court's error: the revulsion the Tribunal spoke of was at the sadism of the strippers, not her nudity. Rape is shown for its terrifying effect, not glorified. The test: for a serious film, ask of each scene — does it advance the message? If so, leave it alone, with an 'A' certificate. A film illustrating a social evil must necessarily show the evil; a film extolling it is impermissible; the depiction must be just sufficient. Deference to the expert multi-member Tribunal (three of four members women); the writ court ought not to have entertained a petition resting on a community slur.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Nudity is not obscene by itself — context and purpose decide; the “advance the message” test that Aveek Sarkar later applied to a photograph.

cards.name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020)
cards.sub: (2020) 3 SCC 637 · N.V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy, B.R. Gavai JJ. · (brief written from Columbia's case analysis plus four

fields.label: Facts
fields.html: 2 August 2019 — J&K; Home Department advises tourists and Amarnath pilgrims to leave; schools and offices closed. 4 August — mobile networks, internet and landlines shut; District Magistrates impose section 144 CrPC. 5 August — the constitutional order ending Article 370's special status. Anuradha Bhasin, editor of the Kashmir Times (Srinagar), unable to publish since 6 August; Ghulam Nabi Azad M.P.; an intervenor noting restrictions described as temporary had lasted over 100 days. The State: cross-border terrorism history (similar steps in 2016); the internet never restricted in Jammu and Ladakh; social media's one-to-many reach; selective blocking not technically possible; newspaper standards do not carry over to the internet.

fields.label: Held
fields.html: (1) Orders must be produced and published — Article 32 remedies and the right to information require it; no law affecting rights should be passed in secret. (2) The internet: the most used and accessible medium of information; trade and commerce through it are protected under 19(1)(g) subject to 19(6); expression through it is integral to 19(1)(a), restrictable only under 19(2) — but no fundamental right of access to the internet was declared (no party argued for one). (3) A restriction may in a proper case amount to complete prohibition, but the government must explain why lesser measures would not do. (4) Proportionality: whether the least restrictive choice was made (para 53), drawing on Modern Dental College; the Court's own five points — legitimate goal, necessity, alternatives considered, least restrictive measure, judicial review; the restriction's degree, scope, territory and duration must match necessity (para 71). (5) Shutdowns: governed by the 2017 Suspension Rules under the Telegraph Act — only the Union or State Home Secretary (or a Joint Secretary in unavoidable circumstances, confirmed within 24 hours); reasons recorded; Review Committee; section 5(2) requires “public emergency” or “public safety” of a serious nature; orders must be published for challenge; complete suspension is drastic — only if necessary and unavoidable after assessing alternatives (para 99); indefinite suspension impermissible. (6) Section 144: only where danger exists or is apprehended, in the nature of an emergency; cannot suppress legitimate expression; orders must state material facts — mechanical or cryptic orders unlawful; repetitive orders are abuse; the concentric circles repeated (para 120). (7) Press freedom valuable under 19(1)(a), but no evidence publication was actually stopped — no sword of Damocles may “hang over the press indefinitely” (para 151). Order: the Government to review all suspension and section 144 orders, publish them, and withdraw those unnecessary or without time limits.

fields.label: Principle
fields.html: Proportionality as the present meaning of “reasonable”; the internet as protected medium (without overstating access as a right); restriction orders must be published and reasoned. Critics note: principles laid down, no immediate relief given.

qa.q:
Q1. Speech is a natural right (a baby cries on birth), so why did it need constitutional status?

Context: Opening question of the lecture; the student answered "so that people can speak freely" and "because those above us in power try to suppress us".
qa.a: Because rights are written down only when somebody has taken them away. The State and those more powerful than the individual suppressed free expression (Socrates, Galileo, the Inquisition, Propaganda Ministry), so the framers gave the natural freedom a constitutional guarantee that is enforceable against the State under Art 32 and 226.

qa.q: Q2. Who suppresses the freedom of speech, and why? (Give a one-word answer in Ambedkar's style)
qa.a:
The State. Reasons: (1) to prevent its wrongdoing from coming out; (2) to protect the established system of knowledge or religion on which its authority rests; (3) because rulers consider their statement final and a challenge a personal affront; (4) to maintain power.

Note the counter-reason given by a student: the other side has a right not to be provoked into violence; this is why the Constitution lets the State impose reasonable restrictions under Art 19(2) but only on the eight listed grounds.

qa.q: Q3. What happened to Socrates? What was his "fault"?
qa.a: He questioned prevailing knowledge, religion and authority in Athens (the Socratic method). He was convicted of impiety and corrupting the youth and executed by drinking hemlock in 399 BCE. His case shows that questioning was treated as a crime.

qa.q: Q4. What happened to the one who said the Earth revolves around the Sun? Who was it, and who punished him?
qa.a: The heliocentric theory is associated with Copernicus (published 1543), and defended by Galileo. The Church (through the Roman Inquisition, 1633) forced Galileo to recant and placed him under house arrest, because the accepted view (Ptolemaic geocentrism, backed by religious authority) was that the Sun moved around the Earth. (Giordano Bruno was burned in 1600.)

qa.q:
Q5. What was the Inquisition?

Context: A student read out the NotebookLM definition at the professor's request: "an institution that actively sought out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established knowledge".
qa.a: A historical institution of the Roman Catholic Church that actively searched out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established religion and knowledge; punishment for heresy could be imprisonment or death. It also operated the Index of Prohibited Books, an early form of prior censorship.

qa.q: Q6. What is the Official Secrets Act, 1923, and how does it classify information?
qa.a: A colonial law (replacing the 1889 Act) punishing spying and unauthorised communication or even retention of official secret information. Government information is graded Restricted, Confidential, Secret and Top Secret. It is a classic example of a law that restricts speech in the name of State security and is read now with Art 19(2) (security of the State) and the RTI Act, 2005.

qa.q: Q7. Why is Article 14 placed before Article 19 in India when America put speech (First Amendment) first?
qa.a: See section 1.6. Short form: the West's main problem was suppression of ideas, so speech came first; India's main problem was social inequality, so equality came first. The Constitution is designed to solve the problems of its own society.

qa.q: Q8. Why is Article 19 given only to citizens?
qa.a: See section 1.7. Short form: Art 19 freedoms are political rights of members of the nation; non-citizens can seek only the "person" rights (Arts 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22), and foreign propaganda was a concern.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 1.1: Write a short article on the examples used in class (Socrates, Galileo/Copernicus, the Propaganda Ministry) and circulate it (professor: "make a small article... circulate by email/video")
qa.a:
Model article (about 250 words, ready to submit):

Why the Constitution Protects Speech: Lessons from History. Freedom of speech is as old as the human voice, yet it has always been fragile. In 399 BCE Athens tried Socrates for questioning the city's gods and for "corrupting the youth"; he was made to drink hemlock. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition, the Church tribunal charged with enforcing orthodoxy, forced Galileo Galilei to recant his support for Copernicus's heliocentric model and confined him to his house for the rest of his life. The Church also maintained an Index of Prohibited Books to control what people could read. In the twentieth century Nazi Germany set up a Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda (1933) which controlled press, radio and film.

These episodes explain why modern constitutions turn a natural human capacity into an enforceable right. The American First Amendment (1791) placed speech first. In India, colonial laws such as the Official Secrets Act, 1923 and the sedition law showed how the State could suppress dissent; the framers therefore guaranteed freedom of speech and expression in Article 19(1)(a) to citizens, subject only to reasonable restrictions on the eight grounds in Article 19(2). Because India's own central problem was inequality, the Constitution places Article 14 before Article 19. The lesson of history is that a society which punishes questions stops learning; free speech is the marketplace in which better ideas defeat worse ones.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 1.2: Remember this sentence (professor: "ये सेंटेंस याद रखना")
qa.a:
"Wherever Western powers went they suppressed freedom of speech (e.g. the Official Secrets Act, 1923), and therefore freedom of expression became essential: Western constitutions listed speech first because suppression was their problem; India listed equality first because inequality was ours."

Use it as the opening line of any answer on the historical background of Art 19(1)(a).

qa.q: HOMEWORK 1.3: Be ready with the definition of the Inquisition and the Official Secrets Act (professor asked students to look them up and read aloud)
qa.a: See Q5 and Q6 above. Learn them word-for-word. The professor expects the phrases "actively sought out and suppressed ideas contradicting the established knowledge" for the Inquisition and "Restricted, Confidential, Secret, Top Secret" for the Official Secrets Act.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 1.4: Habit task: follow the news and general knowledge (professor repeatedly asked students to read news daily and to check facts themselves rather than rely on his statement)
qa.a: Answer-writing tip: when you cite a historical or current example, make sure you can name the year and the authority (for example "Roman Inquisition, 1633"). Accuracy in examples earns marks; vague examples do not.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 2.1: Fit each of the following cases to the theme "we have a fundamental right to give and to receive information" (the professor asked "what are these cases focusing on?")
qa.a:
CaseGive (impart/disseminate)Receive
Romesh Thappar (1950)Right to circulate the journalReaders' access is the purpose of circulation
Odyssey v. Lokvidayan (1988)Right to telecast the serialViewers' right to see lawful content
LIC v. Manubhai Shah (1992)Right to reply / publish counter-viewReaders get both sides
Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)Right to telecast sport through chosen agencyPublic's right to receive information on air

One line for the exam: "Together these cases establish that Art 19(1)(a) protects not only the speaker but the entire chain: production, publication, circulation, broadcast and reception of ideas."

qa.q: HOMEWORK 2.2: Research why, in the "blue drum" murder case, the wife was (as the professor believed) not given the death penalty while the lover was; the professor said "research and tell me why the wife was not hanged"
qa.a:
What the professor said: the lover was sentenced to death, the wife only to about 20 years, and he asked whether the wife (the alleged informer and mastermind) should have been hanged. Students gave different answers (equal participation; the woman has a child; pregnancy).

Legal framework for the answer (valid for any such question):

  • Death is the exception: only in the "rarest of rare" cases (Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, 1980), after weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances for each accused separately (Machhi Singh, 1983). Parity between co-accused is not automatic: courts examine role, age, criminal record, probability of reform, family circumstances.
  • Possible mitigating factors for a woman accused: a young child dependent on her; pregnancy (a death sentence on a pregnant woman is postponed, and customarily commuted: s. 416 CrPC, now the corresponding BNSS provision); no previous criminal record; the possibility of reform.
  • Death sentences by trial courts must be confirmed by the High Court (CrPC s. 366 / BNSS s. 407); the accused can appeal to the Supreme Court and seek mercy under Arts 72 and 161.

Factual update (verify before using in an exam answer): news reports found while preparing these notes state that on 14 October 2026 the Meerut trial court sentenced both the wife and her lover to death. If that is right, the premise in class (wife got 20 years) is outdated or wrong. In an exam, use the case only as an illustration that even Art 21 yields to procedure established by law.

qa.q: Q1. What does Article 19 say? For whom is it? Which Articles are only for citizens?
qa.a: Art 19(1) gives "all citizens" the right to (a) freedom of speech and expression, (b) assemble peaceably and without arms, (c) form associations or unions, (d) move freely, (e) reside and settle anywhere in India, and (g) practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business ((f) was repealed in 1978). It is available only to citizens. Arts 15, 16 and 19 (and 29, 30) are citizen-only; Art 14 and Art 21 apply to every person.

qa.q: Q2. Why did the Supreme Court strike down the Madras order in Romesh Thappar even though the Government allowed the paper to be printed?
qa.a: Because freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation; a paper which can be printed but not circulated has no practical freedom. And the ground of "law and order" (public order) was not in Art 19(2) at that time, so the Court could not uphold the ban. (Parliament then amended Art 19(2) in 1951 to add public order.)

qa.q: Q3. Distinguish law and order, public order and security of the State.
qa.a: See 2.7: three concentric circles. Law and order (individual quarrels) is widest and not a ground; public order (community-level disturbance of peace and tranquillity) is the middle circle, added in 1951; security of the State (rebellion, war, insurrection) is the innermost. A speech that disturbs only law and order cannot be restricted; one that disturbs public order can; one that threatens the State's security can be curbed more severely. (Ram Manohar Lohia, 1966.)

qa.q: Q4. A person abuses you and it is recorded on tape. Is it libel or slander?
qa.a: Libel, because the recording is a permanent form (words fixed in a durable medium that can be reproduced as evidence), even though the original utterance was spoken. Slander covers evanescent spoken words only. (Professor accepted "libel" and said the question should be debated in class.)

qa.q: Q5. What is the difference between a restriction and a reasonable restriction? Which case defines it?
qa.a: A restriction is any limit on the right; to be valid it must be reasonable. State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) defines the standard: restriction by law; on an Art 19(2) ground; real and proximate connection with the protected interest; not arbitrary or excessive; fair procedure and judicial review; judged objectively having regard to the nature of the right, the evil sought to be remedied, its extent and urgency, and the proportion between the two.

qa.q: Q6. Name the eight grounds of Art 19(2), and which amendments added which?
qa.a: Sovereignty and integrity of India (16th Amend., 1963 added "sovereignty and"); security of the State (original); friendly relations with foreign States (1st Amend., 1951); public order (1951); decency or morality (original); contempt of court (original); defamation (original); incitement to an offence (1951). The First Amendment also inserted "reasonable" and "in the interests of".

qa.q: Q7. Which case says pre-censorship of print media is not acceptable, and which case allows it for films?
qa.a: Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950) (print: not acceptable); K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970) (film: allowed because of its greater impact and the need for classification).

qa.q: Q8. Is freedom of speech absolute?
qa.a: No. Even Art 21 (right to life) can be taken away by procedure established by law (death penalty). Art 19(2) lists eight grounds on which reasonable restrictions can be imposed by law. The courts examine reasonableness.

qa.q: Q9. Which cases show that there is a fundamental right to give and receive information?
qa.a: Romesh Thappar (circulation), Odyssey v. Lokvidayan (telecast), LIC v. Manubhai Shah (reply), Cricket Association of Bengal (airwaves, right to receive). See Homework 2.1.

qa.q: Q10. What was the Hicklin test, and was it ever applied in India?
qa.a: English test of 1868: material is obscene if it tends to deprave and corrupt those open to such influences, judged by an isolated passage. The professor suggested it is not in India; in fact it was followed in India until the 1980s-1990s (e.g. Ranjit Udeshi, 1964) and was expressly replaced by the community standards test in Aveek Sarkar (2014).

qa.q: Q11. What is "slander" (spelt "slender" by a student)? Define the two kinds of defamation.
qa.a: Slander (not "slender" or "cylinder") = defamation by transient words; libel = defamation in permanent form; both are forms of defamation, an Art 19(2) ground.

qa.q: Q12. Why do Arts 15, 16 and 19 apply only to citizens when Art 14 applies to everyone?
qa.a: Because these are rights of membership of the political community (discrimination between citizens in public life/employment, political freedoms); the framers extended only the basic equality and life/liberty protections (Arts 14, 20, 21, 22) to all persons within India.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 2.3: Presentation schedule: the professor asked students to prepare a schedule for presentations ("from July") and bring presentations on Khushboo (next day) and Aveek Sarkar
qa.a:
Model 2-minute presentation skeleton (works for any case): 1. Facts in 3 lines; 2. Issue; 3. Decision; 4. Ratio; 5. Why it matters today; 6. One criticism. The case cards in this file follow this pattern.

Khushboo (ready to present): In 2005 actress Khushboo told a magazine that pre-marital sex was not wrong if precautions were taken; 20+ criminal complaints were filed. The Supreme Court (2010) quashed them: expressing an unpopular view is protected by Art 19(1)(a), and there is no offence of discussing pre-marital sex; there was no obscenity, since nothing appealed to prurient interest, and no incitement. Aveek Sarkar (ready to present): see section 2.9: community standards test; nude photo of Becker and Feltus was an anti-racism statement, hence not obscene.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 2.4: Read the original judgments of Romesh Thappar and the debate on the First Constitutional Amendment (and Nehru's speeches); the professor said "I will not explain it, you must read it"
qa.a:
Study map for the First Amendment debate (10 points to take away):

  • Passed 18 June 1951 by the Provisional Parliament (Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951).
  • Occasion: Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan, Master Tara Singh/Punjab HC decisions striking down curbs on speech; the Government's concern about communal propaganda and relations with Pakistan.
  • Nehru argued that the Constitution should not become a hindrance to social progress; he proposed new grounds. Critics (Syama Prasad Mookerjee, H.N. Kunzru, Kamath) objected that it was vague and curtailed civil liberties.
  • Outcome: Art 19(2) rewritten (see 2.6); Arts 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule were also added by the same Amendment (agrarian reforms); Art 15(4) was added to overcome State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) (reservation in educational institutions).

qa.a: See the case card in 2.1.

qa.a: See the case card in 2.10 and the table that compares print with cinema.

qa.q: Q1. A person wanted to speak at Jantar Mantar for/against the CEC, Delhi Police refused, and he sues for violation of freedom of speech. As the court, what will you check first?
qa.a:
Whether he is a citizen of India. Art 19(1) is confined to citizens (hence Arts 15, 16, 19 are citizen-only; Art 14 and 21 are for all persons). If he is a foreigner the Art 19(1)(a) claim fails; he can only invoke Arts 14, 21.

If he is a citizen, test the restriction: (i) by law; (ii) on an Art 19(2) ground; (iii) reasonable/proportionate.

qa.q: Q2. How many grounds are there in Art 19(2)? Recite them.
qa.a: Eight: sovereignty and integrity of India; security of the State; friendly relations with foreign States; public order; decency or morality; contempt of court; defamation; incitement to an offence. (See Lecture 2 for the amendments.)

qa.q: Q3. Can the State restrict speech for "better administration"?
qa.a: No. Restrictions are permitted only on the eight grounds in Art 19(2). "Better administration", "national interest", "economic development" are not grounds.

qa.q: Q4. What does "law" mean in Art 19(2)? Is it the same as in Art 13(3)?
qa.a: It means law duly enacted by Parliament or a State Legislature (and valid subordinate legislation derived from such an Act). It is not to be understood as widely as the Art 13(3)(a) definition (ordinances, orders, bye-laws, custom etc.). Executive instructions without a statutory basis are not "law".

qa.q: Q5. What is "reasonable" today? State the test.
qa.a: Reasonable has become proportionate. Under Anuradha Bhasin the four-fold test: legitimate aim; rational nexus; necessity; balancing (structural proportionality), with judicial review of the order.

qa.q: Q6. What does "legitimate" mean in the proportionality test? Is it the same as a legitimate child?
qa.a: No. It means legal and fair, in the public interest and pursuing recognised aims such as national security, public safety, public order, public health, public morals and protection of the rights and reputation of others (ICCPR Art 19(3), European standards). The family-law "legitimacy" of children (s. 16 HMA) is irrelevant.

qa.q: Q7. What is a "rational nexus"? Apply it to an internet shutdown.
qa.a: The restriction must have a direct connection with the legitimate aim. An internet shutdown can be rationally linked to stopping the spread of incitement or misinformation that may disturb public order or security, but only if the content spreads through that medium, and the restriction is temporary and targeted; a blanket, indefinite shutdown fails necessity and balance (Anuradha Bhasin).

qa.q: Q8. Who must justify a restriction, and can the court say a lesser action would have sufficed?
qa.a: The authority that took the decision must justify it, with recorded reasons ("this is the minimum necessary action in the present situation"). The court reviews proportionality but does not substitute its own policy view for that of the decision-maker, unless the restriction is clearly excessive or less restrictive means were obviously available.

qa.q: Q9. Which case says that evidence obtained by illegal means is inadmissible?
qa.a: In the United States, Weeks v. United States (1914) and Mapp v. Ohio (1961) (exclusionary rule). In India the rule is different: relevant evidence is admissible even if illegally obtained (Pooran Mal, 1974).

qa.q: Q10. Which case dealt with the appointment of the CVC which the Supreme Court quashed? What was the reasoning?
qa.a: Centre for PIL v. Union of India (2011) (P.J. Thomas). The committee ignored relevant material about the candidate's pending corruption case and the Leader of Opposition's dissent; the Court quashed the appointment, emphasising institutional integrity.

qa.q: Q11. Does the mere fact that a newspaper or a leader alleges wrongdoing prove it?
qa.a: No. A press report or allegation is not proof; it triggers a demand for inquiry by a competent authority (court, statutory body, RTI, Parliament), not a verdict by the accuser. This is why speech about public officials is protected but defamation and incitement remain grounds for restriction.
