qa.a: Weeks v. United States (1914); Mapp v. Ohio (1961). Indian position: Pooran Mal (1974). See 3.7.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 3.5: Find which statutory section says "all children are legitimate" (professor accepted "s. 16")
qa.a: Section 16, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages). Not relevant to Art 19.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 3.6: Read the cases yourself before approaching the professor ("read the case first, the answer is there")
qa.a: Reading list from COLA 5 and 6: Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan, V.G. Row, K.A. Abbas, Aveek Sarkar, Khushboo, Anuradha Bhasin, P.J. Thomas. Case cards for all are in this file.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 3.7: Find the year in which two additional Election Commissioners were appointed (the professor asked: "which year?" answer given: 1989)
qa.a: See 3.6 correction: 1989 appointment (withdrawn 1990) versus the October 1993 appointment of two additional Election Commissioners (related to T.N. Seshan); Seshan v. UoI (1995) upheld the multi-member Commission.

qa.q: Q1. What was the new mechanism the Government adopted to suppress press freedom after the courts closed the direct route?
qa.a: After Romesh Thappar, Brij Bhushan, Sakal Papers and Bennett Coleman blocked direct restraints, the State used indirect pressures: newsprint, advertisements, taxation, power and premises, and (in the professor's analysis) the ownership of media houses. The law responds by testing direct and inevitable effect, not form.

qa.q: Q2. What were the earlier "grounds" such as libel and slander, and what were added in 1951 and 1963?
qa.a: Original Art 19(2): libel, slander, defamation, contempt of court, decency or morality, security of the State (undermining or tending to overthrow). 1951: public order, friendly relations with foreign States, incitement to an offence; "reasonable"; 1963: sovereignty and integrity.

qa.q: Q3. Is commercial advertisement protected speech? Which cases?
qa.a: Hamdard Dawakhana (1960): not protected when it merely promotes trade (magic remedies); Tata Press v. MTNL (1995): protected (public right to receive commercial information) provided it is not misleading; misleading ads are punishable (Consumer Protection Act, 2019).

qa.q: Q4. Why did Parliament pass the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954, and was it valid?
qa.a: To stop quackery and false claims of cure (sexual disorders, venereal disease, cancer etc.) that endanger public health. It was upheld in Hamdard Dawakhana (the advertisement of such remedies is not a protected exercise of Art 19(1)(a); it also falls within reasonable restrictions).

qa.q: Q5. Name the Hicklin case and explain the test.
qa.a: Regina v. Hicklin (1868): material is obscene if it tends to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences, judged by isolated passages. Rejected in India in Aveek Sarkar (2014); replaced by the community standards (Miller) test.

qa.q: Q6. State the three-part test that replaced Hicklin.
qa.a: (1) Would the average person applying contemporary community standards find that the work as a whole appeals to prurient interest? (2) Does the work depict sexual conduct in a patently offensive way (as defined by law)? (3) Does the work, taken as a whole, lack serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value? (Miller v. California, 1973; adopted in Aveek Sarkar).

qa.q: Q7. Why can nude depictions in medical textbooks or breastfeeding diagrams not be obscene?
qa.a: Because they have scientific/medical value and fail the third limb (the work as a whole is not lacking in serious scientific value); s. 292(2) IPC exempts material for science, art and learning; the context (instruction) negates prurient appeal.

qa.q: Q8. What additional factor did Tuljapurkar add, and was the poem held obscene?
qa.a: When a historically respected figure (Gandhi) is used as a vehicle for obscene allusions, the community standards test is applied with greater vigour and poetic licence is no defence; the poem was held obscene, but the editor/publisher was discharged because of the passage of time (20 years) and his unconditional apology.

qa.q: Q9. Name the case based on the film "Bandit Queen".
qa.a: Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996): the film was held not obscene, because the scenes had to be judged in the context of the film's message (social oppression, brutality).

qa.q: Q10. Give one example of how community standards differ between places and times.
qa.a: The professor's examples: segregated seating of boys and girls earlier vs students walking arm-in-arm now; purdah among women; a public kiss at an event in Jaipur (Gere-Shetty) judged by local standards. Standards are relative to society and time.

qa.q: Q11. Why did Parliament and the courts treat misleading advertisements differently from other speech?
qa.a: Because they cause economic harm and deceive consumers, they offer no contribution to the marketplace of ideas, and are covered by consumer protection law and Art 19(2) grounds; truthfulness is the condition for protection.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 4.1: Read the original Regina v. Hicklin ("read this case"; the professor said the meaning of the test is in the case itself)
qa.a: Key sentence (Cockburn C.J., 1868): "the test of obscenity is this, whether the tendency of the matter charged as obscenity is to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to such immoral influences, and into whose hands a publication of this sort may fall." Learn it as the "Hicklin test".

qa.q: HOMEWORK 4.2: Read State of West Bengal v. Aveek Sarkar, and Devidas Ramchandra Tuljapurkar v. State of Maharashtra (compulsory reading; the professor "declared" a fact-based question on Tuljapurkar)

qa.q: HOMEWORK 4.5: Recall American cases on obscenity and the Miller test (professor: "and American cases")
qa.a: See the timeline table in 4.5: Hicklin (England), Miller v. California (US, 1973). Also read Roth v. United States (1957) (community standards, prurient interest) and Memoirs v. Massachusetts (1966).

qa.q: HOMEWORK 4.6: Verify before forwarding any news or advertisement (professor's general instruction on misinformation)
qa.a: Practical rule: check source, date and a second reliable source; do not share unverified claims (risk of defamation, IT Act and BNS liability).

qa.q: HOMEWORK 4.7: Google: which newspaper was closed down and its assets disputed (the professor asked "which newspaper?"; answer: National Herald, published by Associated Journals Ltd., founded by Jawaharlal Nehru in 1938)

qa.q: Q1. How is hate speech defined? Where?
qa.a: Not in the Constitution of India. It has been defined by the UN (attack or pejorative/discriminatory language against a person or a group on the basis of religion, ethnicity, nationality, race, colour, descent, gender or other identity factor) and discussed by the Law Commission (267th Report: incitement to hatred against a group). Professor's one-liner: "hate created towards a particular group, which can be classified on any basis".

qa.q: Q2. Why is hate speech an international problem?
qa.a: Because internet and social media make content available across borders (a post on Instagram in America is seen in India); no State can control foreign platforms alone; hence the UN's concern and the need for international co-operation (ICCPR Art 20(2)).

qa.q: Q3. Why is hate speech more serious than an ordinary crime?
qa.a: An ordinary crime (murder, rape) harms one victim or household; hate speech brands an entire group (all people from a place, religion or caste), exposing every member to discrimination and violence; it undermines fraternity, dignity and equal citizenship.

qa.q: Q4. Is the existing law sufficient to control hate speech, or do we need new law? Which Law Commission report should be read?
qa.a: See 5.5. The report is the 267th Report, "Hate Speech" (2017) (Chairman: Justice B.S. Chauhan), which recommended ss. 153C and 505A IPC.

qa.q: Q5. Name the leading Supreme Court case on hate speech brought as a PIL by a "Pravasi" organisation.
qa.a: Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan v. Union of India (2014) 11 SCC 477: the Court directed the Law Commission to examine whether hate speech should be defined; existing laws to be enforced.

qa.q: Q6. How does Shreya Singhal classify speech? Which categories are protected?
qa.a: Discussion, advocacy, incitement. Discussion and advocacy (even of unpopular causes) are protected under Art 19(1)(a); incitement (with a proximate, direct link to harm) alone can be punished under Art 19(2).

qa.q: Q7. Is saying that "my religion is so good that the whole world should adopt it" an offence?
qa.a: No; it is advocacy/propagation (Art 25, Art 19(1)(a)); an offence arises only if there is force, fraud or allurement leading to conversion (anti-conversion statutes upheld in Rev. Stanislaus, 1977) or incitement to violence or hatred.

qa.q: Q8. Is the right to silence part of freedom of speech? Which case, and what were the facts?
qa.a: Yes. Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986): three Jehovah's Witness children stood respectfully but did not sing "Jana Gana Mana" and were expelled; the Court held that freedom of speech includes freedom of silence, and that no law compels singing; expulsion violated Arts 19(1)(a) and 25.

qa.q: Q9. What are "Miranda rights"? State the four warnings. What is the Indian counterpart?
qa.a: US warnings before custodial interrogation: (1) right to remain silent; (2) anything said can be used against you; (3) right to a lawyer present; (4) a lawyer will be appointed if you cannot afford one (Miranda v. Arizona, 1966). In India: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani (1978) under Art 20(3)/Art 21, Art 22(1), D.K. Basu (1997).

qa.q: Q10. Why does the law give an accused the right to silence?
qa.a: Presumption of innocence: the prosecution must prove guilt; the accused cannot be forced to supply the evidence against himself; otherwise the burden of proof would be reversed. It also prevents custodial torture to extract confessions.

qa.q: Q11. Can the police hold a person at the station until she answers? Can they beat a suspect?
qa.a: No. Compelling answers by detention or pressure violates Art 20(3) and Art 21 (Nandini Satpathy). Physical violence is illegal; only a court can punish (D.K. Basu). Police may only ask questions; a person is not bound to answer incriminating ones.

qa.q: Q12. What is the difference between admonition and reprimand? (the Air Force illustration)
qa.a: Admonition is a mild warning; reprimand is a severe, formal and often recorded censure. Both are disciplinary measures imposed by the competent authority, not physical punishment; the professor used it to show that the police and even a judge may only record such censure and cannot beat or abuse.

qa.q: Q13. What are the three types of "silence" in constitutional law?
qa.a: (i) Art 19(1)(a): freedom not to speak (Bijoe Emmanuel); (ii) Art 20(3): privilege against self-incrimination (Nandini Satpathy); (iii) Custodial rights (Art 22(1), D.K. Basu; Miranda in the US).

The professor said: "I am not going to define it because I myself may not remember it; you will read."

qa.q: Q1. Art 19(1) lists (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and then (g). Where is (f)? Whose mistake is it?
qa.a: No one's mistake. Art 19(1)(f) (right to acquire, hold and dispose of property) was repealed by the Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978; the remaining clauses were not re-lettered. The right to property was moved out of Part III into Art 300A.

qa.q: Q2. Dr Ambedkar put the right to property in two places - Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31. Why? Could one not suffice?
qa.a: They served different purposes: Art 19(1)(f) was a citizen's freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property, subject to reasonable restrictions (Art 19(5)); Art 31 governed the State's power of compulsory acquisition/deprivation, for any person - law, public purpose, compensation. In the professor's words, "19 gave us the right to keep property; 31 acknowledged the State's right to take it" - a built-in contradiction that produced decades of litigation and amendments, ending with deletion of both in 1978 and the insertion of Art 300A.

qa.q: Q3. What difference did it make when Arts 19(1)(f) and 31 were removed and Art 300A inserted? Do people now have no right to property?
qa.a: People do have the right - as a constitutional right under Art 300A and a human right, not as a Fundamental Right. Differences: (i) no direct Art 32 petition; remedy is the High Court under Art 226; (ii) property laws are no longer tested against Art 13 on the ground of property, so the State can acquire by ordinary law and does not need a constitutional amendment; (iii) the test is now authority of law + public purpose + fair compensation/procedure (K.T. Plantation; Vidya Devi; Bimal Kumar Shah).

qa.q: Q4. Can the State (or a Professor acting for the State) take a student's mobile phone?
qa.a: Only by authority of law. The university is "State" under Art 12 (statutory, State-funded and controlled - Ajay Hasia), so Part III and Art 300A bind it. Taking the phone without any law violates Art 300A; the State cannot rely on executive discretion (Vidya Devi).

qa.q: Q5. State the three conditions for compulsory acquisition of property.
qa.a: (1) Authority of law (a legislature-enacted statute - not the wide Art 13 "law" of orders and customs); (2) public purpose (never a purely private one); (3) compensation (market value → "amount" → fair compensation under LARR 2013).

qa.q: Q6. What is "eminent domain"?
qa.a: The sovereign power of the State to take private property for public use; Latin dominium eminens; inherent in sovereignty and exercised subject to law, public purpose and compensation.

qa.q: Q7. What does "law" mean in "authority of law"?
qa.a: A valid law enacted by the competent legislature (Parliament or State Legislature) - not a mere executive order or administrative decision. The professor: "law means not the Art 13 'law'; it is law enacted by the legislature."

qa.q: Q8. Can property be acquired for a private farmhouse of a politician?
qa.a: No. Only for a public purpose - education, airports, railways, defence, roads. Acquisition for a private purpose violates Art 300A.

qa.q: Q9. Which constitutional amendment replaced "compensation" with "amount"? What did "compensation" mean earlier?
qa.a: The 25th Amendment (1971) (in force 1972) - Parliament under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Earlier, "compensation" meant the just equivalent / market value of the property (State of W.B. v. Bela Banerjee, 1954; R.C. Cooper, 1970). The change was upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

qa.q: Q10. Which amendment removed the right to property from the Fundamental Rights?
qa.a: The 44th Amendment (1978) - it repealed Art 19(1)(f) and Art 31 and inserted Art 300A (and Art 30(1A)).

qa.q: Q11. Why were so many constitutional amendments needed on property? Who can amend the Constitution?
qa.a: Because Courts struck down acquisition laws that offended Arts 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 (via Art 13), the Government had to amend the Constitution (1st, 4th, 17th, 25th, 42nd); only Parliament can amend (Art 368), subject to the basic structure doctrine.

qa.q: Q12. What is the modern law on compensation for acquisition of land?
qa.a: LARR Act 2013: replaced the 1894 Act; market value with multiplier plus solatium (up to 4x in rural areas, 2x in urban areas), consent, SIA, R&R. Constitutional footing: Art 300A and Entry 42, List III.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 6.1: Google "eminent domain" and be ready to explain it
qa.a: See 6.4. Latin dominium eminens; sovereign power to take private property for a public purpose on payment of compensation.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 6.2: Find out by which constitutional amendment "compensation" was replaced by "amount"
qa.a: 25th Amendment, 1971 (in force 20 April 1972).

qa.q: HOMEWORK 6.3: Read State of W.B. v. Bela Banerjee ("you will enjoy it")
qa.a: See the case card in 6.5: compensation = just equivalent / market value.

qa.q: Q1. Name the grounds on which the right to freedom of speech and expression can be restricted.
qa.a: Under Art 19(2): (1) sovereignty and integrity of India; (2) security of the State; (3) friendly relations with foreign States; (4) public order; (5) decency or morality; (6) contempt of court; (7) defamation; (8) incitement to an offence. There is no ground of "peace" or "tranquillity". (First Amendment 1951 added public order, friendly relations, incitement; 16th Amendment 1963 added sovereignty and integrity.)

qa.q: Q2. How many grounds restrict assembly (19(1)(b)) and association (19(1)(c))? Which is extra in association?
qa.a: Two for assembly (sovereignty and integrity of India; public order). Three for association - the same two plus morality (Art 19(4)).

qa.q: Q3. On what grounds can the right to move freely and to reside be restricted?
qa.a: Under Art 19(5): in the interests of the general public, or for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe (e.g. Inner Line Permit; restrictions on entry/land transfer in tribal areas).

qa.q: Q4. Why are outsiders required to take permits in tribal areas?
qa.a: To protect the land, culture, language and vulnerable communities of the tribes from exploitation and disturbance (and sometimes to protect outsiders from isolated tribes). The restriction is justified by Art 19(5). Legal tools: ILP (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation 1873), Fifth and Sixth Schedule land protections (Samatha, 1997).

qa.q: Q5. Can I practise law, medicine or architecture without the prescribed qualification? Which clause of Art 19 allows the restriction?
qa.a: No. Art 19(6)(i) allows the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications (Advocates Act 1961 ss. 29, 33 for advocates; NMC Act 2019 for doctors; Architects Act for architects). A person may argue their own case, but only enrolled advocates may represent others.

qa.q: Q6. Why does the Constitution allow State monopoly in trade and business?
qa.a: Art 19(6)(ii): the State or State-owned corporation may carry on a trade or business to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens. A welfare State needs to provide both profitable and unprofitable but essential services - monopolies like railways generate surplus to support unprofitable services. Upheld in Akadasi Padhan (1963).

qa.q: Q7. Is the pre-censorship of press valid? Of films? Why the difference?
qa.a: Press: pre-censorship invalid (Brij Bhushan, 1950); films: pre-censorship permissible (K.A. Abbas, 1970) because cinema has a more powerful, immediate impact and a different nature of exhibition; censorship must still be reasonable and limited to Art 19(2) grounds.

qa.q: Q8. Can the Government control newspapers indirectly (price, number of pages, taxes)?
qa.a: No. Control of circulation or content by price/page schedules or newsprint control is a restriction on press freedom (Express Newspapers, Sakal, Bennett Coleman); taxation affecting newspapers must be tested against press freedom (Indian Express, 1985).

qa.q: Q9. Who owns airwaves/spectrum? Can the Government give it to friends on first-come-first-served basis?
qa.a: Airwaves/spectrum are public property (Cricket Association of Bengal; Art 39(b)). The Government is a trustee and must allocate fairly and transparently; first-come-first-served as practised in 2008 was struck down in the 2G case (2012); auction is not the only method (Presidential Reference 2012).

qa.q: Q10. Do voters have a right to know the background of candidates?
qa.a: Yes. Union of India v. ADR (2002) and PUCL (2003): the right to know is part of Art 19(1)(a); candidates must disclose criminal antecedents, assets and qualifications; s. 33B RPA was struck down. (Extended in the Electoral Bonds judgment, 2024.)

qa.q: Q11. Do government employees (or students) have a fundamental right to strike?
qa.a: No. T.K. Rangarajan v. Govt of T.N. (2003) - no fundamental, statutory or moral right to strike; Art 19(1)(c) protects the right to form unions, not to strike.

qa.q: Q12. Can people protest anywhere and for as long as they like?
qa.a: No. Protest is protected by Art 19(1)(a),(b) but may be reasonably regulated - time, place, manner, and numbers (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, 2018); public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely (Amit Sahni, 2020); police action must be proportionate (Ramlila Maidan, 2012).

qa.q: Q13. Can a Minister's statement bind the Government? Are fundamental rights enforceable against private parties?
qa.a: Kaushal Kishor (2023): a Minister's personal statement is not vicariously attributable to the Government under Art 75(3); Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons in appropriate cases; no additional restrictions beyond Art 19(2) on free speech.

qa.q: Q14. Can the State stop publication of an autobiography written in jail?
qa.a: No prior restraint. R. Rajagopal (1994): the State cannot restrain publication in advance; remedies lie after publication; matters of public record and official conduct are open to publication.

qa.q: Q1. What are the main points to write if asked about Art 19(1)(g)?
qa.a: See the seven-point checklist in 8.1. Opening line: "Art 19(1)(g) guarantees citizens the right to practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business; it is subject to reasonable restrictions by law under Art 19(6) in the interests of the general public, including qualifications and State monopoly."

qa.q: Q2. Can a person claim Art 19(1)(g) to sell ganja or run an illegal business?
qa.a: No. Only lawful professions are protected; illegal, immoral or inherently dangerous activities (gambling, narcotics, trafficking, liquor trade as a right) are not (Chamarbaugwala, 1957; Khoday Distilleries, 1995).

qa.q: Q3. Is running a private school or college an occupation or a business? What does the classification achieve?
qa.a: TMA Pai (2002): an occupation (not trade/business in the commercial sense) - therefore (i) restrictions must be reasonable, (ii) by law, (iii) in the public interest; no capitation fee; reasonable surplus allowed; admissions transparent and merit-based.

qa.q: Q4. Name the case that was decided to clarify the ratio of TMA Pai.
qa.a: Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka (2003) 6 SCC 697 (5 judges) - the year 2003, not 2018 (a student's slip in class).

qa.q: Q5. Which case recognises the right to silence under Art 19(1)(a)? Who wrote the judgment?
qa.a: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986) - the National Anthem case; judgment by O. Chinnappa Reddy J. (not B.P. Jeevan Reddy).

qa.q: Q6. Explain the rights of pavement dwellers and hawkers (Olga Tellis; Sodan Singh).
qa.a: Olga Tellis (1985): right to livelihood is part of Art 21; eviction only after fair procedure; no waiver of Fundamental Rights. Sodan Singh (1989): hawking is protected by Art 19(1)(g), but there is no right to trade at a place of one's choice on public property; the State must frame schemes and designate hawking zones; statute: Street Vendors Act 2014.

qa.q: Q7. Is there a right to close down a business?
qa.a: Yes - Art 19(1)(g) includes the right to close (Excel Wear, 1978); reasonable regulation (notice, compensation to workmen) is allowed.

qa.q: Q8. Is prostitution illegal in India? Which acts are prohibited?
qa.a: Prostitution per se is not an offence; the ITPA 1956 prohibits keeping a brothel (s. 3), living on its earnings (s. 4), procuring/inducing (s. 5), prostitution near public places (s. 7) and soliciting in a public place (s. 8). Private, voluntary activity is outside the Act; police misuse is a concern; sex workers have a right to dignity under Art 21.

qa.q: Q9. Was the ban on dance bars valid? Why?
qa.a: No - State of Maharashtra v. IHRA (2013): violated Art 19(1)(g) and Art 14; the ban deprived women of livelihood and the State had not shown that a total ban was necessary; regulate rather than ban.

qa.q: Q10. Explain the law on cattle slaughter and meat bans (Quareshi, Mirzapur, Hinsa Virodhak, Om Prakash).
qa.a: Quareshi (1958): cow/calf slaughter ban valid; ban on useless bulls/bullocks unreasonable. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005): overruled; complete ban on cow progeny valid (Art 48, Art 51A(g), harmonisation after Minerva Mills). Hinsa Virodhak (2008): 9-day closure during Paryushan reasonable. Om Prakash (2004): meat ban in Haridwar/Rishikesh upheld because of traditional religious character.

qa.q: Q11. State the difference between Om Prakash and Ramasamy Udayar.
qa.a: See the table in 8.9: trade ban upheld where the traditional religious character is preserved by law; a religious procession cannot be banned because another community is the local majority (the heckler's veto is not allowed; roads are secular).

qa.q: Q12. Can a person who converts from Hinduism to another religion claim backward-class reservation?
qa.a: Per the Supreme Court (15 October 2026, bench of P.K. Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar JJ.), conversion to a non-Hindu religion does not automatically entitle a person to BC benefits; SC status is lost on conversion to a religion other than Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism; reconversion requires fact-specific verification. See 8.10.

qa.q: Q13. Does the Supreme Court hold that Directive Principles override Fundamental Rights (Art 48 v. Art 19(1)(g))?
qa.a: No. Since Minerva Mills (1980) the position is that FR and DPSP are complementary and must be harmonised; neither overrides the other. (Professor's warning from earlier lectures: writing that "Fundamental Rights override Directive Principles" earns zero marks.) Mirzapur Moti Kureshi shows harmonisation in action.

qa.q: Q1. What was the opinion of the Supreme Court on Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in the beginning of the Republic?
qa.a: In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Court held that Directive Principles are subsidiary to Fundamental Rights and cannot override them. That position has since changed: Minerva Mills (1980) - they are complementary and must be harmonised. (Do not write "in certain cases FR are to be given priority"; it fetches zero.)

qa.q: Q2. Why did the conflict between FR and DPSP arise? Which two Articles created the confusion?
qa.a: Art 32 (enforcement of FR by the Supreme Court) and Art 37 (DPSPs not enforceable by any court). One is justiciable and the other non-justiciable, so courts initially preferred the justiciable FR.

qa.q: Q3. What did Parliament do after Champakam? What did the 25th Amendment add?
qa.a: After Champakam Parliament enacted the First Amendment (1951) adding Art 15(4). The 25th Amendment (1971) added Art 31C: laws giving effect to Art 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged for violating Arts 14, 19, 31, and a declaration of such object cannot be questioned in court.

qa.q: Q4. In which case was Art 31C challenged? What happened?
qa.a: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): the first part of Art 31C (protection for laws furthering Art 39(b),(c)) was upheld; the second part barring judicial review was struck down - judicial review is part of the basic structure.

qa.q: Q5. What did the 42nd Amendment do and what happened to it?
qa.a: It extended Art 31C to all Directive Principles (so a law implementing any DPSP could override Arts 14, 19 and 31) and added Art 368(4),(5). In Minerva Mills (1980) these provisions were struck down; FR and DPSP are complementary and supplementary, to be harmonised.

qa.q: Q6. Who can claim Art 21? Against whom? Does it apply to foreigners and corporations?
qa.a: "No person": all human beings, including foreigners (the procedure established by law must be followed even for a convicted terrorist); not corporations (classroom statement). Traditionally against the State; now also against private persons (horizontal application - Bodhisattwa Gautam 1996, Kaushal Kishor 2023).

qa.q: Q7. What is horizontal application of Fundamental Rights? Name the recent case.
qa.a: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights (here Arts 19 and 21) against non-State actors. Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023) - majority (Ramasubramanian J.) held Arts 19 and 21 can be enforced against private persons; Nagarathna J. concurring in part (see Lecture 7).

qa.q: Q8. What remedy is available if a Fundamental Right is violated and the loss cannot be recouped (e.g. classes lost because of wrongful rustication)?
qa.a: Monetary compensation under Art 32/226: Rudul Sah (1983) – compensation against the State; M.C. Mehta (1987) – absolute liability; Bodhisattwa Gautam (1996) – compensation payable even by a private individual.

qa.q: Q9. How did the Supreme Court interpret "life" in 1950 and in 1962?
qa.a: Gopalan (1950): narrow - bare existence/physical liberty. Kharak Singh (1962): "life" means more than animal existence; night-time domiciliary visits violate personal liberty (Art 21); privacy was recognised in Subba Rao J.'s minority opinion; Gopalan was partially overruled.

qa.q: Q10. What is "personal liberty" after Maneka Gandhi?
qa.a: It includes all liberties not covered by Art 19 and is of the widest amplitude (right to travel abroad, privacy, dignity, livelihood...).

qa.q: Q11. Explain "procedure established by law" and "due process of law". How did Maneka Gandhi change the position?
qa.a: See the table in 9.6. In Gopalan any procedure enacted by the legislature sufficed; in Maneka Gandhi the procedure must be just, fair and reasonable (non-arbitrary) - the Court reads Arts 14, 19 and 21 together (golden triangle), importing due process in substance.

qa.q: Q12. Why did the Constituent Assembly avoid "due process of law"? What was the Lochner problem?
qa.a: Because of Justice Frankfurter's advice to B.N. Rau and the American experience: the judiciary used due process to strike down welfare laws (maximum hours, child labour limits) as an infringement of "freedom of contract" - Lochner v. New York (1905); the Court was supreme over the legislature until the 1937 crisis (court-packing plan).

qa.q: Q13. Name the hotel case which was compulsory reading.
qa.a: State of Maharashtra v. Indian Hotel and Restaurants Association (2013) - the dance bar case (Lecture 8). (The transcript calls it "the hotel case"; this is the case assigned as compulsory reading in the previous lecture.)

Q1. What is the difference between "procedure established by law" and "due process of law"?
qa.a: PEL: the court only checks that the procedure prescribed in the law was followed by the authority implementing it; it does not test the fairness of the law or the procedure. DPL: the court checks both the law (substantive due process) and the procedure (procedural due process) for reasonableness, fairness and justness. Under PEL the proctor's order debarring a student is valid if the university rule was followed; under DPL the court also asks whether the rule is fair and the student was heard. Example: Gopalan (PEL - detention valid) v. Maneka Gandhi (hearing read in; fair procedure demanded).

qa.q: Q2. What do you mean by "procedure established by law"? (Why will you get zero if you write that the law was passed following the proper procedure?)
qa.a: It means the procedure laid down in the law for depriving a person of life or liberty (arrest, trial, detention), not Parliament's law-making procedure. Courts cannot inquire into the internal procedure of Parliament - Art 122 (proceedings not to be questioned on ground of irregularity), Art 110(3) (Speaker's Money-Bill decision final), Art 118 (rules of procedure). The correct answer: "the court will see whether the procedure prescribed in the law was followed while depriving the person."

qa.q: Q3. Define substantive due process and procedural due process.
qa.a: Substantive: the court examines whether the law itself is reasonable, fair and just; if not, it is struck down (Mithu - s. 303 IPC; Navtej Johar). Procedural: the court examines whether the procedure for implementing the law is just, fair and reasonable; if not, the procedure is corrected (Maneka Gandhi - hearing read in).

qa.q: Q4. Give an example of procedural due process.
qa.a: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): s. 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act empowered the authority to impound a passport without a hearing. The Court did not strike the section but held the procedure must be fair and read in a right to be heard; the Attorney General undertook to give Maneka a hearing.

qa.q: Q5. Give an example of substantive due process.
qa.a: Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983): s. 303 IPC (mandatory death sentence for murder by a life-convict) was struck down as unjust, unfair and unreasonable under Arts 14 and 21. Another: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) (s. 377 IPC as applied to consensual adult same-sex acts).

qa.q: Q6. Why did Americans start hating "due process"? Which case?
qa.a: Lochner v. New York (1905), 198 U.S. 45: the US Supreme Court struck down a New York law limiting bakery employees to 60 hours a week as violating the liberty of contract under the 14th Amendment's due process clause. In the "Lochner era" the Court struck down many social-welfare laws on the ground that they were unreasonable, so "due process" became a tool for judges to impose their economic philosophy (the "super-legislature" charge). That is why Justice Frankfurter advised B.N. Rau not to use it and why the Indian Constitution says "procedure established by law".

qa.q: Q7. Why was Art 21 originally given a narrow meaning? Which case and which approach?
qa.a: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950): Art 21's "law" meant any State-made (enacted) law; "procedure established by law" meant procedure prescribed by that law. The Court also adopted the watertight compartments approach - Arts 19, 21 and 22 were mutually exclusive codes. It was weakened by R.C. Cooper (1970) and overruled by Maneka Gandhi (1978).

qa.q: Q8. Name the post-1978 cases in which Art 21 was expanded and the rights recognised.
qa.a: Hussainara Khatoon (speedy trial, free legal aid); Sunil Batra (humane treatment in prison, no fetters); Francis Coralie Mullin (right to live with human dignity); Olga Tellis (livelihood); Sodan Singh (hawkers' trading zones); Parmanand Katara (immediate medical aid); Mohini Jain / Unni Krishnan (education up to 14 → Art 21A); Subhash Kumar / M.C. Mehta (clean environment); Rudul Sah (compensation); Puttaswamy (privacy).

qa.q: Q9. Is there a right to die under Art 21? What was the position in Rathinam and in Gian Kaur?
qa.a: No. In Rathinam (1994) a two-judge bench held that the right to life includes the right not to live and struck down s. 309 IPC. In Gian Kaur (1996) a five-judge bench overruled Rathinam: the right to life is a natural right; suicide is an unnatural extinction of life and inconsistent with Art 21; ss. 306 and 309 are valid. The "right to die with dignity" (passive euthanasia, living wills) was recognised later in Aruna Shanbaug (2011) and Common Cause (2018) within narrow limits.

qa.q: Q10. Why is suicide punished only when it is "attempted"? (professor's question on s. 309)
qa.a: A completed suicide leaves no offender to prosecute; the offence of attempt (s. 309 IPC) applied where the person survived. The rationale offered in the lecture: people face failure repeatedly; the law is to discourage the act and encourage perseverance, rather than leave attempts consequence-free. Present law: s. 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 presumes severe stress and bars prosecution; the BNS, 2023 omits the general offence of attempt; abetment of suicide remains an offence. (For the exam, mention that attempt-to-suicide is better treated as a health issue.)

qa.q: Q11. What are the rights of an arrested person? (D.K. Basu)
qa.a: Right to know grounds of arrest (Art 22(1)); to consult and be defended by a lawyer, with free legal aid if he cannot afford one (Art 22(1), Art 39A); to have a relative/friend informed; to be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours (Art 22(2)); to medical examination at the time of arrest and thereafter; identifiable police and a signed memo of arrest; protection from custodial torture (Art 21, Art 20(3)). D.K. Basu (1997) laid down 11 binding requirements (see 10.5).

qa.q: Q12. Why is a medical examination required at the time of arrest?
qa.a: To record the condition of the arrestee's body at the time he enters custody so that any injury later found can be traced to what happened in custody. It protects against third-degree methods and fixes police accountability; medical care for a disease such as diabetes is only a secondary purpose.

qa.q: Q13. Who was the lecturer's authority for "life is more than animal existence"?
qa.a: The phrase comes from Field J. in Munn v. Illinois (1877) (US), cited by Subba Rao J. (dissenting) in Kharak Singh (1962), adopted in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Francis Coralie Mullin (1981).

qa.a: See 10.6 - arbitrary = capricious, irrational, without adequate determining principle (E.P. Royappa; Shayara Bano's "manifest arbitrariness").

qa.q: Q1. To whom does Article 21 apply - to every citizen or every person?
qa.a: To every person ("No person shall be deprived..."), including foreigners and non-citizens. Art 19 applies to citizens only. (The professor deliberately tested this: the correct word is "person".)

qa.q: Q2. What was discussed under Art 21 in the last class? (vertical and horizontal application, expansion of life, expansion of personal liberty, PEL v. DPL)
qa.a: Vertical = Art 21 against the State; horizontal = against private persons (Kaushal Kishor, 2023; Bodhisattwa Gautam). Expansion of life = life with dignity, livelihood, health, environment, education. Expansion of personal liberty = everything not in Art 19 (travel abroad, privacy, choice of dress/food). PEL v. DPL = see Q 3.

qa.q: Q3. What is the difference between procedure established by law and due process of law?
qa.a: Under PEL the legislature is trusted more and the court only sees whether the prescribed procedure exists and has been followed. Under DPL the judiciary has more power: it tests the quality of the law (substantive due process) and the fairness of the procedure (procedural due process). Example: s. 377 IPC and adultery could be struck down only because of due process; under PEL the Court would only have checked whether someone had been punished under s. 377.

qa.q: Q4. Was there any element of due process in the Constitution before Maneka Gandhi? Give a case.
qa.a: Yes - in Art 14 (reasonable classification) and Art 19 (reasonable restrictions). State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) struck down s. 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 because the classification of cases for special trial was not a valid classification. Only Art 21 had no such test until 1978.

qa.q: Q5. Why was due process not available under Art 21 earlier? (the Lochner-era problem)
qa.a: Because the framers feared the American experience: in the Lochner era the US Supreme Court used due process to strike down social-welfare laws on the basis of "freedom of contract". On Frankfurter's advice to B.N. Rau, "due process of law" was dropped and "procedure established by law" (from Art 31 of the Japanese Constitution) was adopted.

qa.q: Q6. Which article of the Japanese Constitution has "procedure established by law"?
qa.a: Article 31 (not 33 or 39).

qa.q: Q7. Who was the Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly, and what did he do about "due process"?
qa.a: Sir B.N. Rau; he consulted jurists abroad including Justice Felix Frankfurter, who warned that "due process" would give a few judges excessive power over legislation. The phrase was replaced by "procedure established by law".

qa.q: Q8. Why did the American framers/people have "absolute" rights in the Bill of Rights, and how did restrictions come in?
qa.a: The first ten amendments (1791) were demanded as the condition of ratifying the Constitution and are drafted in absolute terms. No right can be absolute in practice, so restrictions came through judicial decisions, unlike India where they are in the text (Art 19(2)-(6)).

qa.q: Q9. What is "fair" in "procedural due process"? Give the professor's example.
qa.a: Fair = just and reasonable, not arbitrary, unjust or unfair. Example: a university holds a test but never checks the answer-books and declares pass/fail. Under PEL the Court would say "a test was conducted"; under procedural due process it would say the procedure is not fair because evaluation is part of fairness.

qa.q: Q10. What are the facts of Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and what did the Court hold?
qa.a: Her passport was impounded under s. 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 in the interest of the general public, without reasons or a hearing. She argued that natural justice was violated. The Government said Art 21 only requires a procedure prescribed by law. The Court held: right to go abroad is part of personal liberty (Satwant Singh, 1967); procedure must be just, fair and reasonable - "any procedure is no procedure"; natural justice is part of Art 21; Arts 14, 19, 21 form a golden triangle; s. 10(3)(c) is valid only if a fair (post-decisional) hearing is provided.

qa.q: Q11. What was Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) and what was its consequence?
qa.a: The Supreme Court held that the right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Art 21 and the executive cannot refuse a passport arbitrarily; a law is needed. Parliament enacted the Passports Act, 1967.

qa.q: Q12. The Government said: if we give notice she will flee. What doctrine did the Court evolve?
qa.a: The doctrine of post-decisional hearing: in a case of urgency (where a prior hearing would defeat the object) the authority can act first and then give the person a hearing; the hearing comes after the decision, but it must be real and meaningful.

qa.q: Q13. When did substantive due process come to India? Name the case and the provision struck down.
qa.a: Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983): s. 303 IPC (mandatory death sentence for a murder committed by a life-convict) was struck down under Arts 14 and 21 because it gave the court no discretion and was arbitrary. (Not Maru Ram.)

qa.q: Q14. Why is the Court's power over the "quality" of a law a feature of due process but not of PEL? Give two examples of laws struck down on that ground.
qa.a: Because only under due process does the court ask whether the law itself is fair. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) struck down s. 377 IPC as applied to consensual adults, and Joseph Shine (2018) struck down adultery (s. 497 IPC); Mithu (1983) struck down s. 303 IPC.

qa.q: Q15. How did Public Interest Litigation begin in India? Name the first Constitution Bench case that accepted PIL.
qa.a: Seed: Bombay Kamgar Sabha (1976) (representative standing). Then Hussainara Khatoon and Sunil Batra (letter petitions). The first Constitution Bench acceptance: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) - the Judges Transfer Case, where advocates were held to have locus standi.

qa.q: Q16. Why did lawyers have locus standi in the Judges Transfer Case?
qa.a: Judges cannot challenge their own transfers (they depend on the Government for postings) and the poor/ignorant are not the aggrieved class here. The Court held that advocates are officers of the court and justice cannot be delivered without the Bar; hence the Bar has a sufficient interest in the independence of the judiciary and can sue in public interest.

qa.q: Q17. Why is it dangerous if the judiciary is under the control of the executive (the professor's point on judge transfers)?
qa.a: Because transfers (e.g. "punishment postings") can be used to pressurise judges; if judges work "under" the executive like administrative officers, justice (especially against the State) will not be available. Independence of the judiciary is part of the basic structure.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.1: Read Lochner v. New York (professor had requested it in earlier classes: "try to read it")
qa.a: See 11.3. 198 U.S. 45 (1905); Holmes J.'s dissent; liberty of contract.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.2: Know the name of the case and Act declared unconstitutional in 1950-52 on Art 14 grounds
qa.a: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952); West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, s. 5(1). See 11.2.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.3: Know the article of the Japanese Constitution from which "procedure established by law" was borrowed
qa.a: Article 31.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.4: Read Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) and the Passports Act, 1967 (s. 10(3)(c))
HOMEWORK 11.5: Find out the name of the doctrine evolved in Maneka Gandhi when the Government argued that notice would let her flee
qa.a: Post-decisional hearing. The administrative-law teacher will teach it in detail.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.6: Check the correct name of the case in which s. 303 IPC was struck down ("Maru Ram" or "Mithu")
qa.a: Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) 2 SCC 277; Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980) is a different case (remission/s. 433A CrPC).

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.7: Google the Shah Commission and read the Emergency-era cases
qa.a: Shah Commission: commission of inquiry (Justice J.C. Shah) set up in 1977 to inquire into excesses during the Emergency. Cases: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976), Kesavananda Bharati (1973) - see Lectures 6-9 and 11.6.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.8: Read Bombay Kamgar Sabha (1976), Hussainara Khatoon, Sunil Batra and S.P. Gupta (Judges Transfer Case)
qa.a: See 11.6 and Lecture 10, 10.3.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.9: Read the original Maneka Gandhi judgments (Bhagwati J., Krishna Iyer J.) in English for language practice
qa.a: See 11.4 and Lecture 9, 9.5.

qa.q: HOMEWORK 11.10: Refer ADM Jabalpur (to be taught next semester)
qa.a: ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) 2 SCC 521: during the Emergency (Art 359 order), the Supreme Court (4:1; Khanna J. dissenting) held that no person had locus standi to move any court for a writ of habeas corpus to challenge detention under MISA. Overruled by K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017); the 44th Amendment made Arts 20 and 21 non-suspendable.

qa.q: Why is classification necessary for the application of Article 14?
qa.a: Because equality is not identical treatment: treating unequals equally is itself a violation of equality. Without classification the State could not legislate for specific groups or problems; the power to classify is an essential incident of legislative power. Article 14 forbids only class legislation, not reasonable classification.

qa.q: What are the two tests for a valid classification? Explain with reference to Anwar Ali Sarkar.
qa.a: (1) Intelligible differentia — a clear, real, substantial basis distinguishing those grouped in from those left out; (2) rational nexus between that differentia and the statute's object. In Anwar Ali Sarkar, Section 5(1) supplied no differentia at all — the executive's unguided pick-and-choose — and the conferral of absolute discretion had no rational connection with speedier trial. Both limbs failing, the provision was void.

qa.q: Why did Anwar Ali Sarkar succeed while a similar provision was upheld in Kathi Raning Rawat?
qa.a: Context and guidance. The Saurashtra Ordinance's preamble supplied the criteria — offences connected with an exceptional breakdown of public order in named regions — channelling the executive's discretion toward a constitutional object. The West Bengal Act had no such internal or contextual guide, leaving naked discretion. Same text, different legal fate.

qa.q: Why is Article 14 placed before Articles 19 and 21 in the Constitution?
qa.a: The lecture leaves this as the question for the next class: is equality more important than life (Article 21) and freedom (Article 19)? The placement is a conscious constitutional choice — the framework for answering it (equality as the first among the rights, and later the Golden Triangle that makes them co-equal) develops over the following sessions.

qa.q: The government, to bring black money into the mainstream and fund new medical colleges, issues Bearer Bonds purchasable by anyone without questions about the money's source; after ten years the investment becomes white. A PIL challenges the Act under Article 14: it is an injustice to honest taxpayers who paid full income tax; it rewards dishonesty and encourages hoarding in expectation of future amnesty schemes. Decide.
qa.a: (1) Presumption of constitutionality: courts presume a parliamentary statute valid; the burden is on the challenger. (2) Judicial deference to economic policy: courts do not intervene in policy, especially economic policy, unless it is manifestly arbitrary. (3) The two tests: intelligible differentia — is there a clear distinction between holders of black money and others? Yes, the classification is clear. Rational nexus — the object is to surface black money, fund medical colleges, improve the doctor-patient ratio; allowing investment without declaring the source directly furthers that object. Nexus exists. (4) Conclusion: the Act is constitutionally valid — it satisfies both limbs and, as an economic policy measure, deserves deference. (This is the pattern of R.K. Garg v. Union of India, the recommended original reading.)

qa.q: A student argues: government priorities after independence were different — first feed the hungry during the Bengal famine, build ISRO, DRDO and the IITs, then turn to traditional knowledge. The professor's response?
qa.a: “Tell me one institute opened to promote Ayurvedic medicine.” When a student mentions AIIMS, he dismisses it as having only a neglected Ayurveda department — no dedicated government institute for Ayurveda was ever established. Even today millets and Indian generic foods have become globally popular — why was this importance not recognised earlier? Seventy years have passed, and the neglect continued throughout. A second student then makes the thoughtful point that those in power can only act on what they know: Nehru and Gandhi were educated abroad, absorbed Western philosophies of freedom and liberty, and naturally implemented what they had learned. The professor acknowledges the argument but, needing to move forward with the syllabus, humorously declares the student has “won for now,” inviting a dedicated debate another day.

qa.q: 1 · Prohibition with exemptions. A State bans liquor entirely in the interest of public health and temperance, but exempts soldiers and sailors consuming foreign liquor in military messes, canteens, warships and troopships, and foreign tourists possessing liquor under a special permit. Ordinary residents get no permit route. Is the exemption of defence personnel (separate service conditions, functional needs aboard ships) and foreign visitors (transient status, different customs) valid, even though allowing them to drink seems to work against the very purpose of temperance among the general population?
qa.a: OFFICIAL SECTION B ANSWER: Defence personnel and vessels were already recognised as a distinct legal category under separate service and discipline laws, and foreigners were distinguished by their transient status and different customs — both real, non-fanciful differentia. The Supreme Court held that special treatment of a class already treated as distinct under other statutes has a rational nexus to practical governance — even though the High Court had earlier found no such nexus and struck the exemption down. (This is the pattern of State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, taught on 30 July.)

qa.q: 2 · The rent-control cut-off. A rent law permanently frees all buildings constructed after a cut-off date from rent control, to encourage fresh construction. Decades later, the “new” buildings are over twenty-five years old, yet their landlords still enjoy total freedom, while equally old pre-cutoff buildings remain regulated forever. The classification made sense when passed — is it still valid to keep exempting them forever, with no time limit?
qa.a: OFFICIAL SECTION B ANSWER (as far as the source preserves it): the classification — date of construction — was valid when first made, a genuine, verifiable distinction with a real incentive-based nexus. But a classification's validity is not frozen... [the source text breaks off here]. COMPLETION ON THE COURSE FRAMEWORK: ...at the date of enactment. The rational nexus between “newness” and the incentive object evaporates once the exempted buildings age into the regulated class's condition; perpetuating the distinction indefinitely, with no sunset, is a continuing failure of the nexus limb as applied today. The better view: the exemption was valid when made but is open to challenge as arbitrary in its continuing operation — the legislature must re-examine the cut-off.

qa.q: 3 · The labour welfare fund. A law requires “establishments” — all factories, plus tramway and motor-bus businesses — to deposit unclaimed wages and bonuses in a welfare fund, but excludes businesses with fewer than fifty employees and government establishments other than factories. Is it valid to regulate only larger establishments and specific sectors, leaving out smaller trade businesses and most government bodies, on the reasoning that the legislature may tackle a widespread problem in phases?
qa.a: VALID. The differentia is intelligible: large factories and public transport undertakings concentrate wage labour and unpaid dues; small trading businesses and non-factory offices present a smaller, more diffuse administrative problem. The nexus with the object — recovering unclaimed dues for workers' welfare where the problem is administratively concentrated — is rational, and the legislature may legitimately attack a widespread evil in phases, beginning where the concern is greatest (the pattern of the phased-approach reasoning taught with this problem).

qa.q: 4 · The flat land tax. A State imposes a single flat rate per acre on “all lands,” so the owner of fertile, income-generating farmland pays the same as the owner of unproductive forest yielding barely any income — one owner earned only a small annual income from roughly 25,000 acres of forest yet faced a tax demand many times his earnings. The law also lets government exempt “any land or class of lands” at its own discretion, with no guidelines. Is a flat rate on wildly unequal land valid, and is the unguided discretionary exemption valid?
qa.a: INVALID ON BOTH COUNTS. First, imposing identical burden on admittedly unequal subjects — fertile versus barren land — is the very “equal treatment of unequals” that Article 14 forbids (the positive concept of equal protection, 27 July lecture): a rational tax would classify by productivity or income. Second, the unguided power to exempt “any land” is Anwar Ali Sarkar's vice in reverse — absolute, unguided executive discretion with no criteria, which fails the intelligible differentia limb and breeds arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa).

qa.q: 5 · The pension line. The government liberalises the pension formula but applies it only to employees retiring on or after a fixed date; employees retired even a day earlier, with identical service of the same kind, quality and length, remain on the old, less generous formula for life. All served the same employer — is a line drawn purely on the date of retirement valid when the object was simply better financial security in old age?
qa.a: INVALID. Cut-off dates are not per se unconstitutional, but the differentia must have a rational nexus with the object. Here the object — old-age financial security for those who rendered comparable service — is indifferent to the day of retirement; the classification neither identifies a class needing different treatment nor serves economy or transition (no such justification appears). Same-service pensioners are similarly situated; the day's difference is arbitrary in effect — the pattern of the cut-off analysis in Ex-Services Association (taught 24–25 July), where a cut-off discriminating between similarly situated groups without reasonable nexus was condemned.

qa.q: 6 · The air hostesses (three sub-questions). An airline has two cabin-crew cadres: male flight pursers and female air hostesses. Air hostesses must retire at 35, or earlier on marriage within the first four years of service, or immediately upon first pregnancy — whichever first; pursers serve until 58. Extension beyond these conditions lies purely in the Managing Director's unguided discretion. (a) Are two separate cadres with different rules valid, given different recruitment sources and historical service conditions? (b) Is termination upon first pregnancy valid, on the theory that pregnancy affects ability to do the job? (c) Is it valid to let one official decide, with no written standard, whose service is extended?
qa.a: (a) VALID — separate cadres recruited from different sources with different historical conditions can constitute an intelligible differentia; that much is not per se objectionable. (b) INVALID — a rule terminating a woman upon first pregnancy draws the line on sex and pregnancy alone. The “ability to do the job” rationale is over-broad: pregnancy is a temporary condition, not a permanent incapacity, and the rule spares the employer any individualised inquiry while visiting the entire burden on women alone — the classification fails the nexus limb and is sex-based discrimination of the kind Articles 14–15 target (Air India v. Nergesh Meerza was the course's designated case for exactly this regulation). (c) INVALID — the Managing Director's unguided discretion to extend service is Anwar Ali Sarkar's absolute, standardless pick-and-choose: wherever there is discretion without criteria, there is room for arbitrariness.

qa.q: 7 · The degree-and-diploma split. Degree-holder and diploma-holder Assistant Engineers had formed one integrated cadre — equal pay, equal promotion prospects. New rules give degree-holders a higher pay scale and reserve promotion to Executive Engineer for degree-holders alone; diploma-holders, however senior, are no longer eligible. Is re-splitting a merged cadre valid, on the reasoning that a degree involves deeper theoretical training better equipping a person for the senior post's technical and managerial responsibility?
qa.a: VALID. The differentia — formal engineering degree versus diploma — is real, verifiable and non-fanciful; the nexus — the senior post's greater technical and managerial responsibility requiring deeper theoretical training — is rational. The prior integration of the cadres is a fact of history, not a constitutional bar: the State may re-classify when the qualification genuinely correlates with the demands of the post. (The answer would flip if the degree bore no rational relation to the post's functions — then the split would be arbitrary.)

qa.q: 8 · The black-money bonds. To pull undisclosed wealth into productive investment, government issues special bonds buyable with black money, granting immunity from questions about its source, protection from tax proceedings and certain exemptions — while honest taxpayers who declared and paid tax on everything receive nothing comparable. Is giving immunities specifically to holders of undisclosed wealth, where the stated aim is productive investment of black money, valid — or does it reward tax evasion at the expense of the honest?
qa.a: VALID — this is the Bearer Bonds problem solved in class (c.31 July) and read as R.K. Garg v. Union of India. (1) Presumption of constitutionality; the burden lies on the challenger. (2) Judicial deference to economic policy unless manifestly arbitrary. (3) Intelligible differentia: holders of undisclosed wealth are a clearly distinct class. (4) Rational nexus: allowing them to invest without declaring the source directly furthers the object — surfacing black money, funding development. The emotional claim of “rewarding dishonesty” does not supply a constitutional ground; the hardship of honest taxpayers is not a listed vice in the classification.

qa.q: 9 · The SC/ST test exemption. Departmental tests must be passed for promotion to a higher clerical grade, but the government may temporarily exempt in-service SC/ST employees for a limited period. A batch of promotions goes largely to exempted employees by seniority, ahead of a general-category employee who passed the tests. Is the temporary exemption valid, where the object is adequate representation of historically disadvantaged communities?
qa.a: VALID. The differentia is intelligible — Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are historically disadvantaged and under-represented communities, the very class the Constitution's scheme of compensatory discrimination addresses (Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are facets of equality, not exceptions — the 13 August lecture). The nexus — securing adequate representation in public service — is direct. That some promoted employees had not passed the test while a general candidate had is within the logic of substantive equality: the Court has upheld even the removal of minimum qualifying marks for reserved candidates (Kumari Nivedita Jain). The exemption is temporary and targeted, not a permanent lowering of standards.

qa.q: 10 · The single-company law. After a special inquiry into one textile mill in financial and managerial trouble threatening the supply of an essential commodity (cloth), Parliament passes a law naming that company alone — removing its managing agents and directors, letting government appoint new ones, curtailing shareholders' voting rights. No other company, even similarly troubled, is touched. Can a law targeting a single named entity be a valid classification, given that a “class” normally means a group of more than one?
qa.a: VALID — a single person or entity can constitute a class where its situation is unique: the special inquiry established this company's specific financial and managerial crisis threatening an essential commodity's supply and a vast workforce's livelihoods — characteristics not shared by “similarly troubled” companies in the abstract. Chiranjit Lal Chowdhury settles that a class of one is permissible if the differentia is intelligible and the nexus rational. The shareholder's “hostile discrimination” argument is the strongest counter, but it fails because the law responds to demonstrated, unique facts, not hostility toward the named entity.

qa.q: 11 · The pick-and-choose special courts. After communal riots, a State law allows Special Courts with a faster procedure dropping safeguards like jury trial and committal, but does not specify which offences, areas or cases go to them — government may by notification pick any individual “case” or “offence,” with no guiding standard. Is free, case-by-case executive selection of who gets the harsher procedure valid?
qa.a: INVALID — this is Anwar Ali Sarkar itself. Both limbs fail: no intelligible differentia (no criteria at all; the selection rests on executive whim — change the officer, change the cases), and no rational nexus (unguided discretion bears no connection to speedy trial). Persons accused of the same offence may face radically different procedures with no justifiable answer to “why me?”

qa.q: 12 · The ordinance with built-in criteria. After integration of princely states, regions of the new State see organised armed robbery, dacoity, looting and murder; an ordinance itself names the disturbed regions and lists the serious violent offences (murder, dacoity, robbery and related) to be tried by a faster special procedure. A convict argues being tried differently from accused persons elsewhere is discriminatory. Does building the criteria into the law, rather than leaving unguided choice, make the classification valid?
qa.a: VALID — this is Kathi Raning Rawat. The differentia is intelligible (named regions suffering an exceptional breakdown of law and order; named grave offences), and the nexus — a speedier, tougher procedure precisely where the ordinary system has broken down — is rational. Contrast Anwar Ali Sarkar: the guidance here is in the law itself, so no standardless discretion exists.

qa.q: 13 · The custody-statement rule. Confessions to police are generally inadmissible, but a person in custody who gives information leading to a fact's discovery (say, a hidden weapon) may have the discovery-related portion of his statement proved — while a person not in custody making a full voluntary confession is governed by ordinary rules instead. Is treating custody statements differently valid?
qa.a: VALID. The differentia is intelligible — persons in police custody face a materially higher risk of police pressure, inducement and fabrication, so their statements warrant a distinct, more restrictive admissibility rule. The nexus is rational: admitting only the discovery-related portion, verified by the actual discovery of the object, is a safeguard precisely calibrated to that risk — the corroboration of the fact guarantees reliability in a way a free-floating confession does not. Differential treatment keyed to a real difference in vulnerability satisfies both limbs.

qa.q: 14 · The two tobaccos. A sales-tax law taxes one premium, largely export-oriented, cigarette-grade variety of tobacco while exempting the more common “country” variety used for chewing and bidi-making. Traders in the taxed variety argue there is no fair reason to single out their product while a competing product goes untaxed. Is taxing one commercial variety while exempting another variety of the same broad category valid?
qa.a: VALID. The two varieties are genuinely different commodities — grown, cured, marketed and used differently; one is a distinct, higher-value, export-oriented product, the other locally consumed. The differentia is real and commercial, not fanciful; the nexus — taxing the higher-value commodity (and, implicitly, sparing the local consumption of the common variety) — is a rational revenue measure. A “same broad category” does not make sub-varieties a single class for all purposes.

qa.q: 15 · The seventeen-month year. On a district's transfer into a newly formed State, a transitional provision fixes the “previous year” for agricultural income tax in that district as seventeen months (instead of twelve), with the rate computed on an adjusted average-annual-income formula; taxpayers elsewhere in the State use the standard year. The transferred district's taxpayers say the result is harsher and discriminatory. Is a temporary, one-time transitional computation valid?
qa.a: VALID. Transitional provisions classify by a real and temporary necessity: reconciling two different accounting-year systems at the merger. The differentia — the transferred district — is intelligible and self-evident; the nexus — an adjusted computation period and averaging formula to bridge the systems — is directly rational. Genuine administrative difficulty at a one-time transition is a classic reasonable classification; it is neither permanent nor capricious.

qa.q: 16 · The adultery exemption. An offence punishes a man for sexual relations with another man's wife without the husband's consent, but expressly exempts the wife — not even as abettor — however great her role. Is criminalising only men while completely exempting women valid, given that special treatment favourable to women is separately and expressly permitted by the Constitution?
qa.a: VALID on the course's framework. The differentia is sex-based, but it operates favourably to women; the Constitution expressly contemplates special provisions for women (Article 15(3) — the “injection” against historically entrenched discrimination, taught 10–11 August). The legislature proceeded on the protective assumption that in the marital context the wife is the victim, not the perpetrator, and therefore withdrew her from criminal liability even as an abettor. A sex-based classification is not per se invalid; what Article 15(1) forbids is discrimination — hostile or prejudicial treatment — not protective differentiation.

qa.q: 17 · The blanket bar on women in liquor premises. An excise law bans the employment of any woman — and any man under twenty-five — anywhere liquor is consumed by the public: bars, hotel restaurants, room service. The stated purpose is protecting women (and young men) from the environment's risks; trained hospitality professionals who are women are completely barred regardless of individual skill, experience or actual workplace safety. Is a blanket protective ban valid, or does it fail because narrower measures (workplace safety rules) could address the same concerns?
qa.a: INVALID. Protective legislation for women is constitutionally contemplated, but the ban is over-inclusive and the nexus fails: the object — safety in the working environment — can be achieved by narrower, individualised means (safety regulations, conditions of service), so a total exclusion from an entire profession based purely on sex and age is disproportionate to the object. The classification assumes what it should prove — that every woman, whatever her training and whatever the actual conditions of a specific workplace, is endangered — and therefore treats the protected class as incapable of choice. The course's test: where a less restrictive measure serves the object equally, the blanket ban is arbitrary.

qa.q: 18 · The fifteen-percent interview. A college admits students by written test plus interview, with more than fifteen percent of total marks allotted to the interview; each interview lasts two to three minutes and consists of formal questions about parentage and residence — nothing that tests merit. Some high-scoring written candidates are kept out while lower scorers enter on unexplained interview marks. Though every candidate passed through the same process, can the weightage be struck down as unfair and arbitrary in effect, even without a “classification” in the traditional sense?
qa.a: INVALID. This is the E.P. Royappa extension: equality is violated not only by bad classifications but by arbitrary process. A component worth fifteen percent of the admission that, by its own design (two-to-three minutes, formal questions on parentage and residence), cannot assess merit, is irrational — the mechanism bears no relation to the object (selecting on merit). The identical application of an irrational process is still arbitrary; unexplained interview marks functioning as an unreviewable discretion fail non-arbitrariness even where every candidate was “treated alike.”

qa.q: 19 · The EWS quota's exclusion. A constitutional amendment allows up to 10% reservation for “economically weaker sections” — but only for those who do not belong to SCs, STs or OBCs (who already have their own separate reservation). It is argued that since poverty exists in every community, excluding the poor of already-reserved communities from the new quota discriminates against the poorest of the poor. Is treating “economically weak general-category citizens” as a distinct class from “economically weak persons from already-reserved communities” valid?
qa.a: VALID — the position of Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, as taught on 10 August. The class “economically weaker sections of citizens not already covered by reservation” is coherent: the excluded communities already possess separate, older reservation benefits rooted in social and educational backwardness, so the new, purely economic quota reaches precisely those whom the existing scheme leaves out. EWS reservation is not caste-based, and it specifically excludes those already receiving benefits — it brings in people from castes previously outside the net rather than enlarging the same castes' entitlement. The classification identifies two genuinely different positions, not one class arbitrarily halved.

qa.q: 20 · The 27% with creamy layer. A government order grants 27% reservation for socially and educationally “backward classes,” identified substantially using caste as an indicator — while excluding the more advanced “creamy layer” within those communities so the benefit reaches the genuinely disadvantaged. Critics say using caste at all, then sub-dividing the backward class, is irrational and that economic status alone should have been the test. Is caste as an indicator (not the sole test) plus creamy-layer exclusion valid?
qa.a: VALID — the position of Indra Sawhney. (1) Caste may be a starting point for identifying social and educational backwardness — in Indian conditions caste is a very real component of social position — but it cannot be the sole criterion; the identification here uses caste as an indicator within a broader assessment. (2) Excluding the creamy layer keeps the benefit targeted at those genuinely, not merely nominally, disadvantaged — the advanced members of a backward class have already escaped the disadvantage the measure targets. Both limbs satisfied: intelligible differentia (genuinely backward versus advanced members) and rational nexus (advancement of the actually disadvantaged).

qa.q: 21 · The juvenile's date. An accused was a minor on the date of the alleged offence but had crossed the juvenile age by the time of investigation or production before the court. One view fixes juvenile status by age on the date of production; the other by age on the date of the offence. Which is more consistent with treating similarly-placed young offenders equally?
qa.a: The date of the offence. The protective juvenile-justice procedure attaches to the person's condition when the act was done — that is the morally and legally relevant moment, common to all young offenders in like circumstances. The date of production is an accident of procedure: it varies enormously with how quickly or slowly a case moves, so two offenders identically situated at the offence would receive different treatment according to docket speed alone. Equality among similarly-placed offenders therefore requires fixing status by age on the date of the offence — the certain, rational basis; the production-date rule creates an arbitrary, litigation-driven lottery.

articles.label: Preamble
articles.title: Preamble
articles.text:
WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;
EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION
articles.note: The words "SOCIALIST SECULAR" and "and integrity" were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held the Preamble is part of the Constitution.

articles.label: Article 12
articles.title: Definitions
articles.text: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, “the State” includes the Government and Parliament of India and the Government and the Legislature of each of the States and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India
articles.note: Tests for "other authorities": Ajay Hasia (1981) and Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002, deep and pervasive control).

articles.label: Article 13
articles.title: Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights
articles.text:
(1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.
(2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void.
(3) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires,—
       (a) “law” includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law;
       (b) “laws in force” includes laws passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not previously repealed, notwithstanding that any such law or any part thereof may not be then in operation either at all or in particular areas.
(4) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368
articles.note: Clause (4) was inserted by the 24th Amendment (1971) after Golak Nath. Doctrines: eclipse (pre-Constitution laws), severability, waiver.

articles.label: Article 14
articles.title: Equality before law
articles.text: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.

articles.label: Article 15
articles.title: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
articles.text:
(1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.
(2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to—
     (a) access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or
     (b) the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public.
(3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children.
(4) Nothing in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.
(5) Nothing in this article or in sub-clause (g) of clause (1) of article 19 shall prevent the State from making any special provision, by law, for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes in so far as such special provisions relate to their admission to educational institutions including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30.
(6) Nothing in this article or sub-clause (g) of clause (1) of article 19 or clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making,—
     (a) any special provision for the advancement of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5); and
     (b) any special provision for the advancement of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5) in so far as such special provisions relate to their admission to educational institutions including private educational institutions, whether aided or unaided by the State, other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30, which in the case of reservation would be in addition to the existing reservations and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the total seats in each category.
     Explanation.—For the purposes of this article and article 16, "economically weaker sections" shall be such as may be notified by the State from time to time on the basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage.
articles.note: Clause (4): 1st Amendment (1951) after Champakam Dorairajan. Clause (5): 93rd Amendment (2005). Clause (6) and the Explanation (EWS): 103rd Amendment (2019), upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).

articles.label: Article 16
articles.title: Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment
articles.text:
