(1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State.
(2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State.
(3) Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing, in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under the Government of, or any local or other authority within, a State or Union territory, any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment.
(4) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State.
(4A) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for reservation in matters of promotion, with consequential seniority, to any class or classes of posts in the services under the State in favour of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes which, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services under the State.
(4B) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from considering any unfilled vacancies of a year which are reserved for being filled up in that year in accordance with any provision for reservation made under clause (4) or clause (4A) as a separate class of vacancies to be filled up in any succeeding year or years and such class of vacancies shall not be considered together with the vacancies of the year in which they are being filled up for determining the ceiling of fifty per cent. reservation on total number of vacancies of that year.
(5) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any law which provides that the incumbent of an office in connection with the affairs of any religious or denominational institution or any member of the governing body thereof shall be a person professing a particular religion or belonging to a particular denomination.
(6) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clause (4), in addition to the existing reservation and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the posts in each category.
articles.note: Clause (4A): 77th (1995) and 85th (2001) Amendments; clause (4B): 81st (2000); clause (6) EWS: 103rd (2019). See Indra Sawhney (1992), M. Nagaraj (2006), Jarnail Singh (2018).

articles.label: Article 17
articles.title: Abolition of Untouchability
articles.text: “Untouchability” is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of “Untouchability” shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.
articles.note: PUDR (1982): Arts 17, 23 and 24 operate against private persons too.

articles.label: Article 18
articles.title: Abolition of titles
articles.text:
(1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State.
(2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State.
(3) No person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State.
(4) No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State shall, without the consent of the President, accept any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.

articles.label: Article 19
articles.title: Protection of certain rights regarding freedom of speech, etc
articles.note: Sub-clause (f) (property) was omitted by the 44th Amendment (1978). Clause (2) was widened by the 1st Amendment (1951: public order, friendly relations, incitement to an offence) and the 16th Amendment (1963: sovereignty and integrity). "Or co-operative societies" in sub-clause (c) was added by the 97th Amendment (2011).

articles.label: Article 20
articles.title: Protection in respect of conviction for offences
articles.text:
(1) No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the Act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.
(2) No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.
(3) No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.
articles.note: Clause (3) — right against self-incrimination: Nandini Satpathy (1978).

articles.label: Article 21
articles.title: Protection of life and personal liberty
articles.text: No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
articles.note: Read with Arts 14 and 19 since Maneka Gandhi (1978). Cannot be suspended in an Emergency (Art 359, as amended by the 44th Amendment).

articles.label: Article 21A
articles.title: Right to education
articles.text: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.
articles.note: Inserted by the 86th Amendment (2002), in force from 1 April 2010 with the RTE Act, 2009.

articles.label: Article 22
articles.title: Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases
articles.text:
(1) No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice.
(2) Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate.
(3) Nothing in clauses (1) and (2) shall apply—
(a) to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or
(b) to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention.
(4) No law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless—
(a) an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention:
Provided that nothing in this sub-clause shall authorise the detention of any person beyond the maximum period prescribed by any law made by Parliament under sub-clause (b) of clause (7); or
(b) such person is detained in accordance with the provisions of any law made by Parliament under subclauses (a) and (b) of clause (7).
(5) When any person is detained in pursuance of an order made under any law providing for preventive detention, the authority making the order shall, as soon as may be, communicate to such person the grounds on which the order has been made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order.
(6) Nothing in clause (5) shall require the authority making any such order as is referred to in that clause to disclose facts which such authority considers to be against the public interest to disclose.
(7) Parliament may by law prescribe—
(a) the circumstances under which, and the class or classes of cases in which, a person may be detained for a period longer than three months under any law providing for preventive detention without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board in accordance with the provisions of sub-clause (a) of clause (4);
(b) the maximum period for which any person may in any class or classes of cases be detained under any law providing for preventive detention; and
(c) the procedure to be followed by an Advisory Board in an inquiry under sub-clause (a) of clause (4).
articles.note: The 44th Amendment's changes to Art 22(4) and (7) have never been brought into force; the original text still applies.

articles.label: Article 23
articles.title: Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
articles.text:
(1) Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.
(2) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them

articles.label: Article 24
articles.title: Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc
articles.text: No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment

articles.label: Article 25
articles.title: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
articles.text:
(1) Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion.
(2) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law—
(a) regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice;
(b) providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.
Explanation I.—The wearing and carrying of kirpans shall be deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion.
Explanation II.—In sub-clause (b) of clause (2), the reference to Hindus shall be construed as including a reference to persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion, and the reference to Hindu religious institutions shall be construed accordingly.

articles.label: Article 26
articles.title: Freedom to manage religious affairs

articles.label: Article 27
articles.title: Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion
articles.text: No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination

articles.label: Article 28
articles.title: Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions
articles.text:
(1) No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to an educational institution which is administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution.
(3) No person attending any educational institution recognised by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction that may be imparted in such institution or to attend any religious worship that may be conducted in such institution or in any premises attached thereto unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto.

articles.label: Article 29
articles.title: Protection of interests of minorities
articles.text:
(1) Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same.
(2) No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.

articles.label: Article 30
articles.title: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
articles.text:
(1) All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
(1A) In making any law providing for the compulsory acquisition of any property of an educational institution established and administered by a minority referred to in clause (1), the State shall ensure that the amount fixed by or determined under such law for the acquisition of such property is such as would not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under that clause.
(2) The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language.

articles.label: Article 31
articles.title: Compulsory acquisition of property
articles.text: [Compulsory acquisition of property.] Rep. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 6 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).
articles.note: Repealed by the 44th Amendment (1978, w.e.f. 20 June 1979); the right to property now lives in Art 300A.

articles.label: Article 31A
articles.title: Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc
articles.text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law providing for—
(a) the acquisition by the State of any estate or of any rights therein or the extinguishment or modification of any such rights, or
(b) the taking over of the management of any property by the State for a limited period either in the public interest or in order to secure the proper management of the property, or
(c) the amalgamation of two or more corporations either in the public interest or in order to secure the proper management of any of the corporations, or
(d) the extinguishment or modification of any rights of managing agents, secretaries and treasurers, managing directors, directors or managers of corporations, or of any voting rights of shareholders thereof, or
(e) the extinguishment or modification of any rights accruing by virtue of any agreement, lease or licence for the purpose of searching for, or winning, any mineral or mineral oil, or the premature termination or cancellation of any such agreement, lease or licence,
shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by [article 14 or article 19:
Provided that where such law is a law made by the Legislature of a State, the provisions of this article shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent:
Provided further that where any law makes any provision for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force or any building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto, unless the law relating to the acquisition of such land, building or structure, provides for payment of compensation at a rate which shall not be less than the market value thereof.
(2) In this article,—
(a) the expression ''estate'' shall, in relation to any local area, have the same meaning as that expression or its local equivalent has in the existing law relating to land tenures in force in that area and shall also include—
(i) any jagir, inam or muafi or other similar grant and in the States of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, any janmam right;
(ii) any land held under ryotwari settlement;
(iii) any land held or let for purposes of agriculture or for purposes ancillary thereto, including waste land, forest land, land for pasture or sites of buildings and other structures occupied by cultivators of land, agricultural labourers and village artisans;
(b) the expression ''rights'', in relation to an estate, shall include any rights vesting in a proprietor, subproprietor, under-proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under-raiyat] or other intermediary and any rights or privileges in respect of land revenue.

articles.label: Article 31B
articles.title: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations
articles.text: Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in article 31A, none of the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule nor any of the provisions thereof shall be deemed to be void, or ever to have become void, on the ground that such Act, Regulation or provision is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by, any provisions of this Part, and notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court or Tribunal to the contrary, each of the said Acts and Regulations shall, subject to the power of any competent Legislature to repeal or amend it, continue in force.

articles.label: Article 31C
articles.title: Saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles
articles.text:
Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by article 14 or article 19 and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy:
Provided that where such law is made by the Legislature of a State, the provisions of this article shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent.
articles.note: The 42nd Amendment's extension of Art 31C to "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980). In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (5 November 2024) a nine-judge bench held that Art 31C continues in the form upheld in Kesavananda — protecting laws giving effect to Art 39(b) and (c). The dataset text below shows the struck-down 42nd-Amendment wording.

articles.label: Article 32
articles.title: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part
articles.text:
(1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.
(2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.
(3) Without prejudice to the powers conferred on the Supreme Court by clauses (1) and (2), Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under clause (2).
(4) The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution.

articles.label: Article 32A
articles.title: Constitutional validity of State laws not to be considered in proceedings under article 32
articles.text: [Constitutional validity of State laws not to be considered in proceedings under article 32.] Rep. by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 3 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978).

articles.label: Article 33
articles.title: Power of Parliament to modify the rights conferred by this Part in their application to Forces, etc
articles.text:
Parliament may, by law, determine to what extent any of the rights conferred by this Part shall, in their application to,—
(a) the members of the Armed Forces; or
(b) the members of the Forces charged with the maintenance of public order; or
(c) persons employed in any bureau or other organisation established by the State for purposes of intelligence or counter intelligence; or
(d) person employed in, or in connection with, the telecommunication systems set up for the purposes of any Force, bureau or organisation referred to in clauses (a) to (c),
be restricted or abrogated so as to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

articles.label: Article 34
articles.title: Restriction on rights conferred by this Part while martial law is in force in any area
articles.text: Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, Parliament may by law indemnify any person in the service of the Union or of a State or any other person in respect of any act done by him in connection with the maintenance or restoration of order in any area within the territory of India where martial law was in force or validate any sentence passed, punishment inflicted, forfeiture ordered or other act done under martial law in such area.

articles.label: Article 35
articles.title: Legislation to give effect to the provisions of this Part
articles.text:
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—
(a) Parliament shall have, and the Legislature of a State shall not have, power to make laws—
(i) with respect to any of the matters which under clause (3) of article 16, clause (3) of article 32, article 33 and article 34 may be provided for by law made by Parliament; and
(ii) for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under this Part;
(b) any law in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution in the territory of India with respect to any of the matters referred to in sub-clause (i) of clause (a) or providing for punishment for any act referred to in sub-clause (ii) of that clause shall, subject to the terms thereof and to any adaptations and modifications that may be made therein under article 372, continue in force until altered or repealed or amended by Parliament.
Explanation.—In this article, the expression “law in force” has the same meaning as in article 372.

articles.label: Article 36
articles.title: Definition
articles.text: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, “the State” has the same meaning as in Part III.

articles.label: Article 37
articles.title: Application of the principles contained in this Part
articles.text: The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.

articles.label: Article 38
articles.title: State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people
articles.text:
(1)The State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life.
(2) The State shall, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vocations.

articles.label: Article 39
articles.title: Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State
articles.note: On clause (b): Property Owners Association (2024) held, 8:1, that not every item of private property is a "material resource of the community".

articles.label: Article 39A
articles.title: Equal justice and free legal aid
articles.text: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.

articles.label: Article 40
articles.title: Organisation of village panchayats
articles.text: The State shall take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government.

articles.label: Article 41
articles.title: Right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases
articles.text: The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of undeserved want.

articles.label: Article 42
articles.title: Provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
articles.text: The State shall make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.

articles.label: Article 43
articles.title: Living wage, etc, for workers
articles.text: The State shall endeavour to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.

articles.label: Article 43A
articles.title: Participation of workers in management of industries
articles.text: The State shall take steps, by suitable legislation or in any other way, to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry.

articles.label: Article 43B
articles.title: Promotion of co-operative societies
articles.text: The State shall endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.
articles.note: Inserted by the 97th Amendment (2011). Parts of that amendment (Part IXB, as applied to State co-operative societies) were struck down in Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021); Art 43B was not.

articles.label: Article 44
articles.title: Uniform civil code for the citizens
articles.text: The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.

articles.label: Article 45
articles.title: Provision for early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years
articles.text: The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
articles.note: Substituted by the 86th Amendment (2002). The original Art 45 (free and compulsory education up to 14 within ten years) became the Fundamental Right in Art 21A.

articles.label: Article 46
articles.title: Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections
articles.text: The State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, and, in particular, of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, and shall protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.

articles.label: Article 47
articles.title: Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living and to improve public health
articles.text: The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people and the improvement of public health as among its primary duties and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption except for medicinal purposes of intoxicating drinks and of drugs which are injurious to health.

articles.label: Article 48
articles.title: Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
articles.text: The State shall endeavour to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and shall, in particular, take steps for preserving and improving the breeds, and prohibiting the slaughter, of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle

articles.label: Article 48A
articles.title: Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life
articles.text: The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country.

articles.label: Article 49
articles.title: Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance
articles.text: It shall be the obligation of the State to protect every monument or place or object of artistic or historic interest, declared by or [under law made by Parliament] to be of national importance, from spoliation, disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal or export, as the case may be.

articles.label: Article 50
articles.title: Separation of judiciary from executive
articles.text: The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

articles.label: Article 51
articles.title: Promotion of international peace and security

articles.label: Article 51A
articles.title: Fundamental duties

articles.label: Article 300A
articles.title: Persons not to be deprived of property save by authority of law
articles.text: No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
articles.note: Inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978). A constitutional (not fundamental) right: K.T. Plantation (2011), Vidya Devi (2020), Bimal Kumar Shah (2024).

articles.label: Article 352
articles.title: Proclamation of Emergency
articles.text:
(1) If the President is satisfied that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India or of any part of the territory thereof is threatened, whether by war or external aggression or armed rebellion, he may, by Proclamation, make a declaration to that effect in respect of the whole of India or of such part of the territory thereof as may be specified in the Proclamation.
   Explanation. — A Proclamation of Emergency declaring that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by war or by external aggression or by armed rebellion may be made before the actual occurrence of war or of any such aggression or rebellion, if the President is satisfied that there is imminent danger thereof.
(2) A Proclamation issued under clause (1) may be varied or revoked by a subsequent Proclamation.
(3) The President shall not issue a Proclamation under clause (1) or a Proclamation varying such Proclamation unless the decision of the Union Cabinet (that is to say, the Council consisting of the Prime Minister and other Ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under article 75) that such a Proclamation may be issued has been communicated to him in writing.
(4) Every Proclamation issued under this article shall be laid before each House of Parliament and shall, except where it is a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation, cease to operate at the expiration of one month unless before the expiration of that period it has been approved by resolutions of both Houses of Parliament:
   Provided that if any such Proclamation (not being a Proclamation revoking a previous Proclamation) is issued at a time when the House of the People has been dissolved, or the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during the period of one month referred to in this clause, and if a resolution approving the Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People before the expiration of that period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution, unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days a resolution approving the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People.
(5) A Proclamation so approved shall, unless revoked, cease to operate on the expiration of a period of six months from the date of the passing of the second of the resolutions approving the Proclamation under clause (4):
   Provided that if and so often as a resolution approving the continuance in force of such a Proclamation is passed by both Houses of Parliament the Proclamation shall, unless revoked, continue in force for a further period of six months from the date on which it would otherwise have ceased to operate under this clause:
   Provided further that if the dissolution of the House of the People takes place during any such period of six months and a resolution approving the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States but no resolution with respect to the continuance in force of such Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People during the said period, the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of thirty days from the date on which the House of the People first sits after its reconstitution unless before the expiration of the said period of thirty days, a resolution approving the continuance in force of the Proclamation has been also passed by the House of the People.
(6) For the purposes of clauses (4) and (5), a resolution may be passed by either House of Parliament only by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the Members of that House present and voting.
(7) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing clauses, the President shall revoke a Proclamation issued under clause (1) or a Proclamation varying such Proclamation if the House of the People passes a resolution disapproving, or, as the case may be, disapproving the continuance in force of, such Proclamation.
(8) Where a notice in writing signed by not less than one-tenth of the total number of members of the House of the People has been given, of their intention to move a resolution for disapproving, or, as the case may be, for disapproving the continuance in force of, a Proclamation issued under clause (1) or a Proclamation varying such Proclamation, —
(a) to the Speaker, if the House is in session; or
(b) to the President, if the House is not in session,
a special sitting of the House shall be held within fourteen days from the date on which such notice is received by the Speaker, or, as the case may be, by the President, for the purpose of considering such resolution.
(9) The power conferred on the President by this article shall include the power to issue different Proclamations on different grounds, being war or external aggression or armed rebellion or imminent danger of war or external aggression or armed rebellion, whether or not there is a Proclamation already issued by the President under clause (1) and such Proclamation is in operation.

articles.label: Article 358
articles.title: Suspension of provisions of article 19 during emergencies
articles.text:
(1) While a Proclamation of Emergency declaring that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by war or by external aggression is in operation, nothing in article 19 shall restrict the power of the State as defined in Part III to make any law or to take any executive action which the State would but for the provisions contained in that Part be competent to make or to take, but any law so made shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect as soon as the Proclamation ceases to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the law so ceases to have effect:
   Provided that where such Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in any part of the territory of India, any such law may be made, or any such executive action may be taken, under this article in relation to or in any State or Union territory in which or in any part of which the Proclamation of Emergency is not in operation, if and in so far as the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of the territory of India in which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply —
(a) to any law which does not contain a recital to the effect that such law is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation when it is made; or
(b) to any executive action taken otherwise than under a law containing such a recital.

articles.label: Article 359
articles.title: Suspension of the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part III during emergencies
articles.text:
(1) Where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, the President may by order declare that the right to move any court for the enforcement of such of the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21) as may be mentioned in the order and all proceedings pending in any court for the enforcement of the rights so mentioned shall remain suspended for the period during which the Proclamation is in force or for such shorter period as may be specified in the order.
(1A) While an order made under clause (1) mentioning any of the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21) is in operation, nothing in that Part conferring those rights shall restrict the power of the State as defined in the said Part to make any law or to take any executive action which the State would but for the provisions contained in that Part be competent to make or to take, but any law so made shall, to the extent of the incompetency, cease to have effect as soon as the order aforesaid ceases to operate, except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the law so ceases to have effect:
   Provided that where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in any part of the territory of India, any such law may be made, or any such executive action may be taken, under this article in relation to or in any State or Union territory in which or in any part of which the Proclamation of Emergency is not in operation, if and in so far as the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of the territory of India in which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.
(1B) Nothing in clause (1A) shall apply —
(a) to any law which does not contain a recital to the effect that such law is in relation to the Proclamation of Emergency in operation when it is made; or
(b) to any executive action taken otherwise than under a law containing such a recital.(
(2) An order made as aforesaid may extend to the whole or any part of the territory of India:
   Provided that where a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation only in a part of the territory of India, any such order shall not extend to any other part of the territory of India unless the President, being satisfied that the security of India or any part of the territory thereof is threatened by activities in or in relation to the part of the territory of India in which the Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, considers such extension to be necessary.
(3) Every order made under clause (1) shall, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before each House of Parliament.
articles.note: The words "(except articles 20 and 21)" were added by the 44th Amendment (1978), after ADM Jabalpur.

articles.label: Article 368
articles.title: Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor
articles.text:
(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.
(2) An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill:
   Provided that if such amendment seeks to make any change in —
(a) article 54, article 55, article 73, article 162 or article 241, or
(b) Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, or Chapter I of Part XI, or
(c) any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule, or
(d) the representation of States in Parliament, or
(e) the provisions of this article,
the amendment shall also require to be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States by resolutions to that effect passed by those Legislatures before the Bill making provision for such amendment is presented to the President for assent.
(3) Nothing in article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article.
(4) No amendment of this Constitution (including the provisions of Part III) made or purporting to have been made under this article [whether before or after the commencement of section 55 of the Constitution (Fortysecond Amendment) Act, 1976] shall be called in question in any court on any ground.
(5) For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that there shall be no limitation whatever on the constituent power of Parliament to amend by way of addition, variation or repeal the provisions of this Constitution under this article.
articles.note: Clauses (4) and (5), inserted by the 42nd Amendment, were struck down in Minerva Mills (1980) but remain printed in the text. Clause (3) and the word "constituent power" were added by the 24th Amendment (1971).

solvers.title: Is the law valid under Article 14?
solvers.use: A law or order treats one group differently from another.
steps: Identify the classification and the object
State who is included, who is left out, and what the law is trying to achieve. Name the object from the statute, its preamble or its context.
Is there a real, understandable difference between those included and those left out — not an arbitrary or fanciful one?
Does that difference have a rational relation to the object of the law? Test it against the object you identified.

Single-entity laws (Chiranjit Lal); unguided discretion (Anwar Ali v. Kathi Raning, Moopil Nair); wide latitude for tax and economic laws (R.K. Garg, East India Tobacco); classification that loses its nexus over time (Motor General Traders); step-by-step, under-inclusive laws (Ambica Mills).
Even if the classification passes, is the State action arbitrary? Arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality.
Valid or invalid, and why — name the limb that decides it. If invalid, say whether the bad part can be severed.

solvers.title: Is the restriction on an Article 19 freedom valid?
solvers.use: A law or order limits speech, assembly, association, movement, residence or occupation.
steps: Art 19 protects citizens only. Companies cannot claim it, but shareholders can; foreigners cannot.
Which freedom, and is it directly affected?
Name the sub-clause. Ask whether the direct and inevitable effect of the measure falls on that freedom.
A restriction must be imposed by law; executive instructions alone are not enough.
A permitted ground in the matching clause
Speech: Art 19(2)'s eight grounds; assembly 19(3); association 19(4); movement and residence 19(5); occupation 19(6). The grounds are exhaustive.

Substance and procedure; nature of the right, the evil, proportion (V.G. Row); proximate, not remote, nexus (Lohia 1960, Rangarajan); only incitement, not discussion or advocacy (Shreya Singhal); not excessive (Chintaman Rao); proportionality (Anuradha Bhasin).
State the result clause by clause; distinguish law and order from public order where relevant (Lohia 1965).

solvers.title: Has Article 21 been violated?
solvers.use: Someone is deprived of life or personal liberty, or a claim is made under the expanded Art 21.
steps: Art 21 protects every person — citizens and non-citizens.
Is life or personal liberty engaged?
"Life" is more than animal existence; it includes dignity, livelihood, privacy, speedy trial, education up to 14 and more.
Is the deprivation by procedure established by law?
There must be a valid law; the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary.
Test the same law against Art 14 and the relevant Art 19 freedoms — the rights are not watertight compartments.
A law can fail even with procedure if it is substantively unjust — for example, a mandatory death sentence.
Arts 20 and 21 cannot be suspended (Art 359 after the 44th Amendment). Compensation is available for custodial violations.

solvers.title: Is the law void under Article 13?
solvers.use: A statute conflicts with a Fundamental Right and you must say what happens to it.
steps: Laws in force before 26 January 1950 fall under Art 13(1); later laws under Art 13(2).
Void only to the extent of inconsistency and only from 26 January 1950; dormant, not dead — it revives if the Fundamental Right is later amended.
Void from inception and not revived by a later amendment — but where the right is for citizens only, the law still operates against non-citizens.
Strike only what is void if the rest is a complete, workable code and the legislature would have enacted it alone.
Uncodified personal law (Narasu Appa Mali) and constitutional amendments (Art 13(4)) are outside Art 13.

solvers.title: Is the constitutional amendment valid?
steps: Special majority in each House; ratification by half the States for the provisos (federal provisions, Art 368 itself).
After the 24th Amendment (Arts 13(4), 368(3)) an amendment is not "law" under Art 13 — Golak Nath no longer applies.
Does the amendment damage or destroy an essential feature — supremacy of the Constitution, judicial review, limited amending power, the FR–DPSP balance, rule of law?
Laws added after 24 April 1973 can be tested against Part III and the basic structure.
Valid, or struck down to the extent it violates the basic structure.

solvers.title: Is the reservation valid (Arts 15(4), 16(4))?
solvers.use: A reservation or special provision for a backward class is challenged.
steps: Is the group a backward class?
Social and educational backwardness; caste can be an indicator but not the sole test for 15(4) (Balaji); for 16(4) a caste can be a class (Indra Sawhney).
The advanced members must be excluded for OBCs; it also applies to SC/ST in promotions (Jarnail Singh).
Reservation should ordinarily not exceed 50%; carry-forward cannot breach it (Devadasan); EWS reservation sits outside it (Janhit Abhiyan).
Arts 16(4A) and (4B); the State must justify inadequacy of representation and keep efficiency in view (Art 335).
Is it equality or an exception?
Arts 15(4) and 16(4) are facets of equality, not exceptions to it.
Backwardness tied to the Hindu social order does not automatically carry over after conversion.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 6 How to Use These Notes These notes consolidate every document in the four classnotes files — raw lecture transcripts, structured lecture notes, the verbatim class record, worksheet problems and the two study companions — into one day-wise, exam-ready compendium. The course ran from 15 July 2026 to 7 October 2026 across twenty-one recorded sessions. Where a document carries no printed date, its position in the sequence has been reconstructed from the teaching flow and is marked with a c. (circa) before the date; nothing else has been re-ordered. Three reading aids run through the document. Case boxes (gold-edged) carry facts, holdings and the single principle each case settles. Professor's Aside boxes reproduce, in italics, the informal, niche and anecdotal things the professor said in class — the stories, jokes, warnings and political commentary that never appear in textbooks but which he repeatedly said would be examined. The professor uses Article 13(2) to open the deepest question of the early course — can personal laws be declared void when they violate fundamental rights? Personal Laws versus Fundamental Rights The professor frames the problem through marriage. Islamic law does not permit a Hindu to marry a Muslim girl unless she converts — and conversion, he asks, why should she want to convert? Article 21, read broadly, says a person may marry anybody. The personal law therefore violates a citizen's fundamental right, and the violation is doubly suspect because it is gender-based: a Muslim boy may marry anybody, including a Hindu girl, but a Muslim girl cannot marry outside her religion without converting. The question for inquiry: can such a Koranic practice, violating Article 21, be declared void under Article 13(2)? A parallel problem comes from constitutional history: by constitutional amendment some fundamental rights have been taken away — above all the right to property. Whether those amendments are valid is studied under Article 13(3). The Reform Record of Parliament — and the POCSO Digression Parliament, the professor argues, has been discriminatory in its reform energy. Starting from the very first Parliament, every manner of reform was introduced among Hindus. In Hindu tradition marriage was a Kanya Daan given before puberty; in Muslim law too the age of puberty was the age of marriage. The age of marriage was later raised to eighteen while the age of consent stood at sixteen — and the professor recounts joining a mild protest against the resulting incoherence: “What is this? Do you want to keep our daughters in adulterous relationships? They cannot marry, but they can have sex? Raise the age of consent to eighteen as well.” Under POCSO the age of consent became eighteen (following the Justice Verma Committee — Verma being originally from Satna, near Indore), and the Supreme Court had remarked only days earlier that such strict laws on the sexuality of girls aged sixteen to eighteen have sent thousands of boys — and girls, the law being gender-neutral — to jail. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE

The First Amendment — Kameshwar Singh and Article 31B Asked why the First Constitutional Amendment came about, a student (Kanishk) answers correctly: Champakam Dorairajan. The professor confirms it was one reason — but the most important was property. He recalls Dr. Ambedkar's final Constituent Assembly speech (assigned as compulsory reading): “Today we are going to start a life of contradictions.” After working the class through the answer, the doctrine emerges: political equality has arrived — one person, one vote; one vote, one value — but a huge gulf persists in the economic and social dimensions of society, and that disparity must be dismantled by the fastest path if the country is to remain united. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE There is a character in our Ramayana — Bali. Whoever fought him, half their power came to him. When even the foolish students of NLU stand up in moot court, the students of traditional colleges think, “Oh dear, this person is from NLU, he will certainly speak well” — half of them fall into depression and their performance deteriorates. That is what economic disparity does to confidence. I have lived outside the village for forty years, and still, sometimes, confidence fails me. Land being a State subject, every State enacted zamindari abolition laws, taking the landlords' land and giving it to the tenants who worked it. The rajas and maharajas — whose rights the professor illustrates with the full style of the complainant in the leading case: “Maharajadhiraj Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga” — challenged the Bihar Act, and the Patna High Court declared it unconstitutional under Article 13(2): property was a fundamental right, and the Act took it away. Nehru, greatly distressed, brought the First Amendment, inserting Article 31A and Article 31B and creating the Ninth Schedule. A student (Sanika) reads Article 31B aloud. Its effect: any Act placed in the Ninth Schedule is deemed never to have become void for violating Part III, notwithstanding any judgment of any court. The original Constitution had eight schedules (which the class was told to memorise on day one); the Ninth was added by the First Amendment. With it, the Kameshwar Singh judgment was reduced to zero — the Bihar Act sailed through. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE If any act is placed in the Ninth Schedule, that act will become like Duryodhan after Gandhari opened her eyes — his body became like a thunderbolt; he could not be killed. The Schedule itself is not immune from review — the Acts placed within it are. The professor's image: “The Constituent Assembly made an umbrella where rainwater would not go. Call that umbrella the 9th Schedule.” Article 368 requires passage by both Houses — under Article 79, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) and the House of the People (Lok Sabha). The Provisional Parliament problem of 1951: elections were held only in 1951–52, so the Rajya Sabha did not yet exist when the First Amendment was passed. Article 379 (now repealed) gave the provisional Parliament all the powers of a regular Parliament; the President could make rules to remove difficulties. “If Rajya Sabha was not there, should the country have been locked up? Or should there be some mechanism for improvement?” Ambedkar's Three Contradictions In his final speech Dr. Ambedkar identified: (1) political equality — “one man, one vote, one vote, one value”; (2) social inequality — hierarchies of caste and class persisting; (3) economic inequality — disparities in wealth and land. The First Amendment's purpose was to remove the economic contradiction by enabling land reform; the constitutional goal is an egalitarian society — justice, social, economic and political. Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India (1951) Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India 5-judge bench · unanimous (5:0) · judgment by M. Patanjali Sastri J. · P.R. Das for petitioners · M.C. Setalvad (first Attorney General of India — a general-knowledge point) for the Union Facts · Zamindars of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh challenged land reform laws as violating Part III. Parliament responded with the First Amendment (Articles 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule). Blocked from attacking the Acts directly, the zamindars challenged the Amendment itself — strategic logic: if the tree falls, the branch falls anyway. Held · The First Constitutional Amendment is valid. (1) Article 368 confers constituent power, distinct from ordinary legislative power under Articles 245–246; Article 13(2) applies only to the latter. (2) The definition of “law” in Article 13(3) deliberately omits “constitutional amendment.” (3) Article 368 contains no exception for Part III — the framers could have written “except Part III” and did not. Principle · Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights; an amendment is not “law” under Article 13(2). The six petitioner arguments — and the lesson in over-pleading # Petitioners' argument Court's response 1 Only a proper two-House Parliament can amend; the one-house provisional Parliament lacked competence Article 379 empowered the provisional Parliament 2 The President wrongly modified Article 368 to permit single-House amendment Considered weak — over-pleading weakens a case: when one ground is found false, the judge may view the entire petition with suspicion 3 An amendment is “law” under Article 13(2) — Parliament is “State” under Article 12 Rejected — see ratio 4 State ratification was necessary (Arts 31A/31B affected court powers) Only direct, not indirect, effects on courts trigger ratification

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 13 # Petitioners' argument Court's response 5 The Bill was changed after introduction Parliament is master of its own procedure — “slave only to the Constitution” 6 Parliament cannot legislate on land (State subject) Conflates legislative power with constituent power The petitioners' case, argument by argument The respondents' two textual pillars: Article 13(3) enumerates ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages — not constitutional amendments; and Article 368 speaks of amending “any provision of this Constitution” without carving out Part III. Both omissions are deliberate. Under constituent power, “Parliament becomes as powerful as the Constituent Assembly itself was. Just as there were no restrictions on the Constituent Assembly, similarly no restrictions will remain with Parliament either, because restrictions are not written anywhere.” Ordinary legislative power Constituent power Derived from Articles 245–246 Derived from Article 368 Subject to Article 13(2) Not subject to Article 13(2) Limited by the Seventh Schedule As powerful as the Constituent Assembly itself Makes ordinary laws Makes and amends the Constitution The two powers of Parliament distinguished Doctrine of harmonious construction Two apparently conflicting provisions are interpreted so that both survive: Article 13 governs legislative power; Article 368 governs constituent power; each operates in its own sphere. Reading Article 13 broadly would render Article 368 “dead” for Part III — an interpretation courts must avoid. “Harmony means making a balance between both, keeping both alive. Lest one dies. Both survive.” Sajjan Singh (1965) — the Seeds of Doubt The Seventeenth Amendment (1964), expanding the Ninth Schedule and amending Article 31A, was challenged. The majority (Gajendragadkar C.J., Wanchoo and Raghubar Dayal JJ.) reaffirmed Shankari Prasad. But two judges — both with Nagpur connections, the professor notes — wrote separate opinions that planted the Basic Structure seed. ●Justice Hidayatullah: Fundamental Rights are “primordial sacrosanct” rights; Article 13(2) does not expressly exclude amendments; rights of such significance cannot be abrogated in the same manner as ordinary provisions; certain rights are inalienable — recognised by the Constitution, not created by it. ●Justice Mudholkar: the comparative argument. At a Banaras Hindu University conference a German professor had described the Basic Law's eternity clause — Article 79(3) entrenches the federal structure, the democratic and social state and the inviolability of human dignity against all amendment. A Pakistan Supreme Court judgment (likely Fazlul Quader Chowdhury, 1963) had similarly limited amending power. And the U.S. Constitution's Article V contains two unamendable matters: the slave-trade clause (temporarily, until 1808) and equal suffrage in the Senate (permanently — no State, without its consent, may be deprived of its equal suffrage). If other constitutions entrench cores, the Indian Constitution too must have essential features beyond

State of Punjab (1967) Golak Nath v. State of Punjab 11-judge bench · 6:5 · majority led by K. Subba Rao C.J. Facts · The validity of the Seventeenth Amendment's protection of land reform laws was again in issue; the Court reconsidered Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh. Held · Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. Article 368 (its marginal heading then reading “Procedure for amendment”) supplies only procedure, not power; the power flows from the residuary legislative power — Entry 97, List I read with Article 248 — making an amendment an exercise of legislative power, hence “law” under Article 13(2), hence void insofar as it abridges Part III. Principle · Fundamental Rights placed beyond the amending power; the doctrine of prospective overruling introduced — the ruling operates only from the judgment date, so all earlier amendments survived. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE That poor guy won the case, but he didn't get any relief — the property already taken remained taken. The 24th Amendment (1971) — Parliament Responds Golaknath holding 24th Amendment's answer Article 368 is merely procedural; power comes from Entry 97 + Art 248 Marginal heading changed to “Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor”; “Power” written into the text An amendment is “law” within Article 13(2) Article 13(4) inserted: “Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment made under article 368” Article 13(2) voids rights-abridging amendments A non-obstante clause — “Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution” — prefixed to Article 368(1); a mirror clause 368(3) added for abundant caution — Presidential assent made mandatory: the President “shall” assent and the Constitution “shall stand amended” — the President becomes a rubber stamp How the 24th Amendment dismantled Golaknath pillar by pillar

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 15 Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — the Middle Path Thirteen judges — the largest bench in Indian history — tested the 24th Amendment. Between Shankari Prasad's unlimited power and Golaknath's no power over Part III, the Court took the middle path: Parliament can amend any provision, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot destroy or abrogate the Constitution's basic structure or essential identity. The 24th Amendment was upheld, but the amending power it confirmed is a limited power. (The case is taught in full detail on 22 July — Day 3.) Issue Shankari Prasad Golaknath Kesavananda Nature of amending power Constituent (distinct) Legislative (same) Constituent but limited Amendment of FRs Permitted Not permitted Permitted, subject to basic structure Art 13 applies to amendments? No Yes No — Golaknath overruled on this point Art 368 provides Power + procedure Procedure only Power + procedure Ultimate limit None Absolute bar Basic Structure Comparative analysis of the three watershed decisions Comparative and Historical References U.S. Article V offers a four-way amendment process (Congress proposes with State legislatures ratifying — the common route; Congress proposes with State conventions ratifying — used once, for the 21st Amendment repealing Prohibition; two-thirds of State legislatures demand a convention — never used; and convention-plus-convention). In the United States amendment is treated as a political question: no judicially enforced basic structure exists there. The German Basic Law (1949), Article 79(3), expressly entrenches the division into Länder, the Länder's participation in legislation, and the principles of human dignity (Article 1) and the democratic, social federal state (Article 20). Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) U.S. Supreme Court · 7:2 Facts · Dred Scott, enslaved, sued for freedom having lived with his owner in a free State and territory. Held · African Americans, enslaved or free, were not citizens and could not sue; the Missouri Compromise was unconstitutional. “Once a slave, always a slave — you can never become a free citizen.” Principle · Widely regarded as the worst U.S. Supreme Court decision; it inflamed public opinion and catalysed the Civil War (1861–65). The Civil War connection to Article 356: Lincoln — a self-educated man of humble origins, early a shoemaker, who had lost almost every election before winning the presidency — sent the military to prevent secession at the cost of roughly 800,000 casualties in a country of 31 million, and was assassinated shortly after. The Indian framers, aware of that bloodshed, designed President's Rule as a constitutional safety valve — a Centre may take over a State's administration when constitutional machinery fails, without armed conflict. (The Second Amendment's right to bear arms, the lecture noted, itself grew from the States' desire to maintain militias against federal overreach.)

The Original Constitution — Art and Symbolism Students are directed to examine the original hand-written Constitution, illuminated by artists: calligraphy by Prem Behari Narain Raizada; depictions of Lord Ram; Lord Krishna imparting the Bhagavad Gita on a chariot — placed in the Directive Principles section to symbolise Raj Dharma; and figures from Islamic history, including Akbar, in Part 8. The artwork is a deliberate choice of the framers to represent India's diverse cultural and religious heritage, directly connected to the constitutional value of secularism. The Case His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala AIR 1973 SC 1461 · 13 judges — the largest Constitution Bench in Supreme Court history · decided 24 April 1973 · a deeply fragmented 7:6 verdict — “a 6.5 to 6.5 judgment” pulled to a majority by the Chief Justice · 66 days of hearing (the longest until the Ayodhya hearings, at about 63) Facts · Kesavananda Bharati, chief of a Kerala religious sect (matha) which owned significant land, petitioned under Article 32 to enforce rights under Articles 25, 26, 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 against the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 and its 1969 Amendment. While the petition was pending, the Indira Gandhi government passed the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments (partly to overcome Golaknath), and the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1971 was placed in the Ninth Schedule. The petition was amended to challenge the amendments themselves. Held · By 7:6 — Parliament may amend any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but cannot abrogate or destroy the Constitution's basic structure or identity. Principle · The Basic Structure Doctrine. Key advocates: for the petitioners, Nani A. Palkhivala (leader) with Daphtary, Chagla, Soli Sorabjee, Deewan and Harindranath; for the State, H.M. Seervai, Advocate General of Maharashtra — “the world's greatest constitutional jurist,” not to be “limited” to a state role.

The word ‘amendment’ postulates that the old Constitution survives without loss of identity despite the change and continues even though it has been subjected to alterations.” A mere retention of trivial provisions while the basic structure is destroyed is no amendment: it is not permissible to touch the foundation or alter the basic institutional pattern. The Sun is the pre-constitutional law radiating legal force; the Moon is the inconsistent Fundamental Right; the shadow is Article 13(1); the Earth is the affected population — for citizens the law is in shadow, for non-citizens it shines fully. When the Moon moves away (the Fundamental Right is amended), the Sun automatically becomes visible again. The problem the doctrine solves: declaring all inconsistent pre-constitutional laws dead would destroy vested rights, past transactions and completed decrees, creating legal chaos. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 22 The four simultaneous states of an inconsistent pre-Constitutional law: (1) as against citizens — dormant or moribund, unenforceable; (2) as against non-citizens — fully operative, since Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30 are citizens' rights (Keshav Madhav Menon); (3) for pre-Constitution transactions — fully effective, Article 13(1) not being retrospective (Bhikaji Narain); (4) potential for revival — automatic when the inconsistency is removed. Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955) 5-judge bench · AIR 1955 SC 781 · locus classicus of eclipse Facts · The C.P. and Berar Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1948 — enacted under the Government of India Act, 1935 by a legislature with plenary powers — created a State monopoly in motor transport, clashing with Article 19(1)(g) as it then stood. The First Amendment (1951) added the state-monopoly clause to Article 19(6). Held · Per B.K. Mukherjea J., unanimously: the impugned law “became, as it were, eclipsed, for the time being, by the fundamental right... Such laws were not dead for all purposes... It is only as against the citizens that they remained in a dormant or moribund condition.” The amendment “removed the shadow”; the 1948 Act revived automatically — no re-enactment required. Principle · Pre-constitutional laws are void only quoad citizens; supervening inconsistency is curable retrospectively by constitutional amendment. Keshav Madhav Menon v. State of Bombay (1951) AIR 1951 SC 128 · per S.R. Das J. Facts · Prosecution under the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931 for publishing a pamphlet without prior authorisation; proceedings had begun before the Constitution. Held · Article 13(1) operates prospectively from the Constitution's commencement; it does not invalidate past transactions or pending proceedings under laws valid when the act was done. “The voidness of the law is from the date of the commencement of the Constitution and not from an earlier date.” Principle · The distinction between void ab initio and void from a future date is the very foundation of the eclipse doctrine. Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1959) AIR 1959 SC 648 · 4:1 · per S.K. Das J. Facts · The U.P. State Road Transport Act, 1951 — a post-Constitutional state monopoly — was challenged under Article 19(1)(g); the State invoked Bhikaji Narain's revival logic. Held · Article 13(2) imposes a constitutional prohibition; the State legislature “had no power to make the impugned law.” A post-Constitutional inconsistent law is “still-born” and void ab initio — “A dead law cannot be revived by any constitutional amendment... it must be re-enacted.” Principle · Eclipse applies exclusively to pre-Constitutional laws under Article 13(1). Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1955) AIR 1955 SC 728 Facts · The U.P. Road Transport Act, 1951 (post-Constitutional) was challenged while the First Amendment's Article 19(6) change was in force. Held · Applying Thomas Cooley's American doctrine: “A statute void for unconstitutionality is dead and cannot be vitalized by a subsequent amendment of the Constitution removing the constitutional objection but must be re-enacted.” Principle · The critical difference between pre- and post-Constitutional laws: a constitutional amendment does not retroactively confer jurisdiction on the legislature that passed the void law.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 23 State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974) AIR 1974 SC 1300 · per H.R. Khanna J. Facts · The Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1953 (post-Constitutional) required employers' contributions; provisions were challenged under Articles 19(1)(f) and 14 by a company (a citizen). Held · A post-Constitutional law void for violating Articles 14 or 19 is void only quoad citizens — the contravention exists only in relation to those entitled to the right. The law remains valid and enforceable against non-citizens. Principle · Modifies the “still-born” theory by making it person-specific: void in personam for citizens, not void in rem against the world. Revival through the Ninth Schedule — and the Dularey Lodh anomaly Article 31B is the one great exception to the re-enactment rule: it deems a listed Act never to have been void — an absolute constitutional fiction applying to pre- and post-Constitutional laws alike. But its limits were later drawn: Waman Rao (1981) held laws added to the Ninth Schedule before Kesavananda (24 April 1973) to be beyond review, while post-1973 insertions remain challengeable; I.R. Coelho (2007, 9 judges) confirmed that any law placed in the Schedule after 24 April 1973 is open to review on the twin grounds of Part III violation and basic structure. Dularey Lodh v. III Additional District Judge, Kanpur (1984) is the anomaly — applying eclipse language to a post-Constitutional statutory bar blocking a decree: once the 1972 Act's bar was removed, “by virtue of the doctrine of eclipse the decree will revive and become at once operative and executable.” It has not been followed as a general principle. The four arguments for extending eclipse to post-Constitutional laws: (1) legislative incompetence is relative to the Fundamental Right, not absolute — the law should not be treated as non-est; (2) Articles 200–201 and 213(3) contemplate laws of doubtful vires, implying some existence; (3) Parliament's power to repeal State laws (Article 252) presupposes their valid existence; (4) practical sense — re-enactment for a cured inconsistency is formalistic waste. The settled position nonetheless remains Deep Chand's: eclipse is for pre-Constitutional laws only. Doctrine of Severability Severability is embedded in the text — “to the extent of such inconsistency” — in both 13(1) and 13(2). Borrowed from American law (the “Doctrine of Separability”), the judicial function is to excise the malignant portion, not kill the organism; but if malignant and healthy tissue are inextricably interwoven, the entire statute falls. The twin test: (1) separability in fact — the valid and invalid parts must be physically and notionally separable; (2) separability in intent — would the legislature have enacted the valid part without the invalid? If either answer is negative, the whole Act falls. Rule Content (R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla, 1957) 1 The intention of the legislature is determinative — the master rule: would it have passed the valid portion knowing the infirmity? 2 Where valid and invalid provisions are inextricably mixed, the invalidity of a part fails the whole 3 Where provisions are distinct and severable, the valid portion survives as a self-contained code 4 Even distinct sections forming a single integrated scheme may fall together — substance over form 5 If the remainder is “so thin and truncated” as to be materially different legislation, all falls 6 Judicial legislation prohibited — if severance would require rewriting, the court strikes down the whole; courts delete, never amend

Union of India (1957) AIR 1957 SC 628 · 5-judge bench · locus classicus Facts · The Prize Competitions Act, 1955 defined “prize competition” broadly enough to cover both skill competitions (crosswords, essays — protected business under 19(1)(g)) and gambling (lotteries, lucky draws — res extra commercium, outside 19(1)(g)). Held · The Act was unconstitutional as applied to skill competitions but valid as to gambling; the distinction was “clear-cut and well-recognized,” and Parliament's primary object was the gambling evil. The Court read down the definition: the Act applies only to gambling competitions. Principle · Severability by restricting application — the classic instance of saving an Act by confining it to the valid class. Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) AIR 1950 SC 124 · 6 judges Facts · Section 9(1-A), Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 — banning entry and circulation of journals “for securing the public safety or the maintenance of public order.” “Public safety” was not a ground in Article 19(2) as it then stood. Held · The provision fell entirely: the distinction between “public safety” and “public order” was “not precise”; severing the words would leave a power still capable of unconstitutional application — danger of misuse is the decisive factor. Principle · Inseverability where permissible and impermissible applications cannot be cleanly separated. State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) AIR 1951 SC 318 Facts · The Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949, challenged on multiple grounds. Held · Eight specific unconstitutional sections were severed; the core Prohibition Act survived as a complete, workable code. Principle · Rule 3 in action — distinct invalid parts removed, the rest upheld. A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) AIR 1950 SC 27 Facts · Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 barred detainees from disclosing grounds of detention to a court. Held · Only Section 14 violated Articles 19(1)(a) and 21; the rest of the Act was a complete code without it. Principle · “Save as much of an Act as can be saved” — declare void only what must be void. Mithu Singh v. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 25 Held · The classification (life convicts versus other murderers) lacked intelligible differentia, and mandatory death excluded judicial consideration of mitigating circumstances, violating Articles 14 and 21. Section 303 was a standalone provision, cleanly severable from the IPC's sentencing scheme (Section 302 continues to govern). Principle · A penal provision excised cleanly; the rest of the Code operates normally. The reconciliation came in Superintendent, Central Prison, Fatehgarh v. Ram Manohar Lohia (1960), per Subba Rao J.: in RMDC the two activities were conceptually distinct with no confusion risk; in Romesh Thappar the two purposes overlapped imprecisely, with a real danger the power granted for the constitutional purpose would be used for the unconstitutional one. The decisive factor is the danger of misuse — essentially a test of overbreadth. Doctrine of Waiver Waiver is the intentional, voluntary relinquishment of a known right. Its elements: (1) knowledge of the right; (2) intention to abandon it; (3) voluntariness — no coercion or duress. Can a citizen waive a fundamental right? The answer is a resounding no. Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959) AIR 1959 SC 149 · 5-judge bench · majority of C.J. S.R. Das, Kapur and Subba Rao JJ.; N.H. Bhagwati J. concurring more broadly; S.K. Das J. dissenting Facts · Basheshar Nath, a wealthy businessman, settled under Section 8A of the Taxation of Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947, agreeing to pay about Rs. 4.5 lakh in instalments. When Section 5(1) of that Act was held unconstitutional in Suraj Mall Mohta (1955), he stopped paying; the Department sought recovery as arrears of land revenue, arguing he had waived his Article 14 right by settling. Held · Fundamental rights cannot be waived. Article 14 is a principle of public policy, the foundation of the Constitution — not a private right to be bartered away. Principle · Justice Subba Rao's rationale: rights are limitations on State power, not gifts; “The large majority of our people are economically poor, educationally backward, and politically not yet conscious of their rights... They may, without understanding the consequences, agree to waive their rights. It would be the duty of the Court to protect them against themselves.” Waiver assumes equal bargaining power — a fiction in India. Bhagwati J. went further: no fundamental right in Part III can be waived. The dissenter S.K. Das J. distinguished rights for the public benefit (Articles 15, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, 24 — non-waivable) from rights for individual advantage (Articles 16, 19, and the Article 14 right at issue — waivable); the settlement falling in the second category, the petitioner had validly waived. The deep rationales of the majority: Part III is a charter of public policy (jus publicum), not a contract; allowing waiver would let the State extract rights-surrenders for licenses and settlements, making rights negotiable commodities; the Indian reality of unequal bargaining power imposes a paternalistic duty; and constitutional morality binds the State even where the individual does not insist. The modern critique Arvind Datar's critique: every right necessarily includes the right not to exercise it — the right to speech includes the right to remain silent; post-Puttaswamy decisional autonomy recognises informed choices to forgo rights (the reality-show contract; the voluntarily posted photograph). Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978) held that the right to carry on business includes the right not to carry it on — a choice inherent in the right. And Olga Tellis: estoppel cannot stand against fundamental rights; no individual act can validate a void law.
