Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 27 DAY 5 c. 23–24 July 2026 Basic Structure Consolidated & Article 14 Introduced 24th Amendment text · 42nd Amendment & Minerva Mills · I.R. Coelho and the Ninth Schedule · Dissecting Article 14 · The Salma & Prapti hypothetical This session (undated; it recaps Kesavananda and sets up the Article 14 sequence) begins with the text of the amended Article 368. The 24th Amendment's Article 368(3) — “Nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article” — and the consequential Article 13(4) were designed as a watertight separation between amending power and fundamental rights: Parliament's direct legislative answer to Golaknath. From Kesavananda to Minerva Mills Kesavananda (7:6) overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment, but on the implied-limitation reasoning of constitutional identity: the Constitution possesses a fundamental identity, an essential character constituting its core; Article 368 grants the power to amend, not to destroy. Illustrative constituents of the basic structure identified across the judgments: supremacy of the Constitution; the republican and democratic form of government (one cannot amend in a monarchy or a foreign ruler); secularism; federalism and the distribution of powers; separation of powers; the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Articles 32, 136, 141 and 142; and Fundamental Rights — while not all FRs are per se basic structure, some are so foundational that their destruction would violate it; the essence of Part III is protected. The executive's retort was the 42nd Amendment (1976), the Emergency-era “Mini-Constitution.” Article 368(4): “No amendment of this Constitution (including the provisions of Part III) made or purporting to have been made under this article whether before or after the commencement of section 55 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 shall be called in question in any court on any ground.” Article 368(5) declared that there shall be “no limitation whatever” on the constituent power. The first clause was a direct ouster of the judiciary's Kesavananda jurisdiction; the second an assertion of unlimited power. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) Y.V. Chandrachud and P.N. Bhagwati JJ. prominent · suo motu cognizance of sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment Facts · The immediate issue was a challenge under Article 31C, but the Court took up the validity of the 42nd Amendment's clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 on its own motion. Held · Twin holdings: (1) the Indian scheme vests supremacy in the Constitution, not in Parliament — Parliament is a creature of the Constitution; (2) judicial review of constitutional amendments is an integral basic feature. Article 368(4) was struck down as violative of basic structure; so was 368(5), which sought to destroy the limited nature of the amending power — itself part of the basic structure. Principle · The final synthesis: Parliament may amend under Article 368; Article 13 does not bar amendments; but any amendment destroying the basic structure is void. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) 9-judge bench · unanimous Facts · Post-Kesavananda legislatures kept adding laws to the Ninth Schedule — some allegedly arbitrary, even near-100% reservation destroying equality. Held · The cut-off is 24 April 1973, the date Kesavananda was decided. Any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule after that date is not immune from judicial review, and can be tested on the twin grounds of Part III violation and basic structure violation; if it fails, it is struck down.

Article 14 — Dissecting the Text “The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.” — Article 14 Element Analysis “The State” — the duty-bearer A vertical right enforceable against the State; Article 12 defines it. Test — Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. IICB (2002): financial, functional and administrative domination, or deep and pervasive government control. Even private universities (e.g. SRM, per the Chennai case) have been held to be “State”; a fortiori a National Law University established by State Act, with the Chief Justice as Chancellor and Secretaries (Finance, Law, Education) on its governing board, receiving substantial state funding — “500% State” “Any person” — the right-holder The word “citizen” is conspicuously absent, unlike Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29. The right extends to non-citizens, aliens, even artificial legal persons (companies) “Within the territory of India” The guarantee operates within the Republic's geographical boundaries — it prohibits discrimination even against a foreign national on Indian soil Three foundational elements of the Article The Salma and Prapti Hypothetical — Deconstructing the Textualist Argument Facts: MNLU Nagpur's admission policy (eligibility for CLAT: “Citizen of India”). Prapti, an Indian citizen with CLAT rank 300, gains admission. Salma, a Pakistani citizen with rank 290 — higher merit — is denied solely for not being an Indian citizen. She petitions under Article 32. Her purely textualist argument: (a) Article 14 says “any person,” not “any citizen”; (b) I am a person; (c) the State (MNLU, through admission committee head Dr. Disha Kher) has denied me equality before the law; (d) the policy discriminates between persons — one citizen, one non-citizen — treating my higher marks as inferior; (e) the policy is unconstitutional on the face of Article 14. The Socratic demolition of the intuitive responses: (1) “The University's bye-law says so” — but the Constitution is supreme (Article 13(2)); a bye-law is tested against the constitutional standard, not on its own terms. (2) “She is not a citizen, so she has no right” — a legislative addition; the framers consciously used “any person” in Article 14 and “citizen” in Article 19; the interpreter cannot insert a word deliberately omitted. (3) “Article 29 (or 15) applies only to citizens” — a non sequitur; a challenge under Article 14 must be answered on the anvil of Article 14: “You cannot defeat a claim for khichdi (Article 14) by serving chicken (Article 29).” (4) “Equality before law differs from equal protection” — a semantic trap; the combined effect is a comprehensive mandate of non-arbitrariness. (5) “There are reasonable restrictions” — unlike Article 19, Article 14 enumerates none; the classification must pass the twin test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus, with the burden on the State. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 29 The unresolved suspense — the threshold question for the next class: if Article 14's text is taken to its logical extreme, every law preferring citizens over non-citizens in state benefits would be unconstitutional — yet such laws are ubiquitous. Find the principle that harmonises the inclusive text of Article 14 with the sovereign right of a State to prefer its own citizens, without importing the word “citizen” into the text. DAY 6 c. 24–25 July 2026 Article 14 — Reasonable Classification & the Nexus Test Treating unequals equally · The two-fold command · Anwar Ali Sarkar — the dacoit case · Kathi Raning — the contrast · Chiranjit Lal — one person, one class The Core Principle — Why Classification Is Essential The right to equality is not a mandate for absolute, mechanical, rigid equality. To treat everyone identically regardless of differing circumstances, needs and conditions is not equality — it is injustice. The foundational maxim: “Equals must be treated equally, and unequals must be treated unequally.” God and nature have created human beings with infinite variety — in upbringing, age, education, income, background and needs — so the law must classify persons and things into groups based on relevant similarities, applying appropriate rules to each. ●Illustration 1 — dietary needs: one person observes a religious fast (sabudana, fruits), another is non-vegetarian. If the mess serves chicken biryani to everyone and compels the fasting student to eat it “in the name of equality,” that violates her rights; equally, forcing the non-vegetarian to eat only khichdi every day because another is fasting is injustice. ●Illustration 2 — regional habits: a person from Uttar Pradesh may eat four or five parathas for breakfast; a person from Maharashtra is satisfied with poha. A uniform “poha only” rule leaves the first hungry — a failure to account for different needs. ●Illustration 3 — age: a sixty-year-old has different physical, medical and dietary requirements from a twenty-year-old; applying the same standard to both is not equal treatment. Hence the two-fold command of Article 14: (1) persons similarly situated (the same class) must be treated alike — if Niyati and Manaswi both fast but Niyati gets plain sabudana worth Rs. 15 while Manaswi gets sabudana vada with raisins and cashews worth Rs. 500, that is discrimination within a class; (2) persons differently situated may — indeed must — be treated differently. The critical question: how do we decide who falls into one class? That is the function of the Doctrine of Reasonable Classification and the Nexus Test. Article 14 does not forbid classification; it forbids class legislation — discrimination against a class without any reasonable basis — while permitting reasonable classification. A legislature that cannot classify cannot govern. The burden of proving unreasonableness lies in the first instance on the challenger, though once a prima facie case of discrimination is made out it may shift to the State.

Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) — the “Dacoit Case” State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar AIR 1952 SC 75 · 7-judge Constitutional Bench · 6:1 majority · Patanjali Sastri C.J. dissenting Facts · The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950 provided for speedier trial of certain offences. Section 5(1) empowered the State Government, by notification, to direct that any particular case or class of cases be tried by a Special Court — with no guidelines, criteria or standards governing the selection. The special procedure was more stringent than the CrPC: ordinary procedural safeguards were withdrawn. Anwar Ali Sarkar and 49 co-accused, caught in an armed dacoity raid, were notified into a Special Court, tried, convicted and sentenced; he challenged Section 5(1) under Article 14. Held · Section 5(1) unconstitutional. Limb 1 failed — no basis or criterion for classifying which cases go to speedier trial; selection rested on the subjective opinion of executive officers; change the officers and different cases would be picked: not “intelligible,” but arbitrary and capricious. Limb 2 failed — how does unguided discretion serve speedier trial? The means (absolute discretion) are not rationally related to the end. Illustration: dacoities in five districts, two dacoits caught in each; District A's pair notified to the harsher Special Court while Districts B–E enjoy ordinary protections — discrimination within a single class (all dacoity accused), with no justifiable answer to “why these two?” Principle · A law conferring absolute, unguided, unfettered discretion on the executive to classify persons or cases, without criteria or standards, violates Article 14.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 31 Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra (1952) — the Contrast Case Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra AIR 1952 SC 123 · text of the impugned section virtually identical to the West Bengal Act Facts · A Saurashtra State Ordinance empowered the government to send cases to Special Courts — but its preamble recited the exceptional law-and-order situation: widespread communal violence, dacoity, breakdown of the ordinary criminal justice system in named disturbed regions. Held · Upheld. In context, the discretion was not unguided: the preamble itself channelled it — cases connected with the breakdown of public order were the legitimate target. The discretion was bounded by the statute's stated objective. Principle · A provision identical in text may be valid or invalid depending on context, purpose, and the presence of guiding principles — in the statute or its surrounding circumstances. Noteworthy: Patanjali Sastri C.J. was a judge in both cases — dissenting in Anwar Ali Sarkar (to uphold) and in the majority in Kathi Raning (upholding). Anwar Ali Sarkar (struck down) Kathi Raning (upheld) Act specified no categories of offences Ordinance specified the categories — in the preamble and the disturbed regions Uncontrolled discretion with the State Government Clear guidance to Executive Magistrates Failed the intelligible differentia test Passed the intelligible differentia test Two virtually identical provisions, two opposite outcomes Can a Single Person Constitute a Class? Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India (1950) AIR 1950 SC 41 Facts · A single “sick” industrial undertaking — a textile mill threatening the livelihood of over 1,30,000 people — was taken over by the government for better management; shareholders objected to being singled out. Held · Yes — a single person or entity can constitute a valid class where it possesses unique characteristics distinguishing it from all others, and the law addresses that unique situation. Illustration offered in class: if one company causes 90% of an industry's pollution, a law addressing that company may be a valid classification. Principle · The test remains the same: intelligible differentia plus rational nexus — even for a class of one. Other Authorities and a Note on Judicial Fallibility ●Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar (1958) — the consolidating authority: several propositions summarising the law on Article 14 and reasonable classification. ●In re: Special Courts Act — further elucidation of the limits of special courts and Article 14. ●Ex-Services Association v. Union of India (2006) — cut-off date (1997) for retired servicemen's medical benefits: those retired before paid nothing, those after paid. The reasoning has been debated; students are encouraged to examine it critically and form their own views, with reasons. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 32 Judges, like all human beings, can err in reasoning. A judgment is not divine law. Justice Endlaw of the Delhi High Court, in the Delhi University photocopying case brought by Oxford University Press, delivered a celebrated judgment: “Copyright is not divine law” — a critique of the colonial mindset of blindly copying Western copyright laws, in a case where the library photocopied expensive textbooks for students who could not afford them. The principle may be right even where a given application is debatable. Questions for Reflection — Answered Q Why is classification necessary for the application of Article 14? A Because equality is not identical treatment: treating unequals equally is itself a violation of equality. Without classification the State could not legislate for specific groups or problems; the power to classify is an essential incident of legislative power. Article 14 forbids only class legislation, not reasonable classification. Q What are the two tests for a valid classification? Explain with reference to Anwar Ali Sarkar. A (1) Intelligible differentia — a clear, real, substantial basis distinguishing those grouped in from those left out; (2) rational nexus between that differentia and the statute's object. In Anwar Ali Sarkar, Section 5(1) supplied no differentia at all — the executive's unguided pick-and-choose — and the conferral of absolute discretion had no rational connection with speedier trial. Both limbs failing, the provision was void. Q Why did Anwar Ali Sarkar succeed while a similar provision was upheld in Kathi Raning Rawat? A Context and guidance. The Saurashtra Ordinance's preamble supplied the criteria — offences connected with an exceptional breakdown of public order in named regions — channelling the executive's discretion toward a constitutional object. The West Bengal Act had no such internal or contextual guide, leaving naked discretion. Same text, different legal fate. Q Why is Article 14 placed before Articles 19 and 21 in the Constitution? A The lecture leaves this as the question for the next class: is equality more important than life (Article 21) and freedom (Article 19)? The placement is a conscious constitutional choice — the framework for answering it (equality as the first among the rights, and later the Golden Triangle that makes them co-equal) develops over the following sessions. HOMEWORK Reading list: Anwar Ali Sarkar; Kathi Raning Rawat; Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri; Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Tendolkar; In re: Special Courts Act; Ex-Services Association (2006, critically).

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 33 DAY 7 27 July 2026 Equality Before Law vs Equal Protection of Laws Scope of “person” · E.P. Royappa introduced · Historical disabilities · The basketball and IAS illustrations · Ten valid and five invalid classes Foundations Article 14's dual mandate: equality before law, a negative concept prohibiting special privileges and disabilities, of English origin; and equal protection of the laws, a positive concept requiring the State to treat equals equally and unequals unequally — justifying affirmative action and reasonable classification — drawn from the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The term “person” includes citizens, aliens (Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka nationals alike) and companies, ensuring the protection against discrimination extends to every individual within Indian territory. Reasonable Classification — The Working Cases E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) (1974) 4 SCC 3 Facts · E.P. Royappa, a senior IAS officer serving as Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu — the highest State-level IAS post — was moved out and made Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission Board (a post declared equivalent in rank and salary), then OSD. He challenged the removal as arbitrary. Held · Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness: a decision that is arbitrary is inherently unequal — a significant expansion beyond the traditional classification test. (The doctrine is taught in full on Day 10.) Principle · The “New Doctrine of Equality”: arbitrariness read as a facet of Article 14. Anwar Ali Sarkar and Kathi Raning Rawat were revisited in compressed form with the comparison table (Day 6), and Federation of Armed Forces v. Union of India was added: a policy requiring retired armed forces personnel to make a one-time payment for lifetime medical facilities while active personnel received free treatment — the cut-off discriminating between similarly situated groups without a reasonable nexus may be unconstitutional. Equality Before Law — The Negative Concept in History The lecture illuminated the disabilities and privileges this concept abolishes through four historical episodes: ●Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa — thrown out of a first-class compartment at Pietermaritzburg despite a valid ticket, solely on race; the turning point of his life. ●The Travancore breast tax — lower-caste women prohibited from wearing upper garments unless they paid it; the tragic protest of Nangeli, who cut off her breasts. ●“No peon, no water” — Dalits denied access to public water sources; Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's own experience of not being allowed to drink water without a peon's assistance. ●Karna's exclusion — denied participation in Draupadi's swayamvar as a Suta-putra, not of royal lineage. Equality before law abolishes these historical disabilities and privileges, creating a level playing field for all.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 34 Equal Protection — The Positive Concept Two illustrations anchored the positive dimension. The basketball example: two players, one six-and-a-half feet tall, one three feet; a uniform twelve-foot hoop advantages the taller — that is merely equality before law. True equal protection may adjust conditions to make the contest fair. The IAS examination example: Person A, born into affluence — optimal nutrition, top-tier education, coaching from infancy, social capital of judges and ministers acquired by daily osmosis; Person B, born into rural poverty — nutritional deficits, late schooling, no social capital. Applying an identical standard (same examination, same age limit, same cut-off) guarantees B's perpetual ineligibility: the competition is rigged not by individual malice but by historically accumulated structural advantage. Criterion Equality Before Law Equal Protection of Laws Origin British legal tradition American legal tradition (14th Amendment) Nature Negative concept Positive concept Command The State shall not deny equality The State shall afford equal protection Function Abolition of special, discriminatory privileges Reasonable classification and positive discrimination to remedy structural disadvantage Concept of equality Formal — treating all alike Substantive — treating unequals differently to achieve genuine equality Illustration First-class ticket: anyone holding it may travel Reservation / quota system in education and employment The two facets of Article 14 compared HOMEWORK Homework: create 10 valid classifications satisfying both the intelligible-differentia and nexus tests, and 5 invalid ones failing them; support each with case law where possible; keep the classes diverse (avoid multiple variations of “committees”). DAY 8 30 July 2026 Session A Positive Discrimination & Social Justice Discrimination as a global phenomenon · Code Noir & the French Declaration · Loving v. Virginia · Forms of affirmative action · Nivedita Jain · Individual exploitation vs social discrimination The Universality of Discrimination A common and erroneous criticism holds that social discrimination — particularly caste and untouchability — was uniquely Indian. Historically, systemic, legally sanctioned discrimination was near-universal. Japan's Burakumin (“hamlet people”) suffered ostracism analogous to untouchability — residential segregation and restrictions on social intercourse — the existence of the very word evidencing institutionalisation. Ancient Mesopotamia, Greece and Rome divided society into rigid classes — free persons, slaves, citizens, non-citizens — with rights to property, contract and courts apportioned by status; law functioned as an instrument of exclusion.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 35 The Code Noir (1685), promulgated by Louis XIV for the French colonies, systematised exploitation in 60 articles: it defined the legal conditions of slavery with precision, classified human beings as movable property (meubles) stripping them of juridical personality, mandated Catholicism and ordered the expulsion of Jews — remaining in force long after France's revolutionary declarations of universal rights. The heritability principle partus sequitur ventrem — the child follows the mother's condition — created the doctrine of “once a slave, always a slave.” A comparative caution: India's bonded labour (prohibited by Article 23, including begar) is brutal, but the bonded labourer retains residual legal personality, unlike the chattel slave who was a res — a thing. The French Declaration of 1789 is celebrated as liberalism's foundational text, yet women were not entitled to citizenship, and property qualifications confined the vote to citoyens actifs; the poor and all women were citoyens passifs — civil rights without political rights. The most vaunted proclamation of equality in the Western canon was, at inception, a document for propertied white males. Racial discrimination in the United States persisted into living memory: until Loving v. Virginia (1967), anti-miscegenation laws were valid — Richard Loving (white) and Mildred Jeter (Black), married in the District of Columbia, were convicted on returning to Virginia under the Racial Integrity Act, before a unanimous Supreme Court held the statutes violative of equal protection and due process. The Nazi Nuremberg Laws (1935) — protecting “German or related blood” (Blutschutzgesetz) — were the most extreme expression of state-sanctioned social discrimination; the lecture also referred to recent conflict reports of checking sexual organs to determine religious identity before execution. KEY POINT Key takeaway: discrimination on grounds of race, caste, religion and sex was a global phenomenon. Indian society has — and continues to have — profound shortcomings requiring rectification; but the portrayal of discrimination as an exclusively Indian pathology is historically false and intellectually dishonest. Every society must confront its own legacy; the Indian constitutional project is a conscious, ongoing effort to dismantle inherited structures of injustice. The Two Dimensions — and the Impossibility of Formal Competition Equality before law is fundamentally prohibitory: post-independence, the sole criterion for a first-class railway compartment is a valid first-class ticket — whether the passenger is Black, White, Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh or Parsi, of any caste or sex. Equal protection, by contrast, authorises and sometimes requires preferential treatment for the historically disadvantaged. The lecture's centrepiece contrast: Child A (the child of privilege — optimal nutrition and healthcare, top-tier resources from infancy, social capital: connections with judges and ministers, knowledge of institutions acquired by osmosis) against Child B (the child of disadvantage — poverty, health deficits, late schooling, informational deficits, systemic barriers). A purely formal, identical standard of competition guarantees B's perpetual exclusion from power, influence and advancement — the competition is inherently rigged by historically accumulated structural advantage. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE The early Indian Civil Services examination is the paradigm. For years no Indian succeeded — not for want of intellect, but because the examination tested a universe of knowledge centred on Christian theology and the Bible, entirely alien to the Indian experience. Questions like “Who gave the apple to whom?” were incomprehensible to a candidate not steeped in scripture. That was structural exclusion — and it shows why the professor says NEET has never operated on a purely meritocratic basis. Forms of Affirmative Action

Kumari Nivedita Jain The limits of reservation Facts · To fill backward-class medical seats, MP progressively lowered the qualifying marks from 50 to 45 to 35 to 30 — then removed the minimum entirely, permitting admission regardless of entrance score, even zero or negative. Held · The Supreme Court upheld the State's action. Principle · The extremity of compensatory discrimination — and, as the professor notes, evidence that medical admissions have grappled with the merit-versus-social-justice tension from the outset; NEET has never been purely meritocratic. State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) The trigger for Article 15(4) Facts · Madras's Communal G.O. allocated medical and engineering seats by caste and community. Held · Struck down under Article 15(1): discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste. Consequence: the First Constitutional Amendment (1951) inserted Article 15(4), empowering special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs. Principle · The case that constitutionalised affirmative action in education. The Taxonomy — Individual Exploitation vs Social Discrimination Individual exploitation arises from personal relationships and private enmities — the abuse of personal power. The case studies from contemporary India: Madhumita Shukla, the poetess murdered by Uttar Pradesh's Amarmani Tripathi when she pressed for marriage after seeking his patronage; Geetika Sharma, the air hostess allegedly coerced into servicing the business clients of Haryana minister Gopal Kanda, who died by suicide leaving a detailed note; Shivani Bhatnagar, the journalist murdered through her entanglement with IPS officer R.K. Sharma in pursuit of access to the Prime Minister's Office; Naina Sahni, the tandoor murder victim of Congress politician Sushil Sharma. “As long as the sun and moon exist, individual exploitation will persist” — rooted in the ineradicable human capacity for passion, jealousy, greed and vengeance; law can punish it, not prevent it. Social discrimination is categorically different: not personal enmity but membership of a targeted group — the victim harmed not for who they are but for what they are within the discriminatory structure. The archetype is Dr. Ambedkar: no personal enmity with anyone (his father was a respected Subedar); forced to sit outside the

Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad of Baroda sponsored his studies abroad on merit. The grounds: sex (Sabarimala entry restrictions, litigated in Indian Young Lawyers' Association; historical denial of property rights, remedied only by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005); caste (hierarchy by birth imposing civil and religious disabilities); race (Jim Crow, apartheid); religion (assertion of one faith's supremacy; extremist interpretations denying the very right to life of others; the Nazi persecution as the extreme); and economic status (the Marxist critique of law as superstructural exploitation; Shakespeare's line — “The first thing we do, let's kill all the lawyers,” Henry VI Part 2 — a critique of law used to oppress the poor). Criterion Individual exploitation Social discrimination Basis Personal enmity, private relationships, individual passion Membership in a targeted group (caste, race, religion, sex) Scope Interpersonal Systemic and structural Target The victim as an individual The victim as a representative of a group Remedy Criminal prosecution and civil action for specific wrongs Constitutional and legislative group measures — affirmative action, reservations, social justice Persistence Ineradicable so long as human passions exist Dismantlable through sustained legal and social reform The taxonomy applied to remedies KEY POINT Social justice is the telos — the ultimate purpose — of equal protection: the set of positive measures by which the State dismantles structures of social discrimination, recognising that formal equality is an insufficient guarantee of a dignified life for those subjected to centuries of systemic subordination. It demands conditions in which the historically disadvantaged participate in the life of the nation on terms of genuine, substantive equality. DAY 9 30 July 2026 Session B Applying the Two-Limb Test — The Prohibition Hypothetical West Bengal Prohibition Ordinance · Finding the true objective · Testing exceptions A, B and C · The classroom vote · NEET rural age concession · R.D. Shetty and reading facts The Hypothetical — West Bengal Prohibition Ordinance A newly elected West Bengal government issues an ordinance imposing prohibition — a total ban on the manufacture, transportation, storage, sale, purchase and consumption of alcoholic liquor. Section 3's proviso exempts: (A) military personnel; (B) foreigners; (C) consumption within 5-star hotels. A citizen — “Niyati,” in the classroom's casting — petitions under Article 14. Her arguments: (1) military personnel are citizens too, and she is “an army in herself, all alone”; (2) is she “any less than a foreigner”?; (3) the 5-star exception is discrimination purely by economic class — if the rich may drink in luxury, why not the person of modest means at home or in a 3-star hotel?

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 38 Step one — identify the true legislative objective The ban is a means, not an end. The deeper objectives are grounded in the Directive Principles: public health (Article 47) — the State shall endeavour to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks injurious to health; public order and safety — prevention of alcohol-related crime and nuisance (the vivid illustration: a rickshaw-puller earning Rs. 300 a day who spends Rs. 500 on a bottle — the cascade of demanding money from and beating his wife, chain-snatching to finance the addiction, further crime under influence); and protection of the vulnerable — a paternalistic, welfarist rationale: the government is not opposed to drinking by those who can “afford and reconcile” it, but is deeply concerned for the poor. Step two — test each exception Exception Intelligible differentia Nexus analysis A — Military personnel A fundamentally distinct class: separate regulated society (cantonments), military discipline, unique stresses and sacrifices Clear: they are not the vulnerable socio-economic class the Act protects; stable state-provided income; “trained enough” to know how much and when to drink. Precedent — upheld in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (AIR 1951 SC 318) B — Foreigners A distinct juridical class: non-citizens, transient, not subjects of the State's socio-economic reform Not offending international sensibilities; facilitating commerce and tourism; in colder-climate cultures (the Sikkim example — universal drinking as thermoregulatory norm) alcohol is integral to meals; the object of protecting the Indian poor does not rationally extend to foreign visitors' cultural habits C — 5-star hotels Economic elite — the clientele is a proxy for socio-economic status For validity: a person spending Rs. 10,000–20,000 is definitionally outside the protected class — his drinking does not produce the theft and domestic violence over a Rs. 200 shortfall the Act targets; the classification perfectly serves the object. For invalidity: facially discriminatory by economic capacity — “it promotes inequality”; if the object were public health per se, the classification fails, for alcohol is equally harmful to the rich liver and the poor Testing the three exceptions against the twin limbs A classroom vote followed: an overwhelming majority held the classification invalid (for the petitioner); a small minority for validity. The lecture's conclusion: both sides are arguable — the outcome depends on which objective the court prioritises. F.N. Balsara is the seminal authority grappling with these precise questions. RESEARCH TASK Research assignment: in Bihar a prohibition law was challenged and initially declared unconstitutional; a subsequent ordinance, its flaws rectified, was upheld. Identify the first ordinance and the flaw in its classification scheme; then the second, and the legislative improvements that satisfied the intelligible-differentia and rational-nexus tests.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 39 Hypothetical — Age Concession for Rural NEET Candidates A Maharashtra ordinance grants a five-year age concession to students of rural (village) background appearing for NEET; city students get none. For validity: rural and urban students are distinct classes — documented lack of access to quality schools, coaching and infrastructure. For invalidity (a student's counter-argument): the classification is over-inclusive and outdated — a village child may attend a school superior to an urban slum's municipal school; a rich landlord's village child has every facility while the urban domestic worker's child in Dharavi has none; the classification fails to distinguish the rural rich from the urban poor. The Supreme Court's view (per the lecture): a blanket “rural” classification is unreasonable — it ignores the disparities within the urban category, particularly the uniquely disadvantaged urban slum-dweller, whose condition is often worse than the rural poor (who may retain community support and access to food). In the same judgment the Court upheld a classification based on mountainous or hilly terrain (the Uttarakhand example): the geographical hardship, sparse population and severe lack of accessible schools place all residents of that terrain at a fundamental disadvantage. State of Tamil Nadu AIR 1974 SC 555 · bench including P.N. Bhagwati and Y.V. Chandrachud JJ. Facts · Royappa, IAS, Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu — the highest State-level IAS post — was removed and appointed Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission Board (the Chairman being the Chief Minister; the Deputy Chairman therefore the post immediately below), then made OSD. An official order declared the posts equivalent in rank and salary to Chief Secretary. Held · He lost — he could not prove arbitrariness — but the principle was established. The petitioner's argument: equality is not determined solely by salary; power, position, prestige, status and respect are essential components (the classroom example: a professor given Rs. 5 lakh but assigned housekeeping duties is not made Vice-Chancellor). The State's answer — equal salary, equivalent posts, no discrimination — missed the point. Bhagwati J.: “Mala fide and arbitrariness are easy to claim, but hardest to prove.” Principle · The flaw in the old law: where there is no comparator class (a person uniquely targeted), discrimination cannot be proven and Article 14 lies dormant. The new perspective: whether or not discrimination exists, if the State has absolute discretionary power or acts arbitrarily, Article 14 is violated. “Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be ‘cribbed, cabined and confined’ within the traditional limits of classification.” What is arbitrariness? A decision based on whims and fancies — without reason, logic or justification; the opposite of a judicious decision. Its characteristics: (1) absence of reason; (2) whims and fancies — “I liked it, so I did it”; (3) lack of evidentiary support; (4) no consideration of relevant factors. Why absolute discretion breeds arbitrariness: every human being has preferences — someone likes chicken, someone biryani — and unfettered power lets personal preference govern. Discretion cannot be eliminated (governance requires it — if a fire breaks out, the teacher must evacuate the class; everything cannot be pre-written), but it must be structured, guided, reasonable. Proving arbitrariness is extremely difficult — “as tough as proving the existence of oxygen without instruments.”

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 42 The Three Pillars Before Maneka Gandhi Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962) first Indian citation of Munn v. Illinois Facts · Police surveillance of a citizen, challenged under Article 21. Held · “Life does not mean mere animal existence. It includes all those things which make life meaningful and beautiful. It includes the right to develop all our faculties.” Principle · The expansive reading of Article 21 from which the rights to privacy, to choose one's partner, and to live with dignity all descend — without this sentence, the constitutional protection for love marriages, personal relationships and individual autonomy would not exist. (Contemporary application: the Allahabad High Court recently scolded police for investigating a married couple's private life — protected under Article 21.) R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) — Bank Nationalisation 11-judge bench — one of only a handful in history Facts · Indira Gandhi nationalised several banks. The petitioner was not a bank but a director and shareholder — because the right to property under Article 19(1)(f) belongs only to citizens, and a company is not a citizen; the bank could not sue, its shareholder-director could. Held · The government argued it need comply only with Article 31, not Article 19. Rejected: “Nothing doing! They cannot be separated. While acting under Article 31, you must also comply with Article 19(1)(f).” Principle · Fundamental rights are not watertight compartments — the foundation stone of the Golden Triangle, expressly acknowledged by Bhagwati J. in Maneka Gandhi. Satwant Singh v. Union of India — the Passport Precedent Facts · Before 1967 India had no Passport Act; issuance was executive discretion. Satwant Singh's passport was refused — “We denied it because we chose to deny it.” Held · The Court directed the government: if you want to deny passports, make a law; write down the reasons. Result: the Passports Act, 1967 — whose Section 10(3) authorised impounding “without assigning any reason, in public interest”: absolute, arbitrary power. Principle · The statutory hook that Maneka Gandhi would strike. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India AIR 1978 SC 597 Facts · Two constables arrived at her residence: “Ministry of External Affairs — please surrender your passport.” On asking why: “Orders from above. We don't know why.” The government invoked Section 10(3) — impounding without assigning any reason — and defended it: “If we tell her the reason, she will run away!” Held · The doctrine of post-decisional hearing evolved: in urgency the State may impound first, but must immediately (1) issue a notice stating the grounds; (2) afford a hearing; (3) continue the impounding only if justified, else return the passport. Section 10(3)'s absolute unguided discretion was arbitrary power, violating Article 14; and Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive — any law depriving personal liberty must satisfy non-arbitrariness (14) and reasonableness (19) as well as Article 21. The Golden Triangle was formally established. Principle · Outcome: Maneka Gandhi did not get her passport back — the case was dismissed on other grounds, continuing the pattern: Marbury (no relief), Kesavananda (no relief), Royappa (no relief), Maneka (no relief). Landmark cases create principles; they do not always grant relief to the petitioner.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 43 Marbury v. Madison (1803) — the Origin of Judicial Review Marbury v. Madison 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137 (1803) · Chief Justice John Marshall Facts · The Constitution was 14–15 years old; no article mentioned judicial review. In the lame-duck period after John Adams lost the 1800 election, his party appointed 40 judges; commissions were signed and sealed, but some undelivered when Jefferson took office at midnight. Jefferson: “Throw these undelivered commissions away!” Marbury sought mandamus against Secretary of State Madison. Held · Three issues: (1) Does Marbury have a right to the commission? Yes — the right vested when signed and sealed; “where there is a right, there is a remedy” (ubi jus ibi remedium). (2) Can the Court issue mandamus to the executive? Yes — in the most famous sentence of American constitutional law: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.” (3) Does mandamus lie in the Court's original jurisdiction? No — Article III, Section 2 does not cover it; Section 13 of the Judiciary Act 1789, which purported to grant it, was unconstitutional and void — the first federal statute ever struck down. Principle · The political genius: the Court asserted the massive power of judicial review yet ordered no relief against the President, avoiding a confrontation Jefferson would likely have defied. “We will show our power, but we will not use it in this case.” Marbury did not get his commission. Applying the Tests — the Bearer Bonds Problem Q The government, to bring black money into the mainstream and fund new medical colleges, issues Bearer Bonds purchasable by anyone without questions about the money's source; after ten years the investment becomes white. A PIL challenges the Act under Article 14: it is an injustice to honest taxpayers who paid full income tax; it rewards dishonesty and encourages hoarding in expectation of future amnesty schemes. Decide. A (1) Presumption of constitutionality: courts presume a parliamentary statute valid; the burden is on the challenger. (2) Judicial deference to economic policy: courts do not intervene in policy, especially economic policy, unless it is manifestly arbitrary. (3) The two tests: intelligible differentia — is there a clear distinction between holders of black money and others? Yes, the classification is clear. Rational nexus — the object is to surface black money, fund medical colleges, improve the doctor-patient ratio; allowing investment without declaring the source directly furthers that object. Nexus exists. (4) Conclusion: the Act is constitutionally valid — it satisfies both limbs and, as an economic policy measure, deserves deference. (This is the pattern of R.K. Garg v. Union of India, the recommended original reading.) EXAM TIPS Examination tips: structure the answer Introduction → Facts (brief) → Legal Provisions → Tests Applied → Case Laws → Conclusion; use headings (“Intelligible Differentia,” “Rational Nexus,” “Non-Arbitrariness,” “Presumption of Constitutionality”); cite cases with name, year and principle; quote judicial observations for weight; do NOT invoke “colourable legislation” unless genuinely applicable — misapplied doctrines cost marks; distinguish “arbitrary” from “mala fide”; always remember the Golden Triangle (cite Maneka Gandhi and R.C. Cooper). “Arbitrariness and equality are sworn enemies. Equality cannot be crippled, cabined, cribbed, or imprisoned in some doctrinal limitations.” — E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 44 DAY 11 3 August 2026 Rule of Law I — Dicey & the Glorious Revolution Meaning and definition · Dicey's book and its three parts · The Glorious Revolution 1688-89 · The three components · How to answer a Rule of Law question Meaning and Definition Rule of Law means that no man is above law and every person is subject to the jurisdiction of ordinary courts of law, irrespective of position and rank. — The working definition The phrase originates in the French La Principe de Legalite — the principle of legality: governance according to law, not according to the whims and fancies of any person. Black's Law Dictionary defines it as governance according to law; the Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary provides a similar definition. Rule of Law is a foundational concept of constitutional jurisprudence ensuring that everything runs by law. Dicey and His Book Professor Albert Venn Dicey systematically articulated the concept in An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885), observing and documenting the prevailing circumstances in England after the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89: the powers of the monarchy curtailed, governance increasingly in the hands of the House of Commons — the common people. Dicey did not create the Rule of Law; he observed and documented it. His book was divided into three parts: (1) The Sovereignty of Parliament — which Dicey took to be fundamental, total and beyond challenge; (2) The Rule of Law; (3) the constitutional conventions. When Irish home rule returned to Parliament's agenda some three decades later, Dicey changed his mind about parliamentary omnipotence: in the final edition of The Law of the Constitution (1915) he lamented that parliamentary sovereignty had fallen prey to the party system. The Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 A watershed in British constitutional history establishing the supremacy of Parliament over the monarchy. It began on 5 November 1688 when William of Orange, backed by a 21,000-strong army, invaded England; uprisings in the north followed; by the end of 1688 James II had fled to France, where Louis XIV offered the king-in-exile his protection. The revolution was driven by a deep-seated fear of Catholicism and the belief that Catholics were plotting the overthrow of church and state — a conspiracy theory given credibility by genuine Catholic subterfuge, most notably the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. James II's authority had appeared secure on his accession in February 1685, but support ebbed as it became clear he wished not only freedom of worship for Catholics but removal of the Test and Corporation Acts so they could occupy public office. In the months after James's flight, a Convention Parliament decided he had effectively abdicated; William and his wife Mary were declared joint monarchs — a minor Dutch prince became King of England. The Bill of Rights (1689) determined the monarch must be Protestant; the Act of Settlement (1701) went further, demanding that whoever inherited the Crown must “joyn in communion with the Church of England as by law established.” The revolution established parliamentary supremacy — though the events of 1688 constituted a foreign invasion by the Dutch Republic; bloodshed in England was limited, but the settlement was secured in Ireland and Scotland by force and much loss of life. The revolution also fostered the growth of slavery by ending the Royal African Company's monopoly on the trade in 1698 — for the non-white inhabitants of the British Atlantic empire it represented not the

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 45 broadening of freedom but the expansion of servitude. The Three Components Dicey's three components — the architecture of the Rule of Law 1. Supremacy of Law “No man shall be punished or made to suffer in body or goods except for the violation of the law, and such violation must be established in an ordinary court of the land and in an ordinary legal manner.” Key elements: no punishment without law; punishment only through the ordinary legal manner; no arbitrary power — government cannot punish by its own fiat; no wide discretionary powers — persons in authority in Britain do not enjoy wide, arbitrary or discretionary powers; and wherever there is discretion, there is room for arbitrariness. The concept was necessary because before its establishment people acted according to their own will. The Anwar Ali Sarkar case exemplifies the violation: unguided State discretion to send cases for speedy trial without rational basis — one Collector might send a rape case for speedy trial because it received good publicity while another ignores a similar case. The law itself should specify what kind of cases go to speedy trial. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE If a student expresses an opinion I disagree with, I cannot throw her out of class simply because I didn't like what she said. That would be acting on individual whims and fancies. The law gives everyone the liberty to hold independent opinions based on their own choice, conviction and thinking. If someone is to be punished, it must be in accordance with the law, not personal preference.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 46 2. Equality before Law “No man is above the law and everyone, whatever his condition or rank, is subject to the ordinary laws of the land. Every person can sue or be sued in a court of law.” Dicey was not concerned with equality in a general sense but with limiting official power in favour of individual legal rights. His two specific ideas: (1) officials as such enjoy no special protection — an official who abuses power is personally liable to anyone whose rights he violates, just as if he were a private citizen; (2) disputes between government and citizen are settled in the ordinary courts according to ordinary law, not in special governmental courts. The framers incorporated this into Article 14: “The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.” Equality before Law (the negative aspect — no special privilege will be created; no untouchability, no caste restrictions, no prohibition on wearing clothes on the upper body, no denial of access to ponds) was borrowed from the British tradition; Equal Protection of Laws (the positive aspect — no discriminatory and depressive status will be created) from the American. 3. Predominance of Legal Spirit “The general principles of the British Constitution and especially the liberties of the individual are judge-made — the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons in particular cases brought before the courts from time to time.” Peculiar to Britain: the rights of individuals form part of and pervade the Constitution because they are secured by the courts. British Constitutional Law is not the source but the consequence of the rights of individuals as defined by courts. Referring to the Habeas Corpus Act, Dicey said it was “worth a hundred Constitutional articles guaranteeing individual liberty.” He accepted there was Rule of Law in the U.S.A. because the rights declared in the Constitution could be enforced, the Constitution giving legal security to the rights declared. The classroom explanation is the lecture's philosophical centre. Think of the hundred people you have known since childhood: how many would you have enmity with? A student estimates 80-20; the professor suggests closer to 90-95 neutral, 5-10 hostile. With most people we do not fight — we do not violate their rights, nor they ours. Even without a teacher or State present, peace prevails, because human beings are usually peaceful. Even before the State or formal law existed, people lived in an orderly, non-volatile manner. The famous maxim: “Your right ends where my nose begins” — possibly originating in France, later used by Abraham Lincoln and others: you may practice punching all you want, but it must not hit someone else's nose. This theory governed society even when there was no sovereign, no State, no king, no Prime Minister — a natural, self-regulating order. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE The State might have made a few laws, but as human society evolved, some laws kept forming along with us. When the State came into existence, there were already existing laws. At the very least, the right to life, the right to food, the right to marry and the right to procreation were certainly already there. These rights were not given by any king or any State. Generally people respected each other and took care of each other — and such practices which became customs were, in essence, laws. The State came later to make it even better. Rule of Law vs Rule by Law Aspect Rule by Law Rule of Law Meaning Work happens according to whatever law exists The law itself must be just, fair and reasonable Quality No concern for justice or quality of the law Law must have inherent quality, respect fundamental rights and human dignity

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 47 Aspect Rule by Law Rule of Law Examples A dictator's orders; oppressive laws Laws respecting fundamental rights and promoting justice The critical distinction ●North Korea: when the father of the “missile man” died, the new ruler ordered all subjects to weep, with tears in their eyes — anyone without tears would be killed. Not illegal, because the sovereign ordered it; but no fairness, no justice, no reasonableness — Rule by Law. (When dictators die, the professor observes, people actually celebrate.) ●Taliban: girls cannot study under existing laws — order without justice. ●Women's rights: in some interpretations Indian girls from Muslim households are given fewer rights, told not to get educated, married off early, made to wear a burqa — contrasted with Iranian girls who protested against the burqa by coming onto the streets and being shot at, some agitating that if forced to wear it they would wear nothing at all. How to Answer a Question on the Rule of Law The ideal structure, displayed on the PPT: (1) Meaning — the general definition; (2) Dictionary definition — Black's Law Dictionary, Oxford; (3) Jurist's view — the historical perspective. Sir Edward Coke, Chief Justice in James I's reign, was the originator of the doctrine in England; but Greek philosophers — Aristotle, Plato and Cicero — first wrote about it. Aristotle notably said that “law should govern and those who are in power should be servants of law.” This introduction pattern (general meaning, dictionary definition, jurist's view) works for any topic — Rule of Law or Natural Justice alike. Significance and Application Dicey's thesis has been criticised from various angles, but his basic tenet stands: power is derived from, and is to be exercised according to, law — the absence of arbitrary and discretionary power, equality before law, legal protection of basic rights. In India the Supreme Court has read Article 14 to encompass non-arbitrariness: E.P. Royappa — arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality. In Kesavananda Bharati, the Court enunciated the Rule of Law as one of the most important aspects of the basic structure doctrine. The broad emphasis: absence of any centre of unlimited or arbitrary power, proper structuration and control of power. Government intervention in citizens' daily activities is ever-increasing, creating possibility of arbitrariness in State action — Rule of Law is the counter, because its basic emphasis is the exclusion of arbitrariness. Lawlessness and unreasonableness in government are its antithesis.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 48 DAY 12 4 August 2026 Rule of Law II — Ancient India, Colonial Erasure & ADM Jabalpur Attendance and honesty · The quasi-federal warning · Rule of Law in ancient India · Article 331 and the Anglo-Indians · ADM Jabalpur and the 44th Amendment · Justice Khanna's legacy Classroom Interaction — the Honesty Principle PROFESSOR'S ASIDE I am not as stupid as students think — I remember faces and names even when students lie. One student claims her attendance is fine; it is actually fifteen percent — fifteen out of thirty-five classes. Lying and saying “I do come” will not help the situation improve; accept the truth so the problem can be addressed. I ask about attendance only for your betterment — I even help students at risk of being debarred, because a full year back is a serious consequence. I am not as cruel as students think; if someone genuinely cannot wake in the morning, I will jokingly arrange for a bucket of water to be poured over them. The rules exist and cannot be bypassed — but there is room for empathy if students are honest about their difficulties. The NLU System — and the Quasi-Federal Warning KEY POINT The professor does not teach by reading from a book: whatever he teaches is what he expects in the examination. He has taught that the Constitution of India is not quasi-federal. Every book and article will say “quasi-federal” — the moment a student writes that word in an exam, they receive a zero and fail; he will not entertain a book brought to argue otherwise. The correct position, as taught: Dr. Ambedkar first said the Constitution is federal; the Supreme Court repeatedly said it is federal; later the Court declared federation part of the basic structure. “Anyone writing quasi-federal is merely acting as a follower of a Western country. I am not Western. I am Indian.” PROFESSOR'S ASIDE A student from Nagpur — a local girl — is threatened, humorously, that eight to ten of us will come to her house for tea and to lodge a complaint about her attendance. In my local rustic language, “abusing” actually means criticism. When I taught IPS officers, criticising corruption — if the SSP is not corrupt, a traffic inspector does not have the courage to take money at a crossroad; the topic was the Prevention of Corruption Act — a huge complaint was made against me for taunting and abusing the very officers who had paid my airfare. And if we eat your salt, we cannot abuse you — but I still promise to visit; Symbiosis often hosts my lectures, so a visit is not impossible. Rule of Law — Its True Origins in Ancient India Since Equality before Law is drawn from the Rule of Law, the professor returns to its deeper origins. The Rule of Law is a concept very difficult to explain but very easy to understand. Books trace it only to Western countries; the professor asserts emphatically that the Rule of Law has always been there in our country — read any story from ancient India and you will find it. Natural justice can be considered part of the Rule of Law: Lord Rama and Ravana — natural justice in the Ramayana Classroom authority for the ancient Indian Rule of Law

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 49 Facts · Rama sent messages to Ravana not once but twice, warning him to return Mother Sita and avoid a destructive war; even during the war he gave repeated warnings. Held · — Principle · Rama told Ravana that he was a great and knowledgeable saint, and needed only to return Sita to be excused — notice and opportunity to amend before force: natural justice. Yudhishthira's exile — the Mahabharata example Facts · Yudhishthira lost the game of gambling; the condition was twelve years of exile and one year in an unknown place. Lord Krishna knew a war would take place — yet did not stop it. Held · — Principle · He insisted that the rule be followed: even the contemplated catastrophe did not justify setting aside the agreed condition. Shravan Kumar — the devoted son Facts · Shravan Kumar was carrying his blind parents; Lord Dasharatha accidentally killed him. Held · — Principle · The Rule of Law demanded that the king take responsibility for the care and protection of the dead boy's parents. King Dasharatha went to them and served them water; they ultimately cursed him to die of the same grief of losing a son. Dasharatha was a king — he could have avoided this, but the Rule of Law bound him. This is the true spirit of the ancient Indian Rule of Law. The Colonial Erasure of Indian Legal Heritage Why are these hundreds and thousands of ancient Indian examples ignored? Because of the British need to show dominance: had the British acknowledged that Indians had good things of their own, the Indian people would never have accepted their superiority. The narrative pushed was that Indians were inferior — “snake charmers.” The professor dislikes the term intensely: charm actually means something good (a charming friend); the real satisfaction comes from the Hindi word sapera. Did the British come all the way to India just to see snakes? If they liked India so much — why didn't they want to go back even after independence? The historical footnote: the British eventually folded their hands before people like Dr. Ambedkar and pleaded — with democracy, the public would elect representatives, but the British had fallen in love with India and were not going back. Since they would not win elections, they asked for representation without elections. Dr. Ambedkar granted the Anglo-Indian community two MPs in Parliament for ten years under Article 331; the professor criticises the Congress Party for repeatedly extending the provision until its removal by the 104th Constitutional Amendment. If India was not good, no one would have wanted to settle here — from the Mughals to the British, everyone who came stayed. Even Mark Tully, the BBC reporter, came to report and stayed — the professor recommends him as an excellent writer. EXAM DIRECTIVE Examination directive: if asked about the Rule of Law, write a little bit about India. The professor states candidly that no matter how hard the “cockroach” tries, he thinks Modi will remain in power another three years and only Modi sympathisers would evaluate their answer sheets — but regardless of who is in power, he will be evaluating their papers. If a student writes that the Rule of Law came from Western countries, three marks will be deducted automatically. Search for and find references to the Rule of Law in ancient Indian literature — even new Indian literature is still older than Western sources. Decolonise your legal thinking.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 50 ADM Jabalpur — the Darkest Hour of the Rule of Law ADM Jabalpur and its correction — the timeline that must be memorised ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla The Emergency case · habeas corpus during MISA detentions Facts · During the Emergency, MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) was applied and everyone was arrested under it; Fundamental Rights stood suspended. Detainees petitioned that they were wrongly detained and should be released. The Supreme Court then had very good judges — at least three beyond doubt: Justice Khanna, a very upright judge; Justice Bhagwati, who called himself the pioneer of human rights; Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, a very good judge — along with Justice Beg (whom the professor harshly calls Indira Gandhi's “peon”) and Chief Justice A.N. Ray (made Chief Justice by Indira Gandhi, later changing his allegiance). It seemed the decision would be 4:1 for liberty. Held · The shocking judgment came — the professor states bluntly that Indira Gandhi bought everyone; the only man who was not sold was Justice H.R. Khanna. The judges held: “The entire repository of the right to liberty is the Constitution. If the Constitution has not given the right, then you do not have the right at all. Since the Constitution and rights were suspended, there was no Right to Life left to protect.” Principle · The core: all rights come only from the Constitution — suspend the Constitution and you have no rights at all. Nani Palkhivala's argument (appearing for the detainees) posed a terrifying hypothetical: suppose a girl committed a crime and the police went to arrest “Ishita,” but by mistake caught an innocent girl, “Aarya,” who protests she is not Ishita — and the police answer, “To hell with it, you are in our hands now.” The darker question: during an Emergency, if a policeman, out of personal enmity or after drinking, simply shoots an innocent person without any crime — is there any remedy? Justice Chandrachud's devastating response: “I am sorry, but the present law does not allow any relief.” A station house officer could come, shoot you, and you would have no legal recourse whatsoever. The professor tells students to read the case themselves — “you will feel like abusing the judges even more” — and recounts visiting Justice Bhagwati's home and bluntly asking him what had happened, whether he had consumed something.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 51 The overruling — the 44th Amendment Because it was a manifestly wrong decision, immediately after the Morarji Desai government came to power the 44th Constitutional Amendment was passed: the Right to Life can never be suspended, even during an Emergency. Two articles cannot be suspended — Articles 20 and 21. The professor made the class chant “twenty and twenty-one” five times to memorise it: this is explicitly written in Article 359, which now reads “except 20 and 21.” Thus ADM Jabalpur stands overruled by the 44th Amendment. The emotional correction — Justice D.Y. Chandrachud Justice D.Y. Chandrachud — son of Justice Y.V. Chandrachud — felt a deep sense of guilt over his father's betrayal. In the landmark Privacy case he wrote a powerful passage, read aloud in class: “Neither life nor liberty are bounties conferred by the State, nor does the Constitution create these rights.” Our life and liberty are not a bounty (a gift) of the State or the Constitution; they are given by Nature or God, and the Constitution has merely accepted this fact — it is not the sole repository of these rights, which existed even before its advent. The exact opposite of what his father had written. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE The parable of the naughty father and the good son: a very naughty father abused everyone in the village his whole life. On his deathbed he told his decent son that everyone would abuse him after his death, and asked the son to do something to make people praise him. The son realised that if he did even dirtier work than his father, people would say the father was better — so while the father only abused, the son started throwing mud and dung at people. After a few days the villagers began saying, “His father was better!” D.Y. Chandrachud did something similar: to make his father look better, he wrote this profound passage — though it was not legally necessary, the 44th Amendment having already fixed the problem — explicitly writing that ADM Jabalpur is overruled, washing away his father's sin. The Visit of Justice Sanjiv Khanna — Reading Cases Pays PROFESSOR'S ASIDE Justice Sanjiv Khanna — nephew of Justice H.R. Khanna — visited the university for convocation. Students, having been taught ADM Jabalpur, were eager for photos with him because of the heroic legacy: for his courageous dissent, H.R. Khanna was not made Chief Justice. I told Justice Khanna he had a huge fan following; he was surprised — Chief Justice for only five or six months, who would know him? I explained: he had converted the injustice done to his uncle into justice by rising to Chief Justice himself. He was pleased immensely and took photos with students for a long time. PROFESSOR'S ASIDE A PhD scholar, on her honeymoon in Kashmir, recognised Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul at her hotel and called me for advice on what to say. I told her: quickly read two or three of his judgments, then tell him how much you appreciated his explanation of proportionality in the Privacy judgment. She did — and it led to a meaningful conversation. When Justice S.K. Krishna — a popular judge, Chairman of the Pay Commission — visited, I could engage him by recollecting his judgments and commission reports. The moral: when students read cases and judgments, they have something substantial to talk about with eminent people. Otherwise they will just come, eat food, leave — and not have a good life.

The professor's response? Rule of Law — Recap and Deeper Exploration Why study the Rule of Law? One of its components, Equality before Law, is part of Article 14. Supremacy of Law means two things: no punishment except for violation of law, and no governance by individual whims and fancies (the classroom example of the opinion-expressing student). Equality before Law — all are equal, but all cannot be equal, which is why the theory of classification exists in both England and India. Predominance of Legal Spirit receives the interactive treatment: the most naughty student in class (Isha, self-certified) considers the hundred people she has known since childhood — her estimate of enmity is 80-20, corrected to 90-95 neutral, 5-10 hostile. With most people we do not fight: rights go unviolated on both sides; peace prevails even without teacher or State, because human beings are usually peaceful. Even before the State or formal law existed, people lived in an orderly, non-volatile manner. FIND OUT Homework attached to the maxim: find out who said “Your right ends where my nose begins” — it may have originated in France and was later used by Abraham Lincoln and others. The idea: you can practice punching all you want, but it should not hit someone else's nose; as long as there is distance, people do not interfere. This theory governed society even when there was no sovereign, no State, no king, no Prime Minister — no Nehru, no Modi. It is a natural, self-regulating order. Students are also directed to read the International Commission of Jurists' modern expansion of the concept. Magna Carta (1215) The professor traces the Rule of Law in England to 1215. Magna Carta was one of the first official documents about human rights — the first written promise by a King not to do certain things. In older times kings levied taxes on the public for personal whims: to fight wars for a princess; to build grand monuments for a deceased wife; simply to display power. The common people's blood was sucked through arbitrary taxation; there was no curb on the king's power. The Barons of England — not the common man, but middle-class people — confronted the king and threatened revolt; the king was compelled to accept: no taxation without consultation. This was the first time a king acknowledged that some people had some rights.

The pattern-answers below the two official ones are reconstruction, clearly marked. The Problems and Answers Q 1 · Prohibition with exemptions. A State bans liquor entirely in the interest of public health and temperance, but exempts soldiers and sailors consuming foreign liquor in military messes, canteens, warships and troopships, and foreign tourists possessing liquor under a special permit. Ordinary residents get no permit route. Is the exemption of defence personnel (separate service conditions, functional needs aboard ships) and foreign visitors (transient status, different customs) valid, even though allowing them to drink seems to work against the very purpose of temperance among the general population? A OFFICIAL SECTION B ANSWER: Defence personnel and vessels were already recognised as a distinct legal category under separate service and discipline laws, and foreigners were distinguished by their transient status and different customs — both real, non-fanciful differentia. The Supreme Court held that special treatment of a class already treated as distinct under other statutes has a rational nexus to practical governance — even though the High Court had earlier found no such nexus and struck the exemption down. (This is the pattern of State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, taught on 30 July.) Q 2 · The rent-control cut-off. A rent law permanently frees all buildings constructed after a cut-off date from rent control, to encourage fresh construction. Decades later, the “new” buildings are over twenty-five years old, yet their landlords still enjoy total freedom, while equally old pre-cutoff buildings remain regulated forever. The classification made sense when passed — is it still valid to keep exempting them forever, with no time limit? A

But a classification's validity is not frozen... [the source text breaks off here]. COMPLETION ON THE COURSE FRAMEWORK: ...at the date of enactment. The rational nexus between “newness” and the incentive object evaporates once the exempted buildings age into the regulated class's condition; perpetuating the distinction indefinitely, with no sunset, is a continuing failure of the nexus limb as applied today. The better view: the exemption was valid when made but is open to challenge as arbitrary in its continuing operation — the legislature must re-examine the cut-off. Q 3 · The labour welfare fund. A law requires “establishments” — all factories, plus tramway and motor-bus businesses — to deposit unclaimed wages and bonuses in a welfare fund, but excludes businesses with fewer than fifty employees and government establishments other than factories. Is it valid to regulate only larger establishments and specific sectors, leaving out smaller trade businesses and most government bodies, on the reasoning that the legislature may tackle a widespread problem in phases? A VALID. The differentia is intelligible: large factories and public transport undertakings concentrate wage labour and unpaid dues; small trading businesses and non-factory offices present a smaller, more diffuse administrative problem. The nexus with the object — recovering unclaimed dues for workers' welfare where the problem is administratively concentrated — is rational, and the legislature may legitimately attack a widespread evil in phases, beginning where the concern is greatest (the pattern of the phased-approach reasoning taught with this problem). Q 4 · The flat land tax. A State imposes a single flat rate per acre on “all lands,” so the owner of fertile, income-generating farmland pays the same as the owner of unproductive forest yielding barely any income — one owner earned only a small annual income from roughly 25,000 acres of forest yet faced a tax demand many times his earnings. The law also lets government exempt “any land or class of lands” at its own discretion, with no guidelines. Is a flat rate on wildly unequal land valid, and is the unguided discretionary exemption valid? A INVALID ON BOTH COUNTS. First, imposing identical burden on admittedly unequal subjects — fertile versus barren land — is the very “equal treatment of unequals” that Article 14 forbids (the positive concept of equal protection, 27 July lecture): a rational tax would classify by productivity or income. Second, the unguided power to exempt “any land” is Anwar Ali Sarkar's vice in reverse — absolute, unguided executive discretion with no criteria, which fails the intelligible differentia limb and breeds arbitrariness (E.P. Royappa). Q 5 · The pension line. All served the same employer — is a line drawn purely on the date of retirement valid when the object was simply better financial security in old age? A

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 58 INVALID. Cut-off dates are not per se unconstitutional, but the differentia must have a rational nexus with the object. Here the object — old-age financial security for those who rendered comparable service — is indifferent to the day of retirement; the classification neither identifies a class needing different treatment nor serves economy or transition (no such justification appears). Same-service pensioners are similarly situated; the day's difference is arbitrary in effect — the pattern of the cut-off analysis in Ex-Services Association (taught 24–25 July), where a cut-off discriminating between similarly situated groups without reasonable nexus was condemned. Q 6 · The air hostesses (three sub-questions). An airline has two cabin-crew cadres: male flight pursers and female air hostesses. Air hostesses must retire at 35, or earlier on marriage within the first four years of service, or immediately upon first pregnancy — whichever first; pursers serve until 58. Extension beyond these conditions lies purely in the Managing Director's unguided discretion. (a) Are two separate cadres with different rules valid, given different recruitment sources and historical service conditions? (b) Is termination upon first pregnancy valid, on the theory that pregnancy affects ability to do the job? (c) Is it valid to let one official decide, with no written standard, whose service is extended? A (a) VALID — separate cadres recruited from different sources with different historical conditions can constitute an intelligible differentia; that much is not per se objectionable. (b) INVALID — a rule terminating a woman upon first pregnancy draws the line on sex and pregnancy alone. The “ability to do the job” rationale is over-broad: pregnancy is a temporary condition, not a permanent incapacity, and the rule spares the employer any individualised inquiry while visiting the entire burden on women alone — the classification fails the nexus limb and is sex-based discrimination of the kind Articles 14–15 target (Air India v. Nergesh Meerza was the course's designated case for exactly this regulation). (c) INVALID — the Managing Director's unguided discretion to extend service is Anwar Ali Sarkar's absolute, standardless pick-and-choose: wherever there is discretion without criteria, there is room for arbitrariness.
