Is re-splitting a merged cadre valid, on the reasoning that a degree involves deeper theoretical training better equipping a person for the senior post's technical and managerial responsibility? A VALID. The differentia — formal engineering degree versus diploma — is real, verifiable and non-fanciful; the nexus — the senior post's greater technical and managerial responsibility requiring deeper theoretical training — is rational. The prior integration of the cadres is a fact of history, not a constitutional bar: the State may re-classify when the qualification genuinely correlates with the demands of the post. (The answer would flip if the degree bore no rational relation to the post's functions — then the split would be arbitrary.) Q 8 · The black-money bonds. A

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 59 VALID — this is the Bearer Bonds problem solved in class (c.31 July) and read as R.K. Garg v. Union of India. (1) Presumption of constitutionality; the burden lies on the challenger. (2) Judicial deference to economic policy unless manifestly arbitrary. (3) Intelligible differentia: holders of undisclosed wealth are a clearly distinct class. (4) Rational nexus: allowing them to invest without declaring the source directly furthers the object — surfacing black money, funding development. The emotional claim of “rewarding dishonesty” does not supply a constitutional ground; the hardship of honest taxpayers is not a listed vice in the classification. Q 9 · The SC/ST test exemption. Departmental tests must be passed for promotion to a higher clerical grade, but the government may temporarily exempt in-service SC/ST employees for a limited period. A batch of promotions goes largely to exempted employees by seniority, ahead of a general-category employee who passed the tests. Is the temporary exemption valid, where the object is adequate representation of historically disadvantaged communities? A VALID. The differentia is intelligible — Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are historically disadvantaged and under-represented communities, the very class the Constitution's scheme of compensatory discrimination addresses (Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are facets of equality, not exceptions — the 13 August lecture). The nexus — securing adequate representation in public service — is direct. That some promoted employees had not passed the test while a general candidate had is within the logic of substantive equality: the Court has upheld even the removal of minimum qualifying marks for reserved candidates (Kumari Nivedita Jain). The exemption is temporary and targeted, not a permanent lowering of standards. Q 10 · The single-company law. After a special inquiry into one textile mill in financial and managerial trouble threatening the supply of an essential commodity (cloth), Parliament passes a law naming that company alone — removing its managing agents and directors, letting government appoint new ones, curtailing shareholders' voting rights. No other company, even similarly troubled, is touched. Can a law targeting a single named entity be a valid classification, given that a “class” normally means a group of more than one? A VALID — a single person or entity can constitute a class where its situation is unique: the special inquiry established this company's specific financial and managerial crisis threatening an essential commodity's supply and a vast workforce's livelihoods — characteristics not shared by “similarly troubled” companies in the abstract. Chiranjit Lal Chowdhury settles that a class of one is permissible if the differentia is intelligible and the nexus rational. The shareholder's “hostile discrimination” argument is the strongest counter, but it fails because the law responds to demonstrated, unique facts, not hostility toward the named entity. Q 11 · The pick-and-choose special courts. After communal riots, a State law allows Special Courts with a faster procedure dropping safeguards like jury trial and committal, but does not specify which offences, areas or cases go to them — government may by notification pick any individual “case” or “offence,” with no guiding standard. Is free, case-by-case executive selection of who gets the harsher procedure valid? A INVALID — this is Anwar Ali Sarkar itself. Both limbs fail: no intelligible differentia (no criteria at all; the selection rests on executive whim — change the officer, change the cases), and no rational nexus (unguided discretion bears no connection to speedy trial). Persons accused of the same offence may face radically different procedures with no justifiable answer to “why me?”

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 60 Q 12 · The ordinance with built-in criteria. After integration of princely states, regions of the new State see organised armed robbery, dacoity, looting and murder; an ordinance itself names the disturbed regions and lists the serious violent offences (murder, dacoity, robbery and related) to be tried by a faster special procedure. A convict argues being tried differently from accused persons elsewhere is discriminatory. Does building the criteria into the law, rather than leaving unguided choice, make the classification valid? A VALID — this is Kathi Raning Rawat. The differentia is intelligible (named regions suffering an exceptional breakdown of law and order; named grave offences), and the nexus — a speedier, tougher procedure precisely where the ordinary system has broken down — is rational. Contrast Anwar Ali Sarkar: the guidance here is in the law itself, so no standardless discretion exists. Q 13 · The custody-statement rule. Confessions to police are generally inadmissible, but a person in custody who gives information leading to a fact's discovery (say, a hidden weapon) may have the discovery-related portion of his statement proved — while a person not in custody making a full voluntary confession is governed by ordinary rules instead. Is treating custody statements differently valid? A VALID. The differentia is intelligible — persons in police custody face a materially higher risk of police pressure, inducement and fabrication, so their statements warrant a distinct, more restrictive admissibility rule. The nexus is rational: admitting only the discovery-related portion, verified by the actual discovery of the object, is a safeguard precisely calibrated to that risk — the corroboration of the fact guarantees reliability in a way a free-floating confession does not. Differential treatment keyed to a real difference in vulnerability satisfies both limbs. Q 14 · The two tobaccos. Is taxing one commercial variety while exempting another variety of the same broad category valid? A VALID. The two varieties are genuinely different commodities — grown, cured, marketed and used differently; one is a distinct, higher-value, export-oriented product, the other locally consumed. The differentia is real and commercial, not fanciful; the nexus — taxing the higher-value commodity (and, implicitly, sparing the local consumption of the common variety) — is a rational revenue measure. A “same broad category” does not make sub-varieties a single class for all purposes. Q 15 · The seventeen-month year. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 61 VALID. Transitional provisions classify by a real and temporary necessity: reconciling two different accounting-year systems at the merger. The differentia — the transferred district — is intelligible and self-evident; the nexus — an adjusted computation period and averaging formula to bridge the systems — is directly rational. Genuine administrative difficulty at a one-time transition is a classic reasonable classification; it is neither permanent nor capricious. Q 16 · The adultery exemption. A VALID on the course's framework. The differentia is sex-based, but it operates favourably to women; the Constitution expressly contemplates special provisions for women (Article 15(3) — the “injection” against historically entrenched discrimination, taught 10–11 August). The legislature proceeded on the protective assumption that in the marital context the wife is the victim, not the perpetrator, and therefore withdrew her from criminal liability even as an abettor. A sex-based classification is not per se invalid; what Article 15(1) forbids is discrimination — hostile or prejudicial treatment — not protective differentiation. Q 17 · The blanket bar on women in liquor premises. An excise law bans the employment of any woman — and any man under twenty-five — anywhere liquor is consumed by the public: bars, hotel restaurants, room service. The stated purpose is protecting women (and young men) from the environment's risks; trained hospitality professionals who are women are completely barred regardless of individual skill, experience or actual workplace safety. Is a blanket protective ban valid, or does it fail because narrower measures (workplace safety rules) could address the same concerns? A INVALID. Protective legislation for women is constitutionally contemplated, but the ban is over-inclusive and the nexus fails: the object — safety in the working environment — can be achieved by narrower, individualised means (safety regulations, conditions of service), so a total exclusion from an entire profession based purely on sex and age is disproportionate to the object. The classification assumes what it should prove — that every woman, whatever her training and whatever the actual conditions of a specific workplace, is endangered — and therefore treats the protected class as incapable of choice. The course's test: where a less restrictive measure serves the object equally, the blanket ban is arbitrary. Q 18 · The fifteen-percent interview. Though every candidate passed through the same process, can the weightage be struck down as unfair and arbitrary in effect, even without a “classification” in the traditional sense? A

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 62 INVALID. This is the E.P. Royappa extension: equality is violated not only by bad classifications but by arbitrary process. A component worth fifteen percent of the admission that, by its own design (two-to-three minutes, formal questions on parentage and residence), cannot assess merit, is irrational — the mechanism bears no relation to the object (selecting on merit). The identical application of an irrational process is still arbitrary; unexplained interview marks functioning as an unreviewable discretion fail non-arbitrariness even where every candidate was “treated alike.” Q 19 · The EWS quota's exclusion. A constitutional amendment allows up to 10% reservation for “economically weaker sections” — but only for those who do not belong to SCs, STs or OBCs (who already have their own separate reservation). It is argued that since poverty exists in every community, excluding the poor of already-reserved communities from the new quota discriminates against the poorest of the poor. Is treating “economically weak general-category citizens” as a distinct class from “economically weak persons from already-reserved communities” valid? A VALID — the position of Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, as taught on 10 August. The class “economically weaker sections of citizens not already covered by reservation” is coherent: the excluded communities already possess separate, older reservation benefits rooted in social and educational backwardness, so the new, purely economic quota reaches precisely those whom the existing scheme leaves out. EWS reservation is not caste-based, and it specifically excludes those already receiving benefits — it brings in people from castes previously outside the net rather than enlarging the same castes' entitlement. The classification identifies two genuinely different positions, not one class arbitrarily halved. Q 20 · The 27% with creamy layer. A government order grants 27% reservation for socially and educationally “backward classes,” identified substantially using caste as an indicator — while excluding the more advanced “creamy layer” within those communities so the benefit reaches the genuinely disadvantaged. Critics say using caste at all, then sub-dividing the backward class, is irrational and that economic status alone should have been the test. Is caste as an indicator (not the sole test) plus creamy-layer exclusion valid? A VALID — the position of Indra Sawhney. (1) Caste may be a starting point for identifying social and educational backwardness — in Indian conditions caste is a very real component of social position — but it cannot be the sole criterion; the identification here uses caste as an indicator within a broader assessment. (2) Excluding the creamy layer keeps the benefit targeted at those genuinely, not merely nominally, disadvantaged — the advanced members of a backward class have already escaped the disadvantage the measure targets. Both limbs satisfied: intelligible differentia (genuinely backward versus advanced members) and rational nexus (advancement of the actually disadvantaged). Q 21 · The juvenile's date. An accused was a minor on the date of the alleged offence but had crossed the juvenile age by the time of investigation or production before the court. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 63 The date of the offence. The protective juvenile-justice procedure attaches to the person's condition when the act was done — that is the morally and legally relevant moment, common to all young offenders in like circumstances. The date of production is an accident of procedure: it varies enormously with how quickly or slowly a case moves, so two offenders identically situated at the offence would receive different treatment according to docket speed alone. Equality among similarly-placed offenders therefore requires fixing status by age on the date of the offence — the certain, rational basis; the production-date rule creates an arbitrary, litigation-driven lottery. The Constitutional Hierarchy — and the Loudspeaker Example Students are directed to examine Article 25: it opens “Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part” — the critical phrase “other provisions of this Part” makes Article 25 subject to the rest of Part III, including Articles 14, 19 and 21. The contemporary illustration: the Supreme Court's ruling on loudspeakers in mosques — used at very high volumes creating noise disturbance, the practice was restricted because Article 21 (the right to life, read to include peaceful living without noise pollution) is superior to Article 25. If anyone's Article 21 rights are disturbed, Article 25 must yield. By the same reasoning, if Article 30 protection for minority institutions conflicts with Article 19(1)(g) rights or the equality framework, Article 30 must yield. Union of India (2023/24) CJI Dhananjaya Chandrachud · argued by Justice Muralidhar (former Chief Justice, Orissa High Court, engaged by the petitioner) Facts · Sukanya — “a very dynamic journalist” — researched and revealed that caste-based discrimination persisted in Indian prisons decades after independence: work assignments were made by caste, Dalit prisoners assigned to dig drains and clean bathrooms, Brahmin prisoners assigned to cook. This despite Congress having amended the Constitution to declare India “Socialist Secular.” Disturbed, she filed a PIL. Held · Counsel argued that Article 15 explicitly prohibits caste discrimination, yet the prison system was recording prisoners' castes and assigning work on that basis. CJI Chandrachud made a landmark observation: there is no need to record caste anywhere, as recording facilitates discrimination. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 65 The Caste Census Debate The professor's critique of the caste census, in layers. Rahul Gandhi's formula: “Jitni jiski sankhya, uski utni hissedari” — as is the population, so is the share. The implied strategy: Dalits plus OBCs — together roughly ninety percent of the population (some add Muslims) — promised seventy to eighty percent reservation would secure their votes. The professor's challenge: is the government distributing stolen goods that must be divided proportionally among thieves? The constitutional anchors: the primary focus of the Constitution is equality; Article 16(2) prohibits discrimination of any kind; Article 16(4) provides reservation only where adequate representation is lacking, read with Article 335's requirement of efficiency of administration — together yielding the Supreme Court's principle that reservation cannot exceed fifty percent. When a student raises the EWS reservation's breach of the fifty percent cap (upheld as part of the basic structure), the professor clarifies: EWS is fundamentally different — not caste-based, and specifically unavailable to those already receiving reservation benefits; it brings in people from other castes previously excluded rather than increasing benefits for the same castes. The dangers of the census: groups learning their exact percentages would demand proportional power — Dalits seeking the Prime Ministership where concentrated, Yadavas their strongholds — precisely the dynamic that led to Partition (Jinnah's argument that Muslims, a minority in a Hindu-majority country, would never genuinely come to power). Proportional reservation demands would bring violent protests, police firing — he predicts at least fifty to a hundred deaths. Vote bank politics is “the biggest evil of democracy”: parties manipulating caste and religious identities, making groups fight while politicians secure votes. Even if seventy to eighty percent of the population belongs to certain castes, giving seventy to eighty percent reservation effectively ends the constitutional commitment to equality; since proportional reservation cannot constitutionally be given, there is no positive gain from determining exact percentages. He acknowledges the current government has also compromised on this principle for votes — but the ideal remains a casteless society. The True Purpose of Reservation — Ending the Ruler-Ruled Divide The professor's philosophical account opens with Manthara's couplet from the Ramayana, in Awadhi: “Koi hoi Ram hame ka hani, cheri chhod na hoi bai rani” — whoever becomes king, I lose nothing; I remain a servant. Under the old order, whoever ruled, the servants remained servants: the line between ruling class and ruled class was absolutely fixed. In monarchical systems no servant, however capable, could become king. Reservation was designed to break this permanent divide. By opening government positions to Dalits and backward classes, it aimed to erase the psychology of “I am the ruler and these are the ruled.” Based on competence, anyone — Dalit or general caste — can become a Collector through the IAS examination, or a representative through votes. Initially Dalits could not pass the IAS examination, necessitating modest reservation to provide the opportunity. The goal was to bridge the gulf so Dalits would not feel disconnected — not “what do we have to do with this country; we are peons anyway” — but rather: “This country is ours too, and we are rulers of this country, and we are protectors of this country, and we have to do good for this country.” Reservation was to transform the psychology of the ruled class, lifting them from inferiority complex into patriotism and ownership — to make the ruled class part of the ruler class. Economic empowerment was never the primary purpose. The professor cites his own son, who never prepared an hour for a government job: a Chief Secretary earns perhaps Rs. 1.5–2 lakh monthly with privileges while in office, but afterward “they'll die of hunger” — one could earn more selling samosas. The craze for government jobs exists because of corruption; the day corruption ends, no child will aspire to government employment. His friend and NLU Jodhpur classmate, now a Group General Counsel, earns Rs. 4 crore annually — far more than any government position — talented people increasingly choose the private sector.

The Delhi Judicial Service Association Case (1991) — the Judge and the Police Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat (1991) Facts · A Gujarat judge, very strict with police officers over investigation quality (“Haven't done investigation, what are you doing?”), generated resentment in an understaffed, overworked force — running between crime scenes (a rape investigation interrupted by a truck-car collision with eight dead). Dr. Ambedkar's Vision The ultimate aim is to have equality. Reservations are a means to achieve that equality, not an end in themselves. — Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly debates on Article 16 Four points from the debates: (1) equality as the ultimate goal — reservations a temporary measure toward a society where they are unnecessary; (2) backwardness as a recognizable, measurable condition requiring state intervention; (3) balancing competing interests while the overall objective survives; (4) reservations as transitional — a mechanism to lift disadvantaged communities to a level where they compete on equal terms. The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 A watershed enacted in response to Supreme Court decisions striking down progressive measures. The primary trigger: Champakam Dorairajan — the Communal G.O., first introduced in 1926-27, allocating educational seats communally (illustratively: Brahmins 3, Harijans 2, Muslims 1, other communities variously), struck down under Article 15(1). The Court's reasoning: the State may make special provisions for backward classes, but they must rest on backwardness, not merely religion or caste — the Communal G.O. did not adequately distinguish the two. The amendment added Article 15(4) to overturn this effect. Three speeches from the Provisional Parliament: Nehru argued passionately that the Constitution must not become an obstacle to social reform; Ambedkar defended the amendment as necessary to the constitutional goal of equality — the Court's interpretation had made upliftment measures impossible; Syama Prasad Mookerjee raised serious objections: the Article 19(2) speech restrictions were being broadened excessively, threatening the democratic fabric; property rights were being eroded; judicial review's scope might shrink, undermining checks and balances. Despite the objections, the amendment passed. Landmark Cases E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu Under Articles 14 and 16 Facts · The Chief Secretary's removal and appointment as OSD. Held · Article 14 (and through it, Article 16) strikes at arbitrariness: “Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be ‘cribbed, cabined and confined’ within the traditional limits of classification.” Administrative discretion is necessary for governance but must rest on relevant considerations, not whims. Principle · The high evidentiary burden of proving arbitrariness — “easy to claim, hardest to prove.” Zoroastrian Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar Cooperative Societies (2005) Facts · A cooperative housing society restricted membership to Zoroastrians (Parsis) only. Held · Upheld: housing societies are not “places of public resort” under Article 15(2); a society may restrict membership by religion or community.

Law changing society: Article 17 abolished untouchability — attitudes have not wholly changed, but the legal prohibition created the framework for challenge and gradually shifted norms; the Domestic Violence Act 2005 and the Criminal Law Amendment 2013 changed attitudes toward violence against women. Procedural Fairness — Hostel Allocation and the Amravati Analogy The hostel allocation anecdote: four beds; four sections (BA, Justicing, BBA and one other); one bed per section by chit-picking, decided in consultation with students; six medical-ground applications (epilepsy, PCOD and other genuine conditions) against four beds. The Amravati analogy for discretion versus arbitrariness: travelling to Amravati, three routes — the super-fast Gadkari highway at Rs. 3,000 toll; a partially developed highway at Rs. 1,500, slightly harder; a toll-free route, longer and slower. The driver (administrator) may choose any, with reasons: the fast highway — “we arrive half an hour early; Rs. 3,000 is worth it”; the free route — “we save Rs. 3,000; the extra time does not matter for a wedding.” Arbitrariness occurs only when there is no reason at all — “I am saying, that's why.” When a relevant reason is given, the decision is not arbitrary, even if another option was better. The Final Article and Its Afterlife Article 10 as amended: (1) equality of opportunity in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State; (2) no ineligibility or discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence; (2a) Parliament's residence-requirement power; (3) reservation for backward classes not adequately represented; (4) religious institutions' office-holders. State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976) 7-judge bench · 5:2 · (1976) 2 SCC 310 Facts · The constitutionality of special treatment for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Kerala government service was at issue before the largest bench then assembled for the question. Held · Five judges held Article 16(4) is NOT an exception to Article 16: it is within the purview of Article 16 as a facet of equality, providing equality of opportunity in line with clause (1), giving positive support and content to 16(1). The Court envisaged not formal or legal equality but proportional equality — the progressive elimination of pronounced inequality. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 79 The same logic extends to 15(4): both rest on Article 14's equality. The theoretical footing is Ronald Dworkin's distinction: the right to equal treatment (formal equality — an equal distribution) versus the right to treatment as an equal (substantive — the fundamental right to be treated with equal concern and respect). Unequal treatment of equals violates equality; so does equal treatment of unequals. Article 15(4) rests not on prejudice, contempt or insult toward forward classes — it promotes equality by requiring affirmative action to remove discrimination. Supporting arguments: (1) constitutional practice — 15(4) and 16(4) have been implemented through executive orders without separate legislation, and courts have consistently upheld this; a fundamental right cannot be taken away without authority of law, so treating these as exceptions would render the executive actions unconstitutional; (2) DPSP harmony — fundamental rights and Directive Principles are read in harmony (itself basic structure): Article 38 (social order for the people's welfare) and Article 46 (promoting the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections) — the pattern of Article 21A's derivation from Article 21 read with Articles 41, 45 and 46; (3) Article 335 — SC/ST claims must be considered “consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration,” a positive obligation, not a device to avoid reservation; (4) Hohfeldian analysis — rights as claims, privileges, powers and immunities: a positive State duty creates a corresponding claim, enforceable under Articles 32 and 226 (mandamus); (5) international recognition — the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights recognises positive rights; (6) comparison — Articles 17, 23 and 24 equally require positive State action, yet are unquestionably fundamental rights: requiring state action does not stop a right from being one. The Birth of Reservation Jurisprudence — Mandal The Mandal Commission was appointed by Prime Minister Morarji Desai on 20 December 1978, chaired by Justice B.P. Mandal, tasked to: (1) determine criteria for identifying socially and educationally backward classes; (2) recommend steps for their advancement; (3) examine the desirability of reservation in appointments and posts; (4) report to the President. The birth story: Dr. Ambedkar did not define “backward class” — when asked, he left it to the government of the day, a strategic avoidance of a politically impossible definition. The report was submitted on 31 December 1980 — and left untouched, gathering dust. The turning point: V.P. Singh's 1990 political crisis, his chair “shaking.” Someone suggested the 50-52% backward classes could save him: he implemented 27% OBC reservation through an executive order — crucial because he lacked parliamentary majority. The 52% thesis: the OBC population was estimated at 52%, hence 27% (within the 50% ceiling). The protests: students preparing for UPSC for three-plus years saw their chances drastically cut — with 500 seats, reservations taking 300 left 200 for the general category. 60-70 people died by self-immolation; around 200 died of burns. The government remained “deaf and blind”; with limited media (no social media, few mobile phones), the government provided incomplete data. The students went to the Supreme Court.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 80 The Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953) — the First Attempt Established 1953 under Kaka Kalelkar; report 1955-56 — the first attempt to identify backward classes. Criteria: (1) traditional apathy for education from social and environmental conditions; (2) occupational handicap; (3) poverty and lack of educational institutions in rural areas; (4) living in inaccessible areas. The failure: no unanimous report — five members recorded minutes of dissent against linking caste with backwardness; even Chairman Kalelkar himself opposed caste as the basis. The Union Government's 1961 memorandum: “It cannot be denied that the caste system is the greatest hindrance in the way of our progress towards an egalitarian society, and the recognition of the specified castes as backward may serve to maintain and even perpetuate the existing distinctions on the basis of caste” — concluding that “some positive and workable criteria should be devised.” No all-India OBC list was drawn; States chose their own criteria; the Centre preferred economic tests. The Mandal Commission's Methodology An empirical survey of 405 of the 406 districts then existing — two villages and one urban area per district — a genuine effort at objectivity. Eleven criteria in three categories: Category Criteria Weight Social (3 points each) Considered socially backward by others; dependent mainly on manual labour; early marriage (25% of females, 10% of males marrying above the State average at a very young age); female work participation at least 25% above the State average (economic compulsion) 12 Educational (2 points each) Children aged 5-15 never attending school at least 25% above State average; dropout rate at least 25% above; matriculates at least 25% below 6 Economic (1 point each) Average family assets at least 25% below State average; families in kutcha houses at least 25% above; drinking water source beyond half a kilometre; landless families or only “khasra” land at least 25% above 4 The eleven indicators of backwardness Castes scoring 11 points (50%) or above were listed as socially and educationally backward; households below 20 for any caste were excluded as too small a sample. The evaluation offered in class: this cannot be called the best method, but it was the best effort — not arbitrary, suited to the task, with economic indicators flowing directly from social and educational backwardness. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 82 DAY 19 14 August 2026 Backward Classes — Four Advocates Argue Indra Sawhney The social-backwardness thesis · Palkhivala · Jethmalani · Parasaran · Venugopal · The Court's holdings · The EWS inconsistency · Quotes to memorise The Core Thesis — All Backwardness Is Rooted in Social Backwardness The Court's causal chain: (1) social backwardness (the caste system's discrimination, stigma and exclusion) is the root cause; (2) it produces educational backwardness (exclusion from access); (3) which produces economic backwardness (no education, no employment) — which in turn reinforces social backwardness. “They feed upon each other, constituting a vicious circle.” The quotes to remember: “Social hierarchy and economic position exhibit an indisputable mutual relationship”; “The lower the caste, the poorer its members. The poorer the members of the caste, the lower the caste.” It is therefore logically flawed to find a person “socially backward but educationally forward” and use that to deny reservation — the categories are intertwined, and the root is social status determined by caste. Why pure economic criteria are rejected: “mere poverty” cannot be the criterion — the vast majority of India is poor, and among the poor are many socially and educationally forward (the professor's example: himself — a “forward community” member, not wealthy, but a PhD professor, certainly not educationally backward). Reservation based on income alone would benefit poor individuals from forward castes, which is not Article 16(4)'s object: correcting a specific historical injustice rooted in caste. From this logic grows the creamy layer: within a backward class, members who have “progressed far enough and far ahead so as to compare favourably with the leading forward class economically, socially and educationally” should not take the benefit — an upper income ceiling secures it “only for such of those members who are still behind, who really deserve.” The Purpose — Sharing State Power, Not Poverty Alleviation Reservation was not designed to make anyone wealthy — a government job cannot do that. The object is to dismantle the historical dominance of certain castes in the State apparatus and enable backward classes to share state power. The pre-independence reality — “It is a well known fact that till Independence, the administrative apparatus was manned almost exclusively by members of the upper caste” — excluded Shudras, SCs, STs and backward groups among Muslims and Christians from any administrative role, leaving them perpetually “ruled.” The goal is empowerment and dignity: moving a community from the feeling of being ruled to being part of the ruling class — bringing pratishtha (prestige), samman (respect) and garv (pride). The textual distinction matters: Article 15(4) reserves in education for classes “socially and educationally backward” (it would be pointless to reserve educational seats for a class educationally forward); Article 16(4) reserves employment for the “backward class of citizens” — where, per Indra Sawhney, social backwardness is the main criterion, and it is incorrect to require the class to be both socially and educationally backward for jobs. Four Advocates, Four Definitions of “Backward Class” Advocate Core position Key arguments Nani Palkhivala A “secular, unified, casteless society is the basic feature of the Constitution” — caste must be erased altogether Since caste is a prohibited ground of distinction, it can never be the basis for determining backward classes under 16(4) — doing so perpetrates the very evil the Constitution abolishes. Accepting the Mandal findings (52% backward) would “seriously jeopardize the efficiency of the administration” and make “merit” disappear

Parasaran The linguistic distinction: reservation is for a “backward class of citizens,” not for “backward citizens” The State must identify a homogeneous group that is backward — a class formed by religion, race, caste, place of birth or another group characteristic — not a collection of backward individuals. If the entire group is backward, reservation may follow. “A very good secular definition” K.K. Venugopal The primacy of economic factors Articles 38(2) and 46 direct the State to minimise income inequalities and promote weaker sections' interests; the economic criterion “must be applied in determining backward class.” (Rejected by the Court for Article 16(4) — the seed of the later EWS controversy) The four arguments before the Court The Supreme Court's Holdings On identification: the Court rejected Palkhivala's extreme (caste irrelevant) and Jethmalani's restriction (only Shudras). The four principal factors of social backwardness — poverty, caste, occupation, habitation: “Poverty, caste, occupation, and habitation are the principal factors which contributed to rank a class as socially backward.” The primary accent of 16(4) is social backwardness; educational backwardness is a requirement of 15(4), not 16(4). # Question Ruling 1 Is a law required for reservation? No — executive order suffices: 16(4) says “provision,” not “law” 2 Is 16(4) an exception to 16(1)? No — a facet, an elaboration of reasonable classification 3 Is 16(4) exhaustive? No — reservation can also be made under 16(1) itself in “very exceptional situations” and “public interest,” not for vote-bank politics 4 Can caste be a starting point? Yes — relevant, but never the sole criterion 5 Economic criteria alone? No — reservation under 16(4) cannot rest purely on economics (the later 10% EWS came by constitutional amendment and remains contested) 6 Sub-categories (“backward” and “more backward”)? Yes — States may sub-classify so benefits reach the most marginalised 7 The limit? Normally 50%; extraordinary circumstances may justify exception 8 Carry-forward? Valid, subject to the 50% ceiling — later addressed by the 81st Amendment (16(4B)) 9 Reservation in promotion? No — but prospective overruling allowed five years' continuation; nullified later by the 77th Amendment (16(4A))

Part 1 — The Constitutional Text Article 19(1) guarantees all citizens the rights to (a) freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout India; (e) to reside and settle anywhere in India; and (g) to practise any profession, or carry on any occupation, trade or business. Sub-clause (f) — acquire, hold and dispose of property — was omitted by the Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978. The words “or co-operative societies” in (c) were added by the Ninety-seventh Amendment, 2011. Each freedom has its own restriction clause: (a) is limited by clause (2), (b) by (3), (c) by (4), (d) and (e) by (5), (g) by (6). Shailabala Devi (1952) The eight grounds — an exhaustive list A restriction “in the interest of the general public” is allowed for trade under clause (6) but not for speech: Sakal Papers; reaffirmed in Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (2023). The 1950 text and the First Amendment As enacted, clause (2) allowed restrictions only relating to libel, slander, defamation, contempt of court, matters offending decency or morality, or which undermined “the security of, or tend[ed] to overthrow, the State.” Two gaps drove the early litigation: no “reasonable,” and no “public order.” Three lines of cases mattered: (1) Romesh Thappar and Brij Bhushan (both 26 May 1950) invalidated provincial public-safety provisions — the Punjab High Court then struck down sedition (section 124A) in Tara Singh Gopi Chand (1950); (2) the Organiser order in Brij Bhushan targeted “news and views about Pakistan” — the government wanted power to curb war-talk after the Nehru–Liaquat Pact of April 1950; (3) the Patna High Court in the Bharati Press case (In re Shailabala Devi, 1950) held even incitement to murder not covered unless it threatened the State — the “Bihar” case the lecturer recalled. The First Amendment (1951) added three grounds — public order, friendly relations with foreign States, incitement to an offence; inserted the word “reasonable,” opening every restriction to judicial review; replaced “libel, slander, defamation” with “defamation” alone and dropped “tends to overthrow the State”; and operated retrospectively — Section 3 deemed the new clause “always to have been enacted,” reviving struck-down laws. The same Act added Article 15(4) (answering Champakam Dorairajan), amended 19(6) for nationalisation, and added Articles 31A and 31B with the Ninth Schedule. The Supreme Court reversed the Patna view in State of Bihar v. Shailabala Devi (AIR 1952 SC 329) a year later — part of the stated need having disappeared, though the text stayed. The Sixteenth Amendment (1963) added “the sovereignty and integrity of India” to clauses (2), (3) and (4), following the November 1962 Committee on National Integration and Regionalism report amid secessionist demands and the war with China; it also changed Articles 84 and 173 and the Third Schedule oaths — candidates, legislators, ministers and judges now swear to uphold sovereignty and integrity. Why Article 19 belongs only to citizens Article Subject Who can claim 14 Equality before law Any person, citizen or not 15 No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth Citizens 16 Equal opportunity in public employment Citizens 19 The six freedoms Citizens 20, 21, 22 Criminal process protections, life and liberty, arrest Any person The constitutional scheme of right-holders Consequences: a foreign national cannot found a claim on Article 19 (Hans Muller of Nuremberg, AIR 1955 SC 367); a company is not a citizen (State Trading Corporation, AIR 1963 SC 1811) but its shareholders and editors can sue for their own rights (Bennett Coleman); in Cricket Association of Bengal the government argued a foreign broadcaster was using an Indian body to claim 19(1)(a) — the majority answered that the citizen-organiser was exercising its own right through an agent.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 87 Articles 17 and 18 in brief Article 17 abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice in any form, and makes enforcement of any disability arising from it an offence — enforced through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989; it binds private persons as well as the State (PUDR, 1982). The lecturer's hygiene-based account of untouchability's origins was expressly his personal view — not a legal proposition; Article 17 treats untouchability as exclusion based on birth, as Dr. Ambedkar described his own experience. Article 18: the State shall confer no title other than military or academic distinction (clause 1); no citizen shall accept a foreign title (clause 2); non-citizen office-holders of profit or trust need the President's consent for foreign titles (clause 3), and no such office-holder may accept presents, emoluments or offices from a foreign State without consent (clause 4). No penalty is prescribed; Parliament may legislate for breach but has not. Category Examples Why Prohibited Knighthood (“Sir”), Rai Bahadur, Khan Bahadur, Dewan Bahadur — colonial or hereditary titles They create a rank above fellow citizens — Article 18's mischief Prohibited to citizens Any title from a foreign State Clause (2) Permitted — military distinction Param Vir Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra, Vir Chakra; military ranks Express exception, clause (1) Permitted — academic distinction “Doctor” for a doctorate; “Professor” Express exception, clause (1) Permitted — professional designation “Advocate”; “Dr.” for a medical practitioner Earned by qualification, not conferred as a title by the State Permitted — national awards Bharat Ratna, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri Not “titles” (Balaji Raghavan) — but must not be used as prefix or suffix; a recipient who does so should forfeit the award Titles under Article 18 — the categories Part 2 — The Landmark Cases Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) AIR 1950 SC 124 · 6 judges · majority per Patanjali Sastri J.; Fazl Ali J. dissenting Facts · Cross Roads, an English weekly printed in Bombay; on 1 March 1950 Madras banned its entry, circulation, sale and distribution under section 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949 “for securing the public safety and the maintenance of public order.” Thappar went straight to the Supreme Court under Article 32. Held · Petition allowed; section 9(1-A) void. Article 32 is itself a fundamental right — the Court cannot turn a petitioner away. Freedom of speech includes freedom to propagate ideas, and propagation is secured by circulation: “Liberty of circulation is as essential to that freedom as the liberty of publication.” “Public order” is a wide expression covering every breach of tranquillity from affray to rebellion — but the 1950 clause (2) spoke only of the security of the State; only aggravated disorder endangering the State's foundations could justify curbing speech. A provision whose language authorises both valid and invalid restrictions cannot be severed — void as a whole. Fazl Ali J.: serious disorder does undermine the State's security, as sedition does. Principle · The first free-speech ruling: circulation is part of speech; the 19(2) grounds are exhaustive and read narrowly; the seed of the overbreadth doctrine. It caused the First Amendment.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 88 Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi (1950) AIR 1950 SC 129 · the same six judges, the same day · Fazl Ali J. dissenting Facts · The Chief Commissioner of Delhi required the weekly Organiser to submit for pre-publication scrutiny “all communal matter and news and views about Pakistan including photographs and cartoons” under section 7(1)(c), East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949. Held · Pre-censorship is a restriction on the liberty of the press, which is an essential part of 19(1)(a); the majority applied Romesh Thappar — public safety/public order is not the security of the State, so clause (2) did not save it. Fazl Ali J. read “public safety” as the security of the State and would have dismissed. Blackstone, quoted: the press's liberty “consists in laying no previous restraint upon publications.” Principle · Press freedom lives inside 19(1)(a) though the Article never says “press”; prior restraint demands justification under clause (2). It does NOT hold all print pre-censorship void — Virendra v. State of Punjab (1957) upheld a time-limited power with a right of representation and struck down one without safeguards. State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) AIR 1952 SC 196 · 5 judges · Patanjali Sastri C.J. Facts · The People's Education Society declared an unlawful association under the 1908 Act's section 15(2)(b) (financing the banned Communist Party); the Madras amendment required stated grounds, allowed representation, and made an Advisory Board's finding bind the government — but the declaration was Gazette-only and membership itself became an offence. Held · Restriction struck down. Reasonableness covers substance and procedure; the test is statute-by-statute — “no abstract standard, or general pattern, of reasonableness.” The factors: the nature of the right, the purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil, the disproportion of the imposition, and prevailing conditions. Shutting out judicial inquiry in favour of executive satisfaction is reasonable only in very exceptional circumstances; the absence of personal notice when membership was criminalised was a serious defect. The Court is “a sentinel on the qui vive.” Principle · The foundational reasonableness test for all of Article 19; the “disproportion” factor is the root of modern proportionality (Modern Dental College 2016; Anuradha Bhasin 2020). Limit noted: it arose under 19(1)(c)/(4) — a ruling on one freedom is weak authority on another. K.A. Abbas v. Union of India (1970) (1970) 2 SCC 780 · 5 judges · Hidayatullah C.J. Facts · Abbas, journalist and film-maker (on the Khosla Committee), made the 16-minute documentary A Tale of Four Cities with a brief blurred red-light-district shot; offered a “U” certificate only with cuts, he challenged pre-censorship itself and the vagueness of the Cinematograph Act's section 5-B(2) directions. Held · Censorship of films including prior restraint is justified; U/A classification is reasonable; directions not void for vagueness but must be supplemented to protect artistic and social value. Film is treated differently from print — instant appeal, realism, combined effect on eye and ear, strong effect on children. American decisions are not decisive: the First Amendment is absolute in form, Article 19(2) expressly permits reasonable restrictions. A law leaving censors “in a boundless sea of uncertainty” would be struck, but courts first construe sensibly. The flaw in the directions: treating artistic and inartistic work alike — censors judge the handling of a theme, not the theme. The Solicitor-General conceded time limits and court- or tribunal-level appeals. Principle · The print-film distinction. Key lines: “The motion picture is able to stir up emotions more deeply than any other product of art”; “our standards must be so framed that we are not reduced to a level where the protection of the least capable and the most depraved amongst us determines what the morally healthy cannot view or read”; “Sex and obscenity are not always synonymous.” Odyssey Communications Pvt. Ltd. v. Lokvidayan Sanghatana (1988) (1988) 3 SCC 410 · per Venkataramiah J.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 89 Facts · Doordarshan was showing Honi-Anhoni; two organisations obtained a Bombay High Court injunction against episodes 12 and 13 in a public interest petition alleging superstition and fright to children — the producer added as a party only the day before the order. Held · Injunction set aside. The right to exhibit a film on Doordarshan, on Doordarshan's terms, is part of 19(1)(a) — like publishing through a newspaper, subject to the medium owner's terms; an interim injunction infringes the producer's right where petitioners show no legal right and no material of real harm; “It spreads superstition” is not a 19(2) ground. The Court expressly left open whether a citizen may set up a private broadcasting station. Principle · Dissemination extends to television; courts must not impose prior restraint by injunction on non-listed grounds. The reserved question was taken up in Cricket Association of Bengal. LIC v. Prof. Manubhai D. Shah (1992) (1992) 3 SCC 637 · two appeals together · per Ahmadi J. Facts · Shah's study paper arguing LIC premiums were unduly high; a member's counter reprinted in LIC's magazine Yogakshema; Shah's rejoinder refused (“in-house publication”). Separately, Doordarshan refused to telecast Beyond Genocide, the Golden Lotus-winning Bhopal documentary holding a “U” certificate, calling it outdated and sub judice. Held · Both appeals dismissed — LIC must print the rejoinder with explanation and apology for delay; Doordarshan must telecast. “Speech is God's gift to mankind.” Freedom includes circulating views through print, radio and television and using the medium to answer criticism. LIC is “State” under Article 12; its publicly funded magazine, open to outside subscribers, must be fair — printing one side and refusing the other violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(a). Once the film-maker's right is recognised, the refusing party bears the burden of showing a 19(2) ground — criticism of government is not one. Ruling confined to “the peculiar facts”: no absolute duty to print whatever any citizen sends. Principle · Right of reply against State-controlled media; burden of justification on the State. It does not create such a right against a private publisher. Secretary, Ministry of I&B; v. Cricket Association of Bengal (1995) (1995) 2 SCC 161 · Sawant and Mohan JJ. jointly; Jeevan Reddy J. concurring Facts · CAB's 1993 Hero Cup: Doordarshan offered Rs. 1 crore; CAB sold worldwide rights to Trans World International for a guaranteed US$550,000 plus 70% of excess; the Telecom Department told VSNL to refuse the uplink and customs detained TWI's equipment; interim orders let both telecast. The 1994 BCCI–ESPN dispute recurred. Held · (para 124) Airwaves are public property; a public authority must regulate their use in the public interest. The right to impart and receive information is part of freedom of speech; a citizen has access to telecasting subject to public-property limits. The Central Government must set up an independent, autonomous public authority to control the airwaves. Sports telecast by a non-profit body has a speech element — earning revenue incidentally does not convert expression into trade. 19(2) permits no monopoly over speech (unlike 19(6) for business). Jeevan Reddy J.'s limits: no citizen has a fundamental right to set up a private broadcasting station — that is for Parliament; “From the standpoint of Article 19(1)(a), what is paramount is the right of the listeners and viewers and not the right of the broadcaster.” Both opinions found the Telegraph Act, 1885 unsuited to broadcasting; the Prasar Bharati Act, 1990 was brought into force in 1997. Principle · The right to receive information; airwaves public property; no broadcasting monopoly. The lecture's version — that the rights-holder must give the feed to Doordarshan — is not in the judgment: that rule comes from the Sports Broadcasting Signals (Mandatory Sharing with Prasar Bharati) Act, 2007. S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal (2010) (2010) 5 SCC 600 · per Chauhan J. Facts · In a 2005 India Today survey the actress endorsed pre-marital sex within committed relationships and girls' self-protection; twenty-three criminal complaints (defamation, obscenity, insult to modesty) followed, mostly from one political party's functionaries.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 90 Held · All quashed. A reference to sex is not per se obscene; the standard is contemporary community tolerance as of an average reasonable person; no identifiable person or definite group was defamed, so the complainants were not “persons aggrieved”; pre-marital sex between consenting adults is no offence, so advocating its acceptance cannot be incitement; the complaints were mala fide, for political mileage. “It is not the task of the criminal law to punish individuals merely for expressing unpopular views”; “Morality and Criminality are not co-extensive”; the law must not have a “chilling effect.” Principle · Unpopular social opinion protected from morality-based prosecution; lays down no new obscenity test (that came in Aveek Sarkar, which cites it). Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014) (2014) 4 SCC 257 · per Radhakrishnan J. Facts · Stern's photograph of Boris Becker nude with his fiancée Barbara Feltus (her father took it), reproduced by Sports World and Anandabazar Patrika in May 1993; an Alipore lawyer's complaint under section 292 IPC; summons issued; the High Court refused to quash. Held · Hicklin is “not the correct test.” Obscenity is judged from the average person's viewpoint applying contemporary community standards, the work as a whole, in its context and for its message; nudity is not obscene per se — only material tending to excite lustful thoughts. The photograph's message was against racism; prosecution quashed. Principle · Hicklin (followed since Ranjit Udeshi 1965) replaced by the community standard test. Note: a two-judge bench displaced a five-judge bench's retention of Hicklin; the judgment reads Udeshi as itself recognising changing standards. Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) (1996) 1 SCC 361 · 5-judge Constitution Bench · per Ahmadi C.J., Kuldip Singh J. concurring Facts · Petitions in Kerala and Madhya Pradesh, transferred to the Supreme Court, challenged the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards as “titles” under Article 18(1). Held · The awards are valid — not titles — but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes; a user should forfeit the award; a high-level committee should set selection criteria. “The theory of equality does not mandate that merit should not be recognized.” Principle · Article 18 targets ranks of nobility and colonial loyal-subject creation; honours recognising work done are compatible with equality. Two cases raised by students Ramesh v. Union of India (1988) — the Tamas case (1988) 1 SCC 668 Facts · A petition to stop Doordarshan showing Tamas, the serial from Bhisham Sahni's Partition novel, alleging it would inflame communal feeling. Held · Refused: two High Court judges had watched it and found a message of peace; the work is judged as a whole by the standard of reasonable, strong-minded people — not of those who sense danger in every hostile view. Principle · Depicting violence is not inciting it. S. Rangarajan v. P. Jagjivan Ram (1989) (1989) 2 SCC 574 — the case a student named “Shankar Asrani v. Jagjivan Ram” Facts · The Tamil film Ore Oru Gramathile criticised caste-based reservation; after agitation threats the High Court revoked its “U” certificate.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 91 Held · Certificate restored. Open criticism of policy is not a restriction ground; the State cannot plead inability to control a hostile audience — freedom “cannot be held to ransom by an intolerant group of people”; the anticipated danger must be “a spark in a powder keg,” justified “on the anvil of necessity and not the quicksand of convenience or expediency.” Principle · The Indian proximity test; the State's duty to protect speech against hostile audiences. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 92 Circulation and the right to receive An idea that cannot be disseminated has not been expressed in any useful sense. Romesh Thappar: a journal's entry ban restricts speech; Sakal Papers: price-by-page laws restrict speech by cutting circulation — the State cannot curb speech to regulate business; Bennett Coleman: newsprint quotas capping pages restrict speech; Odyssey: stopping a telecast restricts the producer; LIC: refusing a reply restricts the critic. Article 19(1)(a) also protects the listener and viewer: Raj Narain — the people's right to know every public act of their functionaries; Indian Express Newspapers — press freedom exists for the public's right to know; CAB — the viewers' interest is paramount; Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) — voters' right to know candidates' antecedents. The Right to Information Act, 2005 is the statutory vehicle. Reasonable restriction — the five-step checklist The five-step checklist for any restriction on speech Points examiners look for: “Law” — the lecturer said only an Act of the legislature; the usual formulation is wider: a statute or a rule made under statutory power qualifies, bare executive instructions do not (the High Court rejected Doordarshan's norms on this basis in LIC). Burden — once the citizen shows a restriction, the State must justify it (LIC; CAB para 46). Proportionality today — legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity, balance (Modern Dental College; Anuradha Bhasin). “In the interests of” — wider than “for the maintenance of” (Ramji Lal Modi, 1957), but the 1960 Lohia case keeps it within proximity. The three tiers of disorder

The test is the act's effect on the community, not its nature (Arun Ghosh v. State of West Bengal, 1970). Proximate and reasonable nexus: a remote, hypothetical or far-fetched connection will not do (Lohia, 1960). Obscenity — from Hicklin to community standards Year Case Contribution 1868 R. v. Abbas (1970) Result Pre-censorship order struck down Prior certification upheld Reason No ground in Article 19(2) supported it Film's stronger impact on a mass audience, including children Limits Can survive only with narrow scope, a time limit and a right of representation (Virendra, 1957) Needs definite standards, room for art, a time limit and an independent appeal Later authority R. Rajagopal v. State of T.N. (1994): no prior restraint on publishing about public officials S. Rangarajan: certification must be reasonable, judged by an ordinary person of common sense Prior restraint across media Incitement, proximity and the remaining grounds Speech becomes punishable when it incites, not when it merely discusses or advocates. United States: Schenck (1919) — clear and present danger from anti-draft leaflets; Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) — advocacy protected unless directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it. India: Kedar Nath Singh (1962) saved section 124A by confining sedition to words with a tendency or intention to create disorder or incite violence — strong criticism of government is protected; Rangarajan (1989) — danger not “remote, conjectural or far-fetched,” a spark in a powder keg; Shreya Singhal (2015) — discussion, advocacy and incitement distinguished; only incitement can be restricted. A caution: Arup Bhuyan v. State of Assam (2011) adopted Brandenburg for membership of banned organisations; a larger bench overruled that holding in 2023, warning against importing American doctrine without regard to 19(2)–(4). A fiery speech nobody acts on is rhetoric, not incitement. Sovereignty and integrity: restricting advocacy of secession or cession of territory; Parliament used it to enact UAPA, 1967; section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 now penalises acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity. A student asked how violation is “quantified” — it is not measured: the State points to a law, shows the speech falls within it, and shows a proximate link to the harm. Balwant Singh v. State of Punjab (1995): raising separatist slogans a few times, with no response and no disorder, is not an offence. Contempt: Articles 129 and 215 and the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; fair criticism of a judgment is permitted (E.M.S. Namboodiripad). Defamation: tort and crime (sections 499–500 IPC, now section 356 BNS); Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) upheld criminal defamation, treating reputation as part of Article 21; Khushboo shows the limit — only a person actually aggrieved may complain. Decency or morality: wider than obscenity, not confined to sexual morality (Ramesh Yeshwant Prabhoo, 1996). Friendly relations: added 1951, rarely litigated — targets propaganda damaging relations with another country, not criticism of its policies. Security of the State: rebellion, waging war — the innermost circle. Part 4 — Comparative Constitutional Law India writes its limits into the constitutional text; the United States leaves them to the courts; the international instruments follow the Indian pattern of right plus limitation clause. Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 96 The First Amendment debate and Nehru's speech Nehru's case: the courts had read Article 19 so widely that Parliament could not legislate for public order. The Bill was introduced 12 May 1951, referred to a Select Committee on 16 May, passed 2 June 1951 by 228 votes to 20. His argument, in paraphrase: the Constitution had been “kidnapped and purloined by lawyers”; judicial readings were blocking social and economic policy; the amendment was enabling only — it restricted no speech itself and restored Parliament's lawmaking power, still subject to judicial review; he criticised the press's tone — freedom carries responsibility; on sedition he called section 124A “highly objectionable and obnoxious” — yet the new public order ground later saved that section in Kedar Nath Singh. The Statement of Objects and Reasons cited courts holding a person not culpable “even if he advocates murder and other crimes of violence” — the Patna ruling. The opposition, led by Syama Prasad Mookerjee, argued a provisional Parliament chosen before the first general election should not cut back fundamental rights — though he accepted that adding “reasonable” was an improvement. For the verbatim speech: Parliamentary Debates of the Provisional Parliament, 16 May to 2 June 1951; book-length accounts: Granville Austin, Working a Democratic Constitution (1999); Tripurdaman Singh, Sixteen Stormy Days (2020). Article 21 and the death penalty — why no right is absolute Article 21's exception is in its text: no deprivation of life or liberty “except according to procedure established by law.” If even life may be taken by law, speech cannot be absolute. Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) upheld the death penalty but confined it to the “rarest of rare”; Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab (1983) requires a balance sheet of aggravating and mitigating circumstances for each accused. The “blue drum” case, corrected: the class was told the lover received death and the wife twenty years — that does not match the record as of 5 October 2026. Saurabh Rajput was killed in Meerut in March 2025, his body found in a cement-filled blue drum; on 30 September 2026 the Meerut district court convicted his wife Muskan Rastogi and Sahil Shukla of murder; sentencing is listed for 14 October 2026, the prosecution seeking death for both. Points of law for the discussion: (1) conspiracy and abetment carry the same punishment as the offence — a student's claim that conspiracy does not attract death is incorrect (Kehar Singh, 1988); (2) sentencing is individual — same murder, different sentences for different roles and mitigating circumstances; (3) murder has only two punishments — death or life; a trial court cannot impose “twenty years”; only the High Court or Supreme Court may fix a term without remission as a death alternative (Swamy Shraddananda, 2008); (4) motherhood is a mitigating factor, not a bar — no rule exempts a mother. The Shabnam case (Amroha): April 2008 — Shabnam and Saleem killed seven members of her family; she was pregnant at arrest, delivered in jail in December 2008, the child fostered at about six; death sentences 2010, confirmed in Shabnam v. State of U.P. (2015), review dismissed January 2020, mercy petitions rejected — a student's claim that she “was hanged” is wrong: the latest reports (2021) record a sentence awaiting a death warrant and no execution. Shabnam v. Union of India (2015) separately holds a death warrant cannot issue until legal remedies are exhausted. Pregnant women: the High Court must commute a pregnant woman's death sentence to life (section 416 CrPC, now section 456 BNSS); before a 2009 amendment it could only postpone execution; Article 6(5) ICCPR likewise forbids execution of pregnant women — the rule protects a woman pregnant when the sentence falls due, which did not help Shabnam, whose child was born before trial ended. Language wide enough for both valid and invalid applications is void as a whole — the overbreadth idea; post-1951 the same ban would be tested for reasonableness and proximity on the public order ground

That it is a restriction needing a 19(2) ground — not that all print pre-censorship is void; the Organiser order would today be tested under public order plus Virendra safeguards 4 Which V.G. Procedural fairness above all — no personal notice though membership was criminalised, and judicial inquiry shut out; a binding Advisory Board cannot cure that except in very exceptional circumstances 5 Abbas's stage-difference vs Blackstone's no-prior-restraint Both hold for different media: prior restraint is permissible only with a legal basis, standards, time limits and appeal — Blackstone's absolute rule belongs to print's history, not Indian law 6 LIC hypotheticals: not “State”; no counter printed; private funding (a) No Article 12 duty — the ruling collapses; (b) no right of reply arises absent the one-sided publication; (c) the public-funds rationale fails — the ruling was confined to its peculiar facts 7 Sawant J. vs Jeevan Reddy J. on private broadcasting Sawant: airwaves public property, independent regulator; Jeevan Reddy: no citizen's right to a station — Parliament decides; a would-be broadcaster must look to legislation 8 Khushboo had she advocated an offence Advocacy is protected until incitement (Shreya Singhal); urging an offence with proximity could be restricted — the reasoning would move from obscenity to incitement analysis 9 Should the message matter in obscenity?
