MTNL 3 Aug 1995 Commercial advertisement held protected Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra 19 Aug 1964 Obscenity — the lecturer credits it with the community standard test, which is wrong Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal 3 Feb 2014 Not named in the lecture, but the real source of the community standard test described Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon 1 May 1996 Bandit Queen and the Phoolan Devi scenes Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India 10 Jan 2020 Proportionality as the modern meaning of “reasonable” Hans Muller v. Superintendent, Presidency Jail 23 Feb 1955 The Netanyahu hypothetical: Article 19 is for citizens only — closing pages only Regina v. Hicklin 1868 The old obscenity test — know it; quoted in full in Udeshi Indian Express Newspapers (Bombay) v. Union of India 1984 Not the case the lecturer described — the other “Indian Express” case, on newsprint duty; skim P.J. Thomas (CVC appointment, 2011); Weeks v. United States (1914); the Election Commissioner case (2023) — Digressions not opened for Article 19 The reading list (the lecturer first said “N.M. Thomas” and corrected himself to P.J. Thomas — N.M. Thomas being a reservation case) CORRECTIONS Where the lecture and the judgments differ — seven points to correct before writing them in an exam: (1) The community standard test is not from Ranjit Udeshi — Udeshi expressly refused to discard Hicklin and only qualified it; Aveek Sarkar (2014) is the authority. (2) The ten-page limit is Bennett Coleman, not Sakal — Sakal (1961) struck down the price-to-pages schedule; Bennett Coleman (1972) struck down the flat ten-page ceiling; the chain the lecturer described (fewer advertisements, higher price, lower circulation, closure) is Sakal's reasoning, repeated in Bennett Coleman. (3) The “Indian Express” lease was never cancelled — Express Newspapers (1985) quashed two show-cause notices (re-entry on the lease; demolition); the other Indian Express case concerns newsprint duty. (4) Tata Press did not overrule Hamdard Dawakhana — a three-judge bench cannot overrule five; it read Hamdard as confined to advertisements of prohibited drugs, relying on Indian Express (1985). (5) This Lohia case is a preventive detention case — the concentric circles come from Hidayatullah J. reading “public order” in rule 30(1)(b) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, while Article 19 stood suspended; the distinction is now used to read “public order” in 19(2), and Anuradha Bhasin repeats the circles when judging section 144 orders. (6) “Law” need not itself be an Act of the legislature — the tested restrictions came through statutory orders and rules (the Price and Page Order 1960 in Sakal; rule 458 of the Telegraph Rules in Tata Press; the Suspension Rules 2017 in Anuradha Bhasin); what fails is bare executive policy with no statute behind it — Beg J.'s ground in Bennett Coleman. (7) Proportionality has more than one formulation — the class's four steps (aim, rational connection, necessity, balancing) are the earlier cases' statement; Columbia's analysis of Anuradha Bhasin reports the Court's own five-point summary (legitimate goal, necessity, alternatives considered, least restrictive measure, judicial review) — the student who added judicial review was right about this case. Two points the lecture got exactly right: “better administration” is not a ground (Sakal — no “interests of the general public” head); and the two-drunks example is Hidayatullah J.'s own illustration in Lohia.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 100 The Briefs Hans Muller v. Superintendent, Presidency Jail, Calcutta (1955) AIR 1955 SC 367 · per Bose J. — closing pages only required Facts · Hans Muller, a West German subject, arrested 18 September 1954 and detained under section 3(1)(b) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 with a view to expulsion; his passport endorsed for return only; a German fraud warrant and extradition request pending; the Centre's signed expulsion order held back once he moved the High Court. Held · (1) Competence: Entries 9–10, Union List — preventive detention connected with foreign affairs; the Foreigners Act, 1946 supported. (2) Articles 21 and 22 protect “citizen and foreigner alike.” (3) Detention to arrange expulsion is genuinely preventive — preventing evasion. (4) A State may act in anticipation of the Centre's order. (5) Excluding certain British subjects from “foreigner” is a reasonable classification. (6) Article 19's rights to move and reside have “no corresponding” foreigner rights — all a foreigner is guaranteed is life and liberty under Article 21. (7) Expulsion power is “absolute and unfettered.” (8) Expulsion is not extradition — the expelled person leaves a free man; government may choose the Foreigners Act route even where extradition is requested. (9) Bad faith not shown. Principle · Cite for: Article 19 is confined to citizens. Be precise — the Court spoke of the rights to move and reside, in an expulsion case; free speech by a foreigner was not in issue. The same visitor still has Articles 14 and 21. Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1965) AIR 1966 SC 740 · Sarkar, Hidayatullah, Raghubar Dayal, Mudholkar, Bachawat JJ. · Lohia argued in person · released 4:1 (Raghubar Dayal J. dissenting) Facts · The 1962 Chinese-attack Emergency; the Defence of India Rules' rule 30(1)(b) permitting detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “public safety” and “maintenance of public order” — not “law and order.” On 9 August 1965 the Patna District Magistrate ordered Lohia's detention to prevent acts prejudicial to “the public safety and the maintenance of law and order”; served 1.40 a.m.; Hazaribagh Central Jail by 3.30 p.m.; Lohia's Hindi letter from jail became the writ petition. Held · (1) The petition was entertainable: the Article 359 order bars petitions only where liberty was taken “under” the Act — whether it was so taken must itself be examined; the President's order “did not make lawless actions lawful.” (2) Sarkar J.: the order is the only warrant and must be strictly in the rule's terms; “public order” in an emergency law means disorder of a grave nature, “law and order” lesser local disorder (rowdiness at Holi); the State cannot use an affidavit to show the order meant what it does not say; one valid and one invalid ground (public safety valid; law and order not) — under Shibban Lal Saksena the whole order falls. (3) Hidayatullah J. (with Bachawat J.): disorder is a spectrum; two drunkards quarrelling cause disorder, not public disorder — if the two belong to rival communities and one stirs communal passion, public disorder is “apprehended”; the circles — “Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State”; by writing “law and order” the Magistrate “was adding a clause to the Defence of India Rules.” (4) Mudholkar J.: the words made the order ambiguous on its face. Dissent (Raghubar Dayal J.): actual satisfaction, not form, controls; the file note showed public order satisfaction. Principle · The three concentric circles; for Article 19(2) only the inner two circles are grounds — a mere law and order problem is not. Sakal Papers (P) Ltd. v. Union of India (1961) AIR 1962 SC 305 · unanimous Constitution Bench · per Mudholkar J. · G.S. Pathak for petitioners; M.C. Setalvad, Attorney-General, for the Union Facts · Sakal, the Marathi daily from Poona (circulation ~52,000 weekdays, 56,000 Sundays; six pages at 7 naye paise, Sunday ten at 12), and two readers' petitions, against the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act, 1956 and the Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Order, 1960 — a schedule fixing maximum pages per price; supplements only on 26 January, 15 August, once a quarter, else by permission.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 101 Held · Section 3(1) unconstitutional. (1) Press freedom is within 19(1)(a) — Brij Bhushan. (2) Circulation is part of the right — “not merely to the matter which he is entitled to circulate, but also to the volume of circulation.” (3) The real purpose was to cut circulation — a minimum price for pages makes papers too costly for a class of readers. (4) Price affects circulation (the Press Commission's findings: Free Press Journal's price cut doubled circulation; two Tamil dailies' price rise lost 33,000 readers). (5) Cutting pages compels restricting news; cutting advertisements forces prices up — “no remote, but a direct consequence,” a vicious cycle ending in closure. (6) Supplement control leaves issues to government's “sweet will and pleasure.” (7) 19(2) is exhaustive — nothing allows restriction for the general public or a section. (8) 19(6) cannot be borrowed — each freedom has its own clause; the State cannot regulate the business side “by directly and immediately curtailing” speech. (9) The test is direct effect: a law capping a named paper's subscribers would be void; achieving it through a rate schedule makes no difference. (10) A good object (checking monopoly) does not save bad means — “a dangerous weapon which is capable of being used against democracy itself.” The Article 14 point and the readers' standing were left undecided. Principle · Indirect restrictions on the press: the State cannot do through price, pages or advertisements what it cannot do directly. Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1972) (1972) 2 SCC 788 · Sikri C.J., Ray, Jaganmohan Reddy, Mathew, Beg JJ. · 4:1 (Mathew J. dissenting) · Palkhivala, Daphtary, Nambyar for petitioners; F.S. Nariman for the Union Facts · Four groups — Bennett Coleman (Times of India), Hindustan Times, Express Newspapers, The Hindu — against the Newsprint Policy 1972-73: a 10-page quota ceiling (Remark V); circulation growth 10% for dailies under 1,00,000 but 3% for larger (VII(a)); a 20% page increase for under-10-page dailies usable only for pages (VII(c)); no page increases by cutting circulation, no quota shifting within common ownership units (VIII); no new newspaper or edition even within quota (X). Held · Two preliminary objections rejected: a company is not a citizen — but under R.C. Cooper shareholders do not lose rights by incorporating; Article 358 (1971 Emergency) does not protect executive action lacking legislative authority. The majority (Ray J.): rationing scarce newsprint is allowed — but “shortage of newsprint can stop with allotment”; the test is direct effect, not pith and substance; the policy directly controlled page growth, circulation and advertisement space. The ten-page ceiling: the three Times editions averaged 13.13, 13.99 and 17.83 pages — cuts of 23.8%, 28.4%, 43.8% against a 4.5% newsprint fall; The Hindu faced 16 to 10. Unequals treated as equals — Article 14 violated. Estimated losses: Rs. 39 lakh (Bennett Coleman), Rs. 44 lakh (Hindustan Times), Rs. 38 lakh (The Hindu). Remarks V, VII(a), VII(c), VIII struck down under Articles 14 and 19(1)(a); X under 19(1)(a). Press liberty is “an Ark of the Covenant.” Beg J. concurring: the conditions had no authority of law at all. Mathew J. dissenting: “an abridgment of speech, but not an abridgment of the freedom of speech”; Article 19(1)(a) is not “the guardian of unlimited talkativeness”; the community's right to hear supports maximum circulation; Article 39(b) validates the small-dailies' classification. Principle · The effect test — judge a measure by its direct effect on the right, not its label or purpose; shareholders and editors can enforce 19(1)(a) through the company. Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India (1985) (1986) 1 SCC 133 · A.P. Sen, Venkataramiah, Misra JJ. · F.S. Nariman for petitioners Facts · The press enclave on Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg; Express Newspapers' plots leased from 1954; building only east of a diagonal sewer under the 1957 agreement; 1977 request to divert and build with double basement; DDA and Ministry approvals (1978); Rs. 1.30 crore spent by February 1980. Then: 17 February 1980 — Jagmohan takes office as Lieutenant-Governor and that Sunday evening calls for the municipal files; 29 February — the Zonal Engineer's locks broken to remove the file; 1 March — press conference announcing an inquiry by three subordinates in three days and a demolition warning, broadcast on radio and television; 1 March — a show-cause notice for demolition; 10 March — a notice to show cause on lease re-entry; 12 March — the committee's report released at another press conference. The Indian Express had published on Jagmohan's role in the Turkman Gate demolitions during the Emergency.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 102 Held · Both notices quashed. The Lieutenant-Governor confused power over Union property (Entry 32, Union List) with his Article 239 powers — nearness to the Centre gave him no authority over its property. A.P. Sen J.: the notices “are intended and meant to silence the voice of the Indian Express” — a direct and immediate threat to press freedom, violating 19(1)(a) read with 14; a writ lies though the matter looks contractual; the re-entry notice was real, not exploratory; summary eviction was unavailable; mala fides — power used for an alien purpose is bad faith; the specific allegations were met only with bare denials; nothing was contemplated before 17 February; promissory estoppel binds the successor government. Venkataramiah J.: arbitrary, without independent application of mind — Article 14. Misra J.: the land rights spring from contract and planning law, not 19(1)(a) — a matter for a civil suit. Principle · Administrative harassment of a newspaper as an indirect attack on press freedom (Sen J.); the model of proving mala fides from a detailed chronology. Do not write that the lease was cancelled — two show-cause notices issued, both quashed. Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) Lal Kuan v. Union of India (1959) AIR 1960 SC 554 · per Kapur J. · K.M. Munshi and N.C. Chatterjee for petitioners; C.K. Daphtary, Solicitor-General, for the Union Facts · The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954: “advertisement” defined widely (labels, cartons, leaflets); “magic remedy” includes talisman, mantra, kavacha; section 3 barred advertisements suggesting drugs for miscarriage, contraception, sexual capacity or venereal disease “or any other disease... specified in rules”; section 8 allowed seizure. Hamdard, the Delhi Unani house, was stopped from advertising forty products; the Poona branch of Sadhana Ausadhalaya was raided without warrant. Held · Method: find the law's true nature and character — history, mischief, remedy; presumption of constitutionality. History: the 1927 Council of State resolution, the Chopra Committee, the Drugs Act 1940, the Bhatia Committee 1953, English statutes. The evil: self-medication driven by extravagant advertising to a credulous public. Article 19(1)(a): “An advertisement is no doubt a form of speech but its true character is reflected by the object for the promotion of which it is employed” — a commercial advertisement does not propagate social, political or economic ideas; advertising prohibited drugs is not speech (relying on Valentine v. Chrestensen). 19(1)(f)/(g): reasonable in the general public's interest. But: section 3(d)'s delegation — naming further diseases by rule with no criteria — “uncanalised and uncontrolled power,” void; the Rules' Schedule fell with it (severable). Section 8's seizure power went far beyond the Act's purpose and lacked safeguards — void; mandamus to return seized goods. Principle · The starting point of the commercial speech story (1959: purely commercial advertising outside 19(1)(a)) — and a leading case on excessive delegation. Confined by later cases to its facts. Tata Press Ltd. v. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. (1995) (1995) 5 SCC 139 · per Kuldip Singh J. · Dr. Abhishek Singhvi for Tata Press; K.K. Venugopal and Arun Jaitley for the Nigam Facts · MTNL (80% government-held, licensee under the Telegraph Act 1885) gave directory publishing to contractors earning from Yellow Pages advertising; Tata Press published its own Yellow Pages buyers' guide (Bombay editions 1992-94); rule 458 of the Telegraph Rules, 1951 bars publishing “any list of telephone subscribers” without permission; the City Court dismissed MTNL's suit, the Single Judge and Division Bench of Bombay reversed and enjoined. Held · Appeal allowed. Hamdard rested on Valentine v. Chrestensen — but American law moved: Sullivan (1964), Bigelow v. Virginia (1975), Virginia State Board of Pharmacy (1976 — a free flow of commercial information is indispensable), Bates v. State Bar of Arizona (lawyer advertising allowed; false and misleading advertising restrainable). The Indian text differs: Article 19(2) itself lists the restrictions — deceptive, unfair, misleading and untruthful commercial speech is hit by 19(2). Hamdard confined: it dealt with prohibited drugs; Indian Express (1985) had already called its wider observations too broad. Advertising pays most of the media's cost (60-80% of newspaper revenue) — Sakal and Bennett Coleman show curbing advertisements hits circulation. The receiver's right: the recipient may have a deeper interest than the advertiser (the life-saving drug example). Holding: “Commercial speech” is part of 19(1)(a). Application: a telephone directory is a public utility the authority may regulate; paid Yellow Pages advertising is not that service; a 19(1)(a) right cannot be denied by creating a government monopoly; Tata's guide is compiled by trade, not by subscription — not a “list of subscribers.” Rule 458 remains mandatory for white-pages entries.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 103 Principle · Commercial advertisements are protected speech; listeners and readers have their own right to receive. Limits: false, misleading or deceptive advertising may be restrained (the judgment does not say which 19(2) head covers it — a gap for critical answers). It did not overrule Hamdard. Ranjit D. Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra (1964) AIR 1965 SC 881 · Gajendragadkar C.J., Wanchoo, Hidayatullah, Shah, Rajagopala Ayyangar JJ. · per Hidayatullah J. · R.K. Garg for the appellant; C.K. Daphtary for the State Facts · Four partners of Bombay's Happy Book Stall found with unexpurgated Lady Chatterley's Lover; one sold a copy to a decoy customer; all convicted under section 292 IPC (fines of Rs. 20); Mulk Raj Anand testified to the novel's literary merit. Held · (1) Section 292 valid — a reasonable restriction in the interests of decency or morality; obscenity has “extremely poor value” in spreading ideas, though where ideas of public interest are conveyed (the medical textbook) the balance tilts toward speech. (2) Knowledge of obscenity is not an ingredient — no “knowingly” in the section; liability is strict, though absence of knowledge may mitigate sentence. (3) The test: Hicklin set out (tendency to deprave and corrupt susceptible minds), “uniformly applied in India”; mere treatment of sex and nudity in art is not obscenity “without something more” — Michelangelo's angels need not wear breeches; but “We do not think that it should be discarded.” Three qualifications: not stray words — the whole work viewed overall; yet the obscene matter also considered “by itself and separately”; art must so preponderate as to throw obscenity into shadow. Obscenity “without a preponderating social purpose or profit” has no protection — judged “by our national standards.” (4) The novel: Lawrence's sincerity accepted, but the sexual descriptions were its only attraction for the common reader; the law protects “not those who can protect themselves”; the impugned portions passed permissible limits; no preponderating social gain shown. Appeal dismissed. (Contrast: the English Central Criminal Court in R. v. Penguin Books had held the same novel not obscene.) Principle · Cite for “Hicklin as modified,” not for the community standard test; and for the seller's strict liability. Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal (2014) — the brief Facts · Stern's Becker-Feltus photograph (taken by her father), reproduced by Sports World (cover story, 5 May 1993) and Anandabazar Patrika (6 May 1993); the Alipore lawyer's complaint under section 292 IPC and section 4 of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986; summons 10 May 1993; the High Court refusing to quash. (An earlier lecture called the fiancée South African; the judgment calls her a dark-skinned film actress, the complainant a German film actress.) Held · Standards change (paras 12-19) — Udeshi, Kakodkar, Samaresh Bose, Khushboo each stressed contemporary values; the yardstick (para 19): “contemporary mores and national standards,” not the susceptible group. Hicklin judged by isolated passages and the most susceptible readers; Roth (1957) moved to the average person; Canada followed in Towne Cinema and Butler. Para 24: “We are also of the view that Hicklin test is not the correct test” — the community standard test applies; nudity is not obscenity per se — only material exciting lustful thoughts; the message and context (paras 25-26, following Bobby Art; Ajay Goswami). The photograph: standing close, Becker's arm covering her breast, taken by her own father; the message — skin colour matters little, love prevails; no tendency to deprave. Proceedings quashed. Principle · Three working rules: the average person, not the most susceptible; the work as a whole; context and message. The standard is national and contemporary. For criticism: a two-judge bench declared Hicklin incorrect although the five-judge bench in Udeshi had declined to discard it. Bobby Art International v. Om Pal Singh Hoon (1996) (1996) 4 SCC 1 · Ahmadi C.J., Bharucha, Kirpal JJ. · per Bharucha J.

Constitutional Law · Day-Wise Class Notes Compiled from classroom lectures · July–October 2026 104 Facts · Bandit Queen, from Mala Sen's book (on sale since 1991 without objection): Phoolan Devi married as a child, raped, humiliated by police, gang-raped, stripped and paraded naked, turning dacoit and to revenge. The Tribunal (Lentin J., retired Bombay High Court, and three women members) allowed the coarse language (ordinary speech in the Chambal), kept the police-beating scene (it explains her turning), cut the second of three rape sequences and trimmed the first and third, kept the naked parade whole — cutting it “would be a sacrilege,” comparing Schindler's List's frontal nudity. The Delhi High Court quashed the certificate. The petitioner: a Gujjar claiming the film slurred his community (the rapist named Babu Gujjar) and Indian womanhood. Held · 'A' certificate restored. The guidelines are broad standards, not a statute — clause 2's sub-clauses cannot outweigh clauses 1 and 3. Where the theme is of social relevance it must prevail; this film “is not a pretty story” — it accuses the society that tormented her. The naked parade: those who stripped her meant to demean her; showing it conveys exactly that — sympathy for the victim, disgust for the perpetrators; “Nakedness does not always arouse the baser instinct.” The High Court's error: the revulsion the Tribunal spoke of was at the sadism of the strippers, not her nudity. Rape is shown for its terrifying effect, not glorified. The test: for a serious film, ask of each scene — does it advance the message? If so, leave it alone, with an 'A' certificate. A film illustrating a social evil must necessarily show the evil; a film extolling it is impermissible; the depiction must be just sufficient. Deference to the expert multi-member Tribunal (three of four members women); the writ court ought not to have entertained a petition resting on a community slur. Principle · Nudity is not obscene by itself — context and purpose decide; the “advance the message” test that Aveek Sarkar later applied to a photograph. Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) (2020) 3 SCC 637 · N.V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy, B.R. Gavai JJ. · (brief written from Columbia's case analysis plus four readable paragraphs — check quotations against the judgment) Facts · 2 August 2019 — J&K; Home Department advises tourists and Amarnath pilgrims to leave; schools and offices closed. 4 August — mobile networks, internet and landlines shut; District Magistrates impose section 144 CrPC. 5 August — the constitutional order ending Article 370's special status. Anuradha Bhasin, editor of the Kashmir Times (Srinagar), unable to publish since 6 August; Ghulam Nabi Azad M.P.; an intervenor noting restrictions described as temporary had lasted over 100 days. The State: cross-border terrorism history (similar steps in 2016); the internet never restricted in Jammu and Ladakh; social media's one-to-many reach; selective blocking not technically possible; newspaper standards do not carry over to the internet. Held · (1) Orders must be produced and published — Article 32 remedies and the right to information require it; no law affecting rights should be passed in secret. (2) The internet: the most used and accessible medium of information; trade and commerce through it are protected under 19(1)(g) subject to 19(6); expression through it is integral to 19(1)(a), restrictable only under 19(2) — but no fundamental right of access to the internet was declared (no party argued for one). (3) A restriction may in a proper case amount to complete prohibition, but the government must explain why lesser measures would not do. (4) Proportionality: whether the least restrictive choice was made (para 53), drawing on Modern Dental College; the Court's own five points — legitimate goal, necessity, alternatives considered, least restrictive measure, judicial review; the restriction's degree, scope, territory and duration must match necessity (para 71). (5) Shutdowns: governed by the 2017 Suspension Rules under the Telegraph Act — only the Union or State Home Secretary (or a Joint Secretary in unavoidable circumstances, confirmed within 24 hours); reasons recorded; Review Committee; section 5(2) requires “public emergency” or “public safety” of a serious nature; orders must be published for challenge; complete suspension is drastic — only if necessary and unavoidable after assessing alternatives (para 99); indefinite suspension impermissible. (6) Section 144: only where danger exists or is apprehended, in the nature of an emergency; cannot suppress legitimate expression; orders must state material facts — mechanical or cryptic orders unlawful; repetitive orders are abuse; the concentric circles repeated (para 120). (7) Press freedom valuable under 19(1)(a), but no evidence publication was actually stopped — no sword of Damocles may “hang over the press indefinitely” (para 151). Order: the Government to review all suspension and section 144 orders, publish them, and withdraw those unnecessary or without time limits. Principle · Proportionality as the present meaning of “reasonable”; the internet as protected medium (without overstating access as a right); restriction orders must be published and reasoned. Critics note: principles laid down, no immediate relief given.

Verbatim Class Notes: Article 13, Personal Laws, and Constitutional Amendments Part I: Personal Laws versus Fundamental Rights — The Conflict under Article 13 and Article 21 The second sentence is more important. Consider this. Islam does not permit a Hindu to marry a Muslim girl unless she converts. And conversion is prohibited—why should she want to convert? Suppose a Muslim girl wishes to marry a Hindu, or a Christian, or a Parsi, without conversion. Now, Islamic law does not allow a girl to marry outside her own religion. Article 21 says that you may marry anybody. So the personal law is violating the fundamental right of a... and especially, this is discriminatory for the fact that a Muslim boy may marry anybody, including a Hindu girl. But a Muslim girl cannot. So it is a gender-based discrimination also—sex-based discrimination. So, such a Koranic practice, if it is violating Article 21 of a citizen, can it be declared to be void under Article 13, sub-clause 2, or not? That is a question for us to inquire. Part II: Constitutional Amendments and the Right to Property Similarly, by constitutional amendment, some of our fundamental rights can be taken away. They have been taken away—especially the right to property. All of you must be aware that a great deal of constitutional amendment has taken place, and the right to property has gone. So, are those constitutional amendments valid or not? This is what we are going to study under Article 13, sub-clause 3. Part III: The History of Personal Law Reforms and the Legislature So far as personal laws are concerned, I must tell you that the Parliament of India has been discriminatory. Starting from the very first Parliament, they tried to introduce all manner of reforms among Hindus. Among Hindus, you see, earlier the age of marriage was before puberty begins, because in Hindu tradition it is a Kanya Daan. The daan is given, and generally—I do not know, I have not read the Vedas—but it is said that the 1

daan is given before puberty starts. Similarly, in Muslim law also, the age of puberty is the age of marriage. But you restricted it... and I am also a part of that; I am also a small participant in that sin. I was also part of a mild protest. Protest, in the sense—protest in discussion. Part IV: The Evolution of Age of Consent and Mar- riage Laws — A POCSO Illustration Earlier, the age of consent was sixteen years. The age of consent—I hope all of you know what that means? [Student: “Yes sir, sixteen years for females, right?”] For females, yes. Now, the Congress government raised the age of marriage to eighteen years, and the age of consent remained at sixteen years. So we pounced upon them. We said, “What is this? Do you want to keep our daughters in adulterous relationships? They cannot marry, but they can have sex? What kind of rule is this? Raise the age of consent to eighteen years as well.” In Indian society, where we cannot expect relationships outside marriage, you are giving this law. Justice Verma—Chief Justice Verma, he was from Indore, from Madhya Pradesh, origi- nally from Satna—the committee that was formed, later, when reforms came, you know that under POCSO the age of consent became eighteen years. In fact, just the day before yesterday, the Supreme Court remarked that making such strict laws regarding the sexu- ality of girls between sixteen and eighteen years of age—how proper is that? Thousands of boys have gone to jail because of this practice. Girls are also in jail—do not think otherwise. This is a gender-neutral law. In sexual offenses... There was some aunt—a chachi—who fell in love with her nephew. This is a story from a few days ago; perhaps some of you have read it. And she conceived from her nephew, who was sixteen or seventeen years old. And now she is compelling the nephew to marry her. Now, a boy of sixteen or seventeen will not be financially independent. He told his mother; the mother told the father. The family spoke to the chachi: “Very well, we will do nothing against you, but you must abort the child and leave this relationship.” The chachi replied, “No. Now I shall marry only him. I will not leave him.” The matter escalated. An FIR was lodged. Now the chachi is in jail, delivering a child. What is to be done? POCSO is a very strict law. You may Google it if you do not believe me. Girls... not chacha—chachi. [Students laugh] Why are you so worried? Worry about the chacha if you must. You worry about the chacha; I am worrying about the law. [The teacher laughs] The chacha is not within our field of study, because he falls outside 2

POCSO. Is that not so? It is the chachi who falls within our field. The one who is within POCSO—that is our concern. Part V: The Judicial Approach to Personal Laws — Shayara Bano, Shah Bano, and Goolrokh Gupta So you see, these laws—they violate our fundamental rights, a great many of them. A Hindu cannot marry more than once. A Hindu cannot marry a Muslim girl. And among Muslims also, there are many instances where their personal law itself violates their fundamental rights. So, will those personal laws be declared void under Article 13, sub-clause 2? Shall we treat them as custom, or shall we treat them as personal law? There is a significant difference between custom and personal law. Is there not? Now, regarding personal law, one thing has been said. For Hindus, considerable reforms were enacted. For Muslims, reforms were not enacted, and Jawaharlal Nehru said that they are not prepared. They have not yet become sufficiently educated to accept reforms. And even today, seventy-five or eighty years later, the same thing is said. Now, the question arises: whatever reforms have taken place in Muslim personal law—were they enacted by overriding personal law, or was something else done? For instance, you must have read a case—the Shah Bano case. In Shah Bano’s case, whether maintenance is to be given beyond the iddat period or not was a very important question. And Islamic law says that maintenance must be given within the iddat period, not beyond that. So, did the court override that law, or did it grant relief under some other law? You will observe that the Supreme Court, with a certain cleverness, grants some rights—it gives relief from the side, as it were—and it does not comment upon the personal law. On the subject of personal law, the Supreme Court refrains, to some extent, from making a direct attack. Even when it declared instant triple talaq unconstitutional, it did so in a roundabout manner; it did not attack personal law directly. There is a Muslim case—Shayara Bano’s case. There was also a Christian lady; she was, I believe, educated at an NLU. She fell deeply in love—she fell in love with someone, and he was not a Parsi. Now, what happened was that her father passed away, and she wished to perform his funeral rites. But Parsi personal law, perhaps, states that if you marry someone from outside the community, you cannot perform the last rites of your parents. So she had to approach the Supreme Court. Now, observe: the Supreme Court granted her permission, but did it make any comment on the personal law? That is what you must examine. You must read this; these are original cases. Write down the name 3

of the case—everyone, write it down. Find out what the name of that case is. I do not remember everything. [A student asks about the court’s behaviour.] A court remains a court only so long as society obeys its orders. Have you observed what happened in Pakistan—how the people burned down the Supreme Court? Read the case of Asia Bibi. And when Asia Bibi’s case... [A student asks about codification of Muslim law.] Vote bank. These days, it is all vote bank. There is no other affliction. Many Muslims do not adhere strictly to the Muslim faith; they offer their prayers and so on, they believe, but they do not follow the rest strictly. Yes, but the government does not have the courage. If reforms had been enacted at that time, they would have been done. Look at how many Islamic countries there are—around sixty, I believe—and in nearly sixty of them, polygamy is prohibited. It is prohibited even in Pakistan. In Pakistan, a Muslim cannot have four wives. But the All India Muslim Personal Law Board will not allow four marriages to be stopped, because if that happens, they will go to jail. This has become a political matter, and in politics, everyone wants votes. Modi also wants votes. [A student speaks about the common man.] That is the worst thing in democracy. Part VI: A Clarification on Talaq Laws — Talaq-e- Biddat versus Talaq-e-Ahsan Yesterday, someone said something, and I became rather quarrelsome about it. Someone from your class—find out who it was. Someone said that you cannot take much action against fifth-year students, because their careers are at stake. And ninety percent of my blood boiled. I said, “These fellows smoke ganja, drink alcohol, call girls to their rooms and make them wear saris—and we should take no action because their careers are at stake? Do the younger students not have careers?” Try to understand that position. They are students; you are a professor. So I said, “If they throw shoes at us, must we, as professors, tolerate it?” This is insolence. The Vice-Chancellor wants to appease the students. The students must not be displeased. “Worry about your own career,” they say. When the student has no such worry—when he is smoking ganja, drinking alcohol, beating people, calling them to his room and abusing them, uttering abusive language—and the Vice-Chancellor says, “No, no action should be taken.” There is a girl, I think, from your class—is she in this class? Ask her. I said that this will not be tolerated. But the Vice-Chancellor has been promoting drunkards for ten years, and 4

that is why many people survive here. Is that not so? And that is why people support the Vice-Chancellor. So, the policy of appeasement—this is the greatest weakness of democracy: that you cannot take strict action... Once, I was delivering a lecture somewhere, and I said, “For five years, this country should make Saddam Hussein its President, because he does not believe in appeasement; whatever is just, he decides accordingly.” So, that Christian... Parsi lady—what is her name—the one regarding her father’s... [Student: “Goolrokh M. Gupta. Goolrokh M. Gupta versus Valsad Parsi Anjuman.”] Yes, she married a Gupta, it seems. Pardiwala? Are there two Pardiwala cases, or does Goolrokh M. Gupta also come under this? Read both cases, whichever they may be. [Student: “2010... this one is from 2017.”] Read both cases, whichever contains the relevant material, all right? What you must observe is this: if her personal law was violating her fundamental right, how did the court find a via-media? Did it directly state whether it was personal law or not? In the same way, I have asked you to examine the Shayara Bano case. And similarly, I mentioned that Indore case—what is its name? The Indore case regarding maintenance during the iddat period—the Shah Bano case. Then there is a Christian case. Christian women did not have guardianship over their children. This exists in every religion; it existed among Hindus as well. Whatever is wrong with Hindu society—untouchability and all that—these things are said to divide Indian society. Read all of it; read all of it. That is why I am not telling you everything; I am making you read. So, for a mother to write her daughter’s or son’s name, the father’s name was necessary, because he was the guardian. Or, say, to open a bank account, the father’s name was required, because he was the first guardian, or something of that sort. So, observe how the court granted relief in that case also, but there too, it would not have commented upon the personal law. And for Hindus, of course, there are very many cases. One case, to start with, you may read—what is the name of that case? Narsu Appa Mali. Yes, Narsu Appa Mali. [Student: “Mali, Mali.”] It is Mali, very well. [Student: “Was he a Mali?”] I do not know; it is a case, that is all. His name is known to us—that much I know. Yes, tell me. No, not in that sense. The name is known to us in that way, not in the other. 5

The useful things, I do not know. And look up one or two more cases that the Supreme Court has decided, taking up personal rights. Please sit down. Let us proceed. [Addressing a student’s response on talaq laws] The day before yesterday, the Supreme Court... Let us construct a hypothesis. Suppose a woman has now reached forty years of age. I am speaking of a matter twenty years hence, for the present purpose. There is a very prominent advocate in Nagpur. And a Muslim friend of his came to him and asked, “I wish to give talaq to my wife. Will our petition lie in the High Court, or in the District Court? How may I give talaq?” So, all of you, tell me, assist me. How will a man who follows the Islamic religion give talaq to his wife? I have heard that talaq has become unconstitutional, illegal. What have you heard? [Student: “You have heard correctly, sir. Triple talaq...”] I have heard correctly? Yes, all right, I have heard correctly. I have heard correctly, have I not? [Student: “One cannot say single talaq, but talaq is valid.”] So, if triple talaq has become invalid, does that mean one must pronounce talaq only once? [Student: “That process itself has become invalid.”] That is precisely what I am saying. When the process has become invalid, then the advocate will require assistance; one must go to court. Not during those days. Now you will have to file a case in court. We are saying, up to now, Muslim law has not even been taught to you... but this much is common sense. What were you doing while preparing for the CLAT? This is a matter of your own timeline. Must I teach common sense also in class? Buy a newspaper sometimes. Why are newspapers printed? To be read. My friend, these days, even in faculty selections, I ask this very question, and everyone becomes confused as to whether one should file a writ petition in the High Court or a case in the District Court. [The teacher laughs] All right? So be very careful with your words. Part VII: A Strict Warning against Generative AI for Legal Research Now we shall come to constitutional amendment. This is for your self-study, but a question will come—it will compulsorily come. You must read it; you must read the original cases. And one thing: do not study from ChatGPT—from Chat G-P-T. But there is a huge gulf in the economic and social dimensions of society. Goodness—an NLU student. Half the time, in moot court... There is a character in our Ramayana—Bali. Half their power. Suppose I go to fight with him, and I am Bali. Then half their power comes to me. So suppose his power is one hundred horsepower. My son tells me, “You are not a villager.” I have lived outside for forty years; I lived in the village for fifteen or sixteen years. But even now, sometimes confidence fails me. [The teacher laughs] Duffers. But my confidence was weakening, and I had to gather it again. Therefore, Dr. Ambedkar said that we must dismantle this disparity by the fastest path, at the earliest, if we wish the country to be united. And it was to remove this very disparity—and this had been discussed during the freedom struggle as well—that the lands of the zamindars should be taken away. To put an end to this, zamindari abolition acts were enacted in almost every state. Land is a state subject; that is why there is no central legislation. All states enacted zamindari abolition acts. What did these acts do? They took the land from the landlords and distributed it among the peasants who were the tenants. He who worked the land, the land now became his. Now the great rajas and maharajas—their lands were taken. And see, there was some trouble here, because they had the right to property. Property cannot be taken—or can it be taken? Ask me tomorrow; do not take me there today, or I shall digress. Ask tomorrow: can property be taken or not? It is called the eminent domain power of the state. Read about it. Some of you may already know; I taught it under Article 2—whether a country can secede. A sovereign nation has certain rights. That is also there. 10

[Student: “Sir, it is in Article 300A, perhaps?”] Wherever it may be, even if it were not written, it would still exist—the eminent domain power of the state. All right? The case which led to the First Constitutional Amendment, pertaining to the right to property. The case decided by a High Court, pertaining to the right to property, which led to the First Constitutional Amendment. And let me quickly add: Champakam Dorairajan was also a reason, but that pertained to another article—Article 15(4). [Student: “Kameshwar Singh versus Province of Bihar.”] Do not call him simply Kameshwar Singh, or he will be displeased. Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes 1 Constitutional Framework 1.1 Schedules of the Indian Constitution Schedule Added By Constitutional Amendment 1st–8th Original Constitution — 9th Schedule First Amendment Act, 1951 Article 31B 10th Schedule 52nd Amendment Anti-defection Law 11th Schedule 73rd Amendment Panchayati Raj 12th Schedule 74th Amendment Municipalities Key Point The 9th Schedule was not part of the original Constitution. At the time of enact- ment, only 8 Schedules existed. 1.2 Purpose and Mechanism of the 9th Schedule The 9th Schedule operates through the following mechanism: (i) Parliament places specific Acts in the 9th Schedule (ii) Such Acts become immune from judicial review for violation of Fundamental Rights (iii) Article 13(2) ceases to apply to these Acts (iv) Even if they violate Articles 14, 19, and 31, they remain constitutionally valid Quote “The Constituent Assembly made an umbrella where rainwater would not go. Call that umbrella the 9th Schedule. Now, if you put any act in the 9th Schedule, then Article 13(2) will not apply to it.” Caution Important Distinction: The 9th Schedule itself is NOT immune from judicial review. Rather, the Acts placed within the 9th Schedule by Parliament become immune from challenge on the ground of violating Fundamental Rights. 1.3 Article 368: Constitutional Amendment Procedure Article 368(1) “Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.” 2

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes Article 368(2) – Key Phrase “...it may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority...” Key Point The Constitution requires passage by both Houses of Parliament. The constitu- tional names (under Article 79) are: • Council of States (Rajya Sabha) • House of the People (Lok Sabha) 1.4 The Provisional Parliament Problem Factual Context (1951): • The Constituent Assembly was functioning as the provisional Parliament of India • Elections for Lok Sabha were held only in 1951–52 • Rajya Sabha could be constituted only after Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies were constituted • Therefore, Rajya Sabha did not exist when the First Amendment was passed Legal Basis for Single-House Amendment: (a) Article 379 (now repealed): Gave the provisional Parliament all powers of the regular Parliament (b) The President was empowered to make rules to remove difficulties in implementing the Constitution Quote “If Rajya Sabha was not there, should the country have been locked up? That the country will not move forward, it will stand right there, and when Rajya Sabha comes, it will be seen? Or should there be some mechanism for improvement?” 2 Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s Vision of Contradictions Dr. Ambedkar, in his final speech to the Constituent Assembly, identified three funda- mental contradictions in Indian society: 1. Political Equality: “One man, one vote, one vote, one value” – All citizens are politically equal 2. Social Inequality: Hierarchies based on caste and class persist 3

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes 3. Economic Inequality: Disparities in wealth and land ownership Quote “On the political front we all are equal now... but on social and economic fronts, we are not.” Purpose of the First Amendment: To remove economic contradictions by en- abling land reform legislation. The 9th Schedule was designed to protect these reforms from judicial challenge. Constitutional Goal: An egalitarian society – ensuring justice, social, economic, and political. 3 Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India 3.1 Case Details Particular Detail Bench Strength 5 Judges Decision Unanimous (5 : 0) Judgment Author Justice M. Patanjali Sastri Petitioners’ Counsel P.R. Das Respondents’ Counsel M.C. Setalvad Key Point M.C. Setalvad was the first Attorney General of India – this is a potential General Knowledge question. 3.2 Factual Background 1. Zamindars (landlords) challenged land reform laws in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh 2. Ground for challenge: These laws violated their Fundamental Rights under Part III of the Constitution 3. To protect these land reform laws from judicial scrutiny, Parliament passed the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 4. This Amendment inserted: • Article 31A • Article 31B • The 9th Schedule 5. Having lost the ability to challenge the Acts directly (due to 9th Schedule protec- tion), the zamindars challenged the First Amendment itself 4

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes Key Point Strategic Logic: “If the tree falls, the branch will fall anyway.” If the First Constitutional Amendment is struck down, the 9th Schedule and all Acts placed within it would automatically fall. 3.3 Petitioners’ Arguments Argument 1: Only a Proper Two-House Parliament Can Amend Article 368 requires passage by each House. The temporary one-house provisional Parliament lacked the competence to amend the Constitution. Argument 2: The President Wrongly Modified Article 368 The President allegedly changed the wording of Article 368 to permit amendment by a single House. Caution Commentary: This argument was considered weak. Over- pleading weakens a case. When even one ground is found to be false, the judge may view the entire petition with suspicion. Argument 3: Constitutional Amendment is “Law” under Article 13 • Article 12 defines “State” to include Parliament • Therefore, whatever Parliament makes is “law” • Article 13(2) states that no law shall violate Fundamental Rights • A Constitutional Amendment, being a “law,” must also comply with Part III • If it violates Fundamental Rights, it must be declared void Argument 4: State Ratification Was Necessary Article 368 requires that certain provisions, when amended, must receive ratification by half of the State Legislatures. Articles 31A and 31B affected the power of courts, which arguably required such ratification. Argument 5: Amendment Procedure Was Not Followed The Amendment Bill was changed after its introduction in Parliament. Caution Commentary: This argument was dismissed as untenable. Par- liament is master of its own procedure and can amend, reject, or modify any Bill. Parliament is “slave only to the Constitution,” not to lawyers or procedural technicalities of this nature. Argument 6: Parliament Cannot Legislate on Land Land is a State subject under the Seventh Schedule. Parliament lacks legislative competence over land matters. 5

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes Caution Commentary: This argument conflated legislative power with constituent power. Parliament did not make a law on land; it amended the Constitution to create the 9th Schedule. These are distinct powers. 3.4 Respondents’ Arguments (Union of India) Response 1: Parliament Has the Power to Amend the Constitution, Including Fundamental Rights Two textual reasons support this: • Article 13(3): When defining “law,” the Constitution makers enu- merated: ordinances, laws, by-laws, regulations, rules, orders, cus- toms, usages. They did not include “constitutional amendment” in this definition. If their intention was to prevent amendment of Fundamental Rights, they would have explicitly mentioned it. • Article 368: When granting the power to amend “any provision of this Constitution,” the framers could have written “except Part III.” They did not. Despite knowing that Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct, they deliberately omitted any such restriction. Key Point Textual Inference: The deliberate omission in both Article 13(3) and Article 368 indicates that the Constituent Assembly did not intend to bind Parliament’s amending power with respect to Fun- damental Rights. Response 2: Constitutional Amendment is NOT “Law” under Article 13 Parliament possesses two distinct powers: Ordinary Legislative Power Constituent Power Derived from Article 245–246 Derived from Article 368 Subject to Article 13(2) Not subject to Article 13(2) Limited by Seventh Schedule As powerful as the Constituent Assembly itself Makes ordinary laws Makes/amends the Constitution Quote “When an amendment is happening under constituent power, Par- liament becomes very powerful. It becomes as powerful as the Con- stituent Assembly itself was. Just as there were no restrictions on the Constituent Assembly, similarly no restrictions will remain with the Parliament either, because restrictions are not written anywhere.” 6

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes Response 3: Provisional Parliament Had Full Powers Article 379 (now repealed) conferred all parliamentary powers on the pro- visional Parliament until the regular Parliament was constituted. Response 4: State Ratification Was Not Required Articles 31A and 31B did not directly reduce the powers of courts. Only provisions that directly affect court powers trigger the ratification require- ment. Indirect effects do not suffice. Response 5: Parliament Could Protect Land Reform Laws Articles 31A and 31B were themselves constitutional amendments. Par- liament possessed the constituent power to enact them. 3.5 The Judgment Case Summary Held: The First Constitutional Amendment is constitutionally valid. Ratio Decidendi – Core Reasoning: (1) Constituent Power vs. Legislative Power Article 368 confers constituent power, which is distinct from the ordinary legisla- tive power exercised under Articles 245–246. Article 13(2) applies only to ordinary legislative power, not to constituent power. (2) Textual Interpretation of Article 13(3) The definition of “law” in Article 13(3) does not expressly include “constitutional amendment.” This omission is deliberate and significant. (3) Textual Interpretation of Article 368 Article 368 does not contain any exception for Part III (Fundamental Rights). The framers could have written “except Part III” but chose not to. This indicates that Parliament’s amending power extends to Fundamental Rights. 3.6 Doctrine of Harmonious Construction Key Point Definition: Harmonious construction is a principle of statutory interpretation where two apparently conflicting provisions are interpreted in a manner that gives effect to both, rather than allowing one to render the other inoperative. Application in Shankari Prasad: 7

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes Article 13(2) Article 368 Harmonious Construction Applies to Applies to Article 13 governs legislative power Article 368 governs constituent power Both provisions survive and op- erate in their respective spheres Reasoning: • If Article 13 were interpreted broadly to include constitutional amendments, Article 368 would become non-operational – it could not amend any Fundamental Right • Such an interpretation would render Article 368 “dead” for the purposes of Part III • Courts should avoid interpretations that make one provision completely ineffective • The harmonious construction: Article 13 applies to ordinary legislation; Article 368 applies to constitutional amendments • Both articles survive and function within their respective domains Quote “Harmony means making a balance between both, keeping both alive. Lest one dies. Both survive.” 4 The Trajectory of Amendment Jurisprudence 4.1 Overview of the Evolution Case Year Held Key Doctrine Shankari Prasad 1951 Amendment power unlimited Constituent vs. Legislative power Sajjan Singh 1965 Doubts expressed Basic Structure (first mention) Golak Nath 1967 No amendment of FRs Prospective Overruling 24th Amendment 1971 Overruled Golak Nath Parliamentary supremacy Kesavananda Bharati 1973 Middle path Basic Structure Doctrine 8

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes 4.2 Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965) Case Summary Key Judges from Nagpur: • Justice M. Hidayatullah • Justice J.R. Mudholkar Both expressed doubts about the unlimited amending power recognised in Shankari Prasad. Significance: (1) The majority followed Shankari Prasad (2) However, two judges expressed doubts about Parliament’s unlimited amending power (3) Justice Mudholkar used the term “basic structure” for the first time in Indian constitutional jurisprudence (4) Both judges agreed that Parliament’s power cannot be unlimited, but they ex- pressed this concern in different ways Caution Task: Identify the precise difference between Justice Hidayatullah’s and Justice Mudholkar’s reasoning. Both concluded that amending power is not unlimited, but their approaches differed. 4.3 Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) Case Summary Bench: 11 Judges Outcome: Overruled Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh Held: Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights Key Reasoning: (1) Article 368 provides only the procedure, not the power The actual power to amend the Constitution is derived from the residuary leg- islative power under Entry 97, List I, Seventh Schedule, read with Article 248 (2) Since the amending power is legislative in nature, a constitutional amendment is “law” within the meaning of Article 13(2) (3) Therefore, any constitutional amendment violating Fundamental Rights is void (4) There is no distinction between constituent power and legislative power 9

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes Key Point Doctrine of Prospective Overruling (Introduced for the First Time) • The Court held that its decision would apply only prospectively (from the date of judgment onwards) • All amendments made before the judgment remained valid • This meant Golak Nath won the case but got no relief – the property already taken remained taken Quote “That poor guy won the case, but he didn’t get any relief.” 4.4 The 24th Constitutional Amendment (1971) Purpose: To overturn the Golak Nath decision. Key Changes: (a) Amended Article 368 to clarify that it confers both power and procedure for amendment (b) Added Article 368(3): “Nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment made under this article” (c) Made Presidential assent to amendment Bills mandatory 4.5 Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) Case Summary Bench: 13 Judges (largest constitutional bench in Indian history) Challenge: Validity of the 24th Amendment Outcome: The Basic Structure Doctrine The Middle Path: Shankari Prasad Unlimited Power (Amend anything) Golak Nath No Power Over FRs (Cannot amend FRs) Kesavananda Bharati Basic Structure Doctrine (Can amend but cannot destroy basic structure) Core Holding: 10

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes (1) Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights (2) However, Parliament cannot destroy or abrogate the “basic structure” or “es- sential features” of the Constitution (3) The 24th Amendment was upheld, but Golak Nath’s core concern (protection against absolute power) was preserved through the basic structure limitation Key Point Key Judges to Study: • Chief Justice S.M. Sikri – Majority view • Justice K.K. Mathew – Distinct reasoning differing from Sikri 5 Comparative Analysis Issue Shankari Prasad Golak Nath Kesavananda Bharati Nature of amend- ing power Constituent power (distinct) Legislative power (same) Constituent power (distinct but lim- ited) Amendment of FRs Permitted Not permitted Permitted, subject to basic structure Art. 13 applies to amendments? No Yes No (overruled Go- lak Nath on this point) Art. 368 provides Power + Procedure Procedure only Power + Procedure Ultimate limit None (unlimited) Absolute (cannot amend FRs) Basic Structure 6 Key Definitions and Concepts Egalitarian Society: A society based on the principle of equality for all its members; the constitutional goal of achieving social, economic, and political justice. Harmonious Construction: An interpretative principle where two conflicting provi- sions are interpreted in a manner that gives effect to both, ensuring neither becomes inoperative. Prospective Overruling: A doctrine where the Court declares the law as it should be from the date of judgment onwards, but does not disturb past transactions decided under the overruled law. 11

Constitutional Amendment Jurisprudence Lecture Notes Basic Structure: The essential and fundamental features of the Constitution that can- not be destroyed or abrogated by any constitutional amendment. First mentioned by Justice Mudholkar in Sajjan Singh and fully developed in Kesavananda Bharati. Constituent Power: The power to frame, make, or amend the Constitution, derived from Article 368. Distinguished from ordinary legislative power. Ordinary Legislative Power: The power to make laws on subjects enumerated in the Seventh Schedule, derived from Articles 245–246, and subject to the restrictions in Article 13(2). 7 Study Tasks Caution Assigned Reading (3 days): 1.
