Part I: The Foundational Conflict – Parliament vs. the Judiciary 1 The Core Constitutional Question The lecture traces one of the most consequential constitutional battles in Indian legal history: the struggle between Parliament and the Supreme Court over the scope and limits of the power to amend the Constitution. The central question is deceptively simple: The Core Question Does Parliament have unlimited power to amend any part of the Constitution, including the Fundamental Rights (Part III), or are there inherent limitations on this amending power? This question engaged the highest constitutional court for over two decades, from Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) to Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), culminating in the enunciation of the Basic Structure Doctrine. 2 The Political and Constitutional Context When the Constitution was adopted, the first generation of India’s rulers were the very freedom fighters who had drafted and enacted the Constitution. There was an implicit trust that these individuals, having sacrificed for the nation, would always act for the welfare of the people. In this climate, the idea that Parliament might abuse its amendment power to dismantle fundamental rights seemed remote. However, as time passed and the political landscape changed, concerns began to emerge. If Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution without limitation, what safeguard existed against the total abrogation of the rights guaranteed to citizens? Could a transient parliamentary majority permanently alter the essential character of the Constitution? 3 The Two Competing Visions Two fundamentally opposed views of constitutional sovereignty emerged: 1. Parliamentary Supremacy (The British Model): Parliament is the supreme law-making body. It can make or unmake any law whatsoever. No person or body has the right to override or set aside legislation. If Parliament amends the Constitution, courts must accept and enforce the amendment. 2. Constitutional Supremacy (The American Model): The Constitution is the supreme law of the land. All organs of the State—legislature, executive, and ju- diciary—derive their authority from the Constitution and are bound by it. An amendment that violates the essential character or fundamental principles of the Constitution is not a valid exercise of the amending power. 3
The Indian Constitution does not explicitly adopt either model in its pure form. The contest between these two visions played out in the courts over two decades. 4

Part II: The Early Cases – The First Stirrings of Doubt 4 Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951) 4.1 Facts and Issue The Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, introduced, among other things, Article 31A and 31B, which sought to protect land reform laws from challenge on the ground that they violated Fundamental Rights, particularly the right to property under Article 31. The amendment was challenged on the ground that it infringed Fundamental Rights and that Parliament lacked the power to amend Part III of the Constitution. 4.2 The Question Before the Court The core legal question was: Is a constitutional amendment a “law” within the meaning of Article 13(2)? Article 13(2) provides that the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III. If a constitutional amendment is “law” under Article 13(2), then Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. If it is not “law,” then the prohibition in Article 13(2) does not apply to constitutional amendments. 4.3 The Judgment The Supreme Court, by a unanimous decision, held that: 1. The word “law” in Article 13(2) refers to ordinary legislation made in exercise of legislative power. It does not include constitutional amendments. 2. A constitutional amendment is made in exercise of constituent power (the power to frame and amend the Constitution), which is distinct from ordinary legislative power. 3. Therefore, Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including the Fun- damental Rights, and such an amendment is not subject to Article 13(2). Ratio: Parliament has unlimited power to amend the Constitution, including Part III. Fundamental Rights are not immune from constitutional amendment. 5 Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965) 5.1 Background The Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, further expanded the Ninth Schedule and amended Article 31A. This was again challenged. A five-judge bench of the Supreme Court was called upon to reconsider the correctness of Shankari Prasad. 5

5.2 The Majority View The majority (Chief Justice Gajendragadkar, Justice Wanchoo, and Justice Raghubar Dayal) reaffirmed the decision in Shankari Prasad. They held that Article 368 confers the power to amend the Constitution and that this power is not subject to Article 13(2). Fundamental Rights can be amended. 5.3 The Seeds of Doubt: Separate Opinions of Justice Mud- holkar and Justice Hidayatullah Although concurring in the result, two judges—Justice J.R. Mudholkar and Justice M. Hidayatullah—wrote separate opinions that planted the first seeds of the Basic Structure Doctrine. While they agreed with the decision, they expressed reserva- tions and raised profound questions about whether there were implied limitations on the amending power. 5.3.1 Justice Hidayatullah’s Opinion Justice Hidayatullah’s reasoning centered on the primacy and sacrosanct character of Fundamental Rights: 1. Fundamental Rights are Primordial and Sacrosanct: Justice Hidayatullah emphasized that Fundamental Rights form a very basic and essential part of the Constitution. They are “primordial sacrosanct” rights. 2. The Article 13(2) Question: He noted that Article 13(2) does not explicitly ex- clude constitutional amendments from the definition of “law.” If ordinary legislation cannot affect Fundamental Rights because of Article 13(2), it seems anomalous that a law derived from Article 368 (which is itself a provision of the Constitution) could abrogate those very rights. 3. Fundamental Rights Cannot Be Amended in the Same Manner as Ordi- nary Provisions: The significance and character of Fundamental Rights demand a higher threshold of protection. They are not ordinary constitutional provisions. The manner in which ordinary provisions may be amended cannot be equally ap- plied to the abrogation of fundamental liberties. 4. Inalienable Rights: The idea that certain rights are inalienable—that they cannot be taken away even by the sovereign—was part of his reasoning. These are rights that inhere in individuals by virtue of their humanity and are constitutionally recognized, not constitutionally created. 5.3.2 Justice Mudholkar’s Opinion: The Comparative Constitutional Argu- ment Justice Mudholkar’s contribution was to introduce a comparative constitutional per- spective. His opinion is remarkable for the breadth of its scholarship, especially given the limited resources available at the time (no internet, limited library access, no SCRs in the modern sense, no interns, typewriters requiring the retyping of entire pages for a single error). 6

The BHU Conference and the German Constitution: A conference was held at Banaras Hindu University (BHU), at which a German professor delivered a lecture on the German Constitution (Basic Law). The Ger- man Basic Law contains an “eternity clause” (Article 79(3)), which expressly pro- vides that certain fundamental principles—including the federal structure, the demo- cratic and social character of the State, and the inviolability of human dignity—cannot be amended. These are eternally entrenched and placed beyond the reach of even the constitution-amending power. The Pakistan Supreme Court Judgment: Justice Mudholkar also referred to a judgment of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, which had similarly held that certain fundamental features of a constitution could not be abrogated by amendment. (The reference is likely to Fazlul Quader Chowdhury v. Muhammad Abdul Haque (1963), where the Pakistan Supreme Court discussed limitations on the amending power.) The United States Constitution – Article V: Justice Mudholkar drew attention to the United States Constitution, Article V, which provides for the amendment process and specifies certain matters that cannot be amended: Article V 1. The Slave Trade Clause (Temporary): The first clause of Article V provided that no amendment could be made prior to the year 1808 that would affect the first and fourth clauses of Article I, Section 9. These clauses related to the prohibition on Congress banning the importation of slaves before 1808. This was a 20-year temporary entrenchment. 2. Equal Suffrage in the Senate (Permanent): The second clause of Article V provides: “No State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.” This is a permanent, unamendable provision. Every state, regardless of its population or size, is entitled to two senators. A small state like Goa (in the Indian analogy) and a large state like Uttar Pradesh have equal representation in the Senate (two senators each). This equality cannot be taken away even by constitutional amendment unless the state itself consents. Justice Mudholkar’s Reasoning: From these comparative examples, Justice Mudholkar reasoned as follows: 1. If the constitutions of Germany, the United States, and other nations recognize that certain things cannot be amended—that there is a “basic structure” or an unamendable core—then it stands to reason that the Indian Constitution, even if not explicitly, must also contain some essential features that are beyond the reach of the amending power. 2. A constitution is not merely a collection of provisions; it has a soul, an identity, a character. That identity cannot be destroyed while still claiming that the same constitution survives. 3. The absence of an explicit “eternity clause” in the Indian Constitution does not mean that Parliament’s amending power is unlimited. Implied limitations may 7

and should be read into the amending power to preserve the essential character of the Constitution. 4. He invited the Court to consider whether there were basic features of the Consti- tution that could not be amended. This was the first use of the conceptual language that would later become the “Basic Structure Doctrine.” 5.4 The Significance of Sajjan Singh Although the majority in Sajjan Singh reaffirmed the Shankari Prasad position, the separate opinions of Justice Mudholkar and Justice Hidayatullah had planted a powerful intellectual seed. They had introduced into Indian constitutional discourse the following ideas: • The concept of implied limitations on the amending power. • The use of comparative constitutional law to interpret the Indian Constitution. • The language of “basic features” and “primordial sacrosanct” rights. • The notion that the identity of the Constitution cannot be destroyed by amend- ment. These ideas would germinate and find full expression in later cases. 5.5 A Note on the Scholarship of the Era The lecture paused to reflect on the extraordinary dedication and scholarship of judges like Justice Mudholkar. In 1964: • There was no internet. • Supreme Court Reports (SCRs) were not as comprehensive or accessible as they are today. • Law libraries were not as well-stocked with international materials. • Judges did not have interns or research assistants (the very concept of an “intern” was virtually unknown in India until the 1990s; the term gained widespread currency only after the Clinton-Lewinsky scandal brought it into global headlines). • Judgments were typed on manual typewriters. If an error occurred on the 21st line of a page, the entire page had to be retyped. There was no “save” or “cut and paste.” Justice Mudholkar was not in line to become the Chief Justice of India. He had nothing personal to gain from writing an elaborate, scholarly, dissenting-in-spirit opinion. He could simply have signed the majority opinion. Yet, he undertook the pain of research and writing because he believed the Constitution and the people of India deserved it. This dedication, this commitment to the constitutional cause without personal incentive, is a model of judicial integrity and intellectual rigour. 8

Part III: The Turn – Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967) 6 Background and Composition of the Bench The question of Parliament’s power to amend Fundamental Rights was revisited by an 11-judge bench of the Supreme Court in Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967). This was the largest bench assembled up to that point, reflecting the gravity and complexity of the constitutional issue. 7 The Core Argument of the Supreme Court The majority in Golaknath (6:5), led by Chief Justice K. Subba Rao, overruled Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh and held that Parliament cannot amend Funda- mental Rights. 7.1 The Reasoning: Article 368 is Procedural, Not Substantive The central plank of the majority’s reasoning was a reinterpretation of the nature of Article 368: 1. Article 368 is Merely Procedural: The marginal heading of Article 368, at the time, read: “Procedure for amendment of the Constitution.” The Court held that Article 368 only lays down the procedure for amending the Constitution. It does not itself confer the power to amend. 2. The Source of the Amending Power: If Article 368 does not confer the power to amend, where does the power come from? The Court answered: Entry 97 of the Union List (List I of the Seventh Schedule), read with Article 248. • Entry 97, Union List: “Any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III including any tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.” This is the residuary power of legislation—the power to legislate on subjects not assigned to the State List or the Concurrent List. • Article 248: “Residuary powers of legislation.—(1) Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List. (2) Such power shall include the power of making any law imposing a tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.” 3. Constitutional Amendment is an Exercise of Legislative Power: Since the power to amend the Constitution is derived from the Legislative Relations chapter of the Constitution (Articles 245–255, read with the Seventh Schedule), a constitutional amendment is, in essence, an act of legislation. It is an exercise of legislative power, not a separate, sui generis “constituent power.” 4. Constitutional Amendment is “Law” under Article 13(2): If a constitu- tional amendment is an exercise of legislative power, it falls within the definition of 9

“law” in Article 13(2). Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making any “law” that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights. Therefore, a constitutional amendment that infringes Fundamental Rights is void under Article 13(2). 7.2 The Conclusion The majority concluded that Parliament has no power to amend Part III of the Constitution (Fundamental Rights). Fundamental Rights were placed beyond the reach of the amending power. This was a dramatic reversal of the position that had prevailed for 16 years since Shankari Prasad. 7.3 The Dissent Five judges dissented, adhering to the view that Article 368 conferred both the power and the procedure to amend the Constitution and that constitutional amendments were not “law” under Article 13(2). 10

Part IV: The Legislative Response – The 24th Amendment (1971) 8 The Political Context The Golaknath decision was a severe blow to the legislative agenda of the government led by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The judgment threatened the validity of numerous land reform laws and other progressive legislation that had been protected by consti- tutional amendments placing them in the Ninth Schedule. The government resolved to overturn Golaknath through a constitutional amendment. 9 The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 The 24th Amendment was a direct and comprehensive legislative response designed to restore the supremacy of Parliament and to negate the reasoning of the Golaknath majority. The amendment made the following critical changes: 9.1 Amendment 1: Change in Marginal Heading and Addition of “Power” The marginal heading of Article 368 was changed from: “Procedure for amendment of the Constitution” to: “Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor” By adding the word “Power”, Parliament sought to make it explicit that Article 368 is not merely a procedural provision; it is the repository of the substantive power to amend the Constitution. The Golaknath argument that the power came from the residuary legislative entry was thus legislatively overruled. The Constitution now stated, in terms, that the power to amend is located in Article 368 itself. 9.2 Amendment 2: Introduction of “Notwithstanding” Clause – Non-Obstante A non-obstante clause was added to Article 368(1): “Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution. . . ” The significance of a non-obstante clause is that it gives the provision overrid- ing effect. It means that no matter what any other provision of the Constitution says—including Article 13—Article 368 prevails. It is a declaration of supremacy: “I am the boss. No other provision, including Article 13, applies to me.” 11

9.3 Amendment 3: Presidential Assent Made Mandatory – “Shall” The language governing the President’s role in the amendment process was changed to make the President’s assent mandatory. The amendment provided that when a Bill to amend the Constitution is passed by both Houses of Parliament and presented to the President, the President “shall” give assent, and upon such assent, the Constitution “shall stand amended.” This removed any possibility that a future President might refuse assent to a con- stitutional amendment, thereby frustrating the will of Parliament. The President was rendered a formal, rubber-stamp authority in the amendment process. 9.4 Amendment 4: Addition of Article 13(4) A new clause was added to Article 13: Article 13(4) – Added by the 24th Amendment “Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368.” This clause explicitly states that Article 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments. The Golaknath argument that a constitutional amendment is “law” un- der Article 13(2) and therefore cannot infringe Fundamental Rights was legislatively nullified. Article 13(4) makes it clear that the prohibitions in Article 13 do not extend to amendments made under Article 368. 9.5 Amendment 5: Addition of Clause (3) to Article 368 A new clause (3) was added to Article 368, which stated in substance that nothing in Article 13 shall apply to any amendment under Article 368. This was essentially a repetition of the point made in Article 13(4), inserted for abundant caution and emphasis. 9.6 Summary of the 24th Amendment’s Strategy The 24th Amendment was a comprehensive legislative masterstroke designed to system- atically dismantle every pillar of the Golaknath reasoning: Golaknath Holding 24th Amendment Response Article 368 is merely procedural; the power to amend comes from residuary legislative power (Entry 97, List I; Arti- cle 248). Added “Power” to the marginal heading and the text of Article 368 to make it the source of substantive amending power. A constitutional amendment is “law” within Article 13(2). Added Article 13(4): “Nothing in this article shall apply to any amend- ment. . . ” Article 13(2) prohibits amendments that take away Fundamental Rights. Added “Notwithstanding” clause to Ar- ticle 368 and clause (3) to override Ar- ticle 13. 12

9.7 The 42nd Amendment (1976) – A Later Exacerbation The lecture noted, in passing, that the 42nd Constitutional Amendment (enacted during the Emergency) went even further. It added clause (4) (later renumbered as clause (5)) to Article 368, which declared, in substance, that there are no limitations whatsoever on the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution. This clause was later struck down as unconstitutional in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) for violating the Basic Structure Doctrine. The point made was that the ruling party had attempted, through constitutional amendments, to assert that whatever Parliament does is valid—a claim of absolute, unchecked power. 13

Part V: The Landmark – Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) 10 The Case and Its Significance Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) is arguably the most important consti- tutional case in Indian legal history. It was decided by the largest-ever bench of the Supreme Court: 13 judges. The case directly confronted the validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments and, in doing so, was called upon to determine, once and for all, the scope of Parliament’s amending power. 11 The Political Atmosphere The atmosphere surrounding the case was intensely political. The Supreme Court had, in effect, become the arena for a fundamental contest between the legislature and the judiciary for constitutional supremacy. The judges were acutely aware that their decision would shape the future of Indian democracy. 12 The Composition of the Bench and the Judicial Alignments The 13 judges can be broadly divided into three groups based on their positions: 12.1 Group 1: Pro-Parliament (Unlimited Amending Power) – 6 Judges These six judges held that Parliament has unlimited power to amend the Consti- tution, including Fundamental Rights. There are no inherent or implied limitations on the amending power. Their view was: • The 24th Amendment is valid. • Article 368 confers plenary (full and absolute) power to amend any part of the Constitution. • The word “amendment” includes the power to alter, modify, or even repeal any provision. • The Constitution cannot be held hostage by a judicially created doctrine of una- mendability. Result: 6 judges in favour of unlimited parliamentary power. 14

12.2 Group 2: Pro-Basic Structure (Limited Amending Power) – 6 Judges These six judges held that while Parliament has wide powers of amendment, the amend- ing power is not unlimited. There are certain essential features or basic elements of the Constitution that cannot be destroyed by amendment. Their view was: • Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. • However, Parliament cannot amend the Constitution in a manner that destroys its identity or basic structure. • The Constitution has a soul, a character, an essential personality. That personality cannot be killed while keeping the body (the text) alive. • The word “amendment” implies that the original Constitution continues to exist in an amended form. It does not contemplate the replacement or abrogation of the Constitution. Variations within Group 2: • Some judges (e.g., Justice Shelat, Justice Hegde, Justice Grover) spoke of “implied limitations” on the amending power. • They identified the identity or essential character of the Constitution as the touchstone. • Different judges used different terminology—some said “basic features,” others said “basic structure,” but the core idea was the same: the identity cannot be de- stroyed. Result: 6 judges in favour of limitations on the amending power (the Basic Structure Doctrine). The Deadlock: 6 judges for unlimited power + 6 judges for limited power = dead- lock. The deciding vote was cast by the 13th judge. 12.3 Group 3: The Swing Vote – Justice H.R. Khanna (1 Judge) Justice H.R. Khanna became the most consequential judge in this historic case. His vote broke the deadlock and created the 7:6 majority. His reasoning is of exceptional importance. 12.3.1 Justice Khanna’s Initial Position: No Inherent Limitations In the first part of his judgment, Justice Khanna appeared to align with the pro-Parliament camp. He stated: • Parliament has no inherent limitation on its power to amend the Constitution. • There is no implied limitation on the amending power. • Parliament has plenary power to amend any part of the Constitution, as and when and as much as it wants. This would have delighted the government, as it suggested that Justice Khanna was the seventh judge in favour of unlimited amending power. 15

12.3.2 Justice Khanna’s Critical Proviso: The Meaning of “Amendment” However, in the very next breath, Justice Khanna introduced a critical qualification that changed the entire trajectory of the case. He stated: Justice H.R. Khanna’s Holding “The word ’amendment’ has its own inherent limitations. Amend- ment does not mean replacement. You cannot replace the Con- stitution. The original Constitution must survive.” Justice Khanna’s reasoning focused on the linguistic and conceptual meaning of the word “amendment”: 1. He consulted dictionaries, including the Oxford Dictionary, to ascertain the or- dinary meaning of “amendment.” 2. “Amendment” means to correct, improve, or modify something while retaining its essential character. 3. “Amendment” does not mean abrogation, repeal, or replacement. 4. A constitution can be amended; it cannot be destroyed under the guise of amend- ment. 5. He posed a rhetorical question: “Does amendment mean changing everything except words like ’is,’ ’am,’ and ’are’?” The answer is manifestly no. The core, the essence, the main substance must remain. 12.3.3 The Path to the Basic Structure Unlike the six judges in Group 2, who arrived at the Basic Structure Doctrine through the concept of the identity or essential character of the Constitution, Justice Khanna arrived at the same destination through a different route: the inherent limitation contained in the word “amendment” itself. His reasoning can be summarized as follows: 1. Parliament has plenary power to amend any part of the Constitution. 2. There is no implied limitation on what can be amended. 3. However, the power to amend is not the same as the power to replace. 4. The word “amendment” contains within itself an inherent limitation: the original must survive. 5. Therefore, while Parliament can amend any provision, it cannot amend the Consti- tution in such a way as to destroy its basic structure or essential framework. 6. The Constitution, as amended, must remain recognizably the same Constitu- tion. 16

12.3.4 The Significance of Justice Khanna’s Vote Justice Khanna’s judgment created the 7:6 majority for the proposition that while Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, it cannot alter or destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution. This is the Basic Structure Doctrine. The Result: • The 24th Amendment was upheld as valid. • However, the power under Article 368, as amended by the 24th Amendment, is subject to the limitation that it cannot be used to destroy the Basic Structure. • The 25th Amendment was partially upheld and partially struck down (the portion that excluded judicial review was held to violate the Basic Structure). 13 The Legacy: The Basic Structure Doctrine The Basic Structure Doctrine, as propounded in Kesavananda Bharati, established the following principles: 1. Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. 2. Parliament cannot destroy or alter the Basic Structure of the Constitution. 3. The Basic Structure is not exhaustively defined. It is an evolving concept. Over time, the Supreme Court has identified several features as part of the Basic Struc- ture, including: • Supremacy of the Constitution • Republican and democratic form of government • Secular character of the Constitution • Separation of powers between the legislature, executive, and judiciary • Federal character of the Constitution • Judicial review • Rule of law • Dignity and freedom of the individual • Harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles 4. The power of judicial review to determine whether an amendment violates the Basic Structure remains with the Supreme Court. 17

14 The Aftermath: Subsequent Developments The lecture noted, in closing, the following subsequent developments: • The 42nd Amendment (1976): Enacted during the Emergency, this amendment added clause (4) (later clause (5)) to Article 368, which declared that there were no limitations on the amending power. This was a direct attempt to overrule Kesavananda Bharati. • Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): The Supreme Court struck down this clause as unconstitutional. The Court held that the power to amend the Constitution is a limited power, not an absolute power. The limitation is the Basic Structure. Any attempt to remove this limitation is itself a violation of the Basic Structure (specifically, judicial review and the harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles). 18

Part VI: Comparative and Historical References 15 The United States Constitution – Article V 15.1 The Amendment Process Article V of the U.S. Constitution provides for a four-way system of amendment: 1. Congress proposes, State Legislatures ratify: This is the most common method. Two-thirds of both Houses of Congress propose an amendment. Three- fourths of the State legislatures (currently 38 out of 50 states) must ratify. 2. Congress proposes, State Conventions ratify: Congress proposes, and ratifi- cation is by conventions in three-fourths of the states. This method has been used only once (for the 21st Amendment, repealing Prohibition). 3. State Legislatures demand a Convention, Congress proposes, States rat- ify: Two-thirds of the state legislatures call for a constitutional convention. Congress then proposes amendments, which are ratified by three-fourths of the states. This method has never been used. 4. Convention proposes, State Conventions ratify: A convention proposes, and state conventions ratify. 15.2 Unamendable Provisions Article V contains two explicit limits on the amending power: (a) Slave Trade (Temporary – 20 years): No amendment could be made before 1808 affecting the clauses relating to the importation of slaves. This was a 20-year entrenchment. (b) Equal Suffrage in the Senate (Permanent): “No State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.” Each state has two sena- tors. This equality of representation cannot be taken away even by constitutional amendment without the consent of the state concerned. 15.3 The Political Nature of Amendment in the U.S. In the United States, the process of constitutional amendment is regarded as a political question, and the judiciary generally does not interfere in the amendment process. There is no judicially enforceable “basic structure” doctrine in the U.S. If an amendment is passed following the procedure in Article V, it is valid. 19

16 The German Basic Law – The Eternity Clause The German Basic Law (Grundgesetz), adopted in 1949, contains an “eternity clause” in Article 79(3). This clause provides that amendments to the Basic Law af- fecting certain fundamental principles are inadmissible (unamendable). These prin- ciples include: • The division of the Federation into L¨ander (states) – the federal structure. • The participation of the L¨ander in the legislative process. • The principles laid down in Article 1 (protection of human dignity) and Article 20 (democratic and social federal state, sovereignty of the people, separation of powers, and the rule of law). This was the provision that the German professor at the BHU conference had dis- cussed, and which Justice Mudholkar cited as an example of a constitution that explicitly entrenches certain core principles against amendment. 17 The American Civil War and Dred Scott v. Sand- ford The lecture drew a historical parallel to illustrate the consequences of judicial decisions on slavery and the constitutional framework. 17.1 Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) Dred Scott was an enslaved African American man who sued for his freedom on the ground that he had lived with his owner in a free state (Illinois) and a free territory (Wisconsin), and therefore, he should be free. The U.S. Supreme Court, by a 7:2 majority, held: 1. African Americans, whether enslaved or free, were not citizens of the United States and could not sue in federal court. 2. The Missouri Compromise (which had prohibited slavery in certain territories) was unconstitutional because it deprived slave owners of their property without due process of law. 3. The Court famously declared: “Once a slave, always a slave. You can never become a free citizen.” This decision is widely regarded as one of the worst in the history of the U.S. Supreme Court. It inflamed public opinion, deepened the sectional divide between the North and the South, and was a direct catalyst for the American Civil War. 20

17.2 The American Civil War (1861–1865) • Abraham Lincoln, a self-educated man from humble origins (a shoemaker by early trade), was elected President. He had lost almost every election in his life but won the presidency. • Lincoln was committed to ending slavery. The Southern states, whose economy depended on slave labour, declared that they would secede (separate) from the Union and form a new country, the Confederate States of America. • Lincoln took the bold decision to send the U.S. military to prevent secession and preserve the Union. The resulting conflict was the American Civil War. • The war resulted in an estimated 800,000 casualties (a staggering number, espe- cially considering the much smaller population of the United States at the time—approximately 31 million in 1860). • Lincoln was assassinated shortly after the war ended. 17.3 The Connection to Article 356 of the Indian Constitution The lecture drew a connection between the American Civil War and Article 356 of the Indian Constitution (President’s Rule in States): • The framers of the Indian Constitution, particularly Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, were deeply aware of the dangers of state secession and the potential for civil conflict. • Article 356 was designed as a constitutional safety valve. If a state government acts in a manner that threatens the unity and integrity of India, or if the consti- tutional machinery in a state fails, the Centre can impose President’s Rule, taking over the administration of the state without resorting to military force. • The lecture contrasted this with the American experience: the U.S. had to fight a devastating civil war with 800,000 dead to prevent secession. India, through Article 356, created a constitutional mechanism to address state-level crises without bloodshed. • The reference was also made to the Second Amendment to the U.S. Constitu- tion (the right to bear arms), which was partly motivated by the states’ desire to maintain militias to protect themselves against federal overreach. 18 Concluding Reflections on Judicial Scholarship and Integrity The lecture concluded with a personal reflection on the dedication of judges like Justice Mudholkar, Justice Hidayatullah, Justice Subba Rao, Justice Krishna Iyer, and others. These judges: • Worked without the modern amenities that contemporary students and profession- als take for granted (internet, computers, comprehensive databases, interns). 21

• Typed their judgments on manual typewriters, where a single error meant re- typing an entire page. • Had no personal career advancement to gain (many were not in line to become Chief Justice). • Yet, they undertook painstaking research and wrote elaborate, scholarly opinions because they believed in the Constitution and the people of India. The lecture urged students to look beyond grades and CGPA and to draw inspiration from the lives of these judges—to cultivate humility, hard work, punctuality, and a commitment to principles rather than personal gain. The example of Amitabh Bachchan, who, despite his stature, reaches the set first, often before the sweepers, and never performs without rehearsal, was cited as an example of dedication to one’s craft. The message was that true achievement lies not in transient accolades but in the lasting impact of one’s work and the integrity with which one performs it. 22

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 2 Preliminary Remarks: Classroom Conduct and Disciplinary Warnings Attendance and Proxy Issues The Professor emphasized strict attendance enforcement and collective responsibility for classroom property. Key points: * • Collective Responsibility: If classroom property (e.g., a malfunctioning device) is damaged and the specific student responsible is not identified, the cost (e.g., 60,000 rupees for a replacement) is to be recovered equally from all students in the class. This is a written rule in the university manual. • Proxy Attendance: The Professor identified instances of students attempting to mark attendance for absent peers (calling out “Present” for multiple roll numbers). The warning was that attendance would be deducted for proxy calls, and fraudulent claims undermine trust. • Medical Leave Abuse: A specific case was cited where a student broke his leg playing football and claimed the university was responsible because the university “gave permission to play,” demanding medical leave. The Professor rejected this logic: “Who asked you to play? Is it compulsory from our side?” He warned against shifting personal responsibility onto the institution. Bar Council of India (BCI) Directions on Conduct BCI Disciplinary Mandate: * • Students must address faculty with proper respect (using “Sir”/“Ma’am”). • Posting on social media regarding protests, or any content that may attract legal action, is prohibited. • The Internship Committee is directed to conduct an orientation using the BCI letter. • Any student found violating these rules should be reported to the BCI for disci- plinary action.

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 3 The Original Constitution of India and the Philosophy of Sarva Dharma Sambhava The Physical Document: Art and Symbol- ism The Professor directed students to examine the original hand-written Constitution of India, illuminated by artists. Key features noted: * • Illustrations: The document contains detailed artwork, including depictions of Lord Ram, Lord Krishna (imparting the Bhagavad Gita on a chariot, located in the Directive Principles section to symbolize Raj Dharma), and figures from Islamic history (e.g., Akbar in Part 8). • Calligraphy: Hand-written by Prem Behari Narain Raizada. • Significance: The artwork is a deliberate choice by the framers to represent India’s diverse cultural and religious heritage, directly linked to the constitutional value of secularism. The True Meaning of Indian Secularism The Professor contrasted Western and Indian secularism. Western Secularism Indian Secularism (Sarva Dharma Sambhava) Based on a strict separation or “distance” between State and Religion. Stemmed from historical conflict between the Church and the Ruler. Based on equal respect for all religions. The State does not distance itself from reli- gion but engages with all faiths equally. Often leads to the exclusion of religious expression from the public sphere. Actively acknowledges and re- spects the positive teachings of all religions. The Constitu- tion does not mandate the “de- struction of India’s ancient cul- ture.” Table 1: Contrasting Models of Secularism “Secularism did not mean keeping a distance from religion. Secularism meant Sarva Dharma Sambhava (equal respect for all religions). ’Destroy India’s

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 4 ancient culture’—it is nowhere written in the Constitution... Those who were making the Constitution wrote it down themselves. Today, if someone men- tions ancient things, a hundred people stand up against it. This is not real secularism.” Universal Teachings: The Bhagavad Gita and the Quran The Professor gave examples of how religious texts contain universal human values, which should be taught to all, irrespective of faith. This, he argued, is the constitutional vision. Teaching from the Bhagavad Gita: Self-Elevation The Professor recited and explained a key verse: Sanskrit Verse: Uddhared atmanatmanam natmanam avasadayet Atmaiva hy atmano bandhur atmaiva ripur atmanah Meaning and Explanation: * 1. Self-Elevation: A human being must elevate themselves through their own in- tellect, willpower, and good deeds. No one else can do this for you. “Who can elevate you? You can! Nobody else can.” External privileges (like a wealthy family) are irrelevant without personal effort. 2. Avoiding Despair: One must not allow oneself to fall into despair, laziness, and bad thoughts. The Professor shared an anecdote about a colleague who would feign illness moments before class out of a lack of confidence, illustrating the need to overcome internal weakness. 3. Mastery of the Mind: The mind itself can be one’s greatest friend or, if uncon- trolled, one’s greatest enemy. An example was given of a woman in Meerut who conspired with her driver to murder her husband, demonstrating the catastrophic consequences of an uncontrolled mind. “Now tell me, where in the Gita is it written that only Hindus have to control the mind? How did this become ’non-secular’? This is for every human being! Do people who follow Islam never go into depression? If they are going into depression, to elevate them, we can tell them from the Quran as well. No, no, tell them from the Gita too!” Teaching from the Quran: Tolerance and Forgiveness The Professor cited a case from Pakistan where the court praised the Quran for identifying the two pillars of Islam as Tolerance and Forgiveness. “If Islam says ’Tolerance and Forgiveness,’ why shouldn’t this be taught to all Hindu children as well? ... See, our religions are one and the same in

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 5 these aspects! They also say tolerance, we also say tolerance. They also say forgiveness, we also say forgiveness. This is what the Constitution wanted!” Critique of Modern “Spiritual” Commercialism The Professor criticized figures like Ramdev for commercializing spirituality, arguing that true adherence to Indian scriptures would preclude becoming a businessman and accumulating wealth, as the scriptures teach that everything must be left behind. This, he noted, is a degradation of religious principles.

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 6 Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): The Case and Its Context Introduction and Significance The Professor introduced the case with high praise for a former student’s presentation, which he used as a benchmark for the depth of analysis expected. * • Full Case Name: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala. • Citation: AIR 1973 SC 1461. • Bench: 13 Judges. This is the largest Constitution Bench in the history of the Indian Supreme Court. • Decision Date: 24th April 1973. • Judgment: A deeply fragmented 7:6 verdict (described as a “6.5 to 6.5 judgment” pulled to a majority by the Chief Justice). • Hearing Duration: 66 days (the longest until the Ayodhya dispute hearings, which lasted around 63 days). • Key Advocates: – For Petitioners: Nani A. Palkhivala (leader), along with Daphtary, Chagla, Soli Sorabjee, Deewan, Harindranath, and others. – For Respondents (State): H.M. Seervai (Advocate General of Maharashtra, described by the Professor as “the world’s greatest constitutional jurist,” not to be “limited” to a state role). Factual Background * 1. The Petitioner: Kesavananda Bharati was the chief of a religious sect (matha) in Kerala. The sect owned significant land. 2. The State Action: The Kerala government enacted the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, and the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1969, which placed restrictions on land holdings. The State claimed ownership of the sect’s land under these laws. 3. Initial Petition: The Swami filed a petition under Article 32 in the Supreme Court to enforce his rights under Articles 25, 26, 14, 19(1)(f), and 31.

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 7 4. The Supervening Event: While the petition was pending, the Indira Gandhi gov- ernment passed the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments (partly to over- come the Golaknath decision of 1967). The Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1971, was also passed, and it was placed in the Ninth Schedule, shielding it from judicial review. 5. The Broadened Challenge: The petition was amended to challenge the validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments themselves. The Central Issue Core Question: What is the extent of the amending power conferred by Article 368 upon Parliament? * • Is the power to amend the Constitution absolute and unlimited? • Or is it subject to inherent or implied limitations that prevent Parliament from destroying the Constitution’s basic features? • Specifically, can Fundamental Rights be abrogated by a constitutional amendment? This was a direct conflict on whether Golaknath was correctly decided and what “amendment” means. Preamble as Part of the Constitution The Professor explained the reasoning for why the Preamble is a part of the Constitution, a key finding in the case. * 1. The Argument: The Preamble was debated, discussed, and passed by the Con- stituent Assembly in the same manner as all other provisions. 2. The Act of Adoption: It was adopted, enacted, and “given to ourselves” with the rest of the Constitution. 3. Declaration of the Constituent Assembly: The framers explicitly adopted it as a part of the Constitution. 4. Conclusion: The Preamble is not a mere guiding philosophy external to the docu- ment; it is an integral part of the Constitution.

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 8 The 13-Judge Bench: Arguments and Judicial Standpoints The Competing Arguments Petitioners’ Arguments (Nani Palkhivala) Respondents’ Argu- ments (State) Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution is limited and restricted. It is not a power to destroy. The power of Parliament to amend the Constitution is absolute, unlimited, and unfettered. The Constitution was granted to secure freedom from tyranny. An unlim- ited amending power can be used to become tyrannical and take away all rights. Unfettered supremacy of Parliament is a basic prin- ciple of the Indian legal sys- tem. The features of freedom are at risk if not constitu- tionally protected from the whims of a transient major- ity. There is a necessity to ful- fill socio-economic obli- gations which may require amending property rights and other FRs. There is a restrictive competence on the amending power, a sus- picion voiced by Justices Hidayatullah and Mud- holkar in Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan. This is not a new idea but a continuation of that judicial caution. Even a democracy can be turned into a one-party rule if power is not checked. (The Professor noted the irony that this was an argument put forward by the State, which was itself trending toward one-party rule). The Political Context: A Biased Bench? The Professor provided a candid assessment of the judges’ perceived leanings, explaining that the 6 judges in the minority in Golaknath were now part of this larger bench. Indira Gandhi attempted to “neutralize” them by appointing new judges. “The biggest servants of Indira Gandhi were these two: Dwivedi and Beg. Dwivedi’s case is understandable; he was related to a Cabinet Minister who was Indira Gandhi’s right hand... What about Beg? ... Beg tried to be even more loyal than Dwivedi to Indira Gandhi, and later became Chief Justice too because Indira Gandhi made him one!”

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 9 “With the Consti- tution” (Majority) “Non- Committed/Reluctant” “With the Govern- ment” (Minority) Judges who held that the amending power is limited and cannot destroy the Constitution’s ba- sic structure. Their loyalty was to the con- stitutional identity. (Chief Justice S.M. Sikri, Justices She- lat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, Reddy). The pivotal judges who were not clearly aligned. Justice H.R. Khanna was the key non- committed judge whose opinion was decisive. Judges who held that Parliament’s power was absolute. The Professor iden- tified Justice S.N. Dwivedi and Jus- tice M.H. Beg as the biggest “servants” of the Indira Gandhi government. Justice A.N. Ray was de- scribed as relatively more “neutral” among the minority. Table 3: Judicial Alignments on the Bench as Described in the Lecture The Majority View: The “Identity” and “Basic Structure” The Professor meticulously went through the opinions of the judges forming the majority, highlighting their different emphases. The students were made to read aloud from the ratios. Chief Justice S.M. Sikri * • Core Phrase: “Identity of the Constitution.” • Ratio: “The expression ’amendment of this Constitution’ does not enable Parliament to abrogate or take away Fundamental Rights or to completely change the fundamental features of the Constitution so as to destroy its identity.” • Emphasis: The Constitution has an identity, and an amendment cannot destroy that identity. Within the limits of preserving this identity, Parliament can amend everything. • Essential Features Listed: (1) Supremacy of the Constitution; (2) Republican and Democratic form of Government; (3) Secular character of the Constitution; (4) Sepa- ration of powers; (5) Federal character of the Constitution. Justices Shelat and Grover * • Core Phrase: “Identity of the Constitution and its basic features.”

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 10 • Ratio: “Though the power to amend cannot be narrowly construed and extends to all the articles, it is not unlimited so as to include the power to abrogate or change the identity of the Constitution and its basic features.” • Essential Features Listed: Supremacy of the Constitution; Republican and Demo- cratic form of government; Sovereignty of India; Secular and Federal character; Demar- cation of power (Separation of powers); Dignity of the individual; Unity and integrity of the country. Justices Hegde and Mukherjea • Ratio: “Though the power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is a very wide power, it does not yet include the power to destroy or emasculate the basic elements or the fundamental features of the Constitution.” Justice P.J. Reddy • Ratio: “Although the power of amendment is wide, it is not wide enough to totally abrogate or emasculate or damage any of the Fundamental Rights or the essential elements in the basic structure of the Constitution or of destroying the identity of the Constitution.” The Decisive, Pivotal Opinion: Justice H.R. Khanna Justice Khanna’s opinion was distinct from both the six “identity” judges and the six “absolute power” judges. He is the reason the Basic Structure Doctrine prevailed. 1. Rejection of Implied Limitations: Justice Khanna began by rejecting the argu- ment that there is an inherent, implied limitation on the amending power. He stated there is no implied limitation. Parliament’s power is wide. This made Indira Gandhi “happy” initially. 2. The Turn: The Meaning of “Amendment”: He then held that the limitation is derived from the word “amendment” itself. 3. The Core Ratio: “The question has been posed during arguments as to whether the power to amend under the above article includes the power to completely abrogate the Constitution and replace it by an entirely new Constitution. The answer to the above question in my opinion should be in the negative... The word ’amendment’ postulates that the old Constitution survives without loss of identity despite the change and continues even though it has been subjected to alterations.” 4. Substance Must Survive: A mere retention of some trivial provisions while the basic structure is destroyed is not a true amendment. The old Constitution must be retained in substance. “...it is not permissible to touch the foundation or to alter the basic institutional pattern. The word ’amendment’... cannot have the effect of destroying or abrogating the basic structure or framework of the Constitution.”

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 11 5. Conclusion: While the power is not inherently limited, the concept of “amendment” necessarily excludes the concept of “destruction.” This creates the limitation: you can change everything, but you cannot destroy the Basic Structure.

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 12 Broader Constitutional Philosophy and Political Commentary The Danger of Absolute Power The Professor connected the legal arguments back to political philosophy, specifically the social contract theory. “What did Indira Gandhi say? ’I am absolute! I have unlimited power, un- fettered power!’ In a limited government... We formed government for con- venience! And because a government was formed, we gave it some power, but power is limited! By giving up freedom, we took guaranteed rights! And... if they misbehave, we can remove them! Locke was proved wrong by Indira Gandhi!” He contrasted this with the Indian constitutional design, which rejected both absolute Parliamentary Sovereignty (British model) and absolute, unrestricted rights (early Amer- ican model). India created a balance: rights are guaranteed but subject to reasonable restrictions (Articles 19(2)-(6)), and Parliament is supreme but not sovereign to the point of destroying the Constitution’s identity. The Basic Structure as a Safeguard Against Tyranny The Professor justified the Basic Structure doctrine, citing a debate with Professor Faizan Mustafa. “If such a restriction of Basic Structure hadn’t been put on Parliament’s power, who knows, today in the Constitution, Indira Gandhi might have brought another amendment stating, ’Even after I die, my descendants shall be Prime Ministers!’ ... Our judgment—today we are all here and can say with assur- ance that there are certain basic things that no matter what majority you get, you cannot change.” Emergency Era and Censorship The discussion naturally led to the Emergency (1975-1977) as a real-world example of what happens when power is unchecked. * • Dismissal of I&B Minister: Inder Kumar Gujral, then I&B Minister, was dismissed for refusing to censor news and submit it for prior approval to Sanjay Gandhi. The Professor quoted the exchange: “Do you want to stay a minister or not?” • Suppression of Press: The electricity of the Indian Express was cut off to prevent printing. This led to the line of Indian Express cases, which are vital to Article 19 jurisprudence.

Lecture Notes: Kesavananda Bharati & Constitutional Philosophy 13 • The Principle of Ramesh Thappar: The Professor invoked the ratio of Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras: “Circulation of the newspaper, dissemination of informa- tion is included within the right to speech and expression!” Meaning, the State cannot circumvent free speech by allowing printing but banning distribution. Final Message: Self-Reliance and the Fed- eral Principle * • Self-Elevation Reiterated: The lecture closed by returning to the Gita’s teaching.
