Part I: The Philosophical Foundation – Why Classification Is Essential to Equality 1 The Core Principle: Treating Unequals Equally Is a Violation of Equality The right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution of India is not a mandate for absolute, mechanical, or rigid equality. It does not command that every person must be treated in an identical manner. To treat everyone identically, regardless of their differing circumstances, needs, and conditions, is not equality—it is injustice. The fundamental premise of Article 14 is captured in the maxim: “Equals must be treated equally, and unequals must be treated unequally.” The Foundational Principle of Article 14 Because all human beings are not equal in their various aspects— in their upbringing, height, weight, age, education, income, back- ground, and needs—treating unequals equally is a violation of equality. 1.1 Illustrations of the Principle Illustration 1: Dietary Needs. Suppose one person observes a religious fast and consumes only specific foods (e.g., sabudana, fruits), while another person is a non- vegetarian. If the mess serves chicken biryani to everyone, including the person observing a fast, and compels them to eat it in the name of “equality,” that is not equality—it is a violation of that person’s rights. Conversely, if the non-vegetarian person is denied chicken and forced to eat only khichdi every day because another person is fasting, that too is injustice. The needs are different, and the treatment must be different. Illustration 2: Regional Dietary Habits. A person from Uttar Pradesh may be accustomed to eating four or five parathas for breakfast. A person from Maharashtra may be satisfied with a serving of poha. If a uniform rule is made that everyone must eat only poha for breakfast, the person from UP will remain hungry. This is not equality; it is a failure to account for different needs. Illustration 3: Age and Requirements. A person who is 60 years old may have different physical, medical, and dietary requirements compared to a person who is 20 years old. Applying the same standard to both, without regard to their differing conditions, is not equal treatment. The Conclusion: God and nature have created human beings with infinite variety. No two individuals are identical in all respects. Therefore, the law must make distinc- tions. It must classify persons and things into groups based on relevant similarities and differences, and apply appropriate rules to each group. The task of Article 14 jurispru- dence is to determine when a classification is valid and when it is discriminatory. 3

2 The Two-Fold Command of Article 14 From this foundational principle, it follows that Article 14 embodies two complementary commands: 1. Persons who are similarly situated (i.e., who belong to the same class) must be treated alike. There must be no discrimination between persons who are in the same group. If Niyati and Manaswi are both observing a fast, but Niyati is given plain sabudana worth 15 while Manaswi is given sabudana vada with raisins and cashews worth 500, that is discrimination within the same class. Persons in the same group must receive the same treatment. 2. Persons who are differently situated (i.e., who belong to different classes) may be treated differently. The law may, and indeed must, make reasonable distinctions between different classes of persons to account for their differing cir- cumstances. The Critical Question: How do we determine who falls into “one group” or “one class”? What principles do we apply to decide whether a group is properly constituted or whether the classification is arbitrary? This is the function of the Doctrine of Rea- sonable Classification and the Nexus Test. 4

Part II: The Doctrine of Reasonable Classification 3 The Necessity of Classification If Article 14 were applied with absolute rigidity—if every law had to apply identically to every person without any distinction whatsoever—the State would be paralysed. It would be unable to legislate for specific groups, to address specific problems, or to make any special provision for any category of persons. The power to classify is, therefore, an essential incident of the legislative power. A legislature that cannot classify cannot govern. The Supreme Court has consistently recognised that Article 14 does not forbid classifi- cation. It forbids class legislation (discrimination against a class without any reasonable basis) but permits reasonable classification. 4 The Two-Fold Test for Valid Classification For a classification to be valid under Article 14, it must satisfy two conditions, both of which must be cumulatively fulfilled: 1. Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia—a clear, logical, and understandable basis that distinguishes the per- sons or things grouped together from those left out of the group. The basis of classification must not be arbitrary, fanciful, or capricious. It must be capable of being understood and rationally explained. 2. Rational Nexus: The differentia on which the classification is founded must have a rational nexus (a reasonable connection) with the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. There must be a logical relationship between the basis of classification and the purpose of the law. It is not enough that the classification is clear; it must also be relevant to the goal the legislature is trying to accomplish. The Two-Fold Nexus Test Test 1 – Intelligible Differentia: On what basis are you classifying? Is the basis logical, clear, and understandable? Test 2 – Rational Nexus: Does the basis of classification have a rea- sonable connection to the objective of the statute? 4.1 A Note on the Burden of Proof The burden of proving that a classification is unreasonable and violative of Article 14 lies, in the first instance, on the person challenging the law. However, once a prima facie case of discrimination is made out, the burden may shift to the State to justify the classification. 5

Part III: Case Law on Reasonable Classification 5 State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) (The “Dacoit Case”) 5.1 Facts and Background The State of West Bengal enacted the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950. The object of the Act was to provide for the speedier trial of certain offences. Section 5(1) of the Act empowered the State Government, by notification, to direct that any particular case or class of cases be tried by a Special Court under the Act. The Act conferred absolute and unguided discretion on the State Government to select which cases would be sent for speedier trial. There were no guidelines, no criteria, and no standards to govern this selection. The procedure under the Special Courts Act was different from the normal procedure under the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Special Courts procedure was more stringent: certain procedural safeguards available to the accused under the ordinary CrPC were not available under the Special Courts Act. The trial was more expeditious but also more rigorous for the accused. Anwar Ali Sarkar and 49 other persons were accused of committing dacoity (armed robbery). They were caught during an armed raid. The State Government issued a notification directing that their cases be tried by a Special Court under the Act. Anwar Ali Sarkar was tried, convicted, and sentenced under the Special Courts Act. Anwar Ali Sarkar challenged the constitutional validity of Section 5(1) of the Act on the ground that it violated Article 14 of the Constitution. 5.2 The Challenge The core challenge was this: The Act gave the State Government unfettered discre- tion to pick and choose which cases would be tried under the special procedure. The same offence (dacoity) committed by different persons could be tried under two differ- ent procedures—the ordinary CrPC procedure and the special procedure—solely at the discretion of the executive, without any guiding principle. This, it was argued, was discriminatory and violated the right to equality. 5.3 The Judgment The case was heard by a 7-judge Constitutional Bench of the Supreme Court. By a 6:1 majority, the Court struck down Section 5(1) as unconstitutional. Chief Justice Patanjali Sastri dissented. The Majority’s Reasoning: The majority applied the Doctrine of Reasonable Classification and the Two- Fold Nexus Test. 1. Intelligible Differentia – NOT Satisfied: The Act did not lay down any ba- sis or criterion for classifying which cases should be sent for speedier trial. The 6

State Government had absolute and unguided discretion. The classification was based solely on the subjective opinion of the executive officers. If the officers changed, different cases would be selected. This was not an “intelligible” basis for classification; it was arbitrary and capricious. 2. Rational Nexus – NOT Satisfied: Even assuming there was some differentia, it had no rational connection to the object of the Act. The object of the Act was to ensure speedier trial. But how was giving unlimited, unguided discretion to the government connected to achieving speedier trial? There was no logical link. The object (speedier trial) could be achieved without conferring arbitrary power on the executive. The means (absolute discretion) were not rationally related to the end (speedier trial). Illustration of the Discrimination: Suppose dacoities occurred in five different districts of West Bengal. In each district, two dacoits were caught. The State Government, in its discretion, sent the cases of the two dacoits from District A to the Special Court for speedier trial, while the cases of the dacoits from Districts B, C, D, and E were tried under the ordinary CrPC procedure. The two dacoits from District A faced a more rigorous procedure with fewer procedural safeguards, while the other dacoits enjoyed the full protections of the ordinary criminal procedure. There was no rational basis for this distinction. Why were these two dacoits singled out? The State could not provide a justifiable answer. This was discrimination within the same class (all persons accused of dacoity). Result: Section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, was declared unconstitutional and void. Anwar Ali Sarkar’s conviction was set aside. He won the case. 5.4 Key Principle A law that confers absolute, unguided, and unfettered discretion on the executive to classify persons or cases, without any criteria or standards, violates Article 14. The power to classify must be exercised based on intelligible principles, not on the whims of officials. 6 Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra (1952) (The Contrast Case) 6.1 The Striking Similarity and the Different Outcome There is a companion case to Anwar Ali Sarkar that presents a remarkable contrast: Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra. The text of the impugned section in this case was virtually identical to Section 5(1) of the West Bengal Act. It also conferred discretion on the State Government to send cases for trial before Special Courts. Yet, in this case, the Supreme Court upheld the provision as constitutionally valid. The Critical Distinction: The Preamble and Context. The difference lay in the preamble and the surrounding circumstances of the Saurashtra Act. Unlike West Bengal, the State of Saurashtra was facing a grave law and order situation. There was widespread communal violence, dacoity, and a breakdown of the ordinary criminal justice system. The preamble of the Saurashtra Act explicitly 7

stated that the Act was enacted to deal with the exceptional situation prevailing in the State. The Supreme Court held that, in the context of this exceptional situation, the discretion conferred on the government was not unguided. The preamble itself provided the guiding principle: the government was to use its discretion to send those cases for speedier trial which were connected to the breakdown of law and order. The discretion was not absolute; it was channelled by the stated objective of restoring public order. The Common Judge: It is noteworthy that Chief Justice Patanjali Sastri was a judge in both cases. He dissented in Anwar Ali Sarkar (voting to uphold the Act) and was part of the majority in Kathi Raning Rawat (upholding the Act). The Lesson: A provision that appears identical in text may be held valid or in- valid depending on its context, purpose, and the presence or absence of guiding principles—whether in the statute itself or in the surrounding circumstances. 7 Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India (1950) This case addressed the question: “Can a single person constitute a class?” The Supreme Court held that yes, a single person can, in certain circumstances, constitute a valid class for the purposes of Article 14. If a single person or entity possesses unique characteristics that distinguish them from all others, and if the law addresses that unique situation, the classification may be valid. The test remains the same: the differentia must be intelligible, and there must be a rational nexus with the object of the law. Illustration: If a single company is responsible for 90% of a particular industry’s pollution, a law addressing that specific company’s conduct may be a valid classification, because the company’s unique characteristics distinguish it from all others. 8 Other Relevant Cases • In re: Special Courts Act — Further elucidation on the limits of special courts and Article 14. • Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S.R. Tendolkar (1958) — A landmark case that consolidated the principles of reasonable classification. The Supreme Court laid down several propositions summarising the law on Article 14. • Ex-Services Association v. Union of India (2006) — A case involving a cut-off date for medical benefits for retired servicemen. Those who retired before 1997 were not required to pay for medical facilities; those who retired after 1997 were required to pay. The reasoning of the Court has been the subject of academic debate. The case illustrates that judicial reasoning is not infallible; judges may de- cide cases based on their view of the situation at the time. Students are encouraged to critically examine the reasoning and form their own views, provided they give proper reasons. 8

8.1 A Note on Judicial Fallibility and the Colonial Mindset The lecture noted that judges, like all human beings, can make errors in reasoning. A judgment is not divine law; it is the product of human deliberation. An example was given of Justice Endlaw of the Delhi High Court, who, in a copyright case (Oxford Uni- versity Press v. Delhi University), delivered a judgment criticising the colonial mindset of blindly copying Western copyright laws. The University of Delhi library had photocopied expensive textbooks (costing over 1 lakh) for students who could not afford them. Oxford University Press sued. Justice Endlaw held, in a celebrated judgment, that “Copyright is not divine law.” The principle is right, but the specific application by a judge in a given case may be debated. Students should know the judgments, but they may differ in their reasoning, provided they articulate their reasons cogently. 9

Part IV: The Primacy of Equality in the Constitutional Scheme 9 Why Is Article 14 Placed First Among the Funda- mental Rights? The Fundamental Rights in Part III of the Constitution are arranged in a specific order. Article 14 (Right to Equality) is placed before Article 19 (Right to Freedom) and Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty). This placement is not accidental; it reflects a conscious constitutional choice. The question for the next class is: Is equality more important than life (Arti- cle 21) and freedom (Article 19)? Why did the framers place equality first? The relationship between these three foundational rights—equality, freedom, and life—is a central theme of constitutional jurisprudence. 10 Preview: Equality Before Law and Equal Protec- tion of Laws In the next class, the discussion will turn to the two distinct concepts embodied in Article 14: • Equality Before Law: A concept of English origin. It is a negative concept implying the absence of any special privilege in favour of any individual. It means that every person, whatever their rank or status, is subject to the ordinary law of the land and the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts. • Equal Protection of the Laws: A concept of American origin (drawn from the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution). It is a positive concept implying the right to equal treatment in equal circumstances. It requires that persons in similar circumstances be treated alike by the law. 10

Introduction to Article 14 1 Foundational Concepts Article 14 of the Constitution of India guarantees the right to equality to all persons. It provides: Article 14 “The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protec- tion of the laws within the territory of India.” 1.1 Scope of “Person” The term “person” under Article 14 includes all human beings, irrespective of nationality, citizenship, or status. This encompasses: • Citizens of India • Aliens (including citizens of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, etc.) • Companies and legal persons (to the extent applicable) The inclusive nature of the term ensures that the protection against discrimination ex- tends to every individual within Indian territory. 1.2 The Dual Mandate Article 14 contains two distinct but complementary concepts: 1. Equality Before Law: A negative concept that prohibits special privileges and disabilities. 2. Equal Protection of Laws: A positive concept that requires the State to treat equals equally and unequals unequally, thereby justifying affirmative action and reasonable classification. 4

Reasonable Classification: The Doctrine of Classification 2 Introduction to Classification Since Article 14 applies to all persons, it does not mean that all persons must be gov- erned by identical laws. The State is permitted to classify persons into different groups for the purpose of legislation, provided such classification satisfies certain constitutional standards. 2.1 Why Classification is Necessary Equality among unequals is itself a violation of the right to equality. Therefore, the law must recognise the inherent differences between persons and groups. Classification is the mechanism by which the law identifies these differences and creates distinct categories. 2.2 The Two-Pronged Test for Reasonable Classification For a classification to withstand constitutional scrutiny, it must satisfy the following two conditions: 1. Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia that distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from those left out of the group. The differentia must be real and substantial, not merely illusory. 2. Nexus with the Objective: The intelligible differentia must have a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved by the law, policy, or decision in question. Illustration: Selection for a Basketball Team Suppose the objective is to select a basketball team. A classification based on height (e.g., selecting persons above 5 feet 8 inches) would likely satisfy the intelligible differentia test. The nexus with the objective of selecting competent players would also be established. However, if it is proven that shorter players are equally or more capable, the classification would fail the nexus test. 3 Cases on Reasonable Classification The lecture discussed several landmark cases to illustrate the application of the reasonable classification doctrine. 3.1 E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) This case is significant for establishing the “New Doctrine of Equality,” which read arbi- trariness as a facet of Article 14. 5

Case Summary Facts: E.P. Royappa, a senior IAS officer, was superseded in his appointment as Chief Secretary to the Government of Tamil Nadu. He challenged the decision on grounds of arbitrariness and violation of Article 14. Held: The Supreme Court held that Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness because a decision that is arbitrary is inherently unequal. This was a significant expansion of the equality doctrine beyond the traditional “classification” test. 3.2 State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) This case is a classic illustration of a law failing the reasonable classification test. Case Summary Facts: The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, provided for the trial of certain offences by special courts. The Act did not specify the categories of offences that would be tried by such courts, leaving it to the discretion of the State Govern- ment. Held: The Supreme Court struck down the Act on the ground that the classification was arbitrary and did not rest on an intelligible differentia. The wide discretion given to the Executive was found to be discriminatory. 3.3 Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra (1952) This case demonstrates a classification that was upheld. Case Summary Facts: The Saurashtra State Ordinance provided for the trial of certain offences by special courts. Unlike the West Bengal Act, the Preamble to the Ordinance specified the types of offences that were to be tried by the Special Courts. Held: The Supreme Court upheld the Ordinance, noting that the Preamble provided sufficient guidance to the Executive Magistrates regarding the category of cases to be sent to the Special Courts. Thus, the intelligible differentia and nexus tests were satisfied. 6

Anwar Ali Sarkar (Struck Down) Kathi Raning (Up- held) Act did not specify the categories of offences. Ordinance specified the categories in its Preamble. Uncontrolled discre- tion given to the State Government. Clear guidance to Ex- ecutive Magistrates. Failed the intelligible differentia test. Passed the intelligible differentia test. Union of India Case Summary Facts: The government introduced a policy requiring retired armed forces person- nel to make a one-time payment to avail lifetime medical facilities, while active personnel received free medical treatment. Issue: Whether the classification be- tween active and retired personnel was reasonable. Observation: The court noted that while classification is permissible, a cut-off date that discriminates between similarly situated groups without a reasonable nexus to the objective may be un- constitutional. 4 Homework Assignment To deepen understanding, students were assigned the following task: Homework 1. Create 10 valid classes (classifications) that satisfy the intelligible differentia and nexus tests. 2. Create 5 invalid classes that fail these tests. 3. Where possible, find case law to support the classification. 4. Ensure the classes are diverse and not repetitive (e.g., avoid creating multiple variations of “committees”). 7

Equality Before Law and Equal Protection of Laws 5 Understanding the Two Concepts As noted earlier, Article 14 contains two distinct concepts. The lecture provided a detailed historical and practical exposition of these concepts. 5.1 Equality Before Law (Negative Concept) This is a negative concept that prohibits special privileges and disabilities. It embodies the rule of law, meaning: • No person is above the law. • Every person, irrespective of status, is subject to the ordinary law of the land. • No special privileges or disabilities exist. 5.1.1 Historical Context The lecture highlighted historical instances of disabilities and privileges: • Mahatma Gandhi in South Africa: Thrown out of a first-class train compart- ment in Pietermaritzburg despite holding a valid ticket, solely on the basis of race. This incident marked a turning point in his life. • Travancore Breast Tax: Lower-caste women were prohibited from wearing upper garments unless they paid a “breast tax.” This led to the tragic incident of Nangeli, who cut off her breasts in protest. • Untouchability and “No Peon, No Water”: Dalits were denied access to public water sources. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s experience of not being allowed to drink water without a peon’s assistance is a stark example of the disabilities imposed by the caste system. • Karna’s Exclusion: In the Mahabharata, Karna was denied the right to partici- pate in Draupadi’s swayamvar because he was a Suta-putra (not of royal lineage). Key Insight “Equality Before Law” abolishes these historical disabilities and privileges, creating a level playing field for all. 5.2 Equal Protection of Laws (Positive Concept) This is a positive concept that requires the State to treat equals equally and unequals unequally. It justifies: • Affirmative action for disadvantaged groups. 8

• Age relaxations for reserved categories. • Special provisions for women, children, and other vulnerable groups. 5.2.1 Illustration: The Basketball Example The Basketball Example Consider two players: one is 6.5 feet tall and the other is 3 feet tall. If the basket- ball hoop is kept at a uniform height of 12 feet, the taller player has an inherent advantage. This is “Equality Before Law”—everyone is subject to the same rule. However, to achieve true equality (“Equal Protection”), the height of the hoop might be adjusted or other concessions made to ensure a fair contest. 5.2.2 Illustration: The IAS Exam Example The IAS Exam Example Consider two individuals: • Person A: Born into an affluent family, received the best nutrition, educa- tion, and coaching from an early age. • Person B: Born into a rural, impoverished family, with limited access to nutrition, education, and coaching. Applying the same age limit and exam criteria to both would be “Equality Before Law” but may not achieve true equality. “Equal Protection of Laws” would justify extending age relaxations and other benefits to Person B to compensate for systemic disadvantages. 6 Summary of the Two Concepts Equality Before Law Equal Protection of Laws Negative concept. Positive concept. Abolishes privileges and disabilities. Requires the State to treat unequals unequally. Originates from the British legal tradition. Originates from the American legal tradi- tion. Prohibits discrimina- tion. Permits reasonable classification. Table 2: Comparison of the Two Facets of Article 14 9

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 3 Part I: Historical and Global Context of Discrimination Universality of Discrimination A common, and often erroneous, criticism directed at India posits that social discrimi- nation—particularly caste-based discrimination and untouchability—was a phenomenon unique to the Indian subcontinent. A historically rigorous examination reveals that sys- temic, legally sanctioned discrimination was a near-universal feature of pre-modern and early-modern societies across the globe. Comparative Instance: Untouchability in Japan The concept of social ostracism based on birth was not confined to India. In Japan, a historically marginalised group known as the Burakumin (, literally “hamlet people”) suffered discrimination analogous to untouchability. The existence of a specific term for this group in the Japanese language itself evidences the insti- tutionalised nature of the practice. The Burakumin were subjected to residential segregation and restrictions on social intercourse, demonstrating that the pathology of caste-like discrimination transcended cultural boundaries. Discrimination in Ancient and Classical Civilisations The legal systems of ancient Mesopotamia, Greece, and Rome institutionalised social stratification: 1. Status-Based Rights: These societies were formally divided into rigid classes—free persons, slaves, citizens, and non-citizens. Legal rights, including the right to property, contractual capacity, and access to courts, were apportioned according to social status. 2. Denial of Rights: The corollary of conferring special privileges upon certain classes was the active and systematic denial of those same rights to others. The law functioned as an instrument of exclusion. The Institution of Slavery and the Code Noir (1685) In Europe, the institution of slavery was governed by elaborate legal frameworks. The principle of partus sequitur ventrem (the child follows the condition of the mother) ensured that slavery was heritable, creating the doctrine of “once a slave, always a slave.” The Code Noir (Black Code) The Code Noir of 1685, promulgated by King Louis XIV of France, represents a noto- rious example of positive law enacted to systematise human exploitation.

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 4 The Code Noir of 1685 Origins: Enacted under the reign of Louis XIV for the regulation of French colonial possessions. Substantive Provisions: The Code consisted of 60 articles that: 1. Defined the legal conditions of slavery with precision. 2. Legally classified human beings as movable property (meubles), stripping enslaved persons of juridical personality. 3. Mandated Catholicism as the only permissible religion in the colonies and or- dered the expulsion of Jewish persons from French colonial territories. Duration: This legal instrument remained technically in effect until France for- mally repealed it, long after its revolutionary declarations of universal rights. Bonded Labour versus Chattel Slavery A comparative analysis warrants caution when equating India’s historical institution of bonded labour with the chattel slavery of the Atlantic world. • Article 23 of the Indian Constitution prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar). This provision is directed at practices akin to bonded labour. • In bonded labour, the labourer, though exploited and coerced through debt, retains a residual legal personality and is not reduced to the status of chattel property. • In chattel slavery, as codified by the Code Noir, the enslaved person was a res (a thing), possessing no rights whatsoever. The distinction, though not mitigating the brutality of bonded labour, is juridically significant. The Hypocrisy of the French Declaration of 1789 The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (D´eclaration des droits de l’homme et du citoyen) of 1789 is celebrated as a foundational text of liberalism. However, its title and content betray a profound exclusionary logic. The Exclusion of Women and the Poor The Lacuna: The Declaration proclaimed the “Rights of Man and of the Citi- zen.” Women were not entitled to the status of “citizen” under the revolutionary dispensation. Citizenship was circumscribed by property qualifications; only active citizens (citoyens actifs) who paid a certain amount of tax could vote. The poor, and all women, were relegated to the status of passive citizens (citoyens passifs), possessing civil rights but not political rights. Conclusion: The most vaunted proclamation of equality in the Western canon was, at its inception, a document for propertied white males. This historical fact is essential context when evaluating the genealogy of rights discourse globally.

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 5 Racial Discrimination in the United States The legal architecture of racial segregation and prohibition of inter-racial marriage per- sisted in the United States well into the twentieth century. Anti-Miscegenation Laws and Loving v. Virginia Until the landmark decision of the Supreme Court of the United States, state laws pro- hibiting marriage between persons of different races were constitutionally valid. Loving v. Virginia Facts: Richard Loving, a white man, and Mildred Jeter, a Black woman, were mar- ried in the District of Columbia. Upon returning to their home state of Virginia, they were charged with and convicted of violating Virginia’s Racial Integrity Act, which prohibited inter-racial marriage. Judgment: The United States Supreme Court, in a unanimous decision, held that the anti-miscegenation statutes violated the Equal Protection Clause and the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amend- ment. Temporal Context: This case was decided in 1967, a mere few decades ago. It stands as a stark refutation of any narrative that suggests racial and social discrimination is a phenomenon peculiar to non-Western societies. The Doctrine of “Pure Blood” The Nazi regime in Germany enacted the Nuremberg Laws (1935), which criminalised marriage and sexual relations between Jews and citizens of “German or related blood.” The rationale was the protection of the so-called purity of the Aryan race (Blutschutzge- setz). This represents the most extreme and catastrophic expression of state-sanctioned social discrimination in modern history. Key Takeaway The historical record demonstrates conclusively that discrimination on the grounds of race, caste, religion, and sex was a global phenomenon. Indian society had—and continues to have—profound shortcomings requiring rectification. However, the portrayal of discrimination as an exclusively Indian pathology is historically false and intellectually dishonest. Every society must confront its own legacy, and the Indian constitutional project is a conscious and ongoing effort to dismantle inherited structures of injustice. Part II: Conceptual Framework of Article 14 The Two Dimensions of Equality Article 14 of the Constitution of India guarantees the Right to Equality in two distinct but complementary formulations:

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 6 1. Equality Before Law: A negative concept, derived from the English common law tradition. 2. Equal Protection of the Laws: A positive concept, drawn from the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States. Equality Before Law: The Negative Right This principle is fundamentally prohibitory in nature. It commands that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law. Its core function is the abolition of special, discriminatory privileges that existed under pre-constitutional regimes. Illustration: First Class Railway Travel Under the colonial regime, special privileges were often attached to racial iden- tity. Post-independence, the condition for entitlement is objective and impersonal. Whether a passenger is Black, White, Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Sikh, or Parsi, and regardless of caste or sex, the sole criterion for travelling in a first-class com- partment is the possession of a valid first-class ticket. The law does not confer any special privilege based on irrelevant personal characteristics. This uniformity of application is the essence of Equality Before Law. Equal Protection of the Laws: The Positive Right Merely treating unequals equally perpetuates, rather than remedies, substantive inequal- ity. The doctrine of Equal Protection of the Laws authorises, and in certain contexts requires, the State to make reasonable classifications and to extend preferential treat- ment to those who have been historically disadvantaged. 6.2.1 The Rationale: The Impossibility of Formal Competition The professor illustrated this with a hypothetical contrasting two individuals:

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 7 Illustration: The Son of Privilege and the Son of Disadvantage Child A (The Child of Privilege): • Born into an affluent family with access to optimal nutrition and healthcare. • Access to top-tier educational resources, coaching, and developmental tools from infancy. • Social capital: familial connections with judges, ministers, and influential persons. Knowledge of institutions and professions is acquired through daily social osmosis, not rote memorisation. Child B (The Child of Disadvantage): • Born into poverty, with consequent health and nutritional deficits. • First exposure to formal schooling occurs at a significantly later age; gradu- ation is correspondingly delayed. • No social capital; must overcome informational deficits and systemic barriers to access even the opportunity to compete. Legal Conclusion: To apply a purely formal, identical standard of competition (e.g., the same qualifying examination with the same age limit and same cut- off marks) to both Child A and Child B would be to guarantee that Child B is rendered perpetually ineligible for positions of power, influence, and economic advancement. The competition is inherently rigged, not by individual malice, but by historically accumulated structural advantage. 6.2.2 Historical Illustration: The Indian Civil Services Examination The professor cited the early years of the Indian Civil Services (ICS) examination under British rule as a paradigmatic example. For many years, no Indian candidate was success- ful. The reason was not a lack of innate intellectual capacity, but that the examination was structured to test a universe of knowledge—centred on Christian theology and the Bible—that was entirely alien to the Indian educational and cultural experience. Ques- tions of the nature, “Who gave the apple to whom?” (a reference to the Biblical narrative of the Garden of Eden and the Fruit of Knowledge) were incomprehensible to a candidate not steeped in Christian scripture. This was a mechanism of structural exclusion. Positive Discrimination and Affirmative Action To remedy structural disadvantage, the State employs instruments of positive discrimi- nation, also known in the United States as Affirmative Action. In India, this takes the form of the Quota System or reservations. Forms of Affirmative Action The professor identified several modalities through which positive discrimination operates:

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 8 1. Preferential Treatment (Tie-Breaker): Where candidates from different social groups achieve identical marks, the candidate from the more disadvantaged group (e.g., a Scheduled Tribe woman) is selected. This recognises that equal achievement in the face of greater disadvantage represents a greater measure of merit. 2. Augmented Scoring (Bonus Marks): A system where additional marks are added to the raw scores of candidates from disadvantaged groups. For example: • General: Raw score. • Other Backward Classes (OBC): Raw score + 5 marks. • Scheduled Caste (SC): Raw score + 10 marks. • Scheduled Tribe (ST): Raw score + 15 marks. • Woman (any category): Additional +10 marks. • Woman with disability: Further +5 marks. Under this model, a disabled ST woman with a raw score of 580 could receive an augmented score of 580+15+10+5 = 610, potentially surpassing a General category candidate with a higher raw score but no augmentation. 3. The Quota System (Reservation): India adopted a more robust mechanism than simple affirmative action. Under the quota system, a fixed percentage of positions or seats is reserved for members of specified backward classes. The critical legal feature is that a candidate from a reserved category may be selected even if their absolute marks are lower than a candidate from the general category, provided they meet the minimum threshold (if any) set for the reserved pool. Case Law: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kumari Nivedita Jain State of Madhya Pradesh v. Kumari Nivedita Jain – The Limits of Reservation Facts: The State of Madhya Pradesh, in an effort to fill seats reserved for backward classes in medical colleges, progressively lowered the minimum qualifying marks. Initially set at 50, the requirement was reduced to 45, then 35, and finally to 30. When even this failed to attract a sufficient number of candidates, the State removed the minimum marks requirement entirely, permitting admission to candi- dates from reserved categories regardless of their entrance examination score—in effect, even a candidate scoring zero or negative marks could be admitted. Issue: The constitutional validity of admitting candidates with abysmally low or nil marks under the reservation policy. Held: The Supreme Court upheld the State’s action. The case illustrates the extremity to which the logic of compensatory discrimination can extend and serves as a focal point for debates on the tension between “merit” and “social justice.” Critical Reflection: The professor noted that this case demonstrates that the NEET examination system, from its inception, has grappled with the challenge of reconciling reservation policies with minimum standards of competence, and has never operated on a purely meritocratic basis.

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 9 Constitutional Foundation: Article 15(4) The constitutional permissibility of such measures was firmly established in the seminal case concerning communal Government Orders in Madras. State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan Facts: The State of Madras had issued a Communal Government Order allocat- ing seats in medical and engineering colleges on the basis of caste and community. Issue: Whether the Communal G.O. violated the fundamental right to equality under Article 14 and the prohibition on discrimination under Article 15(1). Judg- ment: The Supreme Court struck down the order as violative of Article 15(1), which prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Constitutional Consequence: This decision directly led to the First Amendment to the Constitution of India (1951), which inserted Article 15(4). This clause empowers the State to make special provisions for the advance- ment of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens, and for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, notwithstanding the general prohibition on discrimination in Article 15(1). Part III: The Taxonomy of Exploitation and Discrimination The lecture mapped discrimination along two axes: 1. Nature: Negative (Exploitative) vs. Positive (Affirmative/Compensatory). 2. Scope: Individual vs. Social. Individual Exploitation Individual exploitation arises from personal relationships and private enmities. It is a function of interpersonal dynamics and the abuse of personal power. The law can punish specific acts of individual exploitation, but it cannot eliminate the human capacity for malice and the abuse of private trust. Illustrative Examples of Individual Exploitation The professor provided a series of case studies drawn from contemporary Indian society to illustrate the nature of individual exploitation: 1. Madhumita Shukla Case: A poetess who sought the patronage of a politically powerful figure, Amarmani Tripathi of Uttar Pradesh. When the relationship soured and she pressed for marriage, she was murdered. This exemplifies the lethal danger that can arise when personal ambition intersects with asymmetrical power relations.

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 10 2. Geetika Sharma Case: An air hostess who entered a relationship with a Haryana Home Minister, Gopal Kanda. After being exploited, she was allegedly coerced into servicing his business clients. Unable to endure the exploitation, she died by suicide, leaving a detailed note. The case highlights the abuse of employer-employee relation- ships and the commodification of a person. 3. Shivani Bhatnagar Case: A journalist who, in the pursuit of professional access to the Prime Minister’s Office, developed a relationship with a senior IPS officer, R.K. Sharma. The entanglement ended in her murder. This case illustrates how professional ambition can lead individuals into vulnerable personal situations with fatal consequences. 4. Naina Sahni (Tandoor Murder Case): A victim of intimate partner violence, murdered by Sushil Sharma, a Congress politician, who then attempted to dispose of her body by burning it in a restaurant tandoor. The case is a gruesome testament to the extremes of domestic violence. Important Observation The professor observed that as long as the sun and moon exist, individual exploitation will persist. It is rooted in the ineradicable capacity of human beings for passion, jealousy, greed, and vengeance. The function of law is to punish it, but the law cannot, by its nature, prevent every private wrong before it occurs. Social Discrimination Social discrimination is distinct from individual exploitation. It is not predicated on personal enmity but on an individual’s membership in a targeted group. The victim is not harmed because of who they are as an individual, but because of what they are as defined by the discriminatory social structure. The Example of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar The professor invoked the experience of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as the archetypal example of social discrimination. • Dr. Ambedkar, by all accounts, had no personal enmity with anyone. His father was a Subedar in the British Indian Army, a position of considerable respect. • The discrimination he suffered—being forced to sit outside the classroom, being denied access to water by peons—was not a consequence of any personal dispute. It was a function of social boycott based on caste. • Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad of Baroda, recognising his merit, sponsored his stud- ies abroad. This would not have occurred if Dr. Ambedkar had been personally abrasive.

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 11 The Grounds of Social Discrimination Social discrimination operates on multiple, often intersecting, axes: 1. Sex: • Denial of entry to places of worship (e.g., the Sabarimala Temple restrictions, litigated in Indian Young Lawyers’ Association v. State of Kerala). • Historical denial of property rights to women, remedied in India only by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005. • The Champakam Dorairajan litigation itself was rooted in a denial of educational access on grounds of both caste and, implicitly, sex. 2. Caste: The hierarchical ordering of society by birth, imposing civil and religious disabilities on those at the bottom of the hierarchy. 3. Race: Discrimination based on race, as exemplified by the Jim Crow and apartheid regimes. 4. Religion: • The assertion of the supremacy of one faith over all others, and the attendant denial of the right to equal dignity for adherents of other faiths. • The professor noted the existence of extremist interpretations that deny the very right to life of persons of other religions. • The Nazi persecution of the Jews is the most extreme historical example of religion-based social discrimination. The lecture referred to the horrific prac- tice, reported in recent conflicts, of checking sexual organs to determine religious identity before execution. 5. Economic Status: • The Marxist critique, drawing on the works of Karl Marx, posits that all laws are superstructural instruments designed to facilitate the exploitation of the pro- letariat by the bourgeoisie. • The lecture noted the radical literary expression of this sentiment in a Shake- spearean line: “The first thing we do, let’s kill all the lawyers” (Henry VI, Part 2, Act IV, Scene 2), which, in context, was a critique of those who use the law to oppress the poor. Social Justice as the Objective of Positive Discrimination The conceptual framework converges on the concept of Social Justice. Social Justice is the telos—the ultimate purpose—of the doctrine of Equal Protection of the Laws.

Constitutional Law: Equality and Social Justice 12 Definition: Social Justice Social Justice is the set of positive measures undertaken by the State to disman- tle the structures of Social Discrimination. It recognises that formal equality before the law is an insufficient guarantee of a dignified life for those who have been subjected to centuries of systemic subordination. Social Justice demands the creation of conditions in which the historically disadvantaged can participate in the life of the nation on terms of genuine, substantive equality. Constitutional Law: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification 3 Part I: The Foundational Framework of Article 14 Introduction: The Two Dimensions of Equality Article 14 of the Constitution of India guarantees the right to equality in two distinct but complementary formulations: Equality Before Law (a negative, British concept) and Equal Protection of the Laws (a positive, American concept). While Article 14 prohibits class legislation, it permits reasonable classification. A law is not violative of Article 14 merely because it makes a classification; the classification must satisfy a rigorous two-pronged judicial test. The Two-Limb Test for Reasonable Classification A classification under a statute to be valid under Article 14 must satisfy two con- ditions (State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, AIR 1952 SC 75): 1. Intelligible Differentia: The classification must be founded on a clear, real, and substantial distinction that distinguishes those grouped together from those left out of the group. The basis of classification must not be arbitrary, fanciful, or artificial. 2. Rational Nexus: There must be a rational and proximate nexus between the basis of classification and the objective sought to be achieved by the statute in question. The classification must have a direct and reasonable connection to the legislative purpose. Part II: Hypothetical Case Study — The West Bengal Prohibition Ordinance The Factual Matrix The lecture presented a hypothetical constitutional challenge to test the application of the reasonable classification doctrine. The scenario involves a newly elected government in the State of West Bengal that issues an ordinance imposing prohibition. For the purpose of legal analysis, “prohibition” refers to a total ban on the manufacture, transportation, storage, sale, purchase, and consumption of alcoholic liquor.

Constitutional Law: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification 4 The Operative Provisions The West Bengal Prohibition Ordinance (Hypothetical) Section 3 (General Prohibition): No person shall manufacture, transport, store, sell, purchase, or consume alcoholic liquor within the territory of the State of West Bengal. Proviso — Exceptions: Provided that this section shall not apply to: (A) Military Personnel (B) Foreigners (C) Consumption within the premises of 5-Star Hotels The Constitutional Challenge A citizen of West Bengal, represented by a hypothetical petitioner (humorously named “Niyati” in the classroom discussion), filed a writ petition challenging the ordinance as violative of Article 14. The petitioner’s core arguments were: 1. Military Personnel: If military personnel, who are also citizens of India, are permit- ted to consume liquor, why is the petitioner, as an ordinary citizen, denied the same right? The petitioner asserted she is no “weaker” than a military person, describing herself as “an army in herself, all alone.” 2. Foreigners: The petitioner questioned whether she appeared “any less than a for- eigner” and claimed a royal status comparable to that of foreigners. 3. 5-Star Hotels: This exception, the petitioner argued, is a discriminatory classifica- tion based purely on economic class. It creates an unjust distinction between the rich (who can afford to drink in luxury hotels) and the poor (who cannot). If a rich person can consume liquor in a 5-star hotel, why cannot a person of modest means consume it in a 3-star hotel or at home? Applying the Two-Limb Test Identifying the Legislative Objective The first critical step in the rational nexus analysis is to correctly identify the statu- tory objective. The lecture established a crucial analytical point: the objective of a prohibition law is not simply “to ban alcohol.” The ban itself is a means. The true, deeper legislative objectives (the ends) are grounded in the Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV of the Constitution) and include: 1. Public Health (Article 47): The State shall endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption, except for medicinal purposes, of intoxicating drinks and drugs which are injurious to health.

Constitutional Law: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification 5 2. Public Order and Safety: The prevention of alcohol-related crime, domestic vio- lence, and public nuisance. The lecture illustrated this vividly with the example of a rickshaw-puller earning 300 a day who spends 500 on a bottle of liquor. This leads to a cascade of social harm: demanding money from and beating his wife, snatching purses and gold chains (“chain snatching”), and engaging in other petty crimes to finance his addiction, and then committing further crimes under the influence. 3. Protection of the Vulnerable: Specifically, protecting the poor and working classes from the devastating economic and social consequences of alcohol addiction, which traps them in a cycle of poverty and violence. The objective is rooted in a paternalistic, welfarist rationale: the government is not opposed to drinking by those who can “afford and reconcile” it, but is deeply concerned about the impact on the poor. Testing the Exceptions Against the Objective With the objectives (public health, public order, protection of the poor) established, the validity of each exception is tested. Exception A: Military Personnel Intelligible Differentia: Military personnel form a class that is fundamentally distinct from the general civilian population. They live in a separate, highly regulated society (cantonments), are subject to military discipline, and their service involves unique stresses and sacrifices. Rational Nexus: • The nexus with the objective of protecting the poor is clear: military personnel do not belong to the vulnerable socio-economic class the Act seeks to protect. They have a stable, state-provided income and are not at risk of committing street crime or domestic violence in the same manner to finance an addiction. • Furthermore, as argued by the State, military personnel are “trained enough” to know how much and when to drink. The rationale is that their drinking does not pose the same risk to public order as the drinking of an economically precarious civilian. Judicial Precedent: The Supreme Court in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (AIR 1951 SC 318) addressed these very issues. The Court upheld the validity of permitting drinking by military personnel as a reasonable classification. Exception B: Foreigners Intelligible Differentia: A foreigner is a distinct juridical class. They are non-citizens, often in India temporarily, and are not subjects of the state’s socio-economic reform in the same way citizens are. Rational Nexus: • There is a nexus with the objective of not offending international sensibilities and facilitating commerce and tourism. • Additionally, in many cultures, particularly those from colder climates (the example of Sikkim was given, where universal drinking is a cultural norm for thermoregulation), alcohol is an integral part of daily meals. A blanket imposition on all foreigners would be a disproportionate intervention. The objective of protecting the Indian poor does not rationally extend to regulating the cultural habits of foreign visitors.

Constitutional Law: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification 6 Exception C: 5-Star Hotels Intelligible Differentia: The class of persons who consume alcohol in 5-star hotels is primarily the economic elite. The hotel’s clientele is a proxy for a certain socio-economic status. Rational Nexus: • Argument for Validity: The core objective of prohibition is to protect the poor from the economic ruin and social disorder caused by alcohol. A person who can afford to spend 10,000–20,000 in a 5-star hotel is, by definition, not part of the class the Act aims to protect. The consumption by the rich does not lead to the same socially destructive consequences (theft, domestic violence over a 200 shortfall) that the Act is designed to prevent. Therefore, the classification perfectly serves the objective. • Argument for Invalidity (Economic Discrimination): The counter-argument is that this is a facially discriminatory classification based purely on economic capacity, which is a deeply suspect ground. As the student Niyati argued, it “promotes in- equality” by suggesting that a rich person’s drinking is socially harmless while a poor person’s is not. If the objective were public health per se, this classification would fail, as alcohol is equally harmful to the liver of a rich man and a poor man. Classroom Verdict and Discussion A classroom vote was conducted. An overwhelming majority of students voted that the classification was invalid (i.e., in favor of the petitioner, Niyati). A small minority voted for validity. The lecture concluded that both arguments are arguable, and the ultimate validity depends on which objective the court prioritises. The F.N. Balsara case is a seminal authority that grapples with these precise questions. Case Law Research Assignment Research the following: • In Bihar, a prohibition law was challenged and initially declared unconstitu- tional. A subsequent ordinance, after rectifying the flaws, was upheld as valid. • Task: Identify the first Bihar ordinance and analyse what flaw in its classifi- cation scheme made it unconstitutional. Then, identify the second ordinance and explain what legislative improvements were made to satisfy the Intelligible Differentia and Rational Nexus test, thereby making it valid.

Constitutional Law: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification 7 Part III: Additional Hypotheticals and Illustrative Cases Hypothetical 1: Age Concession for Rural NEET Can- didates The Problem The Government of Maharashtra passes an ordinance providing a 5-year age concession for students from rural (village) backgrounds appearing for the NEET medical entrance exam. Students from cities receive no such concession. The classification is “rural origin” vs. “urban origin.” Is this valid? Arguments and Analysis • Argument for Validity (Intelligible Differentia): Village and city students form distinct classes. The rural student faces a well-documented lack of access to qual- ity schools, coaching centres, and educational infrastructure compared to their urban counterpart, as discussed in the class’s previous analysis of privilege and disadvantage. • Argument for Invalidity (Changing Social Realities): A sophisticated counter- argument was presented from a student. The classification may be over-inclusive and outdated. A student from a village may attend a school that is superior to a municipal school in an urban slum. Conversely, a rich landlord’s child from a village may have all the facilities, while the child of an urban domestic worker living in a slum (like Dharavi) has none. The classification fails to distinguish between the rural rich and the urban poor. • The Supreme Court’s View (Per the Lecture): The Supreme Court has held that a blanket classification of “rural” is an unreasonable classification. It ignores the vast disparities within the urban category, particularly the uniquely disadvantaged position of the urban slum-dweller. The condition of the urban poor is often far worse than that of the rural poor, who may still have community support and access to food, as illustrated by the professor’s anecdote of rural community traditions. • Contrasting Valid Classification: In the same judgment, the Court upheld a clas- sification based on mountainous/hilly terrain (e.g., for students in Uttarakhand). The Court found an intelligible differentia grounded in the unique geographical hard- ship, sparse population, and severe lack of accessible schools in the mountains, which places all residents of that terrain at a fundamental disadvantage. Case Law Compendium for Article 14 The lecture referenced a constellation of landmark cases that form the bedrock of Article 14 jurisprudence. Students were directed to read these cases in detail, paying careful attention to the facts that formed the basis of the classification.

Constitutional Law: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification 8 Case Name Basis of Classification / Key Principle State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952) The foundational case establishing the two-limb test of reason- able classification and striking down a law that gave the state unguided discretion to send cases to special courts. State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951) Upheld classifications in a prohibition law permitting drinking by military personnel and foreigners as reasonable. Chiranjit Lal Chowdhury v. Union of India (1950) Valid classification: A single “sick” industrial undertaking was taken over by the government for better management, as it constituted a class in itself. The closure of a large essential commodity factory threatened the livelihood of over 1,30,000 people. Kathi Raning Rawat v. Nergesh Meerza (1981) Tested a service regulation retiring air hostesses on first preg- nancy. The classification based on sex and pregnancy was examined. R.D. Shetty v. Inter- national Airport Authority (1979) A classic example of applying the test. A tender required “5 years of experience in a 3-Star Hotel.” The authority awarded the contract to a person with 10 years of experience running a tea-stall (tapri). The Court struck this down: the class “3-star hotel management” was fundamentally different from “tea-stall management.” The authority failed to respect its own intelligible differentia. Table 1: Landmark Cases on Reasonable Classification under Article 14 The Importance of Reading Facts — The R.D. Shetty Lesson The professor stressed the pedagogical importance of reading case facts with metic- ulous care. He recounted an anecdote where a colleague, preparing to teach R.D. Shetty, repeatedly missed the critical detail that the eligibility criterion was specif- ically “5 years of experience in a 3-Star Hotel.” Because she skipped over the qualifier “3-Star,” she failed to see the legal problem: the authority had equated a 3-star hotel manager’s experience with that of a tea-stall owner. Without grasping the fact, the intelligible differentia at the heart of the case becomes invisible. The lesson is to read facts with precision.

Constitutional Law: Article 14 — Reasonable Classification 9 Part IV: Summary of the Analytical Framework The Method for Solving Article 14 Problems To determine the constitutional validity of a classification under Article 14, the following analytical steps must be applied: 1. Identify the Classification: Exactly what groups has the law created? Who is included, and who is excluded? (e.g., military personnel vs. civilians; rural vs. urban students). 2. Determine the Legislative Objective: Why was this law passed? What social evil, policy goal, or constitutional directive (e.g., DPSPs) is it trying to achieve? This is the most critical step, as the nexus test depends entirely on the objective. A prohibition law’s objective is not “to ban alcohol,” but to achieve public health and public order. 3. Test for Intelligible Differentia: Is the distinction between the groups real, sub- stantial, and non-arbitrary? Are military personnel truly different from civilians in a legally cognisable sense? Is the difference between a rural and an urban student always substantial, or does it fail to distinguish between a rich rural student and a poor urban one? 4. Test for Rational Nexus: Granting that the groups are different, does that spe- cific difference have a direct and rational connection to the legislative ob- jective? Military personnel are different, but is their differentness connected to the objective of preventing alcohol-induced destitution and street crime? If the objective is public health, then all consumption is harmful, and the nexus with all exceptions (including the rich in 5-star hotels) fails. — End of Lecture Notes —

Article 14 The New Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness LECTURE NOTES Article 14: The New Doctrine of Non-Arbitrariness E.P. Royappa, Menaka Gandhi, and the Golden Triangle Constitutional Law — I / II Evolution of Equality Jurisprudence in India Faculty of Law TABLE OF CONTENTS SECTION 1 The Journey from Classification to Non-Arbitrariness 1.1 The Transition in Article 14 Jurisprudence The understanding of Article 14 of the Constitution of India has undergone a profound transformation. The traditional approach required a demonstration of discrimination between classes. The modern approach, crystallized in E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, recognizes that arbitrariness is itself the antithesis of equality. KEY PRINCIPLE: The Core Shift in Article 14 Analysis Old Rule: Equality = Non-Discrimination (Reasonable Classification Test) New Rule: Equality = Non-Arbitrariness (Arbitrariness is the sworn enemy of equality) Arbitrariness and equality are sworn enemies. Equality cannot be crippled, cabined, cribbed, or imprisoned in some doctrinal limitations. 1.2 The Metaphor of the Golden Triangle The constitutional jurisprudence evolved through a series of landmark cases that built upon one another, ultimately creating the Golden Triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21. The foundation of this Golden Triangle was laid in the Bank Nationalization Case (R.C. Cooper v. Union of India), where the Supreme Court held that Articles 19 and 31 could not be read in isolation. This principle was later extended by Justice Bhagwati to encompass Articles 14, 19, and 21 in Menaka Gandhi v. Union of India. SECTION 2 E.P. Royappa v. Applying the Two Tests Under Article 14 7. Key Takeaways, Study Resources, and Examination Tips ARTICLE 21 Life & Liberty /\ / \ / \ / \ / \ / \ ARTICLE 14 ------------ ARTICLE 19 Equality Interlinked Freedoms GOLDEN TRIANGLE Menaka Gandhi (1978) E.P. Royappa was an IAS officer serving as the Chief Secretary of Tamil Nadu — the highest post for an IAS officer at the State level. He was removed from the post of Chief Secretary and was appointed as the Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission Board.

Arguments: The Petitioner's Response — Equality is Not Just Salary: Decision: Significance — The Birth of the Non-Arbitrariness Doctrine: 2.1 What is Arbitrariness? Definition: A decision based on whims and fancies — without reason, logic, or justification. It is the opposite of a judicious decision. Characteristics of Arbitrary Action: Why Absolute Discretion Breeds Arbitrariness: Proving Arbitrariness: SECTION 3 The Three Pillars Before Menaka Gandhi Before the landmark decision in Menaka Gandhi v. Union of India, three crucial cases laid the groundwork for the expansion of fundamental rights. 3.1 Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1962) Year: 1962 Significance: This case, for the first time in Indian constitutional history, quoted an American case (Munn v. Illinois) and held a profoundly important principle. IMPORTANT JUDICIAL OBSERVATION The Chairman of the Planning Commission is the Chief Minister at the State level (and the Prime Minister at the Centre). The Deputy Chairman is, therefore, the post immediately below the Chief Minister. Later, Royappa was made an OSD (Officer on Special Duty). The State Government had issued an official order declaring that the OSD post and the Deputy Chairman post were equivalent in rank and salary to the Chief Secretary. Royappa challenged his removal from the Chief Secretary post as being arbitrary and mala fide, amounting to a violation of Article 14. Petitioner (Royappa): "My demotion has occurred. Though my salary is the same, the post of Chief Secretary is the most prestigious IAS post in the State. Removing me from that post and giving me another post with equal salary is not true equality." State: "Your salary is equal. You remain an IAS officer. We have declared through an official order that the posts are equivalent. Therefore, no discrimination has occurred." Equality is not determined solely by salary. Power, position, prestige, status, and respect are essential components of equality. Example: Giving a Professor a salary of ₹5 lakh and assigning housekeeping work — that does not make the Professor a Vice-Chancellor. The nature of the work, the dignity of the post, and the respect associated with it are intrinsic to equality. The Court accepted the principle that equality is not merely about salary — it encompasses power, prestige, and status. However, Royappa lost the case because he could not prove arbitrariness. As Justice Bhagwati observed: "Mala fide and arbitrariness are easy to claim, but hardest to prove." Before this case, Article 14 required proving a classification and showing that the classification had no rational nexus with the object of the law. Justice Bhagwati recognized a fundamental flaw: if there is no comparator class (e.g., a person is uniquely targeted), discrimination cannot be proven, and Article 14 becomes dormant — unable to grant relief. New Perspective: Whether or not discrimination exists, if the State has absolute discretionary power or acts arbitrarily, it violates Article 14. Arbitrariness and equality are sworn enemies. Arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality. 1. Absence of Reason: No logical basis or justification for the decision. 2. Whims and Fancies: "I liked it, so I did it" — purely subjective preference. 3. Lack of Evidence: Decision not supported by facts or circumstances. 4. No Consideration of Relevant Factors: Ignoring material circumstances. Human Weakness: Every human being has preferences, biases, and inclinations. Someone likes chicken, someone likes biryani; someone likes a particular subject, someone likes another. When a person is given absolute, unfettered discretionary power, these personal preferences can influence decisions. This is why discretion must be structured, guided, and non-arbitrary. Discretion cannot be eliminated (governance requires it), but it must be exercised in a just, fair, and reasonable manner. Example: If a fire breaks out in the classroom, the teacher must have the discretion to evacuate students — everything cannot be pre-written. But that discretion must be exercised reasonably, not arbitrarily. Proving arbitrariness is extremely difficult — "as tough as proving the existence of oxygen without instruments." It requires demonstrating that the decision-maker acted without any rational basis, which is a high evidentiary burden.

"Life does not mean mere animal existence." "It includes all those things which make life meaningful and beautiful. It includes the right to develop all our faculties." Impact: 3.2 R.C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) — The Bank Nationalization Case Citation: Also known as the Bank Nationalization Case Bench: 11 Judges — one of only a handful of such large benches in Indian constitutional history. Facts: The Core Issue — Interconnection of Articles: Foundation of the Golden Triangle: 3.3 Satwant Singh v. Union of India — The Passport Precedent Background: Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967: SECTION 4 Menaka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) Citation: AIR 1978 SC 597 Facts: Government's Defense: This expansive interpretation of the Right to Life under Article 21 became the foundation for numerous rights subsequently recognized by the Supreme Court. The right to privacy, the right to choose one's partner, the right to live with dignity — all trace their lineage to this principle. Contemporary Application: The Allahabad High Court recently scolded police for investigating the private life of a married couple, holding that the private life of a husband and wife is protected under Article 21. If this sentence had not been pronounced in Kharak Singh, the constitutional protection for love marriages, personal relationships, and individual autonomy would not exist today. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi nationalized several banks (Andhra Bank, and others). The case was not filed by the banks themselves, but by R.C. Cooper, who was a Director and Shareholder of one of the nationalized banks. Why did Cooper file and not the bank? Because the Right to Property was under Article 19(1)(f), and Article 19 rights are available only to citizens, not to corporations (which are not citizens). A bank, being a corporate entity, could not enforce Article 19. Its shareholder/director, being a citizen, could. The Government argued that the acquisition of property was under Article 31 and that they were required to comply only with Article 31, not Article 19. The Government claimed Articles 19 and 31 were separate and independent. Supreme Court's Ruling: "Nothing doing! They cannot be separated. While acting under Article 31, you must also comply with Article 19(1)(f)." This established the principle that fundamental rights are not watertight compartments — they are interconnected and must be read together. This case laid the foundation stone of the Golden Triangle. Justice Bhagwati later acknowledged in Menaka Gandhi that the interlinking of Articles 19 and 31 in R.C. Cooper was the precedent that compelled the Court to interlink Articles 14, 19, and 21. Before 1967, India had no Passport Act. The issuance or denial of passports was entirely at the discretion of the executive. Satwant Singh was denied a passport by the Government. When he challenged this, the Government's response was essentially: "We denied it because we chose to deny it." Supreme Court's Response: The Court granted permission for the passport and directed the Government: "If you want to deny passports, make a law. Write down the reasons on which a passport can be denied." This led to the enactment of the Passports Act, 1967. This section authorized the Government to impound a passport "without assigning any reason, in public interest." This provision granted absolute, arbitrary power to the executive — precisely the kind of power that would later be challenged in Menaka Gandhi. Menaka Gandhi's passport was impounded by the Government of India under Section 10(3) of the Passports Act, 1967. Two constables arrived at her residence, stating: "Ministry of External Affairs — please surrender your passport." When she asked for the reason, the response was: "Orders from above. We don't know why." The Government invoked Section 10(3), which allowed impounding "without assigning any reason." Menaka Gandhi challenged this action as being arbitrary and violative of Articles 14, 19, and 21. "If we tell her the reason, she will run away!" "If we give notice that the passport is being impounded because of corruption or involvement in serious crimes, the person will flee the country." Therefore, the Government argued, prior notice and hearing were not feasible.

The Court's Innovation — Doctrine of Post-Decisional Hearing: Application of the Non-Arbitrariness Doctrine: The Golden Triangle Formally Established: Outcome: SECTION 5 Marbury v. Madison (1803) — The Origin of Judicial Review Year: 1803 Constitutional Context: Facts: The Three Issues Framed by the Court: IMPORTANT JUDICIAL OBSERVATION Chief Justice John Marshall's Immortal Words: "It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is." This single sentence established the power of Judicial Review — the authority of courts to interpret the Constitution and declare laws or executive actions unconstitutional. The Doctrine of Constitutional Supremacy: The Supreme Court evolved the Doctrine of Post-Decisional Hearing. Rule: If there is urgency, the Government may impound the passport first. However, immediately thereafter, the Government must: 1. Issue a notice to the passport holder stating the grounds. 2. Provide an opportunity of hearing. 3. If, after hearing, the Government is satisfied that the impounding was justified, it may continue. If not, the passport must be returned. This doctrine balances the State's interest in preventing flight with the individual's right to know the reasons and be heard. The Court applied the principle from E.P. Royappa: arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality. Section 10(3) gave the Government absolute, unguided discretion to impound passports without reason — this was arbitrary power. Arbitrary power violates Article 14. The Court held that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive — they are interconnected and must be read together. Any law depriving a person of personal liberty (Article 21) must also satisfy the requirements of Article 14 (non-arbitrariness) and Article 19 (reasonableness of restrictions). This interconnection is known as the Golden Triangle of the Constitution. Menaka Gandhi did not get her passport back. The case was ultimately dismissed on other grounds. This continues the pattern observed in landmark constitutional cases: Marbury v. Madison (no relief), Kesavananda Bharati (no relief), E.P. Royappa (no relief), Menaka Gandhi (no relief). Landmark cases create principles; they do not always grant relief to the petitioner. The US Constitution was implemented in 1789. Marbury v. Madison was decided only 14-15 years later, at a time when constitutional principles were not yet settled. No article of the US Constitution explicitly mentioned Judicial Review. It was not written anywhere that the Supreme Court could review and invalidate actions of the President or Congress. In the US, the Presidential election occurs in November, but the newly elected President takes the oath of office only in January of the following year. During this lame-duck period, the outgoing President (John Adams) and his party lost control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. To preserve influence in at least one branch of government, the outgoing President appointed 40 judges to the judiciary. Commissions (appointment documents) for all 40 were signed and sealed. However, due to the rush of vacating office, some Commissions were not delivered before the new President (Thomas Jefferson) took over at midnight. The new President ordered: "Throw these undelivered Commissions away! Our people will now make new appointments." William Marbury was one of the appointees whose Commission was not delivered. He filed a case directly in the Supreme Court seeking a writ of mandamus to compel the Secretary of State (Madison) to deliver his Commission. 1. Does Marbury have a right to the Commission? Held: Yes. When the President signed and the seal was affixed, Marbury's interest (right) was created. "Where there is a right, there is a remedy." 2. Can the Supreme Court issue a mandamus to the President/Executive? Held: Yes. The Court delivered what is arguably the most famous sentence in American constitutional law. 3. Does Marbury have the right to come to the Supreme Court under original jurisdiction? Held: No. Marbury's case did not fall within the categories specified in Article III, Section 2 of the US Constitution. Marbury argued that Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 authorized him to come directly to the Supreme Court. The Court framed the crucial question: The Constitution says one thing (you cannot come); an Act of Congress says another (you can come). Which shall prevail? Answer: The Constitution shall prevail. Any law that contradicts the Constitution is void. Section 13 of the Judiciary Act was declared unconstitutional and void — the first time the US Supreme Court struck down a federal law.
