3 August 2026 (CONSTITUTION) Rule of Law: Concept, Components, and Historical Evolution Introduction to Rule of Law The Rule of Law is a foundational concept in constitutional jurisprudence that ensures governance according to established legal principles rather than arbitrary exercise of power. Professor Albert Venn Dicey, in his seminal work "An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution" (1885), systematically articulated the concept as it operated in England following the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89. Dicey did not create the Rule of Law; rather, he observed and documented the prevailing circumstances in England where the powers of the monarchy had been curtailed and governance was increasingly in the hands of the House of Commons—the common people. The Rule of Law is fundamentally about ensuring that everything runs by law, without any person's whims and fancies governing society. Dicey's work was divided into three parts: "The Sovereignty of Parliament," "The Rule of Law," and a third section dealing with constitutional conventions. His book was divided into three parts. The first was "The Sovereignty of Parliament", something which Dicey took to be fundamental, total and beyond challenge. However, when some three decades later Irish home rule returned to Parliament's agenda, Dicey changed his mind about its omnipotence. In the final edition of The Law of the Constitution in 1915 he lamented that parliamentary sovereignty had fallen prey to the party system. The Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 The Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 was a watershed moment in British constitutional history that established the supremacy of Parliament over the British monarchy. The Revolution began on 5 November 1688 when William of Orange, backed by a 21,000-strong army, took the unprecedented step of invading England. Uprisings in the north soon followed, and by the end of 1688 James II had fled to France, where Louis XIV offered the king-in-exile his protection. The revolution was driven by deep-seated fear of Catholicism and the belief that Catholics were actively plotting the overthrow of church and state. This conspiracy theory was given credibility by genuine Catholic subterfuge, most notably the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. James II's authority appeared secure when he succeeded to the throne in February 1685, but initial support for the king ebbed away as it became clear that he wished to secure not only freedom of worship for Catholics, but also the removal of the Test and Corporation Acts so that they could occupy public office. In the months following James's departure from England, established royal practices were overturned. A Convention Parliament decided that James had effectively abdicated, William and his wife Mary were declared joint monarchs, and a minor Dutch prince became King of England. The Bill of Rights (1689) determined that the monarch must be Protestant, and the Act of Settlement (1701) went further and demanded that whoever inherited the Crown must "joyn in communion with the Church of England as by law established". The Glorious Revolution ultimately established the supremacy of parliament over the British monarchy, though the events of 1688 constituted a foreign invasion of England by the Dutch Republic. While bloodshed in England was limited, the revolution was only secured in Ireland and Scotland by force and with much loss of life. The revolution also fostered the growth of slavery by ending the Royal African Company's monopoly on the trade in 1698. For the non-white inhabitants of the British Atlantic empire, the Glorious Revolution represented not the broadening of freedom but the expansion of servitude. The Three Components of Dicey's Rule of Law Dicey's formulation of the Rule of Law incorporated three distinct though kindred ideas: 1. Supremacy of Law The first and most fundamental component of Dicey's Rule of Law is the Supremacy of Law. This principle means that no man shall be punished or made to suffer in body or goods except for the violation of the law, and such violation must be established in an ordinary court of the land and in an ordinary legal manner. The government cannot punish anyone merely by its own fiat, and persons in authority in Britain do not enjoy wide, arbitrary or discretionary powers. Dicey asserted that wherever there is discretion there is room for arbitrariness. The concept was necessary because prior to its establishment, people acted according to their own will. The Anwar Ali Sarkar case exemplifies the violation of this principle. In that case, the State Government had unguided discretion to decide which cases would be sent for speedy trial, without any rational basis. One Collector might send a rape case for speedy trial because it received good publicity, while another Collector might ignore a similar case. Such individual discretion violates the Supremacy of Law because the law itself should specify what kind of cases will be sent for speedy trial. 2. Equality before Law The second component of Dicey's Rule of Law is Equality before Law, which means that no man is above the law and everyone, whatever his condition or rank, is subject to the ordinary laws of the land. Every person can sue or be sued in a court of law. Dicey was not concerned with equality in a general sense; rather, he was concerned with limiting the power of officials in favor of individual legal rights. According to Dicey, this is best achieved if everyone is subject to the same law administered by ordinary courts. Dicey had two specific ideas in mind: first, that officials as such enjoy no special protection, so that if an official abuses his power, he is personally liable to anyone whose property rights or personal freedom he violates just as if he were a private citizen; and second, that disputes between government and citizen are settled in the ordinary courts according to ordinary law rather than in a special governmental court. The framers of the Indian Constitution incorporated this concept into Article 14, which states that "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India." The principle of Equality before Law is distinct from Equal Protection of Laws, which was borrowed from the American constitutional tradition. 3. Predominance of Legal Spirit The third component of Dicey's Rule of Law is the Predominance of Legal Spirit. This principle is peculiar to Britain and emphasizes that the general principles of the British Constitution and especially the liberties of the individual are judge-made—that is, the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons in particular cases brought before the courts from time to time. The British Constitution is judge-made and the rights of the

individual form part of and pervade the Constitution. The rights of individuals are part of the Constitution because these are secured by the courts. British Constitutional Law is not the source, but the consequence, of the rights of individuals as defined by the courts. Referring in particular to the Habeas Corpus Act, Dicey said that it was "worth a hundred Constitutional articles guaranteeing individual liberty." Dicey accepted that there was rule of law in the U.S.A. because there the rights declared in the Constitution could be enforced, and the Constitution gave legal security to the rights declared. The Predominance of Legal Spirit ensures that legal remedies are available to all individuals and that the spirit of law, rather than mere technicalities, guides judicial decision-making. This principle ensures that the ordinary courts and the ordinary law of the land should be supreme, and that there should be no arbitrary or wide discretionary powers. John Austin and The Province of Jurisprudence Determined A significant anecdote from legal history concerns John Austin (1790-1859), who was the first professor of jurisprudence at the University of London. His classic work, "The Province of Jurisprudence Determined," was derived from his course lectures and first appeared separately from the Lectures in 1832. Austin took great pride in his ability to clearly delineate the study of law, taking a surgical approach and creating a stripped-down view of material central to the study of jurisprudence. The story of how Austin's book came to be published is particularly noteworthy. After Austin passed away, his wife found some of his notes on his desk. She was also educated and recognized the value of these notes—the lecture materials Austin had prepared for his courses. She approached a publisher, and the book was published posthumously. Had there not been his wife's intervention, Austin's work might not have achieved the recognition it did. This is why Austin is regarded as the Father of Analytical Jurisprudence, even though Jeremy Bentham was senior to him. Rule of Law versus Rule by Law A critical distinction exists between Rule of Law and Rule by Law. Rule by Law means that work happens according to whatever law exists, regardless of the quality or justice of that law. For instance, in some countries, women may be denied education or forced to follow oppressive practices under existing laws. These laws provide order and rules, but they lack the essential qualities of justice, fairness, and reasonableness. Such laws are an example of Rule by Law, not Rule of Law. Rule of Law, by contrast, requires that the law itself must be just, fair, and reasonable. The law must have inherent quality and must respect fundamental rights and human dignity. This distinction is significant because a society may be governed by laws, yet those laws may be oppressive and arbitrary. The Rule of Law demands not merely the existence of law, but the existence of good law that respects human rights and promotes justice. Significance and Application Dicey's thesis has been criticized from various angles, but the basic tenet expressed by him is that power is derived from and is to be exercised according to law. In substance, Dicey's emphasis is on the absence of arbitrary power and discretionary power, equality before law, and legal protection to certain basic human rights. These ideas remain relevant and significant in every democratic country even today. In India, the Supreme Court has interpreted Article 14 to encompass not only Equality before Law and Equal Protection of Laws but also the principle of non-arbitrariness. As established in E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality, and any arbitrary action violates Article 14. The broad emphasis of Rule of Law is on absence of any center of unlimited or arbitrary power in the country, on proper structuration and control of power, absence of arbitrariness in the government. Government intervention in many daily activities of citizens is on the increase, creating a possibility of arbitrariness in State action. Rule of Law is useful as a counter to this situation because the basic emphasis of the Rule of Law is on exclusion of arbitrariness. Lawlessness and unreasonableness on the part of the government are the antithesis of the Rule of Law. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, the Supreme Court enunciated the rule of law as one of the most important aspects of the doctrine of basic structure. The rule of law in one form or another is a criterion of civilization.

4 August 2026 (CONSTITUTION) Classroom Interaction and Attendance The professor begins by addressing a student's dishonesty about her attendance. He points out that he is not as stupid as the students think, as he remembers faces and names even when students lie. When one student claims her attendance is fine, the professor reveals it is actually 15 percent, meaning she has attended only 15 out of 35 classes. He explains that lying and saying "I do come" will not help the situation improve. Instead, he asks her to accept the truth so the problem can be addressed. The professor clarifies that he asks about attendance only for the student's betterment. He even helps students who are at risk of being debarred due to one attendance, because a full year back is a serious consequence. He states plainly that he is not as cruel as students think, and if someone genuinely cannot wake up in the morning, he jokingly offers to arrange for a bucket of water to be poured over them. The underlying message is that the rules exist and cannot be bypassed, but there is also room for empathy if students are honest about their difficulties. The Importance of Attending and Listening in Class The professor emphasizes the unique nature of NLU's academic system. He explains that he does not teach by simply reading from a book, and by now the students must have realized this. The NLU system is such that whatever the professor teaches is what he expects in the examination. To illustrate this, he gives a powerful example. He has taught that the Constitution of India is not quasi-federal. However, if a student reads any book or article, they will find the term quasi-federal written there. The moment a student writes quasi-federal in an exam, they will receive a zero and fail. He warns that he will not even entertain a discussion if a student brings a book to argue otherwise, because the correct position was already taught in class. He substantiates this by stating that Dr. Ambedkar first said the Constitution is federal, the Supreme Court repeatedly said it is federal, and later the Supreme Court declared that federation is the basic structure of this Constitution. Therefore, anyone writing quasi-federal is merely acting as a follower of a Western country, and the professor firmly declares, "I am not Western. I am Indian." A Humorous Interlude: The Local Student and the IPS Lecture Anecdote The professor engages with a student from Nagpur, a local girl. In a humorous tone, he threatens that 8 to 10 of them will come to her house for tea and also to lodge a complaint against her for her poor attendance. He clarifies that in his local rustic language, "abusing" actually means criticism. He then shares a memorable anecdote from when he was teaching IPS officers. He was criticizing corruption, stating that if the SSP is not corrupt, a traffic inspector does not have the courage to take money at a crossroad. The topic of his lecture was the Prevention of Corruption Act, but a huge complaint was made against him, accusing him of taunting and abusing the officers who had invited him by paying his airfare. This story illustrates his blunt and unfiltered teaching style. Returning to the student, he jokes that if they eat her salt, they cannot abuse her, but he still promises to visit, noting that Symbiosis often hosts his lectures, so a visit is not impossible. Recalling the Previous Lesson The professor then questions another student, who is made to stand as a punishment, about what was taught the previous day. She correctly answers that it was Equality before Law. The professor notes that this topic was actually taught on the first or second day, along with the work of Dicey and the distinction between Equality before Law and Equal Protection of Law, the latter of which was covered just the previous week. The student elaborates that the concept is taken from British rule and comes from a book by A.V. Dicey titled Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution. When asked the year it was written, the student hesitates out of fear, but the professor praises her for having read it, calling her a good girl and encouraging the class to clap for her. He then lightens the mood by joking with a student from Pune, saying he has heard that Pune girls are not scared and that they take people around to show forts. He humorously advises the students, especially a boy who seems scared, to be very careful and not to go if someone takes them around to show places. The Rule of Law: Its True Origins in Ancient India The professor transitions into the main topic, explaining that since Equality before Law is taken from the Rule of Law, he wanted to teach the class about its deeper origins. He makes a critical argument that the Rule of Law is a concept that is very difficult to explain but very easy to understand. While books and articles typically trace it only to Western countries, the professor asserts emphatically that the Rule of Law has always been there in our country. He asks the students to read any story from ancient India and they will find it is the Rule of Law. He gives several powerful examples. Natural justice, he says, can be considered a part of the Rule of Law. In the Ramayana, Lord Rama sent messages to Ravana not once but twice, warning him to return Mother Sita and avoid a destructive war. Even during the war, he gave repeated warnings, telling Ravana that he was a great and knowledgeable saint and only needed to return Sita to be excused. In the Mahabharata, when Yudhishthira lost the game of gambling and the condition was 12 years of exile and 1 year in an unknown place, Lord Krishna, who knew a war would take place, did not stop it but insisted that the rule be followed. The third and most poignant example is that of Shravan Kumar, the devoted son who was carrying his blind parents. When Lord Dasharatha accidentally killed him, the Rule of Law demanded that the king take responsibility for the care and protection of the dead boy's parents. King Dasharatha went to them, served them water, and they ultimately cursed him to die of the same grief of losing a son. The professor emphasizes that Dasharatha was a king; he could have avoided this, but the Rule of Law bound him. This, he says, is the true spirit of the ancient Indian Rule of Law. The Colonial Erasure of Indian Legal Heritage The professor explains why these hundreds and thousands of ancient Indian examples are ignored and discarded today. The reason was the British need to show dominance. He argues that if the British had acknowledged that Indians had good things of their own, then the Indian people would not have

accepted their superiority. To maintain control, the British had to push a narrative that Indians were inferior, calling them things like snake charmers. The professor expresses his strong dislike for the term, because the word charm actually means something good, like a charming friend. The real satisfaction, he says, comes from the Hindi word sapera. He questions, with biting sarcasm, whether the British came all the way to India just to see snakes, and if they liked India so much that they didn't want to go back even after independence. He then points out a historical fact: the British eventually folded their hands in front of people like Dr. Ambedkar and pleaded. Their plea was that now with democracy, the public would elect representatives to Parliament, but the British had fallen in love with India and were not going back. Since they would not win elections, they asked for representation without elections. This led to Article 331, under which Dr. Ambedkar granted the Anglo-Indian community two MPs in Parliament for a period of 10 years. The professor then criticizes the Congress Party for repeatedly extending this provision until it was finally removed by the 104th Constitutional Amendment. He concludes that if India was not good, no one would have wanted to settle here. From the Mughals to the British, everyone who came stayed. Even a modern figure like Mark Tully, a BBC reporter, came to report and liked India so much that he stayed. The professor recommends him as an excellent writer. A Directive for the Examination The professor makes a direct and practical appeal to the students regarding their examinations. He requests that if they are ever asked about the Rule of Law, they should write a little bit about India. He states candidly that no matter how hard the "cockroach" tries, he thinks Modi will remain in power for another three years, and only Modi sympathizers will evaluate their answer sheets. However, he clarifies that regardless of who is in power, he will be the one evaluating their papers. He instructs them to search for and find references to the Rule of Law in ancient Indian literature, noting that even new Indian literature is still older than Western sources. This is a clear directive to decolonize their legal thinking and ground their answers in Indian history and context. Dicey's Three Principles of the Rule of Law The professor moves on to the formal legal doctrine. He states that Dicey stated three things for the Rule of Law: first was the Supremacy of Law, second was Equality before Law, and third was the Predominance of Legal Spirit. He begins by discussing the Supremacy of Law, which he explains is against the concept of Rule by Law. Rule by Law occurs when a dictator, a sovereign, or a king orders something, and whether it is right or wrong, that order becomes the law. He gives the example of the missile man from North Korea. He contrasts this with Iranian girls, who protested against wearing the burqa by coming onto the streets and being shot at. Some even walked completely naked, agitating that if they were forced to wear it, they would wear nothing at all. He mentions the Taliban, where girls cannot study. All of these, he argues, are examples of Rule by Law, where the ruler's command is absolute. Rule of Law in a University Context To make the abstract concept relatable, the professor applies the Rule of Law to their own university setting. He admits that for a long time, Rule by Law was going on in their university under a certain unnamed person. He contrasts this with the Rule of Law. In a system governed by the Rule of Law, the law remains and governs everything uniformly. He gives the example of a 100-mark exam. No matter how much a professor might personally dislike a student, if the attendance system gives them 5 marks, that cannot be changed to 4. It is calculated automatically. Mid-term marks, project marks, and end-term marks are all fixed. He tells the story of a girl from Indore who is "crazy for gold medals." She has already secured 12 gold medals and is trying for 3 more. He confesses that she was not his most liked student; there were other students who were dearer to him and whom he wanted to get good marks. However, she put her life into studying, worked hard, and wrote the exam correctly, so he could not deduct her marks. This is the Rule of Law: his whims and fancies cannot override her merit. He reassures the students that if they have attendance, no one can debar them. If they have given an exam, getting their result is their right. If they passed, being promoted is their right. He then expands the concept, saying the Rule of Law is everywhere in modern times. If you don't get water, it is a violation. If you don't get food on time, it is a violation. The scope of the Rule of Law has become very wide. Explaining the Three Principles Further The professor elaborates further on Dicey's principles. Equality before Law, he explains, means there will be no special privilege or special discrimination. There will be no untouchability or restrictions based on caste, such as being forbidden to wear clothes on the upper body or being denied access to a pond. It means neither a privileged status will be created, nor a discriminatory and depressive one. This is the negative aspect of the principle. The third principle, the Predominance of Legal Spirit, is described as very important and very controversial. The professor states that Dicey wrote this very well and, importantly, Indian culture aligns with it. Dicey argued that the State did not make all laws. It might have made a few, but as human society evolved, some laws kept forming along with us. When the State came into existence, there were already existing laws. At the very least, the right to life, the right to food, the right to marry, or the right to procreation were certainly already there. These rights were not given by any king or any State. This is the Predominance of Legal Spirit. Generally, people respected each other and took care of each other, and such practices which became customs were, in essence, laws. This means that even before the Constitution was formed, there was an order and a decent system in society. The State came later to make it even better. The professor advises the students to read the modern expansion of this concept by the International Commission of Jurists to ease their further studies. ADM Jabalpur Case: The Darkest Hour of the Rule of Law

The professor transitions to the Indian constitutional history of the Rule of Law, beginning with the first important leading case, ADM Jabalpur vs. Shivkant Shukla. He sets the context: during the Emergency, MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) was applied, and everyone was arrested under it. Fundamental Rights were suspended. A writ petition was filed by ADM Jabalpur stating they were wrongly detained and should be released. The case came to the Supreme Court, which at the time had very good judges. At least three were beyond doubt: Justice Khanna, a very upright judge; Justice Bhagwati, who called himself the pioneer of human rights; and Justice Chandrachud (Y.V. Chandrachud), a very good judge. Along with Justice Beg (whom the professor harshly calls Indira Gandhi's peon) and Chief Justice A.N. Ray (who was made Chief Justice by Indira Gandhi but later changed his allegiance), it seemed the decision would be 4-1 in favor of liberty. However, the shocking judgment came, and the professor states bluntly that Indira Gandhi bought everyone. The only man who was not sold was Justice H.R. Khanna. The judges held that the entire repository of the right to liberty is the Constitution. If the Constitution has not given the right, then you do not have the right at all. Since the Constitution and rights were suspended, there was no Right to Life left to protect. Nani Palkhivala's Argument and the Court's Chilling Response The professor narrates the argument made by the legendary lawyer Nani Palkhivala, who was the respondent in the case. Palkhivala posed a terrifying hypothetical scenario to the court. Suppose a girl committed a crime, and the police went to arrest a specific person, say "Ishita." But the police mistakenly catch another innocent girl, "Aarya." Aarya protests that she is not Ishita, but the police say, "To hell with it, you are in our hands now." Palkhivala then asked an even darker question: during an Emergency, if a policeman, due to personal enmity or after drinking, comes and simply shoots an innocent person without any crime, would there be any remedy? The court's response, delivered by Justice Chandrachud, was devastating: "I am sorry, but the present law does not allow any relief." This meant a station house officer could come, shoot you, and you would have absolutely no legal recourse. The professor tells the students to read the case themselves, as they will feel like abusing the judges even more. He recounts visiting Justice Bhagwati's home and bluntly asking him what had happened and if he had consumed something. The core of the judgment was that all rights come only from the Constitution, and if the Constitution is suspended, you have no rights at all. It was declared that the Right to Life can never be suspended, even during an Emergency. Two articles of the Constitution cannot be suspended: Article 20 and Article 21. He makes the students chant "20 and 21" five times to memorize it and points out that this is explicitly written in Article 359, which now states "except 20 and 21." Thus, ADM Jabalpur was overruled by the 44th Amendment. However, there is a deeper, more human story. Justice D.Y. Chandrachud (DYC) , the son of Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, felt a deep sense of guilt over his father's betrayal. In the landmark Privacy case, he wrote a powerful passage to morally correct his father's wrong. The professor asks a student to read the passage aloud: "Neither life nor liberty are bounties conferred by the State, nor does the Constitution create these rights." The professor explains that our life and liberty are not a bounty (a gift) of the State or the Constitution. They are given by Nature or God, and the Constitution has merely accepted this fact. The Constitution is not the sole repository of these rights; they existed even before its advent. This was the exact opposite of what his father had written. The Parable of the Naughty Father and the Good Son To illustrate this act of correction, the professor tells a folk parable. There was a very naughty father who abused everyone in the village his whole life. On his deathbed, he told his very decent son that everyone would abuse him after he died and asked the son to do something to make people praise him. The son was worried. He then realized that if he did even dirtier work than his father, people would say the father was better. So while the father used to abuse, the son started throwing mud and dung at people. After a few days, the villagers started saying, "His father was better!" The professor explains that D.Y. Chandrachud did something similar. To make his father look better, he wrote this profound passage, even though it was not legally necessary because the 44th Amendment had already fixed the problem. He explicitly wrote that ADM Jabalpur is overruled, effectively washing away his father's sin. The Visit of Justice Sanjiv Khanna The professor recounts the visit of Justice Sanjiv Khanna (the nephew of Justice H.R. Khanna) to the university for convocation. The students, having been taught ADM Jabalpur thoroughly, were eager to get photos with him because of the heroic legacy of Justice H.R. Khanna. The professor told Justice Khanna that he had a huge fan following among the students. Justice Khanna was surprised, thinking that as Chief Justice for only 5-6 months, not many students would know him. The professor explained that because of ADM Jabalpur, the injustice done to his uncle (Justice H.R. Khanna was not made Chief Justice for his courageous dissent), Justice Sanjiv Khanna had converted that injustice into justice by rising to the position of Chief Justice. This pleased Justice Khanna immensely, and he took photos with many students for a long time. The professor uses this as a lesson that reading cases has real-life benefits. He shares another story of a PhD scholar who, while on her honeymoon in Kashmir, recognized Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul at her hotel. She called the professor for advice on what to say. He advised her to quickly read 2-3 of his judgments and then tell him how much she appreciated his explanation of proportionality in the Privacy judgment. She did so, and it led to a meaningful conversation. Similarly, when Justice S.K. Krishna, a popular judge and Chairman of the Pay Commission, visited, the professor was able to have an engaging discussion with him by recollecting his judgments and commission reports. The moral of these stories is that when students read cases and judgments, they have something substantial to talk about with eminent people. Otherwise, he says, they will just come, eat food, leave, and not have a good life. How to Answer a Question on the Rule of Law

The professor shifts to practical exam advice and displays a PPT that structures how to properly introduce the Rule of Law in an answer. He asks a student named Athisha to read it aloud. The ideal answer structure begins with the meaning: "Rule of Law means that no man is above law and every person is subject to the jurisdiction of ordinary courts of law, irrespective of position and rank." It then traces the phrase's origin to the French phrase "La Principe de Legalite," which implies the principle of legality. The answer should then cite definitions from authoritative sources like Black's Law Dictionary and the Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary. After defining what it is, the answer should provide a historical perspective by quoting jurists. The student reads that Sir Edward Coke, Chief Justice in James I's reign, was the originator of the doctrine, but the professor notes that Greek philosophers like Aristotle, Plato, and Cicero first wrote about it. Aristotle notably said that "law should govern and those who are in power should be servants of law." The professor explains that this introduction pattern—general meaning, dictionary definition, jurist's view—should be followed for any topic, whether it's the Rule of Law or Natural Justice. He points out that he has provided all this information in a concise seven-page document, acknowledging that the students are "useless" and won't read much, so he has kept it short. The document also covers the Modern Rule of Law as defined by the International Commission of Jurists and the United Nations, which has many parameters with multiple sub-points. The professor emphasizes that the Parliament in England made laws that controlled and limited the power of the monarchy, making the executive subject to the law, which is how the Rule of Law began in its modern English form. The session concludes with a final compliment about the quality of teachers recruited at the university, despite the flaws of a former administrator.

5 August 2026 (CONSTITUTION) Discussion on Indian Heritage, Exports, and Traditional Knowledge The professor begins with a reflection on how Indian traditions and products were systematically neglected after independence. He argues that if sarees had been exported to the world, India could have become economically strong much earlier. He notes that Aishwarya Rai once draped a saree for a European actress, demonstrating the global appeal of Indian attire. The professor humorously suggests that girls who do not feel like studying could go to Europe and open a business draping sarees at weddings and functions. However, due to what he describes as Jawaharlal Nehru's love for the West and disregard for Indian traditions, such opportunities were lost. A student points out that Nehru himself wore kurta-pyjama and Khadi, to which the professor responds that he is not asking Nehru to wear a saree. His larger point is that Nehru focused heavily on imports and neglected exports. He believed there was nothing in India worth exporting, which was a fundamental flaw. The professor gives the example of Sanskrit, which he calls the most scientific language in the world. He points out that research on Sanskrit is happening at NASA, yet Nehru stopped the teaching of Sanskrit in India, insisting that English was essential for progress. The discussion extends to the neglect of religious and cultural heritage. The professor gives the example of Ayodhya, a place of immense faith for crores of Indians, which had no railway station, while Faizabad, just 15 kilometers away, was developed and all trains stopped there. Similarly, Chitrakoot, a major pilgrimage and tourist site, was ignored in favor of Karwi. He argues that tourism in ancient India was connected with religion, and if pilgrimage sites had been developed, local economies would have benefited through rickshaw fares, hotels, and spending. When students suggest that such decisions were made to avoid Hindu-Muslim conflict, the professor counters that no Muslim ever said a railway station should not be built at a Hindu place. He asserts that those who objected should have been sent to Pakistan, as India was divided on the basis of religion, and Hindus in Hindustan must have the right to live as Hindus. He contrasts this with Sardar Patel's approach to the Somnath temple. The temple had been broken 17 times, and after independence, Patel decided to rebuild it. There was a mosque at the site, but Patel requested the local Muslims to agree, noting that the place had no specific Islamic significance like a visit from Prophet Muhammad. The Muslims agreed, and today there is no conflict over Somnath. However, Nehru refused to allow similar temple construction in Uttar Pradesh, which the professor argues was a political calculation to secure votes by maintaining Hindu-Muslim tensions. He laments that the ongoing disputes over Ayodhya and Mathura are a direct result of these early decisions. On the subject of traditional knowledge, the professor shares a personal story. His father used to prepare a medicine for cataract from the juice of a white bush, which could cure even the highest level of cataract. However, Ayurveda was demoted, not promoted, and today, curing someone at home using Ayurveda can even lead to jail. He points out that turmeric, tulsi, and neem are being patented by America, even though Indian mothers have used tulsi water for sick children for generations. India had lakhs of traditional remedies; if these had been patented and exported, the economic gains would have been enormous. He clarifies that he is not against Western medicine or clothing—people can wear pants and suits—but Indian products should have been marketed too. He notes that Modi popularized the Indian jacket, and now 90% of people wear it, proving that such promotion is possible. A student argues that the government's priorities were different after independence: first, they had to feed the hungry during the Bengal famine, build institutions like ISRO, DRDO, and IITs, and then focus on traditional knowledge. The professor counters by asking: "Tell me one institute opened to promote Ayurvedic medicine." When a student mentions AIIMS, he dismisses it as having only a neglected Ayurveda department. No dedicated government institute for Ayurveda was established. He points out that even today, millets and Indian generic foods have become globally popular, so why did the government not recognize this importance earlier? He argues that 70 years have passed since independence, and the neglect continued throughout. A student makes a thoughtful point: those in power can only act based on what they know. If Nehru and Gandhi were educated abroad and absorbed Western philosophies of freedom and liberty, they naturally tried to implement what they learned. They may not have known the traditional Indian knowledge systems well enough to promote them. The professor acknowledges this argument but chooses not to engage further in the debate at that moment, humorously declaring that the student has "won for now" because he needs to move forward with the syllabus. He invites the class to have a separate, dedicated debate on this topic another day. Attendance The professor takes attendance, calling out roll numbers from 1 to 141. There is some confusion about the class strength, with the professor noting that absentees are few but the room looks less full. He makes a light-hearted remark about an absent student, asking if she does not feel like studying in the library and offering to send her there himself. Rule of Law: Recap and Deeper Exploration The professor returns to the topic of the Rule of Law, explaining why it is being studied: one of its components, Equality before Law, is part of Article 14 of the Constitution. He recaps that Dicey gave three components: Supremacy of Law, Equality before Law, and Predominance of Legal Spirit. Supremacy of Law means two things. First, no one can be punished except for violation of law. There must be a law, and only if a person violates that law can they be punished. Second, we should not be governed by individual whims and fancies. The professor uses a classroom example: if a student expresses an opinion he disagrees with, he cannot throw her out of class simply because he did not like what she said. That would be acting on individual whims and fancies. The law gives everyone the liberty to hold independent opinions based on their own choice, conviction, and thinking. If someone is to be punished, it must be in accordance with the law, not personal preference. Equality before Law has been covered in several lectures. The principle is that all are equal, but all cannot be equal, which is why the theory of classification exists in both England and India.

Predominance of Legal Spirit is explained through an interactive example. The professor asks a student named Isha, who claims to be the most naughty in class, to think about the 100 people she has known in her life since childhood. He asks how many she would have enmity with and how many she would have neutral relations with. She estimates 80-20, but the professor suggests it is closer to 90-95 neutral and 5-10 hostile. With most people, we do not fight. Our relations remain fine. This means we do not violate their rights, nor do they violate ours. Even without a teacher or a State present, peace prevails in the class because human beings are usually peaceful. This is the essence of the Predominance of Legal Spirit: even before the State or formal law existed, people lived in an orderly and non-volatile manner. The professor introduces the famous legal maxim: "Your right ends where my nose begins." He asks students to find out who said it, noting that it may have originated in France and was later used by Abraham Lincoln and others. The idea is that you can practice punching all you want, but it should not hit someone else's nose. As long as there is distance, people do not interfere. This kind of theory governed society even when there was no sovereign, no state, no king, no Prime Minister, no Nehru, no Modi. It is a natural, self-regulating order. Magna Carta and the Origin of Rule of Law in England The professor traces the Rule of Law in England to 1215 with the Magna Carta. He asks a student to explain it, and she responds that it was one of the first official documents about human rights. The professor elaborates that it was the first written promise by a King not to do certain things. In older times, kings would levy taxes on the public for personal whims—to fight wars for a princess, to build grand monuments for a deceased wife, or simply to display power. The common people's blood was sucked through arbitrary taxation. There was no curb on the king's power. The Barons of England—not the common man, but middle-class people—confronted the king and threatened to revolt if their demands were not met. The king was compelled to accept and agreed not to tax them without consultation, leading to the principle of "no taxation without consultation." This was the first time a king acknowledged that some people had some rights. The professor clarifies two important points: Magna Carta was not for the common man initially, and it was signed not once, but on several occasions. Whenever a new king came to power, the charter was signed afresh. The first version may have had only 15 items, but later versions expanded to 39 items. Importantly, the word "due process" was used for the first time in Magna Carta, likely in Article 39 of a later version. Rule of Law in India and the Subramanian Swamy Case The professor asserts that the Rule of Law has always existed in India in some form. He then discusses a modern application through the case of Dr. Subramanian Swamy vs. Dr. Manmohan Singh. The issue was that a government servant can be prosecuted for corruption only after obtaining permission from the government. If a minister in Manmohan Singh's government was corrupt, permission to prosecute was needed from Manmohan Singh himself. Naturally, such permission was not granted. A case was filed, and the Supreme Court held that not giving sanction for prosecution of a corrupt official is a violation of the Rule of Law. The professor makes it clear that he is criticizing based on this judicial pronouncement, not personal whims. He declares that reading this case is compulsory and warns that anyone who does not read it will fail the mid-term, though he later admits he has never actually framed a question on this case for his students. The World Justice Project and Measuring Rule of Law The professor discusses the World Justice Project (WJP) , which has attempted to define the Rule of Law in a new way and annually audits countries on their Rule of Law ranking. He expresses some disagreement with their methodology, noting that Scandinavian countries like Norway have smaller, more homogeneous populations and sufficient money, so problems are fewer. India, with its immense diversity, faces unique challenges: give reservation, General gets angry; don't give, the rest get angry. Give permission for Tazia, idol immersers get angry; give permission for idol immersion, Tazia processors get angry. There are, as he puts it, "many arrangements for anger." The WJP's main components are: Accountability, Open Government, Just Law, and Accessible and Impartial Justice. The benefits of effective Rule of Law are significant: where Rule of Law is stronger, the economy is stronger because hard work is rewarded and looting is less. The professor gives the example of Bihar becoming poor because Jungle Raj replaced Rule of Law—no one wants to set up a factory if they have to pay bribes or risk kidnapping. More peaceful countries enjoy greater Rule of Law. People are more educated where Rule of Law exists. People live longer in countries with higher Rule of Law. India is currently ranked around 76th, which the professor feels is lower than deserved. The conceptual framework includes: Constraints on Government Powers (limited by legislature, judiciary, independent audit, and non-governmental checks); Absence of Corruption (in executive, judicial, and legislative branches); Open Government (published laws, Right to Information, civic participation, complaint mechanisms). The professor notes that in India, no matter how good a law Modi makes, Rahul Gandhi will never support it, and vice versa. Party interests are prioritized over national interest, which weakens this component. Further components read by students include: Fundamental Rights (equal treatment, right to life, due process, freedom of opinion, belief, privacy, assembly, and labor rights); Order and Security (crime control, limited civil conflict, no resort to violence for personal grievances); Regulatory Enforcement (effective enforcement without improper influence, no unreasonable delay, due process in administrative proceedings, no expropriation without lawful process and compensation). The Civil Justice parameters include: access and affordability, freedom from discrimination, freedom from corruption, freedom from improper government influence, no unreasonable delay, effective enforcement, and accessible ADR mechanisms. The Criminal Justice parameters include: effective investigation, timely adjudication, effective correctional system, impartiality, freedom from corruption, freedom from improper government influence, and due process rights of the accused. The professor humorously references an incident where a former Home Minister was beaten up, suggesting that such things affect the criminal justice parameter. The professor concludes that Rule of Law can be applied anywhere, in practical terms. Students can measure Rule of Law in their own university by looking at components like whether classes start on time, whether syllabus and reading material are provided, whether teachers come on time,

whether exams and results happen on time. One could even break it down into Academic, Hostel Management, Mess Management, and Placement Cell components to determine the Rule of Law parameter at NLU Nagpur. Homework: Legitimate Expectation and American Equality Cases The professor assigns Legitimate Expectation as homework. Students are to read about what it is, where it started, how it developed, when it traveled to India, and two to four cases on the topic. He also asks whether students want to read American cases on equality violations or move directly to Article 15. The students express interest in the American cases. He assigns two landmark cases: Plessy v. Ferguson (1897) and Brown v. Board of Education (1954) . When a student asks how he remembers exact dates, the professor responds with a quote: "First love is never forgotten." He says an article from BBC London reported that people who tried to find their first love after many years ended up marrying them 80% of the time. For him, the Constitution is his first and last love. Personal Anecdotes and the Scholarship Issue The professor shares stories from his career to emphasize the importance of capability and self-confidence. He recounts an offer to teach for CLAT coaching in 2012. A gentleman approached him looking for a teacher, and he initially refused. When the man persisted, the professor demanded 3000 rupees per lecture (equivalent to 15000 today). The man asked him to first teach a demo class because the students were "very naughty" and had chased away three teachers. The professor replied: "Throw your approval in the dustbin. I don't have time to give a test. If you bring lousy teachers, kids will do this only." He refused to negotiate and insisted on payment for all 30 classes upfront, even joking that the director should not instigate the kids to chase him away after 28 classes to avoid paying. His confidence came from knowing his subject thoroughly. He eventually taught there successfully. He shares that Nidhi Mugreja, a good teacher, currently earns around 6-7 lakh rupees per month teaching at Rahul IAS, possibly even 10 lakhs. The lesson is: "In India, there is no lack of employment; there is a lack of capable people." He emphasizes that he belongs to the General category with no reservation and has changed many government jobs, always thriving because of his competence. He chose to stay in Nagpur because Delhi's pollution gave him respiratory problems and black spots on his heart—doctors told him it looked like he smoked 20 cigarettes a day, though he has never even seen a cigarette up close. Nagpur, especially the Mihan area, offers a peaceful life with morning and evening walks. Finally, the professor discusses the recent scholarship issue at the university. The scholarship is called Merit-cum-Means, which the Vice Chancellor had been interpreting for seven years as "Merit separate, Means separate," giving scholarships under two different heads. When the professor became Chairman of the committee, he argued that "Merit-cum-Means" means "Merit in Means," just as a "Drawing-cum-Dining room" does not mean the dining room and drawing room are separate. He scolded the committee members and, after a world-class research effort, took the matter to the Executive Council, where a judge ruled in his favor. Now, only students whose family income is up to 8 lakh rupees (the government's means criteria) are eligible, and within that group, the toppers receive the scholarship. Those with family income of 1 crore rupees are not eligible at all. He notes that students are still sending letters asking about the separate merit scholarship, but he tells them the VC knows, not him. He concludes that this is Rule of Law in action—and that is why people get angry with him. But if one keeps reading and building capability, one will always find work elsewhere.

Constitutional Law Notes 5 INTRODUCTION TO RULE OF LAW 1 Meaning and Definition Definition Rule of Law means that no man is above law and every person is subject to the jurisdiction of ordinary courts of law, irrespective of position and rank. 1.1 Origins of the Phrase • The phrase originates from the French phrase ”La Principe de Legalite” which implies the principle of legality. • Black’s Law Dictionary defines it as governance according to law. • Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary provides a similar definition. 1.2 Historical Evolution in England The Rule of Law was systematically articulated by Professor Albert Venn Dicey in his seminal work An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885). Important Key Points about Dicey’s Work: • Dicey did not create the Rule of Law; he observed and documented the pre- vailing circumstances in England. • The powers of the monarchy had been curtailed after the Glorious Revolution of 1688-89. • Governance was increasingly in the hands of the House of Commons—the common people. • The Rule of Law is fundamentally about ensuring that everything runs by law, without any person’s whims and fancies governing society. 1.3 Dicey’s Book Structure Dicey’s work was divided into three parts: 1. The Sovereignty of Parliament - Dicey initially took this to be fundamental, total and beyond challenge. 2. The Rule of Law 3. Constitutional Conventions

Constitutional Law Notes 6 Important Note: When Irish home rule returned to Parliament’s agenda some three decades later, Dicey changed his mind about parliamentary omnipotence. In the final edi- tion (1915), he lamented that parliamentary sovereignty had fallen prey to the party system. 1.4 How to Answer Questions on Rule of Law Ideal Answer Structure: 1. Meaning - General definition 2. Dictionary Definition - Black’s Law Dictionary, Oxford 3. Jurist’s View - Historical perspective from jurists Quote Sir Edward Coke, Chief Justice in James I’s reign, was the originator of the doctrine in England. However, Greek philosophers like Aristotle, Plato, and Cicero first wrote about it. Aristotle notably said that ”law should govern and those who are in power should be servants of law.”

Constitutional Law Notes 7 THE GLORIOUS REVOLUTION OF 1688-89 2 Historical Background The Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 was a watershed moment in British constitu- tional history. • Began on 5 November 1688 when William of Orange, backed by a 21,000- strong army, invaded England. • Uprising in the north followed. • By the end of 1688, James II had fled to France. • Louis XIV offered the king-in-exile his protection. 3 Causes of the Revolution • Deep-seated fear of Catholicism • Belief that Catholics were actively plotting the overthrow of church and state • This conspiracy theory was given credibility by genuine Catholic subterfuge, most notably the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 • James II wished to secure not only freedom of worship for Catholics, but also removal of the Test and Corporation Acts so they could occupy public office 4 Key Outcomes • A Convention Parliament decided James had effectively abdicated • William and his wife Mary were declared joint monarchs • A minor Dutch prince became King of England 5 Constitutional Documents 1. Bill of Rights (1689) - Determined that the monarch must be Protestant 2. Act of Settlement (1701) - Demanded that whoever inherited the Crown must ”joyn in communion with the Church of England as by law established”

Constitutional Law Notes 8 6 Significance • Established the supremacy of Parliament over the British monarchy • The events of 1688 constituted a foreign invasion of England by the Dutch Republic • Bloodshed in England was limited, but secured in Ireland and Scotland by force with much loss of life • Fostered growth of slavery by ending Royal African Company’s monopoly on trade in 1698

Constitutional Law Notes 9 DICEY’S THREE COMPONENTS 7 Overview Dicey’s formulation of the Rule of Law incorporates three distinct though kindred ideas: Component Meaning Key Points 1. Supremacy of Law No man shall be pun- ished except for violation of law established in ordinary court No arbitrary power; no discretion; or- dinary court 2. Equality before Law No man is above the law; everyone subject to ordi- nary laws No special privilege; personal liability; ordinary courts 3. Predomi- nance of Legal Spirit General principles of Con- stitution are judge-made; rights secured by courts Natural order; customs; judge-made rights 8 SUPREMACY OF LAW 8.1 Definition Definition ”No man shall be punished or made to suffer in body or goods except for the violation of the law, and such violation must be established in an ordinary court of the land and in an ordinary legal manner.” 8.2 Key Elements 1. No punishment without law - Only violation of law can lead to punishment 2. Ordinary court - Punishment must be through ordinary legal manner 3. No arbitrary power - Government cannot punish by its own fiat 4. No wide discretionary powers - Persons in authority do not enjoy wide, arbi- trary or discretionary powers 5. Wherever there is discretion, there is room for arbitrariness

Constitutional Law Notes 10 8.3 Example: Anwar Ali Sarkar Case Case Law Anwar Ali Sarkar Case • State Government had unguided discretion to decide which cases would be sent for speedy trial. • No rational basis existed. • One Collector might send a rape case for speedy trial because it received good publicity. • Another Collector might ignore a similar case. • Such individual discretion violates the Supremacy of Law. • The law itself should specify what kind of cases will be sent for speedy trial. 8.4 Classroom Illustration Example The professor uses a classroom example: ”If a student expresses an opinion he disagrees with, he cannot throw her out of class simply because he didn’t like what she said. That would be acting on individual whims and fancies. The law gives everyone the liberty to hold independent opinions based on their own choice, conviction and thinking. If someone is to be punished, it must be in accordance with the law, not personal preference.” 9 EQUALITY BEFORE LAW 9.1 Definition Definition ”No man is above the law and everyone, whatever his condition or rank, is subject to the ordinary laws of the land. Every person can sue or be sued in a court of law.” 9.2 Key Elements 1. No special privilege - Officials as such enjoy no special protection 2. Personal liability - If an official abuses power, he is personally liable

Constitutional Law Notes 11 3. Ordinary courts - Disputes between government and citizen settled in ordinary courts according to ordinary law 4. No special governmental courts - No special courts for government officials 9.3 Dicey’s Specific Ideas 1. Officials enjoy no special protection; if an official abuses his power, he is personally liable as if he were a private citizen. 2. Disputes between government and citizen are settled in ordinary courts according to ordinary law, not in special governmental courts. 9.4 Indian Constitution: Article 14 Quote ”The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.” Important Note: The principle of Equality before Law is distinct from Equal Protection of Laws. • Equality before Law was borrowed from British tradition. • Equal Protection of Laws was borrowed from the American constitutional tradition. 9.5 Important Distinction • Equality before Law - Negative aspect: No special privilege will be created • Equal Protection of Laws - Positive aspect: No discriminatory and depressive status will be created What it prohibits: • No untouchability • No restrictions based on caste • No prohibition on wearing clothes on upper body • No denial of access to ponds

Constitutional Law Notes 12 10 PREDOMINANCE OF LEGAL SPIRIT 10.1 Definition Definition ”The general principles of the British Constitution and especially the liberties of the individual are judge-made—the result of judicial decisions determining the rights of private persons in particular cases brought before the courts from time to time.” 10.2 Key Elements 1. Constitution is judge-made - Rights of individuals form part of and pervade the Constitution 2. Rights are secured by courts - Rights are part of Constitution because secured by courts 3. Constitutional Law is consequence - Not the source, but consequence of rights as defined by courts 4. No arbitrary powers - No arbitrary or wide discretionary powers 5. Ordinary courts supreme - Ordinary courts and ordinary law should be supreme 10.3 The Habeas Corpus Act Dicey said it was: Quote ”Worth a hundred Constitutional articles guaranteeing individual liberty.” 10.4 Example in USA Dicey accepted Rule of Law in the U.S.A. because: • Rights declared in the Constitution could be enforced • Constitution gave legal security to the rights declared

Constitutional Law Notes 13 10.5 Classroom Explanation Example The professor asks students to think about the 100 people they have known since childhood. • How many would they have enmity with? • How many would they have neutral relations with? Estimate: 80-20 ratio (but professor suggests closer to 90-95 neutral, 5-10 hostile) Key Insight: With most people, we do not fight. Our relations remain fine. We do not violate their rights, nor do they violate ours. Even without a teacher or State present, peace prevails because human beings are usually peaceful. ”This is the essence of the Predominance of Legal Spirit: even before the State or formal law existed, people lived in an orderly and non-volatile manner.” 10.6 Famous Legal Maxim Quote ”Your right ends where my nose begins.” • May have originated in France • Later used by Abraham Lincoln and others • The idea is: you can practice punching all you want, but it should not hit someone else’s nose • As long as there is distance, people do not interfere Important Key Insight: This theory governed society even when there was no sovereign, no state, no king, no Prime Minister. ”It is a natural, self-regulating order.” 10.7 The State Came Later The professor explains: • The State might have made a few laws • But as human society evolved, some laws kept forming along with us • When the State came into existence, there were already existing laws • At the very least, the right to life, right to food, right to marry, and right to procreation were certainly already there

Constitutional Law Notes 14 • These rights were not given by any king or any State • Generally, people respected each other and took care of each other • Such practices which became customs were, in essence, laws • The State came later to make it even better 11 Summary Table: Dicey’s Three Components Component Meaning Key Points Supremacy of Law No punishment except for violation of law No arbitrary power; no discretion; ordinary court Equality before Law No one above the law No special privilege; personal liability; ordi- nary courts Predominance of Legal Spirit Judge-made constitu- tion Rights secured by courts; natural order; cus- toms

Constitutional Law Notes 15 RULE OF LAW vs RULE BY LAW 12 Critical Distinction Aspect Rule by Law Rule of Law Meaning Work happens according to whatever law exists Law itself must be just, fair, and reasonable Quality No concern for justice or quality Law must have inherent quality Example Dictator’s orders; oppres- sive laws Laws respecting fundamen- tal rights and human dig- nity 13 Rule by Law Examples Example 1. North Korea Example: When the father of the ”missile man” died, the new ruler ordered all subjects to weep and have tears in their eyes. Any- one without tears would be killed. This is Rule by Law—it is not illegal because the sovereign ordered it, but it has no fairness, no justice, and is not reasonable. 2. Taliban Example: Girls cannot study under existing laws. These laws pro- vide order and rules, but they lack the essential qualities of justice, fairness, and reasonableness. 3. Women’s Rights Example: In some interpretations, Indian girls from Muslim households are given fewer rights, told not to get educated, married off early, and made to wear a burqa. 14 Key Insight Important Rule of Law demands not merely the existence of law, but the existence of good law that respects human rights and promotes justice.

Constitutional Law Notes 16 15 John Austin and The Province of Jurisprudence Determined Definition John Austin (1790-1859) - First professor of jurisprudence at the University of London. ”The Province of Jurisprudence Determined” was derived from his course lectures and first appeared separately from the Lectures in 1832. Important Interesting Story: After Austin passed away, his wife found some of his notes on his desk. She was also educated and recognized the value of these notes—the lecture materials Austin had prepared for his courses. She approached a publisher, and the book was published posthumously. Had there not been his wife’s intervention, Austin’s work might not have achieved the recognition it did. • Austin is regarded as the Father of Analytical Jurisprudence • Jeremy Bentham was senior to him

Constitutional Law Notes 17 RULE OF LAW IN ANCIENT INDIA 16 Introduction Quote The professor makes a critical argument that the Rule of Law is a concept that is very difficult to explain but very easy to understand. While books and articles typically trace it only to Western countries, the professor asserts emphatically that the Rule of Law has always been there in our country. 17 Ancient Indian Examples 17.1 Natural Justice in the Ramayana Case Law Lord Rama and Ravana • Lord Rama sent messages to Ravana not once but twice, warning him to return Mother Sita and avoid a destructive war. • Even during the war, he gave repeated warnings. • He told Ravana that he was a great and knowledgeable saint and only needed to return Sita to be excused. 17.2 The Mahabharata Example Case Law Yudhishthira’s Exile • When Yudhishthira lost the game of gambling, the condition was 12 years of exile and 1 year in an unknown place. • Lord Krishna, who knew a war would take place, did not stop it. • He insisted that the rule be followed.

Constitutional Law Notes 18 17.3 Shravan Kumar Example Case Law The Devoted Son • Shravan Kumar was the devoted son who was carrying his blind parents. • Lord Dasharatha accidentally killed him. • The Rule of Law demanded that the king take responsibility for the care and protection of the dead boy’s parents. • King Dasharatha went to them, served them water. • They ultimately cursed him to die of the same grief of losing a son. Important Key Insight: Dasharatha was a king; he could have avoided this, but the Rule of Law bound him. This is the true spirit of the ancient Indian Rule of Law. 18 Natural Justice as Part of Rule of Law The professor explains that natural justice can be considered a part of the Rule of Law. Students should read: • Any story from ancient India—they will find it is the Rule of Law • These hundreds and thousands of ancient Indian examples are ignored today 18.1 Why These Examples Are Ignored Important The reason was the British need to show dominance. If the British had ac- knowledged that Indians had good things of their own, then the Indian people would not have accepted their superiority.

Constitutional Law Notes 21 MAGNA CARTA (1215) 24 Introduction The professor traces the Rule of Law in England to 1215 with the Magna Carta. Definition Magna Carta was one of the first official documents about human rights. It was the first written promise by a King not to do certain things. 25 Historical Background In older times: • Kings would levy taxes on the public for personal whims • To fight wars for a princess • To build grand monuments for a deceased wife • Simply to display power • The common people’s blood was sucked through arbitrary taxation • There was no curb on the king’s power 26 The Barons’ Revolt Important The Barons of England—not the common man, but middle-class peo- ple—confronted the king and threatened to revolt if their demands were not met. • The king was compelled to accept • Agreed not to tax them without consultation • Led to the principle of ”no taxation without consultation” • First time a king acknowledged that some people had some rights 27 Important Points About Magna Carta 1. Magna Carta was not for the common man initially 2. It was signed not once, but on several occasions 3. Whenever a new king came to power, the charter was signed afresh

Constitutional Law Notes 22 4. The first version may have had only 15 items 5. Later versions expanded to 39 items 6. The word ”due process” was used for the first time in Magna Carta 7. Likely in Article 39 of a later version

Constitutional Law Notes 27 ADM JABALPUR CASE (EMERGENCY) 36 Case Details Case Law ADM Jabalpur vs. Shivkant Shukla 37 Historical Context • During the Emergency • MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act) was applied • Everyone was arrested under it • Fundamental Rights were suspended • A writ petition was filed by ADM Jabalpur stating they were wrongly detained and should be released 38 The Supreme Court Bench The Supreme Court at the time had very good judges. At least three were beyond doubt: 1. Justice Khanna - a very upright judge 2. Justice Bhagwati - called himself the pioneer of human rights 3. Justice Chandrachud (Y.V. Chandrachud) - a very good judge 4. Justice Beg - the professor harshly calls Indira Gandhi’s ”peon” 5. Chief Justice A.N. Ray - made Chief Justice by Indira Gandhi but later changed his allegiance Important It seemed the decision would be 4-1 in favor of liberty. However, the shocking judg- ment came. The professor states bluntly that Indira Gandhi bought everyone. The only man who was not sold was Justice H.R. Khanna. 39 The Judgment The judges held that: ”The entire repository of the right to liberty is the Constitution. If the Con- stitution has not given the right, then you do not have the right at all. Since the Constitution and rights were suspended, there was no Right to Life left to protect.”

Constitutional Law Notes 28 40 Nani Palkhivala’s Argument The legendary lawyer Nani Palkhivala, who was the respondent in the case, posed a terrifying hypothetical scenario: Example ”Suppose a girl committed a crime, and the police went to arrest a specific person, say ’Ishita.’ But the police mistakenly catch another innocent girl, ’Aarya.’ Aarya protests that she is not Ishita, but the police say, ’To hell with it, you are in our hands now.” An even darker question: ”During an Emergency, if a policeman, due to personal enmity or after drink- ing, comes and simply shoots an innocent person without any crime, would there be any remedy?” 41 The Court’s Response Justice Chandrachud’s devastating response: Quote ”I am sorry, but the present law does not allow any relief.” Meaning: A station house officer could come, shoot you, and you would have abso- lutely no legal recourse. Important The core of the judgment was that all rights come only from the Constitution, and if the Constitution is suspended, you have no rights at all. 42 The Overruling • Because it was a manifestly wrong decision, immediately after the Morarji Desai government came to power • The 44th Constitutional Amendment was passed • It was declared that the Right to Life can never be suspended, even during an Emergency

Constitutional Law Notes 29 42.1 Two Articles That Cannot Be Suspended Important Article 20 and Article 21 cannot be suspended, even during an Emergency. ”This is explicitly written in Article 359, which now states ’except 20 and 21.”” Note: Thus, ADM Jabalpur was overruled by the 44th Amendment. 43 The Emotional Correction: D.Y. Chandrachud Important Justice D.Y. Chandrachud (DYC), the son of Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, felt a deep sense of guilt over his father’s betrayal. 43.1 The Privacy Case Passage In the landmark Privacy case, he wrote a powerful passage: Quote ”Neither life nor liberty are bounties conferred by the State, nor does the Consti- tution create these rights.” The professor explains: • Our life and liberty are not a bounty (a gift) of the State or the Constitution • They are given by Nature or God • The Constitution has merely accepted this fact • The Constitution is not the sole repository of these rights; they existed even before its advent • This was the exact opposite of what his father had written

Constitutional Law Notes 30 44 The Parable of the Naughty Father and the Good Son Example The Parable: 1. There was a very naughty father who abused everyone in the village his whole life 2. On his deathbed, he told his very decent son that everyone would abuse him after he died 3. He asked the son to do something to make people praise him 4. The son realized that if he did even dirtier work than his father, people would say the father was better 5. While the father used to abuse, the son started throwing mud and dung at people 6. After a few days, the villagers started saying, ”His father was better!” Application: D.Y. Chandrachud did something similar. To make his father look better, he wrote this profound passage, even though it was not legally necessary because the 44th Amendment had already fixed the problem. He explicitly wrote that ADM Jabalpur is overruled, effectively washing away his father’s sin. 45 The Visit of Justice Sanjiv Khanna • Justice Sanjiv Khanna (nephew of Justice H.R.
