Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 3 1 Introduction: The Constitutional Framework of Equal- ity The Constitution of India establishes a comprehensive framework for equality through Arti- cles 14, 15, and 16. While Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of laws as a general principle, Articles 15 and 16 provide specific applications of this princi- ple in the context of discrimination and public employment. This lecture explores the intri- cate relationship between these provisions, their historical evolution through constitutional amendments, and the critical judicial interpretations that have shaped their application. Understanding the distinction between Articles 15 and 16 is fundamental to constitutional law. Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination by the State against any citizen on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, or any of them. This provision covers a wide domain of state action, including access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, and places of public entertainment. Article 16, on the other hand, specifically addresses equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. The narrower scope of Article 16 reflects the special significance of government employment in a welfare state and the need for nuanced provisions addressing residence and descent requirements. 2 Article 15: Prohibition of Discrimination 2.1 Article 15(1): The General Prohibition Article 15(1) provides that: ¿ ”The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them.” The use of the word ”only” in this provision is of paramount importance. It signifies that discrimination cannot be based solely on these enumerated grounds. The State may discrim- inate on other grounds, provided such discrimination is reasonable and serves a legitimate purpose. This interpretive nuance has significant implications for understanding the scope of permissible state action. Key Insight: The word ”only” in Article 15(1) allows the State to consider other factors alongside the enumerated grounds. For instance, if the government decides to provide benefits to economically disadvantaged individuals, and some of those individuals happen to belong to a particular religion or caste, the discrimination is not ”only” on the prohibited ground. 2.2 Article 15(2): Access to Public Places Article 15(2) extends the prohibition against discrimination to private actors in specific con- texts: ¿ ”No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to— ¿ (a) access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or ¿ (b) the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public.”

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 4 This provision is significant because it applies to private individuals and entities, not just the State. A private shop owner cannot refuse service based on caste or religion. A housing society cannot discriminate against potential buyers or tenants based on their religion, caste, or sex. 2.3 Article 15(3) and (4): Special Provisions Article 15(3) empowers the State to make special provisions for women and children. This is a recognition that formal equality may not be sufficient to achieve substantive equality and that protective discrimination may be necessary to address historical disadvantages. Article 15(4) was added by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 in response to the Supreme Court’s decision in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan. This provision allows the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. 2.4 Subsequent Amendments: Article 15(5) and 15(6) Article 15(5) was added by the Ninety-Third Constitutional Amendment Act, 2005, allowing the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally back- ward classes, Scheduled Castes, and Scheduled Tribes in educational institutions, including private unaided institutions (except minority educational institutions). Article 15(6) was added by the One Hundred and Third Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019, allowing the State to make special provisions for the advancement of economically weaker sections (EWS) of citizens, even if they do not belong to any backward class. Table 1: Evolution of Article 15: Key Amendments Amendment Year Key Provision Added First Amend- ment 1951 Article 15(4): Special provisions for backward classes Ninety-Third Amendment 2005 Article 15(5): Educational insti- tutions (private unaided) One Hundred Third Amend- ment 2019 Article 15(6): Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) 3 Article 16: Equality of Opportunity in Public Em- ployment 3.1 Article 16(1) and (2): The General Principle Article 16(1) establishes the fundamental principle: ¿ ”There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State.”

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 5 Article 16(2) provides the specific prohibition: ¿ ”No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State.” The Distinctive Grounds: Two grounds appear in Article 16(2) that are absent from Article 15(1): ”descent” and ”residence.” The inclusion of these grounds reflects the special nature of public employment. Descent is included to prevent hereditary appointments or discrimination based on family background. In feudal societies, certain positions were reserved for particular families or castes by birth. Article 16(2) explicitly prohibits such practices. Residence is included because of the federal structure of India and the need to balance the rights of citizens to employment throughout the country with the interests of states to protect employment opportunities for their residents. Article 16(3) provides an exception to the residence prohibition, allowing Parliament to prescribe residence requirements for employment in certain states or union territories. 3.2 Article 16(3): Residence Requirement Exception Article 16(3) provides: ¿ ”Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing, in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under the Government of, or any local or other authority within, a State or Union territory, any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment.” Critical Point: Under Article 16(3), only Parliament (and not State Legislatures) has the power to enact laws prescribing residence requirements for public employment. This is reinforced by Article 35, which provides that only Parliament has the power to make laws relating to the matters specified in Article 16(3) and other similar provisions. This exclusive parliamentary power ensures uniformity in the treatment of citizens across states and prevents parochialism in state employment policies. 3.3 Articles 16(4), (4A), and (4B): Reservation Provisions Article 16(4) allows the State to make provisions for the reservation of appointments or posts in favor of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State. Article 16(4A) (inserted by the Seventy-Seventh Amendment Act, 1995) allows the State to provide for reservation in matters of promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Article 16(4B) (inserted by the Eighty-First Amendment Act, 2000) deals with the carry- forward of unfilled reserved vacancies. 3.4 Articles 16(5) and 16(6) Article 16(5) provides that nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any law which provides that the incumbent of an office in connection with the affairs of any religious or denominational institution shall be a person professing that particular religion.

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 6 Article 16(6) (added by the One Hundred Third Amendment Act, 2019) allows the State to make provisions for the reservation of appointments or posts in favor of economically weaker sections of citizens, up to a maximum of 10%, in addition to existing reservations, subject to the conditions specified. 4 Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s Vision: Equality as the Ulti- mate Aim Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the principal architect of the Indian Constitution, had a clear vision for Article 16. In the Constituent Assembly debates, he emphasized that the primary and ultimate aim of Article 16 is equality. Ambedkar understood that formal equality of op- portunity was not sufficient; substantive equality required addressing historical disadvantages that had prevented certain communities from accessing public employment. Key Points from Ambedkar’s Constituent Assembly Debates: 1. Equality as the Ultimate Goal: Ambedkar emphasized that while reservations were a temporary measure, the ultimate aim was to create a society where such provisions would no longer be necessary. 2. Backwardness as a Recognizable Category: He argued that backwardness was a recognizable and measurable condition that required state intervention. 3. Balancing Competing Interests: Ambedkar recognized the need to balance the competing interests of different groups while ensuring that the overall objective of equality was achieved. 4. Reservations as a Transitional Measure: He viewed reservations not as a perma- nent feature but as a mechanism to uplift disadvantaged communities to a level where they could compete on equal terms. Ambedkar’s Vision: ”The ultimate aim is to have equality. Reservations are a means to achieve that equality, not an end in themselves.” 5 The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 5.1 Historical Context The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, was a watershed moment in Indian consti- tutional history. It was enacted in response to a series of Supreme Court decisions that had struck down several progressive social welfare measures. The Immediate Trigger: The primary trigger for the amendment was the Supreme Court’s decision in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951). In this case, the Court struck down the Communal G.O. (Government Order) that provided for communal reservation in educational institutions.

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 7 The Court held that such reservation violated Article 15(1), which prohibited discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, etc. The Communal G.O. of 1926-27: The Communal G.O. was first introduced in 1926-27, well before independence. It pro- vided for reservation of seats in educational institutions based on communal representation: - Brahmin: 3 seats - Harijan (Dalit): 2 seats - Muslim: 1 seat - Other communities: Various allocations This system had been in operation since the pre-independence era, with modifications over time. The challenge in Champakam Dorairajan argued that this reservation system violated Article 15(1). 5.2 The Supreme Court’s Decision The Supreme Court struck down the Communal G.O., holding that it was violative of Article 15(1). The Court reasoned that the Constitution prohibited discrimination on grounds of religion, race, and caste, and the communal reservation based on these grounds was uncon- stitutional. The Court emphasized that while the State could make special provisions for backward classes under Article 15(4), such provisions had to be based on backwardness, not merely on religion or caste. The Communal G.O. did not adequately distinguish between backwardness and community membership. 5.3 The First Amendment Response The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, added Article 15(4) to overturn the effect of the Champakam Dorairajan decision. This amendment allowed the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes or for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, notwithstanding the prohibition in Article 15(1). Speeches in the Constituent Assembly (Provisional Parliament): The debates on the First Amendment featured powerful speeches from three key figures: 1. Jawaharlal Nehru: Nehru argued passionately for the need to implement progres- sive social welfare measures despite the constitutional constraints identified by the Supreme Court. He emphasized that the Constitution should not become an obstacle to social reform. 2. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar: Ambedkar supported the amendment, emphasizing that it was necessary to achieve the constitutional goal of equality. He argued that the Supreme Court’s interpretation of Article 15 had made it impossible to implement measures for the upliftment of backward classes. 3. Syama Prasad Mookerjee: Mookerjee raised serious concerns about the amend- ment, particularly regarding the restrictions on freedom of speech under Article 19(2). He feared that the amendment would be used to stifle dissent and limit fundamental freedoms. His critiques highlighted the tension between individual rights and social welfare measures. 5.4 The Syama Prasad Mookerjee Critique Syama Prasad Mookerjee’s objections were significant:

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 8 • Freedom of Speech: He argued that the restrictions on freedom of speech under Article 19(2) were being broadened excessively, threatening the democratic fabric of the nation. • Property Rights: He expressed concern about the erosion of property rights through the amendment. • Judicial Review: He feared that the amendment would limit the scope of judicial review, undermining the checks and balances in the Constitution. Despite these objections, the amendment was passed, and Article 15(4) became part of the Constitution. 6 Landmark Cases and Doctrinal Developments 6.1 E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu This landmark case established the doctrine of non-arbitrariness under Articles 14 and 16. The Supreme Court held that Article 14 strikes at arbitrariness because any arbitrary action is inherently unequal. The Court stated: ¿ ”Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions, and it cannot be ’cribbed, cabined and confined’ within the traditional limits of classification.” Significance: The case emphasized that the concept of equality is not static but evolves to address new forms of discrimination and inequality. It also established that administrative discretion must be exercised reasonably and not arbitrarily. The High Burden of Proof: A crucial aspect of E.P. Royappa is the emphasis on the high evidentiary burden required to prove arbitrariness. The Court recognized that administrative discretion is necessary for effective governance but insisted that such discretion must be exercised based on relevant considerations and not on whimsical grounds. Key Principle from E.P. Royappa: Arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality. Any action that is arbitrary is inherently violative of Article 14. However, proving arbitrariness requires a strong evidentiary foundation showing that the decision lacks any reasonable basis. 6.2 State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) Facts: The case challenged the Communal G.O. (Government Order) that provided for communal reservation in educational institutions based on religion and caste. Held: The Supreme Court struck down the Communal G.O., holding that it violated Article 15(1). The Court reasoned: 1. The Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. 2. The Communal G.O. made distinctions based on religion and caste, which

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 9 was unconstitutional. 3. While the State could make special provisions for backward classes under Article 15(4), such provisions had to be based on backwardness, not merely on religion or caste. Consequence: This decision directly led to the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, which added Article 15(4). 6.3 Zoroastrian Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar Cooperative Societies (2005) Facts: A cooperative housing society restricted membership to Zoroastrians (Parsis) only. The question was whether such a restriction was constitutional. Held: The Supreme Court upheld the society’s right to restrict membership to Zoroastrians. The Court reasoned: 1. Article 15(2) of the Constitution prohibits discrimination in access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, and places of public entertainment. 2. Housing societies, being coopera- tive societies, are not considered ”places of public resort” under Article 15(2). 3. Therefore, a housing society could restrict membership based on religion or community. Critical Analysis: The decision in this case is controversial. Critics argue that it undermines the constitu- tional commitment to secularism and pluralism. The creation of separate pockets for different religious communities may ultimately harm national integration and social harmony. The professor expressed concern about this judgment, noting: ¿ ”I feel in the long run this won’t be right, because we want a plural society. If everyone makes pockets... Muslims here, Hindus here, Yadavs here, Dalits here... our unity will be destroyed.” Limitation of the Judgment: The Court’s reasoning appears to be based on a literal interpretation of Article 15(2), treating housing societies as distinct from places of public entertainment. However, the broader constitutional vision of a secular, egalitarian society might require a more expansive interpretation. 6.4 State of Rajasthan v. Pratap Singh Facts: The case involved the imposition of additional tax and police force in a particular area, allegedly discriminating against a specific community. Held: The Supreme Court examined the constitutionality of the state action. The Court con- sidered whether the discrimination was based ”only” on the prohibited grounds under Article 15(1). The Court held that if there was a rational basis for the action, it would not violate Article 15. Key Principle: The word ”only” in Article 15(1) means that discrimination based solely on the enumer- ated grounds is prohibited. However, if the State can show additional, rational reasons for its action, the discrimination is not prohibited.

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 10 6.5 Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration Facts: The case challenged the routine handcuffing of undertrial prisoners. Held: The Supreme Court held that handcuffing is a form of degrading treatment and should not be used routinely. The Court emphasized: 1. Handcuffing violates the dignity of the individual. 2. It should only be used in exceptional cases where there is a genuine risk of escape or violence. 3. The authorities must justify the need for handcuffing in each case. Relevance to the Lecture: The professor referenced this case when discussing the improper handcuffing of a young boy who had eloped with a girl. The professor invoked Prem Shankar Shukla to argue for the removal of the handcuffs. 7 The Law-Society Interface: Changing Societal Norms 7.1 Does Law Change Society or Society Change Law? This is a fundamental question in legal theory and constitutional law. The relationship between law and society is reciprocal and dynamic. Law Changing Society: • Untouchability: The Constitution abolished untouchability under Article 17. While social attitudes have not entirely changed, the legal prohibition has created a framework for challenging discriminatory practices and has gradually shifted social norms. • Women’s Rights: Laws such as the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, and the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 2013, have changed societal attitudes toward violence against women. Society Changing Law: • Live-in Relationships: The recognition of live-in relationships by the Supreme Court reflects a change in social attitudes. The Court acknowledged that society has evolved, and the law must adapt accordingly. • LGBTQ+ Rights: The decriminalization of homosexuality under Section 377 of the IPC through the Navtej Singh Johar case reflects the Court’s recognition of changing societal attitudes. 7.2 The ”Separate but Equal” Doctrine and Plessy v. Ferguson The professor referenced the U.S. Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which upheld racial segregation under the ”separate but equal” doctrine. The Court, in that case, held:

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 11 ¿ ”Legislation is powerless to eradicate racial instincts, or abolish distinctions based upon physical differences.” This statement reflects a particular judicial philosophy: that law has limited power to change deep-seated social attitudes. The professor expressed some sympathy with this view, acknowledging that social change takes time. However, the professor also noted the eventual reversal of Plessy in Brown v. Board of Education (1954), which recognized that separate but equal was inherently unequal. This illustrates that while law may not instantly change society, it can set a normative framework that eventually leads to social transformation. 7.3 The Babu Jagjivan Ram Story: Social Change Through Inno- vation The professor shared two powerful examples of how social change can be achieved through innovative and sensitive approaches: Example 1: Railway Water Booths Babu Jagjivan Ram, as Railway Minister, appointed Dalit women at railway station water booths. Travelers who needed water had to either drink from the hands of Dalit women or go without. Over time, this forced interaction helped break down caste prejudices. Example 2: The Punjabrao Deshmukh Experiment At a function, Dalit women were dressed elegantly and made to cook and serve food. Guests did not initially realize they were Dalit. After the meal, they were informed. Initially, some felt uncomfortable, but gradually, they realized that the food was not different and the women were not inferior. Key Insight: The professor’s point was that social change requires patience and creativity. One cannot simply expect people to ”accept” change immediately. As he noted: ¿ ”It takes hard work to change society. Saying ’Accept it’ doesn’t work.” This is a crucial insight for understanding the limits of constitutional remedies. While Articles 15 and 16 provide a legal framework for equality, the actual realization of equality requires a broader social transformation. 7.4 The Personal Example: Accepting Diversity The professor shared a deeply personal story about preparing himself mentally to accept the possibility of his son marrying a Kashmiri Muslim girl. He acknowledged the difficulty of such acceptance and the time it takes to overcome deeply ingrained prejudices. The Sociological Perspective: The professor consulted a sociology teacher, Deepmala, who explained: ¿ ”This we have to change slowly. Stigma remains, but slowly...” This reinforces the insight that social change, including the acceptance of diverse com- munities and relationships, is a gradual process.

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 12 8 Reservation, Caste, and Political Manipulation 8.1 The Caste Census Debate The professor discussed the contentious issue of a caste census, which was being advocated by Rahul Gandhi and others. The professor expressed skepticism about the utility of a caste census: ¿ ”What will you do with caste census, cause fights?” The Concern: The professor’s concern was that a caste census would exacerbate social divisions by highlighting and entrenching caste identities. Instead of promoting social harmony, it could lead to increased competition for scarce resources and further political mobilization along caste lines. The Counterargument: Proponents of a caste census argue that accurate data on caste populations is necessary to assess the effectiveness of reservation policies and to ensure that benefits reach the intended beneficiaries. Without such data, it is difficult to measure whether reservations have been successful in uplifting backward communities. 8.2 The Communal G.O. and Reservation Policy The Communal G.O. of 1926-27, which was struck down in Champakam Dorairajan, repre- sents an early attempt to provide reservation based on community identity. However, the G.O. was criticized for being based on religious/caste identity rather than actual backward- ness. The Modern Reservation Framework: Modern reservation policy is based on backwardness, not merely community identity. The Mandal Commission and subsequent judgments have emphasized that backwardness must be assessed based on social, educational, and economic factors. However, the professor expressed concern that reservation policies are often used for political ends: ¿ ”Politicians destroying for votes, increasing caste, religion, not good. Vote should be on development.” 8.3 Right to Information vs. Right Against Misinformation The professor noted a contemporary problem: ¿ ”Today you shouldn’t have Right to Information, but Right against Misinformation! So much misinformation Rahul Gandhi creates.” This reflects a frustration with the spread of false information and the difficulty citizens face in distinguishing fact from fiction.

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 13 9 Procedural Fairness and Non-Arbitrariness 9.1 The Hostel Allocation Dilemma The professor shared an extended anecdote about hostel bed allocation to illustrate the principles of non-arbitrariness and administrative discretion. The Facts: • Four beds were available in the hostel. • Four sections existed: BA, Justicing, BBA, and another section. • The administration decided to allocate one bed per section through a chit-picking process. • This decision was made in consultation with students. • Students who did not get beds accused the administration of arbitrariness. • Six applications were received on medical grounds, but only four beds were available. The Professor’s Analysis: The professor explained why the administration’s decision was not arbitrary: 1. A Reasonable Basis: The decision to allocate one bed per section was based on a reasonable principle—that each section should have equal access to the available facility. 2. Precedents: The chit-picking process had been used in December as well. If students had raised objections at that time, there could have been discussion and potentially better options. 3. Consultation: The decision was made in consultation with students, not unilaterally. 4. No Partiality: The professor emphasized that no favoritism was involved: ”What will we get by doing partiality?” 5. Alternatives: If students had a better alternative, the administration was open to considering it. 9.2 The Amravati Analogy: Administrative Discretion The professor used a powerful analogy to illustrate the difference between administrative discretion and arbitrariness: The Scenario: One must travel from one location to Amravati. There are three routes: 1. A super-fast highway (Gadkari highway) costing 3000 in toll tax. 2. A partially developed highway costing 1500 but slightly more difficult. 3. A toll-free route that is longer and takes more time.

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 14 The Analysis: The driver (administrator) can choose any route based on his wisdom. If he chooses the super-fast highway, he can justify it by saying, ”We will reach half an hour early, and 3000 rupees is worth it.” If he chooses the toll-free route, he can justify it by saying, ”We will save 3000 rupees, and the extra time is not significant for a wedding.” Key Insight: Arbitrariness occurs only when there is no reason at all for the decision—when the deci- sion is based solely on whim or personal preference. When a reason is given, and the reason is relevant, the decision is not arbitrary. The professor emphasized: ¿ ”Arbitrariness happens when there is no reason at all, that ’I am saying, that’s why.’ When I am giving a reason... there is a reason. A better option than this could be, if you have any, then give us.” 9.3 The Medical Grounds Dilemma The hostel allocation case also highlighted the difficulty of accommodating special needs: • Six applications were received on medical grounds. • Four beds were available. • All six applicants had legitimate medical conditions (including epilepsy, PCOD, and other health issues). • The administration was forced to make difficult choices based on limited resources. The professor expressed sympathy but also noted practical constraints: ¿ ”I am having full sympathy with my students. But my limitations are there.” This illustrates the tension between individual rights and resource constraints in adminis- trative decision-making. While equality and non-discrimination are constitutional principles, they must be balanced against practical realities. 10 Critical Analysis: Articles 15 and 16 10.1 Arguments For the Current Framework 1. Historical Justice: Articles 15(4) and 16(4) provide a mechanism for addressing historical injustices and uplifting disadvantaged communities. 2. Substantive Equality: The provisions recognize that formal equality is not sufficient; substantive equality requires addressing structural disadvantages. 3. Constitutional Balancing: The provisions strike a balance between competing in- terests—individual rights versus collective welfare, and equality versus diversity. 4. Evolutionary Framework: The Constitution allows for amendments to adapt to changing social needs, as demonstrated by Articles 15(5), 15(6), and 16(6).

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 15 10.2 Counterarguments and Critiques 1. Reverse Discrimination: Critics argue that reservation policies constitute reverse discrimination against non-reserved categories, violating the principle of equality. 2. Inefficiency: Some argue that reservation policies compromise merit and efficiency in public services and education. 3. Political Manipulation: Reservation policies are often used for political ends rather than genuine social upliftment. 4. Caste Entrenchment: Rather than eliminating caste distinctions, reservation policies may reinforce and entrench them. 5. Inadequate Targeting: The benefits of reservation often go to the ”creamy layer” within backward communities, leaving the most disadvantaged members without ben- efits. 11 Special Emphasis: Homework Assignments and Read- ing Preparation The following homework assignments were specifically emphasized by the professor during the lecture. 11.1 Primary Mandatory Reading and Case Law Analysis 11.1.1 Constituent Assembly Debates on Article 16 Task: Thoroughly read Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s statements and debates regarding Article 16, focusing specifically on his principle that the primary and ultimate aim of the provision is equality. Deliverable: Prepare a presentation on the Constituent Assembly Debates surrounding Article 16, highlighting all key arguments for class discussion. Key Questions to Address: 1. What was Ambedkar’s vision for equality in Article 16? 2. How did Ambedkar view reservations in relation to the ultimate goal of equality? 3. What balance did Ambedkar envision between competing interests? 11.1.2 First Constitutional Amendment Act (1951) Speeches Task: Read the historic speeches delivered by Jawaharlal Nehru, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, and Syama Prasad Mookerjee during the introduction and debates of the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951. Context to Focus On: Understand Syama Prasad Mookerjee’s sharp critiques regarding freedom of speech restrictions under Article 19(2) and the addition of Article 15(4).

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 16 Key Questions to Address: 1. What was Nehru’s rationale for the First Amendment? 2. How did Ambedkar defend the amendment? 3. What were Mookerjee’s specific objections? 4. Were the critiques justified? How do they resonate with contemporary concerns? 11.1.3 Fundamental Case Laws to Read and Analyze Case 1: Zoroastrian Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. v. District Registrar Cooperative Societies (2005) Question: Analyze the constitutional validity of restrictive housing societies based on religion/community. Does such restriction violate Article 15(2)? Issues to Consider: 1. Is a housing society a ”place of public resort” under Article 15(2)? 2. Does the right to property include the right to associate with co-religionists? 3. What are the implications of this judgment for social pluralism? Case 2: State of Rajasthan v. Pratap Singh Question: Study the application of Article 15(1) regarding discrimination and additional tax/police force burdens. Issues to Consider: 1. What does the word ”only” in Article 15(1) signify? 2. When does additional burden on a community constitute discrimination? 3. What justifications can the State provide for differential treatment? Case 3: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) Question: Examine the strike-down of the Communal G.O. (1926-27) under Article 15(1), which directly led to the insertion of Article 15(4). Issues to Consider: 1. Why did the Supreme Court strike down the Communal G.O.? 2. What was the immediate political response to the decision? 3. How did the First Amendment respond to the decision? Case 4: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu Question: Review the doctrine of non-arbitrariness under Articles 14 and 16 and the high evidentiary burden required to prove arbitrariness. Suggested Cases (to be supplemented): 1. E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu 2. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India 3. Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib 4. Delhi Transport Corporation v. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress 5. N. Nagendra Rao v. State of A.P. 6. Indian Railway Construction Co. v. Ajay Kumar 7. Central Inland Water Transport Corp. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly 8. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation 9. K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India 10. Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 18 11.2 Textual Analysis and Comparative Conceptual Questions 11.2.1 Comparative Analysis of Article 15 vs. Article 16 Question: What is the precise distinction between the scope of Article 15 and Article 16? Focus Areas: 1. Article 15 covers a wider general domain, including access to public facilities, while Article 16 specifically targets state/public employment. 2. The grounds listed in Article 16(2) include ”descent” and ”residence,” which are absent from Article 15(1). Why? 3. The scope of discrimination under Article 15 is broader, covering a wide range of state actions, while Article 16 is limited to employment. Question: Why are ”Residence” and ”Descent” explicitly listed in Article 16(2) but omitted in Article 15(1)? Answer to Prepare: • Residence: Included because of the federal structure and the need to balance interstate mobility with state employment interests. The exception in Article 16(3) addresses this concern. • Descent: Included to prevent hereditary appointments and caste-based discrimination in public employment, which was a feudal practice. 11.2.2 Article 16(3) and Article 35 Analysis Question: Explain the constitutional operation of Article 16(3) alongside Article 35. Focus: • Article 16(3) allows Parliament to prescribe residence requirements for public employ- ment in certain states. • Article 35 reinforces this by providing that only Parliament (not State Legislatures) has the power to make laws relating to the matters specified in Article 16(3). • This exclusive parliamentary power ensures uniformity in the treatment of citizens across states and prevents parochialism. 11.2.3 Sub-clause Deep Dive Preparation Task: Prepare for upcoming class coverage on: 1. Article 15(4): Special provisions for backward classes 2. Article 15(5): Educational institutions (private unaided) 3. Article 15(6): Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)

Constitutional Law Lecture Notes 19 4. Article 16(4): Reservation in appointments 5. Article 16(5): Religious/denominational institutions 6. Article 16(6): EWS reservation in employment Key Case for Review: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (on EWS reservation) 12 Conclusion: The Path Forward The constitutional framework for equality, as embodied in Articles 15 and 16, represents one of the most ambitious experiments in social engineering in human history. The framers of the Constitution recognized that formal equality was not enough and that substantive equality required active state intervention to address historical disadvantages. 12.1 Key Takeaways 1. Articles 15 and 16 Are Complementary: While Article 15 provides a general pro- hibition against discrimination, Article 16 specifically addresses equality of opportunity in public employment. 2. The Word ”Only” is Critical: In both provisions, the word ”only” allows the State to consider other factors alongside the prohibited grounds, provided there is a rational basis for doing so. 3. Reservations Are a Means to an End: Dr. Ambedkar emphasized that reserva- tions are a transitional measure to achieve the ultimate goal of equality. 4. Non-Arbitrariness Requires Reasons: Administrative discretion is not arbitrary if there is a reasonable basis for the decision. Arbitrariness occurs when there is no reason at all. 5. Law and Society Are Interconnected: Legal change alone cannot transform society; social change requires patience, creativity, and cultural adaptation. 6. The First Amendment Was Transformative: The First Constitutional Amend- ment Act, 1951, added Article 15(4) and reshaped the constitutional framework for reserva- tion. 7. Judicial Doctrines Evolve: Cases like E.P. Royappa have expanded the concept of equality to include non-arbitrariness and substantive justice. 12.2 Final Reflections The professor’s closing reflections on social change and acceptance are worth highlighting: ¿ ”Society takes time to change. Are we moving towards change or not? Are we same as 70-80 years ago or changed? If changed, progress is there, not bad. But politicians destroying for votes, increasing caste, religion, not good. Vote should be on development.” The constitutional journey of India is a work in progress. Articles 15 and 16 provide the legal foundation for equality, but the actual realization of equality requires a broader societal transformation. As the professor emphasized, this transformation requires patience,

12 August 2026 (Constitution) Detailed Notes on the Constituent Assembly Debate: Draft Article 10 (Equality of Opportunity in Public Employment) I. Overview and Context Date of Debate: 30th November 1948 Draft Article Under Discussion: Article 10 (which later became Article 16 of the Constitution of India) Presiding Officer: Mr. Vice-President (Dr. H.C. Mookherjee) Core Issue: How to guarantee equality of opportunity in public employment while also addressing the historical exclusion of certain communities from government services. II. Preliminary Discussions (New Article 11-B - Capital Punishment) A. Amendment to Abolish Death Penalty Shri Amiyo Kumar Ghosh (Bihar): Shri K. Hanumanthaiya (Mysore): Mr. Vice-President's Ruling: No reference to the "particular individual" was permitted. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's Position: Simply stated, "I do not accept the amendment." Result: The amendment was negatived. III. The Main Debate: Draft Article 10 A. The Core Principle Article 10(1) as originally drafted: "There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters of employment under the State." B. The Amendments and Discussions 1. Amendment No. 338 (Mr. Mohd. Tahir, as modified by Amendment No. 77) Mr. Mohd. Tahir's Original Amendment: Shri M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar's Modification (Amendment No. 77): Accepted by Dr. Ambedkar: Yes. Rationale: To make the language more comprehensive and clarify that both employment and appointment to office were covered. Argument: Opposed incorporating the abolition of capital punishment in the Constitution. Reasoning: The State must retain the power to impose grave penalties in times of crisis. Fettering the State's hands "for all time" through the Constitution was unwise. Alternative Suggestion: Such changes should be made through the Indian Penal Code, which can be amended more easily as circumstances change. Position: Supported the principle of abolishing capital punishment but rejected it as a constitutional provision. Argument: Opposed the amendment from the State's perspective. Key Points: Referenced George Bernard Shaw's play about Joan of Arc, who preferred death over life imprisonment—suggesting that convicts may prefer death to a "dead life" in prison. Argued that society is based not only on reformation but also on the "fear instinct" principle. Without the death penalty, the deterrent value of punishment would be lost. The possibility of early release (after 7-8 years) would "encourage the method of revenge." Referenced a politically sensitive case (the Godse incident) which was interrupted by the Chair. Sought to add the word "acquisition" after "employment" in clause (1). Sought to add "or employment" after "office" in clause (2). Proposed substituting "in matters of employment" with "in matters relating to employment or appointment to office" in clause (1). Proposed inserting "employment or" before "appointment to office" in clause (2).

2. Amendment No. 336 (Mr. Naziruddin Ahmad) Proposed: Substituting clause (2) with: "Every citizen shall be eligible for office under the State irrespective of his religion, caste, sex, descent or place of birth." Dr. Ambedkar's Position: Not accepted. Result: Negatived. 3. Amendment No. 334 (Shri Lokanath Misra) Proposed: Deleting clauses (2), (3), and (4) entirely. Argument: Dr. Ambedkar's Position: Not accepted. Result: Negatived. 4. Amendment No. 339 (Prof. K.T. Shah) Proposed: Adding "in India" after "place of birth" in clause (2). Argument: Dr. Ambedkar's Position: Not accepted. Result: Negatived. 5. Amendment No. 340 (Shri Jaspat Roy Kapoor) Proposed: Adding "or residence" after "place of birth" in clause (2). Argument: Accepted by Dr. Ambedkar: Yes (as modified by Amendments Nos. 81 and 82). Significance: This amendment recognized that discrimination based on residence was as harmful as discrimination based on religion, caste, or sex. 6. Amendment No. 81 (Shri K.M. Munshi) Proposed: A verbal amendment to No. 340, substituting "or residence" with simply "residence" to maintain grammatical consistency. Accepted by Dr. Ambedkar: Yes. 7. Amendment No. 82 (Shri Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar) Proposed Insertion of New Clause (2a): "Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under any State for the time being specified in the First Schedule or any local or other authority within its territory, any requirement as to residence within that State prior to such employment or appointment." The Difficulty Raised by Shri H.V. Kamath: Clause (1) already covers all cases. Clause (3) (reservation for backward classes) puts a "premium on backwardness and inefficiency." Clause (4) is unnecessary because India is a secular state that shouldn't manage religious institutions. Sought to reserve positions for "children of the soil." Referenced discriminatory practices in other Commonwealth countries like South Africa, White Australia, and White Canada. Argued that the country's own citizens should have the first claim on employment. Every citizen should have equal opportunity for employment anywhere in the country. Growing provincialism (e.g., "Bengal for Bengalis," "Madras for Madras") was threatening national unity. Allegation that some provinces were imposing absurd residency requirements (e.g., 52 years). The unity and solidarity of the country must be preserved "at all costs."

Shri K.M. Munshi's Clarification: Dr. Ambedkar's Justification of the "Residence" Amendment: Result: The amendment was adopted. 8. Amendment No. 342 (Shri M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar) Proposed: Adding "or discriminated against" after "ineligible" in clause (2). Argument: Accepted by Dr. Ambedkar: Yes. Result: Adopted. 9. The "Backward Classes" Debate The Three Conflicting Viewpoints (Identified by Dr. Ambedkar): Dr. Ambedkar's Dilemma: The Justification for the Word "Backward": Definition of "Backward": "A backward community is a community which is backward in the opinion of the Government." Justiciability: C. Arguments on the "Backward" Clause Supporters of Reservation Shri Ari Bahadur Gurung (West Bengal): Article 1 defines "States" as those specified in Parts I, II, and III of the First Schedule. Part IV of the First Schedule contains Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are "territories," not "States." The amendment's language ("under any State for the time being specified in the First Schedule") was ambiguous. The heading of the First Schedule is "States and Territories." Parts I, II, and III refer to States with autonomous governments. Part IV (Andaman and Nicobar) refers to territories directly controlled by the Centre. Therefore, "any State" in the amendment naturally refers only to Parts I, II, and III. The Centre cannot discriminate between residents of different provinces for its own services. Principle: Common citizenship throughout India implies that residence should NOT be a qualification for employment. Reality Check: Provinces already had varying residency rules (10 years, 7 years, "domicile," etc.). The Problem: If different provinces had different rules, it would create chaos. The Solution: Only Parliament should have the power to prescribe residential qualifications, ensuring uniformity. Purpose: To prevent people from becoming "mere birds of passage" moving from province to province seeking jobs without any roots. Discrimination can occur not only at the time of appointment but also in promotions and other post-appointment matters. "Ineligible" does not cover these cases. 1. Equality of Opportunity: Every citizen should be free to apply and be judged solely on merit. 2. No Reservations: There should be no reservations of any kind for any class. 3. Special Provisions: Communities historically excluded from administration must have guaranteed entry. If reservations are granted to all communities demanding them, the total reserved seats might reach 70%. This would destroy the very principle of equality of opportunity. Therefore, reservations must be limited to a minority of seats. The original fundamental right passed by the Assembly did not contain the word "backward." The Drafting Committee inserted it to prevent the exception (reservation) from "eating up the rule (equality)." Without such a qualifier, the exception would be so large that the rule would cease to have any meaning. Dr. Ambedkar believed the matter would be justiciable. If a State Government reserved so many seats that equality was destroyed, one could approach the Supreme Court. The Court would decide whether the Government acted "in a reasonable and prudent manner."

Ambedkar's Concluding Speech (in Full) A. Introductory Remarks Sir, I am going to say at the outset, before I deal with the specific questions that have been raised in the course of the debate, that I cannot accept amendment No. 334 moved by Mr. Misra; nor can I accept the two amendments moved by my friend, Mr. Naziruddin Ahmad, Nos. 336 and 337. I am prepared to accept the amendment of Mr. Imam No. 338, as amended by amendment No. 77 moved by Mr. Ananthasaynam Ayyangar. I am also prepared to accept the amendment of Mr. Kapoor, viz., No. 340, as amended by amendments Nos. 81 and 82 moved by my friends Mr. Munshi and Mr. Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar. B. Response to the "Paradise for Lawyers" Criticism I do not think that I am called upon to say anything with regard to amendments Nos. 334, 336 and 337. Such observations, therefore, as I shall make in the course of my speech will be confined to the question of residence about which there has been so much debate and the use of the word "backward" in clause (3) of article 10. My friend, Mr. T. T. Krishnamachari, has twitted the Drafting Committee that the Drafting Committee, probably in the interests of some members of that Committee, instead of producing a Constitution, have produced a paradise for lawyers. I am not prepared to say that this Constitution will not give rise to questions which will involve legal interpretation or judicial interpretation. In fact, I would like to ask Mr. Krishnamachari if he can point out to me any instance of any Constitution in the world which has not been a paradise for lawyers. I would particularly ask him to refer to the vast store house of law reports with regard to the Constitution of the United States, Canada and other countries. I am therefore not ashamed at all if this Constitution hereafter for purposes of interpretation is required to be taken to the Federal Court. That is the fate of every Constitution and every Drafting Committee. I shall therefore not labour that point at all. C. Explanation of the "Residence" Amendment Now, with regard to the question of residence. The matter is really very simple and I cannot understand why so intelligent a person as my friend Mr. T. T. Wanted to ensure that only managing affairs, not all connections, should be restricted by religious qualifications. Gave a sharp critique of the entire article: Called it a "paradise for lawyers." this Constitution or which we propose to establish by this Constitution. We are merely following the practice which has been already established in the various provinces. However, what we found was that while different provinces were laying down a certain period as a qualifying period for posts, the periods varied considerably. Some provinces said that a person must be actually domiciled. What that means, one does not know. Others have fixed ten years, some seven years and so on. It was therefore felt that, while it might be desirable to fix a period as a qualifying test, that qualifying test should be uniform throughout India. Consequently, if that object is to be achieved, viz., that the qualifying residential period should be uniform, that object can be achieved only by giving the power to Parliament and not giving it to the local units, whether provinces or States. That is the underlying purpose of this amendment putting down residence as a qualification. D. Explanation of the Word "Backward" Now, Sir, to come to the other question which has been agitating the members of this House, viz., the use of the word "backward" in clause (3) of article 10, I should like to begin by making some general observations so that members might be in a position to understand the exact import, the significance and the necessity for using the word "backward" in this particular clause. If members were to try and exchange their views on this subject, they will find that there are three points of view which it is necessary for us to reconcile if we are to produce a workable proposition which will be accepted by all. Of the three points of view, the first is that there shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens. It is the desire of many Members of this House that every individual who is qualified for a particular post should be free to apply for that post, to sit for examinations and to have his qualifications tested so as to determine whether he is fit for the post or not and that there ought to be no limitations, there ought to be no hindrance in the operation of this principle of equality of opportunity. Another view mostly shared by a section of the House is that, if this principle is to be operative—and it ought to be operative in their judgment to its fullest extent—there ought to be no reservations of any sort for any class or community at all, that all citizens, if they are qualified, should be placed on the same footing of equality so far as the public services are concerned. That is the second point of view we have. Then we have quite a massive opinion which insists that, although theoretically it is good to have the principle that there shall be equality of opportunity, there must at the same time be a provision made for the entry of certain communities which have so far been outside the administration. As I said, the Drafting Committee had to produce a formula which would reconcile these three points of view, firstly, that there shall be equality of opportunity, secondly that there shall be reservations in favour of certain communities which have not so far had a 'proper look-in' so to say into the administration. If honourable Members will bear these facts in mind—the three principles, we had to reconcile—they will see that no better formula could be produced than the one that is embodied in sub-clause (3) of article 10 of the Constitution; they will find that the view of those who believe and hold that there shall be equality of opportunity, has been embodied in sub-clause (1) of Article 10. It is a generic principle. At the same time, as I said, we had to reconcile this formula with the demand made by certain communities that the administration which has now—for historical reasons—been controlled by one community or a few communities, that situation should disappear and that the others also must have an opportunity of getting into the public services. E. The Danger of Over-Reservation Supposing, for instance, reservations were made for a community or a collection of communities, the total of which came to something like 70 per cent of the total posts under the State and only 30 per cent are retained as the unreserved. Could anybody say that the reservation of 30 per cent as open to general competition would be satisfactory from the point of view of giving effect to the first principle, namely, that there shall be equality of opportunity? It cannot be in my judgment. Therefore the seats to be reserved, if the reservation is to be consistent with sub-clause (1) of Article 10, must be confined to a minority of seats. It is then only that the first principle could find its place in the Constitution and effective in operation. If honourable Members understand this position that we have to safeguard two things namely, the principle of equality of opportunity and at the same time satisfy the demand of communities which have not had so far representation in the State, then, I am sure they will agree that unless you use some such qualifying phrase as "backward" the exception made in favour of reservation will ultimately eat up the rule altogether. Nothing of the rule will remain. That I think, if I may say so, is the justification why the Drafting Committee undertook on its own shoulders the responsibility of introducing the word "backward" which, I admit, did not originally find a place in the fundamental right in the way in which it was passed by this Assembly. But I think honourable Members will realise that the Drafting Committee which has been ridiculed on more than one ground for producing sometimes a loose draft, sometimes something which is not appropriate and so on, might have opened itself to further attack that they produced a Draft Constitution in which the exception was so large, that it left no room for the rule to operate. I think this is sufficient to justify why the word "backward" has been used. F. On Minorities and Justiciability With regard to the minorities, there is a special reference to that in Article 296, where it has been laid down that some provision will be made with regard to the minorities. Of course, we did not lay down any proportion. That is quite clear from the section itself, but we have not altogether omitted the minorities from consideration. Somebody asked me: "What is a backward community"? Well, I think any one who reads the language of the draft itself will find that we have left it to be determined by each local Government. A backward community is a community which is backward in the opinion of the Government. My honourable friend, Mr. T. T. Krishnamachari asked me whether this rule will be justiciable. It is rather difficult to give a dogmatic answer. Personally I think it would be a justiciable matter. If the local Government included in this category of reservations such a large number of seats; I think one could very well go to the Federal Court and the Supreme Court and say that the reservation is of such a magnitude that the rule regarding equality of opportunity has been destroyed and the court will then come to the conclusion whether the local Government or the State Government has acted in a reasonable and prudent manner.

Mr. Krishnamachari asked: "Who is a reasonable man and who is a prudent man? These are matters of litigation". Of course, they are matters of litigation, but my honourable Friend, Mr. Krishnamachari will understand that the words "reasonable persons and prudent persons" have been used in very many laws and if he will refer only to the Transfer of Property Act, he will find that in very many cases the words "a reasonable person and a prudent person" have very well been defined and the court will not find any difficulty in defining it. I hope, therefore that the amendments which I have accepted, will be accepted by the House. V. The Final Article 10 (As Amended) After the debate and voting, the following article was added to the Constitution: Article 10 (as amended): (1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State. (2a) Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing, in regard to a class or classes of employment or appointment to an office under any State for the time being specified in the First Schedule or any local or other authority within its territory, any requirement as to residence within that State prior to such employment or appointment. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens who, in the opinion of the State, are not adequately represented in the services under the State. (4) Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any law which provides that the incumbent of an office in connection with the affairs of any religious or denominational institution or any member of the governing body thereof shall be a person professing a particular religion or belonging to a particular denomination. VI. Subsequent Evolution (Post-Constitution) A. The Reservation Debate Continues The "Exception" Theory: The Shift: Why Article 16(4) is NOT an Exception (The Indra Sawhney Logic): Earlier View Later View (Indra Sawhney) Equality is the rule Equality is the rule Reservation is an exception to equality Reservation is a means to achieve equality Reservation deviates from merit Reservation creates a level playing field Backward classes are like others Backward classes are a separate class B. The "Residence" Exception in Practice Constitutional Position: Why Parliament, Not States? Connecting to Article 301: For several years, the Supreme Court treated Article 16(4) as an exception to Article 16(1). The understanding was that while equality was the rule, reservation was a permissible exception to that rule. In the Indra Sawhney v. Union of India case (1992), the Supreme Court fundamentally recharacterized the relationship. It held that Article 16(4) is not an exception to Article 16(1) but an enabling provision. This is based on the principle of substantive equality—that true equality requires treating unequal situations differently. Under this view, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes are a different class under reasonable classification. Therefore, giving them reservation is not an exception to equality but a fulfillment of equality. Article 16(2) generally prohibits discrimination based on residence. Article 16(3) allows Parliament to create exceptions for certain classes of employment or appointment to an office. States would be selfish and discriminate in favor of their own residents. A uniform national standard is needed to preserve the value of common citizenship. The power was given to Parliament to prevent provincialism from undermining national unity. Article 301 states that "trade, commerce and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free." This is part of the same constitutional philosophy: India is one economic and social unit.

VII. Key Quotes from the Debate Dr. B.R. Ambedkar: "Equality is a general rule, while reservation is an exception." "Unless you use some such qualifying phrase as 'backward,' the exception made in favour of reservation will ultimately eat up the rule altogether. Nothing of the rule will remain." "A backward community is a community which is backward in the opinion of the Government." "The seats to be reserved must be confined to a minority of seats. It is then only that the first principle could find its place in the Constitution and effective in operation." Sardar Hukam Singh: "What would be the fate of the minorities?" Mr. Mohamed Ismail Sahib: "Communalism does not come in because people want their rights. When people find that they are not adequately represented, they rightly feel that they must have due representation and then such a demand comes up." Shri H.J. Khandekar: "Though there are commissions... our candidates will not be able to compete with the candidates of the Brahmin community or the so-called Savarna Hindus." Shri V.I. Muniswami Pillay: "The uplift [of Scheduled Castes] will still stand over [without reservation]." Pandit Hirday Nath Kunzru: "It is not desirable that... any special provisions laid down for [backward classes] should operate indefinitely." Shri T.T. Krishnamachari (Critique): "This chapter of fundamental rights is a paradise for lawyers. And, as a piece of loose drafting, article 10 takes the palm." VIII. Conclusion The debate on Draft Article 10 was a defining moment in India's constitutional history. It established: Dr. Ambedkar's Central Legacy: The Continuing Relevance: Just as goods should flow freely across borders, citizens should be able to move and work freely. 1. The Principle of Equality: No citizen can be denied public employment based on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, or residence. 2. The Exception for Backward Classes: The State can make provisions for reservation in appointments or posts for any backward class of citizens. 3. The "Residence" Limitation: While residence discrimination is generally prohibited, Parliament can create exceptions to ensure both national unity and reasonable state autonomy. 4. The Philosophical Framework: Equality is the rule; reservation is a limited exception designed to make representation meaningful. Dr. Ambedkar is often seen as a leader of Dalits, but his vision was much broader. He was a nationalist who balanced social justice with administrative efficiency. His goal was to uplift the backward classes without destroying the principle of merit. He recognized that India's strength lies in unity, efficiency, and justice—not in any one of these alone. The debate over reservation continues in contemporary India. The tension between equality and affirmative action remains unresolved. The Supreme Court's shift from the "exception" theory to the "substantive equality" theory in Indra Sawhney reflects the ongoing evolution of this principle. Dr. Ambedkar's vision—that the backward should be uplifted without sacrificing national unity—remains the guiding light for constitutional interpretation in this area.

Equal Treatment among Equals: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. Equal treatment of unequals is as much a violation of the Constitution as unequal treatment of equals. Ronald Dworkin’s Distinction: Right to Equal Treatment: The right to an equal distribution of an opportunity or resource. Right to Treatment as an Equal: The fundamental right to be treated with equal concern and respect by the State. Differential treatment (affirmative action) by the State is constitutional as long as it stems from equal concern and respect, rather than prejudice, contempt, or hostility toward any group. Harmonious Construction: Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) must be read in harmony—a principle recognized as part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. Reading DPSPs into Fundamental Rights: Right to Education: Articles 41, 45, and 46 were read alongside Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) to establish the Fundamental Right to Education (Article 21A). Affirmative Action: Articles 15(4) and 16(4) draw substantive meaning from Articles 38 (promoting social welfare) and 46 (promoting the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, and weaker sections). Article 335 mandates that the claims of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in public appointments must be considered consistently with the maintenance of administrative efficiency. Taking SC/ST claims into account under Article 335 does not inherently imply a compromise or reduction in administrative efficiency. Hohfeldian Analysis of Rights: Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld classified rights into Claims, Privileges, Powers, and Immunities. Positive state duties create corresponding enforceable legal claims for protected classes. International and Comparative Standards: Positive state action is recognized internationally (e.g., the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights) and in foreign welfare-state constitutions (e.g., Germany). Judicial Enforcement: Both State action and inaction regarding affirmative duties can be challenged under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution, including through writs such as Mandamus. Singh implemented the Mandal Commission’s recommendation by granting a 27% reservation to Other Backward Classes (OBCs) via an executive order. Key Issues Framed in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India 1. Executive Orders for Reservation: Whether reservation under Article 16(4) can be introduced through an executive order without explicit legislative enactment (Held: Yes). 2. Nature of Article 16(4): Whether Article 16(4) is an exception to Article 16(1) (Held: No, it is an emphatic facet of equality/reasonable classification). 3. Identification of Backward Classes and Role of Caste: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore (1963) previously held that caste alone cannot define a backward class. Indra Sawhney (1992) clarified that a social caste can constitute a "class" for the purposes of Article 16(4) if it is shown to be socially and educationally backward. 4. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s Intent: During the Constituent Assembly debates, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar deliberately refrained from rigidly defining "backward classes" in the text of the Constitution, leaving the operational identification to the executive to allow flexibility over time. 5. Additional Issues Addressed by the Bench: Permissibility of reservation in promotions. Validity of sub-classification within backward classes (e.g., backward vs. more backward). Applicability of the 50% ceiling rule on total reservations. Validity of the "carry forward" rule for unfilled reserved vacancies

Questions asked in the lecture, answered Each question is answered the way the lecture's own context answers it. Where the standard legal record adds or differs, it is marked as an additional note or ⚠ Check. Q1. Is clause (f) missing from Art. 19(1) because Dr. Ambedkar did not know the sequence, or did a typist err? Did the professor or Dr. Ambedkar make the mistake? A. Neither. Clause (f), the Right to Property, did exist in Art. 19(1) and was later deleted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment (Morarji Desai government). A typist error is not the explanation either, because the Constitution was handwritten, not typed. The jokes that 'Congress party' or 'Gen Z' deleted it were banter. Q2. Should 'f' be there between (e) and (g)? Who deleted it, and why? A. Originally yes; the sequence (a) to (g) was complete. It was removed together with Art. 31 by the Morarji Desai government through the 44th Amendment, to avoid future litigation over property as a Fundamental Right. Q3. If the Right to Property was taken away, does that mean she has no right to hold property and I can snatch her iPad or pen on my whims? A. No. Property ceased to be a Fundamental Right, but individuals have no power to take another's property, and neither does the State freely. The State may acquire property only for public interest on three conditions: law, public purpose and compensation. Art. 300A says no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law. Q4. Once Art. 19(1)(f) existed, why was the Right to Property also mentioned in Art. 31? Why two places, and why not one? A. Per the lecture: 19(1)(f) was the citizens' right to property, and by the rule of correlative duty (Hohfeld) it put a duty on the State not to take it. Art. 31 was, in a way, the State's right of acquisition, which also restricted that right. One provision gave the State power to take property while the other said citizens' property could not be taken, a contradiction and confusion, so both were abolished. ⚠ Art. 31 is usually described as a safeguard against deprivation of property for persons; the 'State's right of acquisition' framing is the professor's.

The professor called it a sovereign principle: even if Art. 31 had never been written, the State could still take property under it. ⚠ Additional note, not in the lecture: the term comes from the Latin dominium eminens ('supreme lordship'), associated with Grotius. The professor said he could not recall the meaning of the Latin. Q9. What are the three conditions before the State can take property? A. (1) A law authorising the acquisition; (2) a public purpose (not, for example, a politician's farmhouse); (3) compensation. Procedure was folded into law / public purpose, and compensation was linked to economic interest. ⚠ Art. 300A's text mentions only 'authority of law'; the three-condition formulation is the professor's. The State could take property under Art. 31 too, so that is not the difference. The difference is that property became a constitutional right and not a Fundamental Right, so Art. 13 does not apply (Art. 13 voids any law that abridges Fundamental Rights). A law on acquisition can now survive on its own, whereas earlier states struggled because taking a Fundamental Right needed a Constitutional Amendment, which a state cannot make. Q11. The professor was unsure of the number ('17th or 25th, I believe 25th'), so the lecture's answer is the 25th Amendment. With 'amount' the State could pay any sum (for example ₹10 for 100 acres). Q12. Per the students, compensation is 2x market value in cities and 4x in villages, and the professor accepted this.

Article 19(1)(g) — profession, occupation, trade or business • Text: all citizens have the right “to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business” (the professor said “profess”; the verb is practise). Art 19 rights belong to citizens. • Liberally interpreted — “anything can be covered under this” — so borderline cases arose: prostitution (§3), liquor and gambling (§4), meat trade (§5). • Qualifications: some professions need prescribed qualifications — law professor (LLB, LLM, NET, PhD), doctor, engineer; you cannot simply declare yourself one (Art 19(6)(i)). Where none is needed, anyone may enter — e.g. selling paan on the streets of Varanasi. • State monopoly: the government can create monopolies in some areas for certain reasons (Art 19(6)(ii)). • Restrictions are allowed only in the general public interest and must be reasonable — never arbitrary or excessive (Art 19(6)). CONSTITUTIONAL LAW · LECTURE NOTES Art 19(1)(g) · Art 21 · FR vs DPSP Compiled from the lecture transcript; corrections to the lecture are flagged in red. Page 6 8. Accuracy corrections and clarifications 1. Art 19(1)(g) wording: “practise any profession”, not “profess”. 2. “Nagpur High Court” is the Nagpur Bench of the Bombay High Court. 3. Ireland case: the Irish death was Savita Halappanavar (Ireland, October 2012), who died of septicaemia after being refused termination of a miscarrying pregnancy — not a Norway / caesarean case. The student was right. 4. Cow-slaughter cases: the later case is State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat (2005, seven judges), not “Mirzapur v. State of Bihar”. Quareshi (1958) upheld the ban on cows, calves and milch / draught cattle but struck the ban on useless bulls and bullocks as excessive; Mirzapur overruled that part and upheld the wider ban. Because Minerva Mills (1980) came after Quareshi (1958), the “complementary and supplementary” harmony ratio was applied in the later case. 5. Kesavananda: it upheld the 24th, 26th and 29th Amendments and the 25th except the second part of Art 31C (the bar on judicial review), which it struck down; it also laid down the basic-structure doctrine. So it did not leave every amendment untouched. Minerva Mills later held that the balance of Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure. 6. Scope of Art 31C: it shields laws only against challenge under Arts 14, 19 and 31 (Art 31 was repealed in 1978) — not against Art 21. The “Right to Life” remark was hyperbole. 7. Pairs in the conflict example: Art 48 = cows; Art 46 = SC / ST / weaker sections; Art 40 = village panchayats. The intended clash is Art 21 vs Art 48, and Art 15 / 29 vs Art 46 in Champakam. 9. Exam-ready outline: relationship of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles 1. Starting point — Part III is enforceable through Art 32; Part IV is not enforceable by any court (Art 37), yet is fundamental in governance and binds the State in making laws. 2. FR supremacy (1951) — Champakam Dorairajan: in a clash FR prevail and DPSPs run subsidiary to them. (Added: the First Amendment then inserted Art 15(4).) 3. Shift in attitude (1969) — Chandra Bhavan: DPSPs cannot be ignored; the Constitution imposes duties on the State as well as conferring rights. 4. Parliament lifts DPSPs (1971–76) — 25th Amendment — Art 31C for Art 39(b), (c), upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) except the bar on judicial review; 42nd Amendment extended it to all DPSPs. 5. Harmony (1980) — Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment extension: FR and DPSP are complementary and supplementary, “two wheels of the same chariot”, to be harmoniously construed. 6. Application — Cow-slaughter cases (Quareshi, 1958; Mirzapur, 2005): Art 48 read with Arts 14, 19(1)(g), 21 and 25 — the ban is a reasonable restriction in the public interest, and other meats stay open. The lecture moves from the scope of 19(1)(g), to education as an occupation, closing a business, street vending, the test for reasonable restrictions, and then a run of cases on cow slaughter, meat and liquor bans, and religious practice versus public order. What it covers lawful professions · running educational institutions · closing a business · street vending What it excludes illegal / immoral / inherently dangerous activity · monopoly Education = occupation TMA Pai (and Islamic Academy, which explains it) Limits - Art. 19(6) by law · reasonable · public interest · proportionate Food, animal & liquor bans Quareshi · 7-judge Gujarat case · Paryushan · Rishikesh · Bihar Religion vs public order Coimbatore puja ban · azaan & loudspeakers (Art. 25) Art. 19(1)(g) Freedom of occupation, trade & business (citizens only) 1 Opening correction: Hanif Quareshi (cow slaughter, "milch animals") Yesterday's first cow-slaughter case, Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar, was taught in a hurry. The professor said he had left out one point: the Supreme Court's "milch animals" reasoning, i.e. cows that no longer give milk, or bulls no longer fit for work, may be slaughtered. He asked the class to Google whether the case really says this. Q. Is it like that in the first case (Quareshi)? A. Yes, in substance. Quareshi drew its line at usefulness: • Upheld: total ban on slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of cows and she-buffaloes. • Upheld: ban on slaughter of she-buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks while they remain useful for milk, breeding or draught. • Struck down as unreasonable: a total ban on slaughter of animals after they cease to be useful. So a cow that no longer gives milk, or a bull unfit for work, could be slaughtered. • Caution: the later seven-judge Gujarat case (Section 8) effectively diluted this "aged cattle" view and upheld a total ban, so Quareshi is no longer the last word. Prof. said (informal remarks) • The student's half-answer ("animals that were... allowed...") became a joke: useless old things can be killed, so "in five or six years you people will kill me too!" (a memory hook: the old test was usefulness). • Teaching in a hurry means some things get messed up. What a teacher teaches first stays in memory for ever, and later additions raise doubts "a hundred times", so corrections matter. Every night, before sleeping, he recalls what he taught that day and what he left out. • Academic Committee meetings ate class time; he said he would delete the Academic Committee from his committees "so neither a holiday nor a problem". 2 Article 19: who gets it, and which freedoms • Article 19 is available only to citizens of India. A student asked whether all provisions under Article 19 are citizen-only; the professor said yes. Today's discussion is only 19(1)(g). • Not all fundamental rights are citizen-only. Constitutional Law | Article 19(1)(g) - lecture notes Page 2 Q. "Freedom of what?" And "freedom of cow slaughter?" (the professor's probing of the student reading the six points) A. Article 19 gives six freedoms (table above); the one under study is the freedom of occupation, trade or business. It is not a "freedom of cow slaughter": the student corrected himself, and Quareshi / the Gujarat case treat cow-slaughter bans as reasonable restrictions on trade. 3 Scope of Article 19(1)(g) • Citizens only. • Lawful professions only: medicine, law, teaching, accountancy and so on. Unlawful professions are not covered. • Includes the right to establish and administer educational institutions (Section 4). • Includes the right to close down a business (Section 5). • Street vending is recognised as a legitimate occupation (Section 6). • No protection for illegal, immoral or inherently dangerous activities, even for a citizen. Likewise no right to a monopoly. Prof. said (informal remarks) • You cannot claim a right to bring ganja into the hostels. (English word, per the class: "weed".) "If I ask now, they will tell the shop, the mobile number, everything. Beware!" • On monopoly: he cited the BCCI's hold on cricket (mentioning the Zee Telefilms case); the Court did not break it up, but nothing stops a rival federation from forming its own team and becoming more popular.
