PROTECTED by Art. 19(1)(g) Yes Yes Yes No Art. 19 right (Art. 14 & 21 still protect all persons) No protection - illegal / immoral / dangerous trade (e.g. weed in hostels) No No Next: is the State's restriction valid? (chart below) 4 Education as an occupation: TMA Pai and Islamic Academy Under 19(1)(g) there was a long-standing case on the right to establish and administer educational institutions. The professor said he would not teach much of it, but it is very important. TMA Pai was so hard to read that a new Constitution Bench had to sit just to say what its ratio is: Islamic Academy of Education v. State of Karnataka. 1 · Old tradition Education seen as charity: no fees; guru dakshina, or children begged alms to run the ashram. 2 · Before 1980 Mostly government schools or unpaid private teaching. State capped fees and regulated admissions. 3 · After 1980 Private colleges grow. Capitation abuse: seats go to whoever pays 25-30 lakh. Quality suffers. 4 · Court's view Education is "not a trade or business". Govt regulates; managements hint at colleges abroad. 5 · The squeeze Modern institutions need huge money (labs, infrastructure, good salaries); Govt and Court back off. 6 · TMA Pai Education IS an occupation => Art. 19(1)(g). Islamic Academy later explains what TMA Pai held. Why it mattered. Earlier, education was not treated as a business, and the State could cap fees and control admissions. Once private colleges multiplied, money decided admission (an engineering college with 25,000 applicants could sell seats for 25-30 lakh; the same in medical colleges), and people who paid might be poor students. Yet modern institutions need large sums for infrastructure, labs and good teacher salaries, and teachers work well only when paid well. Managements told the government, off the record, that they would open engineering and medical colleges in nearby countries (Maldives, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan) and Indian students would pay fees there. The Government grew nervous and the Court checked itself. • Holding in TMA Pai: for the first time the Supreme Court said education is also an occupation. Constitutional Law | FR vs DPSP & Article 21 Page 1 CONSTITUTIONAL LAW — LECTURE NOTES Part A: Directive Principles vs Fundamental Rights | Part B: Article 21 — Life, Personal Liberty & “Procedure Established by Law” Abbreviations: FR = Fundamental Rights (Part III) • DPSP = Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) • PEBL = Procedure Established by Law • SC = Supreme Court. Colour key: teal/purple = core law • yellow boxes with italics = professor’s informal remarks • green = lecture questions answered • red = accuracy corrections. Left out of these notes: the professor’s party-political remarks and remarks aimed at individual students. Article 20 was deliberately skipped in the lecture (to be taken later); the lecture moved straight to Article 21. PART A — DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES vs FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS The big picture. The lecture opened by revising how the Supreme Court has handled a clash between FRs and DPSPs. The journey runs from “FR above DPSP” (Champakam Dorairajan) to “FR and DPSP are complementary and must be harmoniously construed” (Minerva Mills). The Constitution is founded on the balance between Part III and Part IV, and neither gets absolute primacy — they are the “two wheels of the same chariot”. EXAM TRAP Do not write “in certain cases Fundamental Rights must be given priority”. Minerva Mills does not say that; it says harmonious construction / balance. The professor said this one sentence earns zero. A.1 Why did the conflict arise? — Articles 32 and 37 Article 32 Article 37 Says Right to Constitutional Remedies: a fundamental right to approach the Supreme Court for enforcement of any FR in Part III. DPSPs are not enforceable by any court, though they are “fundamental in the governance of the country”. Nature Justiciable — courts can enforce it. Non-justiciable — courts cannot enforce it. Logic of the early view: if a dispute reaches court, the court enforces what is justiciable → something justiciable (FR) cannot be overridden by something non-justiciable (DPSP) → FRs get primacy; DPSPs are subsidiary to FRs. The confusion was about reservation (communal quota in college seats), not about the right to property. A.2 Flowchart: how the Court’s position evolved 1951 — CHAMPAKAM DORAIRAJAN State of Madras case on communal reservation in seats. FR supreme; DPSP subsidiary. 1951 — 1st AMENDMENT The “reservation amendment” that followed: Art 15(4) added. 1969 — CHANDRA BHAVAN The “hotel case” (Chandra Bhavan Boarding & Lodging v. State of Mysore). DPSPs can no longer be ignored; FR and DPSP read as balanced. 1971 — 25th AMENDMENT Indira Gandhi’s govt. adds Art 31C: law implementing Art 39(b) & (c) cannot be challenged for violating Arts 14, 19, 31. 1973 — KESAVANANDA BHARATI 25th Am. challenged. 1st part of 31C upheld; 2nd part (bar on judicial review) struck down — judicial review is basic structure. 1976 — 42nd AMENDMENT 31C widened: law implementing any DPSP prevails over FR and cannot be questioned in court. DPSP placed above FR. 1980 — MINERVA MILLS 42nd-Am. extension of 31C (s.4) and review-ouster (s.55) struck down. Balance of Parts III & IV is basic structure. POSITION TODAY 31C survives only in its Art 39(b),(c) form. FR + DPSP = complementary & supplementary; harmonious construction. Art 39(b) & (c) in one line: (b) community resources distributed to serve the common good; (c) the economic system must not concentrate wealth and means of production in a few hands. Why 31C had to be an insertion: an amendment does not stand alone as “the law” (unlike the USA); it must add or change something in the text — the 25th Amendment did so by inserting Art 31C. PROFESSOR'S INFORMAL ASIDES (in italics, as said in class) • Marks policy: “While reading answers, if I see even one poor sentence, marks are cut.” Don’t read notes aloud when asked a question — “use your brain.” • How he knows article numbers: as a game, he asked his 3–4-year-old son to open “page 753”-type pages and read the article numbers; the boy could do it, so “even a child can read from the book — recall it without looking.” • On students answering from notes: “Are you attending my class for the first day?” Understand the thought process behind the cases, not only the names. • Quip on assignments: reading only for the Family Law project is not enough — Constitutional Law cases (e.g. the hotel case) were compulsory reading.

Constitutional Law | FR vs DPSP & Article 21 Page 2 A.3 Case notes in more detail Case Facts / issue Holding & consequence State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951) A communal Government Order allotted seats in State colleges by community. The State defended it by pointing to a DPSP (Art 46, protecting weaker sections); the petitioner relied on the FR against denial of admission on grounds of religion, race, caste or language (Art 29(2)). The order was struck down. The Court held DPSPs cannot override FRs and must “run as subsidiary” to them. Result: Parliament responded with the 1st Amendment (Art 15(4)). Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) Challenge to the 24th and 25th Amendments, including the new Art 31C. Landmark basic structure ruling. 31C’s first part (immunity from Arts 14, 19, 31 for 39(b)/(c) laws) survived; its second part, which shut out courts, was struck down because judicial review is basic structure. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) Challenge to the 42nd Amendment: s.4 (31C extended to all DPSPs) and s.55 (Art 368(4),(5): amendments beyond judicial review). Both struck down. The Constitution rests on a balance between Parts III and IV; giving absolute primacy to either upsets that harmony. Hence “complementary and supplementary”, “two wheels of the same chariot”. KEY TAKEAWAY — PART A Memory chain: Champakam (FR > DP) → 25th Am. + 31C (DP > FR, only for 39(b),(c)) → Kesavananda (trims 31C) → 42nd Am. (31C for all DPSPs) → Minerva Mills (back to balance). Whenever a question asks “what is the present position?”, the answer is harmony, not priority. PART B — ARTICLE 21: LIFE, PERSONAL LIBERTY & PROCEDURE ESTABLISHED BY LAW ARTICLE 21 — THE TEXT “No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.” Only one line long, yet the professor called it among the most important articles: “hardly anybody is conceptually clear on this” — even in interviews and selection committees up to Professor level. He asked students to stop writing and just listen. Four ideas must be understood: 1. “NO PERSON” Every person — citizens and foreigners (e.g. Kasab). Generally human beings only, not corporates. 2. “LIFE” From bare survival → “more than mere animal existence” — everything that makes life meaningful. 3. “PERSONAL LIBERTY” From freedom from physical restraint → widest meaning: all liberties not already covered by Art 19(1)(a)–(g). 4. “PROCEDURE ESTABLISHED BY LAW” Gopalan: any validly enacted law. Maneka Gandhi: procedure must be just, fair & reasonable (due-process flavour). B.1 “No person” — and against whom does Art 21 work? Kasab example: when caught in Mumbai he was not shot or hanged on the spot; the procedure established by law was followed (trial, appeals) — because Art 21 protects everybody, including aliens and Pakistani nationals. VERTICAL (traditional view) HORIZONTAL (modern view) Against The State only. The State is the most powerful actor (money, ED, CID, police), so Art 21 restrains it. If a private person attacks you, the State must act to protect you; you cannot take the law into your hands — go to the constitutional courts. Also private persons and entities (e.g. Facebook, X, LinkedIn) — they cannot violate your FR, especially dignity. Because telling the State to act may be ineffective, rights bite directly. Authority Long-standing position. Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. (3 Jan 2023), 5-judge Constitution Bench, 4:1. Justice B.V. Nagarathna (partly dissenting) wrote separately. Compulsory reading — expect an exam question. Remedy when an FR is violated — flow: FR VIOLATED Right to life/liberty infringed (by State or, now, a private party). WRIT PETITION Art 32 (Supreme Court) / Art 226 (High Court). COMPENSATION v. STATE Rudul Sah (1983): money compensation for FR violation — original loss can’t be undone, but money gives relief. PRIVATE PARTY PAYS Bodhisattwa Gautam v. Subhra Chakraborty (1996): first clear horizontal step. Also M.C. Mehta (1986/87): absolute liability.

B.2 “Life” and “Personal Liberty” — how the meaning grew Case Year What happened / what the Court held A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras 1950 A Communist leader and sitting MP was held under preventive detention. The Court gave life and personal liberty a very narrow meaning (bare existence; no physical restraint) and treated PEBL as any law passed by the legislature — if a law exists, “I cannot help.” Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. 18 Dec 1962 (6 judges) Accused in a dacoity case (released for want of evidence) and placed under police surveillance (UP Police Regulations, Reg. 236); police made night domiciliary visits to check whether he was home. The Court struck down the night visits as violating Art 21 and said life is “not mere animal existence”, a sentence borrowed from the US case Munn v. Illinois (1877). First step away from Gopalan. Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India 1978 Passport impounded without reasons or notice. Personal liberty has the widest amplitude — it covers rights not in Art 19(1)(a)–(g); procedure must be just, fair and reasonable. Gopalan’s narrow reading was abandoned (the 1980s expansion by Justice Bhagwati and others was promised for a later lecture). Examples the professor listed under “meaningful life / liberty”: sleep, reading newspapers, giving a TV interview, no needless handcuffing, water, roads, freedom to love, choice of food, dress and movement. Timeline of Art 21 as seen in this lecture: 1950 — GOPALAN Narrow: any valid law will do; liberty = no physical restraint. 1962 — KHARAK SINGH Life ≠ mere animal existence; night domiciliary visits struck down. 1978 — MANEKA GANDHI Widest liberty; procedure must be just, fair, reasonable. 1983 — RUDUL SAH Compensation for FR violation by the State. 1986/87 — M.C. MEHTA Absolute liability for hazardous industry; heavy deposit ordered. 1996 — BODHISATTWA GAUTAM Rape = Art 21 violation; private accused pays interim compensation. 2023 — KAUSHAL KISHOR Arts 19 & 21 enforceable against private actors (4:1).

Constitutional Law | FR vs DPSP & Article 21 Page 4 B.3 Procedure Established by Law (PEBL) vs Due Process of Law Flowchart: where each phrase came from MAGNA CARTA (1215) Barons’ charter against the king: no punishment except by lawful judgment of one’s peers / law of the land — a restraint on royal power. ENGLAND Law-making needed proper procedure, the king’s council, a local jury (community standards, facts). After 1688 (Glorious Revolution) Parliament is supreme → PEBL. USA Due process (5th/14th Amendments): judges test the quality of laws → powerful judiciary → Lochner era. JAPAN (1946–47) Constitution drafted under US occupation uses PEBL. B.N. RAU + FRANKFURTER India’s constitutional adviser consults US Justice Felix Frankfurter: avoid “due process” — it hands judges too much power over the people’s representatives. INDIA: ART 21 Framers adopt PEBL. GOPALAN (1950) Court checks only whether a law exists. MANEKA GANDHI (1978) Procedure must be just, fair, reasonable → due process in effect. Procedure Established by Law Due Process of Law Who is supreme? Parliament / legislature (“upper hand”). Judiciary (“upper hand”). Court checks Only whether the implementing agency followed the prescribed procedure. The procedure and the quality / reasonableness of the law itself. Exam analogy “Was an exam actually held?” “Was there due notice, a proper gap, and enough time — or 10 questions in 3 minutes?” Risk Partisan law-making goes unchecked. Judicial overreach (Lochner). In India Text of Art 21; Gopalan (1950). Read in through Maneka Gandhi (1978). CASE FILE: THE LOCHNER ERA Lochner v. New York (1905): the US Supreme Court struck down a New York law capping bakers’ working hours, on the ground of “freedom of contract” / laissez-faire under due process. Many welfare laws (hours, wages, children) fell in this “Lochner era”. It ended around 1937: President F.D. Roosevelt threatened “packing the Court” — adding sympathetic justices (one per justice over 70) — and the justices began reading due process more liberally. WHY “JUST, FAIR AND REASONABLE” MATTERS After Maneka Gandhi the Court reads Arts 14, 19 and 21 together (the “golden triangle”): a law that touches life or liberty must be procedurally fair, non-arbitrary and, where Art 19 is engaged, reasonable. Added context — not stated in the lecture; included to explain why PEBL now behaves like due process. PROFESSOR'S INFORMAL ASIDES (in italics, as said in class) • Why he likes due process: “everyone is a little selfish; when I get power I will favour my supporters” — legislators fight elections, judges do not, so they judge laws more neutrally. Due process and the basic structure doctrine are “good”, even if judges adopted them for their own reasons. • Don’t make bad laws while in power — they may bite you: the Passport Act was made in Indira Gandhi’s time, yet when it was used against Maneka Gandhi, she (“the daughter-in-law”) was caught by it; the Court asked for reasons and a hearing. • Freedom to contract, mocked: if everything is “contract”, a rich man can make a poor man pull a hand-rickshaw in Calcutta — the exploitation the laws tried to stop (18-hour days, no minimum wage, no age limit). • Jury trivia: jurors were local people who decided facts by community standards; the case that ended jury trials in India is K.M. Nanavati (a student named Ileana D’Cruz as the heroine of the film version, Rustom). • Presentation task: a student must present on the Lochner era “tomorrow”. Personal liberty Gopalan (physical restraint) → Maneka Gandhi 1978 (all liberties outside Art 19(1)(a)–(g)). PEBL vs due process PEBL: court checks procedure only (legislature supreme). Due process: court also tests the law’s quality (judiciary supreme). Maneka brought due process in by the back door. Lochner era US courts used “freedom of contract” to strike welfare laws; ended by FDR’s 1937 court-packing threat. LECTURE QUESTIONS — ANSWERED Question asked in class Answer What was the SC’s view of an FR–DPSP conflict at the start of the Republic? FRs prevail; DPSPs are subsidiary — State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951). Why did the conflict arise? Which two articles? Art 32 (FR enforceable in the SC) vs Art 37 (DPSPs not enforceable by courts); justiciable vs non-justiciable. It concerned reservation, not property. Name the “hotel case”. Chandra Bhavan Boarding & Lodging v. State of Mysore (1969). What did the 25th Amendment do, and where? Inserted Art 31C: laws to implement Art 39(b)/(c) cannot be held void for violating Arts 14, 19, 31. Which case challenged it? Upheld or quashed? Kesavananda Bharati (1973): partly upheld (immunity of 31C) and partly struck down (clause barring judicial review). Which amendment put all DPSPs above FRs, and what happened? 42nd Amendment (1976); Minerva Mills (1980) struck down that extension (and s.55); harmonious construction restored. Who can claim Art 21? Against whom? Every “person”, citizens or not (Kasab); not corporates. Traditionally against the State; now also private actors — Kaushal Kishor (2023). Remedy for violation of an FR? Writ under Art 32/226; compensation — Rudul Sah (1983); private party liable — Bodhisattwa Gautam (1996, the year the student gave). Case giving “life” a narrow meaning? First liberal case? Source of the “animal existence” line? A.K. Gopalan (1950); Kharak Singh (1962); Munn v. Illinois (USA). Case that widened “personal liberty”? Maneka Gandhi (1978). Who advised B.N. Rau on “due process”? Who “packed the Court”? Which case is “Lochner”? Justice Felix Frankfurter; F.D. Roosevelt; Lochner v. New York (1905). ACCURACY CORRECTIONS (where the spoken lecture slipped) As said in the lecture Correct position Art 21 read as “life and personal liberty” The text says “life or personal liberty”. Student: Art 37 means DPSPs “not enforceable by the State” DPSPs are not enforceable by any court. Early FR-over-DPSP view dated “1950” Champakam was decided in 1951. 25th Am.: laws can’t be challenged for violating “Fundamental Rights” Only for violating Arts 14, 19 and 31 (Art 31 was later repealed). Minerva Mills: 42nd Amendment “totally unconstitutional” Only s.4 (31C extension) and s.55 (Art 368(4),(5)) were struck down. Kharak Singh “1963 / seven judges” Decided 18 Dec 1962 (AIR 1963 SC 1295) by a six-judge bench; only domiciliary visits were struck down. Magna Carta “Article 39 has due process of law” Clause 39 speaks of “law of the land”; the words “due process of law” appear in a statute of 1354. Lochner “1903”, child-labour/18-hour laws Lochner is 1905 and concerned bakers’ hours; child-labour laws fell in other cases. FDR to add “three” judges His 1937 plan: up to six extra justices (one per justice over 70); the Court has nine. Nagarathna’s view prevailed Kaushal Kishor majority (4:1) held Arts 19/21 enforceable against private actors; she partly dissented. Maneka Gandhi decided “to save Indira Gandhi” Passport Act, 1967; passport impounded in 1977 under the Janata government; the Court tested fairness of procedure. Bodhisattwa Gautam: aside on the scholar’s conduct Holding: rape violates Art 21; accused (a private person) ordered to pay interim compensation. The aside is not part of the ratio.

sections.title: Overview
sections.html:
What this section is

Study notes on D.D. Basu's Commentary on the Constitution of India, Article 13: the two clauses on pre- and post-Constitution laws, the meaning of "law" and "void", severability, judicial review and its limits, and the effects of a declaration of unconstitutionality.

The notes are summaries in my own words, not Basu's text. Short phrases from judgments and from the Commentary appear in quotation marks. Use them alongside the book, not instead of it.

How to read them

  • Basu's opinions are marked as his. Where the Supreme Court has since taken a different view (for example on prospective overruling), the notes say so.
  • Citations were checked. Where the Commentary has a wrong name, date, citation or attribution, a red box marked as a slip in the source gives the correct version.
  • Underlined case names open a short summary and the case page, with a link to the judgment.

Chapters

  1. Article 13 at a glance
  2. Clause (1) — pre-Constitution laws and the doctrine of eclipse
  3. Clause (2) — the prohibition on post-Constitution laws
  4. "Shall be void" — still-born laws, relative voidness and non-citizens
  5. Severability and reading down
  6. Clauses (3) and (4) — "law", "laws in force" and constitutional amendments
  7. Judicial review — meaning, foundations and scope
  8. Which courts review, and through what proceedings
  9. Limits on judicial review (1) — limits in the Constitution itself
  10. Limits on judicial review (2) — limits inherent in the judicial function
  11. Self-imposed limits (1) — a real case, a substantial question, decided only as far as necessary
  12. Self-imposed limits (2) — standing, waiver and public interest litigation
  13. Self-imposed limits (3) — advisory opinions, pleadings, timing and justiciability
  14. Self-imposed limits (4) — the presumption of constitutionality and deference to the legislature
  15. Self-imposed limits (5) — stare decisis in constitutional cases
  16. The duty to decide — substance, indirect encroachment and attempts to oust review
  17. Effects of unconstitutionality and prospective overruling
  18. After the declaration — judgment in rem, revival and validating laws

sections.title: The provision in four clauses
sections.html:
In one minute

Clause (1) deals with laws that already existed on 26 January 1950: to the extent they are inconsistent with Part III, they are void.

Clause (2) is a command to the State for the future: it shall not make a law that takes away or abridges a fundamental right, and a law made in breach is void to the extent of the contravention.

Clause (3) defines "law" and "laws in force" inclusively (Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law).

Clause (4), added by the 24th Amendment (1971), says nothing in Art 13 applies to an amendment made under Art 368.

Basu reads the Article as doing two jobs at once. It looks backward, cleaning up the pre-Constitution statute book (cl. 1), and it looks forward, limiting every future exercise of law-making power (cl. 2). The definitions in cl. (3) make sure the limit reaches subordinate legislation and custom, not only Acts of a legislature.

"Inconsistency" (cl. 1) and "contravention" (cl. 2) produce the same result — voidness — but the choice of words is deliberate. A pre-1950 legislature was under no prohibition, so its law can only be inconsistent with rights created later. A post-1950 legislature is under an express prohibition, so its law contravenes that prohibition.

sections.title: Why spell it out? The "abundant caution" point
sections.html:
A written Constitution with a Bill of Rights already implies that courts may strike down laws that breach it. That was how Marshall CJ reasoned in Marbury v. Madison (1803) even though the US Constitution has no clause saying that an unconstitutional law is void.

In A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), Kania CJ said Art 13(1) and (2) were inserted "as a matter of abundant caution": even without them, the Court could have declared an infringing enactment invalid. So Art 13 is not the source of judicial review. It makes explicit what a supreme, written Constitution already implies, so that no one can argue the framers left it to judges to assume the power.

Basu draws two further points:

  • Art 13 expresses a reservation by the people. In giving themselves the Constitution, the people kept certain freedoms out of the reach of ordinary law-making. Art 13 records that reservation rather than creating the rights.
  • The Article is the clearest textual statement in the Constitution that judicial review inheres in Part III. Together with Art 245(1) ("subject to the provisions of this Constitution"), it rules out any claim of parliamentary sovereignty in the English sense.

sections.title: Comparative background
sections.html:
Basu sets Art 13 against other constitutions to show it is part of a common pattern of supremacy clauses:

  • Ireland (1937): Art 15(4) bars the Oireachtas from enacting repugnant laws and makes them invalid to the extent of repugnancy; the High Court and Supreme Court decide validity (Art 34).
  • Japan: Art 98 declares the Constitution the supreme law; contrary laws and acts have no legal force.
  • (West) Germany: Art 1(3) binds legislature, executive and judiciary to the basic rights as directly valid law; Art 19(2) protects the "essence" of a basic right from being infringed.
  • Singapore: Art 4 declares the Constitution supreme and post-commencement inconsistent laws void to the extent of inconsistency.
  • USA: no express voidness clause; the rule comes from Marbury.
Exam use

The comparison is useful in an essay answer on "Is Art 13 necessary?". Answer: not strictly (Kania CJ's "abundant caution"), but it removes doubt, fixes the extent of voidness ("to the extent of"), and defines "law" widely enough to catch delegated legislation and custom.

sections.title: Supremacy and who declares invalidity
sections.html:
Basu stresses one difference from the American model. In the USA, a judgment of unconstitutionality binds the parties; the statute is not formally removed from the statute book. In India, once the Supreme Court declares a statute void, Art 141 makes that declaration binding on every court, so no fresh declaration is needed in later cases. The Court can still revisit the point and, with reasons, overrule its earlier view.

He quotes Brown CJ of Nigeria on the Indian model: Art 13 itself declares inconsistent laws void, and the court's task is only to find the inconsistency; its declaration reaffirms what the Constitution has already said.

Keep the limits in view

Art 13 does not invalidate a whole statute automatically. Only the inconsistent part is void, and whether the rest survives depends on the doctrine of severability (see chapter B5).

sections.title: Rights that impose duties on the State
sections.html:
Basu gathers some cases showing that Art 13 is not only negative. Where a fundamental right exists (e.g. to trade on the street), the State has a corresponding duty to regulate its exercise; inaction that defeats the right can itself be corrected by the Court. And where an order is found arbitrary and violative of a fundamental right, hardship caused by quashing it is no reason to let the breach stand.

He also classifies the limits Part III imposes on the State:

  • Express limits (stated in the text, e.g. Art 14's "The State shall not deny…") and implied limits (e.g. a legislature cannot abdicate its essential legislative function).
  • Direct limits — positive prohibitions such as Arts 14, 15, 16(2), 17, 18(1), 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 27, 28, 29(2), 30(2).
  • Indirect limits — rights stated as guarantees rather than prohibitions, such as Arts 16(1), 19, 25(1), 26, 29(1), 30, 32. They bind the State just as firmly; the injunction flows from the guarantee itself.

ddbu.title: Clause (1) — pre-Constitution laws and the doctrine of eclipse
ddbu.trail: Non-retrospectivity, what "void" means for existing laws, and when a shadowed law revives

sections.title: Part III is prospective
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Fundamental rights did not exist before 26 January 1950. So a pre-Constitution law can become inconsistent with them only from that date. Art 13(1) is wholly prospective: it does not reach back to undo what was done earlier.

The leading authority is Keshavan Madhava Menon v. State of Bombay (1951). A prosecution under the Indian Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931 begun before the Constitution could continue after it, even assuming the Act was inconsistent with Art 19(1)(a). Every statute is presumed prospective unless it says otherwise, and nothing in Art 13(1) suggests retrospective effect.

Basu draws three consequences:

  1. Legislative competence is judged by the Constitution as it stood when the Act was made, unless a constitutional amendment is itself retrospective.
  2. A person may still be prosecuted after 1950 for a pre-1950 offence under a law that is now inconsistent with Part III — but the procedure used after 1950 must itself satisfy the Constitution (Lachmandas v. State of Bombay, (1952) SCR 710; Habeeb Mohammad v. State of Hyderabad, AIR 1953 SC 287).
  3. An order that became final before 1950 cannot be attacked for violating a fundamental right, and rights concluded or extinguished under a valid pre-1950 law cannot be reopened (Nabhirajiah v. State of Mysore, (1951) SCR 744; Pannalal v. UOI, AIR 1957 SC 397).

Two qualifications:

  • If a pre-1950 order inflicts a continuing deprivation from day to day, it becomes void from 26 January 1950 to the extent it collides with a right (Santisarup v. UOI, AIR 1955 SC 624, where both a pre-Constitution U.P. order and a post-Constitution Central order taking away management of a firm were struck down under Art 19(1)(f)). This applies only where the old order was itself invalid under the law then in force (Jagadguru v. Commr., H.R.E., (1964) 8 SCR 252).
  • A pre-Constitution statute enforced after 1950 may be attacked through the executive action taken under it, without challenging the statute itself (Zila Parishad v. K.S. Mills, AIR 1968 SC 98).

sections.title: "Void to the extent of inconsistency" — not repealed
sections.html:
The second big idea of clause (1): an inconsistent existing law is not wiped off the statute book. In Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P. (1954) and Keshavan, the Court put it this way:

  • the law survives for past transactions and rights and liabilities accrued before 1950;
  • it survives after 1950 against persons who hold no such fundamental right (e.g. non-citizens, for rights under Art 19);
  • it becomes ineffective only against those who hold the right, and only so far as it stands in the way of exercising it.

K.K. Poonacha v. State of Karnataka, (2010) 9 SCC 671 restated the point: Art 13(1) did not make inconsistent existing laws void ab initio; it made them ineffective from the commencement of the Constitution in relation to the exercise of fundamental rights.

Basu also notes a modern twist from John Vallamattom v. UOI, AIR 2003 SC 2902 (s. 118, Indian Succession Act struck down under Art 14): a law that was valid when made can become unconstitutional with time, once the purpose that justified it has lost all significance.

sections.title: The doctrine of eclipse
sections.html:
The doctrine in one sentence

A pre-Constitution law that clashes with a fundamental right is not dead but eclipsed: it lies dormant against rights-holders, and if the shadow is lifted (by amending the right), the law revives automatically, without re-enactment.

The phrase is Das ACJ's in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955). The C.P. and Berar Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1947 let the State exclude private operators from motor transport. After 1950 that clashed with Art 19(1)(g) read with the original Art 19(6). The First Amendment (1951) widened Art 19(6) to permit State monopolies. Das ACJ held that the Act had been "eclipsed, for the time being, by the fundamental right"; the amendment "removed the shadow" and the Act became enforceable again from the date of the amendment.

Conditions, as Basu states them:

  • the law must have been valid when enacted (i.e. pre-1950, competent legislature);
  • its later infirmity must come from a supervening event — the arrival of Part III;
  • the shadow must be removed by amendment of the Constitution; and
  • revival runs from the date of the amendment, not earlier, unless the amendment is retrospective.
Case

Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of M.P. (1955)

(1955) 2 SCR 589 · Constitution Bench

Facts

A 1947 Act authorised the State to take over motor transport to the exclusion of private operators. After 26 January 1950 this clashed with Art 19(1)(g); the First Amendment (1951) then expressly permitted State monopolies under Art 19(6).

Held

The Act was not dead. It had been eclipsed by the fundamental right and revived when the First Amendment removed the shadow.

Principle

Doctrine of eclipse — for pre-Constitution laws under Art 13(1).

sections.title: Eclipse does not apply to post-Constitution laws
sections.html:
The contrast with clause (2) is the exam point. A post-1950 law that breaches Part III was made in the teeth of an express prohibition. It is still-born: void from birth, so there is nothing to revive. A later constitutional amendment cannot breathe life into it; the legislature must re-enact it (Deep Chand v. State of U.P. (1959); Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of U.P., AIR 1963 SC 1019). The same goes for an attempt to cure such a law by amending the statute (P.L. Mehra v. D.K. Khanna, AIR 1972 Del 1).

Basu notes two contrary pulls:

  • H.M. Seervai argued that eclipse applies to both pre- and post-Constitution laws, relying on State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills (1974). On his view, a law that violates a constitutional limitation (as opposed to one made without legislative competence) is unenforceable only while the limitation lasts, and operates by its own force once it is lifted.
  • Ninth Schedule inclusion under Art 31B validates a still-born post-Constitution Act retrospectively from its enactment, without re-enactment (L. Jagannath v. Authorised Officer, AIR 1972 SC 425, 7 judges). That is a result of the express words of Art 31B, not of the doctrine of eclipse.

Common slip

Do not write that the First Amendment "validated" the Act in Bhikaji from 1947 or 1950. It became enforceable only from the date the amendment came into force (18 June 1951). And do not apply Bhikaji to a post-1950 Act: Deep Chand and Mahendra Lal Jaini say such a law is void ab initio.

And do not apply Bhikaji to a post-1950 Act: Deep Chand and Mahendra Lal Jaini say such a law is void ab initio .

sections.title: Legislative incompetence vs breach of a limitation
sections.html:
Basu reproduces the distinction drawn by Venkatarama Aiyar J in M.P.V. Sundararamier v. State of A.P., AIR 1958 SC 468, and Seervai's summary of it:

  1. A law made without legislative competence (e.g. a State law on a List I subject) is a nullity from the start and is not revived if competence is later conferred.
  2. A law within competence but violating a constitutional limitation is unenforceable while the limitation stands; when the limitation is removed it can operate without re-enactment.
  3. A court's declaration of unconstitutionality does not repeal or amend the law — that is a legislative function.
  4. "Void" in Art 13 does not mean "repealed"; the law is void only to the extent of the repugnancy.

Basu himself rejects proposition 2 for post-Constitution laws (chapter B4). The Supreme Court in Mahendra Lal Jaini sided with him: Part III is as much a limit on power as the Seventh Schedule.

ddbu.title: Clause (2) — the prohibition on post-Constitution laws
ddbu.trail: "The State shall not make any law", how the Court tests infringement, and the grounds on which a law can and cannot fall

sections.title: A prohibition on power, not just a rule of voidness
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Clause (2) opens with an injunction — "The State shall not make any law…" — and only then states the consequence. Because Art 245 makes legislative power "subject to the provisions of this Constitution", the injunction cuts down the power itself. A post-Constitution law that breaches Part III is therefore void ab initio (still-born), unlike an existing law under clause (1).

The Supreme Court put the contrast this way in State of U.P. v. Nooh, (1957) SCR 595 and Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of U.P., AIR 1963 SC 1019: clause (1) recognises existing laws and then declares them void to the extent of inconsistency; clause (2) forbids the State to make an infringing law at all. The prohibition makes the State as incompetent to abridge fundamental rights as it would be to legislate outside its Seventh Schedule list. And the contravention happens once, at enactment; it is not a continuing matter.

Practical results Basu lists:

  • Validity is judged as at the date of enactment. A later constitutional amendment does not cure the law unless the amendment is expressly retrospective (Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v. State of Bombay, (1955) 1 SCR 613; State of M.P. v. Bharat Singh, AIR 1966 SC 1170).
  • Convictions under such a law must be set aside, and anything done under it, whether complete or pending, is illegal (Janardan Reddy v. State of Hyderabad, [1951] SCR 344).
  • A statute once struck down can come back only through a constitutional amendment that sanctions it or a fresh, modified enactment that complies (UOI v. Raghubir Singh, AIR 1989 SC 1933).

sections.title: "The State shall not make any law"
sections.html:
• "Make any law" covers every post-1950 enactment, including amendments to existing laws. Even an amendment to an Act already placed in the Ninth Schedule must independently satisfy Part III (Sri Ram Ramnarain Medhi v. State of Bombay, AIR 1959 SC 459).
  • The words bite only once a Bill becomes law. A court cannot stop a legislature from passing a Bill on the ground that it will be unconstitutional, and no writ of prohibition lies against the legislature (Chotey Lal v. State of U.P., AIR 1951 All 228). This is the "ripeness" idea: review is of enacted law, at the instance of someone actually aggrieved.
  • "State" carries the Art 12 meaning, so the limit binds the legislature, the executive, instrumentalities and agencies of the State, and quasi-judicial bodies. Sovereign immunity is no defence to a public-law claim for breach of a fundamental right (Consumer Education & Research Centre v. UOI, (1995) 3 SCC 42).
  • Das J in A.K. Gopalan identified two principal limits on legislative power: the law must be within competence (Arts 245–246) and must not take away or abridge Part III rights.

sections.title: How the Court decides whether a law infringes a right
sections.html:
Basu gathers the tests the Court applies before declaring inconsistency or contravention:

  1. Real effect, not label. The Court looks at the actual impact of the law on the right (In re Kerala Education Bill, AIR 1958 SC 956). In Rashid Ahmed v. Municipal Board, Kairana, (1950) SCR 566, a bye-law required permission to open a wholesale market but no bye-law provided for granting permission; the "regulation" was in substance a total prohibition of business under Art 19(1)(g).
  2. Direct and inevitable effect. Direct consequences count; remote or incidental effects do not (Express Newspapers v. UOI, (1959) SCR 12; Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1967 SC 1).
  3. Substance over form. A legislature cannot achieve indirectly what it is forbidden to do directly; the Court looks behind names and forms to the true character of the law (Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spinning Co., (1954) SCR 674).
  4. The means matter, not only the object. A laudable object reached by means that offend a right still fails. In State of Bombay v. Bombay Education Society, (1955) 1 SCR 568, promoting Hindi under Art 351 could not justify refusing admission to English-medium schools to pupils whose mother tongue was not English, because Art 29(2) forbids denial of admission on the ground of language.

From "object and form" to "effect"

The shift worth remembering

Gopalan (1950) looked at the object and form of State action and treated each Article as a separate code. R.C. Cooper v. UOI (1970) rejected that: the test is the direct operation of the law on the right, judged by its effect on the individual. Maneka Gandhi v. UOI (1978) refined it into the "direct and inevitable effect" test.

  • In R.C. Cooper (the Bank Nationalisation case) the majority held that "pith and substance" and the "object of the legislation" are irrelevant to whether a fundamental right is infringed; "direct" refers to the quality of the effect, not the subject-matter. Mathew J's dissenting note was that pith and substance still helps decide whether a law is merely regulatory.
  • In Maneka Gandhi, Bhagwati J added "inevitable": if the effect on the right is direct and inevitable, the State must be taken to have intended it. Basu calls this the doctrine of "intended or real effect".
  • Directness is measured against the protected activity. If the State restricts an activity that is itself a fundamental right, the effect is direct. If it restricts something that is not a fundamental right, any knock-on effect on a right is indirect. These are working formulas, not fixed rules (Peerless General Finance v. RBI, AIR 1992 SC 1033).

sections.title: Grounds on which a law can fall — and cannot
sections.html:
Can be struck down for

  1. Contravening a fundamental right in Part III.

  2. Lack of legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule.

  3. Breaching another mandatory limitation in the Constitution, e.g. Art 301 (freedom of trade).

  4. A State law operating outside the State's territory.

  5. Excessive delegation or abdication of the essential legislative function.

Cannot be struck down because

  1. The law-maker did not apply its mind or had an improper motive (K. Nagaraj v. State of A.P., AIR 1985 SC 551; Rehman Shagoo v. State of J&K, AIR 1960 SC 1).

  2. It breaches a constitutional limitation that did not exist when it was made (R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills, AIR 1977 SC 2279).

  3. It conflicts with a Directive Principle in Part IV (Art 37).

  4. It is merely harsh, or the Court disagrees with its wisdom.

Art 13 targets only the first of these grounds. It applies when (a) the law-maker is "State" under Art 12, (b) the measure is "law" under Art 13(3)(a), and (c) the right infringed is in Part III.

Basu collects the modern restatement from State of M.P. v. Rakesh Kohli, AIR 2012 SC 2351:

  • a statute is presumed constitutional;
  • it can be struck down only for lack of competence or violation of Part III or another constitutional provision;
  • calling it "arbitrary" or "irrational" is not enough without pointing to a constitutional infirmity;
  • the Court is not concerned with the wisdom or justice of the law;
  • hardship is irrelevant to the validity of fiscal or economic legislation, and the legislature has wider latitude in tax classification.

He adds that a law cannot be voided because a judge thinks it offends the "spirit" of the Constitution or some ideal of democracy not written into it (Special Reference No. 1 of 2012 (Natural Resources Allocation); State of A.P. v. McDowell, (1996) 3 SCC 709). Equality under Arts 14 and 16 must be patently infringed (K.B. Nagur v. UOI, (2012) 4 SCC 483).

Tension to note in an answer

Some passages Basu collects (e.g. State of T.N. v. K. Shyam Sundar, (2011) 8 SCC 737) say Art 14 "springs into action" against arbitrary legislation, while McDowell and Rakesh Kohli say arbitrariness alone cannot strike down a statute. After this edition, Shayara Bano v. UOI (2017) recognised "manifest arbitrariness" as a ground for striking down legislation under Art 14, and later benches (e.g. Joseph Shine v. UOI, 2018) applied it. Cite those if the question is about current law.

sections.title: Policy decisions
sections.html: The Court does not review the wisdom of legislative or governmental policy. It will intervene only where a policy is unconstitutional, contrary to statute, outside the delegated power, or arbitrary in the Wednesbury sense. Basu cites the grounds summarised in Sivamurthy v. State of A.P., (2008) 13 SCC 730, and Brij Mohan Lal v. UOI, (2012) 6 SCC 502 (decision to wind up fast-track courts struck down as interfering with speedy trial under Art 21 and with judicial independence). A policy may be withdrawn as freely as it was made, unless the withdrawal is mala fide or an abuse of power.

ddbu.title: "Shall be void" — still-born laws, relative voidness and non-citizens
ddbu.trail: Venkatarama Aiyar J's thesis, its rejection in Mahendra Lal Jaini, and the Ambica Mills exceptions

sections.title: What "void" means here
sections.html:
"Void" ordinarily means without legal force, incapable of being cured. Basu's points on how the word works in Art 13:

  • A void law confers no rights and imposes no duties; contracts resting on it fail and no one can be punished for disobeying it. Basu quotes Cooley's classic statement of this, adopted in Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v. State of Bombay (1955).
  • In Behram, Mahajan CJ said the void part should be treated as "notionally obliterated" from the section. Seervai criticised the phrase: Keshavan had held that "void" does not mean "repealed", so nothing is obliterated, even notionally. A court's declaration does not amend the statute.
  • A law is not treated as void until a court declares it so, on the application of someone who holds the right (State of Madras v. V.G. Row, (1952) SCR 597).
  • Once declared, invalidity dates from 26 January 1950 for a pre-Constitution law and from enactment for a post-Constitution law (Mahendra Lal Jaini).
  • "Void" is a relative word: in Ambica Mills the Court said that a non-citizen cannot rely on the voidness of a law that infringes only citizens' rights. Voidness runs against persons, not in the air.

sections.title: Venkatarama Aiyar J's thesis: "relatively void"
sections.html:
The controversy in brief

Aiyar J (dissenting in Behram, 1955; again in Sundararamier, 1958): a law outside legislative competence is absolutely void, but a law within competence that breaches a fundamental right is only unenforceable. So (a) it revives if the right is later amended away, and (b) the person protected by the right can waive the objection.

Majority (Mahajan CJ in Behram; Deep Chand, 1959; unanimous Constitution Bench in Mahendra Lal Jaini, 1963): Part III limits the power itself. A post-Constitution law that breaches it is as void as one made without competence. No revival, no waiver.

Mahajan CJ's reasoning in Behram: when a written fundamental law restricts law-making power, anything enacted against it is in excess of authority. Arts 245–246 confer power subject-wise; Art 13(2) qualifies that power. Lack of competence and breach of Part III are "two aspects of want of legislative power".

sections.title: Basu's critique of the "academician" (Seervai)
sections.html:
Even after Mahendra, Seervai defended Aiyar J's distinction: a legislature with power can legislate conditionally on a limitation being lifted; one without power cannot legislate at all. Basu answers on three levels:

  1. The American authority was misread. Aiyar J relied on Wilkerson v. Rahrer, 140 US 545 (1891). There, an 1889 Kansas liquor-prohibition law could not reach liquor in its "original packages" from other States because of Leisy v. Hardin (1890). Congress then passed the Wilson Act (1890) subjecting such liquor to State police power, and the Kansas law was enforced without re-enactment. Basu's point: that was a concurrent field, where State power exists until Congress occupies the field. Lifting the federal bar simply let an existing power operate. It says nothing about laws offending the Bill of Rights, and no American case holds such a law revives when the right is amended.
  2. Principle. In a written Constitution with judicial review, every justiciable, mandatory limitation is part of the superior law. A law contravening it is a nullity, whether the limitation is a fundamental right or another clause such as Art 286 (sales tax) or Art 301 (trade). The Court has struck down laws for breaching those clauses without any need for Art 13 (Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar, (1955) 2 SCR 603; District Collector v. Ibrahim, AIR 1970 SC 1275).
  3. Partial invalidity is no different. Aiyar J's further view in Sundararamier — that an unconstitutional part of a statute stays on the book and revives when the bar goes — was tied to the old Art 286(2), under which States lacked power until Parliament legislated. It does not carry over to Part III.
Case

Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of U.P. (1963)

AIR 1963 SC 1019 · unanimous Constitution Bench

Facts

The U.P. Land Tenures (Regulation of Transfers) Act, 1952 annulled transfers by intermediaries and their tenants without compensation. Under Art 31(2) as it stood, read with Subodh Gopal (1954), that was unconstitutional. The State argued the Fourth Amendment (1955), which inserted Art 31(2A), had since cured it.

Held

The Fourth Amendment was not retrospective. The 1952 Act was judged by the Constitution as it stood when the Act was passed, and was void.

Principle

A post-Constitution law that contravenes Art 13(2) is void ab initio — "as void as" a law passed without competence. The doctrine of eclipse does not apply to it.

Basu's conclusion: for post-Constitution laws, there is no room for eclipse or "relative" voidness. That such a law physically remains on the statute book and can be amended or repealed is no objection; the same is true of a law struck down for lack of competence.

sections.title: Does an unconstitutional law still bind non-citizens?
sections.html:
Under clause (1)

Yes. Keshavan held that an existing law inconsistent with a citizens-only right (e.g. Art 19) becomes void only for citizens; it continues to operate against non-citizens. C.R.H. Readymoney Ltd. v. State of Bombay, AIR 1958 Bom 181 drew the same line.

Under clause (2) — the general rule

Das CJ in Bhikaji had suggested the same partial survival applied to future laws too. The majority in Deep Chand (1959) disagreed, and Mahendra confirmed: a post-Constitution law that breaches Part III is dead for all purposes. Wanchoo J called partial validity against non-citizens "hypothetical and pedantic".

The exceptions — Jagannath and Ambica Mills

  • L. Jagannath v. Authorised Officer, AIR 1972 SC 425 (7 judges): once an Act is placed in the Ninth Schedule it is valid notwithstanding earlier invalidity; the Court found it unnecessary to scrutinise the "still-born" line of cases or the doctrine of eclipse.
  • State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills (1974, Constitution Bench, Mathew J): provisions of a post-Constitution labour welfare law, requiring employers to pay unclaimed wages into a welfare fund, were void as violating citizens' rights under Art 19(1)(f). Could a company (not a citizen) treat them as non-existent?
Case

State of Gujarat v. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974)

AIR 1974 SC 1300 · (1974) 4 SCC 656 · Constitution Bench

Facts

Provisions of a post-Constitution labour welfare law were void as infringing citizens' Art 19(1)(f) rights. A company, which has no Art 19 rights, relied on that voidness.

Held

The law was void only as against those whose rights it infringed. It remained operative against non-citizens such as the company, which could still challenge it under Art 14 (a right of "any person").

Principle

"Void" in Art 13(2) means void as against persons whose fundamental rights are abridged, not void in rem. The same scheme runs through both clauses. Mahendra states the general rule; it is subject to exceptions.

Mathew J's reasoning: if a pre-Constitution law can survive against non-citizens under clause (1), there is no principled reason why a post-Constitution law cannot, when "void" bears the same meaning in both clauses. Rights inhere in persons; voidness extends only as far as the contravention. He accepted that a statute declared unconstitutional is generally a nullity for all purposes, but said that is "neither universally nor absolutely true" — even an unconstitutional statute is an "operative fact" until declared invalid.

Basu's reconciliation:

  • Ambica Mills (a Constitution Bench) could not overrule Mahendra (also a Constitution Bench), and Jagannath did not overrule it either.
  • So the general rule remains: a post-Constitution law breaching Part III is still-born. It is read with the exceptions Ambica Mills identified — chiefly that its voidness does not extend to persons who hold no such right.
  • Basu reads Ambica Mills as a pragmatic move away from "absolute nullity" towards a realistic reading of Art 13.

Write it this way

"A post-Constitution law that contravenes Part III is void ab initio (Deep Chand; Mahendra Lal Jaini), but only as against those whose rights it infringes; it remains operative against persons who do not hold the right (Ambica Mills)." That one sentence states both cases correctly.

sections.title: Laws that are — and are not — subject to Art 13(2)
sections.html:
Subject to it: every law made under Arts 245–246, including taxing statutes (Hari Krishna Bhargav v. UOI, AIR 1966 SC 619) and laws made under specific constitutional provisions such as Arts 105(3), 194(3) and 309.

Outside it:

  • a Presidential order under Art 359(1) suspending enforcement of rights during an Emergency is not "law" within Art 13(2) (Mohd. Yaqub v. State of J&K, AIR 1968 SC 765, 7 judges, departing from Ghulam Sarwar v. UOI, AIR 1967 SC 1334). The reason: a power conferred by a specific Article that stands on an equal footing with Art 13 cannot be read as subject to it;
  • laws protected by Arts 31A, 31B (Ninth Schedule) and 31C, which the Constitution itself shields;
  • constitutional amendments under Art 368, by virtue of clause (4) (chapter B6).

ddbu.title: Severability and reading down
ddbu.trail: "To the extent of the inconsistency": when the bad part can be cut out, when the whole law falls, and when the Court narrows the law instead

sections.title: The idea
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Art 13 voids a law only "to the extent of" the inconsistency or contravention. If the offending provision can be separated, only it goes; the rest stands. The test is the legislature's intention: would it have enacted the valid part had it known the rest was invalid? If the two are inseparable, or what remains is a different law, the whole falls.

Severability rests on a presumed intention of the legislature that part-invalidity should not sink the whole. Basu calls it the common-law ultra vires rule imported into constitutional law, founded in equity and prudence: courts save what is sound.

The classic Commonwealth formulation is the Privy Council's in A.G. for Alberta v. A.G. for Canada (1947): is what remains so inextricably bound up with the invalid part that it cannot independently survive, or, on a fair review of the whole, can it be assumed the legislature would have enacted what survives without the invalid part?

sections.title: The R.M.D.C. principles
sections.html:
The Supreme Court's fullest statement is in R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. UOI (1957), restated in Corporation of Calcutta v. Calcutta Tramways Co., AIR 1964 SC 1279:

  1. Intention decides. Would the legislature have enacted the valid part if it had known the rest was invalid?
  2. Inextricably mixed valid and invalid provisions fall together. If, after striking out the invalid part, what remains is a complete code, it is upheld.
  3. Even distinct valid provisions fall if they form part of a single scheme meant to operate as a whole.
  4. If what is left is so thin and truncated that it is in substance a different law from what the legislature passed, it falls.
  5. Substance, not form: it does not matter whether valid and invalid parts sit in the same section or different sections.
  6. If what remains cannot be enforced without rewriting, the whole must go — otherwise the Court would be legislating.
  7. The legislative history, object, title and preamble may be used to find the intention.

On evidence of intention: legislative history is admissible, but the Statement of Objects and Reasons, the mover's speech and floor debates are not (Jai Lal v. Delhi Administration, AIR 1962 SC 1781).

Case

R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla v. UOI (1957)

AIR 1957 SC 628 · Constitution Bench

Facts

The Prize Competitions Act, 1955 defined "prize competition" widely enough to cover both competitions of skill (protected trade under Art 19(1)(g)) and gambling (not protected).

Held

Parliament's real target was gambling, and the two classes were clearly distinguishable. The Act was read as applying only to gambling competitions and upheld to that extent.

Principle

Severability can operate on application, not only on text — the Court confined a single definition to the class Parliament could validly regulate.

sections.title: Two kinds of severability
sections.html:
Basu (following Seervai) distinguishes:

  1. Textual severance. A distinct offending provision is struck out and the rest upheld.
  2. Severability in application or enforcement. Where the impugned provision is one indivisible whole (often a definition) that covers distinct classes, some within and some outside the permitted field, the Court restrains its enforcement against the protected class. R.M.D.C. is the model; Ambica Mills applied the same idea to persons — the law was valid against non-citizens though void against citizens.

Seervai's gloss: in the second type it would be self-contradictory to say there both was and was not power to enact one indivisible law. Better to say the power existed but, as regards certain persons, was exercised in disregard of a constitutional limitation, so the law cannot be enforced against them.

The Federal Court used a version of this in Re Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, AIR 1941 FC 72. The Central Act spoke of "property" generally, but the Centre had no power over agricultural land (a provincial subject). Presuming the legislature meant to act within its powers, the Court read "property" as property other than agricultural land and upheld the Act. It warned, though, that if narrowing general words leaves an Act with "nothing or next to nothing", or an Act different in kind, the whole must fall.

sections.title: Wide language that overreaches: the whole falls
sections.html:
The Romesh Thappar rule

Where a law authorises restrictions in language wide enough to cover restrictions both within and outside the constitutionally permissible limits, it cannot be upheld even for its valid applications. So long as it might be applied to unconstitutional purposes, it is wholly void.

  • Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950): a ban on a journal "for securing the public safety or the maintenance of public order" was not confined to the narrow grounds then permitted by Art 19(2), and could not be saved by reading it down.
  • Chintaman Rao v. State of M.P. (1950): to keep agricultural labour available during the season, the law let the State forbid everyone in notified areas from making bidis — including women, children and the infirm who could never do farm work. The restriction exceeded what Art 19(6) permits and the whole provision fell; it could not be upheld for able-bodied workers alone.

But where the legislature itself divided the subject into categories, the Court can sever by category. In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), the prohibition on "liquor" was void as to medicinal and toilet preparations containing alcohol, but valid as to other liquor, because the Act treated these as separate sub-categories.

Basu also lists US illustrations: a ticket-reseller's conviction for trading without a licence stood even though the resale price-fixing clause was unconstitutional; but where a tax on admitting foreign corporations and a tax on their capital stock were interdependent, the fall of one took the other. The Court cannot "make a new law" by severance (United States v. Reese, 92 US 214 (1876)).

sections.title: Severance can widen a law
sections.html:
There is no rule that severance may only narrow a statute. In D.S. Nakara v. UOI (1983), the Court struck out the cut-off date in a liberalised pension scheme, which had the effect of extending the benefit to all pensioners. Conversely, where invalid sections are bound up with the rest in a single scheme, the whole Act goes (A.N. Parasuraman v. State of T.N., AIR 1990 SC 40).

Modern examples Basu adds:

  • Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu, AIR 1993 SC 412: severability applies even to constitutional amendments — para 7 of the Tenth Schedule was severed from the rest of the anti-defection law.
  • Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. UOI, (2008) 6 SCC 1: asking whether Parliament would have wanted OBC reservation in education to fail altogether if the creamy layer were excluded, the Court severed the creamy-layer inclusion and upheld the rest.
  • Offshore Holdings v. Bangalore Development Authority, (2011) 3 SCC 139: a State law repugnant to a Central law is void only to the extent of repugnancy; severability applies.
  • The doctrine applies to administrative and quasi-judicial orders too.

sections.title: Reading down
sections.html:
Before striking down, the Court should try to read the provision down to a constitutional meaning (Rev. Mark Netto v. State of Kerala, AIR 1979 SC 83; Punjab Dairy Development Board v. Cepham Milk Specialities, AIR 2004 SC 4466). Where a literal reading would make the provision unconstitutional, the Court may depart from it. If no saving construction is possible, the provision must be struck down. The Court may also declare invalidity prospectively to avoid disruption.

Basu notes the English shift from "textual" to "substantial" severability (DPP v. Hutchinson, [1990] 2 AC 783 (HL)): the text may even be modified to achieve severance, but only if that does not change the substantial purpose and effect of the provision.

Don't blur the two

Severance removes the bad part. Reading down keeps the words but narrows their meaning. Romesh Thappar shows the limit of both: a court will not rewrite an over-broad restriction to make it fit Art 19(2).

ddbu.title: Clauses (3) and (4) — "law", "laws in force" and constitutional amendments
ddbu.trail: What counts as law for Art 13, the force-of-law test, custom and personal law, and why amendments are outside

sections.title: "Unless the context otherwise requires"
sections.html:
These opening words of clause (3) do real work:

  • they let custom and usage count as "law" for clause (1) (existing laws), even though a legislature cannot "make" a custom under clause (2);
  • they were also used to argue that constitutional amendments fall outside "law" — the point later made express by clause (4).

sections.title: "Law" — clause (3)(a)
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

"Law" in Art 13 is wider than legislation. It includes Ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and custom or usage — so long as the measure has the force of law. It does not include the Constitution itself, constitutional amendments, or purely administrative instructions.

What Basu shows the courts have treated as "law":

  • Subordinate legislation made under a statute (Bidi Supply Co. v. UOI, (1956) SCR 267).
  • Orders and notifications under a statute, even where the parent statute is valid or unchallenged (Ram Krishna Dalmia v. S.R. Tendolkar, AIR 1958 SC 538). An order must be legislative rather than executive in character to qualify (Edward Mills v. State of Ajmer, AIR 1955 SC 25).
  • A Government resolution fixing dearness allowance under r. 44 of the Fundamental Rules (State of M.P. v. Mandawar, AIR 1954 SC 493).
  • Custom — e.g. a custom of hereditary succession to village offices, void under Art 16(1) (Dasaratha Rama Rao v. State of A.P., AIR 1961 SC 564); a custom of pre-emption based on vicinage (Sant Ram v. Labh Singh, AIR 1965 SC 314).
  • A scheme under the Motor Vehicles Act (Narayanappa v. State of Mysore, AIR 1960 SC 1073).
  • Regulations of statutory corporations such as LIC; bye-laws of public authorities; RBI circulars issued under the Banking Regulation Act (Sudhir Shantilal Mehta v. CBI, (2009) 8 SCC 1); Bombay Stock Exchange bye-laws (Mahesh Ratilal Shah v. UOI, AIR 2010 SC 676).
  • A firman of a former Ruler, which was his command and therefore law (State of Punjab v. Sukhjit Singh, (1993) 3 SCC 459). But a Ruler's executive order, or a grant founded on agreement, is not law — though a grant inconsistent with a fundamental right is still void.

What is not "law" for Art 13:

  • the Constitution itself (R.S. Nayak v. A.R. Antulay, AIR 1984 SC 684);
  • constitutional amendments (Kesavananda Bharati, by majority; now cl. (4));
  • executive or administrative instructions without statutory backing — the U.P. Legal Remembrancer's Manual (State of U.P. v. Johri Mal, AIR 2004 SC 3800); the Flag Code (UOI v. Naveen Jindal, AIR 2004 SC 1559); a circular treating converted members of Scheduled Tribes as STs (State of Kerala v. Chandramohanan, AIR 2004 SC 1672);
  • bye-laws of a co-operative society, which are only a contract among members (Zoroastrian Co-op. Housing Society v. District Registrar, AIR 2005 SC 2306; Co-op. Central Bank v. Industrial Tribunal, AIR 1970 SC 245);
  • a treaty as such (Kunga Nima Lepcha v. State of Sikkim, AIR 2006 Sikkim 1);
  • judicial decisions — law declared under Arts 141–142 is not "law" under Art 13(2), so an overruled decision does not become void ab initio (Ashok Kumar Gupta v. State of U.P., (1997) 5 SCC 201).
Administrative action is still reviewable

That an executive instruction is not "law" under Art 13(3) does not put it beyond challenge. Any act of the "State" under Art 12 that infringes a fundamental right is void; Art 13 was inserted only ex abundanti cautela (Gopalan). Departmental orders have been struck down under Art 29 and Art 30 on that basis (State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, 1951; State of Bombay v. Bombay Education Society, 1955).

sections.title: "Having the force of law"
sections.html:
The Constitution does not define the phrase, so Basu turns to jurisprudence. Holland: law is a general rule of external conduct enforced by a sovereign political authority. Salmond: law is the body of principles recognised and applied by the State in the administration of justice. In a modern State, enforcement means enforcement by the courts. So the test is practical: would the courts enforce this rule? If yes, it has the force of law, whatever it is called.

Basu notes that the related question — how far constitutional conventions have the force of law — was examined by the nine-judge bench in S.C. Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. UOI, AIR 1994 SC 268.

sections.title: Personal law
sections.html:
Whether uncodified personal law (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi) is "law" or "law in force" under Art 13 has been contested:

  • No: State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali, AIR 1952 Bom 84 held that personal law is not "law in force"; Krishna Singh v. Mathura Ahir, AIR 1980 SC 707 said Part III does not touch personal law; Ahmedabad Women Action Group v. UOI, (1997) 3 SCC 573 declined to test Muslim personal law on polygamy and unilateral talaq, treating it as a matter for the legislature; P.E. Mathew v. UOI, AIR 1999 Ker 345 followed.
  • Doubts: the Bombay High Court in Re Amina, AIR 1992 Bom 214 questioned Narasu in light of Dasaratha Rama Rao and Sant Ram, which treat custom and usage as "law in force".
  • Commentators: Seervai argued there is no difference between "existing law" and "laws in force", and since custom, usage and statute are inextricably mixed in personal law, personal law must be "law in force" (Entry 5, List III also treats it as law Parliament can alter). M.P. Jain read the courts' reluctance as judicial policy — leaving reform to the legislature.
  • A Kerala Full Bench (Amini E.J. v. UOI, AIR 1995 Ker 252) held that once a personal-law rule is codified in a statute, it must satisfy Part III even if religiously based.

(Sabarimala) (2018), a judge questioned Narasu. Narasu has not been formally overruled; cite it with that caution.

sections.title: "Laws in force" — clause (3)(b)
sections.html:
• Defined in the same words as Explanation I to Art 372, and there is no material difference from "existing law" in Art 366(10) (Edward Mills).
  • The definition is inclusive: it covers Indian statutes, pre-1950 British statutes still applying to India (most were repealed in 1960), common-law rules applied in India, subordinate legislation, custom and usage.
  • The closing words ("notwithstanding that any such law… may not be then in operation…") bring in any law on the statute book on 26 January 1950, even if not yet brought into force in some or all areas.

sections.title: Clause (4) — constitutional amendments
sections.html:
The sequence to know

  1. Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): an amendment under Art 368 is not "law" under Art 13(2).

  2. Golak Nath (1967): by 6:5, it is "law", so Parliament cannot amend Part III to take away or abridge rights.

  3. 24th Amendment (1971): inserted Art 13(4) and Art 368(3): Art 13 does not apply to amendments under Art 368. In force from 5 November 1971.

  4. Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges): upheld the 24th Amendment and overruled Golak Nath, but held that the basic structure cannot be destroyed by amendment.

  5. 42nd Amendment (1976): inserted Art 368(4)–(5) to bar all judicial review of amendments. Minerva Mills (1980) struck these down as destroying a basic feature (limited amending power and judicial review).

Cases: Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. UOI; Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan; I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab; Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala; Minerva Mills v. UOI.

So an amendment can now be challenged only on two grounds:

  1. Procedural — it was not passed according to Art 368 (Raghunathrao Ganpatrao v. UOI, AIR 1993 SC 1267; R.C. Poudyal v. UOI, 1994 Supp (1) SCC 324);
  2. Substantive — it damages or destroys the basic structure. Under Waman Rao v. UOI (1981), this test applies only to amendments made after 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda judgment.

Basu also notes that individual rights within Part III may themselves be basic features — e.g. Art 14 and Art 32 — even though Part III as such is not immune from amendment.

Two slips in the source text

  1. One passage says the question whether an amendment is "law" under Art 13 was "finally decided in the affirmative". That is backwards: Golak Nath answered yes, but Kesavananda overruled it and the 24th Amendment settled the answer as no.

  2. Kesavananda is described as a "Full Bench". It was a 13-judge bench, the largest the Court has sat.

ddbu.title: Judicial review — meaning, foundations and scope
ddbu.trail: What judicial review is, how the US invented it and India wrote it down, why it is narrower here, and why it is a basic feature

sections.title: What "judicial review" means
sections.html:
In ordinary legal usage "review" means a higher court revising a lower court's decision. That sense has no special constitutional importance. In public law — in the USA and India, not England — it has a technical meaning: the power of the courts to declare a law or official act void because it conflicts with the Constitution.

Definitions Basu collects:

  • the power of courts, in cases actually before them, to examine legislative and executive acts and declare them void if they are prohibited by, or exceed the powers granted by, a written Constitution;
  • the judiciary's oversight of the other co-ordinate organs to keep them within constitutional limits (S.P. Sathe);
  • not an appeal from a decision, but a review of the manner in which it was made (Chief Constable of North Wales Police v. Evans, [1982] 3 All ER 141).

Three branches in India

L. Chandra Kumar v. UOI (1997) identifies three aspects of judicial review in India: (1) review of legislative action, (2) review of judicial decisions, and (3) review of administrative action.

Interpretation lies at the heart of it. Deciding whether a law is intra or ultra vires means reading the Constitution and the statute side by side. Lord Reid called the idea that judges never make law "a fairy tale". Basu sets against that Pavle Nikolic's view that a constitutional court does not write law: it only removes the injury an unconstitutional law does to the Constitution.

sections.title: Origins: limited government and the "two laws"
sections.html:
Judicial review grows from the idea of limited government and of two kinds of law, ordinary and fundamental. If there is a paramount law that is the source of all legislative authority, any ordinary law contradicting it must be void, and some organ must be able to say so.

  • England stopped at the supremacy of law and of Parliament as the sole source of law. Courts there review administrative action on the ordinary-law ground of ultra vires, but not Acts of Parliament.
  • The USA went further: a written law above the legislature itself. Basu notes that the English ultra vires doctrine inspired the American public-law version.

sections.title: The American foundation
sections.html:
The US Constitution does not mention judicial review, and the Philadelphia Convention never debated it. Hamilton argued for it in Federalist No. 78: written limits on the legislature mean nothing unless some independent body can enforce them, and that body cannot be the legislature or the executive, which would then judge their own powers. The courts are an intermediate body between people and legislature; preferring the Constitution to a statute means preferring the will of the people to that of their agents.

Marshall CJ adopted this reasoning almost word for word in Marbury v. Madison (1803): the Constitution is either a superior law unchangeable by ordinary means, or it is on a level with ordinary Acts; it is "emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is"; so a law repugnant to the Constitution is void and the courts cannot give it effect.

In United States v. Butler, 297 US 1 (1936), the Court described its task modestly: lay the Article of the Constitution beside the challenged statute and decide whether the latter squares with the former.

Basu's three criticisms of the American reasoning as a matter of pure logic:

  1. The US Constitution, unlike those of India, Ireland or Japan, has no clause declaring repugnant laws void.
  2. A written Constitution implies a paramount law, but not that the judiciary must be its guardian. France (Fourth and Fifth Republics) gave the job to a non-judicial constitutional council that rules during the legislative process.
  3. Not every part of the US Constitution is justiciable; courts cannot enforce the non-justiciable parts.

Still, judicial review is now as much part of the American system as if it had been written in.

sections.title: Other constitutions
sections.html:
• Ireland: Art 34 gives the High Court jurisdiction over the validity of laws and bars excluding such cases from Supreme Court appeal; Art 15(4) voids repugnant laws.
  • Germany: a separate Federal Constitutional Court decides constitutional questions; ordinary courts must refer them; any person may file a constitutional complaint for violation of basic rights.
  • Japan: Art 81 makes the Supreme Court the court of last resort on constitutionality; Art 98 voids contrary laws. The power has been used sparingly.
  • Bangladesh (Art 7(2), 26, 44, 102), Singapore (Art 4) and South Africa (s. 2 of the 1996 Constitution) all declare constitutional supremacy and voidness of inconsistent law.

sections.title: India: firmer footing, narrower scope
sections.html:
Basu's central thesis

Judicial review in India rests on a more solid basis than in the USA, because the Constitution provides for it expressly. But its scope is narrower, because the Indian Constitution is detailed and easy to amend.

Why firmer

  • Art 13 expressly declares inconsistent laws void; Art 254(1) does the same for repugnant State laws in the concurrent field.
  • Arts 32 and 226 give the Supreme Court and High Courts the power to enforce rights; Arts 132, 228 and 145(3) channel constitutional questions to them; Arts 141 and 144 make the Supreme Court's interpretation binding on all courts and authorities.
  • In a federal Constitution, the division of legislative power needs an umpire other than the legislatures themselves.
  • Dr Ambedkar defended writ jurisdiction against the charge that the Constitution was a "lawyer's paradise", calling it the "heart" and "soul" of the Constitution. Granville Austin describes the Constituent Assembly's view of the judiciary as an extension of the Rights and an arm of the social revolution.

Judicial review is not confined to Arts 13 and 254. It reaches any justiciable, mandatory provision of the Constitution not expressly excluded — e.g. Art 286 (sales tax), Art 301 (trade), the Seventh Schedule. In State of Rajasthan v. UOI, AIR 1977 SC 1361, the Court said the Constitution is the supreme lex; no organ is the sole judge of its own powers; the Court is the ultimate interpreter.

State of W.B. v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, AIR 2010 SC 1476 adds that the separation of powers cannot be invoked to curtail judicial review where rights under Arts 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 are at stake.

Why narrower

In the USA, the Constitution is old, brief, general and very hard to amend. The people have looked to the Supreme Court to adapt it — Bryce's "living voice of the Constitution". Cardozo explained how the open texture of "due process" and "liberty" let the Court swing from striking down minimum-wage laws to upholding them. This led to charges of a "third Chamber of the Legislature" (Laski) and the clash with Roosevelt's New Deal in the 1930s, after which the Court developed self-imposed limits.

In India:

  • the Constitution is detailed — closer to a code — leaving less room for judicial reshaping;
  • it is relatively easy to amend, so the people's representatives can correct a judicial reading they disagree with by amendment under Art 368;
  • so the ultimate supremacy lies with the people's representatives, not the judges — subject to the basic structure.

The Court therefore does not sit as a "super-legislature" on questions of policy (Bennett Coleman v. UOI, AIR 1973 SC 106; BALCO Employees' Union v. UOI, AIR 2002 SC 350). It interferes with policy only for clear illegality, unconstitutionality, mala fides or arbitrariness.

A twist Basu points out

The very ease of amendment widened judicial review in the end. Reacting to frequent amendments, the Court devised the basic structure doctrine in Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which limits the amending power itself.
