sections.title: Judicial review as a basic feature
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Judicial review is part of the basic structure. It cannot be taken away even by constitutional amendment. Arts 32 and 226 are its vehicles, and Art 226 too is part of the basic structure.

Authorities Basu gives: Kesavananda Bharati (1973); Minerva Mills (1980); S.P. Sampath Kumar v. UOI, AIR 1987 SC 386; S.R. Bommai v. UOI, AIR 1994 SC 1918; L. Chandra Kumar v. UOI, AIR 1997 SC 1125 (power of High Courts under Arts 226/227 and of the Supreme Court under Art 32 cannot be ousted; tribunals can only supplement them); I.R. Coelho v. State of T.N. (2007) (Ninth Schedule laws inserted after 24 April 1973 remain open to basic-structure review).

The reasoning: no Act of Parliament can exclude the courts' power to enforce fundamental rights; federal limits need an umpire; Arts 13, 32 and 226 together embed review in the text.

Basu also gathers the modern statements of the expansive approach to rights: since Maneka Gandhi, rights are not "isolated pools" but together a comprehensive guarantee against arbitrary State power (I.R. Coelho). Where a statute touches civil liberties — speech, movement, equality, religion — the courts give it far less latitude than fiscal laws (Govt. of A.P. v. P. Laxmi Devi, AIR 2008 SC 1640).

Keep the balance in an answer

Basu ends this part by noting that giving courts the final word on the limits of the other organs gives them a kind of primacy — which is exactly why they have accepted self-imposed limits (chapter B11).

ddbu.title: Which courts review, and through what proceedings
ddbu.trail: The US hierarchy for contrast; in India, High Courts (Arts 226, 228), the Supreme Court (Arts 32, 131–136) and subordinate courts

sections.title: The contrast with the USA
sections.html:
In the USA, constitutionality can be decided by every court: State courts (subject to appeal on a "federal question"), federal District Courts, the Courts of Appeals and the Supreme Court. Since 1988 nearly all Supreme Court review is by discretionary certiorari, granted for "compelling reasons" such as conflicts between circuits or important unsettled federal questions (Rule 10). Certiorari resembles special leave under our Art 136.

India deliberately avoided that plurality of voices. Only the Supreme Court and the High Courts can decide whether a law is constitutional. Parliament could, under Art 32(3), empower other courts to issue writs, but it has never done so. Because Indian federalism does not rest on State sovereignty, both kinds of court can test both Union and State laws.

Two kinds of proceedings

  1. Under ordinary law — a declaratory suit (s. 34, Specific Relief Act, 1963), or a constitutional objection raised in any civil or criminal case.

  2. Under the Constitution — writs under Arts 32 and 226; appeals under Arts 132–134 and 136; transfer under Art 228.

sections.title: High Courts
sections.html:
Under ordinary law

  • A declaratory suit on the Original Side, where one exists.
  • A constitutional point raised as a defence or in an appeal (e.g. a criminal appellant attacking the statute creating the offence, or the tribunal or procedure used). If decided, appeal lies to the Supreme Court under Art 132 (Lachmandas; Kathi Raning Rawat v. State of Saurashtra, (1952) SCR 435).
  • A case stated by a subordinate court under s. 113 CPC or s. 432 CrPC (now s. 395 of the 1973 Code).

Article 226 — the main avenue

Art 226 lets a High Court issue writs, orders and directions for enforcing fundamental rights and "for any other purpose". That is the largest channel for constitutional litigation:

  • Habeas corpus — a detenu may attack the law under which he is held, for breach of a right or for lack of competence.
  • Mandamus — to restrain the executive from enforcing an unconstitutional law against the petitioner. A real threat is enough; one need not wait for the injury (S.M.D. Kiran Pasha v. Govt. of A.P., (1990) 1 SCC 34).
  • Prohibition — to stop a tribunal acting under an unconstitutional law; certiorari — to quash a decision already made under it.

Points on the scope of Art 226:

  • It is part of the basic structure and cannot be curtailed by statute (L. Chandra Kumar; State of W.B. v. CPDR, 2010).
  • It is a public-law remedy against the State or a body with a public element (State of U.P. v. Rakesh Kumar Keshari, (2011) 5 SCC 341; Air India Statutory Corp. v. United Labour Union, (1997) 9 SCC 377).
  • The grounds are illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety.
  • Alternative remedy is a rule of discretion, not a bar. It does not apply where the action is under an invalid law, without authority of law, in breach of natural justice, or where a fundamental right is to be enforced (Tata Engineering & Locomotive Co. v. Asst. Commissioner, AIR 1967 SC 1401; Harbanslal Sahnia v. IOC, (2003) 2 SCC 107).
  • Once a breach of a fundamental right is found, the High Court is bound to grant relief.

Article 228 — withdrawal of cases

The aim is to make the High Court the sole interpreter of the Constitution within the State and avoid conflicting decisions by subordinate courts. Three conditions:

  1. a case must actually be pending in a subordinate court (not a tribunal: Thakur Jugal Kishore Sinha v. Sitamarhi Central Co-op Bank, AIR 1967 SC 1494);
  2. it must involve a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution — a bare plea of unconstitutionality is not enough;
  3. deciding that question must be necessary for disposing of the case.

Example: in Yusuf Abdul Aziz v. State of Bombay, AIR 1954 SC 321, the accused's challenge to s. 497 IPC (adultery) under Art 14 came up after the case was withdrawn under Art 228.

The CPC and CrPC were amended in 1951 to match: a subordinate court that thinks a statute invalid (and which has not been so declared by its High Court or the Supreme Court) must state a case and refer it to the High Court. There is no duty to refer once a Constitution Bench has upheld the law, since the question is no longer "substantial".

Govt. of A.P. , (1990) 1 SCC 34). Prohibition — to stop a tribunal acting under an unconstitutional law; certiorari — to quash a decision already made under it. Points on the scope of Art 226: It is part of the basic structure and cannot be curtailed by statute ( L. Chandra Kumar ; State of W.B. v. CPDR , 2010). It is a public-law remedy against the State or a body with a public element ( State of U.P. v. Rakesh Kumar Keshari , (2011) 5 SCC 341; Air India Statutory Corp. v. United Labour Union , (1997) 9 SCC 377). The grounds are illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. Alternative remedy is a rule of discretion, not a bar. It does not apply where the action is under an invalid law , without authority of law, in breach of natural justice, or where a fundamental right is to be enforced ( Tata Engineering & Locomotive Co. v. Asst. Commissioner , AIR 1967 SC 1401; Harbanslal Sahnia v. IOC , (2003) 2 SCC 107). Once a breach of a fundamental right is found, the High Court is bound to grant relief. Article 228 — withdrawal of cases The aim is to make the High Court the sole interpreter of the Constitution within the State and avoid conflicting decisions by subordinate courts. Three conditions: a case must actually be pending in a subordinate court (not a tribunal: Thakur Jugal Kishore Sinha v. Sitamarhi Central Co-op Bank , AIR 1967 SC 1494); it must involve a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution — a bare plea of unconstitutionality is not enough; deciding that question must be necessary for disposing of the case. Example: in Yusuf Abdul Aziz v. State of Bombay , AIR 1954 SC 321, the accused's challenge to s. 497 IPC (adultery) under Art 14 came up after the case was withdrawn under Art 228. The CPC and CrPC were amended in 1951 to match: a subordinate court that thinks a statute invalid (and which has not been so declared by its High Court or the Supreme Court) must state a case and refer it to the High Court. There is no duty to refer once a Constitution Bench has upheld the law, since the question is no longer "substantial".

sections.title: The Supreme Court
sections.html:
Constitutional questions reach it by:

  • (a) Art 32 petitions;
  • (b) original suits under Art 131 (Centre–State or inter-State disputes);
  • (c) appeals from High Courts under Arts 132–134;
  • (d) special leave under Art 136.

Article 32 — a fundamental right to a remedy

Art 32(1) makes the right to move the Supreme Court itself a fundamental right. In Romesh Thappar Patanjali Sastri J said this casts on the Court a duty to protect rights — the role of a "sentinel on the qui vive". There is nothing like it in the US Constitution.

Article 32 is confined to Part III

A law can be challenged under Art 32 only for violating a fundamental right. Lack of legislative competence or breach of a provision outside Part III is not enough on its own (Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. UOI, (1950) SCR 869; Ramjilal v. ITO, AIR 1951 SC 97). Those grounds go first to the High Court under Art 226 and reach the Supreme Court on appeal.

So no Art 32 petition lies merely:

  • to enforce a right created by statute or contract;
  • where there is no clear breach of a fundamental right;
  • to press policy preferences (Hindi Hitrakshak Samiti v. UOI, AIR 1990 SC 851);
  • to enforce a Directive Principle;
  • (normally) for disputes covered by the Industrial Disputes Act.

But rights enforceable against private persons (Arts 17, 23, 24) can be enforced under Art 32 against them (PUDR v. UOI, AIR 1982 SC 1473). Basu also notes that in practice the Court has entertained Art 32 petitions raising important legal issues without a clear fundamental-right breach: D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987, repromulgation of ordinances), Sarojini Ramaswami v. UOI (1992, removal of a judge), S.C. Advocates-on-Record Assn. (1993, appointment of judges), Aruna Shanbaug v. UOI (2011, passive euthanasia).

Other features of Art 32:

  • No overt act is needed; a law that abridges a right by its own terms can be challenged at once.
  • Alternative remedy is no ground for refusing relief (Himmatlal Harilal Mehta v. State of M.P., AIR 1954 SC 403).
  • Disputed facts can be gone into (K.K. Kochunni v. State of Madras (1959); Kharak Singh v. State of U.P., 1963), and the Court may appoint commissions (M.C. Mehta v. UOI, 1987) or order disclosure (Ram Jethmalani v. UOI, (2011) 8 SCC 1).
  • The Court is not bound by the technicalities of the English prerogative writs (T.C. Basappa v. T. Nagappa, (1955) 1 SCR 250); it may mould relief and "evolve new tools".
  • In Kochunni, the majority through Das CJ held that declaratory relief may be granted under Art 32, moving away from Chiranjit Lal's doubt.
  • But laches and acquiescence can bar relief (Tilokchand Motichand v. H.B. Munshi, AIR 1970 SC 898).
  • Errors of law or fact under a valid law are not corrected under Art 32 (Ujjam Bai v. State of U.P., AIR 1962 SC 1621).

Compensation as a public-law remedy

Earlier courts refused money claims in writ petitions. It is now settled that compensation can be awarded for breach of fundamental rights, especially Art 21: Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar, AIR 1983 SC 1086; Bhim Singh v. State of J&K, AIR 1986 SC 494 (exemplary costs); Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993); D.K. Basu v. State of W.B. (1997); Consumer Education & Research Centre v. UOI (1995); MCD v. Uphaar Tragedy Victims Assn., AIR 2012 SC 100. It is a public-law remedy, additional to a civil claim in tort; sovereign immunity is no defence; and it does not bar criminal proceedings.

sections.title: Subordinate courts
sections.html:
A subordinate court may hear a suit in which a constitutional question arises (s. 9 CPC), but it cannot decide that question; it must refer it (s. 113 and O. XLVI CPC; Art 228). The question can arise:

  • directly, in a declaratory suit — as in Dwarkadas Shrinivas v. Sholapur Spinning & Weaving Co., (1954) SCR 674, where shareholders sued for a declaration that an Ordinance taking over management was void; the Supreme Court decreed the suit under the then Art 31(2);
  • as a defence — e.g. a defendant attacking the Bombay Prevention of Excommunication Act, 1949 (Sardar Syedna Taher Saifuddin Saheb v. State of Bombay, AIR 1962 SC 853);
  • even where the plaintiff does not rely on the statute: in Ganga Pratap Singh v. Allahabad Bank, AIR 1958 SC 293, the defendant debtor argued that the part of a definition excluding his class from debt relief offended Art 14; the Supreme Court directed the High Court to withdraw the suit and decide the point;
  • in a criminal case, at trial or on appeal.

Citation check

The source text cites the excommunication case as "AIR 1958 SC 253". The correct citation for Taher Saifuddin v. State of Bombay is AIR 1962 SC 853.

ddbu.title: Limits on judicial review (1) — limits in the Constitution itself
ddbu.trail: Cases and controversies, advisory opinions under Art 143, and the express bars in Arts 100(2), 122, 212, 255 and 329

sections.title: Three kinds of limit
sections.html:
The framework

Judicial review is a formidable weapon; used without restraint, it could paralyse government. Basu groups its limits into three kinds, in both the USA and India:

  1. Constitutional limits — written into the Constitution (this chapter);

  2. Intrinsic limits — flowing from the nature of the judicial function (chapter B10);

  3. Self-imposed limits — canons the courts have laid down for themselves (chapters B11–B12).

sections.title: Cases and controversies; advisory opinions
sections.html:
USA. Art III, s. 2 extends federal judicial power only to "cases" and "controversies". From that the Supreme Court derives the rule that the question must arise in a concrete dispute between adverse parties — not a hypothetical, academic or moot question (Aetna Life Insurance Co. v. Haworth, 300 US 227 (1937)). It follows that federal courts give no advisory opinions (United States v. Ferreira, 13 How. 40 (1852)); a declaratory judgment is different because it settles a real dispute between adversaries. Some State constitutions do require their highest courts to advise the legislature or executive.

India. Art 143 lets the President refer a question of law or fact to the Supreme Court. But:

  • the Court is not bound to answer, except under Art 143(2) (In re Kerala Education Bill, AIR 1958 SC 956);
  • an advisory opinion is not executable and cannot invalidate a law, so it is not judicial review in the true sense;
  • in advisory jurisdiction the Court may clarify the ratio of an earlier judgment but cannot overturn a decision between parties (Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012, (2012) 10 SCC 1);
  • since only the Supreme Court is given this power, High Courts cannot be asked for advisory opinions; they decide only adversary litigation.

Other constitutional limits already met: Art 32 is confined to breaches of Part III (chapter B8), and Art 228 keeps constitutional questions away from subordinate courts. Basu notes the Court's warning in Ram Jethmalani v. UOI, (2011) 8 SCC 1 that carving exceptions out of fundamental rights, bit by bit, can hollow out the right itself.

sections.title: Express bars on reviewing legislative proceedings
sections.html:
Arts 100(2) and 189(2) — vacancies and unqualified members

A House's proceedings are not invalid because there was a vacancy in its membership, or because a person not entitled to sit or vote took part. So an Act cannot be annulled on those grounds. But "vacancy" means a vacancy after the House was duly constituted. It does not cure a defect in the constitution of the House: in Vinod Kumar v. State of H.P., AIR 1959 SC 223, the Supreme Court struck down a 1954 land reform Act passed by the Assembly of the old State of Himachal Pradesh, which had ceased to exist under the Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur (New State) Act, 1954, without a new Assembly being convened.

Arts 122(1) and 212(1) — "irregularity of procedure"

The validity of proceedings in Parliament or a State Legislature cannot be questioned in court on the ground of irregularity of procedure. Basu summarises the twenty-one propositions in Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007). The core ones:

  • Parliament is a co-ordinate organ whose views deserve deference, but no constitutional functionary is the sole judge of its own powers.
  • The necessity and expediency of using a privilege is for the legislature; the manner of its exercise is open to review on accepted grounds.
  • Arts 122/212 displace the English doctrine of exclusive cognisance; they protect only against challenges for irregular procedure.
  • Proceedings tainted by substantive or gross illegality or unconstitutionality are not protected. Neither are actions breaching fundamental rights (e.g. Arts 20, 21).
  • There is a rebuttable presumption that privileges were exercised regularly. The court does not examine the truth or adequacy of the material, and the burden of proving mala fides is very heavy.
  • Even a finality clause does not shut out review for lack of jurisdiction, nullity, gross illegality, irrationality, mala fides, breach of natural justice or perversity.

So, Basu concludes, a statute cannot be struck down because:

  • it was passed without a quorum (Art 100(3)–(4) leave quorum to the presiding officer);
  • it lacked the required majority, if the Speaker has certified it as passed — the Speaker's certificate is conclusive, following the English rule (State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh, 1952);
  • members had not taken the oath (Vinod Kumar);
  • a House or committee departed from its own rules (Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Shri Krishna Sinha (II), AIR 1960 SC 1186) — e.g. the record did not show the question was put, or the Deputy Speaker certified a Money Bill under Art 199(4).

But review is available where the defect goes to the due constitution of the legislature, to its power or competence to act, to a condition precedent to the power, or where the proceedings are unconstitutional. The Federal Court case Basu relies on is Umayal Achi v. Lakshmi Achi, AIR 1945 FC 25, where Zafrulla Khan J (dissenting) said the question whether a Chamber had capacity to function at all is not a "mere matter of procedure" but turns on the Constitution Act itself. Compare A.G. for New South Wales v. Trethowan, [1932] AC 526: a "manner and form" requirement that conditions the power to legislate is enforceable.

sections.title: The Speaker's certificate and the English cases
sections.html:
English law will not look behind the Parliament Roll: if both Houses passed a Bill and it received assent, courts will not inquire how it was introduced or carried (Edinburgh & Dalkeith Railway v. Wauchope, 1842; Lee v. Bude & Torrington Railway, 1871; Pickin v. British Railways Board, [1974] AC 765 — no inquiry even into alleged fraud on Parliament).

In India that principle covers mere procedure, not constitutional conditions for passing a Bill:

  • Proviso to Art 3. A Bill altering a State's area, boundaries or name must be referred by the President to the State Legislature for its views. This is jurisdictional; failure is fatal (Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay, AIR 1960 SC 51).
  • Second proviso to Art 200. The Governor must reserve for the President a Bill that would derogate from the High Court's powers. Reservation and Presidential assent are conditions precedent; without them the Act is void.
  • President's assent to an amending Act under the old Art 31(3) may raise a presumption of assent to the parent Act (Venkatrao v. State of Bombay, AIR 1970 SC 126), but Basu reads that as obiter on a record that lacked evidence.
  • Arts 107(5), 196(5). A Bill pending in a House lapses on dissolution of the popular House. If assent is given to a Bill that had lapsed, the Act can be struck down. A Bill already passed by both Houses and awaiting assent does not lapse (Special Reference No. 1 of 2002, AIR 2003 SC 87).
  • Arts 200–201. In Hoechst Pharmaceuticals v. State of Bihar, AIR 1983 SC 1019, the Court held the Governor's decision to reserve and the President's assent are not justiciable, and a reserved Bill that receives assent becomes law; Bharat Sevashram Sangh v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1987 SC 494 followed.
  • Art 254(2). But where a State law repugnant to a Central law claims protection through Presidential assent, the courts can examine whether assent was given after the repugnancy was pointedly placed before the President: Kaiser-I-Hind (P) Ltd. v. National Textile Corporation, AIR 2002 SC 3404. Assent is "express agreement" to what was proposed; a general assent covers everything, a specific one only what it names. Rajiv Sarin v. State of Uttarakhand, AIR 2011 SC 3081 added that the presumption of regular official acts (s. 114(e), (f) Evidence Act) applies unless a specific plea is raised.

Art 255 — curing the lack of prior sanction

Where the Constitution requires the President's or Governor's previous recommendation or sanction for introducing a Bill (e.g. Art 3, Art 117 financial Bills, Art 274, the proviso to Art 304(b)), Art 255 saves the Act if the same Bill later receives assent. It cannot be stretched to let a later validating Act retrospectively cure an earlier Act that failed for want of sanction (Jawaharmal v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1966 SC 764).

sections.title: Art 329 — elections
sections.html:
• Art 329(a): laws on delimitation of constituencies and allotment of seats made under Art 327 or 328 cannot be questioned in court (Meghraj Kothari v. Delimitation Commission, AIR 1967 SC 669; Association of Residents of Mhow v. Delimitation Commission, (2009) 5 SCC 404). Once the electoral roll is finalised, neither the Election Commission nor the court can alter it.
  • Art 329(b): an election can be questioned only by an election petition. Courts, including under Art 226, will not interfere between the start of the process and the result (N.P. Ponnuswami v. Returning Officer (1952); Durga Shankar Mehta v. Raghuraj Singh, AIR 1954 SC 520), save in special situations.
  • Exception: a person elected while statutorily disqualified can be unseated by writ (K. Venkatachalam v. A. Swamickan, AIR 1999 SC 1723).
  • Where neither legislature nor Election Commission has acted, the Court may issue directions under Arts 32, 141–142 — e.g. requiring disclosure of candidates' antecedents (UOI v. Association for Democratic Reforms, AIR 2002 SC 2112).

Don't over-read Arts 122 and 212

They protect only against challenges based on procedural irregularity within the House. They do not protect an Act from review for breach of Part III, lack of competence, or breach of a constitutional condition precedent (Raja Ram Pal; Kihoto Hollohan).

ddbu.title: Limits on judicial review (2) — limits inherent in the judicial function
ddbu.trail: Courts decide cases, not policy; motive is irrelevant; colourable legislation; no a priori theories; federalism after Bommai

sections.title: Courts decide cases, not abstract questions
sections.html:
The first intrinsic limit is that a court acts only on a dispute between adverse parties, brought in the prescribed way. It cannot act on its own initiative or issue general edicts. That is why there is often a long gap between a statute's enactment and a declaration of its invalidity.

In Muskrat v. United States, 219 US 346 (1911), the US Supreme Court refused to answer a question Congress had arranged to put to it: courts give declaratory judgments (which settle an actual dispute, without coercive process) but not advisory opinions (advice on hypothetical questions to another branch).

sections.title: Judges declare law; they do not make it
sections.html:
The orthodox position Basu restates:

  • A court finds and applies the law that already exists; it does not purport to make new rules for the future — that is the legislature's job. It cannot disregard existing law on humanitarian or public-policy grounds.
  • The question before the court is legal, not political: not whether the judges approve of the policy, but whether the Constitution permits the law.
  • The court cannot add words, fill self-perceived gaps, or treat a statutory approval as "deemed" given after a period the statute does not prescribe (Sant Lal Gupta v. Modern Co-op Group Housing Society, (2010) 13 SCC 336).
  • The court cannot direct a legislature to enact a particular law (Suresh Seth v. Commissioner, Indore Municipal Corp., AIR 2006 SC 767), nor rewrite an impugned law, nor act as an appellate authority over it (Chandigarh Administration v. Manpreet Singh, (1992) 1 SCC 380).
  • Nor can it ask whether less would have done, whether the provision is more drastic than the occasion demanded, or whether the purpose could have been achieved differently (All India Bank Employees' Assn. v. National Industrial Tribunal, AIR 1962 SC 171).
  • Shah J for the majority in R.C. Cooper (Bank Nationalisation) said whether rural banking needs were genuine, and whose economic policy was better, had little relevance to legality.

The "vacuum" exception: guidelines until the legislature acts

Basu records the counter-current. Where a statute is silent and the authority has power to act, the Court has issued directions to fill the vacuum until legislation is made, under Arts 32, 141 and 142:

  • Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) — sexual harassment at the workplace;
  • Lakshmi Kant Pandey v. UOI (1984) — inter-country adoption;
  • Vineet Narain v. UOI (1998) — independence of the CBI and CVC;
  • Vishwa Jagriti Mission v. Central Government, (2001) 6 SCC 577 — ragging; Common Cause v. UOI (1996) — blood banks;
  • UOI v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) — candidates' antecedents.

Such directions have the force of law until the legislature acts.

sections.title: Economic policy
sections.html:
• The wisdom of economic policy is not reviewable unless it breaches a statute or the Constitution. Government is entitled to trial and error, so long as both are bona fide and within authority. In BALCO Employees' Union v. UOI, AIR 2002 SC 350, disinvestment of a public enterprise was upheld as policy.
  • But in Centre for PIL v. UOI, (2012) 3 SCC 1 (2G spectrum), a "first-come-first-served" allocation of a natural resource was struck down as arbitrary; the State holds natural resources as a public trustee.
  • Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012 then clarified that auction is not the only constitutionally permissible method; any method that subserves the common good and is not arbitrary will do.

sections.title: Motive of the legislature is irrelevant
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Whether a statute is valid is always a question of power. If the legislature had the power, its motive does not matter; if it lacked the power, motive cannot save the law (Mukherjea J in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, AIR 1953 SC 375). Malice is unknown to the field of legislation.

  • The US Supreme Court takes the same view: in United States v. O'Brien, 391 US 367 (1968) (draft-card burning), it refused to strike down an otherwise valid law on the basis of alleged illicit motive drawn from what a few legislators said. Conversely, however laudable the motive, a law that breaches a constitutional limit falls (McCray v. United States, 195 US 27 (1904)).
  • In India: T. Venkata Reddy v. State of A.P., AIR 1985 SC 724 (abolition of village officers' posts — propriety, expediency and necessity are for the legislature; the Court cannot ask whether the legislature applied its mind); K. Nagaraj v. State of A.P., AIR 1985 SC 551 (retirement age cut); Bhanumati v. State of U.P., (2010) 12 SCC 1; G.C. Kanungo v. State of Orissa, AIR 1995 SC 1665 (an executive's ulterior motive cannot be imputed to the legislature).
  • Abuse of power can make an exercise of rule-making power vulnerable, but does not by itself make the rules ultra vires.

sections.title: Colourable legislation and "fraud on the Constitution"
sections.html:
Motive must not be confused with fraud on the Constitution. The doctrine strikes down a law that, while pretending to use a power the legislature has, in substance does what the Constitution forbids or what lies outside its competence. The transgression is covert rather than overt: the legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly.

Key points Basu collects:

  • The doctrine is about competence, not good or bad faith (State of Bihar v. Kameshwar Singh (1952); Gajapati Narayan Deo (1953); R.S. Joshi v. Ajit Mills, AIR 1977 SC 2279).
  • The inquiry is into the true nature and character of the law — its effect and its object, purpose or design — not into the motives of legislators.
  • Krishna Iyer J in Ajit Mills: "colourable" means it is maya — only in appearance what it purports to be. He also warned that the charge is a "malignant expression" to be used only in plain cases, out of comity between the organs.
  • Once competence is found, the doctrine has no application. It cannot be used through a "side door" to attack a competent law because it nullifies an earlier law or takes away compensation (State of Kerala v. People's Union for Civil Liberties, (2009) 8 SCC 46).
  • S.S. Bola v. B.D. Sardana, AIR 1997 SC 3127 distinguished fraud on legislative power (power exists but is not really exercised — a mere pretence, e.g. "illusory" compensation) from fraud on the Constitution (no power, or a constitutional prohibition, yet the law is made under a pretence of power). Either way the law is void.

Illustrations:

  • K.T. Moopil Nair v. State of Kerala (1961): a land tax under the Travancore-Cochin Land Tax Act, 1955 that could exceed the income from the land many times over was held confiscatory — a cloak to take property — and struck down under Arts 14 and 19(1)(f). An excessive tax alone is not colourable; other circumstances must show the device.
  • Assam Co. Ltd. v. State of Assam, AIR 1970 Gau 40: a notification setting up a town committee for an area already better served than the committee could manage was colourable delegated legislation.
  • Mahendra Lal Jaini: colourability, like any other ground, is judged by the Constitution as it stood when the Act was passed.
  • Challenges failed in many cases — e.g. Jalan Trading Co. (1967), B.R. Shankaranarayana v. State of Mysore, AIR 1966 SC 1571, Hari Krishna Bhargav v. UOI (1966).

sections.title: No a priori theories
sections.html:
The court must not begin with a doctrinaire theory and stretch the Constitution to fit it. Its job, in Roberts J's words in Butler, is to lay the Article beside the statute and see whether the latter squares with the former. Nor can it test validity against an ideal of democracy or the "spirit" of the Constitution not found in the text (Special Reference No. 1 of 2012).

Basu's example: federal supremacy and State of W.B. v. UOI

Basu calls State of West Bengal v. UOI (1963, 7 judges, holding that Parliament can legislate to acquire State-owned property) a "glaring example" of a judgment driven by an a priori assumption that national power must prevail over State power.

His argument:

  • In the USA, enumeration was one-sided (only federal powers listed), amendment was hard, and Art VI contains a Supremacy Clause; so the Court could steadily expand federal power by reading "national concern" into the enumerated powers.
  • In India, there is a double (indeed treble) enumeration in the Seventh Schedule; the Constitution gives the Union overriding power expressly where it wants to (e.g. emergencies); and there is no general Supremacy Clause. So no general presumption of Union paramountcy is legitimate.
  • Hidayatullah CJ: Parliament "is supreme only in so far as the Constitution makes it" (Narasimha Rao v. State of A.P., AIR 1970 SC 422).

The a priori view was repeated in State of Karnataka v. UOI, AIR 1978 SC 68 (Beg CJ, describing "pragmatic federalism" overlaid by unitary features). Basu takes credit that his critique was vindicated by S.R. Bommai v. UOI (1994, 9 judges), where six judges held:

Case

S.R. Bommai v. UOI (1994)

(1994) 3 SCC 1 · 9 judges

Facts

Challenges to dismissals of several State governments under Art 356.

Held

Federalism is a basic feature, not a matter of convenience. The Constitution is more federal than unitary. States are supreme within their sphere; courts must not read Union powers so as to whittle down State powers. The President's satisfaction under Art 356(1) is open to judicial review, and the power cannot be used for political ends.

Principle

The judiciary acts as arbiter even in emergency-type powers; no presumption of Union paramountcy.

Basu adds Kuldip Nayar v. UOI, (2006) 7 SCC 1 for balance: India is federal with a tilt to the Centre — a "holding together", not a "coming together" federation — and federalism here is not territory-based, since Parliament can redraw or extinguish States under Art 3.

sections.title: Not every question is fit for judges
sections.html: Courts decide only "judicial issues" — issues appropriate for judges by the traditions of the courts at Westminster. Both US and Indian courts have excluded political questions as non-justiciable, mainly as a function of the separation of powers (Baker v. Carr, 369 US 186 (1962)). But deciding whether a matter has been committed by the Constitution to another branch is itself constitutional interpretation, and so a matter for the court (chapter B12).

ddbu.title: Self-imposed limits (1) — a real case, a substantial question, decided only as far as necessary
ddbu.trail: Judicial self-restraint; adversary litigation and mootness; "substantial" questions; the doctrine of last resort; saving a statute by construction

sections.title: Self-restraint: the sixteen canons
sections.html:
Judicial review, Basu says, is like Janus: it enforces a written Constitution, but it also risks government by unelected judges. Stone J's dissent in United States v. Butler (1936) states the guiding ideas: courts are concerned only with the power to enact, not its wisdom; and while the other branches are checked by the courts, "the only check upon our own exercise of power is our own sense of self-restraint". Unwise laws are for the ballot box.

The US Supreme Court built rules for itself — most famously listed by Brandeis J (concurring) in Ashwander v. Tennessee Valley Authority, 297 US 288 (1936) — to avoid deciding constitutional questions it need not decide. Basu shows the Indian Supreme Court has adopted most of them:

The sixteen self-imposed limits

  1. Adversary litigation

  2. A real, not hypothetical, controversy

  3. A substantial constitutional question

  4. Constitutionality decided only as a last resort

  5. Decide no more than necessary

  6. The petitioner must have standing

  7. The injury must be personal to the petitioner

  8. Adequate pleading

  9. A specific challenge

  10. Raised at the proper stage

  11. The question must be justiciable

  12. Presumption of constitutionality

  13. Respect for legislative determination

  14. Respect for long-standing legislative practice

  15. Stare decisis

  16. Severability

This chapter covers 1–5. Standing (6–7) is in chapter B12; 8–11 in B13; 12–14 in B14; 15–16 in B15.

sections.title: 1. Adversary litigation
sections.html:
A court cannot think in the abstract. Validity is decided only when someone whose rights are affected brings a dispute that cannot be resolved without deciding it. In Massachusetts v. Mellon, 262 US 447 (1923), the US Court said it has no power "per se" to review Acts of Congress; it acts only when an Act is the basis of a direct injury presenting a justiciable issue.

So friendly or collusive suits fail: the Court refused to decide a rate statute on an agreed statement of facts between friendly parties (Chicago & Grand Trunk Railway v. Wellman, 143 US 339 (1892)), and a challenge where the State had agreed not to enforce the law until the Court ruled (CIO v. McAdory, 325 US 472 (1945)).

In India such suits have hardly arisen, but the same follows from Das J's statement in Dwarkadas Shrinivas: only a person directly affected can challenge a law. The Court will not:

  • decide a constitutional question unless necessary, and only when specifically raised (H.M. Trivedi v. V.B. Raju, AIR 1973 SC 2602; Yadlapati Venkateswarlu v. State of A.P., AIR 1991 SC 704);
  • decide it if the case can be disposed of on another ground (Basheshar Nath v. CIT, AIR 1959 SC 149);
  • lay down important law without a proper lis between parties ranged on opposite sides (Sanjeev Coke Mfg. Co. v. Bharat Coking Coal, AIR 1983 SC 239);
  • decide a challenge argued only in theory, on general pleadings (Brahm Dutt v. UOI, (2005) 2 SCC 431);
  • give advisory opinions under Art 32 (Srinivasa Enterprises v. UOI, AIR 1981 SC 504).

sections.title: 2. The controversy must be real — ripeness and mootness
sections.html:
Ripeness. An assumed or potential invasion of a right is not enough; the petitioner must show an actual or threatened one.

  • United Public Workers v. Mitchell, 330 US 75 (1947): federal employees who merely wished to engage in political activity barred by the Hatch Act got no declaration; only Poole, who had actually been charged, presented a justiciable controversy.
  • Laird v. Tatum, 408 US 1 (1972): fear that Army surveillance might later be misused was too speculative.
  • Coffman v. Breeze Corp., 323 US 316 (1945): a licensor could not get a declaration against a royalty statute until the licensee actually relied on it in a suit.

Mootness is "standing set in a time frame": the personal stake must continue throughout. A case becomes moot if a statute is repealed, a detention order revoked, seized property returned, or a sentence fully served. The US exceptions: collateral consequences of a conviction (deportation, loss of civil rights, heavier future sentences), inability to reach court before the sentence ended, and controversies "capable of repetition, yet evading review".

India applies the same principles:

  • A petition that has become infructuous — e.g. the impugned statute repealed or the Ordinance replaced by an Act — is generally dismissed (Kartar Singh v. Piara Ram, AIR 1976 SC 957; Kishan Prakash Sharma v. UOI, AIR 2001 SC 1493; Dharam Dutt v. UOI, AIR 2004 SC 1295).
  • But where the new law continues the injury, the petitioner may amend and challenge it (Commissioner, H.R.E. v. Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar (Shirur Mutt), 1954).
  • A petition may be heard though infructuous if it raises a substantial question of constitutional interpretation (Ramdas Athawale v. UOI, (2007) 15 SCC 708; Sub-Committee on Judicial Accountability v. UOI, AIR 1992 SC 320).
  • Mootness here is a rule of practice, not jurisdiction (Madhu Limaye v. Superintendent, Tihar Jail, AIR 1975 SC 1505). The Court once declared the Orissa kendu-leaf scheme unconstitutional even though the year in issue had passed, to prevent the mischief continuing (Rasbihari Panda v. State of Orissa, AIR 1969 SC 1081). Basu says this exception should not be enlarged.
  • Locus standi is judged as at the date of filing (D.C. Wadhwa).
  • Outside Art 143, no hypothetical questions: the Court will not rule on a law or part of a law not yet in force (Chandrasekhar v. State of Orissa, AIR 1972 SC 486), unless the Court itself stayed its commencement.

sections.title: 3. The question must be "substantial"
sections.html:
In the US, a question is not "substantial" if earlier decisions have so clearly settled it that no real controversy remains (e.g. vaccination laws: Jacobson v. Massachusetts, 197 US 11 (1905); Zucht v. King, 260 US 174 (1922)).

India writes the requirement into Art 132(1) (and Art 228): a "substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution".

  • A question already settled by the Supreme Court is no longer substantial (T.M. Krishnaswami Pillai v. Governor-General, AIR 1947 FC 37; Pankaj Bhargava v. Mohinder Nath, AIR 1991 SC 1233). The Federal Court in Krishnaswami also said "substantial" implies a difference of opinion.
  • In State of J&K v. Ganga Singh, AIR 1960 SC 356, the Court said the principles of Art 14 were so well settled that applying them is not a substantial question. Basu disagrees: even the US took over a century of "trial and error", and equality has not exhausted its facets. A question of fact may also be so bound up with a constitutional guarantee as to be substantial (State of Mysore v. Chablani, AIR 1958 SC 325).
  • A wrong interpretation of a statute, or whether an Act was correctly applied to the facts, is not a question as to the interpretation of the Constitution.
  • An appellant under Art 132 must confine himself to the constitutional point; exceptionally, an appeal may lie from a single judge where the issue is grave (UOI v. Jyoti Prakash Mitter, AIR 1971 SC 1093).

sections.title: 4. Last resort — and saving statutes by construction
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

The Court will declare a law unconstitutional only if it must: if the case can be decided on another ground — the general law, or an interpretation of the statute that avoids the conflict — it will take that route (Brandeis J in Ashwander; State of Bihar v. Hurdut Rai Moti Lal Jute Mills, AIR 1960 SC 378).

In Hurdut Mills, the High Court struck down a forfeiture proviso in the Bihar Sales Tax Act under Arts 20(1) and 31(2). The Supreme Court held the proviso did not apply to registered dealers at all, so the forfeiture failed on that ground and the constitutional point was academic. Gajendragadkar J: first find the facts and see whether the impugned provision is even attracted.

Construction that saves

The Court interprets both the Constitution and the statute. If the statute can be read consistently with the Constitution, there is no conflict:

  • Of two possible readings, choose the one that saves the statute (ut res magis valeat quam pereat).
  • Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962): read literally, "disaffection" in s. 124A IPC (sedition) would punish mere ill-feeling and offend Art 19(2). The Court confined it to words with an intention or tendency to cause public disorder by violence, and upheld it on that reading. Seervai noted the consequence: a person validly convicted on the narrowed reading still loses his Art 19(1) freedom.
  • Reading in: in State of Mysore v. Bhat, AIR 1975 SC 596, the Court read natural justice into a law instead of striking it down; in Express Newspapers v. UOI (1958) it read "capacity to pay" into the wage-fixing law and quashed the Wage Board's decision instead.
  • Reading down applies to rules too: in Rev. Mark Netto v. State of Kerala, AIR 1979 SC 83, a rule that would have violated Art 30 was held inapplicable to minority institutions. In DTC v. DTC Mazdoor Congress, AIR 1991 SC 101, the Court explained that reading down keeps a statute within its purpose and within the Constitution, but cannot revive a provision whose clear words are unconstitutional.
  • Legislative competence: a legislature is presumed to know its limits, so general words are read as confined to its field (Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act Reference, 1941), unless the narrowed Act would be "nothing or next to nothing" or different in kind (Gwyer CJ).
  • Arts 25–26 and 31: "affairs of the temple" read as secular affairs only (Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1963 SC 1638); "building or work" in an acquisition law read as one serving the public purpose (R.L. Arora v. State of U.P., AIR 1964 SC 1230).

…but the Court cannot rewrite

The limits of saving construction

  • The saving rule applies only where the words admit of two meanings. Clear words must be given effect even if the result is absurd or unconstitutional.

  • The Court cannot add words or recast the Act; "if a gap is disclosed, the remedy lies in an amending Act". In Minerva Mills the Court refused to read down Art 31C, because Parliament had clearly intended an unlimited power.

  • Nor can the Court save a statute by narrowing the Constitution — that would be amendment (S.R. Bommai, 9 judges).

Basu's examples on each side of the line:

  • Rewriting he criticises: in Kishan Chand Arora v. Commissioner of Police, Calcutta, AIR 1961 SC 705, the majority (Wanchoo J) treated licence conditions in the Calcutta Police Act, 1866 as standards guiding the Commissioner's discretion to refuse a licence. Subba Rao J, dissenting, said this was an "unwarranted search for an undisclosed policy in the crevices of the statute" — especially odd for a pre-Constitution law. Basu agrees. (The source text heads this case "Kishan Chand v. State of Rajasthan"; the correct title is Kishan Chand Arora v. Commissioner of Police, Calcutta.) He also treats Vrajlal Manilal v. State of M.P., AIR 1970 SC 129 (reading an unstated exception into the M.P. Tendu Patta Act, 1964) as judicial redrafting.
  • English comparison: Lord Denning (Seaford Court Estates v. Asher, 1949) urged judges to "iron out the creases"; the House of Lords called reading words in "a naked usurpation of the legislative function". In Bangalore Water Supply v. A. Rajappa, AIR 1978 SC 548, the Supreme Court approved Denning partly but said the court's power to go outside the words is "strictly limited".

Over-broad restrictions on rights fall whole

Saving construction does not rescue a restriction on an Art 19(1) freedom framed widely enough to reach purposes outside clauses (2)–(6). Nothing so wide can be "reasonable":

  • Romesh Thappar (1950) and Chintaman Rao (1950) (chapter B5);
  • Superintendent, Central Prison v. Ram Manohar Lohia (1960): s. 3, U.P. Special Powers Act, 1932 punished instigating "any person or class of persons" not to pay dues — even a word to one person about a contractual payment. Saving it would have meant deleting "any person or"; the Court refused;
  • Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar, AIR 1962 SC 1166: a rule banning government servants from any demonstration about service conditions could not be read as banning only violent ones;
  • K.A. Abbas (K.A. Abbas v. UOI, AIR 1971 SC 481) — Hidayatullah CJ: a vague law should be construed if possible, but where those applying it are in "a boundless sea of uncertainty" it must fall, as in the Goonda Act case (State of M.P. v. Baldeo Prasad, AIR 1961 SC 293).

Basu adds that the Court's reluctance to strike down is greatest for social-welfare laws — e.g. laws protecting Scheduled Tribes' land from transfer to non-tribals (Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka, (1984) 3 SCC 301; Lingappa v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1985 SC 389).

sections.title: 5. Decide no more than necessary
sections.html:
The Court does not lay down rules wider than the facts require (Euclid v. Ambler Realty, 272 US 365 (1926)). Gajendragadkar J in Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam, AIR 1961 SC 232: courts "should be slow to embark upon an unnecessarily wide or general inquiry". The Court has called this "empiric adjudication" (Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram, AIR 1975 SC 1331).

Basu's illustrations — the Court deciding piecemeal even at the cost of repeat litigation:

  • Suraj Mall Mohta v. Visvanatha Sastri (1954) struck down s. 5(4) of the Taxation on Income (Investigation Commission) Act, 1947 under Art 14, but declined to examine s. 5(1) because the petitioner's case was under s. 5(4). Meenakshi Mills v. Visvanatha Sastri, AIR 1955 SC 13 then struck down amended s. 5(1), but declined to decide whether it was void from the start because the petitioners did not need that.
  • Bidi Supply Co. v. UOI, (1956) SCR 267 quashed an omnibus transfer order under s. 5(7A), Income-tax Act, 1922 without deciding the section's validity; when Parliament then amended the section to cover omnibus orders, Pannalal Binjraj v. UOI, (1957) SCR 233 had to decide it, and upheld it.
  • If a law falls under one Article (e.g. Art 19(1)(g)), the Court will not go on to decide whether it also violates another (e.g. Art 301) (Saghir Ahmad).

sections.title: The other side: the Court's duty to decide
sections.html:
Self-restraint is not abdication. Basu stresses that once a fundamental right is shown to be infringed:

  • the Court must decide, and must strike down the law if it is unconstitutional, just as it must uphold it otherwise (State of Madras v. V.G. Row; Kochunni; State of Punjab v. Khan Chand, AIR 1974 SC 543);
  • no prejudice need be shown — the violation itself voids the action (A.R. Antulay v. R.S. Nayak, AIR 1988 SC 1531);
  • a condition that obstructs access to the Court is void (Prem Chand Garg v. Excise Commissioner, AIR 1963 SC 996 — security for costs in an Art 32 petition);
  • finality clauses and even constitutional non-obstante clauses (e.g. Art 371F) do not exclude review (R.C. Poudyal v. UOI);
  • the possibility of abuse does not make a valid statute invalid; conversely, reasonable administration cannot save an unreasonable statute (Collector of Customs v. Nathella Sampathu Chetty, AIR 1962 SC 316; Mafatlal Industries v. UOI, (1997) 5 SCC 536).

sections.title: Standing in the USA
sections.html:
Standing asks whether this litigant is entitled to have the court decide the dispute. Even a concrete, adverse dispute fails if the plaintiff is the wrong person. The rationale is separation of powers: courts resolve real grievances of injured people, not "disembodied policy questions"; Congress cannot confer standing on people who lack the constitutional core.

The modern test (Allen v. Wright, 468 US 737 (1984)):

  • Constitutional core (Art III): (a) an injury in fact — "distinct and palpable", not abstract or conjectural; (b) fairly traceable to the defendant's conduct; (c) likely to be redressed by the relief sought.
  • Prudential limits (self-imposed, open to congressional override): no asserting third parties' rights; no generalised grievances shared by everyone; the injury must be within the zone of interests the provision protects.

Illustrations: legislators who lost a vote have no standing to challenge the Act (Raines v. Byrd, 521 US 811 (1997)); a man who never applied to a club cannot attack its membership rules (Moose Lodge No. 107 v. Irvis, 407 US 163 (1972)); a victim of a police choke-hold could sue for damages but not for an injunction, since he could not show he would be choked again (Los Angeles v. Lyons, 461 US 95 (1983)). Interests need not be economic — "aesthetic, conservational and recreational" values count.

Taxpayers. A federal taxpayer's interest in the Treasury is too "minute and indeterminable" to challenge spending (Frothingham v. Mellon, 262 US 447 (1923)), though a municipal ratepayer may. Flast v. Cohen, 392 US 83 (1968) opened a narrow door: a taxpayer may challenge an exercise of the taxing and spending power that breaches a specific limit such as the Establishment Clause. Basu traces the earlier religion-in-schools cases (Everson, McCollum, Doremus, Zorach) to show the law's uncertainty, and notes the Court has never applied the Mellon bar to a challenge to the exaction of a tax (Butler).

Basu's criticism: American standing rulings are inconsistent; sometimes "no standing" is a way to avoid an issue, and where the Court wants to give relief it relaxes the rule. Barrows v. Jackson, 346 US 249 (1953) admitted the bar on raising others' rights is a rule of practice that yields when fundamental rights need protection.

sections.title: Standing in India — the traditional rule
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Only a person whose own right is directly affected can challenge a law (Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. UOI (1950)). Three questions: (a) does the right belong to the petitioner? (b) has it been injured or immediately threatened by the law? (c) is the injury to the petitioner individually?

The right must be the petitioner's.

  • A petitioner cannot complain of discrimination suffered by others (State of A.P. v. McDowell, 1996), nor sue on behalf of a person merely because of that person's religious "obsession" (Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of W.B., (2004) 3 SCC 349).
  • A next friend may act for a minor, a person of unsound mind, or one under a legal disability. In Aruna Shanbaug v. UOI (2011), the hospital staff who had cared for the patient for decades, not a social activist, were treated as her next friend.
  • Habeas corpus and quo warranto are exceptions: anyone who is not an absolute stranger may apply (Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration, AIR 1978 SC 1675 — a prisoner for another prisoner).
  • The rule applies equally to challenges for lack of competence (Calcutta Gas Co. v. State of W.B., AIR 1962 SC 1044); so a law affecting bona vacantia has no one to challenge it.
  • The right must be subsisting when the petition is filed; locus is judged at filing, not by later events.
  • The rule has been applied liberally: an interest with a source in some statute is enough to avoid being a "stranger" (Ghulam Qadir v. Special Tribunal, (2002) 1 SCC 33); the Nair Service Society could challenge Kerala's failure to exclude the creamy layer (Nair Service Society v. State of Kerala, AIR 2007 SC 2891); the Court decided M.S. Jayaraj v. Commr. of Excise, AIR 2000 SC 3266 on merits despite doubts about locus.
  • The right to move the Court can be suspended collectively by a Presidential order under Art 359(1).

The interest need not be proprietary. It may be a right to manage a business, a contractual interest (either party to a contract affected by a statute may challenge it), a trustee's or a lessee's interest. But a person whose title is incomplete, or whose interest has expired or terminated, cannot complain under Art 19(1)(g).

The injury must be direct and imminent.

  • A person outside the class said to be discriminated against cannot challenge the classification.
  • One who never applied for a permit cannot attack the permit law (Harishankar Bagla v. State of M.P., [1955] 1 SCR 380).
  • A notice of tax liability is enough to come to court at once.
  • A law may infringe a right on enactment, without any overt act: in K.K. Kochunni v. State of Madras (1959), a private-member's Act taking away the petitioners' sthanam property rights in favour of rival claimants was challengeable immediately under Art 32.

Liberalisation short of PIL. Every citizen other than an officious busybody has an interest in removing a public grievance (Fertilizer Corporation Kamgar Union v. UOI, AIR 1981 SC 344 — workers challenging the sale of a public-sector plant; Jasbhai Motibhai Desai v. Roshan Kumar, AIR 1976 SC 578).

sections.title: Companies and shareholders
sections.html:
• A company is not a "citizen" and cannot claim Art 19 rights (State Trading Corporation v. CTO (1963); Tata Engineering & Locomotive Co. v. State of Bihar, AIR 1965 SC 40). It can claim rights given to "persons" (Arts 14, 21; the old Art 31 — Coffee Board v. Jt. CTO, AIR 1971 SC 870).
  • Chiranjit Lal: whether the company or its shareholders may sue depends on whose rights are affected. Ordinary shareholders failed there.
  • Dwarkadas Shrinivas: preference shareholders facing calls on their shares were directly affected and could sue.
  • R.C. Cooper v. UOI (1970): a shareholder could challenge bank nationalisation for violating his own rights, even though the measure operated on the bank. Shah J: the test is qualitative, not formal; where State action impairs the rights of both company and shareholders, the Court will not deny relief.
  • Bennett Coleman & Co. v. UOI (1972): shareholders, editors and printers could claim Art 19(1)(a) for a newspaper company; joining the company as co-petitioner did not defeat relief. Followed in Excel Wear v. UOI (1978).
  • Delhi Cloth & General Mills v. UOI, AIR 1983 SC 937 called the law "nebulous" but noted the trend: shareholders' and the company's Art 19 freedoms are co-extensive.

sections.title: Can the right to challenge be lost? Estoppel and waiver
sections.html:
USA

A person may lose standing by estoppel — e.g. one who has voluntarily taken a benefit under a statute (compensation, a licence, property rights) cannot attack its burdens, and one who sought enforcement of a statute cannot later call it unconstitutional. No estoppel arises if the benefit was taken under coercion or protest, if the challenged provision was added later, or as to a severable provision. Constitutional rights such as jury trial and even equal protection in jury selection can be waived (Patton v. United States, 281 US 276 (1930); Michel v. Louisiana, 350 US 91 (1955)).

India — no estoppel or waiver against fundamental rights

The Indian rule

"There can be no estoppel against the Constitution." Fundamental rights are put in the Constitution as a matter of public policy, not only for individual benefit; an individual cannot bargain them away, and a concession not to enforce them binds no one (Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985); Behram (1955); Basheshar Nath v. CIT, AIR 1959 SC 149).

In Basheshar Nath (Constitution Bench) the judges divided on reasons: Das CJ and Kapur J held that Art 14 cannot be waived, because it is an admonition to the State; Bhagwati and Subba Rao JJ went further — no fundamental right can be waived. Consequences Basu lists:

  • a right is not lost by non-exercise;
  • no one can contract not to claim it;
  • the State cannot rely on estoppel, acquiescence or waiver to escape its Part III obligations;
  • accepting retrenchment compensation does not bar challenge to an unlawful termination (Nar Singh Pal v. UOI, AIR 2000 SC 1401); accepting acquisition compensation does not waive Art 300A (Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority v. Devendra Kumar, (2011) 12 SCC 375).

But a mandatory provision enacted only for a party's own benefit can be waived by that party; one enacted in the public interest cannot (State Bank of Patiala v. S.K. Sharma, AIR 1996 SC 1669).

Seervai's dissent, which Basu reproduces at length

  • If American and Indian rights are similar, why can rights be waived in the US but never in India? It is "extravagant" to think only ours rest on public policy.
  • Enforcing rights is part of the administration of justice; rules of procedure, evidence, limitation and res judicata already apply to them — Daryao v. State of U.P., AIR 1961 SC 1457 (res judicata bars repeated Art 32 petitions) and Tilokchand Motichand v. H.B. Munshi (1969) (laches), reaffirmed in Rabindranath Bose v. UOI, AIR 1970 SC 470.
  • Art 14 does confer a right; and since no one is obliged to assert a right at all, public policy cannot consistently forbid him to settle for less. A "nascent democracy begins ill if it begins by countenancing bad faith".
How to use this in an answer

State the settled rule (Basheshar Nath, Olga Tellis: no waiver or estoppel), then note the qualification that procedural doctrines — res judicata (Daryao), laches (Tilokchand) — still apply, and mention Seervai's critique as the leading academic view.

sections.title: From locus standi to public interest litigation
sections.html:
What changed

From about 1980 the Supreme Court relaxed standing so that a public-spirited person or group acting bona fide could move the Court for people who cannot come themselves — because of custody, poverty, disability or social disadvantage — or for a public injury that affects no one individually. Upendra Baxi preferred to call it "social action litigation".

Its features (summarised from S.P. Gupta v. UOI (1981, 7 judges), PUDR v. UOI (1982), Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. UOI (1984)):

  • Standing relaxed: "any citizen who is acting bona fide and who has sufficient interest" may sue for public injury, public duty or "diffused" rights (Bhagwati J in S.P. Gupta).
  • Procedure relaxed: letters and telegrams treated as petitions; suo motu cognisance; affidavits not insisted on at first.
  • Non-adversarial: a "co-operative or collaborative effort" of petitioner, State and Court to secure rights of the vulnerable (PUDR).
  • New remedies: commissions, continuing directions, compensation.

Landmarks Basu cites: Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand, AIR 1980 SC 1622 (Krishna Iyer J — residents could force the municipality to deal with open drains; collective loss of a dignified life is justiciable); Akhil Bharatiya Soshit Karmachari Sangh v. UOI, AIR 1981 SC 298; Sunil Batra (prisoner); PUDR (Asiad construction workers); Bandhua Mukti Morcha (bonded labour); D.C. Wadhwa (an economics professor against re-promulgated Ordinances); S.P. Gupta (lawyers on judicial appointments); the M.C. Mehta environmental cases; Centre for PIL v. UOI (2012, 2G spectrum).

State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal, (2010) 3 SCC 402 describes three phases: (1) access to justice for the marginalised; (2) environment and ecology through an expanded Art 21; (3) probity in governance and corruption.

Limits on PIL

Guard-rails the Court has laid down

  • The petitioner must act bona fide — not for personal gain, private profit, political motive or publicity ("publicity interest litigation") (Janata Dal v. H.S. Chowdhary, (1992) 4 SCC 305; Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar, AIR 1991 SC 420). Vexatious petitions may be dismissed with heavy costs.

  • The Court must check the credentials of the informant, the specificity of the information and the gravity of the complaint; anonymous letters are not PILs (Divine Retreat Centre v. State of Kerala, AIR 2008 SC 1614).

  • Private disputes cannot be dressed up as PILs; no PIL in pending criminal matters — e.g. to cancel bail or monitor a trial after charge-sheet (Rajiv Ranjan Singh "Lalan" v. UOI, (2006) 6 SCC 613).

  • Laches applies: a challenge to a project should come before execution begins (Narmada Bachao Andolan v. UOI, (2000) 10 SCC 664).

  • No intrusion into policy; no direction to legislate; interim stays of public projects only where loss would be irreversible, with security for costs (Raunaq International v. IVR Construction, (1999) 1 SCC 492).

  • High Courts should ordinarily not entertain PILs challenging the validity of a statute, and have no power like Art 142 (Balwant Singh Chaufal).

  • BALCO Employees' Union v. UOI (2002): "PIL is not a pill or a panacea for all wrongs."

Who has been allowed and refused:

  • Allowed: an MP (but not an ordinary advocate without specific interest) on removal proceedings against a judge (Krishna Swami v. UOI, (1992) 4 SCC 605); a labour union by letter; a politician not acting for personal gain; a doctor challenging arrack sales in polythene bags; a professor challenging unqualified appointments.
  • Refused: a stranger pursuing an individual's cause without showing how he is interested; a petition on behalf of a sitting judge; challenges to a conviction by anyone but the convict or his representatives.

Judicial legislation through PIL

Basu quotes S.P. Sathe's criticism: expanding open-textured words like "life" or "liberty" is legitimate judicial law-making, but issuing guidelines on inter-country adoption, sexual harassment (Vishaka) or child labour is legislating and strains the separation of powers. The Court has itself drawn back: in P. Ramachandra Rao v. State of Karnataka, (2002) 4 SCC 578 (7 judges), it held courts cannot prescribe time-limits that bar criminal trials, since that is legislation; Katju J in Common Cause v. UOI, (2008) 5 SCC 511 warned against legislative or executive directions in PILs; V.K. Naswa v. UOI, (2012) 2 SCC 542 said the Court cannot direct the legislature, though it may fill a vacuum while the executive fails to act.

ddbu.title: Self-imposed limits (3) — advisory opinions, pleadings, timing and justiciability
ddbu.trail: Art 143; pleading a constitutional challenge; raising it at the right stage; res judicata; political questions and the non-justiciable parts of the Constitution

sections.title: Advisory opinions — Art 143
sections.html:
The US Supreme Court gives no advisory opinions (Art III "case or controversy"). India's Constitution deliberately departs from that. Under Art 143(1) the President may refer any question of law or fact of public importance that has arisen or is likely to arise; under Art 143(2) pre-Constitution treaty disputes excluded by the proviso to Art 131.

Key propositions Basu collects:

  • Discretion. Under 143(1) the Court may decline, giving reasons — e.g. if the question is purely political or socio-economic, of no constitutional significance, needs expert evidence, or is already settled (Special Courts Bill, In re, AIR 1979 SC 478; Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012). In Ismail Faruqui v. UOI (1994) it declined the Ayodhya reference, as one that did not serve a constitutional purpose and offended secularism. Even 143(2) references may be returned for good reason. A reference cannot, however, be rejected for mala fides.
  • No appeal in disguise. The President may ask the Court to reconsider a view of law, but not to reverse a decision between parties; that would invade judicial independence (Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, In re, AIR 1992 SC 522). The Court may clarify, explain or read down an earlier ratio, and treat remarks as obiter (Special Reference No. 1 of 2012).
  • A settled question cannot be referred. Once the Court has decided a point of law in its adjudicatory jurisdiction, there is no doubt for the President to resolve (Cauvery).
  • Uses so far in testing laws: an existing statute (In re Delhi Laws Act, 1951 — delegated legislation); a Bill passed and reserved (In re Kerala Education Bill, 1958); a draft Bill (In re Sea Customs Act, AIR 1963 SC 875); judicial appointments (Special Reference 1 of 1998); timing of elections after dissolution (Gujarat Assembly Election Matter, (2002) 8 SCC 237).
  • Effect. An opinion is not a judgment inter partes, cannot be executed and does not invalidate a law. It is entitled to great weight and is "normally" followed, though Basu doubts it binds courts under Art 141.
  • Only the Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction; no High Court does.

sections.title: Adequate pleading
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Because a statute is presumed valid, the challenger must plead specific facts showing how it violates the Constitution. Vague allegations, hypothetical facts or a bare plea that a law "offends Art 14" will not do.

  • US: facts must be specifically set out — e.g. that utility rates are confiscatory, that a regulation is arbitrary, or that similarly placed persons were treated differently.
  • India: the petitioner must show how his right is infringed, with averments and supporting documents; in writ proceedings affidavits are both pleading and evidence. A point not pleaded will not be entertained (Bharat Singh; Amrit Banaspati v. UOI, AIR 1995 SC 1340).
  • Art 14 challenges need specific, unambiguous allegations and a factual foundation that the persons compared are similarly situated (V.S. Rice & Oil Mills v. State of A.P., AIR 1964 SC 1781; Chiranjit Lal).
  • Anant Mills v. State of Gujarat (1975): the High Court struck down provisions of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act on presumed facts; the Supreme Court reversed — validity must not be decided on presumptions where direct evidence was available, because the ruling binds everyone affected. Basu adds a qualification drawn from Bhagwati J's dissent in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, (1982) 3 SCC 24: for some laws — given the right affected and the gravity of injury — the Court may call on the State to justify the law instead of presuming validity.
  • Mala fides must be pleaded with particulars; general assertions fail.
  • Averments not specifically denied are deemed admitted; a petitioner who suppresses material facts may be thrown out; a party must come with clean hands.
  • Rule of practice, not jurisdiction: a pure question of law arising on admitted facts may be allowed late, or the pleading amended; a point raised in the rejoinder may be argued. PIL pleadings are relaxed, but there must still be a factual foundation (State of M.P. v. Narmada Bachao Andolan, (2011) 7 SCC 639).
  • The Court decides only the provisions specifically attacked and actually causing injury (Euclid).

sections.title: A specific challenge
sections.html:
The US requires the exact constitutional provision to be named — in one harsh case a writ failed because the petitioner cited the Fifth instead of the Fourteenth Amendment against a State court.

India: allegations must be specific, clear and unambiguous, and the burden is on the challenger (Amrit Banaspati). But:

  • the litigant states facts; the Court takes judicial notice of the law, so a petition is not thrown out for citing the wrong Article — the Court can allow amendment at any stage;
  • because validity is presumed, the Court is not limited to the State's pleadings and may uphold the law under any provision;
  • in Sant Lal Bharti v. State of Punjab, AIR 1988 SC 485, a challenge to s. 4 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act failed because validity cannot be decided in the abstract.

sections.title: The proper stage
sections.html:
• US: constitutional objections must be raised at the earliest practicable moment, or they are forfeited (e.g. not for the first time on appeal), unless the defect could not have been anticipated.
  • India: the rule is applied with care so as not to forfeit a fundamental right. The Supreme Court will not allow a new question that needs fresh investigation of facts, but will allow a pure question of law on undisputed facts, or one going to the root of the matter or to jurisdiction (Rajendra Singh Verma v. Lt. Governor (NCT of Delhi), (2011) 10 SCC 1). In Mohd. Shahabuddin v. State of Bihar, (2010) 4 SCC 653, a challenge to a statute's validity raised for the first time in the Supreme Court was refused.

No "exhaustion" requirement — but res judicata applies

  • The US rule that State remedies must be exhausted before federal review (with its harsh habeas results) has no place in India, which has a single integrated judiciary. Since Art 32 is itself a fundamental right, a petitioner need not first go to the High Court (Romesh Thappar).
  • But after Daryao v. State of U.P., AIR 1961 SC 1457, a High Court decision on the merits under Art 226 is res judicata and bars a fresh Art 32 petition on the same matter; the remedy is appeal under Art 136. Constructive res judicata applies too.
  • Exception — habeas corpus: res judicata does not bar a fresh habeas corpus petition on new grounds (Ghulam Sarwar v. UOI, AIR 1967 SC 1335; Lallubhai Jogibhai Patel v. UOI, AIR 1981 SC 728), though a ground already rejected cannot be re-agitated.

sections.title: Justiciability and "political questions"
sections.html:
The distinction

Judicial review is the power, implicit in a written Constitution, to test any exercise of constitutional power. Justiciability concerns particular matters within that power that courts will not decide, usually for want of judicially manageable standards (A.K. Kaul v. UOI, AIR 1995 SC 1403).

The US doctrine

  • Marshall CJ disclaimed power over acts of the President within his discretion and over questions "in their nature political".
  • Colegrove v. Green, 328 US 549 (1946): Frankfurter J refused to enter the "political thicket" of unequal electoral districts.
  • Gomillion v. Lightfoot, 364 US 339 (1960) and Baker v. Carr, 369 US 186 (1962) narrowed this: a power cannot be used to reach an unconstitutional result (racial gerrymandering, unequal votes). Brennan J's six markers of a political question — chiefly a textually demonstrable commitment of the issue to another branch, or a lack of judicially manageable standards.
  • Applied: Powell v. McCormack, 395 US 486 (1969) — the House cannot exclude a member who meets the constitutional qualifications; justiciable. Nixon v. United States, 506 US 224 (1993) — Senate impeachment procedure is committed to the Senate; non-justiciable. The "republican form of government" guarantee (Luther v. Borden, 1849) and the amendment process (Coleman v. Miller, 1939) were treated as political.
  • Basu's verdict: in the end it is "the wisdom of the Court" that decides what is justiciable. Lord Diplock in the GCHQ case ([1985] AC 374) gave the English list: dissolution of Parliament, appointment of ministers, honours, treaties and foreign affairs.

India — non-justiciable by the Constitution's own text

  1. Directive Principles (Art 37) — "not enforceable by any court"; no law can be struck down for breaching them, and no mandamus lies to enforce them. They may still be used collaterally, e.g. to show a restriction on a right is reasonable (Balsara). Also Arts 350A and 351.
  2. Arts 31A, 31B and 31C — laws protected from challenge under Arts 14 and 19 — but subject to basic structure: Ninth Schedule laws inserted after 24 April 1973 can be tested (Waman Rao; I.R. Coelho); the 42nd Amendment's extension of Art 31C to all Directives was struck down in Minerva Mills; a law claiming Art 31C cover must have a real, not colourable, nexus with Art 39(b)/(c) (Tinsukhia Electric Supply Co. v. State of Assam, (1989) 3 SCC 709).
  3. Art 71(4) — a Presidential or Vice-Presidential election cannot be questioned because of a vacancy in the electoral college.
  4. Art 74(2) (and Art 163(3)) — courts cannot inquire whether and what advice Ministers gave. But the material on which the advice was based is not protected and may be examined (S.R. Bommai); the bar does not allow manifestly arbitrary or mala fide orders.
  5. Arts 77(2), 166(2) — a duly authenticated order cannot be challenged as not being the President's or Governor's order; other grounds remain open.
  6. Art 329 — delimitation laws and election disputes (chapter B9).
  7. Arts 100(2), 122, 189(2), 212 — internal proceedings (chapter B9). Proceedings vitiated by illegality or unconstitutionality, as opposed to irregularity, are reviewable (State of Punjab v. Satya Pal Dang, AIR 1969 SC 903 — a Speaker cannot act contrary to the Constitution); a challenge to the Speaker's own election lies by quo warranto.
  8. Art 255 — cures lack of prior sanction (chapter B9).
  9. Art 363 — disputes arising out of pre-Constitution treaties and covenants with Indian Rulers. UOI (1971); Mullaperiyar Environmental Protection Forum v. UOI, AIR 2006 SC 1428).

Powers based on the executive's "satisfaction"

  • Ordinances (Arts 123, 213). Historically the Governor's satisfaction was not justiciable (Bhagat Singh v. King-Emperor, 1931; Lakhi Narayan Das v. Province of Bihar, AIR 1950 FC 59). UOI, AIR 1982 SC 710 held review is not wholly excluded, but the challenger must first make out a prima facie case. In Satya Pal Dang the Court found no mala fides in proroguing an Assembly to pass the Budget by Ordinance; in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) mass re-promulgation of Ordinances was struck down as a fraud on the Constitution.
  • Emergencies (Arts 352, 356, 360). Once thought wholly non-justiciable (Lakhanpal v. UOI, AIR 1967 SC 243), the satisfaction is now reviewable for mala fides, extraneous considerations and absence of relevant material (S.R. Bommai; State of Rajasthan v. UOI, 1977). Rameshwar Prasad v. UOI, (2006) 2 SCC 1 struck down the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly: the Governor's report must rest on verified, relevant material, and stopping a party from forming a government is not a proper use of Art 356.

Intrinsically non-justiciable matters — and the Indian position after Bommai

Outside these provisions, courts decline only matters with no judicially manageable standards — classic examples being recognition of foreign States, war and peace, treaties. But Basu notes the Indian Court has followed Baker v. Carr and gone further. From S.R. Bommai (9 judges):

  1. Separation of powers is a basic feature, though not rigid; each organ must stay within its domain (Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, (1994) 3 SCC 569).
  2. Interpreting the Constitution is exclusively for the courts; what is supreme is the Constitution as interpreted by the Supreme Court (Art 141).
  3. The power and duty to enforce the Constitution lies on the courts.
  4. Where a statute invades fundamental rights, it cannot be shielded by calling the issue a "political question".
  5. The courts decide what powers each branch has and whether it has transgressed them.

Avoid the shortcut

"Political" is not a magic word in India. A dispute is not non-justiciable just because it is politically sensitive or concerns political rights. Ask: does the text commit the matter to another organ, and are there legal standards to decide it?
