ddbu.title: Self-imposed limits (4) — the presumption of constitutionality and deference to the legislature
ddbu.trail: Who carries the burden, how it shifts, why India rejects "preferred freedoms", and the weight given to legislative judgment, Directive Principles and long practice

sections.title: The presumption
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

"The presumption is always in favour of the constitutionality of an enactment, and the burden is upon him who attacks it to show that there has been a clear transgression of the constitutional principles" (Fazal Ali J in Chiranjit Lal (1950)). The legislature is presumed to understand its people's needs, to act on problems shown by experience, and to have good grounds for its classifications.

It is a self-imposed rule; the Constitution says nothing about it. In the US, it goes back to Fletcher v. Peck (1810) and Ogden v. Saunders (1827): "a decent respect due to the wisdom, integrity and patriotism of the legislative body" requires the court to presume validity, and to strike down only on a "clear and strong conviction" of incompatibility. It does not mean decisions must be unanimous; a majority of the bench decides (in India, constitutional questions need a bench of at least five: Art 145(3)).

The leading Indian restatement (Ram Krishna Dalmia v. S.R. Tendolkar, AIR 1958 SC 538; Amrit Banaspati v. UOI, 1995):

  1. There is always a presumption of constitutionality; the challenger must show a clear transgression.
  2. The legislature understands and correctly appreciates its people's needs; its discriminations rest on adequate grounds.
  3. To sustain the presumption, the Court may consider common knowledge, common report, the history of the times, and assume every state of facts which can be conceived to have existed when the law was made.

Corollaries:

  • The challenger must plead and prove the facts (chapter B13).
  • The Court is not limited to the State's pleadings; it may sustain the law under any provision.
  • Of two readings, the Court adopts the one that saves the law; it reads post-Constitution powers as meant to be exercised consistently with the Constitution (Narendra Kumar v. UOI, 1960). But it cannot give words a meaning they cannot bear — Basu warns against the US cases (Rumely, Harris) where language was strained to save a statute.
  • The presumption is stronger for laws acted on for a long time (Dwarkadas) — but an invalid law does not become valid by not being challenged (Lohia Machines v. UOI, AIR 1985 SC 421).
  • It applies to legislative competence too: a legislature with limited powers is presumed to know its limits, and entries are read widely (Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1995 SC 142).
  • It extends to laws imposing reasonable restrictions, and to a presumption that statutory power will not be exercised arbitrarily (PUCL v. UOI, AIR 2004 SC 1442).
  • The Statement of Objects and Reasons may be used to understand the background and the mischief (Gurudevdatta VKSSS Maryadit v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2001 SC 1980), though the Act stands or falls on its own provisions, not on the State's affidavit (Goa Glass Fibre v. State of Goa, (2010) 6 SCC 499).
  • Under Art 14 the Court hesitates to call a classification irrational, being remote from local conditions (G.K. Krishnan v. State of T.N., AIR 1975 SC 583); the latitude is greatest for tax and economic laws (R.K. Garg v. UOI (1981)).

sections.title: When the presumption gives way
sections.html:
The presumption is one of fact and is rebuttable. Mahajan J in State of W.B. v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952): to presume "some undisclosed and unknown reason" for hostile discrimination would make equal protection "a mere rope of sand". So:

  • It has no force where a law is discriminatory on its face and makes no attempt to classify, or is patently arbitrary (Ram Prasad Narayan Sahi v. State of Bihar, 1953).
  • Art 14: the challenger must place material showing the classification is unreasonable, but once a prima facie case is made, the State must justify it (State of Maharashtra v. Manubhai Pragaji Vashi, AIR 1996 SC 1). Where State action appears uninformed by reason, the State must show it was an informed, reasonable decision (Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P., AIR 1991 SC 537). "Manifest arbitrariness" rebuts it (Bombay Dyeing v. Bombay Environmental Action Group, AIR 2006 SC 1489).
  • Art 19: once the petitioner shows a prima facie infringement of a right in Art 19(1), the burden shifts to the State to bring the law within clauses (2)–(6) and show it is reasonable, with material (Saghir Ahmad (1954); Dharam Dutt (2004); Re Ramlila Maidan Incident, (2012) 5 SCC 1). If the State shows a permitted ground, the burden of proving unreasonableness returns to the petitioner — unless the restriction is unreasonable on its face (Chintaman Rao). The same applies under Art 304.
  • Arts 15 and 16(2): once discrimination on a prohibited ground is shown, the State must bring itself within an exception (Patanjali Sastri CJ in Kathi Raning Rawat). But Basu adds: Art 16(1) works like Art 14 — classification is implicit in it, so the challenger bears the burden (Indra Sawhney, 9 judges). Under Art 16(4), the State must justify reservation above 50%.
  • Gender stereotypes: in Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2008), the ban on women working in bars was struck down; protective legislation built on stereotype must meet a test of proportionality.
  • Where the right and the injury are grave, the Court may demand justification from the State instead of presuming validity — a view Basu takes from Bhagwati J's dissent in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, (1982) 3 SCC 24.

Can evidence be taken?

  • US: usually decided on pleadings and judicially noticed facts, but evidence (even expert) is admitted where reasonableness depends on facts, and cases are remanded to trial courts for it.
  • India: writ proceedings are normally decided on affidavits. High Courts may take evidence on issues like mala fides or allow cross-examination. In Kochunni (1959), Das CJ held the Supreme Court cannot refuse an Art 32 petition because it involves disputed facts; it may decide on affidavits, issue commissions, or even set the matter down for trial. Basu says High Courts should take the same view where fundamental rights are at stake, and criticises later decisions that refused (e.g. Arya Vyasa Sabha v. Commr., H.R.E., AIR 1976 SC 475).

sections.title: "Preferred freedoms" — rejected in India
sections.html:
US: since United States v. Carolene Products, 304 US 144 (1938) (footnote 4), the presumption is weaker where a law touches specific guarantees such as the First Amendment or burdens "discrete and insular minorities". Three tiers developed: strict scrutiny (compelling interest, least restrictive means; presumption reversed), intermediate scrutiny (e.g. sex classifications — important objective, substantially related), and rational basis (very deferential). Critics included Frankfurter J (Kovacs v. Cooper, 1949: "a mischievous phrase") and Jackson J (Brinegar, 1949: preferring some rights relegates others).

The Indian position

There is no hierarchy among fundamental rights and no "preferred position" for any (Madhu Limaye v. S.D.M., Monghyr, AIR 1971 SC 2486). All Art 19(1) freedoms are tested by the same standard of reasonableness. American strict scrutiny is not applied; the burden is on the challenger (Saurabh Chaudri v. UOI, AIR 2004 SC 361; Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. UOI, (2008) 6 SCC 1).

But Basu notes the mixed signals:

  • The Court has called speech "the mother of all liberties" occupying a "preferred position" (Ramlila Maidan, 2012), and in Govt. of A.P. v. P. Laxmi Devi, AIR 2008 SC 1640 it said the "clear and present danger" test should be used for speech restrictions — Basu doubts even the US still applies it that way.
  • Laws touching civil liberties (speech, movement, religion) get less latitude than economic laws (Laxmi Devi; R.K. Garg), and the State may carry a heavier burden to justify censorship (LIC v. Manubhai D. Shah, (1992) 3 SCC 637; Indian Express Newspapers v. UOI, (1985) 1 SCC 641 on newsprint tax).

sections.title: Respect for legislative determination
sections.html:
The Court decides power, not wisdom. In the US the Court long denied deciding policy, yet struck down New Deal and labour laws (Butler, 1936, over Stone J's dissent) until the 1937 turn: "we do not sit as a super-legislature" (Day-Brite Lighting v. Missouri, 342 US 421 (1952)); "courts do not substitute their social and economic beliefs for the judgment of legislative bodies" (Ferguson v. Skrupa, 372 US 726 (1963)).

In India, Patanjali Sastri CJ's caution in State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) is the classic statement: in judging reasonableness the judges' social philosophy inevitably plays a part, so the limit of interference must come from "their sense of responsibility and self-restraint and the sobering reflection that the Constitution is meant not only for people of their way of thinking but for all", and that the people's representatives thought the restrictions reasonable. But the ultimate responsibility is the Court's, and it "must not shirk that solemn duty" (Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar, AIR 1958 SC 731).

Where it shows:

  • Equality: the legislature may recognise degrees of harm, attack the evil where it is clearest, and proceed step by step (Sakhawant Ali v. State of Orissa, AIR 1955 SC 166 — disqualifying lawyers retained against a municipality from standing for its council, without covering litigants, was valid).
  • Legislative findings of fact: a legislative declaration on public conditions deserves great respect (Holmes J in Block v. Hirsch, 1921); recitals in a Preamble are not to be disputed (Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1957 SC 510). Conversely, when Preamble and objects disclose no policy, delegated power may fail (A.N. Parasuraman).
  • Social, labour and economic laws — hours of work, minimum wages (Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer, AIR 1955 SC 33), price control, essential commodities, import-export, closure compensation, s. 25N Industrial Disputes Act (Workmen of Meenakshi Mills v. Meenakshi Mills, (1992) 3 SCC 336): trial and error is the legislature's to make. Welfare statutes are read liberally in favour of the class they protect.
  • Tax laws: the extent of the burden is for the legislature; a tax is struck down under Art 14 only for "palpable arbitrariness" (Kerala Hotel & Restaurant Assn. v. State of Kerala, AIR 1990 SC 913) — though an exorbitant, unscientific increase has been struck down (Bidhannagar (Salt Lake) Welfare Assn. v. Central Valuation Board, AIR 2007 SC 2276).
  • Public servants: conduct rules under Art 309 are respected unless they clearly breach a right (Kameshwar Prasad struck one down).

Directive Principles as a measure of reasonableness

Although not enforceable, Directives inform how the Court reads rights and judges restrictions:

  • A restriction that furthers a Directive is presumptively reasonable and in the public interest (Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of J&K, AIR 1980 SC 1992; Papnasam Labour Union v. Madura Coats, AIR 1995 SC 2200; Laxmi Khandsari v. State of U.P., AIR 1981 SC 873).
  • Examples: cow-slaughter bans under Arts 47–48 (Quareshi, 1958; State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat, (2005) 8 SCC 534); prohibition (Balsara); Wealth Tax and Art 39(a); Kesavananda on Art 39(b); widening List III entries (Welfare Association ARP v. Ranjit Gohil, (2003) 9 SCC 358).
  • Directives are "equally fundamental to the understanding and interpretation" of rights (Olga Tellis); rights are read with Parts IV and IV-A as one scheme.
  • But balance is itself a basic feature: public good may tilt the balance, not overturn individual liberty (I.R. Coelho).

But the ultimate responsibility is the Court's, and it "must not shirk that solemn duty" ( Mohd. Hanif Quareshi v. State of Bihar , AIR 1958 SC 731). Where it shows: Equality: the legislature may recognise degrees of harm, attack the evil where it is clearest, and proceed step by step ( Sakhawant Ali v. State of Orissa , AIR 1955 SC 166 — disqualifying lawyers retained against a municipality from standing for its council, without covering litigants, was valid). Legislative findings of fact: a legislative declaration on public conditions deserves great respect (Holmes J in Block v. Hirsch , 1921); recitals in a Preamble are not to be disputed ( Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan , AIR 1957 SC 510). Conversely, when Preamble and objects disclose no policy, delegated power may fail ( A.N. Parasuraman ). Social, labour and economic laws — hours of work, minimum wages ( Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer , AIR 1955 SC 33), price control, essential commodities, import-export, closure compensation, s. 25N Industrial Disputes Act ( Workmen of Meenakshi Mills v. Meenakshi Mills , (1992) 3 SCC 336): trial and error is the legislature's to make. Welfare statutes are read liberally in favour of the class they protect. Tax laws: the extent of the burden is for the legislature; a tax is struck down under Art 14 only for "palpable arbitrariness" ( Kerala Hotel & Restaurant Assn. v. State of Kerala , AIR 1990 SC 913) — though an exorbitant, unscientific increase has been struck down ( Bidhannagar (Salt Lake) Welfare Assn. v. Central Valuation Board , AIR 2007 SC 2276). Public servants: conduct rules under Art 309 are respected unless they clearly breach a right ( Kameshwar Prasad struck one down). Directive Principles as a measure of reasonableness Although not enforceable, Directives inform how the Court reads rights and judges restrictions: A restriction that furthers a Directive is presumptively reasonable and in the public interest ( Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of J&K , AIR 1980 SC 1992; Papnasam Labour Union v. Madura Coats , AIR 1995 SC 2200; Laxmi Khandsari v. State of U.P. , AIR 1981 SC 873). Examples: cow-slaughter bans under Arts 47–48 ( Quareshi , 1958; State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat , (2005) 8 SCC 534); prohibition ( Balsara ); Wealth Tax and Art 39(a); Kesavananda on Art 39(b); widening List III entries ( Welfare Association ARP v. Ranjit Gohil , (2003) 9 SCC 358). Directives are "equally fundamental to the understanding and interpretation" of rights ( Olga Tellis ); rights are read with Parts IV and IV-A as one scheme. But balance is itself a basic feature: public good may tilt the balance, not overturn individual liberty ( I.R. Coelho ).

sections.title: Respect for long-standing practice
sections.html:
• US: long, unbroken legislative practice can make the presumption nearly conclusive, mainly in foreign affairs, foreign commerce and defence — e.g. broad delegation to the President in foreign affairs (United States v. Curtiss-Wright, 299 US 304 (1936)); tariff powers (Field v. Clark, 143 US 649 (1892)); protective tariffs since 1789 (J.W. Hampton & Co. v. United States, 276 US 394 (1928)).
  • India: contemporaneous exposition and long usage are ordinary common-law aids to construction, usable for the Constitution within limits — e.g. in reading Art 286 (State of Bombay v. United Motors, AIR 1953 SC 252) and "terminal tax" and "octroi" (Burmah Shell v. Belgaum Municipality, AIR 1963 SC 906). Where two readings are possible, the Court is reluctant to upset a long course of action. But practice under the Government of India Acts must be used with care given the different constitutional set-up, and practice can never validate what plainly violates the Constitution.

ddbu.title: Self-imposed limits (5) — stare decisis in constitutional cases
ddbu.trail: Why constitutional courts revisit their own decisions more readily, and the cautions Basu insists on

sections.title: The doctrine
sections.html:
Stare decisis et non quieta movere — stand by decided cases and do not disturb what is settled. It serves certainty, consistency and continuity: people arrange their affairs on the law as declared, and a court that changed its mind often would make the law "an ignis fatuus to mislead". A view that has held the field for long should not be disturbed merely because another view is possible (Shanker Raju v. UOI, (2011) 2 SCC 132).

Vertical precedent is fixed by Art 141: law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts. Within the Court:

  • a bench is bound by a larger bench, and a bench of co-equal strength cannot overrule an earlier one — it must refer the question to a larger bench (UOI v. Raghubir Singh, AIR 1989 SC 1933; Central Board of Dawoodi Bohra Community v. State of Maharashtra, (2005) 2 SCC 673);
  • Raghubir Singh recommended benches of at least three judges for authoritative rulings;
  • a decision per incuriam — given in ignorance of a statute or binding authority — may be disregarded (State of U.P. v. Synthetics & Chemicals, (1991) 4 SCC 139);
  • a Constitution Bench may declare that conflicting decisions "stand denuded of their status as precedents" without naming each one (Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi, AIR 2006 SC 1806).

Basu notes M.P. Jain's surprise when an eleven-judge decision (T.M.A. Pai, 2002) was "interpreted" by five judges (Islamic Academy, 2003) and then by seven (P.A. Inamdar, 2005).

sections.title: Other jurisdictions
sections.html:
• House of Lords: strictly bound by its own decisions from London Street Tramways v. LCC (1898) until the 1966 Practice Statement, which allowed departure "when it appears right to do so", while warning about contracts, property, tax and criminal law. First used in Conway v. Rimmer, [1968] AC 910, overruling Duncan v. Cammell Laird (1942) on Crown privilege.
  • Privy Council: never formally bound, but slow to depart on constitutional questions.
  • USA: because constitutional amendment is so hard, the Court "has freely exercised its power to re-examine the basis of its constitutional decisions" (Smith v. Allwright, 321 US 649 (1944)). "The ultimate touchstone of constitutionality is the Constitution itself and not what we have said about it" (Frankfurter J in Graves v. New York, 1939). Famous reversals: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) ending Plessy's "separate but equal"; Erie Railroad v. Tompkins (1938) overruling Swift v. Tyson; Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) on counsel for indigent accused; Mapp v. Ohio (1961) on illegally obtained evidence.
  • Ireland and Australia treat stare decisis as a policy, not a rule — departure is justified where the earlier case ignored a statute or a binding authority, or rested on a concession without argument.

Attribution slip in the source

Two US dicta are swapped in the source text. "Stare decisis is not, like the rule of res judicata, a universal inexorable command" is Lurton J in Hertz v. Woodman, 218 US 205 (1910). "It is more important that the applicable rule of law be settled than that it be settled right… [but] in cases involving the Federal Constitution… this Court has often overruled its earlier decisions" is Brandeis J, dissenting, in Burnet v. Coronado Oil & Gas, 285 US 393 (1932).

sections.title: India: willing to overrule, especially on the Constitution
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

The Supreme Court is not bound by its own decisions and reconsiders constitutional rulings more readily than others, because the error can otherwise be cured only by constitutional amendment. But it does so sparingly, for compelling reasons, and never merely because a different view is possible or the bench has changed.

Leading reversals:

  • Golak Nath (1967) overruled Sankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh on amendment of fundamental rights; Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges) then overruled Golak Nath.
  • Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar (1955) overruled State of Bombay v. United Motors (1953) on the Explanation to Art 286(1)(a), within two years — the Court said it owed it to the public not to let an erroneous tax ruling stand.
  • Maneka Gandhi (1978) departed from Gopalan on Art 21.
  • Supt. & Remembrancer of Legal Affairs v. Corporation of Calcutta (1967) overruled Director of Rationing v. Corporation of Calcutta (1960) on the State being bound by statutes, as inconsistent with a republican polity.

Reasons for the relaxed approach in constitutional cases:

  1. Statutory errors can be corrected by ordinary legislation; constitutional errors need the special amending process.
  2. The Constitution, not the Court's earlier gloss, is the touchstone; "it is better to be ultimately right than to be consistently wrong" (Ganga Sugar Corp. v. State of U.P., (1980) 1 SCC 223).
  3. Constitutional rulings affect the public at large; a manifestly wrong and harmful one should be corrected, especially if recent and no rule of property has grown around it.
  4. In Punjab University v. Vijay Singh, AIR 1976 SC 1441, the Court said precedents should be "stepping stones and halting places", not shackles; but Cardozo's warning holds — changes in the Court's membership should not bring changes in its rulings.

When the Court will reconsider (collected from Keshav Mills v. CIT, AIR 1965 SC 1636; Maganlal Chhaganlal v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, AIR 1974 SC 2009; Dawoodi Bohra):

  • a patent aspect went unnoticed, a relevant statute or earlier decision was overlooked, or the decision rested on a mistake of fact;
  • it is clearly erroneous and its continuance harms the public, particularly if recent;
  • the contextual values that produced it have substantially changed;
  • it is inconsistent with the legal philosophy of the Constitution.

The Dawoodi Bohra criteria for overruling, summarised: use the power sparingly; do not upset legitimate expectations of those who arranged their affairs on the decision; overrule a construction of a statute only in rare cases; not where consequences cannot be foreseen or where the change should be part of a comprehensive reform; not merely because the earlier case was wrong — there must be some further reason; but do overrule where the ruling causes great practical uncertainty or is out of keeping with contemporary social conditions and public policy.

Basu's cautions

  • Do not overrule with a divided court.
  • Length of time alone is no bar, but be slow where property or contract rights rest on the decision.
  • Never let reversal follow a change in the Court's composition — Venkatarama Aiyar J in Bengal Immunity warned that reopening decisions because a new bench prefers another view would be most damaging to the Court's prestige; compare Frankfurter J's warning that law must not seem "the expression of chance".
  • India sits between England and the US: its Constitution is far easier to amend (Basu counted 78 amendments in 45 years; there have been many more since), so the Court should be slower than the US Court to reverse itself — yet it would be circular to say that both judicial correction and constitutional amendment should be avoided. Hence a via media.
  • In Indra Sawhney (9 judges) the Court summed up its practice: respect a decision that has stood the test of time unless there are compelling reasons; where there is no uniformity, decide the question afresh in light of the Constitution's scheme.
  • A law may also cease to be good law through changed conditions — cessante ratione cessat ipsa lex (minority in State of Punjab v. Devans Modern Breweries, (2004) 11 SCC 26; compare John Vallamattom).

Prospective overruling

Golak Nath used prospective overruling — new law for the future, the old rule for the past — to avoid disturbing past amendments. It does not abolish stare decisis; it confines its effect to past transactions. (Chapter B17 deals with it in detail.)

Advisory opinions as precedent

Strictly, an Art 143 opinion is not an adjudication between parties. In practice lower courts treat it as having the same authority as a judgment, and the Federal Court said advisory opinions were no less binding for being advisory.

ddbu.title: The duty to decide — substance, indirect encroachment and attempts to oust review
ddbu.trail: Courts must decide and strike down when the Constitution requires it; how they find a law's real character; why time, motive and finality clauses do not save it

sections.title: A duty, not a discretion
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

Restraint has a counterpart: once a constitutional question is properly raised and the law clearly transgresses, the court must say so. Marshall CJ (Cohens v. Virginia, 1821): "We have no more right to decline the exercise of jurisdiction which is given, than to usurp that which is not given. The one or the other would be treason to the Constitution."

Basu reconciles Marshall's duty with Brandeis J's avoidance rules in Ashwander (chapter B11): the avoidance rules chart the limits of judicial power (cases, controversies, standing); within those limits, the duty to decide is absolute. The court should not be deterred by:

  1. the risk that the executive will disregard its judgment;
  2. serious economic or social consequences of invalidation;
  3. the smallness of the violation — courts must resist even "petty encroachments" on rights;
  4. its own view that the law is beneficial;
  5. the law's long operation;
  6. likely public reaction.

India. Art 13 makes infringing laws "void"; Art 32 makes the remedy itself a fundamental right; so the Court is the "sentinel on the qui vive" (Romesh Thappar). Once a fundamental right and its breach are prima facie shown, relief follows ex debito justitiae (N. Masthan Sahib v. Chief Commissioner, Pondicherry, AIR 1962 SC 797). The duty is as much to strike down an unconstitutional provision as to uphold a valid one (State of Punjab v. Khan Chand, AIR 1974 SC 543). Gajendragadkar CJ in Devilal v. STO, AIR 1965 SC 1150 confirmed that High Courts under Art 226 are equally bound to protect fundamental rights — Basu's long-held view.

Basu's complaint about "retrograde inroads"

Basu regrets that the Court later treated rights enforcement like ordinary civil remedies: requiring petitioners first to approach the High Court; applying res judicata after an Art 226 dismissal (Daryao); and applying laches (Tilokchand). He attributes this partly to arrears and to the growth in the Court's size. (Seervai, by contrast, defends these procedural limits — see chapter B12.)

sections.title: Look at substance, not form
sections.html:
Courts must not be "beguiled" by the label the legislature chooses; they ascertain the law's real character and its substantial effect on the right "in the light of its practical application in the affairs of men" (US cases such as Near v. Minnesota, 1931). Das CJ in In re Kerala Education Bill (1958): weigh "the real effect and impact" on the right.

What the court looks at to find the "true character":

  • the object, purpose and intention of the law as a whole — Title, Preamble, the mischief it addresses, legislative history and surrounding circumstances (Hamdard Dawakhana v. UOI, AIR 1960 SC 554). A legislature's own statement of purpose deserves respect but is not conclusive (Australian authority Basu cites);
  • the scope, operation and effect of the provisions — not how it has in fact been worked in particular cases, but how it may operate under its terms;
  • the means by which the object is to be secured: a legitimate purpose does not save terms that authorise improper application (Peerless General Finance v. RBI, AIR 1992 SC 1033).

"Direct impact" and its evolution

  • Gopalan (Kania CJ): ask whether the law is directed against the right; a preventive detention law is directed at Art 21, so Art 19 is not engaged.
  • Ram Singh v. State of Delhi (1951) and Express Newspapers (1958): only proximate, not remote or incidental, effects count. The Working Journalists Act was "directed" at journalists' service conditions; its possible strain on marginal newspapers was incidental, not a "direct and inevitable" result.
  • Sakal Papers v. UOI (1962): fixing pages by price under the Newspaper (Price and Page) Act was a direct infringement of Art 19(1)(a), not mere business regulation.
  • R.C. Cooper (1970) and Bennett Coleman (1972): object and form are irrelevant; the test is the effect on the right — "direct" goes to the quality of the effect, not the subject-matter. In Bennett Coleman, newsprint controls limiting pages and circulation infringed Art 19(1)(a) whatever their stated subject.
  • Maneka Gandhi (1978): "direct and inevitable effect"; a law may have to satisfy several rights at once (Bachan Singh).
  • Papnasam Labour Union (1995): a restriction must have a direct, proximate and reasonable nexus with its object and not be excessive.
  • M.H. Devendrappa v. Karnataka State Small Industries Development Corp., AIR 1998 SC 1064: a rule primarily aimed at efficiency and discipline in service is not invalid merely because it incidentally touches other freedoms, provided the impingement is minimal.

Don't confuse "substance" with "pith and substance"

"Pith and substance" (borrowed from Canada) answers a competence question: is the law, as an organic whole, really about a subject in the legislature's List? If so, incidental encroachment on another List does not matter (e.g. the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act upheld as State legislation: Zameer Ahmed Latifur Rehman Sheikh v. State of Maharashtra, (2010) 5 SCC 246). For fundamental rights, the question is different: what is the law's direct effect on the right? Basu regrets that some decisions use "pith and substance" in rights cases and recommends keeping the phrase to competence.

sections.title: Gradual and stealthy encroachment
sections.html:
Bradley J in Boyd v. United States, 116 US 616 (1886): illegitimate practices "get their first footing… by silent approaches and slight deviations"; courts must be "watchful for the constitutional rights of the citizen, and against any stealthy encroachments thereon". Mahajan J applied this in Dwarkadas Shrinivas (1954), and Hidayatullah J in Golak Nath warned that "small inroads lead to larger inroads". So the court must strike down a restriction as soon as it reaches a magnitude that threatens "total annihilation" of the right (Peerless).

Basu ties this to basic structure: features such as constitutional supremacy, separation of powers, republican and secular government, federalism, dignity of the individual, unity and integrity, parliamentary democracy, independence of the judiciary and judicial review, equality, and Art 32 itself cannot be abrogated by amendment (Kesavananda; Minerva Mills; Bommai).
sections.text: Bradley J in Boyd v. United States , 116 US 616 (1886): illegitimate practices "get their first footing… by silent approaches and slight deviations"; courts must be "watchful for the constitutional rights of the citizen, and against any stealthy encroachments thereon". Mahajan J applied this in Dwarkadas Shrinivas (1954), and Hidayatullah J in Golak Nath warned that "small inroads lead to larger inroads". So the court must strike down a restriction as soon as it reaches a magnitude that threatens "total annihilation" of the right ( Peerless ). sections.title: Time does not cure unconstitutionality
sections.html: Long acquiescence calls for caution before striking down, and for saving constructions where possible. But where the invalidity is clear, the court will act however late — many Acts of Congress were struck down decades after enactment. Basu rejects Hidayatullah J's suggestion in Golak Nath that long acquiescence by the people may cure unconstitutionality: popular consent is the foundation of a Constitution as a whole, not a way of ratifying particular breaches of it. Similarly, paying an illegal tax without protest does not bar relief (Amalgamated Coalfields v. Janapada Sabha, AIR 1961 SC 964).

sections.title: Colourable legislation and "illusory compensation"
sections.html:
(See chapter B10 for the general doctrine.) Basu adds:

  • The US used the idea to widen "State action": Texas could not escape the Fifteenth Amendment by letting a party exclude Black voters from primaries (Smith v. Allwright, 1944); a power cannot be used "to accomplish an unlawful end" (Gomillion).
  • Das J in Kameshwar Singh (1952): a law that fails a constitutional condition covertly is a "fraud on the Constitution". Laws giving no real compensation for acquiring estates were struck down on that basis.
  • After the 25th Amendment replaced "compensation" with "amount" in Art 31(2), the majority in Kesavananda held that the amount still could not be illusory, fixed on irrelevant principles, or paid in an arbitrary manner (Sikri CJ: an amount payable at Rs 10 a year would fail). This survives under Art 14 (Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar, 1995).

sections.title: Reading one statute with another
sections.html:
• State of M.P. v. Mandawar, AIR 1954 SC 493: validity under Art 13 is tested on the impugned law itself. Two laws by the same legislature that are in substance one scheme may be read together; but a law cannot be held discriminatory by comparing it with a law of another legislature (Central and State dearness allowance rates could differ).
  • Contrast: where the same authority could acquire land under two Acts paying different compensation, the owner who got less can invoke Art 14 (Nagpur Improvement Trust v. Vithal Rao, (1973) 1 SCC 500).
  • Krishna Sugar Mills v. UOI, AIR 1959 SC 1124 (4:2): the majority (Hidayatullah J) upheld a sugar-export levy as reasonable because a notification under a different Act raised home prices to offset the loss — treating them as one legislative plan. Sarkar and Subba Rao JJ dissented: validity cannot depend on what the executive may do or undo at any time. Basu sides with the dissent.

Can rules made under an Act save the Act?

  • Rules and guidelines may show that a discretion is not uncanalised (Tika Ramji v. State of U.P., (1956) SCR 393; RBI guidelines under SARFAESI in Mardia Chemicals v. UOI, (2005) 4 SCC 311), and may aid construction as contemporaneous exposition.
  • But Basu argues rules cannot cure a defect in the Act, because the executive can change them: Bose J (dissenting) in State of Bombay v. United Motors, AIR 1953 SC 252 — "I am not prepared to agree that rules can save an Act." A statute's competence cannot depend on rules that may be deleted tomorrow (Hotel Balaji v. State of A.P., 1993 Supp (4) SCC 536). Rules may, however, be looked at to find a law's pith and substance or to unmask a fraud on power.

sections.title: Attempts to oust judicial review
sections.html:
The rule

Any law that bars or renders illusory the jurisdiction under Arts 32, 136, 226 or 227 is void; even constitutional amendments cannot exclude it, because judicial review is basic structure.

  • Indirect ouster: s. 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 forbade disclosure of the grounds of detention to the court; it was struck down in Gopalan because it disabled the court from testing detention under Art 22(5) and Art 32. Severing s. 14 left the rest of the Act intact.
  • Finality clauses in statutes do not bar constitutional remedies (Deokinandan Prasad v. State of Bihar, AIR 1971 SC 1409), nor do constitutional finality clauses such as Art 217(3) (UOI v. Jyoti Prakash Mitter, 1971) or Art 311(3) (Satyavir Singh v. UOI, AIR 1986 SC 555).
  • Kihoto Hollohan (1992): para 7 of the Tenth Schedule, excluding courts from disqualification disputes, was invalid for want of ratification under Art 368(2); a finality clause does not protect action that is ultra vires, mala fide or colourable.
  • L. Chandra Kumar (1997): Arts 323A(2)(d) and 323B(3)(d), to the extent they excluded Arts 226, 227 and 32, were unconstitutional.
  • Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): Art 329A(4), inserted by the 39th Amendment to place the Prime Minister's election beyond challenge, was struck down.
  • A rule of the Supreme Court requiring security for costs in Art 32 petitions was itself struck down (Prem Chand Garg, 1963).
  • A general bar on "courts" is read so as not to touch the High Courts and Supreme Court. But a law that incidentally reduces the area of writ jurisdiction (e.g. by creating a new remedy) does not abridge Art 226.
  • In the US, a statute that prevents proof of facts showing a law has no rational basis itself violates due process (Carolene Products).

sections.title: Forms and effects of unconstitutionality
sections.html: C.D. Jha's five forms: (1) lack of competence under the distribution of powers; (2) excessive delegation; (3) breach of Part III; (4) breach of other constitutional restrictions; (5) (in some views) breach of natural justice. Basu's own view (with Behram and Deep Chand) is that both incompetence and breach of Part III make a post-Constitution law void ab initio; Arvind Datar agrees, while Jha follows Sundararamier's distinction (chapter B4).

sections.title: A checklist of canons collected by Basu
sections.html:
When a statute is challenged, the court:

  • presumes it valid and resolves real doubt in its favour; but the presumption does not arise where the law makes no classification at all, and under Art 19(1)(g) the State must justify a facially restrictive law;
  • looks at substance, treating the Act as an organic whole;
  • reads down where possible; strikes down where not;
  • does not rely on the State's affidavit to supply a policy the Act lacks (Seervai's criticism of affidavits filed years later explaining a classification);
  • ignores motive and alleged mala fides of the legislature (no "transferred malice");
  • does not invalidate for hardship, vagueness alone, mere inequality, the possibility of abuse, absence of an appeal (Jamshed N. Guzdar v. State of Maharashtra, (2005) 2 SCC 591), breach of legitimate expectation (Sri Srinivasa Theatre v. Govt. of T.N., 1992), or lack of a hearing before legislation (MRF Ltd. v. Inspector, Kerala Govt., (1998) 8 SCC 227);
  • does not apply basic structure to ordinary legislation (Kuldip Nayar; State of A.P. v. McDowell) — only competence and Part III or other express limits;
  • does not invalidate laws for offending the "spirit" of the Constitution (Kameshwar Singh). Basu points out the paradox: the same Court that refused to apply "spirit" to ordinary laws brought it in "through the backdoor" against constitutional amendments via basic structure;
  • requires the State to be a party before deciding the validity of its law, and does not let a tribunal created by a statute judge that statute's validity;
  • treats delay as no bar to deciding constitutionality where a fundamental right is in issue;
  • considers international obligations, such as the ICCPR (John Vallamattom).

ddbu.title: Effects of unconstitutionality and prospective overruling
ddbu.trail: "As if it had never been", the American retreat after Linkletter, and how India came to accept prospective overruling despite Art 13(2)

sections.title: The basic effect: "as if it had never been"
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

A law that breaches a fundamental right is not void until a competent court declares it so — until then the presumption of constitutionality holds. Once declared, a post-Constitution law is void from enactment (Art 13(2)); a pre-Constitution law only from 26 January 1950 (Art 13(1)). Prospective overruling is the exception: the Supreme Court may say its declaration operates only from a stated date.

  • Declaration needed first. In the USA and India alike, a statute does not become void ipso facto; the challenger must rebut the presumption in a regular proceeding (Chiranjit Lal, Balsara, Behram).
  • The effect once declared. In Behram (1955) the Court adopted the classic formula: where a statute is adjudged unconstitutional "it is as if it had never been". No rights can be built on it, contracts that depend on it are void, it protects no one who acted under it, and no one can be punished for disobeying it before the decision. The same holds for an invalid part of an Act.
  • Not absolute. The Behram formula is qualified by severability (only the inconsistent part goes — Rooplal v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, (2000) 1 SCC 644) and by the relative nature of voidness: a law that breaches only citizens' rights (Art 19) remains good against non-citizens, while one that breaches Art 14 or 21 is void against everyone (Ambica Mills; see chapter B4).
  • Art 13(1) is prospective. A pre-Constitution law becomes void only from the commencement of the Constitution. Past transactions and rights that accrued before 26 January 1950 are unaffected (John Vallamattom v. UOI, (2003) 6 SCC 611, on s 118 Succession Act; Pannalal Binjraj v. UOI, AIR 1957 SC 412). Rights extinguished before 1950 do not revive — the Constitution guarantees the rights a person had at its commencement, and does not add to them. But a discriminatory procedure becomes void after 1950 and cannot be used even to enforce pre-1950 rights (Lachmandas v. State of Bombay, AIR 1952 SC 235).

sections.title: The American position
sections.html:
Before 1965: void ab initio, with exceptions

The early rule was logical: the declaration relates back to the moment of enactment. Field J in Norton v. Shelby County, 118 US 425 (1886): an unconstitutional Act "is not a law; it confers no rights; it imposes no duties; it affords no protection; it creates no office; it is, in legal contemplation, as inoperative as though it had never been passed." The theory behind it was Blackstone's — judges do not make new law but "maintain and expound the old".

But Hughes CJ in Chicot County Drainage District v. Baxter State Bank, 308 US 371 (1940) called this "one of the most difficult questions": the actual existence of a statute before the decision is an "operative fact", and "the past cannot always be erased by a new judicial declaration". So the effects differ by subject:

  • Criminal liability. A void law creates no offence and gives no jurisdiction to convict. A person convicted under it can be released by habeas corpus even after the conviction is final (Ex parte Siebold, 100 US 371 (1880)).
  • Official acts. A void statute creating an office creates no office, so acts done by its holder have no legal validity (Norton).
  • Civil rights. As a rule, vested civil rights created before the declaration are protected. Exceptions: a court that later upholds the statute treats it as valid from the beginning; officials are not personally liable for acts done under the statute before it was struck down; voluntarily paid taxes cannot be recovered; and a judgment based on the statute is not res judicata on a fresh subject-matter.
  • Overruling was retrospective too. When the Court overruled an earlier constitutional decision, the new rule applied to past cases — prisoners convicted under a procedure later held unconstitutional could be released.

After 1965: Linkletter and prospective overruling

Case

Linkletter v. Walker (1965)

381 US 618

Facts

Wolf v. Colorado (1949) had held that the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule did not bind State courts. Mapp v. Ohio, 367 US 643 (1961) overruled Wolf, applying the rule to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment. Linkletter, whose State conviction on illegally seized evidence had become final before Mapp, sought habeas corpus.

Held

Relief refused. "The Constitution neither prohibits nor requires retrospective effect." The Court may decide whether a new rule operates prospectively by weighing its purpose, the reliance placed on the old rule, and the effect on the administration of justice. Illegally seized evidence, unlike a coerced confession, is not unreliable, so retroactivity would not serve the purpose of Mapp.

Principle

The US Supreme Court may limit an overruling constitutional decision to the future.

Cases that followed Linkletter (new rule not applied to past cases):

  • Tehan v. US ex rel. Shott, 382 US 406 (1966) — the rule against comment on the accused's silence (Griffin v. California, 1965).
  • Johnson v. New Jersey, 384 US 719 (1966) — Escobedo (1964) and Miranda (1966) applied only to trials beginning after those decisions, even though the evidence affected could be unreliable.
  • Stovall v. Denno, 388 US 293 (1967) — right to counsel at pre-trial identification.
  • DeStefano v. Woods, 392 US 631 (1968) — jury trial in State criminal trials and serious criminal contempts (Duncan v. Louisiana; Bloom v. Illinois).
  • Desist v. US, 394 US 244 (1969) — Katz v. US (1967), which dropped the "trespass" requirement for electronic surveillance.
  • Williams v. US, 401 US 646 (1971) — Chimel v. California (1969) on searches incident to arrest.
  • Adams v. Illinois, 405 US 278 (1972) — Coleman v. Alabama (1970) on counsel at preliminary hearings.

Cases that did not follow it (new rule applied retrospectively):

  • Roberts v. Russell, 392 US 293 (1968) — Bruton v. US (1968), overruling Delli Paoli (1957), held that admitting a co-accused's confession at a joint trial breaches the Confrontation Clause even with a jury warning. Applied retroactively because the error presents "a serious risk that the issue of guilt or innocence may not have been reliably determined".
  • Berger v. California, 393 US 314 (1969) — Barber v. Page (1968) on confrontation with an absent witness was applied to a conviction that became final before it, because the defect went to the fact-finding process and Barber had been foreshadowed by Pointer v. Texas (1965).
  • US v. US Coin & Currency, 401 US 715 (1971) — Marchetti and Grosso (1968), overruling US v. Kahriger, were applied retroactively to forfeitures. The Court distinguished procedural rules that do not affect the accuracy of fact-finding (Linkletter applies) from rules that the conduct cannot constitutionally be punished at all (Linkletter does not).
  • US v. Johnson, 457 US 537 (1982) reviewed the exceptions and applied Payton v. New York (1980) to cases pending on direct appeal.

Basu's verdict: the American law is a "maze" in which the answer turns on the composition of the Court and its discretion. His question is whether so nebulous a doctrine can be read into the express word "void" in Art 13(2).

Slips in the source

  • Field was an Associate Justice, not "Chief Justice", when he wrote Norton v. Shelby County.

  • Linkletter concerned the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments; the text says "Fifteenth" at one point.

  • The case cited as "Donald v. California, 21 L.Ed.2d 508" is Berger v. California, 393 US 314 (1969).

  • One footnote dates Roberts v. Russell to 1962; it was decided in 1968, after Bruton.

sections.title: India: Golak Nath and the Art 13(2) objection
sections.html:
What the doctrine means

Prospective overruling means that when the final court changes the law, it may confine the new rule to the future, so that its impact does not fall on past transactions. It presupposes an earlier decision on the same issue that is being overruled (Somaiya Organics (India) Ltd. v. State of U.P., (2001) 5 SCC 519). As collected in later cases, its features are that it:

  • arises in constitutional matters;
  • can be applied only by the Supreme Court (P.V. George v. State of Kerala, (2007) 3 SCC 557; a High Court may mould relief under Art 226 in equity, but not by invoking this doctrine);
  • is discretionary, and rests on Arts 141 and 142;
  • applies only where the overruling judgment expressly says so — otherwise a Supreme Court decision is taken to state the law from inception, and a High Court cannot make it prospective;
  • does not apply where an earlier judgment is set aside on review — the review judgment is the only judgment.
Case

I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967)

AIR 1967 SC 1643 · [1967] 2 SCR 762 · 11 judges, 6:5

Facts

Challenge to the First, Fourth and Seventeenth Amendments, which protected land reform laws under which the petitioners' land was taken.

Held

Parliament cannot amend Part III so as to take away or abridge fundamental rights. But Subba Rao CJ (for five judges) applied prospective overruling: the earlier amendments, and the laws they protected, stayed valid; the new rule bound only future amendments. "Our Constitution does not expressly or by necessary implication speak against the doctrine of prospective overruling", and Arts 32, 141 and 142 give the Court power to mould the effect of its decisions.

Principle

First Indian use of prospective overruling. Overruled on the amendment question by Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

Wanchoo J, for three of the five dissenters, was emphatic: "in view of Article 13(2), it would be impossible to apply the doctrine of prospective overruling in our country particularly where a law infringes a fundamental right."

Majority figures

The source describes the majority as "8 against 3". Golak Nath was decided 6:5. Wanchoo J wrote for three of the dissenters (himself, Bhargava and Mitter JJ); Bachawat and Ramaswami JJ dissented separately. Hidayatullah J made up the majority of six with a separate concurring opinion; the prospective-overruling reasoning is that of Subba Rao CJ and the four judges who joined him.

Basu's argument against it under Art 13(2)

  • Linkletter rested on the premise that the US Constitution says nothing about the effect of a decision. The Indian Constitution does — Art 13(2) (and Art 254) say a contravening law "shall be void". Void cannot mean "void for tomorrow but valid for yesterday".
  • Art 13(2) opens with a prohibition on power — "The State shall not make any law…" — so the defect strikes at the law's inception. Subba Rao CJ cited Arts 32, 141 and 142 but did not mention Art 13(2).
  • In the US, the American doctrine was confined mainly to criminal procedure; it was never applied to constitutional amendments, the very area where Golak Nath used it. Even in criminal law it was applied unevenly.
  • The doctrine was raised by the Chief Justice himself, not argued by the Bar; in Kesavananda nobody referred to it. Basu thought it had "died a natural death".
  • Golak Nath in any case used it differently: in the US a law struck down is invalid from the date of decision, whereas Golak Nath left the impugned amendments valid for ever (M.P. Jain calls this a dilution).
  • Basu also argued that Golak Nath, Kesavananda and Waman Rao concerned constitutional amendments under Art 368 and so cannot decide the meaning of "void" for ordinary laws; and that Karunakar and Atam Prakash (below) did not discuss the word "void" at all.

S.P. Sathe adds a jurisprudential point: the Golak Nath rule against amending fundamental rights was not, strictly, ratio — the actual decision upheld the amendments, and the "futuristic mandate" had no link to the result. In practice it was treated as law by the Court and by Parliament, which amended the Constitution to overturn it.

How the Court has applied it since

Case

Managing Director, ECIL v. B. Karunakar (1993)

(1993) 4 SCC 727 · Constitution Bench

Facts

Whether a delinquent employee must be given the inquiry officer's report before the disciplinary authority decides, following UOI v. Mohd. Ramzan Khan, (1991) 1 SCC 588.

Held

Non-supply of the report breaches natural justice and Art 311(2). Contrary two-judge decisions were no longer good law — "but this shall have prospective application and no punishment imposed shall be open to challenge on this ground" (para 75). The Court reviewed the case law and treated prospective overruling as a way of moulding relief.

Principle

Prospective overruling extended beyond the constitutionality of statutes, to administrative action.

  • Atam Prakash v. State of Haryana, (1986) 2 SCC 249 — provisions of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 struck down under Art 14 (an earlier Constitution Bench had upheld the Act under Art 19(1)(f)), but decrees that had become final were saved. Basu: no overruling, and no discussion of "void".
  • Govt. of A.P. v. Bala (1995) 1 SCC 184 — a G.O. held to breach Arts 14 and 16(1) was declared inoperative from the date of judgment.
  • Babu Ram v. C.C. Jacob, (1999) 3 SCC 362 — prospective declaration is a device to avoid reopening settled issues and multiplicity of proceedings; actions taken before the declaration are treated as validated in the larger public interest, and lower courts apply the new law only to future cases.
  • Somaiya Organics, (2001) 5 SCC 519 — the doctrine is "a rule of judicial craftsmanship" for a smooth transition; it does not hold an invalid law valid, it only directs that the declaration of invalidity take effect from a future date.
  • Kailash Chand Sharma v. State of Rajasthan, (2002) 6 SCC 562 — weightage for residence in public employment held arbitrary; earlier decisions were overruled, but appointments already made were protected.
  • Waman Rao v. UOI (1981) — amendments adding laws to the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda) are valid; those made on or after that date can be tested against the basic structure. A prospective cut-off in all but name.
  • Basu notes the principle that a later decision normally only "discovers" the correct law and so applies retrospectively, except to matters that are res judicata or settled accounts; prospective operation is the exception.

Outside fundamental rights: competence cases

Basu calls these "recent aberrations", because the defect was want of legislative competence, which also makes a law void from inception:

  • India Cement Ltd. v. State of T.N., AIR 1990 SC 85 (7 judges) — a cess on royalty was beyond State competence; H.R.S. Murthy v. Collector of Chittoor (1965) was overruled; the declaration operated prospectively so that amounts already collected need not be refunded.
  • Orissa Cement Ltd. v. State of Orissa, AIR 1991 SC 1676 — the Orissa cess on royalty was ultra vires; the declaration took effect from the High Court's judgment (22 December 1989), not from 1962, and refunds were refused on grounds of "equity". Basu: equity has no room under Art 13(2).
  • Federation of Mining Associations of Rajasthan v. State of Rajasthan, AIR 1992 SC 103 — the Rajasthan Land Tax Act, 1985 was unenforceable only from the judgment (30 August 1991); tax collected need not be refunded and arrears for earlier periods were still payable.

The justification the Court gives: a law made without competence is non est, but it stays on the statute book until a court declares it void; when declaring it void, the Court may mould relief under Art 142 so that the declaration takes effect from a future date.

The Court's answer to the Art 13(2) objection

  • Indra Sawhney v. UOI (1992) held that Art 16(4) does not permit reservation in promotions, overruling General Manager, Southern Railway v. Rangachari, AIR 1962 SC 36, which had stood for three decades. The ruling was to take effect only after five years. (Parliament later inserted Art 16(4A) by the 77th Amendment, 1995.)
  • In Ashok Kumar Gupta v. State of U.P., (1997) 5 SCC 201 this postponement was challenged as contrary to Art 13(2). The Court rejected the challenge: Art 13(2) deals with legislative or executive action; when the Court declares the law under Art 141 and directs under Art 142 that the new rule operates from a given date, that is a judicial tool, not a "law" made by the State.
  • Githa Hariharan v. RBI, (1999) 2 SCC 228 read "after" in s 6(a) of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 as "in the absence of", so that the mother can act as natural guardian when the father is not in charge, and saved the provision from Arts 14 and 15. The commentary records this too as a reading given only prospective effect, to save past transactions.
Basu's conclusion vs. the current position

Basu: the doctrine "can have no application" to cases under Art 13(2); the express word "void" leaves nothing to judicial imagination, and no "judicial jugglery" can give retrospective validity to a law that was void at birth.

ddbu.title: After the declaration — judgment in rem, revival and validating laws
ddbu.trail: Who is bound by a declaration of invalidity, when a constitutional amendment can save a dead law, and how far a legislature can validate it

sections.title: Does a declaration of unconstitutionality bind everyone?
sections.html:
Exam snapshot

USA: a judgment holding a statute unconstitutional binds only the parties; for everyone else it is just a precedent (Willoughby).

India: because of Art 141, a Supreme Court declaration that a law is void operates in effect as a judgment in rem. Courts must ignore the law; a later litigant need not prove its invalidity again (Behram, 1955).

USA

Willoughby's statement of the American rule: the court "does not annul or repeal the statute"; it simply refuses to recognise it and decides the rights of the parties as if it had no application. "There is no judgment against the statute." Another litigant can sue on the same statute, and the earlier decision counts only as a precedent, not as estoppel or res judicata. Two consequences:

  • If the Court later changes its mind and upholds the statute, it is treated as valid from the beginning.
  • In the converse case (valid, then invalid), the Court protected people who had relied on the earlier decisions — for example, purchasers of municipal bonds who had bought them on the faith of decisions upholding the authorising statute were still entitled to interest. Basu notes this rested on features peculiar to the US: the Contract Clause and the diversity of State and federal law.

India

Case

Behram Khurshed Pesikaka v. State of Bombay (1955)

AIR 1955 SC 123 · (1955) 1 SCR 613

Facts

Prosecution under the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949, part of which (relating to medicinal and toilet preparations containing alcohol) had already been declared void in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951).

Held

Mahajan CJ, for the majority: under Art 141 the American doctrine stated by Willoughby has no application. Once a statute is declared void under Art 13(1) or 13(2), the declaration "has the force of law", and the statute is no longer law for persons whose fundamental rights it infringes. No court can take notice of the void part, and the accused bears no onus to prove its invalidity afresh. The prosecution must prove a breach of the part of the section that remains valid.

Principle

A declaration of invalidity by the Supreme Court operates, in effect, in rem. Also: "when the law-making power of a State is restricted by a written fundamental law, then any law enacted and opposed to the fundamental law is in excess of the legislative authority and is thus a nullity."

Later cases develop the point:

  • The declaration does not physically remove the statute from the book, and a law void for breach of a citizens-only right stays effective against non-citizens; but the effect of the decision is not confined to the parties (Deep Chand v. State of U.P., AIR 1959 SC 648).
  • "Law declared" under Art 141 is wider than "law found or made"; the Court "as a wing of the State is by itself a source of law. The law is what the Court says it is" (Nand Kishore v. State of Punjab, (1995) 6 SCC 614).
  • The State and its officers must follow the law declared, whether or not they were parties. To say that a ruling on the validity of a levy binds only the parties before the Court would "make the mandate of Article 141 illusory".
  • What binds is the ratio decidendi — the principle on which the case was decided, read as a whole in light of the questions raised. A conclusion reached without reasons, or a sentence that depends on the facts of one case, is not "law declared".
  • A High Court's declaration of invalidity binds the courts and tribunals within its State, so long as there is no contrary Supreme Court decision. The difference from the Supreme Court is only one of territorial reach.

sections.title: Void ab initio — for all parts of the Constitution
sections.html:
Basu's position: the rule that unconstitutionality makes a law void from the start applies to every justiciable limit in the Constitution, not only Part III. Those limits are of three kinds:

  1. legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule;
  2. fundamental rights in Part III;
  3. other mandatory provisions, such as Arts 286 and 301–304.

The Court has treated breach of Part III as want of power, just like breach of the Lists (Behram; Mahendra Lal Jaini, AIR 1963 SC 1019; In re Article 143 (Keshav Singh), AIR 1965 SC 745; Jagannath v. Authorised Officer, AIR 1972 SC 425). It follows that the doctrine of eclipse does not apply to post-Constitution laws: a law void under Art 13(2) does not revive if the right is later amended (Deep Chand; Abu Khan v. UOI, (1984) 1 SCC 88). Seervai disagrees, arguing that eclipse applies to both pre- and post-Constitution laws.

The exceptions acknowledged in and after Ambica Mills

Ambica Mills (1974) is sometimes read as having abandoned the "void ab initio" rule. Basu says a five-judge bench could not overrule the seven-judge decisions and did not try to: it stated exceptions to an unquestioned principle.

  • Persons without the right. A law void for breaching a fundamental right is void for those who hold that right; it remains operative against those who do not. Note that Art 21 protects every person, citizen or not — tourists and other foreigners included (Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das, (2000) 2 SCC 465). A law void against citizens is not revived by a later amendment of their right; it must be re-enacted.
  • Ninth Schedule. A law void under Art 13(2) can be shielded retrospectively by placing it in the Ninth Schedule under Art 31B; it then operates from the date it was enacted (Jagannath v. Authorised Officer; UOI v. Hari Krishan Khosla, 1993 Supp (2) SCC 149). But for additions made on or after 24 April 1973, the protection is subject to the basic structure (Waman Rao; I.R. Coelho).
  • Prospective overruling (chapter B17).
Case

I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)

(2007) 2 SCC 1 · AIR 2007 SC 861 · 9 judges

Facts

Whether laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda enjoy blanket immunity from Part III.

Held

Laws added on or after 24 April 1973 are not immune. If such a law abrogates or abridges Part III rights and thereby damages the basic structure — as reflected in Art 21 read with Arts 14 and 19, and the principles underlying them — it can be struck down. Each law is tested individually by its actual impact on rights ("rights test" and "essence of right test"), not its form. Parliament cannot grant fictional immunity from judicial review, since Art 32 is itself part of the basic structure. The greater the invasion of essential freedom, the greater the justification required, and the degree of invasion is for the court to decide.

Principle

The Ninth Schedule cannot be used to exclude Part III review of post-1973 additions.

Stale passage in the source

The source still says the impact of Ninth Schedule inclusion "is now referred to a larger Bench". That reference was decided in I.R. Coelho (2007), summarised above.

  • B. Shama Rao v. Union Territory of Pondicherry, AIR 1967 SC 1480: an Act void for excessive delegation is still-born; an amending Act passed while the challenge was pending could not cure it. The whole Act had to be re-enacted in modified form.

Name slip

The source calls this case "Sharma Rao"; the appellant's name is B. Shama Rao.

sections.title: Can a constitutional amendment save a law already struck down?
sections.html:
Yes, if the amendment is retrospective. The constituent body may direct that the Constitution be read, as amended, from its inception. The offending statute then never violated the Constitution: the amendment does not resuscitate a dead statute but removes the cause of its invalidity ab initio. Nothing in the Constitution limits the amending body's power to act retrospectively (Shankari Prasad; Jagannath v. Authorised Officer).

No, if it is prospective. A law is judged by the Constitution as it stood when the law was made. In Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P. (1954), the First Amendment's change to Art 19(6) could not save the U.P. Road Transport Act, 1951, already void when passed: "a statute void for unconstitutionality is dead and cannot be vitalised by a subsequent amendment of the Constitution removing the constitutional objection, but must be re-enacted" (Mukherjea J). Wanchoo J in Mahendra Lal Jaini called it "absolutely elementary" that constitutionality is judged as at the date the Act was passed, subject to any retrospective amendment. Likewise, a proclamation of emergency suspending Art 19 does not revive a law that was void when enacted (State of M.P. v. Thakur Bharat Singh, AIR 1967 SC 1170).

Amendments overriding judicial decisions

  • USA. Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 US (19 How) 393 (1857) — holding that a slave was property, that a person of African descent could not be a citizen, and that Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories — was undone by the Thirteenth (1865) and Fourteenth (1868) Amendments. Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co., 158 US 601 (1895), striking down the federal income tax as an unapportioned direct tax, was overridden by the Sixteenth Amendment (1913).
  • India. Hidayatullah J in Golak Nath thought validating a law declared void by overriding the judgment was not within the power to "amend". Basu disagrees: the amending power is plenary. In Sasanka Sekhar Maity v. UOI, AIR 1981 SC 522, the Constitution Bench held that Parliament, acting in its constituent capacity under Art 368 ("Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution", added by the 24th Amendment, 1971), may validate State laws by placing them in the Ninth Schedule, even though as a legislature it could not validate a State Act on a List II subject. Art 31B "extends a protective umbrella"; after inclusion, a challenge lies only for want of legislative competence (and, after 1973, the basic structure).

But the constituent power is itself subject to the basic structure:

Case

AIR 1975 SC 2299 · 1975 Supp SCC 1 · Constitution Bench

Facts

After the Allahabad High Court set aside the Prime Minister's election, the 39th Amendment (1975) inserted Art 329A. Clause (4) said that no election law would apply to the Prime Minister's election, that her election would not be void, and that any court order declaring it void "shall be deemed always to have been void"; clause (5) required pending appeals to be decided accordingly.

Held

Clauses (4) and (5) were struck down as damaging basic features — free and fair elections, democracy, the resolution of disputes by judicial process, and equality. The constituent body may validate an election by retrospectively changing the law that caused the disqualification, but it cannot withdraw all election law and then decide the dispute itself by a "legislative judgment".

Principle

The constituent power under Art 368 differs from the plenary power of a Constituent Assembly; it is bound by the basic structure.

sections.title: Validation by ordinary legislation
sections.html:
USA

The general rule: since invalidity attaches at enactment, a later amendment of the statute cannot cure it ab initio, though it can make the statute valid for the future by removing the objectionable provisions. A declaratory Act retrospectively validating proceedings under a statute held void is not possible, as it would interfere with the judicial function contrary to the separation of powers.

India: the governing principles

Exam snapshot — validating Acts

A legislature cannot simply overrule a judgment, declare it not binding, or set aside a decision between particular parties. It can remove the basis of the decision — retrospectively changing the law so that, had the new law existed then, the court could not have decided as it did — provided it has competence and the new law is itself constitutional.

The three tests for a validating Act (T.N. Saksena v. State of M.P., (1976) 4 SCC 750; Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain; Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala, (1996) 7 SCC 637):

  1. Does the legislature have competence over the subject?
  2. Has the validation removed the defect the court found in the earlier law?
  3. Is the validating law consistent with Part III (and the rest of the Constitution)?

The principles collected in Indian Aluminium (and repeated in State of T.N. v. K. Shyam Sunder, (2011) 8 SCC 737):

  • A bare declaration cannot directly overrule, revise or override a judicial decision.
  • A legislature can make a decision ineffective by enacting a valid law within its field that fundamentally changes the conditions on which the decision rested, so that the decision could not have been given had those conditions existed.
  • It may do so retrospectively, from a deeming date or any particular date.
  • It may change the character of a tax from impermissible to permissible, provided the levy answers that character, and validate collections, or make recovery from the State ineffective.
  • The court cannot validate an invalid law or legalise a tax illegally collected; that is the legislature's province, so doing it is no encroachment on judicial power.
  • The common thread: no direct overruling, but the legislature may remove the base on which the decision rested, if it has the competence and acts consistently with the Constitution.

Further points from the cases:

  • The legislature may change the law in general, affecting a class of persons and events at large; it cannot set aside an individual decision inter partes — that would be acting as an appellate court (In re Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal, 1993 Supp (1) SCC 96 (II); S.R. Bhagwat v. State of Mysore, (1995) 6 SCC 16). The same applies to statutory arbitration awards (G.C. Kanungo v. State of Orissa, (1995) 5 SCC 96).
  • It is open to the legislature to pass a new law or amend the old one to remove the unconstitutionality, and provide that what was done under the old law is deemed done under the new one (Sadasib Prakash Brahmachari v. State of Orissa, AIR 1956 SC 432). A "legal fiction" in the validating Act may be used.
  • Where a tax is held illegally levied, the legislature cannot merely declare that the decision is not binding or validate the collection on the footing that the court was wrong (B. Krishna Bhat v. State of Karnataka, (2001) 4 SCC 227).
  • Careless drafting may defeat validation; a validating Act that declares non-existent facts to exist can also fail if that declaration breaches the Constitution.
  • A later Act does not annul a judicial order unless it says so or removes its basis; legislation that neither notices the order nor contains a non obstante clause leaves the order in force.
  • Where an earlier ruling of invalidity lapsed with an Ordinance (the appeal being dismissed as infructuous), a later Act on the same lines is judged on its own merits; the old judgment is not res judicata (Dharam Dutt v. UOI, (2004) 1 SCC 712).
  • A legislature cannot enact an "invalidation Act" nullifying a statute that a court has upheld (K. Shyam Sunder).
Case

Janapada Sabha, Chhindwara v. Central Provinces Syndicate Ltd. (1970)

AIR 1971 SC 57 · (1970) 1 SCC 509

Facts

The Supreme Court had held certain cesses invalid. The legislature passed an Act that in effect set aside the decision.

Held

"It is not open to the Legislature to say that a judgment of a court properly constituted and rendered in exercise of its powers in a matter brought before it shall be deemed to be ineffective and the interpretation of the law shall be otherwise than as declared by the Court." The legislature may amend the Act retrospectively and declare what the law shall be deemed to have been, but the judgment bound the parties and, under Art 141, all courts.

Principle

A legislature may change the law; it may not overrule the court.

Fundamental rights as a bar to validation

Here Basu parts company with some of the Court's statements.

The Court's view. In West Ramnad Electric Distribution Co. v. State of Madras, AIR 1962 SC 1753, Gajendragadkar J reasoned: if a legislature can retrospectively validate action taken under a law void for want of competence, it can equally validate action under a law void for breach of fundamental rights. Rai Ramkrishna v. State of Bihar, AIR 1963 SC 1667 accepts that a legislature may cure an infirmity and make an earlier law effective from its original date — but adds that, under a written Constitution, "neither prospective nor retrospective laws can be made to contravene fundamental rights".

Basu's view. Validation is impossible where the illegality is a breach of a constitutional limit that is still in force, because the validating law itself breaches the same limit.

Case

Antill Ranger & Co. v. Commissioner for Motor Transport (1956)

[1956] AC 527 · (1956) 3 All ER 106 · Privy Council

Facts

New South Wales charges on inter-State road transport were void under s 92 of the Australian Constitution (freedom of inter-State trade). The State then legislated to bar actions to recover the charges collected.

Held

"Neither prospectively nor retrospectively… can a State law make lawful that which the Constitution says is unlawful." A statute keeping illegally imposed charges would be valid if the illegality rested only on State law, but not if it arose from the Constitution itself. To validate an exaction that s 92 makes unlawful would be "a mockery of the spirit of the Constitution".

Principle

Retrospective validation cannot cure a breach of a constitutional limitation that still stands.

Applying Antill, Basu argues West Ramnad is wrong, for two reasons:

  1. Even where a legislature newly acquires competence, its retrospective law is still subject to other limits — e.g. Art 20 or 19 — that may make the retroactivity unconstitutional.
  2. If the fundamental right still stands as it did when the void law was made, the validating Act offends the same right. The same is true if the right has been amended only prospectively. Only a retrospective constitutional amendment removes the obstacle.

So a notification taking property under a void law (or without authority) breached old Art 31, read with Art 13(3)(a), and was instantly void; no later law could revive it retrospectively without itself breaching Arts 13 and 31(1). Basu adds that Art 245(1), which permits retrospective laws, makes all legislative power "subject to the provisions of this Constitution", and that all fundamental rights — not only Art 20 — limit retrospective legislation (Art 14: State of Gujarat v. Raman Lal, AIR 1984 SC 161).

Two cases examined

Case

Sadasib Prakash Brahmachari v. State of Orissa (1956)

AIR 1956 SC 432 · (1956) SCR 43

Facts

In Mahant Jagannath Ramanuj Das v. State of Orissa, (1954) SCR 1046, the Court struck down ss 38–39 of the Orissa Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1939, which let government officers settle schemes for maths at their discretion; schemes framed under them fell. Orissa then amended and brought into force a 1952 Act under which a judicial Commissioner framed schemes by a suit-like procedure, with an appeal to the High Court. Its s 79A deemed schemes "purporting to have been settled" under the old ss 38–39 to have been settled under the new Act, subject to an appeal within 60 days.

Held

The new procedure was a reasonable restriction. Section 79A was valid: it did not deem the old schemes validly settled under the old law (that would be overriding unconstitutionality), but took them up as schemes settled under the new Act, open to any objection available under the new law, to avoid the public inconvenience of redoing them. Art 32 was not curtailed — the remedy failed this time only because the unconstitutionality had been removed.

Principle

A legislature may adopt past acts under a new, valid law.

Basu's criticism: s 79A did more than adopt the schemes prospectively; it enforced them from their original dates, defeating both the earlier judgment and Art 19. Giving such retrospective effect was itself an unreasonable restriction on the mahant's rights under Art 19(1)(f), a point the Court did not consider. "Not uncommon in legislative practice" is true only in systems without fundamental rights; and "public inconvenience" is no excuse for unconstitutionality. The decision overlooked Antill and, in Basu's view, was wrong on s 79A.

Case

State of Mysore v. D. Achiah Chetty (1969)

AIR 1969 SC 477

Facts

Land in Bangalore could be acquired under the Mysore Land Acquisition Act or the Bangalore City Improvement Act, which gave owners a more beneficial procedure. Acquisitions under the former were held discriminatory under Art 14. Pending appeal, the legislature passed the Bangalore Acquisition of Lands (Validation) Act, 1962, making the Land Acquisition Act the sole procedure and validating past acquisitions under it.

Held

Valid. "What the Legislature has done is to make retrospectively a single law for the acquisition of these properties." It could have repealed the Improvement Act retrospectively; the result was no different.

Principle

Where the vice is discrimination between two procedures, retrospectively removing one procedure removes the vice, and past action can be validated.

Basu treats Achiah as only an apparent exception. The procedure followed had no intrinsic vice; the complaint was only that a better one existed. Removing the alternative advances the purpose of the Constitution rather than flouting it, as in Antill. The appeal could also have been decided on the simpler ground that an appellate court applies the law as it stands at the time of its decision.

A later court cannot rewrite the statute

Where a statute has been declared unconstitutional in whole or part, a later court must ignore the invalid part. It has no power to rewrite the statute, tear out pages, or add a proviso to make it constitutional — amendment is for the legislature. Jagannadhadas J assumed otherwise in Behram; Mahajan CJ's view prevailed. The legislature, for its part, may remove the defect so far as the Constitution allows (S.S. Bola v. B.D. Sardana, (1997) 8 SCC 522).

sections.title: What this guide is
sections.html:
What this section is

A study guide to D.D. Basu, Commentary on the Constitution of India (9th ed., Vols 1–6), from the Introduction to Art 35A. For each Article or group of Articles it gives three things:

  • In brief — what the provision does and what the commentary covers, summarised in my own words;
  • Where Basu discusses it — topics with the volume and PDF page where each discussion begins;
  • Leading cases — the main decisions in the commentary, each with a one-line note. Underlined names open the case card already on this site.

None of this is Basu's text. It is a map and a summary, meant to be used with the book open, not instead of it.

Page numbers

Pages are PDF page numbers in the LexisNexis downloads (the number your PDF viewer shows), not the printed page numbers of the book. Article 13 also has the fuller D.D.B.U notes.

Where a case was decided after this edition (e.g. Puttaswamy, 2017) or a holding has since been overruled, the case note says so.
