sections.title: Opening the PDFs at the right page
sections.html:
Each page reference is a link to basu/volN.pdf#page=P. The PDFs are not in this repository and never should be: it is public, and the repository is set to ignore the basu/ folder so they cannot be uploaded by mistake.

On the public site the links cannot open your files; the page number tells you where to go in your own copy.

To make the links open the PDFs, run the site from your own computer:

  1. Put a copy of the repository on your computer (GitHub Desktop: Clone).
  2. Inside it, make a folder named basu and copy your six PDFs in, renamed as in the table below.
  3. Open a terminal in the repository folder and run python -m http.server 8000.
  4. Visit http://localhost:8000. The page links now open the right page.

guide.title: Introduction and the general Appendix
guide.trail: What a constitution is, the character of the Indian Constitution, and the rules for interpreting it

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
The Introduction is a long essay (about 370 pages) that sets up the whole Commentary. It moves from general theory to Indian specifics in three stages.

  • Theory. What a State is (with competing definitions from international law and jurisprudence), what a constitution is, and how written and unwritten constitutions differ.
  • The Indian Constitution. Its federal-but-centralised character, the place of private property, constitutional developments since 1950, the reservation debate, and the proposals for reviewing the Constitution.
  • Interpretation. General canons (literal meaning, the mischief and purposive approaches), presumptions, internal and external aids such as debates and committee reports, and the special rules that apply when the text being read is a constitution rather than an ordinary statute.

Near the end there is a topic-wise digest of recent Supreme Court decisions (constitutional mechanics, education, elections, environment, equality, judiciary, labour, life, PIL, women). It is a quick way into case law but is organised by subject, not by Article.

The Appendix to the Introduction (Vol 1, from p. 371) is reference material: lists of Presidents, Prime Ministers, Chief Justices, Chief Election Commissioners, Speakers, spells of President's Rule, and the amendment Acts year by year.

How to use it. Read the interpretation chapters before an exam answer that turns on "how should this Article be read" (literal v purposive, use of Constituent Assembly debates, harmonious construction). The rest is background.

sections.title: Leading cases
sections.html:
• Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, (1973) 4 SCC 225 — Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but not its basic structure — the case the Introduction keeps returning to.
  • A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, AIR 1950 SC 27 — The early, compartmentalised reading of fundamental rights, later abandoned.
  • I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab, AIR 1967 SC 1643 — Held amendments were "law" under Art 13(2); overruled in Kesavananda.
  • State of West Bengal v. Union of India, AIR 1963 SC 1241 — States are not sovereign units; Parliament may acquire State property — central to the federalism discussion.
  • Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 — Limited amending power and the balance between Parts III and IV are themselves basic features.
  • I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2007) 2 SCC 1 — Ninth Schedule laws added after 24 April 1973 are open to basic-structure review.

guide.title: The Preamble
guide.trail: Purpose, legal status, the objectives it names, and whether it can be amended

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Basu treats the Preamble in three layers.

  • Comparative. Preambles of other constitutions (the US above all) and what courts there have made of them.
  • Legal status. Whether the Preamble is part of the Constitution, what work it can do in interpretation, and the shift from Berubari (not part, and no source of power) to Kesavananda (part of the Constitution, and a guide to its basic features).
  • The words, one by one. Sovereign, socialist (and the "socialistic pattern"), secular (with a separate discussion of secularism in politics), democratic and republic. Then the three kinds of justice — social, economic and political — including justice for women. Then liberty, equality and fraternity.

The chapter closes with judicial review and activism, and with amendment of the Preamble: the 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted "socialist", "secular" and "integrity", and the courts have treated the Preamble as amendable subject to the basic structure.

Exam point. The Preamble cannot override a clear provision. Where the text is ambiguous, it is a legitimate guide, and it is a main source for identifying the basic structure.

• In re Berubari Union , AIR 1960 SC 845 — Preamble described as a key to the framers' minds but not a source of power; cession of territory needs an Art 368 amendment.

guide.title: Arts 1–4 — the Union, its territory, and new or reorganised States
guide.trail: "Union of States", territory and its acquisition, admitting new States, and reorganising existing ones

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 1 (pp. 528–563): India is a Union of States, not a compact the States can leave. Basu uses the article to list the essential features of Indian federalism. He then distinguishes States from Union territories and covers the old position of Jammu & Kashmir. A long passage draws on international law: how a State acquires territory (cession, conquest, occupation), territorial waters, when territory counts as "acquired", and what happens to existing law and private rights when sovereignty changes.

Art 2 and 2A (pp. 564–572): Parliament can admit or establish new States on terms it chooses. Sikkim is the worked example — first "associated" under the 35th Amendment (Art 2A), then made a full State by the 36th, which repealed Art 2A.

Art 3 (pp. 573–590): Parliament may form new States and alter areas, boundaries or names by ordinary law. The President's recommendation is needed, and the affected State Legislature's views must be sought, but they do not bind Parliament. A Bill may be amended after the reference without a fresh one. Ceding Indian territory to a foreign State is different: Berubari held that needs a constitutional amendment.

Art 4 (pp. 591–595): laws under Arts 2–3 may amend the First and Fourth Schedules and make consequential provisions, and are not amendments under Art 368.

guide.title: Arts 5–11 — Citizenship
guide.trail: Who was a citizen on 26 January 1950, the Partition provisions, loss of citizenship, and Parliament's power

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Arts 5–8 settled citizenship only as of the commencement of the Constitution; everything after is left to Parliament under Art 11 and the Citizenship Act, 1955.

  • Art 5 (pp. 596–658) — the main test: domicile in India plus birth, parentage or five years' ordinary residence. This leads Basu into a long treatment of domicile (of origin and of choice, mostly from English private international law), the difference between citizenship and nationality, the rights of citizens and the disabilities of aliens and "foreigners", and whether there is State domicile in India (there is only one domicile — Pradeep Jain).
  • Art 6 (pp. 659–664) — migrants from Pakistan, with the 19 July 1948 cut-off and registration for later arrivals.
  • Art 7 (pp. 665–673) — migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 are not citizens, unless they returned under a resettlement permit. Covers the meaning of "migrated", and the position of married women and minors.
  • Art 8 (pp. 674–676) — persons of Indian origin abroad, through registration with Indian missions.
  • Art 9 (pp. 677–690) — voluntarily acquiring a foreign citizenship ends Indian citizenship. Whether and when a person acquired foreign nationality is for the Central Government under s. 9(2) of the Citizenship Act, not the courts.
  • Arts 10–11 (pp. 691–773) — continuance, subject to Parliament. Art 11 carries most of the Citizenship Act material: acquisition, termination and deprivation, plus later developments on illegal migrants.

guide.title: Part III in general — what fundamental rights are
guide.trail: History, meaning and need of fundamental rights, and how other systems secure individual rights

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Before the Article-by-Article commentary on Part III, Basu writes a general essay of about a hundred pages.

  • History. From Magna Carta and the English petitions, through the American and French declarations, to the demands of the Indian national movement and the Constituent Assembly.
  • Meaning. A fundamental right is one placed beyond ordinary legislative majorities and made judicially enforceable. That is what separates it from a right that is merely legal or moral.
  • Need. Arguments for entrenching rights at all, given parliamentary democracy.
  • Comparison. Different methods of securing individual rights: the English reliance on the common law and parliamentary restraint, the American Bill of Rights with judicial supremacy, and others. Then the Indian scheme — detailed rights, built-in limits, and a guaranteed remedy (Art 32).

Much of the US material (due process, privacy, the exclusionary rule) explains why the Indian framers chose "procedure established by law" and how Maneka Gandhi later moved Indian law towards substantive fairness.

guide.title: Art 12 — "the State"
guide.trail: Which bodies are bound by fundamental rights, and whether courts are "the State"

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 12 decides against whom most fundamental rights can be enforced. The commentary works through each element of the definition: the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and Legislature of each State, local authorities, and "other authorities" within India or under the control of the Government of India.

The core of the chapter is the expansion of "other authorities":

  • early on, from bodies with statutory power to make binding rules (Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal);
  • through the instrumentality-or-agency tests of R.D. Shetty and Ajay Hasia;
  • to the stricter "deep and pervasive control" test of Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002).

There is a long list of bodies held to be, or not to be, "the State": universities, banks, cooperatives, NCERT, BCCI and more. After that, the chapter turns to State action: fundamental rights are mainly guarantees against the State, with American comparisons such as Smith v. Allwright and Blum v. Yaretsky.

Finally, Basu takes up the old question whether the judiciary is "the State". Naresh Mirajkar (1966) held a judicial order cannot violate fundamental rights so as to attract Art 32. A.R. Antulay later qualified this, and the chapter separates judicial from administrative and rule-making functions of courts.

guide.title: Art 13 — laws inconsistent with fundamental rights
guide.trail: Map of the Vol 2 commentary; the detailed notes are in the D.D.B.U chapters

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Article 13 already has its own detailed own-words notes on this site: the D.D.B.U chapters. This page is the map back into the book.

The Vol 2 commentary runs about 350 pages in two halves.

  • Art 13 itself (to about p. 35): pre-Constitution laws and eclipse, the prohibition on post-Constitution laws, "law" and "laws in force", voidness, severability, and whether constitutional amendments are "law".
  • Judicial review (from p. 35 to the end): its meaning and foundations, which courts review and how, and a long survey of limits — limits in the text, limits in the judicial function, and self-imposed limits such as standing, ripeness and the presumption of constitutionality. It ends with prospective overruling and validating laws.

guide.title: Art 14 — equality before law and equal protection
guide.trail: The longest single commentary in the set: equality, administrative law, classification and arbitrariness

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
The Art 14 commentary runs to over a thousand pages because Basu uses it to house most of Indian administrative law. Treat it as three books.

  • Equality in general (pp. 351–378): international charters and other constitutions, rules for reading Art 14, and the "new dimension" of non-arbitrariness (Royappa, Maneka). Also natural justice, the duty to give reasons, and affirmative action.
  • Equality before the law (pp. 378–791): the Diceyan rule of law and its exceptions (official immunities, s. 197 CrPC), equal access to courts and legal aid (Art 39A), and excessive bail or fines. Then a full treatise on delegated legislation and ultra vires, administrative tribunals, judicial review of discretion (proper purposes, relevant considerations, abuse of power, subjective satisfaction), errors of fact and law, consultation, notice and hearing, promissory estoppel and legitimate expectation, natural justice, fact-finding review, policy decisions and mala fides.
  • Equal protection of the laws (pp. 791–1143): the classification test (intelligible differentia, rational nexus), with an A-to-Z of subjects from admissions to working journalists. Also taxation, procedural laws, special courts, single-person legislation, unguided discretion and excessive delegation, government contracts and largesse, service conditions (a very long section), criminal trials, presumption of constitutionality, pleading and burden, standing, State action, and equality as a basic feature.

Where Basu takes a position: he offers critiques of Maganlal Chhaganlal (procedural equality), of R.K. Garg (the bearer-bonds case, on whether morality bears on reasonableness), and of Naresh Mirajkar (discrimination by judicial acts). He also contends that the Union and each State count as juristic persons, and considers what follows for equal protection.

sections.html:
• State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, AIR 1952 SC 75 — Special Courts Act struck down: unguided power to pick cases for a special procedure.

  • Delhi Transport Corporation v. DTC Mazdoor Congress, 1991 Supp (1) SCC 600 — A rule allowing termination by notice without reasons held arbitrary.
  • R.K. Garg v. Union of India, (1981) 4 SCC 675 — Greater latitude for economic legislation; bearer bonds upheld.
  • Tata Cellular v. Union of India , (1994) 6 SCC 651 — Limits of judicial review of tenders and contracts.
  • State of M.P. v. Rakesh Kohli , (2012) 6 SCC 312 — Presumption of constitutionality; a statute is not struck down merely as arbitrary or unwise.

guide.title: Art 15 — prohibition of discrimination
guide.trail: The forbidden grounds, access to public places, special provisions for women, children and backward classes

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Basu begins by placing Arts 14, 15 and 16 in relation to each other. Art 15 is a particular application of equality, operating on named grounds and protecting citizens only.

  • Clause (1) — the State may not discriminate only on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. A law based on one of those grounds plus some other factor can survive. Each ground gets its own treatment, with comparative material (UK, Canada, US, Germany, UN instruments) on race and sex.
  • Clause (2) — access to shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks and public places, which also binds private persons.
  • Clause (3) — special provisions for women and children, framed as protective discrimination. The National Commission for Women is noted here.
  • Clause (4) (First Amendment, 1951, after Champakam) — the longest part. Is it an exception to cl. (1) or a facet of equality? What makes a class "socially and educationally backward": poverty, occupation, residence, education, and the vexed role of caste. Also reservation of seats in educational institutions, the 50% ceiling, "fraud on the Constitution", and SC/ST status on migration and conversion.
  • The chapter ends with standing, waiver, pleading, onus and clause (5) (93rd Amendment, 2005) on admission to private institutions.

guide.title: Art 16 — equality of opportunity in public employment
guide.trail: Equal opportunity in State service, forbidden grounds, residence, and reservation in appointments and promotions

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Over four hundred pages. The bulk sits under clause (1), read as covering every "matter relating to employment": appointment, pay, seniority, promotion, termination, compulsory retirement, regularisation and more. In practice this is a service-law treatise built on Art 16, so use the page map rather than reading straight through.

  • Relation to other provisions: Art 16 is an instance of Art 14, so reasonable classification is allowed. Also its relation to the pleasure doctrine in Art 310.
  • Clause (2): no ineligibility or discrimination only on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence. Includes compassionate appointment, and whether Art 15(3) can support preferences for women in employment.
  • Clause (3): Parliament alone may prescribe residence requirements.
  • Clause (4): reservation for backward classes "not adequately represented", read with Arts 46 and 335. Covers its relation to cl. (1) (exception, or facet of equality after N.M. Thomas and Indra Sawhney), extent, and judicial review.
  • Clauses (4A) and (4B): promotion reservation and carry-forward of unfilled vacancies, both added after Indra Sawhney and tested in Nagaraj.
  • Clause (5): denominational offices. Then remedies, standing, parties and onus.

guide.title: Arts 17–18 — untouchability and titles
guide.trail: Abolition of untouchability and its enforcement; abolition of titles and the national awards

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 17 (pp. 568–584) abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice "in any form". Unlike most of Part III, it binds private persons as well as the State, and it is enforced through legislation: the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955, later the Protection of Civil Rights Act, and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. Basu discusses:

  • what "untouchability" means — the historical practice tied to caste, not every social exclusion;
  • the phrase "in accordance with law";
  • analogous legislation, including temple-entry laws, and their relation to denominational rights under Art 26.

Art 18 (pp. 585–590) abolishes titles other than military and academic distinctions, bars citizens from accepting foreign titles, and limits acceptance of foreign presents or offices by State servants. The main issue is whether the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are titles. In Balaji Raghavan (1996) the Supreme Court held they are not, provided they are not used as prefixes or suffixes to names.

guide.title: Art 19 (part I) — the six freedoms and how they may be limited
guide.trail: Vol 3: general principles that apply to every clause of Art 19

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
The Vol 3 portion of Art 19 lays the groundwork that applies to all six freedoms before Vol 4 takes them one by one.

  • Scope. Art 19 guards against State action, not private action. It belongs to citizens only, which raises the question of corporations: shareholders can sue where company action hits their rights (R.C. Cooper, Bennett Coleman). Also the relation of Art 19 to Arts 21 and 22.
  • Displacement. Provisions of the Constitution that exclude Art 19, loss of standing, and suspension during Emergency under Arts 358–359, including what changed in 1978.
  • Restrictions in general (clauses 2–6). How far the American "police power" idea fits. Whether the listed grounds are exhaustive. The scope of judicial review compared with the US. What counts as a "restriction". The conditions of a valid restriction: authority of law, a listed ground, and reasonableness in substance and procedure.
  • Conflicts. Is Art 19(1) subject to other provisions of the Constitution? Basu comments on Sharma v. Sri Krishna (privilege v. free speech) and the 1964 Special Reference, and covers how competing fundamental rights are adjusted.
  • Burden. Who must prove (un)reasonableness, and why a presumption of constitutionality applies. Then "due process" versus "reasonableness".

Commentary: Vol 3, PDF pp. 591–943. Opening page: Vol 3, p. 591.

guide.title: Art 19 (part II) — each freedom and its restrictions
guide.trail: Vol 4: speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession — with cll. (2)–(6)

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Vol 4 takes the freedoms in order. Each sub-clause is followed by its restriction clause, and each opens with comparative law (US First Amendment cases especially).

  • 19(1)(a) speech and expression (pp. 2–340), by far the largest. Covers the rationale of free speech, the meaning of "speech" and "expression", the right not to speak, the right to know and access to information, privacy, official secrets and speech-plus-conduct. Under cl. (2): what a restriction is, regulation versus prohibition, anticipatory restraint, and each ground in turn. Also sedition, airwaves, campuses, advocacy, the press (censorship, taxation, price-page control, reporting of legislative and court proceedings), mail, customs, licensing, leaflets, loudspeakers, drama, films, television, advertising, symbolic speech, picketing, and the speech of government servants and prisoners.
  • 19(1)(b) assembly (pp. 341–413): public meetings, highways, government property, when a lawful meeting turns unlawful, arms, loudspeakers, processions and their regulation.
  • 19(1)(c) association (pp. 414–478): includes the right not to join, recognition, collective bargaining, the absence of a fundamental right to strike, lock-outs, cooperatives, and restrictions on police and military associations.
  • 19(1)(d)–(e) movement and residence (pp. 478–516): externment, the overlap with Art 21, leaving India, and re-entry.
  • 19(1)(g) profession, trade and business (pp. 518–end): the meaning of each term, closing a business, contracts with government, lawyers and doctors, educational institutions, and cl. (6) (regulation, State monopoly, reasonableness).

19(1)(f) (property) gets only a note, since the 44th Amendment deleted it. See Arts 31–31C.

guide.title: Art 20 — protection in respect of conviction for offences
guide.trail: No ex post facto offences or penalties, no double jeopardy, no compelled self-incrimination

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
• Clause (1) — no conviction except for violating a law in force when the act was done, and no penalty greater than the one then in force. It applies to criminal law and penalties, not civil liability or procedure. A beneficial change in penalty can be given to the accused (T. Barai, Rattan Lal). The commentary deals with "offence", "law in force", and the converse case of a later reduction.
  • Clause (2) — no prosecution and punishment twice for the same offence. Narrower than the US and English versions: there must have been a prior prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, for the same offence. Departmental proceedings do not count. The chapter compares this with autrefois acquit and convict, res judicata in criminal matters, and s. 300 CrPC.
  • Clause (3) — no person accused of an offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. The longest part. Basu asks when a person becomes "accused", what "compelled" means, and whether being a witness covers documents, silence and comment on it, searches and seizures (ss. 91, 93 CrPC), wire-tapping, physical examination, fingerprints and handwriting specimens. Also confessions (involuntary, retracted, s. 27 Evidence Act), and the effect of breach and waiver. Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) and Selvi (2010) — narco-analysis, polygraph and brain mapping — are the anchor cases.

guide.title: Art 21 — protection of life and personal liberty
guide.trail: From Gopalan to Maneka, the meaning of life and liberty, capital punishment, prisoners, and compensation

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
The chapter opens with a long comparative survey: Magna Carta and the English rule of law, the US due process clauses, and international charters. The point is that the Indian phrase "procedure established by law" was a deliberate choice against American due process.

  • Framework. Scope and object, and how Art 21 relates to Arts 14, 19, 22, 33 and 359. Who is a "person". What counts as being "deprived".
  • "Life". Beyond mere animal existence to life with dignity, including health, environment, shelter, livelihood and privacy. Basu adds a section on what privacy is, and one on the unborn child.
  • "Personal liberty". The Gopalan reading (physical restraint only) against the expanded reading after Kharak Singh, Satwant Singh and Maneka.
  • "Procedure established by law". The meaning of "law" and "established", grounds for challenging a law, and whether an Art 21 law must also satisfy Arts 14 and 19 (yes, after Maneka). Investigation and speedy trial, with a summary of the present interplay of Arts 14, 19 and 21.
  • Specific applications. The constitutionality of the death penalty and the effect of delay in execution, rights of prisoners, deprivation by judicial order, protective relief and compensation for violations, strict construction of penal statutes, onus in detention cases and good faith.
  • Emergency. Arts 21–22 under Art 359. ADM Jabalpur, and the 44th Amendment, which makes Arts 20–21 non-suspendable.
  • A closing catalogue of other rights read into Art 21 and further material on prisoners.

guide.title: Art 21A — right to education
guide.trail: Free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen; the RTE Act

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
A short chapter. Art 21A was added by the 86th Amendment (2002), which also rewrote Art 45 (early childhood care) and added a parent's duty in Art 51A(k). It makes free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 a fundamental right, "in such manner as the State may, by law, determine". That law is the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, reproduced as Appendix V of Vol 5 (pp. 869–884).

Basu sets out the Statement of Objects and Reasons and the line of cases leading to the amendment. Mohini Jain (1992) first located education in Art 21. Unni Krishnan (1993) confined the enforceable right to age 14.

He then covers the challenges to the RTE Act. Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan (2012) upheld the 25% quota for disadvantaged children in unaided schools. Pramati Educational Trust (2014) later exempted minority schools, aided and unaided.

guide.title: Art 22 — arrest and preventive detention
guide.trail: Rights on arrest (cll. 1–2) and the constitutional limits on preventive detention (cll. 3–7)

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Clauses (1)–(2) give every arrested person four rights:

  • to be told the grounds of arrest "as soon as may be";
  • to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice;
  • to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours;
  • not to be held beyond that without the magistrate's authority.

The commentary covers what happens when grounds are not supplied, whether the rights extend to arrest under a warrant, and the overlap with Art 21 and with D.K. Basu-type safeguards.

Clause (3) takes enemy aliens and preventive detainees out of cll. (1)–(2). The rest of Art 22 is a code for preventive detention, and the chapter is as much a guide to detention law as to the Article. It covers the history of detention laws in India (from 1950 to MISA, NSA, COFEPOSA, TADA and beyond), how detention differs from prosecution, and the validity of the Act and of the order. Then:

  • what courts can and cannot review;
  • onus, bona fides, and detention after discharge or acquittal;
  • the Advisory Board (cl. 4);
  • the right to grounds and to make a representation (cl. 5) — what must be communicated, in what language, how quickly, the effect of delay in considering it, vague or irrelevant grounds, and severability of grounds;
  • non-disclosure in the public interest (cl. 6) and Parliament's power (cl. 7).

guide.title: Arts 23–24 — exploitation, forced labour and child labour
guide.trail: Traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour, compulsory public service, and children in hazardous work

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 23 (pp. 782–815) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and similar forced labour, and makes breach an offence. Like Art 17, it binds private persons too. The commentary covers:

  • trafficking of women as a modern form of slavery;
  • the meaning of begar;
  • the reading of "forced labour" in PUDR (1982) — paying less than the minimum wage is itself force, because economic compulsion counts.

Clause (2) allows compulsory service for public purposes, such as conscription or emergency duty, without discrimination on religion, race, caste or class.

Art 24 (pp. 816–825) bars employment of children under 14 in factories, mines and other hazardous work. Basu covers "hazardous employment", the legislation, and the protective scheme around it in Arts 39(e)–(f), 45 and 21A. M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) directed a rehabilitation fund for children taken out of hazardous industries.

Appendices I–IV reproduce the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976, the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, the National Commission for Women Act 1990, and the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993. These are public statutes, also available on India Code.

guide.title: Art 25 — freedom of conscience and religion
guide.trail: Profess, practise and propagate; the essential practices test; State power over secular and reform matters

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Over a quarter of the chapter is comparative, especially the US Establishment and Free Exercise clauses, since Basu wants to show where India departs from them.

  • Clause (1). The freedom is subject to public order, morality and health, and to the other provisions of Part III. It belongs to "all persons", not only citizens. Basu covers the relation of religious speech to Art 19(1)(a), freedom of conscience and the absence of an established church, and each verb in turn — profess, practise, propagate. Processions, the meaning of "religion", a summary of the freedom, and the State's power to acquire or tax religious property are also here.
  • Clause (2). The State may regulate secular activities associated with religion (economic, financial, political), and legislate for social welfare and reform, including throwing open Hindu religious institutions to all classes. The key question is who decides whether a practice is essential to a religion. The courts do (Shirur Mutt, Durgah Committee).
  • Personal law. Its status under the Constitution, custom, and Art 44 (uniform civil code), with Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal and Lily Thomas.
  • Secularism. What Indian secularism means, how it differs from the American model, the rights of the majority community, and whether "propagate" includes a right to convert (no — Stainislaus).

guide.title: Arts 26–28 — denominations, religious taxes, religious instruction
guide.trail: Rights of religious denominations; no taxes for a particular religion; religious instruction in schools

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 26 (pp. 202–245) gives every religious denomination four rights, subject to public order, morality and health:

  • to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes;
  • to manage its own affairs in matters of religion;
  • to own and acquire property;
  • to administer that property "in accordance with law".

The commentary covers what makes a group a "denomination" (a common faith, organisation and distinctive name), the overlap with Art 30, excommunication (Saifuddin), the clash between Art 26(b) and temple-entry laws under Art 25(2)(b), taxation, and the property rights of mathadhipatis and shebaits.

Art 27 (pp. 246–262): no one can be compelled to pay taxes specifically appropriated to promote a particular religion. A fee for services to religious institutions is not a tax (Shirur Mutt). Spending on commemorating religious figures as national figures is discussed, with US comparisons.

Art 28 (pp. 263–274) has three tiers:

  • no religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State;
  • an exception for institutions administered by the State but set up under an endowment that requires it;
  • in recognised or aided institutions, attendance must be voluntary.

"Religious instruction" is distinguished from education about religions (Aruna Roy, 2002).

guide.title: Arts 29–30 — cultural and educational rights of minorities
guide.trail: Conserving language and culture; admission without discrimination; minority educational institutions

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 29 (pp. 275–295).

  • Clause (1): any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture may conserve it. This is not limited to minorities.
  • Clause (2): no citizen may be denied admission to a State-run or State-aided institution only on religion, race, caste or language. The commentary covers the meaning of "aid", and the relation to Arts 15(1), 15(4) and 25. Champakam and Bombay Education Society are the starting points.

Art 30 (pp. 296–407) gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. This is the heart of the chapter. Basu covers:

  • who is a minority — determined State-wise (T.M.A. Pai);
  • the meaning of "establish" and "administer" (Azeez Basha on establishment);
  • "of their choice";
  • regulation versus destruction of the right — regulation for excellence, and against maladministration, is allowed; admissions, fees, medium of instruction and staff conditions are the main areas;
  • linguistic minorities and non-interference in policy.

Then clause (1A) (compensation on acquisition of minority institution property), State control through recognition and aid, university affiliation, waiver, and relations with Arts 19, 28(3), 29, 351, Entry 25 of List III and the Directive Principles. Clause (2) bars discrimination in grant-in-aid.

guide.title: Arts 31–31D — the old right to property and the saving clauses
guide.trail: History of Art 31 and 19(1)(f), agrarian reform, the Ninth Schedule, and laws implementing Art 39(b)–(c)

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 31 (pp. 408–445) was repealed by the 44th Amendment (1978); the right to property now sits in Art 300A as a constitutional, not fundamental, right. Basu keeps the chapter for history:

  • eminent domain and police power;
  • successive amendments on "compensation" and "amount";
  • the uneasy relation between Arts 31 and 19(1)(f).

Art 31A (pp. 446–548) protects five kinds of law from Arts 14 and 19:

  • acquisition of "estates" (agrarian reform);
  • State takeover of management of property;
  • amalgamation of corporations;
  • changes in the rights of managers and shareholders;
  • changes in mining leases.

The two provisos require Presidential assent for State laws and market-value compensation for land within the ceiling under personal cultivation. Much of the chapter concerns the meaning of "estate" (jagir, inam, janmam, ryotwari land) and a list of land-reform Acts tested under it.

Art 31B (pp. 549–564) — the Ninth Schedule. Basu covers its object, scope and validity, and how far later amendments of a scheduled Act are protected. Since Coelho (2007), laws added after 24 April 1973 are open to basic-structure review.

Art 31C (pp. 565–584) protects laws giving effect to Art 39(b)–(c). Kesavananda struck down the bar on judicial inquiry into whether a law in fact gives that effect. Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension to all Directive Principles. The chapter also covers whether the legislature's declaration is conclusive, and the meaning of Art 39(b).

Art 31D (p. 585), on anti-national activities, was added in 1976 and omitted in 1977.

guide.title: Art 32 — the right to constitutional remedies
guide.trail: Enforcing fundamental rights in the Supreme Court; writs; PIL; procedure; Art 32A

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
The second-longest commentary in the set (over 700 pages). Art 32 is itself a fundamental right — the right to move the Supreme Court — and a basic feature.

  • Clause (1): the guarantee. What it covers, and what the Court will and will not do. Then particular areas: contracts, legislative privileges, preventive detention, taxation, service matters and the armed forces. Next comes judicial review in general, including its new human-rights dimension, and territorial reach. Last, the grounds for refusing relief: alternative remedy, delay and laches (with exceptions), misrepresentation, malice, and petitions that have become infructuous.
  • Standing and PIL. Who may apply. Loss of standing. Judicial activism, and the long section on public interest litigation (epistolary jurisdiction, S.P. Gupta, Bandhua Mukti Morcha, the M.C. Mehta line, continuing mandamus).
  • Procedure. Against whom a petition lies; certiorari against judicial decisions; declarations; interim relief; fact-finding and evidence; pleading, onus and counter-affidavits; parties, intervention by law officers, abatement; costs; res judicata (Daryao); compliance with orders; and the relation of Art 32 to Arts 226, 132–134 and 136.
  • Clause (2): the writs. The power to issue directions, orders and writs; concurrent jurisdiction with High Courts; then habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition and quo warranto in detail.
  • Clauses (3)–(4). Parliament may confer the power on other courts; the right may be suspended only as the Constitution provides (Art 359).

Art 32A (p. 1294), added in 1976 to bar challenges to State laws under Art 32, was omitted in 1977.

sections.title: Leading cases
sections.html:
• Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, AIR 1950 SC 124 — The Supreme Court is the protector of fundamental rights; no need to go first to the High Court.
  • Daryao v. State of U.P. , AIR 1961 SC 1457 — Res judicata applies to writ petitions decided on merits.
  • K.K. Kochunni v. State of Madras, AIR 1959 SC 725 — The Court can decide disputed questions under Art 32; the remedy is itself a right.
  • S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981 Supp SCC 87 — Relaxed standing; public interest litigation.
  • Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India , (1984) 3 SCC 161 — Letters as petitions; commissions to gather facts.
  • M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas) , (1987) 1 SCC 395 — Absolute liability; power to award compensation under Art 32.
  • Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa, (1993) 2 SCC 746 — Public-law compensation for custodial death.
  • Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, (1997) 6 SCC 241 — Guidelines filling a legislative gap, drawing on international conventions.
  • L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India , (1997) 3 SCC 261 — Judicial review under Arts 32 and 226 is a basic feature.

guide.title: Arts 33–35A — armed forces, martial law, and implementing Part III
guide.trail: Modifying rights for the forces; indemnity after martial law; Parliament's exclusive power; the former Art 35A

sections.title: In brief
sections.html:
Art 33 (pp. 1295–1359) lets Parliament restrict or abrogate fundamental rights for the armed forces, para-military and public-order forces, intelligence organisations and their telecom staff, so far as discipline and duty require. Basu covers:

  • military law in India and the "dual position" of service personnel as soldiers and citizens;
  • courts martial, and the absence of an appeal to ordinary courts;
  • writ control of courts martial on jurisdiction, natural justice, reasons and proportionality of sentence (S.N. Mukherjee, Ranjit Thakur);
  • the armed forces and human rights.

Art 34 (pp. 1360–1385) lets Parliament indemnify acts done to maintain or restore order where martial law was in force. The Constitution does not define martial law; Basu draws on English, Commonwealth and US practice (Duncan v. Kahanamoku, Marais, Tilonko). He discusses how martial law may be imposed, the need for an Act of indemnity, and whether habeas corpus lies.

Art 35 (pp. 1386–1394) gives Parliament alone power to make laws under Arts 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34, and to prescribe punishment for acts declared offences in Part III (untouchability, forced labour). It also continues pre-Constitution laws on those matters.

Art 35A (pp. 1395–1396) saved Jammu & Kashmir laws on permanent residents. It was added by the 1954 Presidential Order and ceased to apply after the August 2019 orders under Art 370.

Commentary: Vol 6, PDF pp. 1295–1396. Opening page: Vol 6, p. 1295.

sections.title: Leading cases
sections.html:
• Ram Sarup v. Union of India , AIR 1965 SC 247 — Army Act provisions upheld under Art 33.
  • Prithi Pal Singh Bedi v. Union of India , (1982) 3 SCC 140 — Service personnel keep fundamental rights except as validly restricted under Art 33.
  • S.N. Mukherjee v. Union of India , (1990) 4 SCC 594 — Reasons for confirming a court-martial verdict not required, but review is available.
  • Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India , (1987) 4 SCC 611 — A court-martial sentence can be set aside if grossly disproportionate.
  • Duncan v. Kahanamoku , 327 U.S. 304 (1946) — Military trial of civilians in Hawaii during war held unlawful.
  • Naga People's Movement of Human Rights v. Union of India , (1998) 2 SCC 109 — AFSPA upheld; it is not martial law.
